Key features and challenges:
An adulticidal oviposition trap is designed to attract egg-laying Aedes aegypti mosquitoes to deposit their eggs in the trap. When the mosquitoes come into contact with the trap, they are killed by an insecticide inside it. Larvicidal traps, on the other hand, aim to kill mosquitoes that are still in their larval stage, for example by destroying eggs by regular drainage of water from the trap. Both approaches reduce the number of mosquitoes and consequently control transmission of Aedes-borne diseases.

The ALO trap is a larvicidal trap designed to attract Aedes mosquitoes to deposit their eggs into the provided artificial water bodies (180 x 180 mm), where they will be destroyed by physical means before they can develop into adult mosquitoes. The current version of ALO is fully autonomous and communicates with human operators via the Internet.

Currently under Vector Control Advisory Group (VCAG) review for assessment of public health value as of 01/03/2020.ALO concept reviewed in May 2019.

Name: Advantage MAL Card
Developers: J. Mitra and Co
Indication: Indicated for the diagnosis of P. falciparum, P. vivax and other malarial strain infections
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Key features and challenges:
Advantage MAL Card is an immunoassay based on the “Sandwich principle” .The conjugate contains colloidal gold conjugated to monoclonal anti-pan specific pLDH (plasmodium lactate dehydrogenase) antibody. The test uses monoclonal anti-Pf pLDH antibody (test line F) & monoclonal anti-Pan specific pLDH antibody (test line P) immobilized on a nitrocellulose strip. The test sample is added to the device. On addition of assay buffer, the red blood cells get lysed. If the sample contains P.falciparum or P.vivax/P.malariae/P.ovale, the colloidal gold conjugate complexes the P.f specific pLDH/Pan specific pLDH in the lysed sample. This complex migrates through the nitrocellulose strip by capillary action. When the complex meets the line of the corresponding immobilized antibody, the complex is trapped forming a purplish pink band which confirms a reactive test result. Absence of a coloured band in the test region indicates a negative test result. To serve as a procedural control an additional line of anti-mouse antibody has been immobilized on the strip as control.

Mechanism of action: Combines coagulation activation (D-dimer) and glycemic control (HbA1c) markers to identify maternal risk states linked to placental insufficiency and IUGR.
Key features and challenges:
A. muciniphila (Am) is a bacterium of oval shape, strictly anaerobic, non‐motile and gram‐negative and forms no endospores. A significant reduction of Am in murine PE models was discovered. The therapeutic potential of Am was demonstrated in mice with PE induced by NG‐nitroarginine methyl ester hydrochloride (L‐NAME, an inhibitor of nitric oxide synthase activity). It was demonstrated that EVs produced by Am reached the placenta and promoted placentation via the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)–phosphatidylinositol‐3‐kinase (PI3K)–protein kinase B (AKT) signalling pathway. Overall, the findings reveal new host–microbiome interactions associated with PE and suggest probiotics that can potentially be used for PE intervention.

The therapeutic potential of AmEVs in preventing PE warrants further investigation, particularly in understanding their specific mechanisms and optimizing delivery strategies. Future studies may explore AmEVs' impact on fetal neurodevelopment and their ability to traverse the placental barrier, offering promising avenues for developing targeted therapies against PE and related pregnancy complications.

Indication: Indicated for the diagnosis of ovarian and peritoneal endometriosis.
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Tracer uptake in endometriotic lesions.
Key features and challenges:
Al¹⁸F-NOTA-FAPI-04 PET/CT imaging is a molecular imaging modality that utilizes a radiolabeled fibroblast activation protein inhibitor (FAPI) to target fibroblast activation protein (FAP), which is overexpressed in activated fibroblasts within inflammatory and fibrotic tissues. Because endometriotic lesions are characterized by fibrosis, stromal activation, and chronic inflammation, FAP-targeted imaging has emerged as a potential non-invasive diagnostic approach for endometriosis.
A 2025 preclinical study evaluated the efficacy of Al¹⁸F-NOTA-FAPI-04 PET/CT in a Sprague–Dawley rat model of endometriosis established through autologous transplantation of uterine endometrial tissue to the ovary and abdominal wall (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1687850725003917?via%3Dihub). 
Small-animal PET/CT imaging performed 60 minutes after tracer injection demonstrated significantly higher uptake in ovarian endometriotic lesions (OELs; SUVmax = 2.53 ± 0.61) compared with adjacent non-lesional ovarian tissue (1.28 ± 0.46; P = 0.031) and contralateral ovarian tissue (1.15 ± 0.49; P = 0.016). Peritoneal endometriotic lesions (PELs) similarly showed elevated tracer uptake (SUVmax = 1.74 ± 0.15) compared with surrounding peritoneal tissue (0.97 ± 0.13; P = 0.001) and abdominal wall muscle (0.83 ± 0.12; P = 0.0004). Histopathological and immunohistochemical analyses confirmed correlation between FAPI uptake and lesion presence.
These findings indicate that Al¹⁸F-NOTA-FAPI-04 PET/CT can effectively distinguish endometriotic lesions from normal tissue in a preclinical setting, suggesting potential utility as a non-invasive diagnostic tool for ovarian and peritoneal endometriosis.
Key challenges include the current limitation to animal models, with no published human clinical validation for endometriosis detection. PET/CT involves radiation exposure and requires specialized nuclear medicine infrastructure, potentially limiting routine use, especially in reproductive-age women. Cost, tracer availability, and regulatory approval pathways must also be considered. While promising for detecting fibrotic and inflammatory lesions, further clinical studies are necessary to evaluate diagnostic accuracy, safety, and comparative effectiveness relative to existing modalities such as MRI and laparoscopy.

Name: Alendronate
Developers: Islamic Azad University; Teijin Pharma
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: Dimethylallyltranstransferase inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Alendronic acid (alendronate) is a second-generation bisphosphonate primarily indicated for the treatment of osteoporosis and Paget’s disease of bone. It inhibits osteoclast-mediated bone resorption by targeting the mevalonate pathway, thereby preserving bone density. Chemically, alendronate is a 1,1-bis(phosphonic acid) compound with a hydroxy and 3-aminopropyl group and functions as a dimethylallyltranstransferase inhibitor.
https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/2088
Interest in alendronate as a potential therapy for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) arose from computational drug-repurposing analyses. A 2022 molecular docking and molecular dynamics study screened 1,614 FDA-approved drugs and identified alendronate as demonstrating promising binding interactions with the aromatase receptor, suggesting theoretical potential as an alternative to letrozole for ovulation induction.
https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07391102.2023.2190411
A subsequent 2024 preclinical study evaluated alendronate in a letrozole-induced PCOS model in female Wistar rats. Treatment was associated with reductions in serum testosterone and luteinizing hormone (LH) levels, decreased numbers of cystic and atretic ovarian follicles, and increased healthy follicular development. These findings suggest potential restoration of ovarian function in this animal model.
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0753332224003883?via%3Dihub
Despite these exploratory findings, alendronate has no approved indication or registered clinical trials for PCOS. Its primary mechanism of action relates to bone metabolism rather than reproductive endocrinology, and the translational relevance of aromatase-binding predictions remains uncertain.
Key challenges include the absence of human clinical data, potential reproductive safety concerns, and the long skeletal half-life of bisphosphonates, which raises considerations for women of reproductive age due to prolonged bone retention and possible fetal exposure. The biological plausibility of sustained aromatase modulation by a bisphosphonate in vivo also requires further mechanistic clarification.
Alendronate represents an early-stage, computationally identified repurposing candidate with supportive preclinical data in animal models of PCOS. However, it remains highly investigational and would require substantial mechanistic validation and clinical evaluation before consideration in PCOS management.

Name: Alma system
Developers: ResQ Medical Ltd
Indication: Indicated for the temporary control or reduction of postpartum uterine bleeding when conservative management of uterine bleeding is warranted.
Mechanism of action: Doppler measurement of uterine artery resistance to assess impaired uteroplacental perfusion.
Key features and challenges:
The Alma System utilizes vacuum-based technology to mimic and support the natural contraction of the uterus, which in turn leads to the cessation of bleeding as would occur naturally in any normal birth. It is specifically tailored to manage abnormal postpartum uterine bleeding and postpartum hemorrhage, providing a swift and efficient treatment option. (https://resq-med.com/) 

The safety and efficacy of the Alma System is currently being tested in a prospective, non-randomized, feasibility pilot study. Women with vaginal deliveries in a hospital setting who have failed first-line therapies for postpartum haemorrhage will be treated with the Alma System. The outcomes studied include the rate of cessation of uterine bleeding and the incidence, severity, and seriousness of device-related adverse events experienced by participants. The trial is expected to be complete in 2025. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06166771)

Name: Aloe vera–Derived Gold-Coated Iron Oxide Nanohybrids (Au-IONPs)
Developers: Guang’anmen Hospital of the Chinese Academy of Traditional Chinese Medicine
Indication: Experimental nanohybrids designed to enhance thermosensitization, radiosensitization, and MRI-guided HIFU ablation of uterine fibroids, evaluated through in-vitro cytotoxicity assays, hyperthermia experiments, radiotherapy interactions, and apoptosis analyses in human uterine leiomyoma (ht-UtLM) cells.
Target:
Functional targets include:
-Enhancement of HIFU energy deposition
-Radiosensitization (↑ ROS, ↑ DNA damage)
-Hyperthermia-induced apoptosis
-Mechanical cavitation effects
Mechanism of action:
Au-IONPs combine gold’s photothermal/radiosensitizing properties with iron oxide’s magnetic and hyperthermia capabilities. In ht-UtLM cells:
Thermosensitization:
-Au-IONPs increase heat generation under mild hyperthermia (42°C), amplifying cell death.
Radiosensitization:
-Au-IONPs enhance X-ray dose absorption.
-Increase ROS production, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial depolarization, leading to apoptosis.
-Dose-enhancement observed at both 2 Gy and 4 Gy radiation.
Synergy with HIFU (High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound):
-Nanoparticles significantly amplify cavitation & mechanical disruption of fibroid cells.
-Dramatic drop in cell viability (>50%) under HIFU with nanoparticles.
Apoptosis induction:
-Annexin-V/PI flow cytometry shows,
• ~21–26% apoptosis (hyperthermia + radiation)
• ↑ to 42–45% apoptosis when Au-IONPs are added
-Apoptosis also accompanied by necrosis at high frequencies of insonation.
Technology type: Nanoparticle theranostic agent for thermosensitization and radiosensitization
Key features and challenges:
Au-IONPs are Aloe vera–mediated gold-coated magnetic iron oxide nanohybrids engineered for combined thermosensitizing, radiosensitizing, and HIFU-enhancing treatment of uterine myomas. Physicochemical characterization confirmed stable, mono-disperse nanoparticles (30–60 nm), negative zeta potential, and coexistence of Au and γ-Fe₂O₃ crystalline phases. In vitro studies using human fibroid (ht-UtLM) cells demonstrated concentration-dependent cytotoxicity beginning at doses ≥15 μg/mL, efficient cellular uptake, and strong apoptosis induction. Au-IONPs amplified hyperthermia-induced cell killing, significantly enhanced cell death under megavoltage X-ray irradiation, and dramatically increased apoptosis under combined HIFU + radiation + nanoparticle treatment. Mechanistic analyses revealed ROS generation, membrane disruption, cavitation, mitochondrial damage, and impaired DNA repair as major contributors to cell death.
However, findings are limited to in-vitro cell-line studies, with no in vivo fibroid models or clinical translation. Key challenges include potential systemic toxicity, need for targeted delivery, uncertainties around reproductive safety, nanoparticle clearance/biodistribution, and translation of HIFU–nanoparticle interactions to human anatomy. Clinical applicability requires rigorous toxicology, biodistribution profiling, and device-compatibility validation. Nonetheless, Au-IONPs represent a promising nanotheranostic platform with potential to meaningfully enhance HIFU and radiotherapy outcomes in fibroids.
Source: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02726351.2024.2364867#d1e239
Recent updates:
A 2024 in-vitro study demonstrated potent HIFU-enhancing, hyperthermia-boosting, and radiosensitizing effects of Aloe vera–mediated Au-IONPs in human uterine fibroid cells. No in vivo or clinical development exists.
Source: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02726351.2024.2364867

Name: Alpha 2 PeptiGel
Developers: University of Manchester
Indication: Indicated for the prevention of Endometriosis recurrence following laparotomy.
Mechanism of action: Reduces final lesion volume.
Key features and challenges:
The aim of a 2024 project was to design a biocompatible, hydrogel-based localised therapy that can prevent endometriosis lesion recurrence. A self-assembling peptide hydrogel (SAPH) has been explored to meet this need as they have the potential to be administered during laparotomy, increasing drug availability whilst mitigating systemic side effects.  
Analysis of hydrogel performance was achieved through four objectives: to characterise drug-loaded SAPHs; to investigate SAPH localisation and stability in vivo via fluorescence imaging; to establish and validate a murine model of endometriosis recurrence and to utilise this model to test the efficacy of systemic and local therapies. 
In vitro degradation and cell culture studies highlighted the adhesive and bio-compatible properties of the chosen SAPH (Alpha 2 PeptiGel®). Drug-loading of solubilised and lyophilised drugs had a distinct effect on hydrogel structure and drug release, which appeared to be due to changes in electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions between drug and peptide. The SAPH was successfully functionalised with an infrared tag (IR750) without compromising its physio-chemical properties. In vivo and ex vivo imaging showed that the IR750-tagged SAPH administered onto the parietal peritoneum of mice remained in situ for up to 22 days. There was no visible peptide bio-accumulation within the organs, and accumulation within the cartilage was temporary. A murine model of endometriosis recurrence was successfully developed by implanting donor uterine tissue onto the parietal peritoneum of recipient mice during laparotomy. A second laparotomy was conducted 14 days later, which confirmed all tissue fragments formed fluid-filled lesions. Lesions that were aspirated and partially removed during this laparotomy consistently recurred after 28 days. There were no signs of distress or disturbances to the oestrous cycle. Therefore, this model was deemed suitable for testing the efficacy of localised and systemic therapies on lesion recurrence. Neither systemic nor localised treatments completely prevented lesion recurrence, but growth rate was attenuated with localised treatment as the drug loaded hydrogels produced an average final lesion volume significantly lower than hydrogel control. Localised application also significantly reduced final lesion volume compared to volume at removal. This effect was also observed for systemic, however, contraceptive effects associated with the therapeutic were observed via disruption of the oestrous cycle. 
In conclusion, utilising a drug-loaded SAPH during the peri-operative window could be a suitable alternative to conventional post-operative treatment to prevent lesion recurrence. This local treatment was well tolerated; efficacious in reducing lesion volume, without systemic side effects (https://www.liebertpub.com/doi/full/10.1089/ten.tea.2024.06979.abs).

Name: Alpha-fetoprotein
Developers: University of Basrah
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Measures serum alpha-fetoprotein as a biomarker reflecting metabolic or hepatic alterations associated with PCOS-related endocrine dysfunction.
Key features and challenges:
Alpha-Fetoprotein (AFP) is a glycoprotein produced primarily by the liver and yolk sac during fetal development. It is commonly used as a biomarker in diagnostics for liver function and certain cancers, particularly hepatocellular carcinoma and germ cell tumors, as well as in the context of neural tube defects during pregnancy.

A 2023 study assessed the potential of AFP as a marker for diagnosing PCOS-related non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). The study found higher AFP levels in women with PCOS (80 ± 0.22) compared to healthy controls (0.67 ± 0.19), with a significant increase observed across most BMI categories, except for those of normal weight. This suggests that AFP could serve as a useful, cost-effective diagnostic tool for identifying PCOS and its association with fatty liver disease. However, further research is needed to validate these findings in clinical practice. (https://www.jptcp.com/index.php/jptcp/article/view/1412/1566)

Name: Amino acid - L-arginine - PTL/PTB
Developers: University of Adelaide; Harvard School of Public Health (HSPH)
Indication: Prevention of preterm labour/birth in at risk women
Mechanism of action: Facilitates nitric oxide production by conversion from nitric oxide synthase
Key features and challenges:
L-arginine is a semi-essential amino acid whose methyl derivatives, in particular symmetric Dimethylarginine (ADMA), is an active inhibitor of nitric oxide synthase. Nitric oxide diffuses into the underlying vascular smooth muscle cells and mediates vasodilatation and platelet stabilisation by a cyclic GMP-dependant process. It is therefore an important regulator of placental perfusion and placental vascular endothelial function, and plays a vital role in labour, cervical ripening, preeclampsia, and intrauterine growth restriction. 
A review of the role of L-arginine (and L-citrulline) in pregnancy outcomes has noted that existing studies of L-arginine supplementation in pregnancy in high-resource settings have shown improved maternal and foetal hemodynamics, prevention of preeclampsia, and improved birth outcomes including higher birth weight and longer gestation(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31075164/). A 2017 study in Tanzania showed that women recieving higher doses of L-arginine supplementation had reduced risk of preterm birth compared to others in lower dose groups (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5860425/).
Clinical studies have reported a reduction in preterm labour/birth risk in women at risk for preeclampsia treated with L-arginine versus placebo. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24172291/). Early (around 16 weeks gestation) and continuous intervention with L-arginine is found to be most effective, which is consistent with results for other nitric oxide drugs. Other larger clinical trials have found similar results. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28911008/)
L-citrulline is naturally found in many foods and is changed into amino acid, L-arginine, in the body. L-arginine is important for the growth of a healthy placenta and healthy baby. Adding L-citrulline to the diets of pregnant women may be an effective and affordable way to improve the health of their babies. In 2023, the AGREE trial was initiated to test whether a dietary supplement containing a common food component, an amino acid called L-citrulline, can help pregnant Kenyan women at risk of malaria have healthier pregnancies and healthier babies. 2,960 pregnant Kenyan women will be enrolled and randomly assigned to take either a twice daily dietary supplement containing L-citrulline or a placebo supplement without additional L-citrulline. The trial is set to be completed in 2026.
(https://classic.clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT05934318)
Recent updates: N/A

Name: Amino acid - L-citrulline - PE/E
Developers: University Medical Center Mainz; Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz; French University Hospital Centre of Nantes, Centre Hospitalier Universitaire de Nantes
Indication: Prevention of preeclampsia in high risk women
Mechanism of action: Precursor to L-arginine (an NO donor)
Key features and challenges:
L-citrulline is a naturally occurring amino acid, synthesised endogenously and also found in high concentrations in certain foods, such as watermelon. Citrulline is a natural amino acid precursor to arginine, produced as a byproduct of the enzymatic production of nitric oxide from the amino acid arginine, catalyzed by nitric oxide synthase. It is currently available as a dietary ingredient in dietary supplement products.

Because preeclampsia is associated with reduced nitric oxide (NO) availability, several preclinical studies and clinical trials have tested the effect of NO donors such as L- arginine.
L-citrulline however, in contrast to L-arginine, escapes uptake in the liver and appears directly in the peripheral blood converted by the kidneys from L-arginine, and released into the systemic circulation. As such, L-citrulline may therefore be more effective in the treatment of preeclampsia than L-arginine alone. 

Most relevant preclinical studies looking directly at L-citrulline versus L-arginine have focused on general hypertension, with positive results. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24113064/). Pregnancy-related studies appear to date focused on L-arginine supplementation. However, a Phase II/III trial was recently competed that evaluated the efficacy of citrulline supplementation on the delay of delivery for women hospitalized for sever preeclampsia (CITRUPE). Results are pending.

Intravenous L-citrulline is also currently under development in Phase II trials for COVID-19 and Phase III trials for Acute lung injury. This includes by Asklepion, under a license from Vanderbilt University, for prevention of acute post-operative lung injury and SARS-COV-2 acute respiratory disease, and under late stage clinical development in the US, Israel, Germany and Austria for prevention of clinical sequelae of acute lung injury and SARS-COV-2 acute respiratory disease.

2025 Study: In patients with preeclampsia, the placental IGF-1 (insulin-like growth factor 1) expression was significantly reduced compared with healthy pregnancy, associated with a downregulation of ZEB1 (zinc finger E-box binding homeobox 1) and an upregulation of miR-486-5p and miR-210. L-citrulline supplementation in preeclampsia rats significantly increased the placental expression of IGF-1 and ZEB1 and reduced the expression of miR-486-5p and miR-210. Total serum polyamine level was reduced in patients with preeclampsia and pregnant Dahl salt-sensitive rats, while L-citrulline treatment maintained the serum polyamine level in Dahl salt-sensitive rats during pregnancy. Placental IGF-1 expression was positively correlated to serum polyamine levels. Moreover, both L-citrulline and polyamines normalized the expression of IGF-1 and some antiangiogenic markers in cultured human placental vascular endothelial cells treated with preeclampsia serum. Results from IGF-1 siRNA experiments indicate that part of the L-citrulline effects on gene expression was dependent on IGF-1.
CONCLUSIONS:
L-citrulline supplementation improves the IGF-1 signaling pathway in preeclampsia, at least partly, via polyamine production. Maternal supplementation with L-citrulline or polyamine may represent a safe and effective therapeutic strategy for preeclampsia. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40452593/)
Recent updates:
In 2016, Nantes University Hospital registered the CITRUPE clinical trial (NCT02801695) to evaluate the efficacy of citrulline supplementation on the delay of delivery for women with preeeclampsia, which completed in December 2020. No results have been published.

2025 study demonstrated L-citrulline supplementation improves the IGF-1 signaling pathway in preeclampsia, at least partly, via polyamine production. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40452593/)

Name: Amino acid signatures
Developers: Peking University Third Hospital
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Profiles plasma amino acid patterns to identify metabolic dysregulation associated with insulin resistance in PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Amino acid signatures refer to specific patterns or profiles of amino acids that may be used as biomarkers for diagnosing or understanding certain diseases. Research into amino acid signatures for PCOS is still in its early stages, but there is growing interest in how metabolic alterations, including amino acid metabolism, could play a role in PCOS diagnosis and management.

A study of 380 Chinese Han women examined plasma amino acid profiles. Thirty-one amino acids showed abnormal levels in PCOS, with 28 upregulated and 3 downregulated. Thirteen amino acids were identified as potential metabolic markers for PCOS, with 10 having high sensitivity and specificity for diagnosis. Specific amino acids were linked to obesity, insulin resistance, and metabolic syndrome in PCOS. Altered levels of certain amino acids, including tyrosine, lysine, and methionine, were associated with these metabolic risks. The study suggests that amino acid signatures could serve as effective markers for diagnosing PCOS and predicting metabolic disturbances.
(https://www.rbmojournal.com/article/S1472-6483(21)00583-6/abstract)

Name: Aminophylline
Developers: Imperial College London
Indication: Prevention or treatment of preterm labour/birth
Target: cGMP-inhibited 3',5'-cyclic phosphodiesterase A; Adenosine receptor A1; Adenosine receptor A3; Histone deacetylase 2
Mechanism of action: Phosphodiesterase inhibitor/Adenosine receptor antagonist/Histone deacetylase activator; increases intracellular cAMP levels, reducing inflammation
Key features and challenges:
Aminophylline is a non-specific phosphodiesterase inhibitor drug combination of theophylline and ethylenediamine in a ratio of 2 to 1. There are various proposals for the molecular mechanism for theophylline, but not all of them take place at clinically effective concentrations. Aminophylline relaxes smooth muscles, particularly bronchial muscles. This xanthine most likely exerts its effect by inhibiting cAMP or cGMP phosphodiesterases, thereby increasing levels of the second messenger cAMP or cGMP intracellularly. Other mode of actions include an adenosine antagonistic effect on the activity of CD4 lymphocytes and mediator release from mast cells thereby decreasing lung sensitivity to allergens and other substances that cause inflammation. Aminophylline also acts as a CNS stimulant and exerts a positive chronotropic and inotropic effect on the heart.

Preclinical studies on aminophylline have been directed towards the addition of aminophylline to progesterone to increase intracellular cAMP levels which might improve the efficacy of progesterone (P4) in the prevention of preterm labour/birth. A study in mice reported that the combination of P4 and aminophylline has a more potent anti-inflammatory effect than either agent alone and may be an effective combination in women at high-risk of preterm labour/birth. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31295341/)

A Phase I Progesterone and Aminophylline for the Prevention of Preterm Labour (PROGRAM) clinical trial (NCT03152942) investigating whether the combination of aminophylline and P4 is acceptable to women at high-risk of preterm labour/birth was completed in 2019 (no publications available).

In 2022, the contraction-blocking potency of three novel tocolytics - 2-APB, glycyl-H-1152, HC-067047 was comprehensively assessed and compared to other tocolytic agents including aminophylline. The IC50 concentrations were 53 µM for 2-APB, 18.2 µM for glycyl-H-1152, 48 µM for HC-067047, 318.5 µM for aminophylline, 4.3 µM for rolipram, 10 nM for nifedipine, and 59.5 µM for indomethacin. A single treatment with each drug at the determined IC50 concentration was confirmed to reduce contraction performance (AUC) by approximately 50%. However, of all the drugs examined, the overall order of contraction-blocking potency in decreasing order was nifedipine > rolipram > glycyl-H-1152 > HC-067047 > 2-APB > indomethacin > aminophylline. (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43032-022-01000-2)
Recent updates:
2019: Aminophylline and progesterone prevent inflammation-induced preterm parturition in the mouse. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31295341/)

2024 (AAA): New preclinical data added to key features

Name: Aminospectinomycin
Developers: Microbiotix, Inc.
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis
Key features and challenges:
Aminospectinomycin (amSPC) antibacterials are a series of novel small-molecule derivatives of spectinomycin (SPC), developed to address antimicrobial resistance in sexually transmitted infections (STIs), particularly Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Like spectinomycin, amSPCs inhibit bacterial protein synthesis by targeting the 30S ribosomal subunit. Spectinomycin remains a second-line gonorrhea treatment in some regions; however, increasing resistance and limited therapeutic options have driven efforts to optimize this scaffold.
Preclinical data indicate that amSPCs demonstrate improved in vitro potency against N. gonorrhoeae compared with parent spectinomycin, along with reduced cytotoxicity. These compounds are being developed as broad-spectrum agents targeting N. gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, with potential utility in co-infections. Given their low oral bioavailability, amSPCs are intended for parenteral administration, consistent with aminoglycoside-class therapies and current standard-of-care treatment such as ceftriaxone.
A Phase I research program aims to advance amSPCs as parenteral therapies for bacterial STIs by maintaining potency against N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis, demonstrating activity against additional bacterial STIs, and confirming efficacy in murine models of gonorrhea (https://reporter.nih.gov/search/dAlQ5rAGAUGIgFvGIAV21g/project-details/9547245). 
In the subsequent Phase II program, lead candidates will undergo expanded in vivo efficacy testing in murine models of N. gonorrhoeae infection and N. gonorrhoeae–C. trachomatis co-infection, alongside pharmacokinetic and toxicology studies to establish an in vivo safety index and support selection of a final preclinical candidate.
Key challenges include the early preclinical stage of development, the need to demonstrate durable activity against resistant strains, and confirmation of safety and pharmacokinetic suitability in humans. Parenteral administration may limit outpatient convenience compared with oral agents, though it aligns with current gonorrhea treatment practice. Regulatory pathways for novel antimicrobials in the context of resistance will also require robust clinical data.
Overall, aminospectinomycin derivatives represent a promising next-generation protein synthesis inhibitor platform with enhanced in vitro potency against drug-resistant gonorrhea. Further preclinical validation and eventual clinical evaluation will determine their potential role in the STI treatment landscape.

Name: Aminothiazoles
Developers: Erasmus University (including Erasmus University Medical Center)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Mycetoma.
Mechanism of action: Unknown.
Key features and challenges:
The open-source drug discovery program for mycetoma, MycetOS, screened a series of compounds for in vitro activity against M. mycetomatis.
Aminothiazoles were one series selected for further testing, and were subsequently identified as a novel lead compound given that they were highly active against M. mycetomatis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9516133/).

Name: Amiodarone
Developers: Sungkyunkwan University; IP Korea
Indication: Treatment of MERS-CoV infection (repurposed candidate)
Target: Host endosomal/lysosomal pathways (acid sphingomyelinase, endosomal pH regulation).
Mechanism of action: Weak base that alkalizes lysosomes, inhibiting acid sphingomyelinase and blocking coronavirus entry via endosomal/lysosomal pathway.
Key features and challenges:
-FDA-approved antiarrhythmic with known safety profile.
-Potent against MERS-CoV pseudovirus and live virus in vitro (EC50 ~3–10 µM).
-Broad-spectrum activity: also effective against SARS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2, HCoV-229E, and HCoV-OC43.
-Stronger efficacy at early stages of infection; reduced potency when administered later.
-Challenges: Cardiac side effects (QT prolongation, bradycardia) make systemic antiviral use problematic.
Recent updates: -Was assessed early in COVID-19 repurposing screens (2020–2021) but not pursued clinically due to cardiotoxicity risks.

Name: Amiodarone/Benznidazole
Developers: Oswaldo Cruz Foundation (FIOCRUZ), Fundação Oswaldo Cruz (including FIOCRUZ Amazonia and Instituto Leônidas & Maria Deane (ILMD))
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Chagas disease.
Target: Trypanosoma cruzi lipids, RNA, DNA and proteins
Key features and challenges:
AMD monotherapy did not impact parasitemia, parasite load, TNF concentration and production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in cardiac tissue. Alike Bz therapy, the combination of Bz and AMD (Bz/AMD), improved cardiac electric abnormalities detected T. cruzi-infected mice such as decrease in heart rates, enlargement of PR and QTc intervals and increased incidence of atrioventricular block and sinus arrhythmia. Further, Bz/AMD therapy ameliorated the ventricular function and reduced parasite burden in the cardiac tissue and parasitemia to a degree comparable to Bz monotherapy

The combination treatment (Bz/AMD) proved to be the most effective in mitigating the ventricular dysfunction caused by the infection, while also modulating crucial pathogenic factors of CCC, including TNF production, ROS levels, fibronectin deposition and, Cx-43 expression in cardiac tissue (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0753332224006267)
Recent updates: Preclinical study finds combination to be effective over ineffective monotherapy with Bz or AMD (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0753332224006267)

Name: Amioder
Developers: Medical University of Warsaw; Universidade Do Grande Rio
Indication: Investigated for the treatment of Trichomoniasis.
Mechanism of action: Causes increase in [Ca2+] and the collapse of the electrochemical potential of the mitochondrial membrane; alkalinization of the parasite’s acidocalcisomes; morphological changes (deformed and aggregated cells and alterations in the hydrogenosomes); cell death by apoptosis.
Key features and challenges:
Amioder is a synthetic benzofuran derivative structurally based on amiodarone, an antiarrhythmic agent approved in the United States in 1985 for conditions such as atrial fibrillation. Structural modifications of amiodarone have been explored for antiparasitic applications. Amioder has demonstrated activity against protozoan parasites, including Trypanosoma cruzi and Leishmania donovani, where it inhibits parasite growth and disrupts intracellular calcium (Ca²⁺) homeostasis. Mechanistic studies in L. donovani showed collapse of mitochondrial membrane potential and alkalinization of acidocalcisomes, leading to parasite death.
In 2022, a study evaluated amiodarone, amioder, and dronedarone against Trichomonas vaginalis, the causative agent of trichomoniasis (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00436-022-07521-8). Amioder exhibited dose-dependent inhibitory activity with an IC₅₀ of 3.5 μM. At a concentration of 10 μM, inhibition of T. vaginalis was comparable to that observed with 2 μM metronidazole, the current first-line therapy. These findings suggest that amioder has meaningful in vitro antitrichomonal activity and may represent a potential alternative or adjunct candidate, particularly in the context of emerging metronidazole resistance.
Key challenges include the preclinical stage of evidence, absence of in vivo efficacy data in trichomoniasis models, and lack of human safety and pharmacokinetic evaluation for this indication. Given its structural similarity to amiodarone, careful assessment of off-target effects and cardiotoxicity risk will be necessary. Further translational studies are required to evaluate selectivity, toxicity, resistance potential, and formulation suitability.
Overall, amioder demonstrates promising in vitro activity against Trichomonas vaginalis and represents a potential novel candidate for trichomoniasis chemotherapy. However, advancement into in vivo and clinical studies will be essential to determine its safety and therapeutic feasibility.

Name: Amixicile
Developers: Virginia Commonwealth University
Indication: Investigated for the treatment of Trichomoniasis.
Target: Inhibitor of enzyme pyruvate ferredoxin oxidoreductase.
Mechanism of action: Amixicile targets vitamin B1, a cofactor of the pyruvate ferredoxin oxidoreductase enzyme, a key player in the energy metabolism of anaerobic bacteria.
Key features and challenges:
Amixicile is a novel antimicrobial derived from an FDA-approved drug, nitazoxanide, currently used in the treatment of Cryptosporidium and Giardia.  Amixicile has shown efficacy in preclinical animal model studies against periodontal anaerobes, Clostridiodes difficile, and Helicobacter pylori.  It has demonstrated high potency as well as low toxicity in animals, and has been shown to be non-inhibitory to various healthy bacteria and to support rapid repopulation of healthy mibrobiomes.  Development of resistance is considered unlikely, as mutations to the drug’s target would potentially lead to loss of function of the pyruvate ferredoxin oxidoreductase enzyme and would therefore be lethal for the pathogen.
A study published in 2022, tested the efficacy of amixicile against Trichomonas vaginalis in vitro reported a minimum inhibitory concentration of 6.25 μM.  In contract, the MIC for the current drug of choice, metronidazole, and nitazoxanide was 12.5 μM and 100 μM, respectively.  Given that T. vaginalis was found to be consistently more susceptible to amixicile at lower concentrations compared to both metronidazole, and nitazoxanide, amixicile may be highly active against T. vaginalis and warrants further investigation as a potential alternative in the treatment of trichomoniasis (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00436-022-07567-8).

Name: Amlodipine
Developers: Hanmi Pharmaceutical
Indication: Management of hypertension in preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: Inducing vasodilation by inhibiting uptake of calcium ions into both vascular smooth muscle and cardiac muscle cells
Key features and challenges:
Amlodipine is a long-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker indicated for the treatment of hypertension and coronary artery disease. It exerts its antihypertensive effect by inhibiting calcium influx into arteriolar smooth muscle cells, resulting in vasodilation and reduced peripheral vascular resistance. Amlodipine is marketed in several salt formulations (e.g., besylate, mesylate, maleate). Patent protection for the originator product (Norvasc®, Pfizer) expired in 2007, and the drug is now widely available in generic form.
Preclinical research published in 2019, in Tg-AT1B2 mouse models demonstrated that amlodipine treatment prevented features consistent with preeclampsia (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30503206/). 
In a small clinical study reported within the same investigation (n=8; 4 per group), amlodipine reduced blood pressure and was associated with a statistically significant prolongation of pregnancy compared with nifedipine, with delivery occurring on average four days later in the amlodipine group. However, the sample size was extremely limited.
In 2019, A clinical study assessing first-trimester exposure in women with chronic hypertension reported no increased risk of major congenital malformations associated with amlodipine use (https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/JAHA.119.012093).
Amlodipine has been investigated for use in pregnancy-related hypertension, primarily in the context of chronic hypertension rather than preeclampsia. Examples are two studies below, published in 2020.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32420783/),
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32199925/). 
Key challenges include limited high-quality clinical data specifically addressing preeclampsia, small sample sizes in early studies, and lack of large randomized controlled trials evaluating maternal and perinatal outcomes. While safety data in chronic hypertension during pregnancy are reassuring, further robust trials are required to determine efficacy and optimal positioning in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
Recent updates:
2024: In the study period, 88 maternal deliveries with preeclampsia met the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Methyldopa, nifedipine, and amlodipine were used in the study population whereas amlodipine with metildopa or nifedipine with metildopa were the option of antihypertensive combination. Nifedipine or amlodipine? The choice for hypertension during pregnancy: a systematic review and meta-analysis. https://www.researchgate.net/publication/359343202_Nifedipine_or_amlodipine_The_choice_for_hypertension_during_pregnancy_a_systematic_review_and_meta-analysis#:~:text=In%20the%20study%20period%2C%2088,the%20option%20of%20antihypertensive%20combination.

2019: Beta-Arrestin1 (via amlodipine) prevents preeclampsia by downregulation of mechanosensitive AT1-B2 receptor heteromers. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30503206/)

Name: Amniotic fluid sludge
Developers: Hacettepe University; Bezmialem Vakif University; National and Kapodistrian University of Athens
Indication: Prediction of PTL
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Ultrasound detection of echogenic intra-amniotic debris indicating inflammation or infection associated with increased risk of spontaneous preterm labour.
Key features and challenges:
Amniotic fluid sludge represents a collection of bacterial and inflammatory cells embedded in an amorphous material consistent with microbial biofilm. On aspiration, amniotic fluid sludge is usually cloudy and thick with an elevated white cell count and may be due to a microbial invasion of the amniotic cavity. It is a finding in obstetric transvaginal ultrasound scanning. It is defined as free-floating hyperechogenic material in close proximity to the cervical internal os within the amniotic cavity of women with intact fetal membranes. It images as a dense, homogenous mass. (https://radiopaedia.org/articles/amniotic-fluid-sludge-ultrasound) 

Amniotic fluid sludge has been identified as a potential marker of adverse pregnancy and perinatal outcomes. Amniotic fluid sludge is associated with spontaneous pre-term labour and, therefore, lower gestational age at birth, lower neonatal birthweight, and increased neonatal intensive care unit admission rate and neonatal death. Amniotic fluid sludge has been found to be an independent predictor of preterm birth in asymptomatic women, and the combination of a short cervix and sludge confers improved prediction for preterm delivery at <28 weeks gestation (OR: 14.8; compared with OR: 9.9 for sludge alone) (https://radiopaedia.org/articles/amniotic-fluid-sludge-ultrasound and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30337215/).

Name: AnAPN-1
Developers: GeneDesign Inc (including Ajinomoto Group); PATH (including Meningitis Vaccine Project (MVP) and Malaria Vaccine Initiative (MVI)); Johns Hopkins University (including the Bloomberg School of Public Health); Centre de Recherches Médicale de Lambaréné (CERMEL); University of Tubingen (including the Natural and Medical Sciences Institute, NMI); University of Florida; Sabin Vaccine Institute
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against malaria caused by P.falciparum
Target: P. falciparum Anopheline Alanyl aminopeptidase N (AnAPN1)
Mechanism of action: Elicits immune response where polyclonal antibodies block parasite invasion of mosquito midgut epithelial cells
Key features and challenges:
The vaccine immunizes mosquitos against infection by the blood-borne Plasmodiumparasites that cause malaria, after they ingest the blood of a person who has malaria but who has received the vaccine.After being exposed in this way, the mosquitoes cannot transmit the parasites and infect other people.
The vaccine targets a surface molecule in the midgut ofAnophelesmosquitoes that the parasites need to complete their life cycle. This molecule is not transmitted to people when they are bitten by the insects; but when introduced to animals in lab studies, the animals made antibodies against it. When these antibodies were introduced back into mosquitos along withPlasmodium, the parasites were blocked from infecting the mosquito. This breaks a key step in the malaria transmission chain.
Phase I trial completed in 2023 (NCT05905432).
Recent updates: Phase I trial completed in 2023 (NCT05905432)

Name: Anakinra - PTL/PTB
Developers: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA); CHU Sainte-Justine Research Center, Centre de Recherche du CHU Sainte-Justine; Swedish Orphan Biovitrum AB
Indication: Prevention or treatment of preterm labour/birth through inflammation reduction
Mechanism of action: Inhibition of IL-1, blocking inflammation
Key features and challenges:
Anakinra is a recombinant, nonglycosylated human interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra). The difference between anakinra and the native human IL-1Ra is that anakinra has an extra methionine residue at the amino terminus. It is manufactured by using the E. coli expression system. Anakinra is composed of 153 amino acid residues. It was FDA approved in 2001. It is marketed and used as a second line treatment to manage symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis after treatment with a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) has failed.
Anakinra has been examined in preclinical studies for efficacy in blocking IL-1 action, which appears to be central to foetal inflammatory injury associated with preterm labour/birth (PTL/PTB), and sufficient to trigger foetal loss. In a study published in 2017, it was however found that Kineret exerted only modest effects and no benefit for gestation length, neonatal mortality, or placental inflammation in an LPS-induced models of infection-associated PTL/PTB. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28148737/)
In a prospective cohort study published in 2018, on the safety of use in pregnancy, some cases of oligohydraminos following fetal renal pathology was observed in pregnant women. Given previously reported cases of congenital renal anomalies associated with both antenatal anakinra use and maternal hyperthermia, the relationship between maternal IL-1 inhibitor use, uncontrolled maternal febrile disease and fetal outcomes should be further explored. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29660063/)
In addition, because IL-1 has a role in the physiological process of labour, total inhibition of IL-1 signaling could influence the normal parturition process. For these reasons, optimisation of the pharmacological and biochemical properties of IL-1 receptor antagonists, like anakinra is desirable before they are used as preventive therapeutics for PTL/PTB.
An NIH grant was awarded to the University of California in 2023 to study the efficacy of Anakinra as a novel therapy in preventing preterm labor and intrauterine inflammation in Rhesus macaques. The completion of the study is planned for 2025.
(https://reporter.nih.gov/search/FxA8bn0-1UCHstjkAR0LGQ/project-details/10618171)
Recent updates: 2024 (AAA): Changed from inactive to active based on multiyear NIH funding for preclinical studies: https://reporter.nih.gov/search/FxA8bn0-1UCHstjkAR0LGQ/project-details/10618171

Name: Anastrozole intravaginal ring
Developers: Peking Union Medical College Hospital
Indication: Management of pain and lesions in endometriosis
Mechanism of action: Aromatase inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Anastrozole, a non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor, reduces estrogen levels in postmenopausal women with estrogen-responsive breast cancer, offering advantages over steroidal inhibitors like exemestane by avoiding steroid-related side effects. Aromatase inhibitors, including anastrozole, are preferred over older estrogen receptor modulators like tamoxifen due to their better efficacy and safety profile. (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB01217)
In endometriosis, aromatase inhibitors combined with progestogens or oral contraceptive pill or gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analogues have demonstrated positive impact on pain scores, lesion size and quality of life. 
(https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1471-0528.2008.01740.x)
An intravaginal ring made from ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA) and containing anastrozole (ATZ) has been developed for the long-term management of endometriosis. The ring aims to provide a more cost-effective and environmentally friendly alternative to oral tablets. A 2023 trial involved pharmacokinetic studies and mucosal irritation assessments of the intravaginal ring in mini pigs. The effectiveness of the ring was compared to oral ATZ tablets (Aida). A bioassay using LC-MS/MS with terfenadine as an internal standard was developed for accurate determination of ATZ levels. Results indicated comparable pharmacokinetic parameters between the intravaginal ring and oral tablets, with the ring showing a favorable targeting effect and acceptable irritation levels, suggesting its potential for long-term endometriosis management. (https://analyticalsciencejournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1002/bmc.5627)

Name: Andrographolide therapy
Developers: University of Tripoli
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of deep Endometriosis.
Mechanism of action: Reduction in M2 macrophages and increase in M1 macrophages.
Key features and challenges:
Andrographolide (HMPL-004) is a botanical product extracted from a herb that occurs naturally in China. The herb has an extensive history of use in TCM for the treatment of upper respiratory tract infections and other inflammatory and infectious diseases.
In endometriosis, M2 macrophages promote the disease, while M1 macrophages inhibit its progression. A 2025 thus sought to determine whether Andrographolide can modify the M1/M2 ratio, aligning with the pattern observed with standard treatment for deep endometriosis.
This experimental study used a post-test-only research design with a control group of 42 female Balb/C divided into 6 groups. Mice in group N (normal), normal control (KN) endometriosis (END) without therapy, while the positive control (KP) group received endometriosis + dienogest, group (P1) END and 0.05 mg/kg BW andrographolide (AND), group (P2) END + 0.1 mg/kg BW AND, group (P3) (END + 0.2 mg/kg BW AND. CD86 (M1) macrophages, while CD163 (M2) macrophages examine the number of M1 and M2 cells via flow cytometry in a specific colour.
There was a significant difference in M1, which was higher than M2 in the AND group, compared with KP. The number of M2 macrophages in the P2 group was significantly lower than that in the KN group. Similarly, the number of M2 macrophages in the P3 group was significantly lower than that in the KN group.
M1 was superior to M2 in the andrographolide group and exhibited a similar trend in the vissane group. This study serves as a preliminary investigation using experimental animals and can be further developed as a foundation for research on andrographolide as an alternative therapy for endometriosis (https://www.openveterinaryjournal.com/?mno=242571)
(https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB05767).

Name: Angel Touch device
Developers: Chiba University Hospital; Peace of Mind Co., Ltd
Indication: Treatment of endometriosis pain
Mechanism of action: Undefined
Key features and challenges:
The Angel Touch device (AT-04) is a portable magnetic field irradiation tool designed to alleviate endometriosis-related pain. It utilizes a combination of mixed alternative magnetic fields at 2 kHz and 83.3 MHz. The device builds on the proven efficacy of AT-02, a predecessor shown to be effective and safe for pain relief in fibromyalgia patients.
(https://academic.oup.com/painmedicine/article/21/2/326/5511537)
A phase III multicenter, randomized, sham-controlled, double-blind study involving premenopausal women with moderate to severe endometriosis-related pain was commenced in 2024. Participants will be randomly assigned to receive either treatment with the AT-04 device or a sham device for 16 weeks, with a subsequent 4-week period where all participants use the AT-04 device. The primary outcome is the change in Numeric Rating Scale score for pain, while secondary outcomes include various types of pelvic pain and quality of life improvements. The study, approved by the Clinical Study Review Board of Chiba University Hospital, aims to assess the effectiveness and safety of the AT-04 device in managing endometriosis-related pain.
(https://reproductive-health-journal.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12978-024-01739-8; https://jrct.niph.go.jp/en-latest-detail/jRCTs032230278)

Name: Angiopoietin Like Protein-3 (ANGPTL-3)
Developers: Bursa Yüksek İhtisas Training and Research Hospital
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS and PCOS-related metabolic features
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Quantifies circulating ANGPTL-3 to assess dysregulated lipid metabolism and insulin resistance associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Angiopoietin Like Protein-3 (ANGPTL-3) is a protein that regulates lipid metabolism by inhibiting lipoprotein lipase, which breaks down triglycerides. This leads to higher triglyceride levels in the blood. ANGPTL-3 is also linked to insulin resistance and metabolic conditions like obesity, cardiovascular disease, and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), where its elevated levels are associated with metabolic disturbances.

A study published in 2023 investigated the relationship between serum ANGPTL-3 levels and clinical, biochemical, and hormonal parameters in PCOS. It included 95 women, with 50 diagnosed with PCOS and 45 in the control group. ANGPTL-3 levels were higher in PCOS patients, particularly in those with hyperandrogenism, and were associated with insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and hyperandrogenemia. A cut-off value of 29.46 ng/ml for ANGPTL-3 showed good sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing PCOS. The study suggests that ANGPTL-3 could be a useful biomarker in PCOS diagnosis and treatment. (https://www.rbmojournal.com/article/S1472-6483(23)00653-3/abstract)

Name: Anogenital distance - Endometriosis
Developers: Tenon University Hospital; Institut National de la Santé et de la Recherche Médicale; Universitas Hasanuddin
Indication: Diagnosis of endometriosis
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Mechanism of action: Measures anogenital distance as an anatomical marker of altered prenatal hormonal exposure associated with endometriosis risk.
Key features and challenges:
In a French study published in 2020, the potential of anogenital distance (AGD) as a marker of endometriosis was explored.
AGD is a marker of intrauterine androgen exposure and exposure to oestrogen-like chemicals such as phthalates. Exposure to endocrine disruptors, such as organochlorine chemicals, is associated with endometriosis. It has been suggested that a short AGD in women is associated with an increased risk of endometriosis based on clinical and ultrasound exams.

A prospective cohort study published in 2020 included 168 adult women undergoing pelvic surgery. Of the 168 women included, 98 patients had endometriosis (endometriosis group) and 70 did not (non-endometriosis group). An operator (not the surgeon) measured the distance from the clitoral surface to the anus (AGD-AC) and from the posterior fourchette to the anus (AGD-AF) before surgery using a millimetre accuracy ruler. Endometriosis was diagnosed on exploration of the abdominopelvic cavity, and the r-ASRM and ENZIAN scores were calculated. All removed tissues underwent pathological examination.
Results:  AGD-AF had a better predictive value than AGD-AC for discriminating the presence of endometriosis (AUC = 0.840 (95% CI 0.782-0.898) and 0.756 (95% CI 0.684-0.828)), respectively. For AGD-AF, an optimal cut-off of 20 mm had a specificity of 0.986 (95% CI 0.923-0.999), sensitivity of 0.306 (95% CI 26.1-31.6) and positive predictive value of 0.969 (95% CI 0.826-0.998). In multivariable analysis, the diagnosis of endometriosis was the only variable independently associated with the AGD-AF (β = -9.66 mm 95% CI -12.20--7.12), P < 0.001). (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32529050/)

The same team also explored the screening accuracy of AGD measured by MRI on the same sample and found the same association: short MRI-AGD was a strong diagnostic marker of endometriosis, and had more accuracy than clinically assessed AGD.
(https://academic.oup.com/hropen/article/2021/1/hoab003/6140894#google_vignette)

An Indonesian study published in 2023 also found a strong correlation between AGD and endometriosis. The study compared the length of AGD in 35 endometriosis patients and 35 controls (AGD-AF and AGD-AC). In the multivariate logistic regression test, AGD-AF length was a single significant predictor (p <0.001). Based on the ROC curve, the length of AGD-AF with a cut-off of
23.35 mm has a sensitivity and specificity value of 97.1% and 65.7%.
(https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/d3a6/fad0bcadcc7d7236590959d1d0f5df9cb514.pdf)

However, an Italian case control study published in 2022 found no significant association between AGD and endometriosis.
(https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43032-022-01009-7)

Name: Anogenital distance - PCOS
Developers: 'Virgen de la Arrixaca' University Clinical Hospital; Amsterdam University Medical Centre
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Mechanism of action: Measures anogenital distance as an anatomical biomarker reflecting prenatal androgen exposure associated with PCOS risk.
Key features and challenges:
Anogenital distance (AGD) can serve as a life-long indicator of androgen action in gestational weeks 8–14. AGD has been used as an important tool to investigate the exposure to endocrine-disrupting compounds in newborns and in individuals with male reproductive disorder. Two measurements can be used: distance from the clitoral surface to the anus (AGD-AC) and distance from the posterior fourchette to the anus (AGD-AF).
Based on animal models showing that prenatal androgenization can produce PCOS-like phenotypes, which include excessive luteinizing hormone (LH) and metabolic abnormalities, along with hyperandrogenism, oligoovulation, and polyfollicular ovaries, a 2021 systematic review explored the potential correlation between PCOS and abnormal AGDs. They found six studies focusing on PCOS, suggesting that AGD is longer in PCOS patients (diagnosed with the Rotterdam criteria) than in controls. Moreover, higher testosterone, high LH and the presence of polycystic ovaries were individually associated with longer AGD.
(https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/endocrinology/articles/10.3389/fendo.2021.696879/full)
Three Spanish studies published between 2017 and 2022 found that AGDAC and AGDAF were longer in PCOS patients than healthy controls, but after adjusting for BMI, age, and episiotomy, only AGDAC remained significant. AGDAC was associated with all PCOS phenotypes and with severity. The AUC for AGDAC (using the optimal cut-off of 81.9 mm) for all PCOS phenotypes was 0.61, achieving a poor sensitivity and specificity even after adding Anti Müllerian Hormone.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32713212/; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29025054/; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30361047/)
Another Dutch study found a significant positive association between biochemical hyperandrogenemia and AGDAC, but not AGDAF.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33036791/)

Name: Anti-CSP monoclonal antibody
Developers: Eisai Co. Ltd.
Indication: Indicated for the prevention of malaria caused by P. falciparum
Mechanism of action: Neutralizing mAb response to PfSPZ
Key features and challenges: The project team aims to isolate and develop a potent anti-CSP mAb for malaria prevention. The project is enabled by access to a panel of potent anti-CSP mAbs, identified from volunteers who were protected against P. falciparum challenge following immunization with RTS,S. Applying in silico, in vitro, and in vivo methodologies the project team characterized hundreds candidate mAbs and optimize the selected 4 mAbs for enhanced potency and serum stability. After further evaluation for to address potential safety concerns, one final mAb will be advanced to further preclinical and clinical development as a tool for malaria intervention.

Name: Anti-GP38 mAb
Developers: US Army Medical Research Institute for Infectious Disease (USAMRIID)
Indication: Therapeutic (passive immunotherapy; adjunct to antiviral/vaccine strategies)
Mechanism of action: GP38 is a secreted viral factor that induces endothelial barrier dysfunction and vascular leak, enhancing viral dissemination. Anti-GP38 mAbs do not neutralize virus directly, but they block GP38-induced vascular permeability, reducing vascular leak and limiting virus spread. They also reduce circulating GP38 levels.
Key features and challenges:
-GP38 acts similarly to flaviviral NS1 as a viral toxin promoting vascular leak and endothelial dysfunction.
-Anti-GP38 mAbs, especially those targeting region 2, significantly inhibit endothelial hyperpermeability in vitro and prevent vascular leak and tissue dissemination in vivo.
-Neutralizing anti-Gc mAbs only reduce viral load, but do not prevent vascular leak, highlighting the unique protective mechanism of GP38 mAbs.
Recent updates:
2025: 
-Discovered that GP38 functions as a secreted virulence factor inducing vascular permeability and virus dissemination.
-Anti-GP38 mAbs (region 2) were shown to block this pathogenic mechanism, offering a new modality of protection distinct from conventional neutralizing antibodies.

Name: Anti-Müllerian hormone
Developers: Roche Diagnostics
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Measurement of AMH levels in the blood to evaluate ovarian reserve and function.
Key features and challenges:
Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) plays a significant role in the diagnosis of PCOS, serving as a potential biomarker due to its correlation with ovarian follicle activity. Women with PCOS typically exhibit elevated serum AMH levels, reflecting increased antral follicle counts, a hallmark of the syndrome. This has led researchers to explore AMH as an alternative to ultrasound for diagnosing PCOS, particularly when imaging results are inconclusive.

AMH levels are also being studied to refine diagnostic criteria, as variations in cutoff values impact sensitivity and specificity. Furthermore, AMH's regulatory role in ovarian function—suppressing follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and follicle recruitment—has been linked to the anovulatory and hyperandrogenic features of PCOS. However, differences in AMH thresholds across populations and assays remain challenging for its widespread clinical use.

AMH is also a critical tool for assessing the impact of surgical or medical interventions on ovarian reserve, despite its limitations in long-term predictions of premature ovarian insufficiency. Its significance continues to grow as research examines its role in broader contexts, including monitoring interventions and managing complex reproductive conditions like PCOS. (https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jog.15818)

Roche Diagnostics has proposed that the Elecsys AMH Plus assay could serve as a surrogate biomarker for Antral follicle count  (AFC) in diagnosing PCOS. (https://diagnostics.roche.com/global/en/products/lab/elecsys-amh-plus-cps-000433.html)

A study published in 2024 aimed to define AMH and AFC cut-off values for PCOS diagnosis based on JSOG 2024 and Rotterdam/IEBG 2023 criteria. Data from 986 PCOS cases and 965 controls showed higher AMH levels in the PCOS group, with AMH correlating with AFC and negatively with age. Age- and assay-specific cut-offs for AMH and AFC were established, with AFC showing more variability. AMH was found to be a reliable surrogate marker for ovarian morphology in PCOS diagnosis. (https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jog.15972) (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/03007995.2023.2204768#abstract)

A 2023 study found that Sudanese women with PCOS exhibited elevated serum AMH levels, a higher LH:FSH ratio, and increased total testosterone (TT) levels compared to controls. Among these markers, AMH demonstrated superior discriminative power and diagnostic accuracy for identifying PCOS in this population. (https://www.dovepress.com/diagnostic-performance-of-anti-mllerian-hormone-luteinizing-hormone-to-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-IJWH)

A 2022 prospective cohort study determined that higher levels of serum AMH in PCOS women required higher doses of oral ovulagen clomiphene citrate and that patients with ultra high levels of AMH may require adjuvant therapy. (https://www.fertstert.org/article/S0015-0282(22)01140-2/fulltext)

A 2022 study showed Anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) levels were elevated in adolescents with PCOS, distinguishing them from healthy controls, even though ovarian volume and endometrial stripe thickness did not align with typical adult PCOS characteristics. This finding underscores the need for adolescent-specific diagnostic criteria and highlights AMH as a potential biomarker for PCOS pathogenesis in this age group. (https://www.jpagonline.org/article/S1083-3188(22)00067-5/fulltext)

Name: Anti-Müllerian hormone biosensor
Developers: National Institute of Pharmaceutical Education and Research S.A.S. Nagar (NIPER S.A.S. Nagar / NIPER Mohali)
Indication: PCOS diagnosis via AMH level detection
Health care facility level: IVDs for research use only
Mechanism of action: Biosensor-based quantification of anti-Müllerian hormone to detect increased follicle number and ovarian dysfunction characteristic of PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
A 2-D rGO/MoS2/PANI nanocomposite-based immunosensor is a type of biosensor that combines two-dimensional materials to create a highly sensitive device for detecting specific biomarkers in biological samples.

To improve PCOS diagnostic efficiency, a novel immunosensor was developed using a 2-D electro-conductive composite of reduced graphene oxide (rGO), molybdenum disulfide (MoS2), and polyaniline (PANI) to detect anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), an early biomarker for PCOS. The sensor leverages monoclonal Anti-AMH antibodies immobilised on the electrode via EDC-NHS chemistry and was validated through electrochemical techniques, showing high sensitivity (LOD ~2.0 ng/mL) and a linear range up to 100 ng/mL. Requiring minimal sample volume (>5 μL), the immunosensor offers a low-cost, rapid, and accurate alternative for PCOS diagnosis.
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1567539424000434?via%3Dihub)

Name: Anti-Müllerian hormone/free testosterone
Developers: Capital Medical University
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Combines AMH and free testosterone measurements to assess ovarian follicle excess and hyperandrogenism consistent with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) and free testosterone are both important biomarkers in the diagnosis and management of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). The combination of AMH and free testosterone enhances the diagnostic accuracy for PCOS, especially in reproductive-age women. While AMH helps assess ovarian reserve and follicular count, free testosterone is an indicator of hyperandrogenism, a key feature of PCOS.

A study published in 2022 aimed to establish a cutoff value for AMH in diagnosing PCOS and assess the predictive value of AMH combined with androgens in Chinese women. It included 550 women, 450 with PCOS and 100 healthy controls. AMH was measured using the Elecsys AMH Plus immunoassay, and androgens were also tested. The cutoff value for AMH was 4.64 ng/mL, with an AUC of 0.938, 81.6% sensitivity, and 92.0% specificity. Combining AMH with free testosterone improved the AUC to 94.8%, with 86.1% sensitivity and 90.3% specificity, offering higher diagnostic accuracy for PCOS.
(https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/09513590.2023.2206927#abstract)

Name: Anti-NP monoclonal antibody (mAb-9D5)
Developers: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID); Defense Threat Reduction Agency
Indication: Indicated as prevention and immunotherapeutic for post-infection of Crimean-Congo Haemorrhagic Fever (CCHF) caused by Crimean-Congo Haemorrhagic Fever virus
Mechanism of action: Non-neutralizing antibody that limits early viral spread and tissue pathology. Protection is independent of Fc receptor or complement functions—suggesting intracellular mechanisms like TRIM21 may mediate protection. NP is also present on the surface of infected cells, enabling antibody-mediated clearance.
Key features and challenges:
-Prophylactic efficacy: In IFNAR⁻/⁻ mice, prophylactic administration (days –1 and +3) of mAb-9D5 conferred ~50% survival and significantly delayed disease compared to controls (median survival: 14 vs 5 days).
-Partial post-exposure benefit: When given post-exposure (days +1 and +4), mice showed delayed weight loss but succumbed by day 8—indicating limited therapeutic window.
-Heterologous protection: mAb-9D5 provided stronger protection (80% survival) against a heterologous strain (Afg09-2990) compared to the homologous IbAr 10200 strain (50%)—consistent with higher binding affinity 
Histopathological delay: Treatment delayed liver and spleen pathology, preserved Kupffer cells, and delayed immune cell infiltration.

https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04182373

Name: Apelin-13
Developers: GMR Foundation
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Target: G-protein coupled receptor angiotensin II protein J
Mechanism of action: Endogenous ligand for G-protein coupled receptor angiotensin II protein J
Key features and challenges:
Apelin is an endogenous adipokine first identified in 1998 as the natural ligand for the G protein–coupled receptor APJ. The apelinergic system is expressed in multiple tissues, including adipose tissue, cardiovascular structures, and the ovary, where it regulates steroidogenesis, follicular development, cell proliferation, and apoptosis. Dysregulation of metabolic pathways involving obesity and insulin resistance—central features of many PCOS phenotypes—has been linked to alterations in circulating apelin levels. However, human studies report conflicting findings regarding whether serum apelin concentrations are elevated or reduced across lean and obese PCOS subgroups, highlighting phenotypic heterogeneity and incomplete mechanistic understanding.
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S104346662400142X?via%3Dihub
Apelin-13 is one of the most biologically active isoforms of apelin and binds the APJ receptor with high affinity (EC50 ≈ 0.37 nM). It is widely distributed in central and peripheral tissues and exerts vasodilatory, antihypertensive, and metabolic effects. Beyond cardiovascular physiology, apelin-13 has been investigated in metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes models, reinforcing its relevance to insulin resistance–associated disorders.
https://www.medchemexpress.com/apelin-13.html
A 2024 preclinical study evaluated modulation of the apelin/APJ system in a letrozole-induced hyperandrogenic mouse model of PCOS. Treatment with apelin-13 improved ovarian morphology, increased corpus luteum formation, reduced androgen levels, and significantly suppressed oxidative stress and apoptosis. These findings suggest that activation of the APJ pathway may mitigate hyperandrogenism-related ovarian dysfunction and inflammatory stress in PCOS models.
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S104346662400142X?via%3Dihub
Despite promising mechanistic data, apelin-13 remains a preclinical candidate with no published human interventional trials in PCOS. The dual findings that both APJ agonism (apelin-13) and antagonism (e.g., ML221) can ameliorate certain PCOS phenotypes underscore complexity in apelin signaling biology and the need for deeper pathway clarification. Additionally, long-term endocrine, metabolic, and cardiovascular safety of systemic APJ modulation has not been established.
Overall, apelin-13 represents a biologically plausible experimental candidate targeting the apelin/APJ axis in PCOS. While animal data indicate potential benefits on ovarian morphology and oxidative stress, substantial translational research and controlled human studies are required before clinical applicability can be determined.

Name: Arterial pulse wave analysis (PWA)
Developers: University of Thessaloniki; McGill University; University of Glasgow
Indication: Diagnostic and prediction of preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Combines placental stiffness, volumetric ultrasound, and MRI oxygenation metrics to assess placental function and predict preeclampsia risk.
Key features and challenges:
Pulse wave analysis allows estimation of cardiac output based on continuous analysis of the arterial blood pressure waveform, a complex physiological signal determined by an interplay of left ventricular stroke volume, systemic vascular resistance, and vascular compliance. 

Measures: arterial stiffness/hardness, augmentation index, carotid–femoral pulse wave velocity, and carotid–radial pulse wave velocity 
 
Evidence for the relevance of PWA measurements for the detection and prediction of preeclampsia is contradictory. 
 
In a 2012 systematic review and meta-analysis, a significant increase in all arterial stiffness indices combined was observed in women with preeclampsia vs. women with normotensive pregnancies; carotid–femoral pulse wave velocity and augmentation index were also significantly increased, whereas carotid–radial PWV increase did not reach significance. Significant increases in arterial stiffness measurements were noted in women with preeclampsia compared with those with gestational hypertension. 
(https://journals.lww.com/jhypertension/abstract/2012/01000/the_association_between_preeclampsia_and_arterial.3.aspx) 
 
However, a 2013 study investigating both arterial stiffness and augmentation index found no difference in any parameter of arterial wave reflection between non-pregnant and pregnant women, nor between those who developed preeclampsia and those who remained normotensive, when examined at weeks 16 and 28 or postnatally. (https://www.nature.com/articles/jhh201364) 
 
A more recent study published in 2022 found pulse wave velocity and augmentation index at a heart rate of 75 beats per minute higher in pregnancies complicated by PE, in comparison with normotensive pregnancies, as well as in early-onset PE, in comparison with late-onset PE. 
(https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2021.2014553)
The PULSE study, coordinated by McGill University Health Centre, started in 2021 to examine the diagnostic value of a non-invasive test for the measurement of arterial stiffness. No results have been published yet.
(https://classic.clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT04783597)
