Name: Aspirin - PCOS
Developers: Sanandaj University of Medical Sciences
Indication: Treatmnet of PCOS infertility
Mechanism of action: Inhibiting COX-1, therefore inhibiting platelet aggregation via TXA2, which slows down progression of placental diseases
Key features and challenges:
Acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) with anti-inflammatory, antipyretic, and antiplatelet properties. It irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes, thereby reducing prostaglandin synthesis and platelet aggregation. Aspirin is widely used in cardiovascular prevention and in selected obstetric indications such as preeclampsia prevention.
https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/Aspirin
Interest in aspirin for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) stems from its anti-inflammatory effects and potential influence on ovarian steroidogenesis. A 2022 computational study using molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations demonstrated that aspirin exhibited binding affinity to the aromatase receptor, suggesting a theoretical capacity to modulate estrogen synthesis and potentially influence ovulation pathways.
https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07391102.2023.2190411
Building on this hypothesis, a 2022 registered randomized clinical trial is evaluating the effect of low-dose aspirin (80 mg daily) as an adjunct to ovulation induction therapy in women with PCOS. The study enrolls 80 women aged 20–35 years with BMI <30 kg/m² diagnosed according to Rotterdam criteria. Participants are randomized into four groups: clomiphene citrate + placebo, clomiphene citrate + aspirin, letrozole + placebo, and letrozole + aspirin. Treatment continues for three months or until pregnancy.
https://irct.behdasht.gov.ir/trial/66832
At present, aspirin is not guideline-endorsed for ovulation induction in PCOS and remains investigational in this context. While anti-inflammatory mechanisms and theoretical aromatase interactions provide biological plausibility, clinical efficacy data are limited.
Key challenges include the lack of robust clinical outcome data demonstrating improved ovulation or live birth rates with aspirin use in PCOS. Aspirin carries dose-dependent risks, including gastrointestinal irritation and bleeding, although low-dose regimens are generally well tolerated. Its mechanism in PCOS remains speculative, and comparative effectiveness relative to established ovulation induction agents is unproven.
Aspirin represents an exploratory adjunctive strategy in PCOS, primarily based on anti-inflammatory and theoretical endocrine-modulating effects. Its clinical role in ovulation induction or broader PCOS management remains investigational pending results from controlled clinical trials.

Name: Aspirin - PTL/PTB
Developers: Menoufia University; The Chinese University of Hong Kong
Indication: Prevention of preterm labour/birth in at risk women
Mechanism of action: Inhibiting COX-1, therefore inhibiting platelet aggregation via TXA2, which slows down progression of placental diseases
Key features and challenges:
Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is a non-selective cyclooxygenase (COX) inhibitor with anti-inflammatory, antipyretic, and antiplatelet effects. While standard-dose aspirin and other NSAIDs are contraindicated in the third trimester of pregnancy, low-dose aspirin (typically 75–150 mg daily, commonly 81 mg) is considered safe in pregnancy and is recommended off-label by the WHO from 16 weeks’ gestation for prevention of preeclampsia in high-risk women.
Low-dose aspirin has also been evaluated for prevention of preterm labour/birth (PTL/PTB), with evidence suggesting benefit is greatest when initiated early in pregnancy. A 2020 study reported that initiating low-dose aspirin between 6+0 and 13+6 weeks’ gestation reduced preterm delivery before 37 weeks and reduced perinatal mortality (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31982074/). 
In 2021, a study assessing low-dose aspirin in combination with dipyridamole reported reductions in PTL/PTB risk, with strongest effects when treatment started at or before 16 weeks’ gestation (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33795180/). 
A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis (35 trials) further reported that aspirin prophylaxis during pregnancy substantially reduced risks of preeclampsia, preterm birth, perinatal mortality, and intrauterine growth restriction without increased bleeding risk.
In 2023, a Phase IV trial at Menoufia University (Egypt) evaluated vaginal progesterone alone versus vaginal progesterone combined with aspirin (100 mg daily) for prevention of recurrent preterm birth; results have not yet been published (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05319834). 
Most recently, a 2025 clinical trial assessing pregnancies at high risk for preterm preeclampsia found that low-dose aspirin use was associated with later gestational age at delivery, suggesting a protective effect against early preterm birth (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40454801/).
Key challenges include ensuring appropriate patient selection (highest benefit appears in high-risk pregnancies), optimizing timing of initiation (earlier initiation appears more effective), and clarifying the incremental value of combination regimens. While low-dose aspirin is inexpensive and widely available, its apparent impact on PTL/PTB may be mediated partly through reduction of placental dysfunction and preeclampsia-related pathways rather than a direct effect on preterm labour mechanisms.
Recent updates:
2025: Clinical trial results examined whether taking low‑dose aspirin could delay preterm birth in pregnancies at high risk for preterm pre‑eclampsia, and it found that aspirin use was linked to a later gestational age at delivery. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40454801/)

Late stage trials are at the planning stage to assess the efficacy of Aspirin in preventing preterm labour. The use of aspirin in combination with other medications is also being explored. (e.g. NCT04051567; ChiCTR2000034662)

Name: Asprosin
Developers: Hangzhou Ninth People’s Hospital; Santiago University Clinical Hospital
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS (biomarker for insulin resistance)
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Asprosin levels can be measured through blood tests using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) or Western blotting.
Key features and challenges:
Asprosin is a fasting-induced hormone primarily secreted by white adipose tissue. It plays a key role in regulating glucose homeostasis and energy metabolism. During periods of fasting, asprosin is released into the bloodstream, where it targets the liver to stimulate glucose production. This process helps maintain normal blood glucose levels.

Asprosin levels can be used as a potential biomarker for diagnosing polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) due to their association with insulin resistance (IR), a common feature of PCOS. Elevated asprosin levels have been observed in women with PCOS, and research suggests that they may be independently correlated with insulin resistance and inflammation markers such as C-reactive protein (CRP).

A retrospective case-control study published in 2023 examined the relationship between asprosin levels and insulin resistance (IR) in 213 patients with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) compared to 213 age- and BMI-matched controls. Results showed that serum asprosin levels and insulin resistance (measured by HOMA-IR) were significantly higher in PCOS patients than in controls. Asprosin was independently correlated with insulin resistance and CRP levels. The study also found that asprosin demonstrated good diagnostic potential for identifying IR in PCOS, with a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) result of 0.826. These findings suggest that elevated asprosin levels are associated with PCOS and could serve as a novel biomarker for assessing insulin resistance in these patients.
(https://journals.lww.com/md-journal/fulltext/2023/04140/serum_asprosin_levels_are_increased_and_associated.62.aspx)

The role of asprosin in the development of PCOS remains unclear. Some studies show higher levels of circulating asprosin in women with PCOS compared to controls. However, a cohort study of 444 women with PCOS found no significant difference in asprosin levels between patients and controls. A more recent study reported slightly lower asprosin levels in women with PCOS who had hyperandrogenism or insulin resistance (IR), compared to those without these conditions.
(https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/endocrinology/articles/10.3389/fendo.2022.1101091/full)

Name: Astaxanthin (ASX)
Developers: Isfahan University of Medical Sciences, Iran
Indication: Treatment of PCOS - Metabolism; Fertility
Target: Oxidative stress and inflammatory pathways (e.g. Nrf2/Keap1/HO-1 axis)
Mechanism of action: Astaxanthin is a lipid-soluble xanthophyll carotenoid with potent antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity. Its polar–non-polar structure allows it to span cell membranes and neutralise reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, modulate Nrf2/Keap1 signalling and related phase II enzymes, and down-regulate pro-inflammatory mediators. In PCOS models and clinical studies, ASX has been shown to improve systemic and follicular oxidative stress markers, enhance granulosa-cell Nrf2/HO-1/NQ-1 expression, and modulate ER-stress and apoptosis pathways, with downstream effects on oocyte/embryo quality and metabolic parameters.
Key features and challenges:
Astaxanthin (ASX) is a natural xanthophyll carotenoid found in microalgae such as Haematococcus pluvialis, as well as in certain yeasts and marine organisms. It is a lipophilic antioxidant that integrates into cell membranes and has been widely marketed as an oral dietary supplement, typically at doses of 4–12 mg per day. ASX has been investigated for its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and metabolic effects across multiple conditions.
https://www.webmd.com/vitamins/ai/ingredientmono-1063/astaxanthin
Mechanistic and translational studies suggest that ASX may target several pathophysiological pathways relevant to polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Experimental evidence indicates that ASX enhances total antioxidant capacity, increases catalase activity, activates the Nrf2/Keap1/HO-1 signaling axis, and reduces oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum stress in granulosa cells.
A randomized, placebo-controlled trial (NCT03991286) published in 2022 evaluated 8 mg/day ASX for 40 days in infertile women with PCOS undergoing assisted reproductive technology (ART). The study reported improved serum antioxidant markers, upregulation of Nrf2, HO-1, and NQ-1 expression in granulosa cells, and higher numbers of mature (MII) oocytes and good-quality embryos. However, no significant differences were observed in chemical or clinical pregnancy rates between groups.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35237893/
A subsequent randomized study (2024) from the same research group demonstrated modulation of apoptosis-related markers in granulosa cells, suggesting that ASX may help rebalance dysregulated apoptosis signaling in PCOS.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39036884/
Building on these findings, a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (NCT06642363) initiated in 2024 is currently recruiting overweight women with PCOS (BMI 25–35 kg/m²) to receive 10 mg/day ASX for 12 weeks. The trial aims to evaluate effects on insulin sensitivity, lipid profile, malondialdehyde (MDA), hirsutism severity, and depressive symptoms, positioning ASX as a potential adjunctive cardiometabolic and symptom-targeted therapy.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06642363
Despite promising mechanistic rationale and early clinical signals, the overall evidence base remains limited. Existing trials are small, conducted in single countries, and of short duration. Outcomes have largely focused on intermediate biomarkers (oxidative stress indices, granulosa-cell gene expression, oocyte and embryo quality) rather than core clinical endpoints such as sustained ovulation, live birth, long-term cardiometabolic risk reduction, or meaningful improvement in hyperandrogenic symptoms.
Astaxanthin is not licensed as a medicinal product for PCOS by any regulatory authority and is instead marketed as a dietary supplement. This results in substantial variability in dose, formulation, and manufacturing quality across products. While short-term use at 4–12 mg/day appears generally well tolerated in adults, long-term safety, optimal dosing, and use during conception or pregnancy remain insufficiently characterized.
https://www.jmolpat.com/jmolpat-articles/antioxidant-effects-of-astaxanthin-in-various-diseasesa-review.pdf
https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/18/3/403
Recent updates:
2022: Double-blind RCT in infertile PCOS patients (NCT03991286, Tehran, Iran) reported improvements in antioxidant status and granulosa-cell Nrf2-pathway activation with 8 mg/day ASX for 40 days, plus higher MII oocyte and high-quality embryo rates, but no difference in pregnancy rates.
Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35237893/
2023: Linked mechanistic RCTs showed ASX modulates ER-stress and apoptosis markers in PCOS granulosa cells. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36854788/
2024: Phase 1 double-blind RCT (NCT06642363) initiated in Isfahan, Iran, evaluating 10 mg/day ASX for 12 weeks on cardio-metabolic profile, hirsutism and depression in overweight women with PCOS; trial currently recruiting (anticipated completion 2025).
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06642363

Name: Atorvastatin - Endometriosis
Developers: Chongqing Medical University, China; Pennsylvania State University; University of Health Sciences, Istanbul, Turkey; Pfizer
Indication: To inhibit the growth of ectopic lesions and inflammation and improve ovarian function
Mechanism of action: competitive inhibitor of the enzyme HMG-CoA; pleiotropic effects relevant to endometriosis include apoptosis induction and anti-inflammatory effects
Key features and challenges:
Atorvastatin, marketed as Lipitor, is a widely used lipid-lowering medication belonging to the statin class. Statins work by competitively inhibiting the enzyme hydroxymethylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) Reductase, a key catalyst in the body's cholesterol production pathway. This inhibition reduces the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonic acid, leading to lower levels of cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein (LDL), and very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) in the blood. By lowering these lipid levels, atorvastatin effectively reduces the risk of cardiovascular events, making it a standard prescription for patients with existing cardiovascular disease or those at high risk of developing it. Its well-established safety profile and long-term benefits have contributed to its widespread use across North America.
Emerging research has explored the potential of atorvastatin as a therapeutic agent for endometriosis. Patients with endometriosis often exhibit lipid dysfunction, heightening their cardiovascular disease risk. A 2024 study by Chongqing Medical University on a rat model has shown that atorvastatin not only inhibits the growth of ectopic lesions associated with endometriosis but also preserves ovarian function and fertility. In experimental models, daily intraperitoneal administration of atorvastatin led to the regression of endometriotic lesions without adversely affecting ovarian health. Additionally, atorvastatin demonstrated a protective effect on ovarian reserve, likely due to its anti-inflammatory properties. These findings suggest that atorvastatin could offer a promising dual benefit in both managing endometriosis and mitigating its associated cardiovascular risks. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0014299923007756?via%3Dihub#sec4)
A 2023 study from the Istanbul University of Health Sciences also studied atorvastatin in combination with Metformin and letrozole, and showed apoptosis induction and anti-inflammatory effects on both ovarian and peritoneal endometriosis in experimental models.
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0344033822001959?via%3Dihub)

Name: Atorvastatin - PCOS
Developers: Pfizer
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitor
Key features and challenges:
Atorvastatin (Lipitor®) is a lipid-lowering statin that competitively inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol biosynthesis. By reducing hepatic cholesterol production, atorvastatin lowers low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol and reduces cardiovascular risk. It has been widely prescribed since its FDA approval in 1996 and remains a first-line therapy for dyslipidaemia and cardiovascular disease prevention.
https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB01076
Interest in atorvastatin for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is based on its lipid-lowering, anti-inflammatory, and potential anti-androgenic effects, given the increased cardiometabolic risk observed in women with PCOS.
A 2021 Cochrane review reported that atorvastatin reduced total testosterone levels in women with PCOS, although subgroup analyses by treatment duration did not demonstrate a consistent overall effect across all studies.
https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD008565.pub3/full
Another 2021 Cochrane review found that atorvastatin reduced total testosterone, free androgen index (FAI), androstenedione, and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS) in women with PCOS.
https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD013211.pub2/full
A 2021 comparative meta-analysis reported significant improvements in lipid parameters and reductions in C-reactive protein (CRP) with atorvastatin compared with placebo or other metabolic agents.
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/cen.14636
A 2023 systematic review evaluating atorvastatin in PCOS reported improvements in lipid profiles and CRP levels, reductions in fasting insulin in some studies, decreases in HOMA-IR, and reductions in testosterone. However, findings regarding insulin levels were inconsistent across trials.
https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD008565.pub3/full
Two 2024 registered studies are further evaluating atorvastatin in PCOS populations. One study examines the addition of atorvastatin to metformin in women undergoing embryo transfer, assessing metabolic parameters and pregnancy outcomes.
https://irct.behdasht.gov.ir/trial/74127
Another randomized phase III trial compares atorvastatin and metformin (Glucophage) for their effects on insulin resistance and follicular fluid biomarkers, including antioxidants and oocyte growth factors, over six weeks.
https://irct.behdasht.gov.ir/trial/75112
Despite evidence of lipid-lowering and modest androgen-reducing effects, atorvastatin is not guideline-endorsed as a standard therapy for PCOS. Statins are contraindicated in pregnancy due to teratogenic risk, which limits their use in women actively seeking conception. Additionally, improvements in reproductive outcomes remain uncertain.
Overall, atorvastatin may offer metabolic and anti-inflammatory benefits in women with PCOS, particularly those with dyslipidaemia or elevated cardiovascular risk. However, its use in reproductive-age women requires careful consideration due to pregnancy safety concerns, and its role in improving fertility or long-term endocrine outcomes remains investigational.

Name: Atovaquone
Developers: National Institute for Infectious Diseases, Tokyo; Japanese National Institute of Infectious Diseases (NIID)
Indication: Treatment of mpox
Target: Host enzyme dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) (pyrimidine biosynthesis); indirectly impairs viral DNA replication.
Mechanism of action: Inhibits DHODH, disrupting pyrimidine nucleotide synthesis and thereby blocking efficient orthopoxvirus genome replication and virion production.
Key features and challenges:
-Identified by repurposing screen of 132 approved drugs.
-Potent in vitro activity against multiple MPXV strains (IC50 ≈ 0.51 μM; IC90 ≈ 3.25 μM), more potent than cidofovir.
-Effective at clinically relevant concentrations (Cmax ~31 μM; half-life ~67 h).
-Electron microscopy: inhibited virion formation before maturation step.
-Mathematical modeling predicted atovaquone reduces viral burden by ~91.6% and shortens shedding by ~7 days at clinical dosing.
-Synergy with tecovirimat observed (greater viral DNA suppression in vitro).
-Already used clinically for malaria and Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia; well-established safety profile.
Recent updates:
Suggested as one of the most clinically viable repurposing drugs for mpox.
Combination with Tecovirimat highlighted as promising for outbreak preparedness.
DHODH confirmed as a critical host target for orthopoxvirus replication; atovaquone validated as a first-in-class host-targeting mpox antiviral.
Potential to develop atovaquone analogues for even greater potency.

Name: Atovaquone/Proguanil-loaded nanoparticles
Developers: Pravneer Singh Institute of Technology (PSIT)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of malaria caused by P. falciparum
Target: P. falciparum electron transport complex I and tetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase
Mechanism of action: Inhibit pyrimidine biosynthesis and mitochondrial electron transport
Key features and challenges: Atovaquone-Proguanil-loaded nanoparticles employing a 3^2 factorial design prepared from combinations of Poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) and Eudragit L100 polymers and different concentrations of PVA (polyvinyl alcohol). Based on the results obtained the formulations were characterized for the particle size, zeta potential, encapsulation efficiency, and percent drug release. Among the nine formulations, F5 proved to be the most favorable in the biophysical parameters with a particle size of 176.3 nm, a zeta potential of −33.5 mV, and an encapsulation efficiency of 86% was found in the present investigation. Experimental dissolution profile analysis indicated that F5 had a slow and controlled-release profile where approximately 92.5%. Besides, cytotoxicity studies employing MTT, LDH (lactate dehydrogenase), and Trypan blue reduction test also supported the biocompatibility of nanoparticles and F5 had the highest cell viability (96%) with the least LDH release of 4%. In stability studies conducted for six months, F5 was found to remain stable regarding physicochemical characteristics and drug release profile at different temperature conditions such as room temperature, 4 °C, and 45 °C. The use of folic acid-functionalized nanoparticles is more effective, according to parasitemia, survival rate, and weight loss in mice treated with the nanoparticles. (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/09205063.2024.2422704)
Recent updates: Drug optimisation and evaluation published in 2024 (http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/09205063.2024.2422704).

Name: Auranofin
Developers: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University (Virginia Tech)
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Target: Peroxiredoxin-5, mitochondrial; inhibitor of nuclear factor kappa-B kinase subunit beta
Mechanism of action: The treatment with auranofin may increase the production or reactive oxygen species and caused elevation of intracellular calcium concentration in platelets, leading to cell death. Furthermore, auranofin may enhance the production of free radicals, governing T-cell activation.
Key features and challenges:
Auranofin is a gold salt that is capable of eliciting pharmacologic actions that suppress inflammation and stimulate cell-mediated immunity. It has subsequently been listed by the World Health Organization as a member of the antirheumatic agent category. Auranofin appears to induce heme oxygenase 1 (HO-1) mRNA. Heme oxygenase 1 is an inducible heme-degrading enzyme with anti-inflammatory properties.
There is an urgent need to find new antibiotics to treat gonococcal infections. In a previous study, the gold-containing drug auranofin demonstrated potent in vitro activity against clinical isolates of N. gonorrhoeae, including multidrug-resistant strains. Therefore, the aim of this 2022 study was to investigate the in vivo activity of auranofin against N. gonorrhoeae using a murine model of vaginal infection. A significant reduction in N. gonorrhoeae recovered from the vagina was observed for infected mice treated with auranofin compared to the vehicle over the course of treatment. Relative to the vehicle, after three and five days of treatment with auranofin, a 1.04 (91%) and 1.40 (96%) average log10-reduction of recovered N. gonorrhoeae was observed. 
Since gonococcal infections have previously been treated with a combination of two drugs, azithromycin and ceftriaxone, it was proposed that the combination of auranofin with azithromycin or ceftriaxone may possess a synergistic effect against N. gonorrhoeae in vivo. However, this must be investigated in a future study.
Overall, auranofin has the potential to be further investigated as a novel, safe anti-gonococcal agent to help meet the urgent need for new antimicrobial agents for N. gonorrhoeae infection.
(https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0266764)

Name: Automated NG phenotypic AST platform
Developers: Acenxion Biosystems
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoea and antimicrobial susceptibility
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Neisseria gonorrhoeae phenotypic Antibiotic Susceptibility Testing platform
Key features and challenges:
Acenxion Biosystems proposes to develop the first fully automated NG phenotypic AST platform that both satisfies the current CDC guidance for surveillance and fulfils an unmet clinical need for AST-guided “directed” antibiotic therapy. The system consists of Hardware; Software & Firmware; and Consumables that are single-use disposable. The system allows the growth of fastidious Neisseria gonorrhoeae while continuously monitoring for growth or lack thereof in the presence of antibiotics in real time, displaying reports via a user-friendly interface. The samples tested include QC strains and challenge strains of N. gonorrhoeae along with select isolates across multiple antibiotics of relevance at multiple concentrations. All testing has been done in parallel with the phenotypic broth dilution method for verification in-house and/or compared against expected or published results. The results of the analysis of gonococcal strains are generated in as little as four (4) hours and are based on phenotypic and broth dilution methodology. We show (a) results from analysis of quality control strains, and CDC/FDA Antibiotic Resistance (AR) Bank and (b) a demonstration of easy integration using clinical laboratory sample workflow. In 100% of cases, our method produced a clear selection of the MIC and corresponding S/I/R interpretations allowing for calculated Categorical Agreement. (https://reporter.nih.gov/search/Pj_i336pPE60DBr67yvp4Q/project-details/10544166)
(https://acenxionbiosystems.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/2023-APHL-Poster-web.pdf)
(https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10676950/)

Name: Autophagy-related-gene based signature
Developers: Zhejiang University; Zhejiang University
Indication: Prediction of pregnancies with PE
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Identification of 20 potential autophagy-related genes of preeclampsia
Key features and challenges:
An autophagy-related gene (ATG)-based signature represents a computational diagnostic approach that leverages differential gene expression profiling to identify molecular biomarkers associated with preeclampsia (PE). Autophagy is a cellular homeostatic process involved in degradation and recycling of intracellular components and has been implicated in placental development, angiogenesis, oxidative stress responses, and immune regulation. Dysregulated autophagy has been associated with abnormal trophoblast function and impaired placentation, both central to PE pathophysiology.
A 2023 study investigated mRNA expression profiles from placental and peripheral blood samples of women with preeclampsia compared with healthy pregnancies (https://www.imrpress.com/journal/FBL/28/7/10.31083/j.fbl2807132). 
Twenty autophagy-related genes were identified as differentially expressed. Functional enrichment analyses linked these genes to biological processes including autophagy, apoptosis, angiogenesis, inflammation, immune response, and signaling pathways such as HIF-1, FoxO, and AMPK. Machine learning approaches, including least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression and support vector machine–recursive feature elimination (SVM-RFE), were used to refine the candidate list to 12 ATGs that effectively distinguished PE from normal pregnancy. Four genes—LEP, ERO1L, PIK3CB, and MAPK8—demonstrated strong diagnostic potential. Additionally, analysis of miRNA dataset GSE84260 identified 11 relevant miRNAs, enabling construction of a miRNA–mRNA regulatory network that may contribute to PE development.
These findings suggest that an ATG-based gene expression signature may serve as a novel molecular diagnostic tool for preeclampsia and provide mechanistic insight into disease pathways.
Key challenges include reliance on bioinformatic and retrospective transcriptomic analyses without prospective clinical validation. The diagnostic performance of the gene signature in diverse populations and across gestational stages remains unconfirmed. Standardization of sample collection, assay platforms, and computational pipelines would be required for clinical implementation. Furthermore, integration into routine clinical workflows would necessitate cost-effective, rapid testing platforms. While promising as a precision medicine approach, further validation in large, prospective cohorts is essential before translation into clinical practice.

Name: Azithromycin - PTL/PTB
Developers: Beni-Suef University; University of Melbourne (including the Australian Venom Research Unit (AVRU) and Bio21 Institute)
Indication: For preventing premature labour
Mechanism of action: Noninvasive hemodynamic assessment measures maternal cardiac output index to identify impaired cardiovascular adaptation associated with placental insufficiency.
Key features and challenges:
Azithromycin [9-deoxo-9a-aza-9a-methyl-9a-homoerythromycin] is a part of the azalide subclass of macrolides, and contains a 15-membered ring, with a methyl-substituted nitrogen instead of a carbonyl group at the 9a position on the aglycone ring, which allows for the prevention of its metabolism. This differentiates azithromycin from other types of macrolides.

The drug is a broad-spectrum macrolide antibiotic with a long half-life and a high degree of tissue penetration. It was initially approved by the FDA in 1991. It is primarily used for the treatment of respiratory, enteric and genitourinary infections and may be used instead of other macrolides for some sexually transmitted and enteric infections. It is structurally related to erythromycin.

Related to this indication, researchers have evaluated the benefit of the addition of azithromycin to standard treatments to prolong pregnancy in women having intact membranes and at risk of or in preterm labour. The phase 2/3 clinical trial is underway and expected to complete in May 2024. 
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05971654)

Ongoing clincial trial in Australia is examining the Efficacy of Azithromycin for Short cervix and Amniotic fluid sludge for the Prevention of Preterm birth (ASAPP Pilot trial) and is expected to complete in 2028.  (https://anzctr.org.au/Trial/Registration/TrialReview.aspx?ACTRN=12624000960550)

Name: B- and T-cell Multi-epitope Vaccine
Developers: Bacha Khan University
Indication: Prophylactic Prevention
Target: Surface-associated viral proteins MPXVgp002 (YP_010377003.1) and MPXVgp008 (YP_010377007.1); selected epitopes KCKDNEYRSR, RSCNTTHNR, RTRRETGAS.
Mechanism of action: Vaccine construct joins predicted B- and T-cell epitopes using GPGPG linkers and adjuvant (cholera toxin B subunit via EAAAK linker). Designed to stimulate both humoral and cellular immune responses by binding to TLR-2, TLR-3, TLR-4, and TLR-8 receptors, activating immune signaling pathways.
Key features and challenges:
-Designed construct includes 103 amino acids (11.5 kDa) with predicted high antigenicity, non-allergenicity, and water solubility.
-Molecular docking showed strong binding affinities: –888.7 kcal/mol (TLR-2), –976.3 kcal/mol (TLR-3), –801.9 kcal/mol (TLR-4), –955.4 kcal/mol (TLR-8).

-Predicted 99.74% global population coverage, with ≥97% coverage in China, India, Pakistan.
-Disulfide bond engineering improved structural stability (Gly1-Ser82, Cys7-Tyr10, Phe51-Ile55).
Recent updates:
Confirms immunoinformatics-driven multi-epitope vaccines as a promising strategy for mpox.
Several parallel studies (2022–2023) have reported similar mpox epitope-based constructs (Aiman et al., 2022; Bhattacharya et al., 2022; Shantier et al., 2022).
This design is noted for high predicted population coverage and TLR docking stability compared to earlier efforts.

Name: B026 neutralizing antibodies
Developers: Shenzhen Bay Laboratory
Indication: Treatment (therapeutic antibody)
Target: B6R protein (enveloped virion [EV] surface glycoprotein of MPXV)
Mechanism of action: Binds to the stalk region of B6R (residues 240–279), blocking EV formation, stability, and cell-to-cell spread. Neutralizes MPXV and VACV in vitro; enhances complement recruitment and antibody-dependent clearance.
Key features and challenges:
-Isolated from a human antibody phage display library (2.2 × 10¹¹ diversity, from >2000 donors).
-Demonstrated very high binding affinity (EC50 < 0.5 ng/mL) and potent neutralization (IC50 < 0.5 nM) against MPXV EV.
-Cross-neutralized MPXV Clade IIb (2022 outbreak lineage) and VACV.
-In vivo mouse studies:
i) Prophylactic administration: Single dose gave partial protection; 66% survival at high-dose VACV challenge.
ii) Therapeutic administration: Reduced viral loads in lung, liver, and spleen.
iii) best efficacy when combined with A138 (anti-M1R) → complete protection and undetectable viral loads.
-Bispecific antibody constructs (A138-B026 scFv formats) also showed high binding and neutralization but were slightly less effective than the combination therapy in vivo.
Recent updates:
-Patent filings cover B026 and related MPXV mAbs.
-Identified as one of the lead human anti-MPXV antibodies with translational potential.
-In vivo BALB/c MPXV challenge confirmed B026 reduced viral loads in major organs.
-Dual-targeting strategies (M1R + B6R antibodies) emerging as optimal approach for orthopoxvirus mAb therapies.

Name: B6R-specific mAb B7C9
Developers: Southern University at Shreveport
Indication: Treatment (therapeutic antibody)
Target: B6R protein (extracellular virion [EV] glycoprotein of MPXV, homologous to VACV B6R).
Mechanism of action: Binds to EV B6R protein, neutralizing extracellular virions before cell entry and inhibiting cell-to-cell viral spread.
Key features and challenges:
-Identified as the only B6R-targeting antibody among screened candidates to show neutralizing activity.
-Exhibited strong binding to VACV lysates but weaker binding to purified recombinant B6R protein, suggesting recognition of conformation- or modification-dependent epitopes.
-In vitro neutralization of EV form of VACV and MPXV confirmed.
-In mice, treatment with B7C9 significantly reduced lung viral loads and protected against weight loss.
-Lower neutralizing potency compared with M1R-specific antibodies (M1H11/M3B2).
-Antigen density on EV particles is relatively low, potentially reducing efficacy.
Recent updates:
B7C9 showed enhanced neutralization when combined with M1R-targeting antibodies.
Identified as a lead EV-targeting antibody but requires further optimization (e.g., humanization, Fc engineering).

Name: B7-33
Developers: University of Mississippi Medical Center; Texas A&M University; Wright State University
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: Activates the CAMP-PKA pathway to relax blood vessels.
Key features and challenges:
B7-33 is a novel H2 relaxin B-chain–only peptide variant under investigation for the treatment of preeclampsia (PE). It is designed to mimic the vasodilatory and antifibrotic effects of relaxin while offering improved pharmacological properties. Preclinical evaluation has focused on its ability to ameliorate placental ischemia and hypertension in experimental models of PE.
In a preclinical study using the Reduced Uterine Perfusion Pressure (RUPP) rat model, B7-33 and its modified formulations (B7-33-Fc and B7-33-HSA) were assessed for therapeutic efficacy (2023: https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/hyp.81.suppl_1.16). RUPP rats were randomized into four groups (vehicle, B7-33, B7-33-Fc, B7-33-HSA; N=8 per group) and treated intravenously twice weekly from gestational day (GD) 10 to GD20. Mean arterial pressure (MAP) was measured via carotid catheterization, and uterine artery resistance index (UARI) was assessed by Doppler sonography. Biomarkers including nitric oxide bioavailability, soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1), and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) were quantified. The study aimed to determine whether B7-33 could reduce hypertension, improve uteroplacental perfusion, and modulate key pathogenic mediators implicated in preeclampsia.
Key challenges include the absence of published human clinical data, uncertainty regarding translation from animal models to pregnant populations, and the need for safety evaluation in maternal–fetal contexts. While preclinical findings are mechanistically promising, further development and clinical trials will be required to establish therapeutic potential in preeclampsia.

Name: BeiDouGen capsule
Developers: Peking University Third Hospital
Indication: Treatment of PCOS - Metabolism; Fertility
Target: Multiple metabolic and hormonal pathways implicated in PCOS
Mechanism of action: BeiDouGen is a standardised traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) herbal capsule formulated to regulate reproductive endocrine function and metabolic homeostasis. Although its exact composition and mechanistic pathways are not publicly detailed in Western literature, TCM research frameworks suggest multi-target effects through modulation of hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian (HPO) axis signalling, improvement of insulin–glucose metabolism, reduction of systemic inflammation, and potential antioxidant or follicular microenvironment benefits. The ongoing Phase 2 trial evaluates its impact on menstrual recovery, insulin resistance, lipid profile, androgen levels, and quality of life metrics, reflecting a presumed multimodal mechanism typical of botanical formulations.
Key features and challenges:
BeiDouGen capsule is a traditional Chinese medicine (TCM)–based oral herbal formulation developed for the management of endocrine and metabolic disturbances associated with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Consistent with TCM pharmacological principles, the formulation is presumed to combine multiple plant-derived components intended to act synergistically on hormonal regulation, insulin resistance, and inflammatory pathways relevant to ovulatory dysfunction and hyperandrogenism. The precise herbal composition has not yet been fully disclosed in English-language clinical trial documentation.
TCM-based formulations have been increasingly investigated for PCOS, targeting menstrual irregularity, ovulation induction, metabolic dysfunction, and androgen excess. These multi-component botanical therapies are hypothesised to exert pleiotropic effects across endocrine and metabolic axes, although mechanistic characterization varies widely between formulations.
A Phase 2 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (NCT06587698), sponsored by the Guangdong General Medical Welfare Foundation (China), is evaluating BeiDouGen capsule in 116 women aged 18–40 years with PCOS. Participants receive either BeiDouGen or placebo for 12 weeks. The primary endpoint is the proportion of participants achieving menstrual cycle recovery (cycle length 21–35 days). Secondary outcomes include time to cycle recovery, ovulation status, metabolic parameters (HOMA-IR, lipid profile), androgen levels, and patient-reported outcomes including PCOSQ scores. The study includes biochemical safety monitoring and is scheduled for completion in 2025.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06587698
Despite growing interest in botanical therapies for PCOS, BeiDouGen remains an early-stage investigational candidate. The undisclosed exact herbal composition limits mechanistic interpretation and reproducibility. No peer-reviewed preclinical or clinical efficacy data are currently available. Additionally, variability in herbal quality control, standardization, and regulatory classification across jurisdictions presents challenges for broader adoption. Evidence from other TCM formulations cannot be directly extrapolated to this specific product without published comparative data.
BeiDouGen capsule represents a multi-component botanical candidate targeting ovulatory and metabolic dysfunction in PCOS. Its clinical utility, safety profile, and regulatory trajectory will depend on transparent formulation disclosure and outcomes from ongoing randomized controlled trials.

Name: Biogenic nanocopper (BNC)
Developers: Tokat Gaziosmanpasxa University
Indication: Investigated for the treatment of Trichomoniasis.
Mechanism of action: Unknown.
Key features and challenges:
Biogenic nanocopper (BNC) refers to copper nanoparticles synthesized using biological methods, including plant extracts, bacteria, or fungi, rather than conventional chemical approaches. Copper nanoparticles (CuNPs) possess antimicrobial, antitumor, antioxidant, and catalytic properties; however, traditional chemical synthesis methods are often associated with toxic reagents, environmental concerns, and higher energy demands. Biogenic synthesis approaches are considered more sustainable, cost-effective, and potentially less cytotoxic to healthy cells, offering advantages for biomedical applications (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42452-020-2279-1
; https://www.mdpi.com/1420-3049/28/12/4838).
In 2022, a study evaluated the synthesis of BNCs using L-ascorbic acid as a reducing agent in combination with varying concentrations of copper (II) chloride, followed by in vitro assessment against Trichomonas vaginalis (https://www.liebertpub.com/doi/10.1089/jmf.2021.0151). Among the formulations tested, CuNP-3x demonstrated complete (100%) reduction in parasite viability at concentrations of 8 µg/mL after 3 hours and 4 µg/mL after 12 hours of exposure. Other formulations (CuNP-4 and CuNP-4x) achieved complete parasite inhibition at higher concentrations (128 µg/mL and 16 µg/mL, respectively) after 24 hours. These findings suggest that CuNP-3x, in particular, exhibits potent in vitro antitrichomonal activity and warrants further pharmacological investigation.
Key challenges include the early preclinical stage of development, absence of in vivo efficacy data, and limited understanding of toxicity, tissue distribution, and long-term safety in humans. Nanoparticle-based therapies also face regulatory considerations related to manufacturing consistency, characterization, and potential off-target effects. Further translational studies will be required to establish therapeutic index, formulation suitability, and comparative efficacy versus existing treatments such as metronidazole.
Overall, biogenic nanocopper represents a novel, sustainable nanoparticle-based approach with promising in vitro activity against Trichomonas vaginalis. Advancement into in vivo models and safety evaluation will be essential to determine its feasibility as a future therapeutic option for trichomoniasis.

Name: Bivalent Typhoid Paratyphoid A conjugate vaccine
Developers: International Vaccine Institute (IVI); Serum Institute of India (SII)
Indication: Indicated for the prevention of enteric fever caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi and Paratyphi A.
Target: Vi capsular polysaccharide and O-specific polysaccharide (OSP)
Mechanism of action:
**MOA of Bivalent Typhoid-Paratyphoid A Conjugate Vaccine**  

The vaccine stimulates immunity against *Salmonella Typhi* and *Salmonella Paratyphi A* by using capsular polysaccharides conjugated to a protein carrier. This enhances antibody production, ensuring robust and long-lasting protection, even in young children, by preventing bacterial colonization and severe disease.
Key features and challenges:
The bivalent typhoid-paratyphoid A conjugate vaccine offers the potential for dual protection against *Salmonella Typhi* (typhoid fever) and *Salmonella Paratyphi A* (paratyphoid fever), addressing the significant burden of these diseases in endemic regions. By leveraging conjugate technology, the vaccine links polysaccharide antigens to a protein carrier, enhancing immune response and providing long-lasting protection, even in young children. Its ability to target both diseases in a single vaccine simplifies immunization programs, improves efficiency, and increases overall coverage for enteric fevers.  

However, the vaccine faces challenges, including the complexity of developing an effective formulation that ensures strong protection against both pathogens. Clinical trials are ongoing to establish safety, efficacy, and durability of immune response. Additionally, the need for sufficient funding, streamlined manufacturing, and eventual regulatory approval are critical steps before the vaccine can be widely available. Despite these hurdles, this vaccine represents a significant advancement in the fight against enteric fevers, particularly in low-resource settings where the burden is highest.

Name: Blood pressure polygenic risk score
Developers: University of Turku
Indication: Prediction of risk of preeclampsia based on genotype
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: Genotype, nucleotide polymorphisms associated with blood pressure risk.
Mechanism of action: Aggregates genetic variants associated with hypertension to estimate inherited susceptibility to preeclampsia.
Key features and challenges:
A polygenic score (PGS) or polygenic risk score (PRS) is an estimate of an individual's genetic liability to a trait or disease, calculated according to their genotype profile and relevant genome-wide association study (GWAS) data.
Preexisting hypertension increases risk for preeclampsia. Researchers from the University of Turku (Finland) examined whether a generic blood pressure polygenic risk score (BP-PRS), compared with a preeclampsia-specific polygenic risk score (PE-PRS), could better predict hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
Their study sample included 141 298 genotyped FinnGen study participants with at least one childbirth and followed from 1969 to 2021. They calculated polygenic risk scores for systolic blood pressure and preeclampsia using summary statistics for greater than 1.1 million single nucleotide polymorphisms.
They observed 8488 cases of gestational hypertension (GHT) and 6643 cases of preeclampsia. BP-PRS was associated with GHT [multivariable-adjusted hazard ratio for 1SD increase in PRS (hazard ratio 1.38; 95% CI 1.35–1.41)] and preeclampsia (1.26, 1.23–1.29), respectively. The PE-PRS was also associated with GHT (1.16; 1.14–1.19) and preeclampsia (1.21, 1.18–1.24), but with statistically more modest magnitudes of effect (P = 0.01). The model c-statistic for preeclampsia improved when PE-PRS was added to clinical risk factors (P = 4.6 × 10–15). Additional increment in the c-statistic was observed when BP-PRS was added to a model already including both clinical risk factors and PE-PRS (P = 1.1 × 10–14).
The study demonstrated a strong association between BP-PRS and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and suggests that the BP-PRS could capture the genetic architecture of preeclampsia better than the current PE-PRSs. The clinical utility of a BP-PRS for preeclampsia prediction warrants further investigation.
(https://journals.lww.com/jhypertension/fulltext/2023/03000/associations_of_polygenic_risk_scores_for.2.aspx)

Name: Blood pressure-based preeclampsia risk prediction model
Developers: Kaiser Permanente Northern California; Tianjin Medical University
Indication: Prediction of preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Mechanism of action: Analyzes longitudinal maternal blood pressure trends to estimate probability of developing preeclampsia.
Key features and challenges:
While blood pressure measurements is a common diagnostic tool for preeclampsia, several research teams have investigated blood pressure trajectories in early pregnancy to see whether these patterns could predict the development of preeclampsia before the occurrence of clinical signs.

In a study published in 2023, researchers from Kaiser Permanente Northern California used early pregnancy BP patterns up to 20 weeks' gestation combined with clinical, social, and behavioral factors to develop a risk prediction model. They used a retrospective cohort (n=249 892) of pregnancies considered to be at low-to-moderate risk of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (excluding preexisting hypertension, heart, kidney, or liver disease, or prior preeclampsia).  The sample was randomly split into development (N=174 925; 70%) and validation (n=74 967; 30%) data sets. Predictive performance of multinomial logistic regression models for early‐onset (<34 weeks) preeclampsia, later‐onset (≥34 weeks) preeclampsia, and gestational hypertension was evaluated in the validation data set. There were 1008 (0.4%), 10 766 (4.3%), and 11 514 (4.6%) patients with early‐onset preeclampsia, later‐onset preeclampsia, and gestation hypertension, respectively. Models with 6 systolic BP trajectory groups (0–20 weeks' gestation) plus standard clinical risk factors performed substantially better than risk factors alone to predict early‐ and later‐onset preeclampsia and gestational hypertension, with C‐statistics (95% CIs) of 0.747 (0.720–0.775), 0.730 (0.722–0.739), and 0.768 (0.761–0.776) versus 0.688 (0.659–0.717), 0.695 (0.686–0.704) and 0.692 (0.683–0.701), respectively, with excellent calibration (Hosmer‐Lemeshow P=0.99, 0.99, and 0.74, respectively). The researchers concluded that early pregnancy BP trajectories improve risk stratification to reveal higher‐risk individuals hidden within ostensibly low‐to‐moderate risk groups.
(https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/JAHA.123.029617)

Another 2023 study by Tianjin Medical University explored the associations between blood pressure trajectories during pregnancy and risk of future pre-eclampsia in a large cohort enrolling pregnant women (N=5 560) at gestational age of ~12 weeks from community hospitals in Tianjin. Latent class growth modeling (LCGM) was used to model the blood pressure trajectories, based on 5 antepartum examinations before gestational week 28, i.e., week 12, week 16, week 20, week 24 and week 28. 
Univariate logistic regression and multivariate logistic regression showed the higher baseline SBP level and DBP level were related with increased risk of preeclampsia. Four distinctive SBP trajectories and DBP trajectories from 12 weeks to 28 weeks of gestation were identified by LCGM. After controlling for potential confounders (baseline BMI, being primipara or not, white blood cell counts, hemoglobin level, platelet counts and alanine aminotransferase level), the OR for SBP latent classification trajectory_ 4 was 4.023 (95%CI: 2.368 to 6.835, P<0.001), and the OR for SBP latent classification trajectory_3 was 1.854 (95%CI: 1.223 to 2.811, P=0.004). Logistic regression showed that using the DBP latent classification trajectory_1 as the reference group, the OR for DBP latent classification trajectory_4 was 4.100 (95%CI: 2.571 to 6.538, P<0.001), and 2.632 (95%CI: 1.570 to 4.414, P<0.001) for DBP latent classification trajectory_2. 
Therefore, BP trajectories from 12 weeks to 28 weeks identified by LCGM served as novel risk factors that independently associated with the occurrence of preeclampsia after 28 weeks of gestation. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis showed incremental diagnostic performance by combing baseline blood pressure levels with blood pressure trajectories.
(https://rs.yiigle.com/cmaid/1446408)

Name: Botulinum toxin A - Endometriosis
Developers: Merz Pharma; National Institutes of Health
Indication: Treatment of endometriosis-related pain by relieving muscle contraction and spasm
Mechanism of action: neuromuscular transmission on motor or sympathetic nerve terminals, inhibiting the release of acetylcholine
Key features and challenges:
Botulinum toxin type A is a purified toxin used to block acetylcholine release, treating chronic sialorrhea, muscle spasticity, dystonia, and wrinkles. It is also used off-label for conditions like TMJ disorders, neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome, and neuropathic pain. The toxin relieves muscle contraction and spasm by causing partial chemical denervation, which may lead to muscle atrophy and reinnervation over time. Effects are typically seen 4-7 days after injection. (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB00083)

Merz Pharma is developing a purified botulinum toxin type A product (NT 201) free from complexing proteins, aimed at treating conditions such as blepharospasm, spasmodic torticollis, essential tremor, and muscle spasticity. Launched in multiple countries, it may reduce neutralizing antibodies over time and is currently in clinical development for intradermal use in Germany and other locations worldwide. (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800014538) This form of the medication was also examined in patients with chronic pelvic pain of uterine origin including those with superficial endometriosis. (https://adis.springer.com/trials/700374024)

In a randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled trial, with results published in 2021, the efficacy of botulinum toxin (BoNT) in alleviating endometriosis-related chronic pelvic pain (endo-CPP) was evaluated. Women aged 18-55 with endo-CPP, who had optimized hormonal treatment, received 100U botulinum toxin A or placebo injections into pelvic floor muscles. Results showed that BoNT provided significant and longer-lasting pain relief compared to placebo, with 73% of BoNT recipients reporting benefit at 1 month versus 29% of placebo recipients. BoNT also led to a greater reduction in pelvic floor muscle spasm and less pain medication use. Benefit was more pronounced in those with focal pelvic pain, and BoNT was well tolerated with mild adverse events. (https://www.fertstert.org/article/S0015-0282(21)00747-0/fulltext)

Overall, these results suggest brilacidin is a promising candidate for further study (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40471977/)

Name: Bromoageliferin
Developers: King Saud University (KSU, formerly Riyadh University)
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Marine-derived alkaloid that inhibits bacterial growth through disruption of essential cellular processes.
Key features and challenges: This 2025 study highlights that the enzyme penicillin-binding protein 2 (PBP2) is essential for cell wall synthesis during N. gonorrhoeae growth. It aims to explore the molecular interactions of three PBP2 variants with halogenated marine sponge metabolites using molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and ADMET analysis. Docking results were assessed with the glide gscore, and the top 20 compounds for each PBP2 receptor were selected. These compounds then underwent ADMET analysis, showing potential for therapeutic development. Among them, Bromoageliferin showed the highest affinity for PBP2, Psammaplysin E for the penicillin-resistant PBP2 variant, and Preaxinellamine for the cephalosporin-resistant variant. MM-GBSA binding free energy and molecular dynamics simulations further supported the docking results. The findings suggest these compounds could be used to treat gonorrhoea, though additional in-vitro research is needed to develop them into clinical drugs (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38088353/).
Recent updates: ADMET study published in 2025 identified three compounds active against gono, targeting penicillin-binding protein 2 (PBP2), including Bromoageliferin (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38088353/)

Name: Bromocriptine - Endometriosis
Developers: Shiraz University of Medical Sciences (SUMS); Santarus; Mylan Laboratories Ltd (previously Matrix Laboratories); Zydus Life Sciences
Indication: Reduction of ovarian endometriomas
Mechanism of action: Dopamine D2 receptor agonist
Key features and challenges:
Bromocriptine mesylate is a semisynthetic ergot-derived dopamine agonist that suppresses prolactin secretion through stimulation of dopamine D2 receptors. It is approved for the treatment of hyperprolactinemia, acromegaly, and Parkinsonian syndromes. Although previously used to inhibit physiological lactation, this indication was withdrawn by the US FDA in 1995 due to safety concerns. Known adverse effects include rare but serious complications such as pulmonary fibrosis (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/31101).
Prolactin has been implicated as a potential autocrine and paracrine growth factor in uterine leiomyomas and endometrial tissue. Elevated prolactin signaling may contribute to proliferation and persistence of ectopic endometrial lesions. Bromocriptine, by reducing circulating prolactin levels, may exert anti-proliferative effects on endometrial cells and inhibit lesion growth in endometriosis.
A 2022 double-blind randomized clinical trial conducted at Shiraz University of Medical Sciences evaluated bromocriptine combined with medroxyprogesterone for three months in 60 women with ovarian endometriomas (https://irct.behdasht.gov.ir/trial/16857). 
Endometrioma size and symptoms including dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and pelvic pain were assessed before and after treatment. Subsequent publication of the trial results demonstrated significant reductions in endometrioma size and symptomatic improvement in both groups, with the bromocriptine–medroxyprogesterone combination producing greater reductions compared to medroxyprogesterone alone (https://www.ijwhr.net/pdf/pdf_IJWHR_647.pdf).
Key challenges include limited sample size and short treatment duration, which restrict assessment of long-term efficacy and recurrence rates. Safety concerns related to ergot-derived compounds, including rare fibrotic complications, warrant careful monitoring. The precise mechanism of prolactin signaling in endometriosis pathophysiology remains incompletely defined. Larger, multicenter randomized trials are needed to confirm efficacy, establish optimal dosing strategies, and evaluate long-term safety before bromocriptine can be considered a standard therapeutic option in endometriosis management.

Name: Budigalimab +/- ABBV-382
Developers: AbbVie; University of the Witwatersrand (RHRU) (including Wits RHI)
Indication: Indicated for the control of HIV-1 infection.
Target: α4β7 integrin; Programmed cell death 1 receptor
Mechanism of action: α4β7 integrin agonist; Programmed cell death 1 receptor antagonist
Key features and challenges:
ABBV-1882 is an investigational therapy developed by AbbVie, combining two monoclonal antibodies: budigalimab (an anti-PD-1 antibody) and ABBV-382 (an anti-α4β7 integrin antibody). This combination aims to achieve a functional cure for HIV by targeting specific immune pathways.
Budigalimab is a monoclonal antibody that may delay HIV rebound or maintain low viral load in people who cease antiretroviral therapy.  It works by blocking the programmed cell death 1 (PD-1) receptor on immune cells (https://www.aidsmap.com/news/oct-2023/pd-1-inhibitor-budigalimab-may-delay-viral-rebound#:~:text=Budigalimab%2C%20a%20monoclonal%20antibody%20that,immune%20responses%20against%20malignant%20cells.).
ABBV-382 is a novel anti-human α4β7 monoclonal antibody that inhibits HIV-1 replication/cell-to-cell spread via direct antagonism of the interaction of α4β7 with its cognate ligand MAdCAM-1 or HIV-1 gp120 (https://www.croiconference.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/posters/2024/411.pdf).
A Phase 2, multicentre (includes HICs and LMICs), randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study will evaluate the efficacy, safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of Budigalimab and/or ABBV-382 in people living with HIV on stable antiretroviral therapy undergoing analytical treatment interruption.
Investigators anticipate that there may be higher treatment burden for participants in this trial compared to their standard of care.
Currently recruiting.  Estimated completion = 03/2027
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06032546).
Recent updates: Phase II trial ongoing in HICs and LMICs and estimated to be completed in 2027 (NCT06032546). Phase I trial in Chinese adults investigating IV and SC routes commenced in 2024 (NCT06632938).

Name: Burulivac
Developers: University of London (Including Royal Veterinary College)
Indication: Indicated for active immunisation against Mycobacterium ulcerans infection
Mechanism of action: Designed to induce cellular immune response.
Key features and challenges:
Buruli ulcer pathogenesis relies on the lipid-like toxin mycolactone, which diffuses through tissue away from the infective organism. A 2019 study hypothesised that inducing a strong immune response to mycolactone could confer protective immunity to Mycobacterium ulcerans, with preliminary results showing its immunogenicity in triggering cellular immune responses. (https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/ntds/buruli-ulcer/meeting-reports-who-tag-bu/2019-who-meeting-bu-skin-ntds-mtg-final-report.pdf?sfvrsn=85e1a53c_9&download=true)

Progressing this research, a 2024 study introduced "Burulivac," a mycolactone-based vaccine combining antigens Ag85A, Polyketide Synthase Enzyme Ketoreductase A (KRA), and mycolactone, formulated with Quil-A adjuvant. Burulivac elicited antigen-specific antibodies, T-cell responses, and elevated Interleukin-10 levels, providing complete protection against Buruli ulcer in a mouse footpad model over 14 weeks, outperforming BCG and an avirulent M. ulcerans strain. These findings highlight Burulivac as a promising candidate for further development. (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.11.21.624625v1.full)
Recent updates: Study published in 2024 - 26https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.11.21.624625v1.full

Name: Bushen Huoxue
Developers: Naval Medical University, Shanghai; Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Endometriosis, including related infertility.
Target: Tumour necrosis factor-α, transforming growth factor-β1 and interleukin-12 in peritoneal fluid, and M2/M1 ratio of peritoneal macrophages.
Mechanism of action: Improves immune microenvironment via decreased tumour necrosis factor-α, transforming growth factor-β1 and interleukin-12 in peritoneal fluid and decreased M2/M1 ratio of peritoneal macrophages.
Key features and challenges:
Bushen Huoxue is a traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) prescription formulated to “tonify the kidney and activate blood circulation,” and has been explored as a complementary therapy for endometriosis (EM). Endometriosis is characterized by ectopic endometrial growth, chronic inflammation, fibrosis, and immune dysregulation, including altered macrophage polarization within the peritoneal cavity. Modulation of the local immune microenvironment represents a potential therapeutic strategy.
A 2025 preclinical study investigated the immunological mechanisms of Bushen Huoxue prescription in a mouse model of endometriosis established by intraperitoneal injection of endometrial tissue fragments (https://www.cabidigitallibrary.org/doi/full/10.5555/20250115596). 
Mice were randomized into three groups: model, gestrinone (0.325 mg/kg twice weekly), and Bushen Huoxue prescription (43.68 g/kg daily) for 28 days. Compared with the untreated model group, both the Bushen Huoxue and gestrinone groups demonstrated significantly reduced ectopic lesion volume and lower abdominal adhesion scores (P < 0.05). Histological analyses showed reduced fibrosis within lesions. Levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1), and interleukin-12 (IL-12), were significantly decreased in peritoneal fluid (P < 0.05). Additionally, the M2/M1 macrophage ratio was significantly reduced (P < 0.01), indicating modulation of macrophage polarization, although macrophage phagocytic function remained unchanged. Outcomes in the Bushen Huoxue group were comparable to those observed with gestrinone treatment.
These findings suggest that Bushen Huoxue may exert therapeutic effects in endometriosis by improving the peritoneal immune microenvironment, particularly through regulation of macrophage polarization and reduction of inflammatory and fibrotic pathways.
Key challenges include the exclusive reliance on animal models and the absence of robust human clinical trials. Standardization of herbal composition, dosing, and quality control presents additional barriers to reproducibility and regulatory approval. The pharmacokinetic profile and potential interactions with conventional therapies remain unclear. While preclinical data indicate immunomodulatory and anti-fibrotic potential comparable to gestrinone, well-designed randomized controlled trials are required to determine safety, efficacy, and translational relevance in women with endometriosis.

Name: C type natriuretic peptide
Developers: Cyprus International University
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for research use only
Mechanism of action: Measures circulating C-type natriuretic peptide to assess ovarian and metabolic signaling alterations associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP) is a hormone produced in blood vessel endothelial cells that helps regulate vascular tone, promote vasodilation, and reduce vascular resistance. Unlike other natriuretic peptides, CNP primarily affects blood vessels, supporting endothelial function rather than influencing blood pressure or fluid balance.

In the context of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), elevated CNP levels may be associated with androgenic imbalance or anovulation, though the exact mechanisms linking CNP to PCOS are not yet fully understood. CNP is still an emerging area of study and is being explored for its potential as a diagnostic marker for PCOS and other conditions involving vascular or metabolic disturbances.

A 2019-2020 study compared serum CNP and androgen levels in 36 women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and 30 healthy controls. The results showed that PCOS patients had significantly higher CNP, total testosterone, free testosterone, and androstenedione levels, along with a lower sex-hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) level. The study concluded that elevated CNP levels in PCOS patients suggest a potential link to hyperandrogenism or anovulation, though further research is needed to understand the mechanism.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04006171)
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36373234/)

Name: C103
Developers: Vicore Pharma Holding
Indication: Treatment of preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: Measures circulating syndecan-1 to detect endothelial and placental barrier injury associated with growth restriction.
Key features and challenges: C103, a promising angiotensin II type 2 receptor agonist (ATRAG), has been selected by Vicore Pharma Holding AB for advancement into toxicology studies and a phase 1 trial for PE. This compound exhibits exceptional selectivity for the AT2R over the AT1R, with preclinical data demonstrating over 40,000 times higher affinity for AT2R stimulation. The AT2R is a resolution and repair receptor whereas AT1R stimulation increases blood pressure and promotes inflammation and fibrosis. Designed to avoid the undesirable effects associated with AT1R activation, C103 shows potential for treating conditions such as preeclampsia, where maintaining blood pressure without exacerbating inflammation and fibrosis is crucial.  This profile makes C103 particularly suitable for indications such as preeclampsia where any AT1R stimulation is undesirable. (https://vicorepharma.com/mfn_news/interim-report-january-march-2024/)
Recent updates:
On 12 Oct 2022: According to a Vicore Pharma media release, the company expects to start this study in H2-2023. No updates since then.

The pipeline shows that this category of drugs are still in preclinical stages. https://vicorepharma.com/our-programs/pipeline/

Name: CAI-based Inhibitor
Developers: Purdue University
Indication: Treatment off gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Inhibition of N. gonorrhoeae carbonic anhydrase
Key features and challenges:
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (CAI)-based compounds are being developed as a novel antimicrobial strategy targeting Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Building on prior findings that FDA-approved carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as acetazolamide and ethoxzolamide exhibit clinically relevant in vitro activity against N. gonorrhoeae, this program focuses on validating gonococcal carbonic anhydrase (NgCA) as a therapeutic target. Mechanistic studies have demonstrated that these molecules inhibit NgCA, impairing essential bacterial metabolic processes. Importantly, CAIs and related analogues appear to have limited activity against commensal bacteria, potentially reducing the risk of antibiotic-associated dysbiosis.
The current research program aims to optimize CAI-based analogues using structure-based drug design to enhance potency and improve permeability across the Gram-negative bacterial membrane (https://reporter.nih.gov/search/E8Hs8cwDCEuBpcp2k_QFWg/project-details/10683068). 
Compounds are being evaluated in in vitro antimicrobial assays, with prioritized candidates advancing to pharmacokinetic (PK) and pharmacologic profiling. Lead molecules will then be assessed for in vivo efficacy in murine gonorrhea models, alongside safety and PK studies to support selection of a preclinical development candidate and future investigational new drug–enabling activities.
Key challenges include demonstrating durable efficacy against drug-resistant gonococcal strains, ensuring adequate intracellular penetration, and confirming safety and selectivity in vivo. As this approach targets a bacterial metabolic enzyme distinct from conventional antibiotic targets, resistance development pathways and combination therapy potential will require further evaluation. Regulatory advancement will depend on successful translation from preclinical validation to human clinical studies.
Overall, CAI-based inhibitors represent a mechanistically novel, host-sparing antimicrobial strategy targeting gonococcal carbonic anhydrase. Continued lead optimization and preclinical validation will determine their potential as future therapeutics for drug-resistant gonorrhea.

Name: CATD-3
Developers: ICMR-National Institute of Virology
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of CHIKV infection
Target:
CHIKV non-structural proteins:
-nsP4 RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp).
-nsP2 helicase.
-nsP1 methyltransferase (moderate affinity).
Mechanism of action:
-Does not block entry, but inhibits CHIKV replication in the post-entry stage.
-Binds nsP4 RdRp (ΔG −13.2 kcal/mol), forming stable interactions with catalytic Asp350 and other palm domain residues → disrupts viral RNA synthesis.
-Also interacts with nsP2 helicase (Thr233, Asp235, Phe286) and nsP1 methyltransferase, potentially impairing unwinding and 5′ capping.
-Likely interferes with early replication complex formation (1–3 h post infection).
Key features and challenges:
1. In vitro efficacy:
-Vero cells: IC₅₀ = 11.49 µM, Selectivity Index (SI) = 13.39.
-≥1 log₁₀ viral titer reduction at 50 µM (post-infection treatment).
-Similar efficacy confirmed in HeLa cells (IC₅₀ ~12.5 µM effective dose).
2. Cytotoxicity: CC₅₀ ~153 µM (Vero cells), 35 µM (HeLa cells).
3. Docking/MD: strongest binding to nsP4 RdRp; maintained stable interactions (RMSD ~2.5 Å in 100 ns MD).
4. ADMET: obeys Lipinski’s rule of five, good GI absorption, favorable solubility, low predicted toxicity.
Recent updates:
2025: 
-First report of CATD-3’s anti-CHIKV effect; showed post-entry inhibition and specific targeting of viral RdRp and helicase.
-Identified as the most potent among 10 cinnamic acid derivatives tested.
-Authors recommend further in vivo validation and structural optimization.

Name: CAd3-Marburg vaccine
Developers: Sabin Vaccine Institute; US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease (NIAID); GlaxoSmithKline (GSK); Texas Biomedical Research Institute (Texas Biomed); ReiThera Srl
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against Marburg virus infection

05/08/2025 JI:

Name: CBP-4888 (sFlt-1-targeting siRNA)
Developers: Sanofi; McGill University; University of Massachusetts Medical School (including MassBiologics); Charite - University Medicine Berlin, Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin; Silence Therapeutics (including Atugen AG); Sumitomo Dainippon Pharma Co., Ltd.; Comanche Biopharma
Indication: Treatment of preeclampsia
Target: sFlt-1; Endothelin A receptor; Protein kinase N3; Vascular endothelial growth factor receptor-1
Mechanism of action: RNA interference; Vascular endothelial growth factor receptor-1 antagonists; Endothelin A receptor antagonists; Protein kinase N3 inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1 or sVEGFR-1) is a tyrosine kinase protein with antiangiogenic properties. A non-membrane associated splice variant of VEGF receptor 1 (Flt-1), sFlt-1 acts as a decoy receptor and binds the angiogenic factors VEGF (vascular endothelial growth factor) and PlGF (placental growth factor), reducing blood vessel growth through reduction of free VEGF and PlGF concentrations. sFlt-1 is commonly overexpressed in the pathogenesis and presentation of preeclampsia.
Preeclampsia is most probably multifactorial and caused by several placental dysfunctions. As an important mediator, sFlt-1 is induced in the placenta and in the serum of preeclamptic women, acting as a decoy receptor for placenta like growth factors and inducing an antiangiogenic balance. Therefore, RNAi mediated gene specific silencing could represent a new therapeutic option in preeclampsia management. Preclinical studies using rats showed through biodistribution experiments that this biologic was able to decrease sFlt-1 mRNA expression in placenta, especially in the labyrinth layer. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30451990/)
Silence Therapeutics are developing stabilised short (small) interfering RNA (siRNA) molecules, called AtuRNAi Silence's double-stranded siRNA induce post-transcriptional silencing of specific genes in cells. The siRNA molecules are stabilised against degradation by serum nucleases and are identical to human nucleotides thereby reducing the risk of unwanted adverse effects. The company also developed a liposomal-based delivery system, called AtuPLEX, that is designed to deliver these siRNA molecules via systemic circulation to sites of disease. The potency of the siRNA molecules have been demonstrated to be 10- to 100-fold better than antisense oligonucleotides. 
Comanche Biopharma are also developing conjugated siRNA compounds that accumulate in the placenta where they selectively down-regulate multiple mRNA isoforms coding for sFLT-1 while leaving important angiogenic factors unaffected. In addition, an NIH funded a research project on an siRNA-based candidate (sFLT1-i13-2283/sFLT1-i15a-2519) by the University of Massachusetts Medical School (https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/9942489) is expected to completed on 30 June 2021.
Pharmacodynamics data from a preclinical study in preclampsia presented at the Council on Hypertension Scientific Session 2017 (AHA-ASH-2017) for AtuPLEX - sFlt-1-specific siRNA formulated with the liposomal siRNA delivery system. (Abstract: https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/hyp.70.suppl_1.p310)
In May 2023, phase 1 trials commenced to evaluate the safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of  siRNA-based candidate - now called CBP-4888 - in Healthy, Non-Pregnant Female Subjects. (https://www.clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT05881993)
Recent updates:
In August 2023, Comanche Biopharma received the Fast Track designation (FTD) from the US FDA for CBP 4888 for the treatment of preeclampsia (sFlt1-mediated pre-term preeclampsia).

In January 2024, Comanche Biopharma anticipate to initiate clinical trials for CBP 4888 for preeclampsia, later in 2024

Name: CCHA-VLP

Mechanism of action: Induces both humoral (IgG, mucosal IgA) and cellular (IFN-γ secreting T cells) immunity; HA provides subtype-specific neutralization; M2 and NA stalk broaden cross-protection; IL-12 enhances T-cell response.

Name: CCHF mAb, Mapp Biopharmaceutical

Indication: Indicated as an immunotherapeutic for post-infection of Crimean-Congo Haemorrhagic Fever (CCHF) caused by Crimean-Congo Haemorrhagic Fever virus

Name: CCHF multi-epitope vaccine (CTL+HTL/TLR adjuvant)

Name: CCHF virus-like replicon particle (VRP) vaccine
Developers: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC); University of Georgia (UGA), (including the Center for Vaccines and Immunology)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against CCHF

Key features and challenges:
For VRP production, the plasmid containing the full-length M genome segment (pT7-M) is replaced with a plasmid producing
the codon-optimized GPC of the Oman-1998 strain (pCAGGS-GPC-Oman, Figure 1(a)). Absence of the M segment in VRP particles limits their replication to a single cycle. To maximize the probability of generating strong immunity to the VRPs, GPC-Oman was selected because it was previously found to improve the capacity of CCHF virus-like particles to enter specialized antigen-presenting cells like human macrophages

Name: CCHFV-MAfg09
Developers: US Army Medical Research Institute of Infectious Diseases (USAMRIID)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against CCHF
Target: CCHFV M segment proteins: structural glycoproteins (Gn and Gc) and the non-structural glycoprotein GP38.
Mechanism of action:

-CD8⁺ T-cell–dependent protection demonstrated in knockout mouse models (µMT, TCRα/β⁻/⁻, CD8⁻/⁻)

Name: CD40.HIVRI.Env (VRIPRO) + Poly-ICLC-adjuvant

Name: CD40.NiV
Developers: Inserm Transfert

-Induced high and durable neutralizing antibody titers in mice and hamsters with a single low dose.
