Name: CD44/FKBPL strip-based lateral flow assay
Developers: University of Technology Sydney; University of Melbourne, Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology
Indication: Detection of PE in the first trimester
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Target: Plasma levels of FKBPL and CD44 as biomarkers of PE
Mechanism of action: Strip-based LFA - biomarker test
Key features and challenges:
A point-of-care strip-based lateral flow assay (LFA) is under development by researchers at the University of Technology Sydney to predict and support diagnosis of preeclampsia using the CD44/FKBPL biomarker ratio.
FK506-binding protein-like (FKBPL) is a divergent member of the immunophilin protein family involved in angiogenesis, inflammation, and vascular development. Dysregulation of angiogenic pathways has been implicated in the pathogenesis of preeclampsia. A 2021 study demonstrated that the ratio of FKBPL to its target protein CD44 in maternal plasma at 20 weeks’ gestation could predict the risk of preeclampsia, particularly late-onset preeclampsia, and assist in diagnosis.
(Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32617576/)
Building on this finding, researchers developed a strip-based LFA incorporating lanthanide-doped upconversion nanoparticles conjugated to specific antibodies to detect CD44 and FKBPL. In validation studies, the CD44/FKBPL ratio demonstrated predictive capability, with a proposed cut-off value of 1.24 yielding a positive predictive value of 100% and a negative predictive value of 91%. The estimated cost of the assay was approximately USD 2 per strip, with an associated reader costing under USD 100, although the reader requires a 980 nm laser and supporting optical system.
(Source: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ange.202301193)
Overall, the CD44/FKBPL strip-based assay represents a low-cost, point-of-care diagnostic approach aimed at improving early identification of women at risk of preeclampsia. Further large-scale validation studies are required to confirm diagnostic performance across diverse populations and clinical settings.

Name: CD4BS CH505M5 Pr-NP1, CH505 TF chTrimer, lipid nanoparticles or 3M-052-AF + alum adjuvant
Developers: US National Institutes of Health (NIH); Department of Health and Human Services (US); Duke University; Access to Advanced Health Institute (AAHI) (formerly Infectious Disease Research Institute IDRI)
Indication: Indicated for the prevention of HIV-1 infection

Name: CD81 and CLDN1 inhibitors
Developers: Jazan University
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of hepatitis C infection.
Mechanism of action: Binds to CD81 and CLDN1 receptors to inhibit viral entry.
Key features and challenges:
Abstract
The hepatitis C virus (HCV), which causes hepatitis C, is a viral infection that damages the liver and causes inflammation in the liver. New potentially effective antiviral drugs are required for its treatment owing to various issues associated with the existing medications, including moderate to severe adverse effects, higher costs, and the emergence of drug-resistant strains. The objective of the current study was to utilize computational techniques to assess the anti-HCV efficacy of certain phytochemicals against tetraspanin (CD81) and claudin 1 (CLDN1) entry proteins. A 200-nanosecond molecular dynamics (MD) simulation was employed to examine the stability of the lead-protein complexes. Free binding energy and molecular docking calculations were conducted utilizing MM/GBSA method, and the selectivity of hit compounds for CD81 and CLDN1 was determined. Five significant CD81 and CLDN1 inhibitors were identified: Petasiphenone, Silibinin, Tanshinone IIA, Taxifolin, and Topaquinone. The MM/GBSA analysis of the compounds revealed high free binding energies. All the identified compounds were stable within the CD81 and CLDN1 binding pockets. This study indicated the promising inhibitory potential of the identified compounds against CD81 and CLDN1 receptors and might develop into potential viral entry inhibitors. However, to validate the chemotherapeutic capabilities of the discovered leads extensive preclinical research is required (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07391102.2023.2263588).

Name: CEU/MB and B-flow/M-mode ultrasonography - PE
Developers: University of Maryland, Baltimore (including CVD)
Indication: Prediction of PE
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: volume/lumenal area of and flow within the uterine spiral arteries
Mechanism of action: Point-of-care nucleic acid amplification test that detects pathogen-specific genetic sequences to diagnose gonorrhea.
Key features and challenges:
Contrast-enhanced ultrasonography (CEU)/microbubble (MB) imaging is used to assess blood flow diagnostically in men and non-pregnant women, but currently cannot be performed in pregnant women carrying to term. Researchers at the University of Maryland Baltimore proposed that CEU/MB could provide a real-time acoustic snapshot of the volume/lumenal area of and flow within the uterine spiral arteries as structural and functional indices of uterine artery remodelling, which underlies IUGR, PTL/PTB and PE/E. Ultrasound B-flow is a 4D non-Doppler technology and researchers superimposed M-mode on B-flow to quantify, with exceptional spatial resolution, uterine spiral artery diameter and mural distensibility (https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/9426883). 
 
Researchers at the University of Maryland Baltimore aimed to establish CEU/MB and B-flow/M-mode as novel prototypes to quantify uterine spiral artery volume/flow and diameter/distensibility, respectively, as complementary structural and functional indices of uterine artery remodelling across normal and abnormal pregnancy. They firstly tested the hypothesis that CEU/MB and B- flow/M-mode provided state-of-the-art approaches to quantify uterine spinal artery perfusion and diameter/distensibility (as indices of uterine artery remodelling) in baboons untreated or treated with E2, which suppresses uterine artery remodelling. Maternal, placental, and fetal physiological parameters were ascertained in baboons after CEU/MB to establish safety standards for the application of CEU/MB to human pregnancy. Secondly, they tested the hypothesis that ultrasound B-flow/M-mode would provide a novel method to quantify uterine spiral artery diameter/distensibility, as structural and functional indices of uterine artery remodelling, across normal pregnancy and as an early marker of abnormal human pregnancy. Completion of this study is expected to establish innovative imaging methods that will lead to more effective prediction and management of adverse human pregnancy arising from defective UAR. Results demonstrated that B-flow/STIC M-mode ultrasonography provides a novel real-time non-invasive method to detect a decrease in uterine spiral artery luminal diameter and volume flow during the cardiac cycle, reflecting decreased distensibility of the vessel wall, in the first trimester in a non-human primate model of defective SAR (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34358371/).

Name: CHIK E1 E2 CP vaccine
Developers: Xiangya Hospital
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against CHIKV infection
Target: CHIKV structural proteins (E1, E2 glycoproteins, capsid protein)
Mechanism of action: Combines predicted cytotoxic T-lymphocyte (CTL), helper T-cell (HTL), and linear B-cell epitopes from CHIKV E1, E2, and capsid proteins with β-defensin adjuvant; designed to bind strongly to MHC alleles and Toll-like receptors (TLR3/TLR8), thereby eliciting both cellular and humoral immune responses.
Key features and challenges:
-Constructed with 6 CTL, 6 HTL, and 16 B-cell epitopes linked by suitable spacers.
-Designed to cover ~99.9% of global population based on MHC allele distribution.
-In silico docking and molecular dynamics simulations confirmed stable interactions with MHC alleles and TLR3.
-Immune simulations predicted strong induction of IgM/IgG antibodies, B-cell memory, T-cell responses, and cytokines (IFN-γ, IL-2, IL-10).
-Codon-optimized sequence cloned into E. coli K12 expression vector (Pet28a+).
-Challenges: Still only computational; no in vitro or in vivo validation yet. Translation to practical vaccine development will require experimental testing and safety validation.
Recent updates: As of Sept 2025, no published in vitro or animal model validation yet. Other epitope-based CHIKV vaccines are also under investigation; this candidate remains a computationally proposed construct.

-Removal of N-linked glycosylation sites alters antigen processing and epitope exposure, modulating antibody vs T-cell response balance.
Key features and challenges:
1. Four DNA constructs tested in mice:
-Full-length E → highest IgG and neutralizing antibody titers.
-E I/IIΔGln (truncated, non-glycosylated) → strongest T-cell cytokine responses (IFN-γ, IL-6).
2. PRNT assays showed protective neutralizing activity in sera from vaccinated mice.
3. Demonstrated that N-linked glycosylation can dampen T-cell responses while enhancing antibody titers.

Recent updates:
Sept 2024:

-Provides rationale for designing non-glycosylated E I/II constructs to enhance T-cell responses.
Suggests glycan removal may unmask epitopes useful for universal CHIKV vaccine strategies.

Name: CHIKV V5040 iDNA Vaccine

Name: CITED2 and PRX4
Developers: Children’s Hospital of Shanxi Province
Indication: Indicated for the diagnosis of Preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for research use only
Mechanism of action: ELISA based assay to quantify CITED2 and PRX4
Key features and challenges: This study aims to investigate the differential level of CITED2 and PRX4 in the serum of preeclampsia (PE) patients and to explore their clinical value in PE diagnosis, severity assessment, and pregnancy outcomes. A total of 110 singleton pregnant women with PE were included, consisting of 57 cases of mild PE and 53 cases of severe PE, with 110 healthy singleton pregnant women enrolled as the normal control. The baseline clinical characteristics were analyzed using chi-square test and independent samples t-test. CITED2 and PRX4 concentrations were measured by ELISA and their diagnostic efficacy for PE was evaluated through ROC curves. Multivariate logistic regression analysis was conducted to identify factors associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes in PE patients. Compared to the healthy group, CITED2 serum levels in PE patients were significantly increased, while PRX4 levels were significantly decreased. CITED2 and PRX4 can diagnose PE, distinguish between mild and severe PE, and be associate with adverse pregnancy outcomes in PE patients. The diagnostic efficacy was better when CITED2 and PRX4 were combined. The serum levels of CITED2 were further elevated and PRX4 levels were further reduced in patients with severe PE and adverse pregnancy outcomes. CITED2 was an independent risk factor and PRX4 was a protective factor for adverse pregnancy outcomes in PE patients. In conclusion, CITED2 and PRX4 can diagnose PE, assess PE severity, and are associated with PE outcomes.

Name: CMP-nonulosonates
Developers: University of Massachusetts Medical School (including MassBiologics)
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Incorporation of CMP-nonulosonates into Ng lipooligosaccharide renders bacteria susceptible to complement and CAMPs
Key features and challenges:
CMP-nonulosonates (CMP-NulOs) are investigational host-targeted agents designed to disrupt immune evasion mechanisms of Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Gonococci evade host immunity by sialylating their lipooligosaccharide (LOS) using host-derived CMP-Neu5Ac via the surface LOS sialyltransferase (Lst). LOS sialylation enhances resistance to complement-mediated killing and cationic antimicrobial peptides (CAMPs). It has been demonstrated that when gonococci are supplied with alternative CMP-NulOs—such as CMP-legionaminic acid (CMP-Leg5,7Ac2) and CMP-ketodeoxynonulosonate (CMP-Kdn)—these analogues are incorporated into LOS, rendering bacteria more susceptible to complement and CAMPs.
Preclinical studies have shown that incorporation of CMP-NulOs into gonococcal LOS significantly shortens the duration and burden of vaginal colonization in murine models. Cathelicidin, a CAMP, was identified as a key mediator of the mechanism of action. Efficacy, safety, and stability evaluations have supported CMP-Leg5,7Ac2 and CMP-Kdn as promising candidates for intravaginal delivery to prevent gonococcal acquisition (https://reporter.nih.gov/search/9WTg1xKrUEODsrTLyN0iag/project-details/10216069).
The development program includes: (1) production, pharmacoeconomic analysis, and scale-up assessment of CMP-NulOs; (2) investigation of safety and efficacy determinants; (3) formulation into intravaginal rings (IVRs) with in vitro and ovine pharmacokinetic studies, including evaluation of vaginal microbiota biofilm formation; (4) validation of activity against genetically and geographically diverse gonococcal isolates; and (5) regulatory preparation culminating in a pre-IND meeting with the U.S. FDA.
Key challenges include translation of murine efficacy to human prevention, optimization of intravaginal delivery systems, assessment of long-term safety and mucosal tolerability, and evaluation of impact on the vaginal microbiome. As a prophylactic strategy rather than a conventional antibiotic, demonstration of consistent protection across diverse strains and populations will be critical for advancement.
Overall, CMP-nonulosonates represent a novel immune-modulating, anti-virulence approach aimed at preventing gonorrhea acquisition by reversing LOS-mediated immune evasion. Continued preclinical optimization and regulatory engagement will determine readiness for first-in-human evaluation.

Name: CMS-D002
Developers: China Medial System
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of endometriosis
Mechanism of action: gonadotropin-releasing hormone receptor antagonist
Key features and challenges:
CMS-D002 is a small molecule antagonist of the gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) receptor. GnRH, a hormone produced by the hypothalamus, regulates hormone release in the reproductive system. By competing with endogenous GnRH for binding to the GnRH receptor on the pituitary gland, CMS-D002 blocks the pituitary gonadal axis, reducing the release of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH). This inhibition lowers the secretion of estrogen, progesterone, and testosterone, potentially alleviating sex hormone-related conditions. Demonstrating strong efficacy and safety in preclinical trials, CMS-D002 shows promise for treating endometriosis. (https://web.cms.net.cn/en/2024/02/ind-approvals-two-of-cmss-innovative-drugs-highly-selective-tyk2-inhibitor-cms-d001-and-gnrh-receptor-antagonist-cms-d002-are-approved-for-drug-clinical-trials/)
A 2024 registered CT investigates the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of CMS-D002 for endometriosis. The study is structured in five parts. TParts 1 and 2 focus on evaluating the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics (PK), pharmacodynamics (PD), and the effect on the cardiac QT interval of single or multiple oral doses of CMS-D002. Part-3 (Food Effect Study) investigates how food impacts the exposure to CMS-D002 and its safety under fasting and fed conditions. Part-4 (Combination with ABT Study) assesses the effect of daily CMS-D002 with ABT on sex hormone levels over four weeks, along with safety, tolerability, and the relationship between PK and PD. Lastly, Part-5 (Metabolism and Excretion Study) examines the extent of CMS-D002 and its metabolites excreted in urine and feces after a single dose, along with its PK and safety profile. (https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=225560)

Name: CRH antagonists
Developers: Sur180 Therapeutics
Indication: Indicated for the management of tissue migration and lesions in endometriosis
Mechanism of action: Corticotropin-releasing hormone antagonist
Key features and challenges:
Corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) is a central regulator of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis and is released in response to stress. Beyond its endocrine role, CRH also acts locally in peripheral tissues, including the uterus and gastrointestinal tract, through activation of CRH receptor 1 (CRHR1) and CRH receptor 2 (CRHR2). Dysregulated stress signaling and neuroinflammation have been implicated in endometriosis pathophysiology, particularly in relation to lesion progression, inflammation, and pain sensitization.
CRH receptor antagonists have primarily been investigated for psychiatric and stress-related disorders such as depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder. More recently, preclinical research has explored CRHR1 blockade in abdominal and pelvic inflammatory diseases, including irritable bowel syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease, enteritis, and endometriosis, demonstrating beneficial effects of CRHR1 inhibition on inflammatory pathways (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0264909).
A 2018 preclinical study using the CRHR1 antagonist antalarmin in a rat model of endometriosis reported a significant reduction in both the size and number of endometriotic lesions following receptor blockade (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30427841/). These findings suggest that CRH signaling contributes to lesion establishment and progression, and that CRHR1 inhibition may represent a novel non-hormonal therapeutic strategy.
Sur180 Therapeutics is currently developing an undisclosed CRHR1 antagonist for endometriosis. The program builds on prior evidence demonstrating lesion reduction and symptom improvement with CRHR1 blockade. The candidate compound, previously tested in clinical trials for mood and gastrointestinal disorders, is being evaluated in preclinical rat models to assess efficacy in reducing endometriotic lesion development and to determine its impact on hormonal and inflammatory pathways (https://reporter.nih.gov/search/N27n6Ho1b0SXQi4tl7DGUw/project-details/10746682
; https://reporter.nih.gov/search/N27n6Ho1b0SXQi4tl7DGUw/project-details/10602801
; https://legacy.www.sbir.gov/node/2300729).
Key challenges include the early preclinical stage of development for endometriosis, with no published human clinical trial data in this indication. The complexity of stress–immune–endocrine interactions in endometriosis requires careful mechanistic validation. Long-term safety, potential neuropsychiatric effects, and reproductive safety must be evaluated. While CRHR1 antagonists offer a promising non-hormonal and potentially disease-modifying approach, further translational and clinical research is necessary to establish efficacy and safety in women with endometriosis.

Name: CT-001
Developers: Coagulant Therapeutics
Indication: Indicated for the treatment or control of postpartum haemorrhage.
Mechanism of action: Promoting coagulation via Factor VIIa and Factor X-mediated pathways
Key features and challenges:
CT-001 is a next-generation recombinant activated factor VIIa (FVIIa) variant under development by Coagulant Therapeutics, licensed from Bayer, for the treatment of acute bleeding associated with postpartum haemorrhage (PPH). The molecule was originally developed using Maxygen’s MolecularBreeding platform technology. CT-001 incorporates amino acid substitutions (P10Q and K32E) designed to increase affinity for negatively charged phospholipid surfaces at sites of vascular injury. It is further engineered with four desialylated N-glycans to promote more rapid hepatic clearance. These modifications aim to enhance localization to active bleeding sites, improve coagulation efficacy, and reduce systemic thrombotic risk compared with conventional recombinant FVIIa (rFVIIa). Preclinical data suggest that this engineered FVIIa variant may demonstrate improved safety and hemostatic activity relative to standard rFVIIa (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/rth2.12530).
In January 2022, CT-001 (human recombinant factor VIIa variant) received Orphan Drug Designation from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of postpartum haemorrhage. In February 2023, Coagulant Therapeutics reported enhanced hemostatic activity in ex vivo peripartum blood samples. A Phase I clinical trial in severe PPH was planned to commence in mid-2023; however, no further public updates on trial initiation or results have been reported (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800069371).
Key challenges include the absence of published clinical trial data in humans with PPH, uncertainty regarding development timelines, and potential safety considerations inherent to procoagulant therapies. While molecular engineering aims to mitigate systemic thrombosis risk, robust clinical evidence will be required to establish safety, efficacy, and positioning relative to existing haemostatic agents.

Name: Cabergoline - Endometriosis
Developers: Pfizer; Kissei Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd.; Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujib Medical University
Indication: Treatment of endometriosis associated pain and angiogenesis
Mechanism of action: Dopamine D2 receptor agonist
Key features and challenges:
Cabergoline is a synthetic ergoline derivative and a potent, long-acting dopamine D2 receptor agonist. It exerts inhibitory effects on prolactin secretion by acting on dopamine receptors in the pituitary gland, making it effective in managing hyperprolactinemia and related disorders. Cabergoline's binding to dopamine D2 receptors also influences motor control, making it useful in treating Parkinson's disease. Additionally, cabergoline has neuroprotective and antioxidant properties due to its free radical scavenging activity. Despite its low affinity for other receptors like dopamine D1, serotonin, and adrenergic receptors, cabergoline remains an effective treatment for conditions such as hyperprolactinemia, Parkinson's disease, and medically necessary suppression of lactation. (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/54746)
Cabergoline has demonstrated therapeutic efficacy across various conditions, leading to its approval in the EU for preventing lactation and treating hyperprolactinemia, as well as in Europe and Japan for Parkinson's disease. Although the drug was in phase III trials for Parkinson's disease in the U.S., development was discontinued. Pharmacia also explored cabergoline's potential for restless legs syndrome in phase II trials, with promising results reported in 2003. Additionally, cabergoline was investigated in phase I trials in Italy for treating breast and pituitary cancers, but development was halted. In a more recent clinical trial, cabergoline is being studied as an adjunct therapy to hormonal treatment for reducing pelvic pain in adolescents and young women with surgically proven endometriosis. (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800000741)
Preclinical studies showed cabergoline reduced endometriotic implant volume and inflammatory markers, with combined treatment (etanercept + cabergoline) showing increased CD25+ and CD5+ cells and a significant decrease in TNF-α staining in the ovary. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S016503782100070X?via%3Dihub)
Other clinical trials investigating the use of cabergoline as a treatment for endometriosis, focusing on its potential as an alternative to current angiogenesis inhibitors are as follows:
A randomized, double-blind study exploring cabergoline as a non-hormonal, non-surgical approach to address endometriosis in adolescents and young women, aiming to offer a safer option given the limitations of current treatments. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03928288)
A phase 3 trial with 72 patients, evaluating the efficacy of cabergoline in reducing pain compared to a control group using a randomized, block design. (https://irct.behdasht.gov.ir/trial/65818)
A phase 3, triple-blind study involving 200 patients, comparing the effects of cabergoline versus placebo on pelvic pain following laparoscopic surgery for endometriosis, with rigorous blinding and randomization procedures to ensure unbiased results. (https://irct.behdasht.gov.ir/trial/75813)
Recent updates: TM 14/12/2025: Trial identified from CT.gov (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06560814).

Name: Cabergoline - PCOS
Developers: Kissei Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd.; Pfizer; Aborihan Pharmaceuticals
Indication: Indicated for the prevention of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome in PCOS fertility treatments.
Mechanism of action: Dopamine D2 receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
Cabergoline is an N-acylurea compound and a long-acting dopamine D2 receptor agonist, derived from ergot. It is primarily used to manage Parkinson's disease and disorders associated with hyperprolactinaemia, acting as a dopamine agonist, antiparkinson drug, and antineoplastic agent. Its potent activity on dopamine D2 receptors makes it effective for treating hyperprolactinemic disorders and Parkinsonian syndrome. (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/54746)

In PCOS, Cabergoline is investigated for its protective effect against ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) in fertility treatments.

A 2024 published cross-sectional study found that the incorporation of cabergoline in fertility treatments did not lead to significant differences in ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome severity, hospitalization rates, or albumin needs between letrozole treated and control groups. Overall, the findings indicate that the combination of cabergoline and letrozole does not effectively reduce the severity of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome in PCOS patient population. (https://kneopen.com/ijrm/article/view/16165/)

Another study registered in 2023 aims to compare two methods of cabergoline administration to prevent ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome in patients with polycystic ovary syndrome. Designed as a randomized, single-blind clinical trial with 200 infertile women at high risk for OHSS, participants will be divided into two groups. Group one will receive 0.5 mg of oral cabergoline daily for 15 days, starting with the GnRH antagonist, while group two will take the same dosage for 8 days, beginning with the GnRH agonist trigger. The main outcome is the incidence of OHSS. (https://irct.behdasht.gov.ir/trial/70355)

Name: Cabergoline - Uterine fibroids
Developers: Kissei Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd.; Iran University of Medical Sciences,
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of heavy menstrual bleeding or pelvic pain related to uterine fibroids, and as part of a pre-surgical regimen to shrink fibroids and reduce symptoms before surgical intervention.
Mechanism of action: Dopamine D2 receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
Cabergoline is an ergot-derived dopamine D2 receptor agonist with potent and long-lasting inhibitory effects on prolactin secretion. It is commonly used in the treatment of hyperprolactinemia and related disorders. By suppressing prolactin production from the pituitary gland; and potentially local prolactin signaling within uterine tissues, cabergoline may influence pathways implicated in uterine fibroid (UF) growth.
Prolactin is expressed in both pituitary and uterine tissues and has been proposed to act as a local growth factor in the myometrium through autocrine and paracrine mechanisms. Elevated prolactin activity may contribute to myoma growth and extracellular matrix accumulation. Prolactin-lowering agents such as cabergoline have therefore been investigated for their potential to inhibit fibroid growth, reduce fibroid size, and improve symptoms including heavy menstrual bleeding and pelvic pain.
www.ejog.org/article/S0301-2115(16)30861-2/pdf
https://www.jimc.ir/article_207816.html
A registered clinical study (IRCT20201209049567N1; trial ID 60616) evaluated cabergoline in comparison with letrozole (an aromatase inhibitor) and triptorelin (a GnRH agonist) for the treatment of uterine myomas. The study aimed to assess relative efficacy in reducing fibroid size and improving clinical symptoms.
https://irct.behdasht.gov.ir/trial/60616
Although preliminary studies suggest that cabergoline may reduce fibroid size and symptom burden, evidence remains limited and largely based on small clinical investigations. Long-term safety, comparative effectiveness against established hormonal therapies, and durability of response require further evaluation. As a dopamine agonist, cabergoline carries potential adverse effects including gastrointestinal symptoms, hypotension, and rare valvular cardiac complications with prolonged use.
Cabergoline represents a hormonally targeted, repurposing candidate for uterine fibroids based on prolactin pathway modulation. While early clinical data suggest possible benefit, robust randomized controlled trials are needed to define its efficacy, safety profile, and role relative to standard fibroid therapies.

Name: Calcium-creatinine ratio
Developers: Tanta University; Ain Shams University; Ahmadi Hospital, Kuwait Oil Company (KOC); Shri B M Patil Medical College

Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories

Key features and challenges:
​Several studies have investigated the potential of urine calcium-creatinine ratio for the screening of preeclampsia. 
 
In a prospective comparative study conducted between 2018 and 2020, the urine calcium-creatinine ratios (CCR) of 246 women were measured: CCR > 0.04 was considered 
negative, while CCR ≤ 0.04 was considered positive. Within the cohort, 86 women developed preeclampsia and 164 had normotensive pregnancies. The calcium-creatinine ratio was found to be significantly lower in the studied PE group (0.04 ±0.16) compared to normotensive controls (0.11 ±0.21). When evaluated as a potential screening test, the calcium-creatinine ratio ≤ 0.04 had 79.3% sensitivity, 96.3% specificity, 91.5% PPV, 90.3% NPV, and 90.7% overall accuracy in predicting PE. This study suggests the use of CCR in spot urine sample for screening and early detection of PE 
(https://anzctr.org.au/Trial/Registration/TrialReview.aspx?ACTRN=12618000497202). 
 
A study in India that began in 2020 is exploring how well a combined model—measuring mean arterial blood pressure, urinary calcium-creatinine ratio, and uterine artery Doppler between 18 and 20 weeks of pregnancy—can predict outcomes. The findings haven’t been released yet. 
(https://www.ctri.nic.in/Clinicaltrials/pmaindet2.php?trialid=41389).

Name: Calcyphosin
Developers: University of Anbar
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for research use only
Mechanism of action: Measures calcyphosin expression or circulating levels to detect cellular signaling alterations associated with PCOS-related metabolic dysfunction.
Key features and challenges:
Calcyphosin (CAPS) is a protein that is involved in regulating calcium signaling and is found in various tissues. It is known to play a role in cellular processes, such as calcium-dependent signaling pathways, that influence cell function, apoptosis, and tissue development. In the context of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), research has suggested that elevated levels of calcyphosin may be linked to the disease, potentially acting as a biomarker for diagnosis.

A study conducted on 100 Iraqi women (60 with PCOS and 40 healthy controls) examined the relationship between lipid profile and calcyphosin A (CAPS) levels. The results revealed significantly higher CAPS levels in women with PCOS compared to healthy controls. Additionally, women with PCOS had elevated levels of total cholesterol, triglycerides, HDL, and VLDL. While no significant changes were observed in other lipid parameters, the study concluded that serum CAPS levels could serve as a novel biomarker for detecting PCOS, potentially aiding in its diagnosis.
(https://www.pnrjournal.com/index.php/home/article/view/719/547)

Approved by the FDA in 2013 for managing type 2 diabetes, it aids blood glucose control alongside diet and exercise. In 2018, it received a second approval to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events in diabetes patients, making it the first oral antidiabetic drug with such an indication.
(https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800026535)

A 2022 randomized controlled trial compared the efficacy and safety of Canagliflozin (CANA) plus Metformin (MET) versus MET monotherapy in overweight and obese women with PCOS. CANA/MET combination therapy showed more significant reductions in total testosterone, glucose, and insulin resistance compared to MET alone, while both treatments were similar in improving menstrual frequency, weight control, and other metabolic parameters. (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/endocrinology/articles/10.3389/fendo.2022.1003238/full)

A 2024 initiated clinical trial examines biomarkers for diagnosing PCOS with NAFLD using advanced chromatography-mass spectrometry. It also assesses Canagliflozin's role in improving treatment outcomes. Fifty non-diabetic PCOS women will receive either Canagliflozin plus Metformin or Metformin alone for three months, with assessments of cardiovascular, metabolic, and liver health. The study aims to identify diagnostic markers and evaluate treatment efficacy and safety. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06256289)

A study commenced in 2022 aims to assess the combined effect of canagliflozin, and metformin on insulin resistance in women with PCOS. The focus is on evaluating its efficacy in managing insulin resistance in non-diabetic PCOS patients, as current evidence on SGLT-2 inhibitors in this population is limited.(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04973891)

A slightly older study commenced in 2020 compares the safety and efficacy of canagliflozin versus metformin in treating insulin resistance (IR) in women with PCOS. Conducted as a randomized, open-label trial, it enrolled 68 women aged 18-45, measuring changes in HOMA-IR and other metabolic, hormonal, and anthropometric outcomes over 12 weeks of treatment. Name: Cananga oil (Ylang-ylang oil)
Developers: The First Hospital of Jilin University
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Salmonella typhimurium infection.
Target: Purine metabolism and the tricarboxylic acid cycle.
Mechanism of action: Disrupts the balance of purine metabolism and the tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA cycle) in Salmonella, interfering with redox processes. This leads to energy metabolic disorders and oxidative stress damage within the bacteria, resulting in bacterial shock, enhanced membrane damage, and ultimately bacterial death.
Key features and challenges:
Cananga oil (CO) is derived from the flowers of the traditional medicinal plant, the ylang-ylang tree. As a traditional antidepressant, CO is commonly utilized in the treatment of various mental disorders including depression, anxiety, and autism. It is also recognized as an efficient antibacterial insecticide, and has been traditionally utilized to combat malaria and acute inflammatory responses resulting from bacterial infections both in vitro and in vivo.
Aim of the study
The objective of this study is to comprehensively investigate the anti-Salmonella activity and mechanism of CO both in vitro and in vivo, with the expectation of providing feasible strategies for exploring new antimicrobial strategies and developing novel drugs.
Methods
The in vitro antibacterial activity of CO was comprehensively analyzed by measuring MIC, MBC, growth curve, time-killing curve, surface motility, biofilm, and Live/dead bacterial staining. The analysis of the chemistry and active ingredients of CO was conducted using GC-MS. To examine the influence of CO on the membrane homeostasis of Salmonella, we conducted utilizing diverse techniques, including ANS, PI, NPN, ONPG, BCECF-AM, DiSC3(5), and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis. In addition, the antibacterial mechanism of CO was analyzed and validated through metabolomics analysis. Finally, a mouse infection model of Salmonella typhimurium was established to evaluate the toxic side effects and therapeutic effects of CO.
Results
The antibacterial effect of CO is the result of the combined action of the main chemical components within its six (palmitic acid, α-linolenic acid, stearic acid, benzyl benzoate, benzyl acetate, and myristic acid). Furthermore, CO disrupts the balance of purine metabolism and the tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA cycle) in Salmonella, interfering with redox processes. This leads to energy metabolic disorders and oxidative stress damage within the bacteria, resulting in bacterial shock, enhanced membrane damage, and ultimately bacterial death. It is worth emphasizing that CO exerts an effective protective influence on Salmonella infection in vivo within a non-toxic concentration range.
Conclusion
The outcomes indicate that CO displays remarkable anti-Salmonella activity both in vitro and in vivo. It triggers bacterial death by disrupting the balance of purine metabolism and the TCA cycle, interfering with the redox process, making it a promising anti-Salmonella medication (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0378874124001636?via%3Dihub).

Unlike tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), which is a psychoactive component with partial agonist activity at cannabinoid receptors, CBD functions mainly as a negative allosteric modulator at the CB1 receptor and affects several other receptor systems, including serotonergic and vanilloid receptors. CBD is available in Canada as Sativex for multiple sclerosis symptoms and Epidiolex in the US for treating rare epilepsies, showing significant clinical improvement in these conditions.

30 patients, split into a CBD group and a placebo group, receiving HempFlex 3000, a natural cannabis oil, with dosages increasing weekly. Name: Carbamazepine
Developers: Griffith University (including the Institute for Glycomics and GRIDD)
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Sodium channel antagonists; Inhibition of gonococcal adherence to cervical cells in patients with therapeutic carbamazepine levels
Key features and challenges:
Carbamazepine is a widely used anticonvulsant indicated for seizure disorders and neuropathic pain, including trigeminal neuralgia. Recent research has explored its potential repositioning as a host-targeted therapy for Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection. Mechanistically, carbamazepine has been shown to block the interaction between gonococcal pili and the I-domain of human complement receptor 3 (CR3), a host–pathogen interaction critical for infection of cervical epithelial cells.
In 2023, preclinical and translational data demonstrated that carbamazepine could clear established N. gonorrhoeae infection in primary human cervical cell models (https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/aac.00968-22).
 The study further quantified carbamazepine concentrations in serum, saliva, and vaginal fluid from 16 women, comparing individuals regularly taking carbamazepine with controls. Detectable levels were found in lower reproductive tract secretions of treated women, and concentrations present in vaginal fluid were sufficient to achieve greater than 99% reduction in viable gonococci within 24 hours in ex vivo cervical infection models. These findings support further investigation of carbamazepine as a host-directed therapeutic strategy for gonococcal cervicitis.
Building on these data, a clinical study registered in 2024 in Australia aims to evaluate the efficacy of oral carbamazepine for uncomplicated cervical N. gonorrhoeae infection in women (ACTRN12624000420549; https://anzctr.org.au/Trial/Registration/TrialReview.aspx?ACTRN=12624000420549). 
The study employs a window-of-opportunity design, enrolling asymptomatic women identified as sexual contacts of confirmed gonorrhea cases and administering carbamazepine while awaiting standard-of-care test results.
Key challenges include confirming clinical efficacy in vivo, ensuring appropriate dosing that balances antimicrobial activity with known neurological adverse effects, and assessing potential drug–drug interactions. As carbamazepine is a systemic medication with established safety considerations, including hepatic enzyme induction and central nervous system effects, careful evaluation in the context of STI treatment is warranted. Additionally, integration into current gonorrhea treatment algorithms, which rely on antibiotics, would require demonstration of either standalone efficacy or synergistic benefit.
Overall, carbamazepine represents a novel host-targeted repurposing strategy with promising preclinical and early translational data against gonococcal cervicitis. Ongoing clinical evaluation will determine whether this established anticonvulsant can be repositioned as an effective treatment option for uncomplicated gonorrhea.

Name: CeO2@RSV
Developers: Wuhan University
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: The synthesised CeO2@RSV nanoparticles mainly possess the following advantages: (1) The chemical bonding of RSV to CeO2 expands the antioxidant activity of the CeO2 nanozymes. (2) Surface-bound RSV may extend the anti-inflammatory capacity and play a congenerous role in dual-directional immunoregulation via macrophage polarization. (3) The CeO2@RSV nanocomposites also exhibited high biocompatibility and drug delivery capabilities to the ovaries and ameliorated ovarian injury in vivo. As a result, the NPs can effectively suppress inflammation response-mediated injury and alleviate endocrine dysfunction
Key features and challenges:
CeO₂@RSV is a nanotherapeutic formulation consisting of octahedral cerium oxide (nanoceria) nanoparticles conjugated with resveratrol, an anti-inflammatory and antioxidant polyphenol. Nanoceria exhibits catalytic redox activity, enabling sustained scavenging of reactive oxygen species (ROS), while resveratrol contributes anti-inflammatory and endocrine-modulating effects. This dual-action design aims to target oxidative stress and inflammation—key pathophysiological contributors in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
PCOS is increasingly recognised as a condition associated with chronic low-grade inflammation and immune dysregulation within the ovarian microenvironment. Macrophages play a central role in this inflammatory milieu, and restoration of M2 phenotype polarization has been proposed as a strategy to reduce ovarian inflammation and support granulosa cell function. Oxidative stress further contributes to follicular dysfunction, endocrine imbalance, and ovarian structural damage.
A 2023 preclinical study evaluated CeO₂@RSV nanoparticles in a dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA)-induced mouse model of PCOS. The formulation demonstrated significant anti-inflammatory and antioxidative effects, alleviating endocrine dysfunction, reducing ovarian inflammation, and improving ovarian histopathology. Treatment promoted granulosa cell proliferation and reduced markers of oxidative damage. The nanoparticles were reported to modulate the proinflammatory ovarian microenvironment, potentially through macrophage phenotype regulation and ROS scavenging.
https://jnanobiotechnology.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12951-023-02182-w
Although the findings suggest promising therapeutic potential, evidence is currently limited to animal models. No human clinical trials have evaluated the safety, pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, or reproductive outcomes associated with CeO₂@RSV in women with PCOS. Nanoparticle-based therapies also raise considerations regarding long-term tissue accumulation, immunogenicity, and translational feasibility.
CeO₂@RSV represents an early-stage, nanotechnology-based investigational approach targeting inflammation and oxidative stress in PCOS. While mechanistically innovative, its role in PCOS management remains experimental pending clinical validation in human populations.

Name: Cell-penetrating peptide
Developers: San Francisco VA Medical Centre
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Inhibiting the biosynthesis of lipid A components with LpxC inhibitors and disrupting outer membrane integrity with CPP may impact bacterial viability and host response to N. gonorrhoeae
Key features and challenges:
Cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) are being investigated as a novel antimicrobial strategy against Neisseria gonorrhoeae, particularly multidrug-resistant (MDR) strains. The therapeutic rationale is based on targeting lipid A, a key component of gonococcal lipooligosaccharide (LOS). Lipid A is a major inducer of cytokine-mediated inflammation and contributes to bacterial survival and infection. Inhibition of lipid A biosynthesis, particularly through targeting LpxC—the enzyme catalyzing the second step of lipid A synthesis—has been shown to be bactericidal in gonococcal strains.
Preclinical research demonstrated that LpxC inhibitors were bactericidal against nine MDR and human challenge strains of N. gonorrhoeae, while also reducing cytokine induction without evident cytotoxicity to human cells. Building on this concept, a 12-amino acid CPP was evaluated for direct membrane-disruptive activity. The CPP penetrated the bacterial membrane and exhibited bactericidal activity against all tested MDR and human challenge strains. Notably, no apparent resistance developed in surviving bacteria upon retreatment, as susceptibility remained unchanged. These findings support the hypothesis that disrupting lipid A biosynthesis and outer membrane integrity can compromise bacterial viability and attenuate host inflammatory responses (https://reporter.nih.gov/search/HMceDDvDcky0PU-xSQWWQg/project-details/10363529).
The research program aims to further validate LpxC inhibition and CPP-mediated membrane disruption as complementary antimicrobial strategies in both in vitro and in vivo models of gonococcal infection. Key development steps include evaluating efficacy in relevant animal models, assessing safety and pharmacokinetics, and determining durability of response against resistant strains.
Key challenges include translating in vitro bactericidal activity into clinically meaningful in vivo efficacy, ensuring selectivity and safety in human tissues, and addressing delivery and stability considerations for peptide-based therapeutics. Regulatory advancement will require comprehensive preclinical validation and demonstration of sustained antimicrobial activity without rapid resistance emergence.
Overall, CPP-based strategies targeting lipid A biosynthesis and membrane integrity represent a mechanistically novel approach to combating multidrug-resistant N. gonorrhoeae. Continued preclinical development will determine their potential as future therapeutic options for resistant gonorrhea.

Name: Cervical consistency index (CCI)
Developers: University of Campania "Luigi Vanvitelli"; Leuven University; University of Barcelona, Universitat de Barcelona
Indication: Prediction of PTL
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Quantifies cervical compressibility using ultrasound before and after compression to assess cervical softening associated with preterm birth.
Key features and challenges:
Cervical consistency index (CCI) has been proposed as a sonographic marker, designed to assess cervical softness as a predictor of PTB. CCI measurement is performed using transvaginal sonography (TVS). In brief, the anteroposterior diameter at rest (AP) is measured as a line perpendicular to the longitudinal axis of the cervix at its midpoint. The same diameter is then measured while applying maximal pressure on the cervix with the TVS probe (APc). The CCI calculation, reflecting the compressibility of the cervix, is the ratio between APc and AP, expressed as a percentage. (https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/uog.21927) 
 
A prospective cohort study of twin pregnancies found CCI performed better than other transvaginal ultrasound markers to predict sPTB < 34+0 in twin gestations, and the best diagnostic accuracy was achieved by combining parity, chorionicity (the type of placentation), CCI, and UCA (uterocervical angle) (https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/9/6/1784). 
A group of researchers from the University of Barcelona has published two studies in 2018 demonstrating predictive potential of CCI for PTB in both low-risk patients (measured at 19 -24 + 6 weeks, AUROC 0.84, and <34 weeks, AUROC 0.87) and high-risk patients (AUROC 0.73 < 37 weeks; 0.68 < 34 weeks).
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28370687/; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29560285/)
 
A clinical trial also tested the cervical consistency index and the cervical length, compared to the cervical length alone in predicting preterm birth. However, results of the study are unknown (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04444206).
Another trial is currently underway in Thailand exploring the potential of CCI for prediction of spontaneous preterm birth in singleton pregnancy.
(https://www.thaiclinicaltrials.org/show/TCTR20230807001)

Mechanism of action: Doppler measurement of ovarian artery resistance to assess altered ovarian perfusion associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
The cervical sliding sign is the ultrasound observation of the anterior cervical lip “sliding” on the posterior lip when gentle pressure is applied. 
A 2019 study from the University of Parma demonstrated that the presence of this sign is associated with reduced cervical length and is an independent predictor of delivery within 7 days (AUROC 0.69) in symptomatic singletons.
(https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/uog.20395)

This was also demonstrated in a 2023 prospective study of singletons (n = 88) with preterm premature rupture of membranes (AUROC 0.75) . 
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35942714/)

A 2022 case-control study performed an elastographic assessment of the cervix in 82 cases of preterm birth (preterm group) and 451 control pregnancies (control group) between the 20th and 37th week of gestation. The anterior cervical lip was divided first into two ("Intern2", "Extern2") and into three sectors ("Intern3", "Middle3", "Extern3"). The tissue deformation pattern after local compression with an ultrasound probe was recorded. The study also distinguished between an irregularly distributed ("Spotting") and homogeneous pattern presentation. Additionally, the presence of a sliding of the anterior against the posterior cervical lip (positive CSS) during compression was evaluated. A logistic regression analysis and the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) were used to estimate the probability of sPTB and to select a prediction model.
The study found that spotting and positive CSS occurred more frequently in the preterm group compared to control group (97.8 vs. 2.2%, p<0.001; 26.8 vs. 4.2%, p<0.001; respectively). The model with the parameters week of gestation at ultrasound examination, Intern3, Middle3 and CSS was calculated as the highest quality model for predicting sPTB. The AUC (Area Under the Curve) was higher for this parameter combination compared to cervical length (CL) (0.926 vs. 0.729).
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35969418/)

Name: Cervical strain elastography
Developers: Capital Medical University; University of Michigan; Intermountain Healthcare (IHC Health Services); Tufts Medical Center; NICHD/NIH/DHHS; Wayne State University
Indication: Prediction of PTL
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: stiffness or elasticity of the cervix
Mechanism of action: Assesses cervical tissue stiffness using ultrasound elastography to detect biomechanical softening associated with early cervical remodeling.
Key features and challenges:
Ultrasound elastography of cervical tissue strain (TS) is a technique that evaluates how stiff or elastic the cervix is. It works by using ultrasound sound waves to see how much the cervical tissue changes shape when pressure is applied. Shifts in cervical stiffness can hint at the risk of preterm labor, premature birth, or other pregnancy issues, and this method may help assess those risks—especially when used alongside measurements like cervical length or other biochemical markers.(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25084285/#full-view-affiliation-1). 

Cervical elastography typically includes measurements like Elasticity Contrast Index (ECI), Cervical Hardness Ratio (CHR), Closed Internal cervical ostium Strain rate (CIS); External cervical ostium strain rate (ES), CIS/ES ratio and Cervical Length (CL).
 
A study explored the link between cervical tissue strain and spontaneous preterm birth. Using ultrasound elastography, researchers measured cervical strain in three anatomical planes: one mid-sagittal, matching the plane for cervical length measurement, and two cross-sectional images at the internal and external cervical os. In each plane, they examined two regions of interest—the endocervix and the entire cervix. Results showed that strain values from all six regions had only a weak correlation with cervical length. However, low strain values at the internal cervical os were tied to a significantly reduced risk of spontaneous preterm delivery before 37 weeks of gestation. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24356388/).

Researchers have looked into how well cervical elastography parameters can predict outcomes compared to cervical length. A 2018 meta-analysis of seven studies involving 1,488 pregnant women found that cervical elastography had a sensitivity of 0.84 (95% CI: 0.68–0.93), a specificity of 0.82 (95% CI: 0.63–0.93), a diagnostic odds ratio of 25 (95% CI: 7–93), and an SROC AUC of 0.90 (95% CI: 0.87–0.93). In contrast, cervical length measurement had an SROC AUC of 0.60 (95% CI: 0.56–0.64), showing cervical elastography outperformed cervical length in diagnostic performance.
(https://www.webofscience.com/wos/woscc/full-record/WOS:000480742900034?SID=EUW1ED0FD3X8WYTZOSgDiBRQjFiIy)

A study running from 2023 to 2028 is aiming to compare the predictive power of the fully quantitative cervical elastography system (Q-CES) with that of cervical length.
(https://reporter.nih.gov/search/yhdsoi8le0-DAZ7Ennuh0Q/project-details/10657884)

Cervical elastography can be combined with cervical length measurement, and in a group of women with a history of PTB, adding the cervical hardness ratio to cervical length improved the ability to predict outcomes.(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2468784723000843?via%3Dihub)

Name: Cervical texture
Developers: University of Barcelona, Universitat de Barcelona; Sant Joan de Déu-Barcelona Children's Hospital (SJD Hospital); Transmural Biotech S. L
Indication: Prediction of preterm birth
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Calculates ratio of total testosterone to sex hormone–binding globulin to estimate biologically active androgen levels.
Key features and challenges:
Ultrasound images of the cervix can be analyzed using a method based on comparison of speckle patterns surrounding each pixel of the image, in order to characterize the cervical microstructure or texture. 
Researchers from the University of Barcelona conducted two prospective cohort studies (2018-2021) to analyze sagittal cervical ultrasound images of patients with singleton pregnancies (n = 310 and n = 633) at 19 + 0-24 + 6 weeks. A learning algorithm was developed to obtain the combination of cervical texture (CTx) features best associated with spontaneous preterm birth (sPTB) based on feature transformation and discriminant analysis regression. The ability of the learning algorithm to predict sPTB was evaluated using a leave-one-out cross-validation technique, which produced a CTx-based score for each participant. Both studies demonstrated that a lower cervical texture score was significantly associated with preterm birth <37 weeks (AUROC 0.77/0.63). The larger study also concluded that predictive potential could be improved by including cervical length.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28508418/ ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33811232/)

Name: Cervical volume
Developers: Brigham and Women's Hospital
Indication: Prediction of PTL
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Ultrasound-based measurement of cervical volume to detect structural shortening and remodeling associated with increased preterm birth risk.
Key features and challenges:
Cervical volume (CV) can be measured through transvaginal ultrasound using the VOCAL Sphere application, starting with an initial sphere volume of 100 cm³ (±2 cm³). A study looking at CV in normal pregnancies across gestation found a moderate correlation between CV and cervical length (CL) over time (r=0.5). Mean (SD) CV for the three gestational age ranges—16+0 to 19+6 weeks, 20+0 to 23+6 weeks, and 24+0 to 27+6 weeks—was 70.9 (23.5), 73.9 (18.3), and 71.7 (11.0) cm³, respectively. CV varied by maternal parity only between 16 and 19.9 weeks (58.9 vs. 77.7 cm³, p=0.04). While CL showed a significant correlation with gestational age (p=0.001), CV did not (p=0.39). Since CV remains stable, researchers suggested it could be a useful complement to CL in evaluating preterm birth risk.
 (https://www.ajog.org/article/S0002-9378(15)02014-1/fulltext). 

However, another study conducted in Istanbul, Turkey, involving 111 women found that cervical volume, along with vascularisation parameters, was not useful in predicting preterm labour.(https://www.degruyter.com/document/doi/10.1515/jpm.2010.087/html)

A new clinical trial was planned to begin in 2024 at Assiut University to assess the predictive value of 3D cervical volume and 3D power Doppler indices in predicting pregnancies at risk of preterm labor.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06190496)

Name: Cervix Monitor device
Developers: Rutgers New Jersey Medical School (NJMS); Advanced Tactile Imaging, Inc.; St. Luke's Hospital and Health Network
Indication: Prediction of PTL
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Mechanism of action: Non-invasive device that continuously monitors cervical or uterine activity signals to detect early physiologic changes preceding preterm labour.
Key features and challenges:
The Cervical Monitor (CM) is a vaginal probe that assesses cervical elasticity (stiffness) and cervical length (effacement) to identify pregnant women at high risk of spontaneous PTL/PTB. The CM was designed as a cart-based device with a medical grade touchscreen computer and a detachable single-use cervix probe. The CM probe contains a tactile array with four sensors and an ultrasound transducer. The ultrasound 3.0 MHz transducer, working in the pulse-echo mode with data acquisition resolution of 20 ns (50 MHz sample rate), measures 3.5 mm in diameter. 

Ten non-pregnant and ten pregnant women were examined with the probe. The study demonstrated clinically acceptable measurement performance and reproducibility. The availability of stress-strain data allowed the computation of cervical elasticity and length. The study concluded that the CM has the potential to provide cervical markers to predict spontaneous preterm delivery. (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7055710/)

Name: Cesarean scar distance to internal cervical os
Developers: University College London Hospital (UCLH)
Indication: Prediction of PTL in women with history of cesarean section
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: Cesarean scar position relative to the internal cervical os
Mechanism of action: Ultrasound measurement of scar proximity to the cervical os to assess structural weakness associated with preterm labour risk.
Key features and challenges:
A study published in 2023 focused on pregnant women with a history of full-dilatation cesarean delivery and investigated cesarean scar parameters (position relative to the internal cervical os) as potential predictors of preterm labour. A multiparameter model based on absolute scar distance from the internal os best predicted spontaneous preterm birth (area under the receiver operating characteristics curve, 0.73; 95% confidence interval, 0.57–0.89; detection rate of 60% for a fixed 25% false positive rate). Models based on the relative anatomic position of the cesarean delivery scar to the internal os and the cesarean delivery scar position with niche parameters (length, depth, and width) best predicted the development of a short cervical length (area under the receiver operating characteristics curve, 0.79 [95% confidence interval, 0.71–0.87]; and 0.81 [95% confidence interval, 0.73–0.89], respectively; detection rate of 73% at a fixed 25% false positive rate). Spontaneous preterm birth was significantly more likely when the cesarean delivery scar was <5.0 mm above or below the internal os (adjusted odds ratio, 6.87; 95% confidence interval, 1.34–58; P =.035).
(https://www.ajogmfm.org/article/S2589-9333(24)00024-7/fulltext)

Name: Cesarean section scar thickness
Developers: University College London Hospital (UCLH); Assiut University
Indication: Prediction of PTL in women with history of cesarean section
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Ultrasound measurement of lower uterine segment or scar thickness to assess myometrial integrity and risk of uterine dehiscence or preterm complications.
Key features and challenges:
Previous studies have associated the formation of a uterine scar with compromised uterine function in future pregnancies. The caesarean section scar can cause problems with placental function and embryo attachment. A study that looked at past pregnancies across multiple studies found that having a scar in the uterus from a previous pregnancy could raise the risk of preterm birth (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30870524/). 
 
A clinical trial (NCT04554745) enrolled women with a history of previous caesarean to assess cervical length and caesarean section scar thickness measured via ultrasound as a predictor for preterm labour. The trial was completed in 2022 but no results have been published yet except for a Master thesis manuscript (http://srv3.eulc.edu.eg/eulc_v5/Libraries/Thesis/BrowseThesisPages.aspx?fn=PublicDrawThesis&BibID=13004417).​

Name: ChAd3-SUDV
Developers: ReiThera Srl; Sabin Vaccine Institute; US National Institutes of Health (NIH); GlaxoSmithKline (GSK); ReiThera SRL
Indication: Indicated for active immunization of individuals aged 6 and up to protect against Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) caused by Sudan Ebola virus

The ChAd3-SUDV vaccine is based on the previously tested GSK ZEBOV vaccine. To date, studies have been performed in non-human primates with challenge using Boniface and Gulu strains of SUDV, which were reported to show protection up to 12 months and to yield a potential candidate correlate of protection. US and Uganda Phase I trials are complete and Phase II trial is planned in Africa. Planned regulatory pathway: animal rule but open to other pathways.
The candidate was included in the Tokomeza ring vaccination trial in Uganda in 2022. This was ranked second as there was considerable clinical trial experience with the company’s ChAd3 vaccine with the Zaire strain involving over 5000 recipients including 600 children plus over 50
recipients of the ChAd3-SUDV strain vaccine. Immunogenicity and challenge studies involving 123 NHPs had been conducted at two independent laboratories. Protection was rapid and durable over 12 months.
Single dose.

Phase 1 trial (NCT04041570): Open-label, dose-escalation (1×10¹⁰ and 1×10¹¹ particle units), 40 healthy adults in Uganda (Makerere University–Walter Reed partnership). Enrolled July–October 2019.

Phase 2 study ongoing: In Uganda and Kenya, conducted by Sabin Vaccine Institute under IAVI protocols. Aims to evaluate safety/tolerability and immunogenicity in the context of recent SUDV outbreaks.

Name: ChAd63-KH
Developers: University of York; University of Edinburgh
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Leishmaniasis
Mechanism of action: Undefined mechanism
Key features and challenges:
Adenovirus-based vaccine ChAd63-KH, which encodes two Leishmania antigens, kinetoplastid membrane protein-11 (K; KMP-11) and hydrophilic acylated surface protein B (H; HASPB), both with prophylactic and therapeutic vaccine efficacy when used as monovalent vaccines in pre-clinical animal models (mouse, hamster, or dog), has been shown to be safe and immunogenic in healthy UK volunteers and in Sudanese patients with persistent PKDL

It was uniquely engineered to reflect repeat domain polymorphisms and arrangements identified from clinical isolates. Recent updates:

Name: ChAd63/MVA ME-TRAP
Developers: European Vaccine Initiative (EVI); University of Oxford (including Oxford University Clinical Research Unit Vietnam (OUCRU), Nuffield Department of Women's and Reproductive Health (NDWRH)); Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI); GlaxoSmithKline (GSK)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against malaria caused by P. falciparum
Target: P. falciparum ME-TRAP (multiple epitope string with thrombospondin-related adhesion protein)
Mechanism of action: Elicits humoral immune response to TRAP protein, inhibiting sporozoites
Key features and challenges:
The University of Oxford investigated in a phase II trial, the efficacy of AdCh63 ME-TRAP + MVA ME-TRAP malaria vaccines versus rabies vaccine in healthy volunteers. The primary endpoint was time to first episode of P. falciparum infection, defined as 2 or more consecutive blood samples confirmed positive by PCR; this was assessed at 18 weeks (NCT01658696). The trial enrolled 120 volunteers in Senegal and was completed in December 2013. Another phase II trial evaluated the efficacy, immunogenicity and safety of AdCh63 ME-TRAP + MVA ME-TRAP malaria vaccines versus rabies vaccine [Verorab®] (controls) in 120 healthy men in Kenya (NCT01666925). It was completed in September 2012.

The University of Oxford is conducting a phase I/II trial to investigate the safety and protective efficacy of concomitant administration of the combination malaria vaccine candidate regimen of RTS,S/AS01B + ChAd63 (GSK 257049) [see RDI profile 800011712] and MVA encoding ME-TRAP and also RTS,S/AS01B alone (NCT02252640; EudraCT 2014-001301-40). The trial began in January 2015. It enrolled 60 patients in the UK and was completed in October 2015.

The University of Oxford has also completed several phase I/II trials of malaria vaccine in the UK. One trial tested the efficacy of two prime-boost malaria vaccine regimens (ChAd63 CS then MVA CS versus AdCh63 ME TRAP then MVA ME TRAP) compared with unvaccinated controls in 36 healthy volunteers in the UK (NCT01623557). The tolerability of two formulations of AdCh63 ME-TRAP or MVA ME-TRAP followed by sporozoite challenge after boost or re-challenged with sporozoite (in protected subjects) or mixture of both formulations followed by sporozoite challenge 3 weeks after last vaccination for prevention of Falciparum malaria, was evaluated in 55 volunteers in the UK (NCT00890760). Another completed trial evaluated the efficacy of 2 different malaria vaccination regimens using the ChAd63 (AdCh63) and MVA vectors encoding ME-TRAP, CS or AMA1 versus an unvaccinated control group to prevent Falciparum malaria in 48 healthy volunteers (NCT01739036). Results demonstrated 50% efficacy in vaccinated individuals.

A completed phase I/II trial evaluated the efficacy, immunogenicity and tolerability of prime boost vaccination with AdCh63 ME-TRAP + MVA ME-TRAP versus rabies vaccine in 730 healthy Burkinabe infants and children (NCT01635647).

Phase I/II trial commenced in 2025 comparing safety and protective efficacy of the whole Plasmodium falciparum sporozoite chemoprophylaxis vaccine candidate PfSPZ-CVac and prime- target vaccination with viral vectored vaccine candidate regime MVA ME-TRAP/ ChAd63 ME-TRAP in malaria-naïve, adults in Germany (NCT05441410).
Recent updates: Phase I/II trial commenced in 2025 (NCT05441410).

Name: ChAd63/MVA PvDBP
Developers: International Centre for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology (ICGEB), India; University of Oxford (including Oxford University Clinical Research Unit Vietnam (OUCRU), Nuffield Department of Women's and Reproductive Health (NDWRH))
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against malaria caused by P. vivax

Name: ChAdOx1 Chik
Developers: University of Oxford (including Oxford University Clinical Research Unit Vietnam (OUCRU), Nuffield Department of Women's and Reproductive Health (NDWRH)); University of Texas Medical Branch, Galveston
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against CHIKV infection
Target: CHIKV nucleocapsid protein (C), glycosylated E proteins (E1, E2, E3) and glycoprotein 6K
Mechanism of action: ChAdOx1-Chik contains the full-length polyprotein of CHIKV, including capsid, 6k, and envelope E3, E2, and E1.  Broadly neutralizing antibodies against the four CHIKV lineages were found in all participants as early as 2 weeks after vaccination
Key features and challenges: ChAdOx1 Chik is a chimpanzee adenoviral vector vaccine expressing the CHIKV structural proteins: Capsid, E3, E2, 6 K, and E1. Previous studies have shown, by transmission electron microscopy, that expression of the CHIKV structural cassette in mammalian cells leads to the formation of virus-like particles (VLPs) that resemble wild-type CHIKV particles15. This suggests that vaccination with ChAdOx1 Chik can induce the formation of CHIKV VLPs, which mimic the tridimensional antigen structure of CHIKV particles released during CHIKV infections.
Recent updates:
21/07/2025: No updates since the trial ended in 2019.

Safety and Immunogenicity of a Candidate CHIKV Vaccine (CHIK001)/ NCT03590392, was a phase I dose escalation study to assess the safety and immunogenicity of the candidate vaccine ChAdOx1 Chik in healthy volunteers. Start date: 2018-07-31, ended: 2019-09-30.  In summary, ChAdOx1 Chik showed excellent safety, tolerability and 100% PRNT50 seroconversion after a single dose.

Name: ChAdOx1 Lassa
Developers: University of Oxford (including Oxford University Clinical Research Unit Vietnam (OUCRU), Nuffield Department of Women's and Reproductive Health (NDWRH)); Janssen Vaccines & Prevention B.V.
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against LASV infection
Key features and challenges: This vaccine comprises of proprietary chimpanzee adenovirus vector platform (ChAdOx1) expressing the Josiah strain LASV GPC: ChAdOX1- Lassa-GP, this vector is derived from chimpanzee adenovirus Y25 (Purushotham et al., 2019). ChAdOx1-vectored Lassa fever vaccine encodes the full-length Josiah strain LASV GPC sequence (ChAdOx1-Lassa-GPC) and protective efficacy was seen after one single dose was given to guinea pigs (Fischer et al., 2021). The vaccine was developed by the University of Oxford and Janssen Vaccines & Prevention B.V. and is being funded by CEPI (Purushotham et al., 2019).
Recent updates: A Phase 1 first-in-human trial of ChAdOx1 LassaJ (ISRCTN16084957) is planned or has recently begun in the UK, targeting safety, tolerability, and immunogenicity in approximately 51 healthy adult volunteers (ages 18–55), with dose escalation and two doses given 12 weeks apart. Preclinical models (mice and guinea pigs) have demonstrated 100% protection against lethal LASV challenge and strong cellular/humoral immune responses, validating advancement to human evaluation. CEPI has prioritized ChAdOx1 Lassa for further clinical development. Source: https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN16084957

Name: ChAdOx1-HBV
Developers: Vaccitech Limited; University of Oxford (including Oxford University Clinical Research Unit Vietnam (OUCRU), Nuffield Department of Women's and Reproductive Health (NDWRH))
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of chronic HBV infection
Target: Precore (PreC), core, polymerase (Pmut, with 8 point-mutations), preS1, preS2, and surface proteins
Mechanism of action: Stimulate an antibody and mixed CD4+/CD8+ T cell immune response
Key features and challenges:
VTP 300 is a therapeutic viral vaccine being developed by utilizing Vaccitech’s ChAdOx1-MVA prime-boost combination to elicit an immune response against Hepatitis B. It is an antigen insert with multigenic construct based on group C hepatitis B viruses developed in the laboratory at Oxford University. The vaccine regimen consists of Chimpanzee Adenovirus Oxford, ChAdOx1-HBV (the prime). It also has a second non-replicating viral vector, a Modified Vaccinia Ankara (MVA), delivering the same HBV antigens (the boost). The vaccine delivers three full-length HBV antigens to stimulate a vigorous antibody and mixed CD4+/CD8+ T cell immune response. Clinical development is underway in the UK, South Korea, Australia and Taiwan.

The ChAdOx1-MVA platform has demonstrated robust activation of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells (immune cells associated with clearance of HBV infected cells), which are believed to have the potential to lead to a functional cure in combination with current anti-viral therapy and a low-dose checkpoint inhibitor.

Phase II trial commenced in 2022, including trial site in Thailand (NCT05343481).

Name: Chiglitazar
Developers: Affiliated Hospital of Nantong University; Shengjing Hospital of China Medical University; Chipscreen Biosciences
Indication: PCOS insulin resistance, menstrual regulation, glucose homeostasis
Target: Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor delta; Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma
Mechanism of action: Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha agonists; Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor delta agonists; Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma agonists
Key features and challenges:
Chiglitazar is an orally bioavailable, non-thiazolidinedione small molecule and pan-agonist of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARα/δ/γ), developed by Chipscreen Biosciences. By activating all three PPAR isoforms, chiglitazar modulates lipid metabolism, glucose homeostasis, insulin sensitivity, and inflammatory pathways. It has been approved in China for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), frequently in combination with metformin, and is also under clinical development for non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), reflecting its metabolic and potential hepatoprotective profile.
https://adisinsight.springer.com/drugs/800021164
Given the central role of insulin resistance and metabolic dysfunction in many PCOS phenotypes, chiglitazar presents a biologically plausible therapeutic candidate. A clinical trial initiated in 2022 (NCT05760677) is evaluating the efficacy and safety of chiglitazar sodium in women with PCOS and coexisting T2DM. In this randomized study of 142 participants, patients receive lifestyle intervention plus background metabolic therapy (including metformin and orlistat), with comparison between pioglitazone and chiglitazar over three months. Outcomes include changes in body weight, menstrual regularity, and glycaemic control.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05760677
In 2023, another clinical trial (NCT06125587) commenced to directly compare chiglitazar with metformin in women with PCOS, focusing on insulin resistance as a primary endpoint. This study aims to clarify whether pan-PPAR activation offers incremental benefits over standard first-line insulin sensitization.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06125587
Despite promising mechanistic rationale, chiglitazar remains investigational in the PCOS context. Current evidence is limited to early-phase or ongoing trials, with no published large-scale randomized data in PCOS populations. Its approval is currently limited to T2DM in China, and broader regulatory acceptance has not yet occurred. As a PPAR agonist, safety considerations similar to other agents in this class—such as weight changes, edema, cardiovascular considerations, and long-term metabolic safety—require continued evaluation. Additionally, its role relative to established therapies such as metformin or pioglitazone remains to be defined.
Recent updates:

Abstract
In this study, we aimed to evaluate the immunogenic profile of a chimeric DNA-based hepatitis C virus (HCV) vaccine candidate encoding the full-length viral core-E1-E2 (HCV-CE) fragment. The vaccine candidate was designed to uniformly express the HCV genotype 4 core-E1-E2 protein. The recombinant HCV-CE protein was bacterially expressed in C41 (DE3) cells, and then BALB/c mice were immunized with different combinations of DNA/DNA or DNA/protein prime/boost immunizations. The proper construction of our vaccine candidate was confirmed by specific amplification of the encoded fragments and basic local alignment search tool (BLAST) results of the nucleotide sequence, which revealed a high degree of similarity with several HCV serotypes/genotypes. The platform for bacterial expression was optimized to maximize the yield of the purified recombinant HCV-CE protein. The recombinant protein showed high specific antigenicity against the sera of HCV-infected patients according to the ELISA and western blot results. The predicted B- and T-cell epitopes showed high antigenic and interferon-γ (IFN-γ) induction potential, in addition to cross-genotype conservation and population coverage. The mice antisera further demonstrated a remarkable ability to capture 100% of the native viral antigens circulating in the sera of HCV patients, with no cross-reactivity detected in control sera. In conclusion, the proposed HCV vaccination strategy demonstrated promising potential regarding its safety, immunogenicity, and population coverage (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38995715/).

Key features and challenges:
Chlorhexidine was developed in the UK by Imperial Chemical Industries in the early 1950s and was introduced to the US in the 1970s. Chlorhexidine is a broad-spectrum antimicrobial biguanide used as a topical antiseptic and in dental practice for the treatment of inflammatory dental conditions caused by microorganisms. It is one of the most common skin and mucous membrane antiseptic agents in use today. The molecule itself is a cationic bis-guanide consisting of two 4-chlorophenyl rings and two biguanide groups joined by a central hexamethylene chain. Topical chlorhexidine for disinfection, as well as oral rinses for dental use, carries activity against a broad range of pathogens including bacteria, yeasts, and viruses. 

The FDA withdrew its approval for the use of chlorhexidine gluconate topical tincture 0.5%, due to a significant number of reports concerning chemical and thermal burns associated with the use of this product. Other formulations of chlorhexidine continue to be available.

A clinical study evaluating the efficacy of a universal strategy of primary prevention of preterm birth using intravaginal chlorhexidine (CLX) applied before 16 weeks was completed in 2023.
