Name: Chloroquine/Hydroxychloroquine - PE/E
Developers: Assiut University; Precision Nanosystems, Inc.; VG Life Sciences Inc. (formerly Viral Genetics); APT Pharmaceuticals Inc
Indication: Prevention or treatment of preeclampsia through suppression of inflammatory responses
Mechanism of action: Suppression of cytokine production and protection against oxidative stress
Key features and challenges:
Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine are antimalarial agents with immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory properties. Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ), a derivative of chloroquine, has been widely used in the management of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and rheumatoid arthritis and was approved for medical use in the United States in 1955. In addition to antimalarial activity, hydroxychloroquine suppresses pro-inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), and inhibits NADPH oxidase (NOX) activity, thereby reducing oxidative stress.
Preclinical and translational evidence suggests that these mechanisms may be relevant to the pathophysiology of preeclampsia (PE), which involves endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and oxidative stress. A 2017 review highlighted the potential of antimalarials, particularly hydroxychloroquine, as a novel therapeutic class for prevention and treatment of preeclampsia (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28142291/
). Given its established safety profile in pregnant women with SLE and rheumatoid arthritis, hydroxychloroquine is considered relatively safe in pregnancy at therapeutic doses. However, overdose—although rare—can be severe or fatal.
A clinical trial initiated in 2021 (NCT04755322) is investigating the efficacy of hydroxychloroquine in the treatment of preeclampsia, with intrauterine growth restriction included as an outcome measure. The trial is currently recruiting.
Key challenges include limited direct clinical evidence supporting efficacy in preeclampsia, uncertainty regarding optimal timing and dosing in non-autoimmune populations, and the need to demonstrate meaningful improvement in maternal and perinatal outcomes beyond blood pressure control. Robust randomized controlled trial data will be necessary to determine whether hydroxychloroquine can be safely and effectively repurposed for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.

Key features and challenges:
Chloroquine is an aminoquinolone derivative first developed in the 1940s for the treatment of malaria. Chloroquine and its derivative hydroxychloroquine have since been repurposed for the treatment of a number of other conditions including HIV, systemic lupus erythematosus, and rheumatoid arthritis.
Chloroquine has been tested using an ex vivo contractility assay and human myometrium and shown to have tocolytic and uterotonic effects. In isolated single mouse myometrial cells, chloroquine reverses the rise in intracellular Ca2+ concentration and cell shortening induced by uterotonics. Chloroquine also prevents PTB induced by LPS or mifepristone more often than current commonly used tocolytics, and this prevention is largely lost in α-gustducin-knockout mice. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28559440/).
A 2021 Danish nation wide cohort study was published in May 2021. It found there was no increased risk of major birth defects, preterm birth, or SGA among pregnancies exposed to 4-aminoquinolines (chloroquine and HCQ) (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33232466/).
University of Massachusetts Medical School received an NIH grant for the period of 2018-2023 to examine the role of TAS2R family as a therapeutic target and bitter tastants (including chloroquine) as new and more effective tocolytics for PTB management. (https://grantome.com/grant/NIH/R01-HD095539-02)
Stanford University School of Medicine also received an NIH grant for the period 2020 - 2023 to determine whether preeclampsia risk is reduced in women who use HCQ during pregnancy. (5R01AR077103-04).

Developers: Sobhan Darou Company; Allergan; Lundbeck Foundation

Key features and challenges:
Citalopram is an antidepressant that belongs to the class of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). It is a bicyclic phthalate derivative with a unique structure, containing a tertiary amine and two nitrogen-containing metabolites. Citalopram works by inhibiting serotonin reuptake, enhancing serotonergic transmission, and has minimal effects on dopamine, norepinephrine, and other receptors. It was approved by the FDA in 1998 for treating depression in adults aged 18 and older.
In 2008 a study aimed to evaluate citalopram's effectiveness in treating chronic pelvic pain by assessing changes in pain severity, depressive symptoms, and functional disability. In a 12-week, open-label study of 14 women, depression scores significantly decreased, pain severity showed a trend toward improvement, but there was no significant reduction in disability. Most participants (91.7%) chose to continue citalopram after the study. The results suggest that citalopram is effective in reducing depressive symptoms and shows potential in managing pain, though its impact on disability is minimal. Further larger studies are needed to confirm these findings. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18441724/)
More recently, a pilot clinical trial has aimed to assess the effect of citalopram on endometriosis symptoms in patients undergoing medical treatment. The primary outcomes being measured are dysmenorrhea (painful periods), dyspareunia (painful intercourse), and dyschezia (painful bowel movements).(https://irct.behdasht.gov.ir/trial/70756)
Results from this trial are already available; Significant improvements were noted in emotional well-being, social support, dysmenorrhea, dyschezia, and chronic pelvic pain in the citalopram group. Dyspareunia showed no significant change. The ENDOPAIN-4D questionnaire highlighted significant improvements in most domains except pain-related disability. The study concluded that citalopram significantly reduces pain and enhances quality of life in endometriosis patients, with future research needed to refine dosages and compare SSRIs.(https://www.oncologyradiotherapy.com/articles/efficacy-of-adjunct-therapy-with-citalopram-to-improve-healthrelated-quality-of-life-and-associated-symptoms-in-patients-with-endo-107180.html)

Name: Citral
Developers: Brazilian Federal University of Pelotas, Universidade Federal de Pelotas (UFPEL)
Indication: Treatment of Trichomoniasis
Target: thioredoxin reductase (TvTrxR), purine nucleoside phosphorylase (TvPNP), and methionine gamma lyase (TvMGL)
Mechanism of action: Terpenoid aldehyde that damages protozoal membranes and impairs cellular metabolism.
Key features and challenges: A 2025 study highlights growing resistance of Trichomonas vaginalis to the only approved drug class, the 5-nitroimidazoles, fueling interest in new treatments for this common non-viral STI. Researchers are looking at natural products, focusing on citral (3,7-dimethyl-2,6-octadienal), the main component in lemongrass essential oil. Findings show citral has a minimum inhibitory concentration of 100 μM, halting T. vaginalis growth within 12 hours, and an IC50 of around 40 μM after 24 hours. Tests on nitric oxide levels indicate citral may also have antioxidant properties. Molecular docking suggests it binds weakly to three parasite proteins: thioredoxin reductase (TvTrxR), purine nucleoside phosphorylase (TvPNP), and methionine gamma lyase (TvMGL). The study presents citral as a possible non-nitroimidazole option for treating trichomoniasis and emphasizes the need to learn more about its mechanism (https://www.mdpi.com/2036-7481/16/5/96).
Recent updates: Discovery study published in 2025 showed citral exhibits a minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of 100 μM, effectively inhibiting the growth of T. vaginalis trophozoites within 12 h of exposure, and a 50% inhibitory concentration (IC50) of approximately 40 μM after 24 h (https://www.mdpi.com/2036-7481/16/5/96)

Name: Clade 2.3.4.4 H5 chimeric cold-adapted attenuated influenza vaccine
Developers: Jilin Agricultural University; Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences; Shandong Normal University
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against influenza A, caused by H5
Target: Hemagglutinin (HA) ectodomain of clade 2.3.4.4 H5 AIVs
Mechanism of action: Induces systemic, mucosal, and cellular immune responses against H5Nx antigens; avoids reassortment risk with IAV by using an IBV backbone; elicits cross-protective antibodies and T-cell responses.
Key features and challenges:
-Designed to mitigate reassortment risks inherent in IAV-based LAIVs.
-Cold-adapted and temperature-sensitive phenotype confirmed.
-Induced cross-clade humoral (IgG, IgA), mucosal, and T-cell immunity.
-Provided 100% survival in two-dose immunized mice against lethal H5Nx challenge, partial protection after one dose.
Demonstrated cross-protection in ferrets (reduced lung virus titers, survival, and IFN-γ responses).
Challenge: antibody titers lower than inactivated vaccines; broader validation in non-human primates needed.
Recent updates:
As of 2024–2025, no further published animal model studies identified. WHO and Chinese CDC continue to list clade 2.3.4.4 H5Nx as a pandemic concern, keeping interest in preclinical LAIVs active.
Related earlier work (2021) by the same group developed H5N1 chimeric cold-adapted vaccines, suggesting continued progression toward broader clade coverage.

Name: Clarithromycin + rifampicin
Developers: Erasmus University (including Erasmus University Medical Center)
Indication: Post-exposure prophylaxis for leprosy close contacts.
Target:
Clarithromycin: 50S subunit of bacterial ribosome
Rifampicin: RNA-polymerase.
Mechanism of action:
Clarithromycin: Binds to the 50S subunit of bacterial ribosomes, which prevents bacteria from making proteins
Rifampicin: Inhibits of DNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
Key features and challenges:
Stop the Transmission of Leprosy (NL-OMON23060).
The PEP++ study uses a cluster-randomised controlled trial design to test the efficacy of an enhanced chemoprophylaxis regimen against leprosy.  Clusters of persons affected by leprosy will be identified by GIS mapping to target blanket campaigns where chemoprophylaxis will be provided to around 100 close contacts per leprosy patient. In the intervention areas, twenty close contacts of leprosy patients will receive enhanced chemoprophylaxis (i.e. PEP++ regimen (3 doses of clarithromycin and rifampicin)) and an additional eighty contacts will receive SDR-PEP.  In the control areas, all contacts will receive SDR-PEP. Outside the cluster areas, twenty close contacts will receive the PEP++ regimen in the intervention areas and SDR-PEP in control areas. The SIMCOLEP mathematical model predicts that this combination of interventions will result in a 50% reduction in new case detection rate in a 5-year period. The PEP++ project targets India, Brazil and Indonesia because 81% of all the new leprosy cases globally are detected in these three countries.
Primary outcome:
- Rate ratio of the case detection rate among close contacts treated with PEP++ over the case detection rate among close contacts treated with SDR-PEP
- Percentage decline in case detection rate in the study districts over 2023 compared to 2019
(https://onderzoekmetmensen.nl/en/trial/23060).

Name: Class 5a fimbrial tip fusion vaccine
Developers: Not specified
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against moderate to severe diarrhoea caused by ETEC infection
Mechanism of action: Targets structural tip proteins responsible for initial host cell contact, neutralizing colonization potential
Key features and challenges: A subunit fusion immunogen built on the CFA/I adhesin-pilin (CfaEB) fused to colonization-factor pilins of CS14 and CS4, targeting the class 5a fimbrial tip adhesins that mediate ETEC's initial host-cell contact to neutralise colonization. Given orally or intramuscularly.
Recent updates: In an Aotus nancymaae non-human-primate challenge model, four intradermal doses of the CfaEp3 (CfaEB-CsuA2-CsfA) candidate with dmLT adjuvant conferred 91% protection against CS14+ ETEC (WS3294A) but only 20% against CFA/I+ ETEC (H10407), indicating limited cross-protection within subclass 5a (Open Forum Infectious Diseases 2025;12(Supplement_1)).

Name: Clofazamine
Developers: University of Hong Kong (including HKU-CTC)
Indication: Treatment of MERS-CoV infection (repurposing)
Target: Coronavirus replication (post-entry, RNA replication and possibly viral helicase/ion channel interference)
Mechanism of action: Broad-spectrum antiviral activity via interference with viral replication complexes and host lipid/redox pathways; previously shown to inhibit replication of MERS-CoV, SARS-CoV, and SARS-CoV-2 in vitro.
Key features and challenges:
-FDA-approved for leprosy; known safety profile in humans, oral bioavailability.
-Demonstrated in vitro activity against MERS-CoV with EC50 in low micromolar range.
-Broad-spectrum activity (MERS, SARS, SARS-CoV-2) supports coronavirus drug repurposing.
-Challenges: cytotoxicity at higher concentrations; unclear in vivo efficacy against MERS (no published animal challenge studies)
-Skin pigmentation and GI side effects common with chronic dosing
Recent updates:
-Clofazimine has been further studied in SARS-CoV-2 hamster models, showing oral efficacy and synergy with remdesivir.
-WHO and repurposing consortia have considered clofazimine in COVID-19 adaptive platform trials, but no MERS-specific clinical entries exist yet as of Sept 2025.
-Remains a candidate for broad-spectrum coronavirus preparedness, including MERS, due to oral dosing and existing approval.

Name: Clomiphene Citrate - Endometriosis
Developers: sanofi-aventis; EMD Serono; A-S Medication Solutions; Cosette Pharmaceuticals, Inc
Indication: Endometriosis associated menstrual cycle regulation and fertility
Mechanism of action:
Selective estrogen receptor modulator; details unclear. see below

the release of gonadotropins, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), and leuteinizing hormone (LH), which leads to the development and maturation of ovarian follicle, ovulation, and subsequent development and function of the coprus luteum, thus resulting in pregnancy. Gonadotropin release may result from direct stimulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis or from a decreased inhibitory influence of estrogens on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis by competing with the endogenous estrogens of the uterus, pituitary, or hypothalamus. Clomifene has no apparent progestational, androgenic, or antrandrogenic effects and does not appear to interfere with pituitary-adrenal or pituitary-thyroid function.
Key features and challenges:
Clomiphene Citrate is the citrate salt form of clomiphene, a triphenylethylene nonsteroidal ovulatory stimulant evaluated for antineoplastic activity against breast cancer. Clomiphene has both estrogenic and anti-estrogenic activities that compete with estrogen for binding at estrogen receptor sites in target tissues. This agent causes the release of the pituitary gonadotropins follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH), leading to ovulation. (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/Clomiphene%20Citrate)
In a randomized trial comparing clomiphene citrate (CC) and letrozole (LTZ) for fertility in women with minimal to mild endometriosis published in 2021, both medications significantly increased ovulation rates (LTZ 88.7%, CC 84.5%) compared to control. However, there were no significant differences in cumulative clinical pregnancy or live-birth rates between the groups at 3, 6, and 12 months post-laparoscopy. This suggests that while LTZ and CC are effective for inducing ovulation, they do not offer a substantial advantage over laparoscopy alone in terms of pregnancy or live-birth outcomes, highlighting the need for further research. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34020578/)

Name: Clotrimazole
Developers: Universidade do Estado do Rio de Janeiro; Centro Universitário Estadual da Zona Oeste (UEZO)
Indication: Prevention and treatment of endometriosis associated abnormal tissue growth
Target: Fungal cell membrane; unclear what the target is in endometriosis
Mechanism of action: Broad-spectrum antifungal agent that inhibits the growth of pathogenic yeasts by changing the permeability of cell membranes; unclear what the mechanism is in endometriosis
Key features and challenges:
Clotrimazole, a broad-spectrum antifungal agent belonging to the imidazole class of azole antifungals, was discovered in the late 1960s. It is available in various forms including creams, pessaries, and troches. While its primary use is for treating fungal infections such as vaginal yeast infections and athlete's foot, it has also attracted interest for its potential in treating diseases like sickle cell disease, malaria, and some cancers. Its minimal side effects and uncomplicated metabolic profile contribute to its widespread use. (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB00257)
Currently, clotrimazole is being explored in Brazilian preclinical studies for endometriosis. However, the mechanism by which it may aid in lesion regression remains unclear.
A 2020 study evaluated the impact of clotrimazole (CTZ) on estrogen production in endometriosis using a rat model, showing that CTZ treatment significantly reduced serum estrogen levels and endometriotic lesion size by downregulating estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) and cytochrome P450 aromatase (CYP19). Both oral and intraperitoneal administration of CTZ led to decreased lesion size and reduced estrogen production, suggesting its potential as a therapeutic agent for managing endometriosis. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32240980/)
More recently, animal studies published in 2023, explored clotrimazole's mechanism and adverse effects in endometriosis by treating rats with either CTZ or vehicle for 15 days after endometrial implantation. CTZ significantly reduced lesion growth, nitric oxide levels, and markers of oxidative stress, while enhancing antioxidant activity in the liver, suggesting it promotes lesion regression through inhibition of reactive nitrogen species, with minimal adverse effects on the brain and liver.(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0303720723000345#:~:text=Clotrimazole%20is%20effective%20for%20the,as%20a%20treatment%20of%20endometriosis.)

Name: ClpC1
Developers: TB Alliance

Name: CoV-RBD-scNP-001+3M-052-AF
Developers: Duke University
Indication: Prevention of COVID-19 and potentially other SARS-related coronavirus diseases
Target: SARS-CoV-2 spike receptor-binding domain (RBD) (sarbecovirus RBD epitope focus).

Name: Coagulation factor XIII concentrate
Developers: CSL Behring; University of Zurich
Indication: Indicated for the treatment or control of postpartum haemorrhage.
Mechanism of action: Promotes coagulation by cross-linking fibrin, resulting in increased mechanical strength and resistance to fibrinolysis of the fibrin clot.
Key features and challenges:
Factor XIII concentrate is a purified form of Factor XIII that is used to prevent and treat surgical bleeding in patients with a Factor XIII deficiency. It is also known as Fibrin Stabilizing Factor (FSF). Factor XIII is an endogenously produced coagulation factor and the final enzyme within the blood coagulation cascade. It cross-links fibrin and other proteins resulting in increased mechanical strength and resistance to fibrinolysis of the fibrin clot. This contributes to enhanced platelet and clot adhesion to injured tissue, thereby improving blood coagulation and maintenance of hemostasis. Exogenous replacement of Factor XIII is a cornerstone of treatment for bleeding associated with congenital Factor XIII deficiency.
A study compared European recommendations about patient blood management in postpartum haemorrhage (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/tme.12927#tme12927-bib-0018). 
A group of Portuguese specialists recommended its use at a dose of 30 IU/kg in a situation of low clot strength evidence, even with adequate levels of fibrinogen. ASCS (German) guidelines mentioned its use at a dose of 15–20 IU/kg if needed, but did not specify any clinical criteria. The majority of the publications in the study did not contemplate the use of FXIII. 
A multi-center, prospective, randomized-controlled interventional trial by the University of Zurich started in 2023 to evaluate the effect of replenishment of coagulation factor XIII in women with PPH on measured blood loss. Seven perinatal centers across Switzerland will participate. In case of PPH, women in the study group will receive FXIII at an early stage of PPH. Further management in both groups shall move along the national guideline for the treatment of peripartum hemorrhage. (https://data.snf.ch/grants/grant/213591)

Name: Coagulation profiles
Developers: Shanghai University of Medicine and Health Sciences
Indication: Prediction of preeclampsia in the first trimester
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: Coagulation profile:  activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), prothrombin time (PT), increased D-dimer, and mean platelet volume
Mechanism of action: Measures clotting parameters to identify hypercoagulability and endothelial dysfunction associated with preeclampsia.
Key features and challenges:
Normal pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state with an increase in coagulation factor levels and a decrease in natural anticoagulation. However, a higher hypercoagulable state with prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), prothrombin time (PT), increased D-dimer, and mean platelet volume is seen in women with preeclampsia at the time of onset. In addition, endothelial dysfunction occurs before the clinical symptoms of preeclampsia. 

Researchers from Shanghai University of Medicine and Health Sciences conducted a study published in 2023 to investigate the coagulation profile in the first trimester in women who developed preeclampsia later. A total of 853 pregnant women with singleton births at the Obstetrics and Gynecology Hospital of Fudan University between January 2021 and December 2021 were included in this case-control study. In the comparison with the controls (n = 531), the mean value of D-dimer, APTT, thrombin time (TT), antithrombin (AT)), and fibrin degradation products (FDP) was significantly lower in preeclamptic women at the time of diagnosis (n = 322). The changes in the coagulation profile were not associated with the severity or the time of onset. The reduced values of D-dimer, AT, and FDP, and increased values of TT were also observed in the first trimester in women who developed preeclampsia later and were not associated with the severity, or the time of onset of preeclampsia. After adjusting for maternal age and BMI, the values of D-dimer and AT in the first trimester were correlated to the risk of developing preeclampsia. 

These results suggest that there is an abnormal maternal response to the hemostatic system in early gestational age in women who developed preeclampsia later and measuring the coagulation profile could be an additional predictive marker of preeclampsia.
(https://www.cell.com/heliyon/fulltext/S2405-8440(23)05191-5?_returnURL=https%3A%2F%2Flinkinghub.elsevier.com%2Fretrieve%2Fpii%2FS2405844023051915%3Fshowall%3Dtrue)

Name: Cold-Adapted Live-Attenuated MERS-CoV Vaccine
Developers: PioneerVaccine Inc
Indication: Prevention of MERS-CoV infection
Target: Whole live-attenuated virus (multigenic antigens; protective immunity directed primarily against Spike/DPP4 entry).
Mechanism of action: Limited replication of temperature-sensitive, attenuated virus in upper airway induces mucosal (IgA) and systemic neutralizing antibody plus Th1-skewed cellular responses, blocking DPP4-mediated entry and preventing disease.
Key features and challenges:
-Single intranasal dose (2×10⁴ pfu) in K18-hDPP4 mice gave complete protection from lethal challenge; no weight loss or detectable virus in nasal turbinates, brain, lung, kidney. 
-Strong nAb titers (≈1:1,280–1:5,120) and tissue IgA; IFN-γ–positive splenocytes and TNF-α predominance indicate Th1 bias. 
-Temperature-sensitive phenotype (little/no growth at 41 °C); 16 AA changes across ORF1a/S/M; RBD sequence unchanged. 
-Challenges: live-attenuated CoV raises reversion/recombination and manufacturing biosafety considerations; no clinical data/registrations. (Stability after 15 passages at 37 °C reported, but further studies needed.)
Recent updates:
2024: Follow-on study reports the cold-adapted strain remained attenuated after 15 passages at 37 °C (no reversion to wild-type pathogenicity in mice). 
-The same cold-adapted strain served as antigen source for an inactivated split MERS-CoV vaccine tested preclinically in 2024 (protective in K18-hDPP4 mice). 
-Ongoing human studies for other MERS platforms continue (e.g., MVA-MERS-S phase 1b; ChAdOx1-MERS phase 1 data), but no clinical listing found for a cold-adapted live MERS-CoV vaccine.

Name: Colistin + Rutin
Developers: South China Agricultural University
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of MDR Salmonella Typhimurium.
Mechanism of action: RT disrupts iron homeostasis to inactivate the PmrA/PmrB system, thereafter reducing the bacterial membrane modifications for enhancing CS binding.
Key features and challenges: The wide dissemination of multidrug-resistant (MDR) Gram-negative bacteria poses a significant global health and security concern. As developing new antibiotics is generally costly, fastidious, and time-consuming, there is an urgent need for alternative therapeutic strategies to address the gap in antibiotic discovery void. This study aimed to investigate the activity of colistin (CS) in combination with a natural product, rutin (RT), to combat against Salmonella Typhimurium (S. Tm) in vitro and in vivo. The results showed that a combination with RT enabled the potentiation of CS efficacy. Further mechanistic analysis indicated that RT disrupted iron homeostasis to inactivate the PmrA/PmrB system, thereafter reducing the bacterial membrane modifications for enhancing CS binding. Besides enhancing bactericidal activity of CS, RT was also observed to mitigate the CS-induced nephrotoxicity, by which the dosing limitation of CS was overcome for better pathogen clearance. The animal trial eventually confirmed the in vivo synergistic interaction of RT with CS to treat the bacterial infection. To sum up, the present study uncovered the potential of RT as a viable adjuvant of CS to eradicate the infection and protect the hosts, which might serve as a promising alternative to combat infections caused by MDR Gram-negative bacteria.

Name: Collectin Surfactant Protein A (SP-A)
Developers: NORTHSHORE UNIVERSITY HEALTHSYSTEM
Indication: For the prevention and treatment of preterm birth
Mechanism of action: Modulates intrauterine immune signaling and inflammatory pathways that regulate parturition and initiation of labour.
Key features and challenges:
SP-A protein is a member of a subfamily of C-type lectins called collectins. The encoded protein binds specific carbohydrate moieties found on lipids and on the surface of microorganisms. This protein plays an essential role in surfactant homeostasis and in the defense against respiratory pathogens.

Findings from a mouse model of infection and inflammation showed a powerful anti-labor effect of exogenously administered surfactant protein A (SP-A), a protein produced by fetal and maternal tissues. Newer data suggest that this effect persists even when SP-A is administered systemically (i.e. intravenously) and hours after the labor-inducing stimulus has taken hold, distinctions that are important for potential clinical use. 

A study started in 2021 aiming to identify the crucial domain(s) of the SP-A molecule (i.e. the minimal functional unit, or MFU) for its anti-labor and anti- inflammatory functions during labors due to either live bacterial infection or sterile inflammatory states in the mouse, assess the safety of the SP-A MFU in mice and their offspring; and test the hypothesis that the above effects of SP-A are dependent upon engagement of toll-like receptor (TLR) 2 and its downstream signal transduction mechanisms. 
(https://reporter.nih.gov/search/sYdz6O_VX0qjmMjcEbwvpw/project-details/10146441)

Name: Combined NLR, HGB and PDW markers
Developers: Fujian Maternal and Child Health Hospital
Indication: Prediction of PTL
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Measures systemic inflammatory and hematologic indices (neutrophil–lymphocyte ratio, hemoglobin, platelet distribution width) to identify inflammatory states associated with preterm labour.
Key features and challenges:
A Chinese study started in 2019 at the Fujian Maternal and Child Health Hospital with the goal of investigating whether complete blood cell (CBC) count parameters at 20-30 weeks of gestation can predict asymptomatic preterm birth. 
The retrospective case-control study reviewed the clinical data of all (15 387 total) pregnant women for preterm deliveries and term deliveries between January and December 2017 at Fujian Provincial Maternity and Children's Hospital, China. 
 
CBC parameters used in the study were as follows: white blood cell; neutrophil count; lymphocyte count; monocyte count; haemoglobin; haematocrit; red cell distribution width; platelet count; mean platelet volume; plateletcrit; platelet distribution width; neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio; lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio; and PLR, platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio. 
 
The study showed that combined marker of neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), haemoglobin (HGB), and platelet distribution width (PDW) could accurately predict PTB at a cutoff value of 0.25, with sensitivity and specificity of 88.6% and 40.5% and negative and positive predictive value of 97.9% and 10.2%, respectively. 
 
The researchers concluded that combined marker of CBC parameters can supplement other markers to predict PTB about 10 weeks in advance. This combined marker had a very high negative predictive value for PTB. Therefore, in subjects with normal combined marker value, further screening tests for PTB may be eliminated unless clinical suspicion is high. 
(https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jcla.23313)​

Name: Combined SIT/IIT Approach
Developers: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO); International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA); WHO: Special Programme for Research and Training in Tropical Diseases (WHO / TDR); Sun Yat-sen University
Indication: Prevention and control of Aedes mosquito-borne arboviral diseases
Mechanism of action: Reduce pathogen transmission by vector manipulation
Key features and challenges:
Currently under Vector Control Advisory Group (VCAG) review for assessment of public health value as of 01/03/2020.VCAG reviewed one RCT protocol in February 2019.

The Combined Sterile Insect Technique (SIT) and Incompatible Insect Technique (IIT) approach is an innovative strategy designed to suppress or eliminate populations of disease-carrying mosquitoes, such as Aedes aegypti. By integrating these two methods, this approach addresses the limitations of each technique when used individually, enhancing its effectiveness. In the SIT component, male mosquitoes are sterilized using radiation, preventing them from producing viable offspring when they mate with wild females. Over time, this technique reduces mosquito populations by disrupting their reproductive cycle. On the other hand, IIT involves infecting male mosquitoes with a specific strain of Wolbachia, a bacterium that induces cytoplasmic incompatibility. When these Wolbachia-infected males mate with wild females, their eggs fail to hatch, further suppressing the mosquito population.

The combined SIT/IIT approach ensures robust results. While SIT can sometimes weaken the competitiveness of sterilized males in the wild, pairing it with IIT enhances the suppression effect. Additionally, IIT reduces the risk of releasing fertile females, a concern when relying solely on SIT. Together, these techniques offer a complementary and effective solution for controlling mosquito populations and reducing the transmission of mosquito-borne diseases.
Recent updates: As of 21 Mar 2023-FAO/IAEA provided an update on advances in mass rearing, sex separation, automatic mosquito release systems and the use of X-rays for inducing mosquito sterility. There are currently 42 trials being undertaken, all with epidemiological end-points. Some of the trials are using SIT only and others are employing the combined SIT/IIT approach. While most of these trials are at the stage of collecting baseline data, there are four large-scale, pre-operational SIT/IIT trials underway in China, Mexico, Singapore and Thailand. Multiple pilot studies of SIT alone to target Ae. albopictus are ongoing in several European countries and in Sri Lanka. SIT studies targeting Ae. aegypti have been conducted and others are underway in several sites in the Americas, including Brazil, Mexico and the United States of America. https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240066021

Name: Combined SW elastography, VOCAL technique and T2* MRI predictive model
Developers: Zigong Hospital of Woman and Children Healthcare
Indication: Predict pre-eclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Combines placental stiffness, volumetric ultrasound, and MRI oxygenation metrics to assess placental function and predict preeclampsia risk.
Key features and challenges: In 2023, researchers from the Zigong Hospital of Woman and Children Healthcare, Zigong, Sichuan, China published their study findings on the clinical value of combining shear wave elastography (SWE) with the Volumetric Organ Computer-Aided AnaLysis (VOCAL) technique and T2* magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to predict pre-eclampsia (PE). Differences in placental elasticity, vascularization index (VI), flow index (FI), vascularization flow index (VFI), and T2* MRI perfusion fraction (f) were compared between PE and non-PE pregnant women. Received operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to evaluate the diagnostic value of placental elasticity, VI, FI, VFI, f, and their combination for predicting PE. Placental elasticity was higher in the observation group than in the control group, while VI, FI, VFI, and f were lower in the observation group (all p < 0.05). SWE combined with VOCAL technique and T2* MRI has high value for predicting PE and can provide reference information for clinical diagnosis. (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jcu.23575)

Name: Combined arterial tonometry + endothelial glycocalyx measurement
Developers: IRCCS Azienda Ospedaliero-Universitaria di Bologna; University of Bologna
Indication: Prediction and diagnosis of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Arterial tonometry (Pulsepen), in vivo darkfield microscopy (Glycocheck) to evaluate endothelial and vascular function, urine sample and a blood sample for specific study analyses on metabolic profile, endothelial and angiogenic markers
Key features and challenges:
Combined arterial tonometry and endothelial glycocalyx measurement is being investigated as a multiparametric, non-invasive approach to assess maternal vascular function in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, including preeclampsia. Arterial tonometry evaluates arterial stiffness and pulse wave characteristics, while endothelial glycocalyx assessment reflects microvascular endothelial integrity. Together, these measures aim to provide a comprehensive evaluation of macrovascular and microvascular function during pregnancy.
A 2023 prospective study (NCT05999851) is examining whether the combination of arterial tonometry and endothelial glycocalyx measurement can predict the development of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and future maternal cardiovascular risk (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05999851). Participants undergo two vascular assessments during pregnancy. The study will evaluate associations between vascular measurements and circulating biomarkers of angiogenesis and endothelial dysfunction, including ANG-1, ANG-2, endothelin-1 (ET-1), ICAM-1, and VCAM-1. Trends in serum uric acid, lipid profiles, and xanthine oxidase activity will also be analyzed in normotensive and hypertensive pregnancies. Pregnancy outcomes are collected at delivery, and long-term cardiovascular outcomes are assessed through follow-up interviews five years postpartum. Serum endothelial and angiogenic markers are measured in participants who develop hypertensive disorders and in matched controls.
Key challenges include the complexity of multiparametric vascular assessment, requirement for specialized equipment and trained operators, and the need for longitudinal validation to establish predictive accuracy and clinical utility. Integration into routine antenatal care will depend on demonstration of added prognostic value beyond established clinical and biochemical screening models, as well as cost-effectiveness in diverse healthcare settings.

Name: Compound 20
Developers: North-West University
Indication: Investigated for the treatment of Trichomoniasis.
Mechanism of action: Substrate for ferredoxin
Key features and challenges:
Compound 20 is a metronidazole–Schiff base hybrid synthesized as part of a 2022 medicinal chemistry study aimed at developing improved treatments for protozoan infections, including Trichomonas vaginalis, Plasmodium falciparum, and Trypanosoma brucei (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ardp.202200409). 
The design strategy preserved the metronidazole core—critical for nitroimidazole activation and radical generation—while introducing arylidene substitutions to create Schiff base derivatives with potentially enhanced antiparasitic activity.
Among the synthesized series, Compound 20 emerged as the most potent antitrichomonal agent in vitro against T. vaginalis. Structurally, it contains a benzylidene moiety substituted with nitro and trifluoromethyl groups. These electron-withdrawing substituents are hypothesized to enhance activity by facilitating intracellular radical formation within the parasite’s hydrogenosome, similar to the established mechanism of metronidazole. Structure–activity relationship analyses in the study supported the importance of these substitutions in improving antiparasitic potency.
Key challenges include the early in vitro stage of development, absence of in vivo efficacy data, and the need to evaluate toxicity, pharmacokinetics, and selectivity relative to host cells. As metronidazole resistance is an emerging concern in trichomoniasis, demonstration of retained activity against resistant strains would be particularly relevant. Further optimization and translational studies are required before clinical development can be considered.
Overall, Compound 20 represents a promising next-generation metronidazole hybrid with enhanced in vitro activity against Trichomonas vaginalis. Advancement into in vivo models and safety evaluation will be essential to determine its therapeutic potential.

Name: Condom catheter
Developers: West Bengal University of Health Sciences
Indication: Indicated for the temporary control or reduction of postpartum uterine bleeding when conservative management of uterine bleeding is warranted.
Mechanism of action: Provides direct intrauterine pressure/tamponade to promote haemostasis.
Key features and challenges:
A condom catheter may be used as an improvised intrauterine balloon tamponade device for the management of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), particularly in low-resource settings. The device is typically assembled using a condom secured to a Foley catheter or simple rubber tubing with sterile string and inflated with saline via syringe to provide intrauterine tamponade. Materials required are generally inexpensive and widely available, making the approach accessible where commercial balloon systems are unavailable. An innovative adaptation, the Chhattisgarh condom balloon device, incorporates a central drainage channel, allowing real-time assessment of ongoing bleeding while the balloon remains inflated (2018: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13224-018-1185-6).
A 2012 systematic review assessed the use of condom catheters for PPH management in resource-poor settings (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22882240/). Across reported studies, the device was used in 193 cases of PPH, achieving haemostasis in 186 cases. Reported duration of placement varied substantially, ranging from 6 to 72 hours. In three studies involving 87 women, the device was retained for less than 24 hours. The findings suggested that improvised condom catheter tamponade may be an effective and practical intervention for controlling PPH when standard uterotonic therapy fails and advanced surgical options are limited.
Key challenges include variability in assembly technique, lack of standardized protocols, risk of infection or retained components, and limited high-quality comparative data against commercially manufactured balloon tamponade devices. While widely adopted in low-resource environments, further rigorous evaluation would strengthen the evidence base for broader guideline endorsement.

Developers: Dhaka Medical College and Hospital; University of Illinois at Chicago; The Ohio State University College of Medicine; Gynuity Health Projects

Key features and challenges:
Congo Red Dot Paper Test is an inexpensive rapid test based on the use of Congo red staining of misfolded and damaged proteins in the urine of women with PE. It has diagnostic and prognostic potential since it precedes the onset of clinical manifestations and correlates with disease severity. 
 
Principle: 
CR [the sodium salt of 3,3'-(1,1'-biphenyl-4,4'-diyl) bis (4-aminonaphthalene-1-sulfonic acid)] is an organic compound, water-soluble, first identified as a pH indicator, currently utilised for tinting sediments or atherosclerotic lesions and inflammation of blood vessels, urine or the cytoplasm. 
Using an impartial large-scale study of proteins, Buhimschi et al observed that women with severe PE (sPE) necessitating medically indicated delivery for PE exhibited a peculiar set of proteomic biomarkers, which included albumin and nonrandom proteoforms of SERPINA1 gene. This finding carried diagnostic and prognostic potential, a positive test preceding the beginning of clinical manifestations, and corresponded with the severity of the disease. A simple method was designed, whereby, urine that had been combined with CR was dripped on a baseless nitrocellulose sheet, which was then washed with increasing concentrations of solutions of methanol. Spots after testing urine from women with sPE, but not healthy pregnant controls, remained red after the methanol wash, demonstrating that women with PE exhibit urinary congophilia. 
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18984079/) 
 
Several studies have confirmed the diagnostic potential of a point-of-care CRD paper test, which can be superior to traditional urine and serum analysis. 
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31193633/) 
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33385127/) 
 
Challenges: Women with chronic kidney disease without PE and nonpregnant women with lupus nephritis have increased urine congophilia levels when compared with healthy pregnant women. The test cannot differentiate between reasons for elevated levels of urine congophilia.​

Name: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) Device
Developers: University of California, San Francisco (UCSF)
Indication: Treatment of PCOS targeting metabolic or reproductive effects
Mechanism of action: Increase oxygen levels for metabolic or reproductive benefits
Key features and challenges:
Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) is a non-invasive device-based therapy widely used for the treatment of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). CPAP maintains upper airway patency during sleep by delivering continuous pressurized air, thereby reducing apneic episodes, intermittent hypoxia, sympathetic activation, and sleep fragmentation. It is considered safe, effective, and relatively affordable for long-term management of moderate-to-severe OSA.

Obstructive sleep apnea is increasingly recognized as a common comorbidity in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), particularly among those with obesity and insulin resistance. OSA may exacerbate cardiometabolic dysfunction through mechanisms including intermittent hypoxia–induced oxidative stress, systemic inflammation, sympathetic overactivation, and worsening insulin resistance. These pathways overlap with core pathophysiological features of PCOS, suggesting a potential bidirectional relationship between OSA and metabolic and reproductive dysfunction.

While CPAP is well established for improving excessive daytime sleepiness, blood pressure control, and cardiovascular outcomes in symptomatic OSA, its effects on metabolic and reproductive endpoints in PCOS remain insufficiently characterized. Current clinical practice does not routinely recommend CPAP for individuals with OSA who lack significant daytime sleepiness or overt cardiovascular symptoms, even when metabolic risk is present.

The ongoing U.S.-based clinical trial NCT05920694 is evaluating whether CPAP therapy can provide metabolic or reproductive benefits in women with PCOS and moderate-to-severe OSA who do not exhibit excessive daytime sleepiness. The study examines potential improvements in insulin resistance and related metabolic parameters, exploring mechanistic links between OSA treatment and PCOS-related health outcomes.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05920694

Key challenges include limited PCOS-specific evidence, as most CPAP data derive from general OSA populations. The impact of CPAP on androgen levels, ovulatory function, menstrual cyclicity, and long-term reproductive outcomes in PCOS remains largely unexplored. Additionally, adherence to CPAP therapy can be variable, which may influence treatment effectiveness in real-world settings. As a device-based intervention targeting a comorbidity rather than primary ovarian pathology, CPAP would likely function as an adjunctive metabolic strategy rather than a core PCOS therapy.

Name: Corallopyronin A
Developers: Emory University
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Inhibits the bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
Key features and challenges:
Corallopyronin A is a natural antibiotic isolated from Corallococcus coralloides and belongs to a class of RNA polymerase inhibitors distinct from rifamycins. It has demonstrated antimicrobial activity against a range of bacterial pathogens, including Chlamydia species. Its mechanism of action involves inhibition of the bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, thereby suppressing transcription and bacterial replication.
In 2022, the activity of corallopyronin A against Neisseria gonorrhoeae was evaluated, including assessment of mutation frequency and potential resistance mechanisms (https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/msphere.00362-22). 
The compound exhibited potent antimicrobial activity against both antibiotic-susceptible and antibiotic-resistant gonococcal strains. In vitro experiments using primary human cervical epithelial cells demonstrated eradication of gonococcal infection. The study also explored resistance development, providing early insights into mutation frequency and potential mechanisms of reduced susceptibility.
Key challenges include the preclinical stage of development, need for pharmacokinetic and safety evaluation in vivo, and assessment of efficacy in animal models of gonococcal infection. As a novel RNA polymerase inhibitor, evaluation of cross-resistance with existing transcription-targeting agents and long-term resistance development will be important. Formulation, route of administration, and compatibility with current gonorrhea treatment strategies must also be established.
Overall, corallopyronin A demonstrates promising in vitro activity against drug-susceptible and drug-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Further preclinical development will determine its potential role as a novel antimicrobial candidate for gonorrhea treatment.

Name: Cordycepin
Developers: Zibo Central Hospital
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Preeclampsia
Target: Macrophage Polarization; AMPK Signaling Pathway; Inflammatory Mediators
Mechanism of action: Restores the balance between pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cells in the placenta. It shifts macrophage polarization from the pro-inflammatory M1-type (dominant in PE) toward the anti-inflammatory M2-type
Key features and challenges:
Cordycepin (3′-deoxyadenosine) is a bioactive compound derived from Cordyceps species with reported anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties. It is being investigated as a potential therapeutic candidate for preeclampsia (PE) based on its effects on inflammatory signaling and immune regulation.
A 2024 preclinical study evaluated cordycepin in a lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced preeclampsia-like rat model (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/08820139.2024.2418572). Pregnant rats received LPS (1 μg/kg) via tail vein injection and were treated with cordycepin at doses of 5, 25, or 50 mg/kg from embryonic day 6 to day 18. Cordycepin administration significantly reduced systolic blood pressure and proteinuria compared with untreated preeclampsia-like controls. Improved pregnancy outcomes were observed, including increased fetal body length and weight. Biochemically, cordycepin reduced circulating sFlt-1 levels, increased placental growth factor (PlGF) levels, decreased placental pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6, MCP-1, MIP-2), and increased anti-inflammatory IL-10 levels. The treatment also modulated macrophage polarization, contributing to restoration of immune balance in placental tissue.
Key challenges include the fact that evidence is currently limited to animal models, with no clinical trials reported in pregnant women. Safety, optimal dosing, pharmacokinetics in pregnancy, and potential fetal effects remain unknown. Translation from LPS-induced rodent models to human preeclampsia requires cautious interpretation, and substantial clinical validation would be necessary before consideration for therapeutic use.

Name: Coumarins
Developers: Purdue University; University of Florence, Università degli Studi di Firenze
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: DNA topoisomerase type II inhibitor
Key features and challenges:
Coumarins are a group of secondary metabolites obtained from plants that are formed through the phenylpropanoid pathway. Coumarins are known to act as prodrug inhibitors of mammalian α-carbonic anhydrases, but they were not yet investigated for the inhibition of bacterial α-CAs. The 2021 study demonstrates that such enzymes from the bacterial pathogens Neisseria gonorrhoeae (NgCAα) and Vibrio cholerae (VchCAα) are inhibited by a panel of simple coumarins incorporating hydroxyl, amino, ketone or carboxylic acid ester moieties in various positions of the ring system. The nature and the position of the substituents in the coumarin ring were the factors which strongly influenced inhibitory efficacy.  The findings are relevant for discovering coumarin bacterial CA inhibitors with selectivity for the bacterial over human isoform, with potential applications as novel antibacterial agents. This investigation warrants further studies in order to find effective non-sulphonamide CAIs which may be useful for exploring antibacterials that can revert the extensive drug resistance observed with the clinically used anytibiotics.
As per the study published in 2022, coumarins are inhibitors of DNA topoisomerase type II that are essential for DNA replication. Coumarins inhibit nucleic acid formation, suppress the quorum-sensing network of the microorganism resulting in the lack of biofilm formation and the production of virulence factors. These inhibitions and suppression of coumarins ultimately lead to the cell death of microorganisms.
(https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14756366.2021.2012174#abstract)

Developers: Clover Biopharmaceuticals Australia; Dynavax Technologies Corporation

Mechanism of action:
The Clover COVID-19 vaccine uses a recombinant spike protein subunit to stimulate the immune system. The vaccine introduces a stabilized trimeric spike (S) protein, mimicking the structure of the SARS-CoV-2 virus's spike protein, which is critical for the virus to enter human cells.  

Adjuvants **CpG 1018** and **Alum** are included to enhance the immune response. CpG 1018 activates Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9), promoting a robust immune reaction, while Alum further boosts the immunogenicity.  

Upon administration, the immune system recognizes the spike protein as foreign, leading to the production of neutralizing antibodies. These antibodies block the virus from binding to and entering cells during subsequent exposure. Additionally, the vaccine induces a T-cell response, contributing to long-term immunity by targeting infected cells.  

This dual activation of antibody-mediated and cellular immunity equips the body to prevent infection and severe disease caused by SARS-CoV-2.
Key features and challenges:
Vx Schedule: Day 0 + 21

The Clover Biopharmaceuticals COVID-19 vaccine, also known as SCB-2019 (CpG 1018/Alum), is a protein-based vaccine developed by Clover Biopharmaceuticals in collaboration with global health organizations like CEPI. It utilizes a stabilized trimeric form of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein combined with two adjuvants. CpG 1018, a TLR9 agonist, and Alum, a widely used adjuvant. to enhance the immune response. This approach is based on proven protein subunit vaccine technology, ensuring safety and scalability.

The vaccine demonstrated promising results in Phase III trials, with over 70% efficacy against symptomatic COVID-19 and 100% protection against severe cases, including effectiveness against variants like Delta and Gamma. It is designed to be stored at standard refrigeration temperatures (2–8°C), making it easier to distribute in low-resource settings. Supported by CEPI, the vaccine aims to address inequities in vaccine access, particularly in underserved regions.

Despite its advantages, the vaccine faces challenges, including competition with established mRNA and adenovirus-based vaccines and the need to demonstrate effectiveness against newer variants like Omicron. Additionally, gaining regulatory approvals and achieving widespread adoption may take time. However, SCB-2019 remains a valuable candidate for improving global COVID-19 vaccine accessibility, particularly in regions with limited infrastructure.

Name: Cryptotanshinone
Developers: Guangzhou University of Traditional Chinese Medicine
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Endometriosis.
Mechanism of action: Modulates the expression of immunosuppressive genes and proteins associated with MDSCs through the JAK2/STAT3 pathway.
Key features and challenges:
Endometriosis (EMS), a well-recognized chronic inflammatory disorder, characterized by significant immune dysregulation, in which myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) are essential for facilitating immunosuppression and driving to disease progression. Cryptotanshinone (CTS) is an active compound capable of modulating MDSC-mediated immunosuppression; however, its therapeutic effects and mechanisms in the treatment of EMS remain unclear.
A 2025 study aims to investigate the therapeutic potential of CTS in modulating MDSCs through JAK2/STAT3 signalling pathway and to evaluate its effects on immune microenvironment and endometriotic lesion growth in EMS.
Transcriptomic data (GSE141549) and single-cell RNA sequencing data (GSE213216) were analysed to compare immune cell populations in control endometrium (CE), utopic endometrium (EuE) and ectopic endometrium (EcE) of patients with EMS. Network pharmacology analysis, surface plasmon resonance (SPR) and cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA) were utilized to explore the molecular mechanism of CTS's effects on MDSCs. A C57BL/6J EMS mice model was established to evaluate CTS's influence on MDSC-mediated immune response in vivo. Flow cytometry and immunofluorescence were used to analyse the immune cell populations, particularly MDSCs and CD8+ T cells. Ex vivo bone marrow (BM)-derived MDSCs were prepared to investigate the modulatory activities of CTS on the frequency and function of MDSCs. The impacts of CTS on JAK2/STAT3 pathway were further examined by western blot.
Bioinformatic analysis revealed that, among the three progression stages (CE, EuE, and EcE), the EcE stage exhibited a relatively elevated level of MDSCs and a reduced level of CD8+ T cells. Network pharmacological analysis, along with SPR and CETSA identified that CTS potentially modulates MDSCs in EMS by targeting the JAK2/STAT3 pathway. In vivo studies demonstrated that a relatively high dose of CTS treatment (60mg/kg) effectively inhibited lesion growth, reduced the population of MDSCs, and enhanced CD8+ T cell infiltration. Ex vivo experiments showed that CTS decreased the BM-derived MDSC frequency and rescued the suppressive ability of MDSC upon CD8+ T cells in a dose-dependent manner. Further mechanism analysis confirmed that CTS modulates the expression of immunosuppressive genes and proteins associated with MDSCs through JAK2/STAT3 pathway.
This study demonstrates that CTS is a promising natural compound for EMS treatment by inhibiting MDSC accumulation and modulating MDSC-mediated immune responses. Its therapeutic efficacy is linked to the modulation of the JAK2/STAT3 signalling pathway (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0944711324008845?via%3Dihub).

Name: Cu-phendione
Developers: Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul
Indication: Under investigation for potential antiparasitic effects on T. vaginalis.
Mechanism of action: Under investigation. Inhibition of T. vaginalis peptidases (cysteine- and metallo-type).
Key features and challenges:
Cu-phendione is a copper(II) complex of 1,10-phenanthroline-5,6-dione (phendione), a compound recognized for its chemical versatility and biological activity. Phendione and its metal complexes, including silver and copper derivatives, have demonstrated antibacterial activity against multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and antiparasitic effects against protozoa including Leishmania spp. and Trichomonas vaginalis. Mechanistic studies indicate that interaction with parasite metallo-peptidases is a key component of its antiparasitic activity (https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0817/12/5/745).
Preclinical investigations evaluating Cu-phendione against T. vaginalis have reported minimum inhibitory concentrations comparable to metronidazole. Additionally, Cu-phendione and metronidazole demonstrated synergistic effects, enhancing trophozoite killing when used in combination (https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0817/12/5/745). 
Mechanistic analyses have shown that Cu-phendione induces redox homeostasis imbalance and apoptosis in T. vaginalis, a mode of action distinct from metronidazole (https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0817/12/5/745
; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0923250822000961?via%3Dihub). 
Treatment with Cu-phendione significantly disrupted proteolytic pathways, reducing trophozoite capacity to cleave peptide substrates and impairing essential biological functions. A 2023 study further reported a cytoprotective effect during parasite interaction with vaginal and renal epithelial cells following Cu-phendione exposure (https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0817/12/5/745).
In 2023, research efforts advanced toward development of an intravaginal nanotechnological formulation containing Cu-phendione, aiming to optimize local delivery and therapeutic efficacy (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0923250822000961?via%3Dihub).
Key challenges include the preclinical stage of evidence, need for in vivo efficacy and toxicity evaluation, and assessment of safety for intravaginal administration. Metal-based complexes may require careful evaluation of systemic absorption, local tolerability, and long-term safety. Regulatory considerations related to nanotechnology-based formulations will also influence development pathways.
Overall, Cu-phendione demonstrates promising in vitro antitrichomonal activity, including synergy with metronidazole and a distinct mechanism involving redox imbalance and apoptosis. Further translational studies and formulation development will determine its feasibility as a novel therapeutic option for trichomoniasis.

Name: Cu/Eu@H-β-CD-ZNPs
Developers: Taihe Hospital, Hubei University of Medicine; Xi’an Daxing Hospital
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Preeclampsia
Target: TLR4, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and trophoblast cells
Mechanism of action: Downregulation of TLR4 and p65 (NF-κB) protein expressions
Key features and challenges:
Cu/Eu@H-β-CD-ZNPs is a nanoformulated therapeutic candidate designed for the treatment of preeclampsia (PE). The formulation consists of zein protein nanoparticles (ZNPs) functionalized with hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin (H-β-CD) and co-encapsulating curcumin (Cu) and eugenol (Eu), two bioactive compounds with anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. The platform aims to enhance bioavailability and targeted therapeutic delivery.
A 2025 preclinical study evaluated this nanoformulation in both in vitro and in vivo models of preeclampsia (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08853282251322272). Under hypoxic conditions, treated trophoblast cells demonstrated improved proliferation, invasion, and migration, suggesting restoration of trophoblast function. In an LPS-induced pregnancy rat model of hypertension, administration of Cu/Eu@H-β-CD-ZNPs significantly reduced systolic blood pressure and downregulated serum and placental pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1β, and IFN-γ. Additionally, expression of TLR4 and NF-κB p65 proteins was reduced, indicating modulation of inflammatory signaling pathways. The formulation was associated with improved hypertension-related outcomes in the animal model.
Key challenges include the fact that evidence is currently limited to preclinical models, with no human clinical data available. Nanoparticle safety, placental transfer characteristics, pharmacokinetics in pregnancy, and long-term fetal effects remain undefined. Regulatory complexity and scalability of nanoformulations also represent potential barriers to translation. Substantial clinical validation will be required before consideration for therapeutic use in preeclampsia.

Key features and challenges:
Curcumin is a bioactive natural compound with a hydrophobic polyphenolic structure, which is extracted from the rhizomes of Curcuma longa belonging to the Zingiberaceae family.  It has been found to have antibacterial, anti-tumor, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant effects and has been
approved as a food additive by the WHO.  Curcumin acts to treat trichomoniasis via a multifaceted attack against Trichomonas vaginalis.  This includes damaging the parasite by interfering with signalling molecules and iron transport.  It also has antioxidant qualities that impact host energy metabolism.
Novel delivery systems like niosomes can enhance drug efficiency and decrease side effects and toxicity.  Niosomes have been used as a vesicular drug delivery system to increase the rate of drug delivery, particularly in skin drug delivery, sustained drug delivery, or controlled drug release, with greater stability and lower cost than liposomes.  Drug encapsulation in niosomes is also another strategy to overcome drug resistance in different resistant pathogens.  Studies have shown that curcumin nanoparticles inhibit the growth of Staphylococcus epidermidis 
A study evaluating the effect of curcumin on the trophozoite stage of T. vaginalis, was published in 2022, and reported that curcumin entrapped modified nano-niosomes at concentrations of 1, 10, and 100 after 24 h had the
same ability as metronidazole to treat trichomonosis with 95-100% of its effectiveness.  The drug, even at the highest concentration (400 mg/ml), had no toxic effect on the fibroblast cell line.  It can therefore be concluded that the compound is a promising therapeutic candidate for trichomonosis.  Further investigations regarding anti-trichomonal effects of the curcumin and its derivative niosomes on animal models are required (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35809560/#:~:text=The%20results%20showed%20that%20quercetin%20and%20curcumin%20at,inhibition%20had%20better%20performance%20than%20positive%20control%20%28metronidazole%29).

Name: Cyclosporin A
Developers: Novartis; Abliva; APT Pharmaceuticals Inc; Maas Biolab; PendoPharm Inc; Sublimity Therapeutics Limited
Indication: Prevention or treatment of preeclampsia through suppression of inflammatory responses
Mechanism of action: Suppression of inflammatory cytokines
Key features and challenges:
Cyclosporin A (CsA) is a calcineurin inhibitor derived from the soil fungus Tolypocladium inflatum Gams. It suppresses immune responses by blocking the activation and proliferation of cytotoxic T-cells, thereby prolonging survival following organ and bone marrow transplants. This drug prevents and controls serious immune-mediated reactions including allograft rejection, graft versus host disease, and inflammatory autoimmune disease. Initially manufactured by Sandoz and approved for use by the FDA in 1983, cyclosporin is now available in various products by Novartis (previously known as Sandoz) for a range of indications including prevention of organ rejection following a kidney, liver or heart transplant and autoimmune disorders such as psoriasis, myasthenia gravis and rheumatoid arthritis
Because preeclampsia pathogenesis is associated with hyperinflammation and associated immune responses, Cyclosporin A (CsA), which is an effective immunosuppressant, has been proposed as a potential therapeutic to attenuate these systemic inflammatory responses.
Preclinical studies in rat models have demonstrated that CsA effectively attenuated preeclampsia manifestation and eclampsia-like seizure severity. In addition, CsA treatment significantly reduced the inflammatory cytokine levels and improved pregnancy outcomes following eclampsia-like seizures. The decreased inflammatory cytokines in preeclampsia are coincident with attenuated preeclampsia manifestation after CsA treatment, suggesting that CsA treatment might decrease the eclampsia-like seizure severity through decreasing systemic inflammation in preeclasmpsia/eclampsia. (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41440-019-0387-3)

Name: DAISY uterine drain
Developers: Raydiant Oximetry, Inc.
Indication: Indicated for the prevention of postpartum haemorrhage following caesarean delivery.
Mechanism of action: Ultrasound-based speckle tracking quantifies fetal cardiac size and function to detect hemodynamic compromise.
Key features and challenges:
The DAISY uterine drain is inserted post-caesarean delivery and is intended to provide a channel through the cervix for fluid drainage preventing the build-up of fluid and allowing for the restoration of uterine tone. It consists of a soft silicone drainage tube (proximal end) attached to a semi-flexible catheter, inserted through the hysterotomy created at the time of the caesarean delivery. The DAISY drain will be placed intraoperatively after delivery of the placenta, stabilization of the patient, and cleansing of the uterine cavity but prior to closure of the hysterotomy. The drain will be placed through the hysterotomy and threaded through the cervix and vaginal canal, out the introitus, so the distal end is accessible outside of the body. The drain is then placed on continuous suction for the first two postpartum hours or more if required. 

The use of the DAISY drain is being studied with the goal of obtaining user feedback from staff and obstetrical surgeons. In this study, once the drain has been placed, an abdominal ultrasound will be performed to document device placement and to assess uterine involution, approximate uterine size and uterine cavity size, presence of intrauterine clots or retained products of conception. The user will remove the drain after at least two hours post caesarean delivery based on clinical management. The DAISY drain and Instructions for Use (IFU) will be evaluated qualitatively for the following including: ease of drain placement by obstetrician-surgeon, appropriate size of drain, appropriate final location of the deployed drain and incidence of improper placement, ease of drain connection to suction tubing, ease of drain removal, perceived effectiveness of suction and clarity of the IFU. The study is intended to be completed at the end of 2024. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06219538)

According to the company pipeline, preparation for a Phase I clinical study is currently ongoing.
Overall, DARE-PTB1 represents a sustained-release progesterone delivery platform intended to improve adherence and provide more consistent progesterone exposure for preterm birth prevention. Clinical safety and efficacy remain to be established in human trials.

Key features and challenges:
Anoikis, a specific form of apoptosis, occurs when cells detach from the extracellular matrix. Recent research has revealed that anoikis resistance is the most important prerequisite for endometriosis development, but it's still not entirely apparent, yet, what part anoikis plays in endometriosis pathogenesis. 
In a 2025 study, researchers obtained the GSE141549 dataset from the GEO database, which served as a training cohort. Anoikis-related genes (ANRGs), sourced from the GeneCards database, were integrated with differentially expressed genes (DEGs) identified in GSE141549. Consequently, researchers obtained a collection of differentially expressed anoikis-related genes (DE-ANRGs). Next, machine learning algorithms were employed to screen for key diagnostic DE-ANRGs and developed a nomogram model to predict and diagnose endometriosis. Ultimately, findings were validated through in vitro experiments and an online endometriosis database. Within the training cohort, a total of 47 DE-ANRGs were identified. Furthermore, three machine learning methods pinpointed four diagnostic genes (CAV1, PDK4, CSPG4, SERPINE1). Based on these genes, a nomogram was constructed to facilitate the prediction and clinical diagnosis of endometriosis. To assess model's predictive accuracy, clinical adaptability, and discriminative ability, authors performed calibration curves, Receiver Operating Characteristic curves and decision curve analysis. All assessments demonstrated the model's outstanding performance. Ultimately, consistent expression trends of four genes were observed in GSE7305 test cohort, clinical specimens, and the Turku database when compared to the training cohort. In addition, the research revealed the immune landscape differences, which may offer new promising immunotherapeutic targets for endometriosis patients in the future. In addition to offering novel perspectives on the role of anoikis in endometriosis pathogenesis, the analysis also identified a panel of distinctive biomarkers with significant diagnostic potential (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10528-025-11151-x).

Name: DLBS1442
Developers: Dexa Medica Group
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of endometriosis associated pain and infertility.
Target: Angiogenesis; cell migration; estrogen receptors; progesterone receptors; eicosanoid signaling pathway; NFκB (nuclear factor kappa B); inducible nitric oxide synthase.
Mechanism of action: inhibits angiogenesis and cell migration; induces apoptosis in endometrial cells; downregulates oestrogen receptors; upregulates progesterone receptors; disrupts the eicosanoid signalling pathway
Key features and challenges:
DLBS1442 is a bioactive fraction derived from Phaleria macrocarpa Boerl fruit, developed by Dexa Laboratories of Biomolecular Sciences (DLBS). It has been investigated for the treatment of primary dysmenorrhea and for alleviating symptoms associated with endometriosis. As a plant-derived extract, DLBS1442 is proposed to exert anti-inflammatory, anti-angiogenic, and pro-apoptotic effects relevant to endometriosis pathophysiology.

Preclinical investigations published in 2015 demonstrated that DLBS1442 exhibits dose-dependent inhibition of angiogenesis and cell migration, increases apoptosis, and reduces cell viability with an IC50 of approximately 100 μg/mL (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25678821/). 
Mechanistically, DLBS1442 was shown to downregulate estrogen receptor expression, upregulate progesterone receptors, and inhibit the eicosanoid signaling pathway by reducing NFκB transcription and inducible nitric oxide synthase levels. These findings suggest modulation of inflammatory and hormone-responsive pathways implicated in endometriosis.
A Phase 2/3 three-arm, prospective, randomized, double-blind, controlled study (NCT01942122) was completed in 2021 to evaluate DLBS1442 for the treatment of pain in patients with suspected endometriosis (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01942122). 
The trial hypothesized that administration of DLBS1442, irrespective of dosage regimen, would result in a significantly greater reduction in composite pain intensity (measured by Visual Analog Scale [VAS]) from baseline to week 8 compared with control. While the study has been completed, publicly available data detailing efficacy outcomes and safety findings remain limited.
Key challenges include limited availability of peer-reviewed clinical efficacy data, unclear regulatory status, and absence of published long-term safety outcomes. As a botanical extract, standardization, reproducibility, and regulatory pathway considerations may also influence development and market access. Further confirmatory trials and transparent reporting of clinical results are required to define DLBS1442’s role in endometriosis management.
Overall, DLBS1442 demonstrates biologically plausible anti-inflammatory and hormone-modulating effects supported by preclinical evidence and a completed late-phase trial. However, limited publicly available clinical outcome data currently constrain assessment of its therapeutic positioning in endometriosis.
Recent updates: TM 13/12/2025: Study datamined from EMBASE (https://rjptonline.org/AbstractView.aspx?PID=2024-17-8-40).

Name: DM199
Developers: DiaMedica Therapeutics Inc
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: DM199 functions as a protein replacement therapy to restore levels of KLK1, a protein that is typically deficient or impaired in preeclampsia
Key features and challenges:
DM199 is a recombinant formulation of human tissue kallikrein-1 (KLK1), an endogenous serine protease that cleaves kininogen to generate bradykinin. Bradykinin is a potent vasodilator that activates the bradykinin B2 receptor on vascular endothelium, stimulating nitric oxide and prostacyclin production and promoting smooth muscle relaxation. In addition to vasodilatory effects, bradykinin signaling may exert pro-angiogenic, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory actions. Given that preeclampsia (PE) is characterized by endothelial dysfunction, impaired vasodilation, and reduced placental perfusion, therapies that restore vascular function represent a mechanistically attractive approach.
DM199 is structurally identical to endogenous KLK1, with the exception of two amino acid differences. Preclinical and animal toxicology studies, along with clinical trials in non-pregnant populations, have demonstrated that DM199 is generally safe and well tolerated. As a protein-based therapy, it is considered unlikely to cross the placenta in significant amounts, potentially limiting direct fetal exposure. Its vasodilatory properties may improve maternal blood pressure control and enhance uteroplacental perfusion, suggesting potential utility in both PE and fetal growth restriction (FGR).
A 2024 Phase II unblinded clinical trial (PACTR202404895013782) is evaluating the safety and dose optimization of DM199 in women with preeclampsia and/or fetal growth restriction. The study aims to determine an effective and safe dosing regimen in this population, representing one of the first investigations of recombinant tissue kallikrein therapy in pregnancy complicated by placental vascular disorders.
(https://pactr.samrc.ac.za/TrialDisplay.aspx?TrialID=29416).
Key challenges include the limited pregnancy-specific safety data to date and the need to confirm maternal and fetal safety in the context of altered hemodynamics during PE. The unblinded design may limit interpretability of early efficacy signals. Additionally, careful monitoring of potential hypotension, fluid shifts, and off-target vascular effects is required. While DM199 offers a mechanistically targeted strategy addressing endothelial dysfunction, further controlled clinical trials are necessary to establish efficacy, optimal dosing, and long-term maternal and neonatal outcomes.

Name: DUB-negative rMERS-CoV(MA)

Key features and challenges:
-Attenuation: Replicates robustly in hDPP4-KI mice lungs but causes no clinical disease; cleared by day 14 post-infection.
-Immunogenicity: A single intranasal dose induced neutralizing antibody titers (~1:320 by week 7), durable up to ≥11 weeks.
-Protection: Provided sterilizing immunity against lethal wt rMERS-CoVMA challenge; no detectable lung virus, no weight loss, no mortality.
-Passive protection: Transfer of sera from vaccinated mice protected naïve hDPP4-KI mice (71% survival vs 0% controls).
-Cellular responses: Induced IFN-γ producing T-cells; enhanced early innate immune responses (IFN-β, IFN-λ, TNF-α, IL-6) vs wt virus.
-Genetic stability: V1691R mutation retained after serial passages; no reversion to wt detected.
-Challenges: Only tested in hDPP4-KI mice; durability and safety in larger animals or camels unknown; risk of reversion requires further safeguards.
Recent updates:
-Recognized in 2024–2025 reviews as a novel MLV approach for MERS-CoV, exploiting viral immune-evasion factors (PLpro DUB) rather than Spike alone.
-Concept extended to other coronaviruses: DUB-negative SARS-CoV and MHV also show attenuation with preserved immunogenicity, supporting broader vaccine platform potential.

Name: Daflon
