Key features and challenges:
Daflon is a micronised purified flavonoid fraction (MPFF) composed primarily of diosmin (90%) and hesperidin (10%). It is widely used for the management of chronic venous insufficiency due to its venotonic, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant properties. Its mechanisms include improving vascular tone, reducing capillary permeability, and modulating inflammatory pathways.
In 2023, Daflon 500 mg was investigated for potential therapeutic effects in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). The study evaluated its impact on oxidative stress, inflammatory markers, hormonal balance, insulin resistance (measured by HOMA-IR), and PCOS-related clinical symptoms. Quality of life was assessed using the Women’s Health Questionnaire (WHQ), alongside sonographic evaluation of ovarian morphology. The investigation aimed to determine whether Daflon’s antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties could improve metabolic and reproductive parameters in PCOS.
Clinical trial source: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06083935
A separate 2023 preclinical study examined the effects of Daflon and myoinositol in a letrozole-induced rat model of PCOS. PCOS was induced in Wistar rats using letrozole combined with a high-fat diet over 21 days. PCOS-induced rats exhibited disrupted estrous cycles, hormonal imbalance, increased cystic follicles, and reduced numbers of developing follicles. Treatment with Daflon (100 mg/kg) and myoinositol significantly restored estrous cyclicity, improved hormonal profiles, and enhanced ovarian morphology. A lower dose of Daflon (50 mg/kg) demonstrated reduced efficacy. The findings suggest that Daflon’s antioxidant activity may contribute to improvements in reproductive function in PCOS models.
https://rjptonline.org/AbstractView.aspx?PID=2023-16-6-32
Collectively, emerging evidence indicates that Daflon may have therapeutic potential in PCOS through modulation of oxidative stress and inflammatory pathways; however, further clinical studies are required to establish efficacy and long-term safety in human populations.

Developers: Viramal Limited
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Endometriosis.
Mechanism of action: Actin modulators; Capillary permeability modulators; Estrogen receptor alpha antagonist; Testosterone congener stimulants
Key features and challenges:
Danazol is a synthetic steroid with antigonadotropic and anti-estrogenic properties, primarily used to treat endometriosis and benign breast disorders. It works by suppressing the pituitary-ovarian axis, inhibiting the release of gonadotropins, and reducing ovarian estrogen production. This suppression leads to the inactivation and atrophy of both normal and ectopic endometrial tissue, resulting in anovulation and amenorrhea. While danazol was initially the first FDA-approved treatment for endometriosis, its use has been largely replaced by GnRH agonists. Additionally, danazol may directly inhibit ovarian steroidogenesis and bind to various hormone receptors. It also helps manage hereditary angioedema by increasing C1 esterase inhibitor levels. (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB01406)
VML 0501 is a vaginal formulation of danazol under development by Viramal for the treatment of endometriosis and infertility. Originally approved in the 1970s for endometriosis, oral danazol is now being explored in a new form. 
As of September 2023, a Phase IIb trial for infertility is ongoing at an undisclosed location, and the danazol cream is still in Phase II development for endometriosis as of April 2021. 
A previous Phase II trial, completed in May 2020, compared the vaginal cream to oral danazol capsules in women with suspected or confirmed endometriosis, involving 30 participants in Italy. (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800051887)

Name: Dapagliflozin
Developers: Zahedan University of Medical Sciences; Beni-Suef University; Southern Medical University ; AstraZeneca
Indication: PCOS metabolic disorders, insulin resistance, obesity, infertility, and dyslipidemia
Mechanism of action: Sodium-glucose transporter 2 inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Dapagliflozin (Forxiga®), developed by AstraZeneca, is an oral sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor approved for type 2 diabetes, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease. It lowers plasma glucose by inhibiting renal glucose reabsorption, promoting glycosuria and improving glycaemic control. Fixed-dose combinations with metformin are available in several markets.
https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800021756
Although not guideline-endorsed for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), dapagliflozin has been investigated for its potential to address insulin resistance, obesity, and cardiometabolic dysfunction in PCOS.
A completed 2021 clinical study (NCT02635386) compared exenatide once weekly, dapagliflozin, their combination, dapagliflozin/metformin XR, and phentermine/topiramate ER in overweight or obese, non-diabetic women with PCOS. Dapagliflozin improved metabolic parameters, while dual therapy with exenatide and dapagliflozin demonstrated superior metabolic outcomes compared to monotherapy.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02635386
https://academic.oup.com/jcem/article/106/10/3019/6294193
A clinical trial completed in 2022 (NCT04213677) evaluated the efficacy and safety of dapagliflozin in improving insulin resistance and hyperandrogenemia in obese women with PCOS.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04213677
A 2022-initiated randomized clinical trial (NCT05601336) is comparing metformin monotherapy, dapagliflozin monotherapy, combined therapy, and control in 200 infertile women with PCOS to assess hormonal, metabolic, and clinical outcomes.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05601336
In 2024, additional trials are evaluating dapagliflozin in ovulation induction and assisted reproduction settings. One trial (NCT06405178) is assessing dapagliflozin, metformin, and combination therapy as adjuvant treatments during letrozole-induced ovulation, focusing on ovulation and pregnancy rates.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06405178
Another 2024 study is examining dapagliflozin–metformin combination therapy in women with PCOS undergoing IVF.
https://irct.behdasht.gov.ir/trial/75855
Preclinical evidence from an obese PCOS mouse model demonstrated that dapagliflozin reduced weight gain, improved insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance, normalized lipid profiles, and improved adipose tissue morphology compared with controls and metformin-treated groups.
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0014299924004308?via%3Dihub
Despite promising metabolic benefits, dapagliflozin is not currently included in PCOS management guidelines. Its effects appear primarily metabolic rather than directly ovulatory or endocrine-modifying. Safety considerations include genital mycotic infections, volume depletion, and rare risk of ketoacidosis, particularly in insulin-deficient states.
Dapagliflozin represents an emerging metabolic adjunct therapy for PCOS, with growing clinical evidence supporting improvements in insulin resistance and cardiometabolic parameters. Its definitive role in ovulation induction and fertility outcomes remains under investigation in ongoing randomized trials.

Name: Dapivirine + levonorgestrel intravaginal ring

A paper describing the results of both the MTN-030/IPM 041 and MTN-044/IPM 053/CCN019 studies was published in the open access journal PLoS One on June 5, 2024. 
A 90-day Phase Ib study of the safety and PK of two different vaginal ring formulations (NCT05041699) has been completed at sites in Oregon and Pennsylvania.
Recent updates: Phase Ib study completed in 2024 (NCT05041699).

Name: Dasatinib and Quercetin (DQ)
Developers: University of Tokyo (including the Graduate School of Agricultural and Life Sciences)
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Target: Senescent cells, particularly within ovarian and adipose tissues
Mechanism of action: Dasatinib and Quercetin target and eliminate senescent cells, reducing inflammation, oxidative stress, and fibrosis. In PCOS, this may improve ovarian and metabolic functions.
Key features and challenges:
Dasatinib and quercetin (DQ) is a senolytic combination therapy that selectively targets and eliminates senescent cells. Dasatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor approved for certain hematologic malignancies, while quercetin is a plant-derived flavonoid with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. Interest in DQ for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) arises from emerging evidence that cellular senescence contributes to ovarian dysfunction, chronic inflammation, and insulin resistance—key features of PCOS.
Early experimental work suggested that senescent cell accumulation may impair granulosa cell function and follicular development in PCOS, providing a rationale for senolytic intervention https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jog.15918
. Building on this, a 2024 preclinical study demonstrated elevated senescence markers in ovarian tissue from both PCOS patients and letrozole-induced PCOS mouse models. Hyperandrogenism was shown to induce granulosa cell senescence, while DQ treatment reduced senescence markers, improved ovarian morphology, and partially restored follicular structure https://academic.oup.com/molehr/article/30/5/gaae015/7644292
These findings position DQ as a mechanistically novel therapeutic approach targeting a potentially upstream driver of PCOS pathology—cellular aging and inflammatory signaling—rather than solely managing downstream hormonal or metabolic consequences. However, current evidence remains preclinical. Dasatinib carries known safety concerns, including myelosuppression and cardiovascular effects, and the safety profile of intermittent senolytic therapy in reproductive-age women has not been established. Human clinical trials in PCOS have not yet been conducted.

Name: Deb 1453
Developers: Debiopharm
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Inhibits the fatty acid synthesis (FASII) pathway in N. gonorrhoeae by interfering with FabI, an enoyl-acyl carrier protein (ACP) reductase
Key features and challenges:
Debio 1453 is a novel antibiotic candidate developed by Debiopharm for the treatment of Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections. It selectively targets FabI (enoyl-acyl carrier protein reductase), an essential enzyme in bacterial fatty acid biosynthesis required for the growth and survival of N. gonorrhoeae. By inhibiting FabI, Debio 1453 disrupts membrane lipid synthesis, leading to bactericidal activity.
The compound has demonstrated potent in vitro activity against N. gonorrhoeae, including strains resistant to currently available antibiotics. Its species-targeted mechanism is designed to minimize disruption of commensal microbiota, thereby reducing selective pressure on non-target organisms and potentially lowering the risk of broader antimicrobial resistance development. This microbiota-sparing profile represents a strategic advantage compared with broad-spectrum antibiotics traditionally used in gonorrhoea treatment.
Debio 1453 is being advanced with support from the Combating Antibiotic-Resistant Bacteria Biopharmaceutical Accelerator (CARB-X), reflecting its potential role in addressing antimicrobial-resistant gonorrhoea. A clinical trial registered in the European Union (EUCT 2024-519328-26-01) is evaluating its safety, tolerability, and efficacy in human subjects.
https://euclinicaltrials.eu/search-for-clinical-trials/?lang=en&EUCT=2024-519328-26-01
Despite promising microbiological activity, clinical evidence remains limited pending results from ongoing trials. Key considerations include resistance emergence, pharmacokinetic optimization for urogenital and extragenital infection sites, and confirmation of microbiota-sparing effects in vivo.
Debio 1453 represents a targeted antimicrobial approach with a novel mechanism of action against N. gonorrhoeae. Its development aligns with global efforts to address antibiotic-resistant gonorrhoea, although clinical validation is required to establish efficacy and safety in patients.
Recent updates: First-in-class antibiotic to treat NG, targeting Fabl (enoyl-acyl carrier protein (ACP) reductase)

Name: DeepHit/PE
Developers: Harvard Medical School; University of Washington; Brigham and Women’s Hospital
Indication: Indicated for the detection of Preeclampsia risk
Health care facility level: IVDs for research use only
Mechanism of action: Nonparametric neural network architecture that captures complex, time-varying relationships between clinical variables
Key features and challenges: In this 2024 study, the authors present a methodology to model the temporal risk of preeclampsia during pregnancy and investigate the associated clinical risk factors. A retrospective study utilized a dataset including 66,425 pregnant individuals who delivered in two tertiary care centers from 2015-2023. The authors modeled the preeclampsia risk by modifying DeepHit, a deep survival model, which leverages neural network architecture to capture time-varying relationships between covariates in pregnancy. The results demonstrated that DeepHit can effectively handle high-dimensional data and evolving risk hazards over time with performance similar to the Cox Proportional Hazards model, achieving an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.78 for both models. The deep survival model outperformed traditional methodology by identifying time-varied risk trajectories for preeclampsia, providing insights for early and individualized intervention. K-means clustering resulted in patients delineating into low-risk, early-onset, and late-onset preeclampsia groups— notably, each of those has distinct risk factors (https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.01.18.24301456v1)

The drug, approved by the FDA for prostate cancer on December 24, 2008, is a linear decapeptide amide containing seven unnatural amino acids, five of which are D-amino acids. (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800016314; https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/16136245)
An abstract from 2023 reported on a study which examined three animals, including one with previous ovariectomy, which received 40 mg of Degarelix every 40 days for one year. The treatment led to significant reductions in endometriosis-associated pain and improvement in symptoms, as evidenced by lower levels of FSH, LH, and estradiol. The study suggests that Degarelix is a promising and affordable option for managing endometriosis in laboratory animals. (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10597326/)

Name: Delta-cadinene
Developers: Universidade Federal de Pernambuco
Indication: Treating Trichomoniasis infection
Mechanism of action: Cytotoxic Activity
Key features and challenges:
Delta-cadinene is a sesquiterpene identified as a major bioactive component of essential oils derived from Myrtaceae plants, particularly Eugenia pohliana. Essential oils from this species (EOEp) have been investigated as potential antiparasitic agents against Trichomonas vaginalis, especially in the context of emerging resistance to standard 5-nitroimidazole therapies.
In a 2022 study, EOEp demonstrated in vitro activity against both reference and clinical strains of T. vaginalis (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14786419.2022.2101050). 
The antiparasitic effect was attributed to the complex phytochemical profile of the essential oil, with delta-cadinene identified as a principal component likely contributing to activity. The study reported moderate cytotoxicity to mammalian cells; however, EOEp showed favorable selectivity toward vaginal epithelial cells, suggesting potential suitability for localized application. Additionally, a synergistic interaction between EOEp and metronidazole was observed, indicating that combination therapy could enhance efficacy against T. vaginalis.
Key challenges include the early in vitro stage of evidence, variability inherent to plant-derived essential oil compositions, and the need for standardized extraction, characterization, and formulation processes. Further evaluation in in vivo models is required to confirm efficacy, safety, and tolerability. Regulatory considerations for botanical or essential oil–based therapeutics may also influence development pathways.
Overall, delta-cadinene–containing essential oils from Eugenia pohliana demonstrate promising in vitro antitrichomonal activity, including synergy with metronidazole. Advancement into in vivo studies and standardized formulation development will be essential to determine their therapeutic potential in trichomoniasis.

Name: Dexamedtomidine - PE/E
Developers: Assiut University
Indication: Improve intracranial pressure in pre-eclampsia
Mechanism of action: Dexmedetomidine is a specific and selective alpha-2 adrenoceptor agonist. By binding to the presynaptic alpha-2 adrenoceptors, it inhibits the release of norepinephrine, therefore, terminate the propagation of pain signals. Activation of the postsynaptic alpha-2 adrenoceptors inhibits the sympathetic activity decreases blood pressure and heart rate.
Key features and challenges:
Preeclampsia is associated with significant maternal complications, including cerebral edema. The cerebral edema observed in severe cases is predominantly vasogenic and may result from impaired cerebral autoregulation, leading to hyperperfusion, blood–brain barrier disruption, and endothelial dysfunction.
The optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) has been used as a non-invasive surrogate marker of intracranial pressure (ICP), as the optic nerve subarachnoid space communicates directly with the intracranial subarachnoid space. Increases in ONSD correlate with elevations in ICP and may reflect central nervous system involvement in preeclampsia.
Magnesium sulphate (MgSO₄) remains the standard therapy for seizure prophylaxis in preeclampsia and eclampsia and is believed to exert neuroprotective effects through multiple mechanisms.
Dexmedetomidine is a selective alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonist that induces cerebral vasoconstriction through postsynaptic alpha-2 receptor stimulation on cerebral blood vessels, resulting in decreased cerebral blood flow. This mechanism has led to investigation of dexmedetomidine as a potential adjunct therapy to reduce intracranial pressure and mitigate cerebral complications in preeclampsia.
A registered clinical trial (NCT05119101) is evaluating the role of dexmedetomidine in patients with preeclampsia, including its effects on optic nerve sheath diameter and related cerebral parameters.
(Source: https://classic.clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT05119101)
Overall, dexmedetomidine is being explored for its potential neuroprotective and cerebral hemodynamic effects in PE/E. Clinical efficacy and safety data in this population remain under investigation.

Mechanism of action: Immunomodulation through the induction of Th1 cytokine phenotypes, triggering a high apoptotic profile, reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, and antioxidant enzymes.
Key features and challenges: 2024 study aimed to explore diallyl sulfide (DAS), a dynamic constituent of garlic, alone and in a mixture with meglumine antimoniate (MAT as standard drug) using in vitro and animal model experiments against Leishmania major stages. The binding affinity of DAS and four major defense elements of the immune system (iNOS, IFN-ɣ, IL-12, and TNF-α) was used to predict the predominant binding mode for molecular docking configurations. Herein, we conducted a broad range of experiments to monitor and assess DAS and MAT potential treatment outcomes. DAS, combined with MAT, displayed no cytotoxicity and employed a powerful anti-leishmanial activity, notably against the clinical stage. The function mechanism involved immunomodulation through the induction of Th1 cytokine phenotypes, triggering a high apoptotic profile, reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, and antioxidant enzymes. This combination significantly decreased cutaneous lesion diameter and parasite load in BALB/c mice. The histopathological findings performed the infiltration of inflammatory cells associated with T-lymphocytes, particularly CD4+ phenotypes, as determined by biochemical markers in alleviating the amastigote stage and improving the pathological changes in L. major infected BALB/c mice.

Name: Diastolic notch + Doppler Ultrasound indices
Developers: Government Thoothukudi Medical College; Government Sivagangai Medical  College,
Indication: Indicated for the prediction of preeclampsia at 20-24 weeks of pregnancy
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Mechanism of action: Identifies impaired trophoblastic invasion and high-resistance uteroplacental circulation
Key features and challenges:
Uterine artery Doppler ultrasound assessment, including evaluation of diastolic notching and Doppler indices such as systolic/diastolic (S/D) ratio, resistance index (RI), and pulsatility index (PI), is a non-invasive tool used to assess uteroplacental blood flow. Abnormal uterine artery Doppler findings reflect increased vascular resistance and impaired placental perfusion, which are central features in the pathophysiology of preeclampsia (PE). A persistent early diastolic (ED) notch is considered a marker of abnormal trophoblastic invasion and reduced spiral artery remodeling.
A 2024 prospective observational study involving 150 high-risk antenatal mothers evaluated the predictive value of uterine artery Doppler findings performed at 20–24 weeks’ gestation (https://academicmed.org/Uploads/Volume6Issue1/314.%20[2307.%20JAMP_Mohamed%20Ali]%201582-1585.pdf). 
Preeclampsia developed in 24 (16%) patients. Among 30 women with abnormal uterine artery Doppler indices (S/D ratio, RI, PI), 24 subsequently developed PE, yielding a sensitivity of 91.67%, positive predictive value (PPV) of 73.33%, and overall accuracy of 93.3%. A persistent ED notch was observed in 14 of the 24 PE cases, corresponding to a sensitivity of 58.33%, PPV of 87.5%, and accuracy of 92%. These findings suggest that abnormal Doppler indices may have strong predictive utility for PE in high-risk populations, while persistent ED notch alone may demonstrate lower sensitivity but relatively high PPV.
Key challenges include variability in operator technique, equipment standardization, and interpretation thresholds across settings. Doppler screening performance may differ in low-risk versus high-risk populations. Additionally, while predictive accuracy appears high in this cohort, the modest sample size and single-center design limit generalizability. Integration of Doppler findings with other predictive markers—such as angiogenic biomarkers or clinical risk models—may improve overall screening performance. Further large-scale prospective validation is needed to define optimal use in routine antenatal screening for preeclampsia.

Name: Dichromatic CD81 protein biosensor
Developers: Nanjing University of Science and Technology
Indication: Prediction of preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: Protein CD81 levels in biological samples
Mechanism of action: Detects CD81 protein expression using optical biosensing to identify placental extracellular vesicle signatures associated with preeclampsia.
Key features and challenges:
Researchers at Nanjing University of Science and Technology are creating a sensor for the protein CD81, identified as a new biomarker for PE. They’ve proposed a highly sensitive dichromatic biosensor using plasmonic ELISA for early screening. The design features a new chromogenic substrate [(HAuCl4)-(N-methylpyrrolidone)-(Na3C6H5O7)] based on the H2O2 dual catalysis reduction of Au ions. The amount of H2O2 reflects CD81 levels and controls the formation of differently sized AuNPs. When analytes are present, the solution turns blue; without them, it turns red. This color change allows bimodal detection with signals at 550 nm (on) and 600 nm (off). The method shows a linear response to CD81 concentrations from 0.1–1000 pg/mL, with detection limits of 86 fg/mL and 152 fg/mL at the two wavelengths. Low false positives result from serum-related nonspecific coloration, which enhances color contrast. These findings suggest the sensor could serve as a visual platform for detecting CD81 in biological samples and holds promise for diagnosing preeclampsia.
(https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/2023/an/d3an00213f)

Name: Didroxyprogesterone
Developers: Sun Yat-sen University
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of endometriosis symptoms and infertility
Mechanism of action: binds to progesterone receptors, leading to changes in gene expression that support the maintenance of pregnancy and the regulation of the menstrual cycle
Key features and challenges:
Didroxyprogesterone is a synthetic progestogen with properties closest to natural progesterone. It is commonly used in luteal phase support and treatment of threatened abortion. Unlike other hormonal therapies, didroxyprogesterone does not inhibit ovulation and is considered safe for embryos, making it suitable for women with endometriosis who are trying to conceive.  In recent years, clinical studies have found that it is helpful to the natural pregnancy of patients with endometriosis after operation, and is beneficial to improve pain symptoms and reduce the recurrence rate. Basic studies have also confirmed the inhibitory effect of didroxyprogesterone on endometriosis. 
A multicenter, prospective, open, randomized controlled clinical trial started in 2022 to investigate the effectiveness of didroxyprogesterone in improving postoperative natural pregnancy rates in women with endometriosis. Women aged 22-35, diagnosed with mild to moderate endometriosis by laparoscopic surgery and had undergone surgical treatment are stratified and randomized based on their fertility index (EFI) score. The trial compares a didroxyprogesterone group with a control group that receives no medication, monitoring pregnancy rates, endometriosis recurrence, and related symptoms over 12 menstrual cycles. The primary outcomes include pregnancy status and safety assessments, with follow-ups occurring at specific intervals throughout the study to gather data on endometriosis symptoms, recurrence, and drug safety.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05467852).

Name: Dienogest - Uterine Fibroids
Developers: Esfahan University of Medical Sciences; Bayer Healthcare
Indication: uterine fibroids associated pain and fibroid volume
Mechanism of action: Progesterone receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
Dienogest is a progestogen with selective progesterone receptor binding, high progestational and anti-androgenic activity, and moderate anti-gonadotrophic effects. It inhibits ovulation, transforms the endometrium, and has anti-proliferative effects. Developed by Bayer HealthCare Pharmaceuticals and originally by Jenapharm (Schering AG), dienogest is used for contraception, menopausal syndrome, dysmenorrhea, and endometriosis. It is approved in many countries for endometriosis treatment and is currently under clinical development for adenomyosis and endometriosis in various regions. (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800008297)

A 2024 retrospective analysis of dienogest in patients with endometriosis or adenomyosis combined with uterine fibroids, showed it can effectively relieve the patient's pain symptoms and significantly reduce the sizes of ovarian endometriotic cysts, but it cannot inhibit uterine fibroid growth. (http://dx.doi.org/10.12998/wjcc.v12.i21.4601)

In a 2011 published other study, it was found that, Uterine myoma volume was successfully reduced by use of dienogest. Consideration of GnRHa disadvantages may lead to short- or long-term management of women with myoma who are to be managed transiently, and who wish to avoid surgical intervention, especially perimenopausal women. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21052701/)

Most recently, a 2023 2 arm randomized clinical trial aimed to assess the impact of Dienogest and N-Acetyl Cysteine on volume reduction of uterine leiomyoma. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06115408)

Name: Diffusion tensor imaging
Developers: Assistance Publique - Hôpitaux de Paris
Indication: Indicated for the diagnosis of nerve damage in pelvic endometriosis.
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: MRI-based diffusion mapping evaluates tissue microstructure and nerve involvement to identify endometriosis-associated fibrosis and lesions.
Key features and challenges:
This 2025 clinical trial (NCT06908655) focuses on evaluating the ability of diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) to detect nerve damage in pelvic endometriosis. The primary objective is to visualize pelvic nerve plexuses to better understand the mechanisms of endometriosis-related neuropathic pain. Secondary objectives include comparing nerve damage between women with and without endometriosis.
The trial includes 110 women with symptoms compatible with endometriosis, in Paris hospitals (Hôpital Cochin and HEGP). The expected duration of the research is 2 years, with individual participation of 3 months (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06908655).

Name: Dihydroartemisinin
Developers: Shanghai Zhongshan Hospital
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of PCOS-related hyperandrogenism
Mechanism of action: Cell inhibitors; Free radical stimulants; Sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium-transporting ATPase inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Dihydroartemisinin is the active metabolite of all artemisinin compounds (artemisinin, artesunate, artemether, etc.). It is a semi-synthetic derivative of artemisinin and is widely used as an intermediate in the preparation of other artemisinin-derived antimalarial drugs. It is marketed for the treatment of malaria in combination with Piperaquine.

Two studies investigated the therapeutic potential of artemisinin derivatives for PCOS. A phase II study completed in 2023 in Shanghai aimed to investigate the effect of artemisinin on improving menstrual regularity, ovarian morphology and serum androgen levels in PCOS subjects. No results have been published yet.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05465135) 
A study estimated to complete in 2025, aims to explore the therapeutic effects of dihydroartemisinin in patients with PCOS who met at least two of three (≥2) Rotterdam Criteria. Outcomes measures are menstrual regularity, number of immature follicles and serum anti-Mullerian hormone and Free androgen index. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06417099)

Name: Dihydrofuro[3,2-c]coumarins
Developers: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Marathwada University (BAMU)
Indication: Investigated for the inhibition of Trichomoniasis.
Target: Catalytic cleft of purine nucleoside phosphorylase of Trichomonas vaginalis.
Mechanism of action: Selective binding at the highly conserved active site catalytic cleft of Trichomonas vaginalis purine nucleoside phosphorylase (TvPNP), the indispensable enzyme of the protozoan purine salvage pathway and potent anti-trichomoniasis drug target.
Key features and challenges:
The dihydrofuro[3,2-c]coumarin (DHFC) derivatives synthesized through a one-pot, three-component reaction display promising potential as anti-trichomoniasis agents. Utilizing aryl/hetryl aldehydes, substituted phenacyl bromides, and 4-hydroxycoumarin in an N,N-diisopropyl ethyl ammonium acetate (DIPEAc) medium, this novel approach efficiently produces diversely substituted DHFC compounds. These derivatives were modeled in silico to selectively bind at the active site of the enzyme purine nucleoside phosphorylase (TvPNP), a critical target for inhibiting the protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis. Molecular dynamics simulations and binding affinity predictions indicate these DHFC compounds possess strong binding affinities, suggesting their potential as therapeutic leads for trichomoniasis treatment.
A 2022 publication presents a streamlined synthetic method to generate DHFC derivatives and evaluates their potential as anti-trichomoniasis drugs. By modeling the interaction of these compounds with the TvPNP enzyme through pharmacophore analysis, researchers could observe selective binding in the enzyme’s catalytic cleft. This binding was further supported by simulations, which predicted favorable free energy profiles and strong affinity for the active site. The structural resemblance of these derivatives to FormycinA, an established TvPNP inhibitor, underscores their potential. The study’s quantitative structure–function analysis suggests these DHFC derivatives could be promising therapeutic leads against trichomoniasis, paving the way for future drug development efforts. (https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/2022/nj/d2nj03838b).

Name: Dihydrotestosterone
Developers: All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS)
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS via detection of hyperandrogenism
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Measures circulating dihydrotestosterone to assess potent androgen activity and hyperandrogenism associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Dihydrotestosterone (DHT) is a potent androgen derived from testosterone, often elevated in women with PCOS, contributing to symptoms like hirsutism and acne. It is a reliable biomarker for diagnosing biochemical hyperandrogenism due to its stability and strong androgenic effects. Studies show DHT has high diagnostic accuracy, making it useful for confirming PCOS and distinguishing it from other conditions. Blood tests measuring DHT levels can aid in diagnosis and guide treatment.

A study on PCOS in North Indian women evaluated androgens in 137 cases and 49 controls, finding elevated levels of testosterone, FAI, DHEAS, androstenedione, and Dihydrotestosterone. 
Dihydrotestosterone was the most reliable biomarker, with significantly higher levels in PCOS cases (mean 584.27 pg/mL) compared to controls (257.15 pg/mL) and the highest diagnostic accuracy (ROC 0.895). The study identifies DHT as the best diagnostic marker for hyperandrogenemia in PCOS women from this population. (https://www.jcdr.net/article_fulltext.asp?issn=0973-709x&year=2022&month=February&volume=16&issue=2&page=QC09-QC14&id=15962)

Name: Diltiazem
Developers: Assembly Biosciences Inc; Beijing CoSci Med-Tech Co Ltd; Women's hospital, Hospital de la Mujer; SLA Pharma AG; Blue Note Therapeutics
Indication: Management of postpartum preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: Inducing vasodilation by inhibiting calcium ion influx into cardiac and vascular smooth muscle cells
Key features and challenges:
Diltiazem is a benzothiazepine derivative with antihypertensive and vasodilating properties. It was approved in 1982 by the FDA and is used clinically as an antihypertensive, anti-arrhythmic, and as an anti-anginal agent due to its potent vasodilation effect. Apart from its main FDA-approved indications, diltiazem has also been used for numerous off-label indications, such as anal fissures (in topical formulations), migraine prophylaxis, pulmonary hypertension, and rest-related cramps in the lower extremities. 
A clinical study (NCT04222855) was conducted in 2009 to investigate the efficacy of diltiazem for blood pressure control in puerperal patients with severe preeclampsia. It showed that Diltiazem controlled arterial hypertension in a more effective and uniform manner in patients under study than nifedipine. Patients treated with diltiazem also had fewer collateral effects and spent less time in the hospital. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32774912/)
Blue Note has initiated phase III development of an immediate/extended-release combination product, called BNP 32762, for the treatment of hypertension and angina pectoris. However, no recent development has been reported.
A 2023 meta-analysis and systematic review shows that of eight RCTs included in the study, Diltiazem was the most effective in reducing blood pressure in PE patients; Labetalol and Nicardipine also had good effects. Diltiazem is preferred for the treatment of patients with severe PE and high blood pressure (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10641955.2024.2329068)
Recent updates:
2023: According to the eight RCTs included in this study, Diltiazem was the most effective in reducing blood pressure in PE patients; Labetalol and Nicardipine also had good effects. Diltiazem is preferred for the treatment of patients with severe PE and high blood pressure. https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10641955.2024.2329068#:~:text=Conclusion-,According%20to%20the%20eight%20RCTs%20included%20in%20this%20study%2C%20Diltiazem,and%20high%20blood%20pressure%20levels.

2020: Results of the 2009 trial (NCT04222855) were published. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32774912/).

Name: Dimethyl itaconate
Developers: Shahid Chamran University of Ahvaz
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: DMI interacts with key pathways in inflammation and oxidative stress. it is known to suppress inflammatory cytokines like TNF-α and IL-1β and reduce oxidative stress markers
Key features and challenges:
Dimethyl itaconate (DMI) is a cell-permeable derivative of itaconic acid known for its anti-inflammatory and antioxidative properties. It exerts its biological effects primarily through modulation of macrophage activity, suppression of pro-inflammatory signaling pathways, and reduction of oxidative stress. These mechanisms are relevant to polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), where chronic low-grade inflammation, oxidative stress, and insulin resistance contribute to ovarian dysfunction and metabolic disturbance.
A 2024 preclinical study evaluated the effects of DMI in a testosterone enanthate–induced PCOS rat model. Forty-eight female Wistar rats were divided into six groups, including untreated PCOS, PCOS treated with DMI, and PCOS treated with metformin. After 30 days of treatment, DMI significantly improved insulin resistance and reduced inflammatory cytokines, including TNF-α and IL-1β. It also decreased oxidative stress index (OSI). Histological assessment demonstrated improved steroidogenesis and folliculogenesis, with reduced cystic follicle formation and partial restoration of normal ovarian architecture. These findings indicate that DMI may address multiple core PCOS mechanisms, including metabolic dysregulation, inflammation, oxidative stress, and ovarian structural abnormalities.
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0960076024000943?via%3Dihub
However, the evidence remains limited to animal studies. No human clinical trials have yet evaluated DMI in PCOS populations, and its safety profile, optimal dosing, pharmacokinetics, and long-term effects in reproductive-age women are unknown. Additionally, translation from rodent models to human endocrine-metabolic conditions requires careful validation.
Dimethyl itaconate represents an early-stage, mechanistically plausible candidate targeting inflammatory and oxidative pathways in PCOS, but substantial clinical research is required before it can be considered for therapeutic use in humans.

Name: Dimorphic invasion-involved protein A multi-epitope vaccine
Developers: Cairo University; University of Tubingen (including the Natural and Medical Sciences Institute, NMI)
Indication: Indicated for the prevention of Streptococcus pneumoniae.
Mechanism of action: Ilicits immune response.
Key features and challenges:
A promising replacement for the current capsular antigen vaccines is the use of epitope-based vaccinations, which may contain various combinations of conserved virulence proteins.
This study explains the design of a novel multi-epitope vaccine using Dimorphic invasion-involved protein A (DiiA) as a target protein. For designing the vaccine, the sequence of DiiA was obtained and various bioinformatics tools were employed to predict multiple CTL, HTL, B lymphocyte epitopes of DiiA. After evaluating antigenicity, allergenicity, toxicity, and immunogenicity, the most promising epitopes were chosen for constructing the vaccine, followed by an analysis of their physicochemical and immunological characteristics. The prediction, refinement, and validation of the 3D structure of the vaccine were carried out. Molecular docking, molecular dynamic simulation, and immune simulation were executed to examine the binding affinities and biological interactions at the atomic level between the vaccine and Toll-like receptor (TLR4). Vaccine translation, codon optimization were performed and expression efficiency was assessed through an in-silico cloning experiment performed to transfer into pET28a(+) plasmid vector. The obtained results proved that the vaccine maintained structural stability and possessed the capability to stimulate an efficient immune response against S. pneumoniae infection. The constructed vaccine has the potential for subsequent wet lab experimentation, leading to the development of an innovative vaccine
(https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2023.09.26.559565v1.full).

Name: Dipyridamole
Developers: Hebrew University of Jerusalem; Magee-Womens Research Institute & Foundation; Kaplan Medical Center
Indication: Indicated for the prevention of preeclampsia
Target: platelet hyperactivity, vascular dysfunction, and excessive placental inflammation
Mechanism of action: Dipyridamole acts as a phosphodiesterase inhibitor and adenosine reuptake inhibitor mitigating the underlying placental insufficiency by improving blood flow and reducing placental damage.
Key features and challenges:
Dipyridamole is an antiplatelet and vasodilatory agent traditionally used for prevention of thromboembolic events. It inhibits phosphodiesterase activity and blocks cellular uptake of adenosine, leading to increased intracellular cyclic AMP and enhanced vasodilation. Beyond its vascular effects, emerging evidence suggests dipyridamole may exert antioxidant properties and modulate oxidative stress pathways. Given that preeclampsia (PE) is characterized by endothelial dysfunction, angiogenic imbalance, and placental oxidative injury, drug repurposing strategies targeting these mechanisms have been explored.
A 2025 study investigated oxidized phosphatidylethanolamines in placental tissues from women with preeclampsia compared with normotensive controls using redox phospholipidomics (https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/HYPERTENSIONAHA.125.25003). 
Preeclamptic placentas demonstrated significant accumulation of oxidized phosphatidylethanolamines. In placental explants, induction of ferroptosis—an iron-dependent form of lipid peroxidation–mediated cell death—increased soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1) release, a key anti-angiogenic factor implicated in PE pathogenesis. Inhibition of ferroptosis using Ferrostatin-1 and deferoxamine significantly reduced sFlt-1 levels (P<0.01). A high-throughput screen of 6,520 compounds identified dipyridamole and promethazine as potent ferroptosis inhibitors in primary trophoblasts. Dipyridamole reduced lipid peroxidation, preserved glutathione levels, and decreased sFlt-1 release in preeclamptic explants, suggesting modulation of oxidative and angiogenic dysregulation.
These findings support placental ferroptosis as a mechanistic contributor to early preeclampsia and identify dipyridamole as a candidate for therapeutic repurposing.
Key challenges include the limitation of current evidence to in vitro and ex vivo models, without clinical data demonstrating efficacy in pregnant populations with PE. Although dipyridamole has an established cardiovascular safety profile, pregnancy-specific pharmacokinetics, optimal dosing, and maternal–fetal safety require thorough evaluation. Additionally, PE is multifactorial, and targeting ferroptosis alone may not address all pathogenic pathways

Name: Diterpenoid compound 9
Developers: Kunming Medical University (formerly known as Kunming Medical College); Yunnan University; Yunnan Key Laboratory of Cross-border Infectious Disease Prevention and Control and New Drug Creation, Kunming
Indication: Antiviral therapy against ZIKV infection
Mechanism of action: Directly inactivates ZIKV virions by altering physicochemical properties (reducing surface charge, increasing particle size distribution), enhancing prM protein thermal stability, and binding/stabilizing prM via hydrophobic interactions; disrupts viral particle integrity and reduces viral load.
Key features and challenges:
Features:
-Potent in vitro anti-ZIKV activity (EC₅₀ ≈ 3.95 µM; CC₅₀ ≈ 272 µM; high selectivity index).
-More effective than ribavirin in comparative assays.
-Reduces viral plaque formation and replication in ZIKV-infected Vero cells.

Challenges:
-Potential limitations due to natural product variability and large-scale production.
Recent updates: 2025 Publication: Identified compound 9 as a lead diterpenoid from Euphorbia helioscopia with direct ZIKV inactivation properties via prM protein targeting.

Name: Dolutegravir + Lamivudine
Developers: Johns Hopkins University (including the Bloomberg School of Public Health and the Center for Health Security)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of HIV-1 infection.

Mechanism of action: HIV integrase inhibitors; HIV integrase inhibitors, Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors; Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors; Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors; Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, Nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors; Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors; Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors; Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors; Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, Nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors; Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, Nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors; Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, Nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors
Key features and challenges: A small-molecule oral antiretroviral combination pairing an HIV integrase strand-transfer inhibitor with a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor to block viral integration and reverse transcription. Taken orally. Investigated in HIV-1 and broader HIV infection.
Recent updates: A Phase 3 trial (NCT06497465) evaluating dual therapy versus standard of care in antiretroviral-naive people with HIV-1 receiving rifampin-based tuberculosis treatment began in 2025 and is recruiting.

Name: Dolutegravir + Lamivudine + Tenofovir
Developers: University of Nairobi
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of HIV-1 infection.
Mechanism of action: HIV protease inhibitors
Key features and challenges: A small-molecule oral antiretroviral combination intended to suppress HIV-1 replication. Taken orally. Investigated in HIV-1 infection.

Name: Doramectin
Developers: Sun Yat-sen University; South China Normal University; Guangdong Pharmaceutical University
Indication: Treatment of ZIKV infection; prevention of neurological complications (microcephaly, GBS, meningoencephalitis).
Target: ZIKV NS5 RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), “N pocket” near the active site
Mechanism of action: Directly binds ZIKV RdRp (Kd ~16.9 μM by SPR), interfering with RNA synthesis; inhibits viral replication with EC50 values 0.85–3 μM in Vero, A549, and SNB19 cells; suppresses ZIKV NS5 and E protein expression; prevents ZIKV infection in cell-based assays without significant cytotoxicity (CC50 >50 μM).
Key features and challenges:
-Potent in vitro anti-ZIKV activity with high selectivity index (>59 in Vero cells).
-Veterinary-approved drug with some safety history in animals, including pregnant cows.
-Potential suitability for pregnant women suggested, but human PK/safety data for antiviral use lacking.
-Needs further optimization for bioavailability and translation beyond animal health.
FDA-approved veterinary macrolide antiparasitic repurposed as antiviral (macrocyclic lactone)
Recent updates:
-2024–2025 reviews highlight doramectin among macrocyclic lactones with antiviral promise (building on ivermectin precedent).
-No registered clinical trials for ZIKV, but interest remains in structure-guided RdRp inhibition for flaviviruses.

Name: Doravirine + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir
Developers: University Hospital of Pitié-Salpêtrière, Hôpital Universitaire Pitié-Salpêtrière
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of HIV-1 infection.

Mechanism of action: Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors; Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors
Key features and challenges: A small-molecule fixed combination pairing a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor with a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor to block HIV reverse transcription. Taken orally. Components have also been investigated for hepatitis B and related conditions.
Recent updates: A Phase 2 trial (NCT06774872) comparing doravirine/lamivudine with dolutegravir/lamivudine as maintenance ART in successfully suppressed people with HIV began in 2025 and is recruiting.

Name: DotEndo
Developers: DotLab
Indication: Diagnostic of endometriosis
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: miRNAs (miR-125b-5p, miR-150-5p, miR-342-3p, miR-451a, miR-3613-5p, and let-7b)
Mechanism of action: Point-of-care immunoassay detecting endometriosis-related protein biomarkers to support rapid, minimally invasive diagnosis.
Key features and challenges:
DotEndo is a blood test developed by DotLab that analyzes the expression of microRNA biomarkers associated with endometriosis to provide a clear positive or negative result.
(https://www.dotlab.com/science)

The biomarkers were validated via a prospective study evaluating subjects with a clinical indication for gynaecological surgery in an academic medical centre. Serum samples were collected prior to surgery from 100 subjects. Women were selected based on the presence of symptoms, and laparoscopy was performed to determine the presence or absence of endometriosis. The control group was categorized based on absence of visual disease at the time of surgery. Circulating miRNAs, miR-125b-5p, miR-150-5p, miR-342-3p, miR-451a, miR-3613-5p, and let-7b, were measured in serum by quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction in a blinded fashion without knowledge of disease status. Receiver-operating characteristic analysis was performed on individual microRNAs as well as combinations of microRNAs. An algorithm combining the expression values of these microRNAs, built using machine learning with a random forest classifier, was generated to predict the presence or absence of endometriosis on operative findings. This algorithm was then tested in an independent data set of 48 previously identified subjects not included in the training set (24 endometriosis and 24 controls) to validate its diagnostic performance. 
Individual microRNAs had receiver-operating characteristic areas under the curve ranging from 0.68 to 0.92. A classifier combining these microRNAs yielded an area under the curve of 0.94 when validated in the independent set of subjects not included in the training set. Analysis of the expression levels of each microRNA based on revised American Society of Reproductive Medicine staging revealed that all microRNAs could distinguish stage I/II from control and stage III/IV from control but that the difference between stage I/II and stage III/IV was not significant. Subgroup analysis revealed that neither phase of the menstrual cycle or use of hormonal medication had a significant impact on the expression levels in the microRNAs used in the algorithm.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32165186/)

The EMPOWER study, a multi-centre, prospective, observational study in women undergoing laparoscopy, laparotomy or other pelvic surgical procedure for endometriosis, infertility or another benign gynaecological indication was conducted between 2020 and 2024. Participants underwent 2 study visits for collection of blood and saliva and completion of study questionnaires. Results haven't been published yet.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04598698)

Name: Double A35R–M1R Immunogen (DAM)
Developers: Universidad de Las Americas
Indication: Prevention of mpox infection
Target: MPXV extracellular enveloped virus (EEV) antigen A35R and intracellular mature virus (IMV) antigen M1R
Mechanism of action: DAM fuses the epitopes of A35R and M1R antigens into a single-chain dimer, maintaining natural conformational structure. It induces both humoral and cellular immune responses, generating cross-reactive neutralizing antibodies against MPXV and orthologous antigens (VARV A36, VACV A33).
Key features and challenges:
-Provides a 28-fold stronger MPXV-specific neutralizing response compared to live VACV scarification.
-Generates cross-reactive antibodies across orthopoxviruses while focusing potency on MPXV A35.
-Aluminum-adjuvanted DAM formulation protected mice against lethal VACV challenge with no adverse reactions.
-Pilot-scale production confirmed high yield and purity, supporting scalability.
Recent updates: Published in 2024 in Nature Immunology (Wang et al.), showing DAM outperformed co-immunization with single antigens. Review (2025) highlights DAM as a promising next-gen mpox vaccine with strong preclinical efficacy. No clinical trials yet reported.

Name: Double-quenched TaqMan PCR assay - Gonorrhea
Developers: Vietnam National University
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoea
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Real-time PCR assay utilising double-quenched TaqMan probes
Key features and challenges:
The double-quenched TaqMan PCR assay is an in-house, multiplex real-time PCR platform developed for the simultaneous detection of nine sexually transmitted infection (STI) pathogens, including Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The assay incorporates double-quenched TaqMan probes containing an additional internal quencher (e.g., ZEN or TAO) positioned between the 5′ fluorescent reporter and the 3′ quencher. This configuration shortens the distance between the reporter and quencher, resulting in enhanced quenching efficiency, reduced background fluorescence, and improved signal-to-noise ratio during amplification.
In a 2023 study, the assay demonstrated high sensitivity and specificity for detection of common STI pathogens prevalent in Vietnam, with applicability to other settings (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0282439). The total turnaround time was approximately two hours. Cost analysis showed that the three master mixes required for the in-house assay amounted to approximately USD 2.34, representing an estimated eight-fold reduction compared with commercially available kits. The study highlighted the assay’s time efficiency and cost-effectiveness, particularly for resource-limited settings where large-scale use of imported diagnostic kits may not be feasible.
Key challenges include the need for external validation across diverse laboratory environments, quality assurance and standardization procedures, and regulatory approval pathways for diagnostic assays. Performance in low-burden settings and integration into national STI screening algorithms will also influence adoption. Comparative evaluations against established commercial multiplex platforms may be required to confirm reproducibility and clinical utility.
Overall, the double-quenched TaqMan PCR assay represents a rapid, cost-effective diagnostic approach for gonorrhea and other STIs, with particular relevance for low- and middle-income settings. Broader validation and regulatory alignment will determine its potential for widespread implementation.

Name: Double-quenched TaqMan PCR assay - Mycoplasma genitalium

These findings support the assay’s time efficiency and cost-effectiveness, particularly in resource-limited environments where access to imported diagnostic kits may be constrained.
Key challenges include the need for external validation across diverse laboratory settings, quality control standardization, and regulatory approval for routine clinical use. Performance benchmarking against established commercial nucleic acid amplification tests for M. genitalium will be important, particularly given the organism’s association with antimicrobial resistance and the need for accurate detection.
Overall, the double-quenched TaqMan PCR assay represents a rapid, affordable diagnostic option for Mycoplasma genitalium and other STIs. Broader validation and regulatory alignment will determine its potential for widespread implementation in clinical and public health settings.

Name: Double-quenched TaqMan PCR assay - Trichomoniasis
Developers: Vietnam National University
Indication: Detection of T. vaginalis
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Real-time PCR assay utilising double-quenched TaqMan probes
Key features and challenges:
The double-quenched TaqMan PCR assay is an in-house multiplex real-time PCR platform developed for the simultaneous detection of nine sexually transmitted infection (STI) pathogens, including Trichomonas vaginalis. The assay utilizes double-quenched TaqMan probes incorporating an additional internal quencher (e.g., ZEN or TAO) between the 5′ fluorescent reporter dye and the 3′ quencher. This design shortens the reporter–quencher distance, enhances quenching efficiency, reduces background fluorescence, and improves signal detection sensitivity during amplification.
In a 2023 study, the assay demonstrated high analytical performance for detection of common STI pathogens prevalent in Vietnam, with potential applicability in other epidemiological settings (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0282439).
The total turnaround time was approximately two hours. Cost analysis indicated that the three master mixes required for the in-house assay cost approximately USD 2.34, representing an estimated eight-fold reduction compared with commercial diagnostic kits. These findings support its utility as a rapid and cost-effective diagnostic tool, particularly in resource-constrained environments.
Key challenges include the need for broader external validation, quality control standardization, and regulatory approval for routine clinical use. Performance across different specimen types and laboratory infrastructures, as well as integration into national STI screening programs, will influence scalability. Comparative assessments against established commercial nucleic acid amplification tests may also be required.
Overall, the double-quenched TaqMan PCR assay represents a rapid, affordable diagnostic option for detection of Trichomonas vaginalis and other STIs. Further validation and regulatory alignment will determine its potential for wider implementation in clinical and public health settings.

Name: Droplet digital PCR
Developers: Sun Yat-sen University
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoea
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: droplet digital PCR
Key features and challenges:
Droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) is an advanced nucleic acid amplification technology designed to enable absolute quantification of target DNA with high sensitivity and precision. A ddPCR system has been developed for the detection of Neisseria gonorrhoeae, targeting the pgi1 gene as a specific molecular marker.
In a 2024 study, the ddPCR assay demonstrated robust amplification efficiency and completed the detection process within approximately 94 minutes (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0732889324001809?via%3Dihub). 
The method achieved a sensitivity of up to 5.8 pg/μL and exhibited high specificity, with no positive microdroplets detected among nine tested non-target control pathogens. Repeatability was strong, with a reported coefficient of variation (CV) of 4.2%. The ddPCR platform provides absolute quantification without reliance on standard curves, enhancing stability, reproducibility, and diagnostic accuracy.
Key challenges include higher equipment and operational costs compared with conventional real-time PCR, the need for specialized instrumentation, and limited availability in low-resource settings. Clinical validation across diverse specimen types and comparison with established nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) will be necessary to confirm real-world diagnostic performance. Integration into routine clinical workflows and cost-effectiveness assessments will also influence adoption.
Overall, ddPCR represents a highly sensitive and specific diagnostic approach for Neisseria gonorrhoeae with the added benefit of absolute quantification. Broader clinical validation and assessment of implementation feasibility will determine its role in gonorrhea diagnostics.

Name: Dydrogesterone - PTL/PTB
Developers: Abbott Laboratories; AbbVie; Chulalongkorn University
Indication: Reducing recurrent uterine contraction in preterm labour
Mechanism of action: Dydrogesterone, a stereoisomer of progesterone, binds to the progesterone receptor (progesterone receptor agonist).
Key features and challenges:
Dydrogesterone is an oral progestin structurally and pharmacologically similar to natural progesterone. It is marketed under brand names including Duphaston, Dydroboon, and Femoston (in combination with estradiol for menopausal hormone therapy). It has been used for multiple gynecologic and obstetric indications, including threatened miscarriage, luteal insufficiency, and menstrual disorders. Unlike many other progestins, dydrogesterone does not inhibit ovulation or increase basal body temperature and has minimal androgenic or estrogenic effects. It is widely marketed internationally but has been discontinued in the United States.
A 2011 prospective study reported that dydrogesterone administration in women at risk of preterm delivery was associated with increased progesterone-induced blocking factor (PIBF) production and interleukin-10 (IL-10) concentrations, reduced interferon-gamma (IFNγ) levels, and longer gestational duration.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22032897/)
A 2016 randomized trial evaluating adjunctive oral dydrogesterone (20 mg) in women with preterm labour found no significant prolongation of the latency period compared to placebo.
(Source: 2016 – https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26856618/)
A 2018 in vitro study investigating various progesterone compounds demonstrated that dydrogesterone uniquely produced a rapid and dose-dependent inhibition of myometrial contractions, suggesting a potential direct uterine relaxant effect.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29981319/)
A 2021 randomized controlled trial assessing 30 mg oral dydrogesterone as adjunct therapy in preterm labour similarly reported no significant extension of latency period compared to placebo.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33509129/)
In 2023, Gorgan University of Medical Sciences completed recruitment for a Phase III clinical trial evaluating dydrogesterone and progesterone for prevention of preterm birth in women with a short cervix; results have not yet been reported.
(https://irct.behdasht.gov.ir/trial/66703)
Overall, dydrogesterone demonstrates biological plausibility for uterine relaxation and immunomodulation. However, randomized clinical trials to date have not shown consistent efficacy in prolonging latency in established preterm labour. Ongoing Phase III research may further clarify its role in PTL/PTB prevention.
Recent updates: 2021: An RCT reported that adjunctive treatment with 20mg and 30 mg of oral dydrogesterone could not prolong latency period in preterm labor when compared to placebo. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33509129/))

E-Cervix is a recent quantification tool to measure the stiffness of the cervix using strain elastography. This technology could increase reproducibility and reduce interobserver variance using the sum $of 50 elastographic images acquired over 3.5 s.

Developers: China CDC
Indication: Treatment of mpox infection; potential post-exposure prophylaxis (neutralizing antibodies)
Target: MPXV E8 (IMV surface protein; structural/functional homolog of VACV D8)
Mechanism of action: Neutralization of intracellular mature virion (IMV) via E8 epitope binding (attachment/entry interference); strong IMV activity, no EEV neutralization; complement markedly enhances anti-VACV activity but not MPXV.
Key features and challenges:
-Potent binding to E8/D8; C9 cross-neutralizes authentic MPXV in vitro (IC50 ~3.0–3.2 µg/mL ± complement).

-No activity vs VACV EEV; IMV-specific.

-Complement enhances anti-VACV neutralization >50-fold, but not MPXV (likely due to mpox complement-evasion features), implying limited leverage of CDC/ADCC for MPXV.
Recent updates:
-Additional anti-MPXV mAb modalities are advancing: two non-competing human mAbs to B6 (EEV antigen) showed protection in models, underscoring cocktail strategies that pair IMV and EEV targets. 
-Bispecific anti-A29/B6 antibodies reported antiviral efficacy, reinforcing multi-antigen designs complementary to E8/D8 approaches. 
-mRNA-encoded anti-orthopox mAbs (LNP-mRNA) yield rapid in-vivo expression and broad neutralization in mice—an alternative delivery format for anti-E8/D8 concepts. 
-Nanobody programs (including bivalent sdAbs) show potent mpox neutralization and may offer manufacturability/thermal-stability advantages for LMIC settings. 
-Clinical backdrop: multiple RCT/observational datasets indicate mixed/limited benefit of tecovirimat, accelerating interest in antibody therapeutics and combinations targeting entry proteins (e.g., E8/D8, A16/G9).

EG-101 is an investigational injectable therapy being developed for the treatment of preeclampsia. Preeclampsia is characterized by hypertension and end-organ dysfunction, often associated with vascular endothelial dysfunction and abnormal placentation. In preclinical animal models of preeclampsia, EG-101 has demonstrated improvements in hypertension and proteinuria, supporting its potential therapeutic relevance in modulating vascular and endothelial pathways (https://en.egpharm.com/product/index.html).
In 2026, a Phase I single-center, randomized, open-label, four-period, three-way crossover, single-dose study was initiated to evaluate the safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of ascending intravenous doses of EG-101 in healthy volunteers 
(NCT07327255; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07327255). 
The study plans to enroll 24 participants, with eight subjects assigned to each dosing sequence under fasted conditions. The dosing period is expected to last approximately four weeks, followed by a post-treatment follow-up phase. This early-phase study represents the first step in clinical evaluation and does not yet include pregnant participants.
Key challenges include the early stage of clinical development, absence of human efficacy data in pregnant populations, and the complexity of conducting interventional trials in preeclampsia due to maternal–fetal safety considerations. Demonstration of a favorable safety profile in healthy volunteers will be a prerequisite before advancing into trials involving pregnant women. Regulatory and ethical requirements for obstetric drug development may also influence timelines.
Overall, EG-101 has shown encouraging preclinical activity in animal models of preeclampsia and has entered Phase I clinical evaluation. However, its clinical efficacy and safety in pregnant women with preeclampsia remain to be established through subsequent trials.
Recent updates: As of April 2022, EG 101 is in IND-authorization phase for the treatment of preeclampsia in China (Evergreen Therapeutics pipeline, April 2022)

Name: EHG signal dynamics
Developers: University of Novi Sad, Serbia; Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam; Bialystok University of Technology; Research Center for Intelligent Healthcare, Institute of Health and Wellbeing; Universitat Politècnica de València
Indication: The evaluation of the electrical activity of the uterus to predict and prevent preterm labour.
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Electrohysterogram (EHG) signal collects electrical activity of the uterus via electrodes placed on the abdominal surface of pregnant women. The electrodes analyze the cyclic depolarization and depolarization of muscle cell membranes and provide the sequence of contractions and relaxations of the myometrium.
Key features and challenges:
Electrohysterography (EHG) is a non-invasive technique that records uterine electrical activity through abdominal surface electrodes. By analysing myometrial electrophysiological signals, EHG aims to predict the onset of labour and identify women at risk of preterm labour (PTL). Signal interpretation typically relies on computational algorithms that assess frequency, amplitude, propagation, and temporal dynamics of uterine contractions.
In 2017, a study analysing EHG signals from 20 women between 24 and 28 weeks’ gestation with threatened PTL reported that signal dynamics could support detection of preterm labour risk using advanced signal-processing methods.
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0169260717307198?via%3Dihub)
In 2018, Despotovic et al. applied machine learning techniques to the Term-Preterm EHG (TPEHG) database using recordings obtained between 22 and 25 weeks’ gestation. The predictive model reported 99.23% accuracy, 98.40% sensitivity, and an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.99.
(https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8524818)
In 2020, a feasibility study assessed prediction of labour within 7- and 14-day horizons in women presenting with threatened PTL, including those receiving tocolytics. The study concluded that EHG could reliably predict imminent labour irrespective of tocolytic treatment stage.
(https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7248811/)
In 2022, multichannel EHG recordings were used to examine uterine electrical signal propagation and spatiotemporal excitation patterns in human myometrium, contributing to improved physiological understanding and informing predictive modelling approaches.
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0169260722003492)
In 2023, Fischer et al. applied deep learning models to the same TPEHG dataset and reported an AUC of 0.58. The study also evaluated whether adding clinical data improved performance and concluded that integration of available clinical variables did not significantly enhance predictive accuracy.
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0010482523003116?via%3Dihub)
Overall, EHG represents a promising non-invasive approach for predicting preterm labour through analysis of uterine electrical activity. However, reported predictive performance varies substantially depending on analytical methodology and dataset, and further validation in prospective clinical settings is required before routine clinical implementation.

Name: EVX-B2
Developers: Evaxion Biotech; University of Massachusetts Medical School (including MassBiologics)
Indication: Prevention of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Elicits bactericidal Abs and attenuates Ng colonisation
Key features and challenges:
EVX-B2 is a multivalent vaccine candidate targeting Neisseria gonorrhoeae, developed through a collaboration involving Evaxion Biotech. The vaccine strategy builds on the immunogenic properties of the 2C7 lipooligosaccharide (LOS) epitope, which is expressed by more than 95% of N. gonorrhoeae strains in vivo. Mutants lacking the 2C7 epitope demonstrate attenuation in murine models, supporting its relevance as a vaccine target. A peptide mimic (mimitope) of the 2C7 epitope, configured as a multi-antigen peptide (MAP), has been shown to elicit bactericidal antibodies and reduce vaginal colonization in mice. Complement-mediated killing, through membrane attack complex formation, has been identified as a mechanistic correlate of protection.
Subsequent antigen discovery efforts screened 30 candidate antigens for immunogenicity, bactericidal activity, and in vivo efficacy in a mouse vaginal colonization model. Two cell division proteins were identified as promising targets. When combined as a fusion (chimeric) protein, enhanced in vivo activity was observed compared with individual proteins. This chimeric construct, together with the 2C7 mimitope, forms the basis of the current multivalent vaccine strategy. A multivalent approach is intended to broaden strain coverage, enhance efficacy, and reduce the likelihood of immune escape.
The ongoing preclinical program includes evaluation of DNA vaccine constructs incorporating the 2C7 LOS mimitope (configured as an octameric concatemer), the cell division protein chimera, or a combination of both. Parallel development using an mRNA vaccine platform is also underway, with assessment of serum and vaginal antibody responses, serum bactericidal activity, T-cell responses, and efficacy in murine infection models (https://reporter.nih.gov/search/7IDHrLHBZ06aRqyuKgFJLQ/project-details/10539860).
Key challenges include demonstration of durable mucosal immunity in humans, confirmation of broad strain coverage, scalability of DNA or mRNA vaccine platforms for gonorrhea, and progression from murine models to human clinical trials. The absence of naturally acquired protective immunity to gonorrhea further underscores the need for robust immunogenicity data.
Overall, EVX-B2 represents a promising multivalent vaccine strategy leveraging LOS mimitope and conserved protein antigens, with parallel DNA and mRNA platform development. Successful completion of preclinical studies will determine its readiness for advancement into clinical evaluation.

Name: EXPAR
Developers: Linear Diagnostics Limited
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoea
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Exponential amplification reaction
Key features and challenges:
Exponential amplification reaction (EXPAR) is an isothermal nucleic acid amplification technique designed to amplify short oligonucleotides. The reaction is initiated by a DNA trigger and proceeds through repeated exponential amplification using a nicking enzyme and a strand-displacing polymerase.
Linear Diagnostics has developed a rapid molecular assay based on EXPAR technology that delivers diagnostic results in under 10 minutes. The assay is integrated into a fully self-contained point-of-care (POC) device incorporating a novel rapid detection mechanism. The test is designed to enable detection of Chlamydia trachomatis (CT) and Neisseria gonorrhoeae (NG) from rectal and throat swabs.
Initial clinical evaluations published in 2022, have demonstrated detection of CT/NG-positive patient samples within 10 minutes of DNA amplification at a constant temperature. The platform aims to facilitate faster and more accurate diagnosis at the point of care, potentially improving timely treatment and patient outcomes (https://sti.bmj.com/content/98/Suppl_1/A44.1).

Name: Easy Loop Amplification POCT
Developers: National University of Quilmes
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoea
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Mechanism of action: Easy Loop Amplification
Key features and challenges:
Easy Loop Amplification (ELA) is an isothermal nucleic acid amplification methodology developed as a rapid and affordable molecular point-of-care test (POCT) for the diagnosis of Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Conventional diagnosis of gonorrhea relies primarily on PCR-based techniques, which, although highly sensitive and specific, require specialized equipment and infrastructure that may not be available in low-complexity or remote health centers.
ELA addresses this gap by coupling isothermal nucleic acid amplification with a pH-sensitive dye for simplified visualization, thereby streamlining the amplification and detection steps of molecular diagnostics. This approach eliminates the need for complex thermocycling equipment and allows the assay to be performed using portable devices. The system has demonstrated adaptability across both human and veterinary pathogens, supporting its flexibility as a platform technology.
Evaluation of the ELA system for N. gonorrhoeae demonstrated specificity and detection limits comparable to those achieved with quantitative PCR (qPCR) methodologies (https://www.conicet.gov.ar/new_scp/detalle.php?keywords=&id=34238&congresos=yes&detalles=yes&congr_id=11735095).
The assay is designed to function without sophisticated laboratory infrastructure, supporting its potential application in decentralized settings and resource-limited environments.
Key challenges include the need for broader clinical validation across diverse specimen types, integration of sample preparation (extraction) into a fully streamlined POCT workflow, regulatory approval, and field performance assessment under real-world conditions. Cost-effectiveness, ease of use by minimally trained personnel, and robustness in varied environmental settings will also determine scalability.
Overall, Easy Loop Amplification represents a promising low-cost, portable molecular diagnostic approach for gonorrhea, with performance characteristics comparable to qPCR. Further validation and product development will determine its feasibility as a widely implemented POCT solution in low-resource settings.
