Name: Ebopiprant
Developers: Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany (also known as EMD Group, including Sigma-Aldrich, MilliporeSigma and EMD Serono); ObsEva SA
Indication: Treatment of preterm labour/birth through tocolytic/relaxant effects on myometrial contraction
Mechanism of action: A specific prostaglandin antagonist, which reduces uterine contractions and cervical maturation through inhibition of prostaglandin F2 alpha.
Key features and challenges:
Ebopiprant (OBE 022), a prodrug of OBE 002 (prostaglandin F2 alpha receptor antagonists; AS-604872) is a first-in-class, orally active, selective prostaglandin F2-alpha (F2α) receptor antagonist. It is designed to control preterm labour by reducing inflammation, decreasing uterine contractions, preventing cervical changes and foetal membrane rupture without causing potential serious side effects to the foetus as observed with non-specific prostaglandin inhibitors.

Preclinical development has shown orally active OBE022 and OBE002 both exhibit potent tocolytic effects on human tissues ex vivo and animal models in vivo without causing the adverse foetal side effects seen with indomethacin (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29777040/). 

In 2018, OBE 022 underwent clinical trial in post-menopausal women to assess pharmacokinetics. OBE022 was safe and had favourable pharmacokinetic characteristics (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29708281/).

Clinical development for preterm labour is underway in Finland, Spain, Czech Republic, Russia, Switzerland and Vietnam. The agent is believed to have been developed under ObsEva and Merck Serono's research programme focused on developing a series of selective prostaglandin F2α receptor (FP) antagonists as tocolytic agents for the treatment and prophylaxis of premature birth. These non-prostaglandin-like FP antagonists belonged to a distinct class of compounds, called thiazolidinyl sulphanomides, that exhibited a high degree of selectivity for all known prostaglandin receptors and oral efficacy in several animal models of preterm labour. Such features offered an alternative over conventionally used tocolytic agents like ritodrine, which lack uterine selectivity thereby causing foetal and maternal side effects (https://adisinsight.springer.com/drugs/800046988)

AS 604872 was also identified as a lead candidate from this research programme. However, although preclinical development for AS 604872 was underway in the US, no recent developments have been reported, and it is assumed that Merck and ObsEva have either ceased all activity in this indication, or AS 604872 is the actually the same candidate as OBE 002 - the parent drug to OBE 022 (ebopiprant).

In 2021, ObsEva officially announced its intention to discuss with European regulators for accelerated registration program for ebopiprant. ObsEva was planning to initiate a phase 2b/3 adaptive, dose-ranging study of Ebopiprant, with the potential to support an accelerated registration program in Europe.

In November 2022, ObsEva sold and assigned to XOMA all its rights to Ebopiprant, including the Company's license agreement with Organon, and the intellectual property estate. No further clinical trials have been announced. (https://www.xoma.com/opportunities/assets-available-for-license/ebopiprant/)
Recent updates:

June 2021: According to an ObsEva media release, data from the Phase II trial will be presented at the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG) Virtual World Congress 2021.  

May 2021: ObsEva plans Phase IIb dose ranging trial for Preterm labour in Europe and Asia, in Q4 2021. ObsEva plans to discuss with the European regulators for a possible accelerated registration program based on a phase IIb/III adaptive design

February/March 2021: ObsEva officially announced its intention to discuss with European regulators for accelerated registration program for ebopiprant; to submit regulatory application for preterm labour; and to launch ebopiprant for preterm labour.

August 2018: First-in-human pharmacokinetics, safety and tolerability study of OBE022 found it had favourable pharmacokinetics and indicated that further investigation into OBE022 a suitable candidate for further investigation for preterm labour (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29708281/).

Name: Echinomycin
Developers: OncoImmune, Inc.
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of fibroid growth and development
Target: GC-rich regions of DNA; Hypoxia-inducible factor 1 alpha
Mechanism of action: DNA synthesis inhibitors; Hypoxia-inducible factor 1 alpha inhibitors; RNA synthesis inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Echinomycin, primarily known for its use in cancer research, works by inhibiting DNA transcription through binding to GC-rich DNA sequences. This mechanism could theoretically affect uterine fibroids if they rely on similar transcriptional processes for growth. However, its application for uterine fibroids is not well-established and remains largely experimental.
The key features of echinomycin in this context include its potential to disrupt cellular growth and proliferation, which might offer a new treatment avenue for fibroids, particularly in cases where conventional therapies fall short. Despite this potential, there are several significant challenges.
First, there is limited research on echinomycin specifically for uterine fibroids. Most existing studies focus on its role in cancer, leaving a gap in understanding its effects on fibroid tissue. Additionally, echinomycin's powerful action on DNA transcription could result in considerable side effects, including impacts on normal tissue function. Finally, moving echinomycin from its current use in cancer to treating uterine fibroids would require extensive clinical trials to thoroughly evaluate its safety, efficacy, and appropriate dosing for this new application.
In a 2022 published study carried out in mice, echinomycin showed antitumor effects against uterine fibroids both in vitro and in vivo. These findings support the potential use of HIF-1 inhibitors for the treatment of uterine fibroids.
(https://www.fertstertscience.org/article/S2666-335X(22)00005-2/fulltext)

Name: Echocardiographic prediction model
Developers: Peking University Third Hospital
Indication: Prediction of preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Uses maternal cardiac structure and function parameters to detect hemodynamic maladaptation associated with preeclampsia development.
Key features and challenges:
A 2023 study by Peking University evaluated the association between maternal echocardiographic changes and the occurrence of preeclampsia (PE) in twin pregnancies. Additionally, a prediction model for PE in twin pregnancies was established and validated.

The first part of this study was retrospective and included data from 854 twin pregnancies that received antenatal care at Peking University Third Hospital (training cohort). Overall, 159 women who underwent transthoracic echocardiography were included in the analysis. To build a predictive model, cardiac findings were compared between normotensive women and those with PE. The model was then validated in a prospective longitudinal cohort (test cohort) that included 109 women with twin pregnancies who underwent two consecutive transthoracic echocardiography examinations during the second and third trimesters.

Fifty-four normotensive women and 105 women with PE were analysed in the retrospective cohort that was used to build the model in which later preeclampsia was associated with echocardiographic changes. The optimised PE prediction model based on the interventricular septal thickness, left atrial anteroposterior diameter, A, peak early diastolic myocardial velocity and pre-pregnancy bodyweight index was then established. The model was tested in the prospective cohort including 87 normotensive women and 22 women with PE; the validation test showed that the prediction model in the second trimesters had high discriminative ability and calibration.

Maternal echocardiographic changes in twin pregnancies are associated with the development of preeclampsia. The model constructed, based on the echocardiographic parameters and body mass index, provides novel ideas for the prediction of PE. 
(https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/aogs.14651)

-Capsid protein (CP) binding (suggested by biochemical binding assays) in addition to possible host/viral factors involved in replication machinery.
Mechanism of action:
-In vitro, efavirenz inhibits CHIKV replication at low micromolar concentrations (EC₅₀ ~1.1-1.3 µM) in relevant cell lines. 
-Time-of-addition assays and minus-sense specific RT-PCR indicate inhibition of viral RNA synthesis early after entry. 
-Efavirenz shows binding affinity to purified CHIKV capsid protein (CP), suggesting CP might also be a target. 
-In vivo (mouse model), treatment with efavirenz reduces CHIKV viral load.
Key features and challenges:
-Oral bioavailability, long half-life, low cost (from its HIV use) make it attractive for repurposing.
-Broad alphavirus activity: also inhibits Sindbis virus (SINV) in cell culture (EC₅₀ ~0.7 µM) in this study, indicating potential cross-alphavirus utility.
Recent updates:
2025:
-Confirmed antiviral efficacy in vitro at ~1-1.3 µM EC₅₀ in two cell lines. 
-Demonstrated reduction in viral load in mouse model. 
-Binding of EFV to CHIKV capsid protein identified, widening possible mechanisms of antiviral action.

Name: Ejiao compound
Developers: Guangzhou University of Traditional Chinese Medicine
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of iron deficiency anaemia in the post-partum period.
Mechanism of action: Rapid molecular assay amplifying pathogen-specific nucleic acids to detect Trichomonas vaginalis infection near patient care.
Key features and challenges:
Ejiao is an ancient traditional Chinese medicine. It is composed of donkey-hide glue, Ginseng, codonopsis pilosula, prepared rhizome of rehmannia, and crab apple, which has been widely used in the treatment of various types of anaemia in China for decades. (https://classic.clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT02656225)

In a study conducted by the Guangzhou University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, the investigators aimed to conduct a randomised controlled trial to assess the efficacy and safety of Ejiao compound comparing with oral iron in the treatment of mild postpartum anaemia with or without iron deficiency. A total of 275 patients after normal labour with Hb 70g/L-100g/L were randomised into trial group（n = 141）and control group（n= 134). The trial group was treated with CES orally, and the control group was treated with polysaccharide iron complex orally. Compared with oral iron supplements, CES improved the hematopoietic function and increased Hb level of postpartum anaemia women rapidly and significantly, while having no significant effect on the serum ferritin level and having lesser side effects. (https://www.cnki.net/kcms/doi/10.13359/j.cnki.gzxbtcm.2018.04.006.html and https://classic.clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT02656225)

In 2023, a randomised, double blind, placebo controlled trial began looking to show safety and efficacy of the compound in mid and late stage pregnancy. The sample size of this trial is expected to be 360 and is taking place in 11 sites in China. https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=211259 

A second trial began in 2023 to investigate safety and efficacy in post-partum anaemia. For this trial the compound will be given with iron supplements. It is a Chinese multi-centre, double blind, placebo-controlled trial with sample size of 360. This trial is sponsored by DongE E Jiao Coporation Limited - the company who sells this Chinese medicine. 
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06175117

Name: Elagolix - PCOS
Developers: AbbVie
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: Elagolix works by blocking the action of GnRH in the pituitary gland, reducing the secretion of luteinising hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone. This reduction leads to a decrease in oestrogen production, suppressing the ovarian cycle and reducing symptoms associated with high levels of ovarian hormones.
Key features and challenges:
Elagolix is an oral gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) receptor antagonist developed for the treatment of endometriosis and uterine fibroids. By competitively inhibiting GnRH receptors in the pituitary, it suppresses luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) secretion, resulting in reduced ovarian estradiol and progesterone production. Its dose-dependent suppression of the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian (HPO) axis underpins its therapeutic role in estrogen-dependent gynecologic disorders.
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is characterised by altered gonadotropin secretion, including relatively elevated LH levels that contribute to ovarian androgen excess. Suppression of LH through GnRH antagonism has therefore been explored as a potential strategy to reduce hyperandrogenism and restore menstrual cyclicity in PCOS.
A Phase 2 randomized, placebo-controlled trial (NCT03951077) evaluated elagolix in 114 women with PCOS over 16 weeks. Participants were assigned to varying doses of elagolix or placebo. Primary and secondary outcomes included menstrual cycle normalization, ovulation rates, and changes in gonadotropin levels. Elagolix effectively reduced LH concentrations compared with placebo. However, it did not significantly increase regular menstrual cycles nor achieve the targeted ovulation rates within the study population.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37398623/
Although elagolix demonstrates pharmacodynamic efficacy in suppressing LH, broader clinical benefits in PCOS remain uncertain. Suppression of ovarian hormone production may require careful dose balancing, as excessive estrogen reduction can result in hypoestrogenic adverse effects, including hot flashes and decreased bone mineral density. In other indications, add-back therapy is often required to mitigate these effects.
Elagolix remains investigational for PCOS. While mechanistically rational for targeting LH-driven hyperandrogenism, current evidence does not demonstrate clear improvement in ovulatory or menstrual outcomes. Larger and longer-duration studies would be required to determine its therapeutic value and safety profile in reproductive-age women with PCOS.

Name: Elagolix/Estradiol/Norethindrone Acetate
Developers: Novo Nordisk Pharmaceuticals
Indication: Uterine fibroid heavy menstrual bleeding
Mechanism of action: Estrogen receptor agonists; Progesterone receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
Elagolix/estradiol/norethindrone acetate (E2/NETA) is an oral combination regimen developed for the management of heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) associated with uterine fibroids. Elagolix is a non-peptide gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) receptor antagonist that suppresses pituitary LH and FSH secretion, thereby reducing ovarian estrogen and progesterone production and decreasing fibroid growth and bleeding. Estradiol (1 mg) and norethindrone acetate (0.5 mg) are administered as hormonal add-back therapy to mitigate hypoestrogenic effects, particularly vasomotor symptoms and bone mineral density (BMD) loss, while preserving efficacy.
Two identical, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, 6-month Phase III trials (ELARIS UF-I and UF-II) evaluated elagolix 300 mg twice daily with add-back therapy in women with fibroid-associated bleeding. The primary endpoint required menstrual blood loss (MBL) <80 mL during the final treatment month and ≥50% reduction from baseline. Elagolix with add-back therapy significantly improved bleeding outcomes compared with placebo. An elagolix-alone arm demonstrated greater hypoestrogenic adverse effects, confirming the benefit of add-back therapy.
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1904351
ELARIS UF-I and UF-II safety analyses (updated through 2022) reported manageable safety profiles, with expected hypoestrogenic events such as hot flushes and mild BMD reductions. No unexpected safety signals were identified.
https://adis.springer.com/trials/700267034
In 2021, a population pharmacokinetics analysis across 13 clinical trials found no patient-related factors requiring dose adjustments for elagolix 300 mg twice daily with estradiol 1 mg/norethindrone acetate 0.5 mg daily in women with HMB associated with uterine fibroids.
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40262-021-01096-w
In 2022, long-term safety data (24 months) showed that elagolix 300 mg twice daily with add-back therapy maintained a consistent safety profile, with BMD changes remaining limited and stable over time and no new safety signals identified.
https://www.fertstert.org/article/S0015-0282(22)00683-5/fulltext
Also in 2022, a comparative review of oral GnRH antagonists (relugolix, elagolix, linzagolix) concluded that these agents, alone and in combination with E2/NETA, demonstrated superior efficacy to placebo in improving bleeding, pain, fibroid size, and quality of life in premenopausal women with symptomatic uterine fibroids, while maintaining acceptable safety profiles.
https://www.jogc.com/article/S1701-2163(22)00684-3/abstract
In 2023, Phase IIIb data from study NCT03271489 evaluated 36-month exposure to elagolix 300 mg twice daily with add-back therapy. Interim findings showed relatively stable BMD through 36 months, with mean percentage changes comparable to 12- and 24-month results. The study has been completed, with final updates pending.
https://www.fertstert.org/article/S0015-0282(23)01410-3/fulltext
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03271489
Elagolix/E2/NETA represents a clinically validated oral therapy for heavy menstrual bleeding due to uterine fibroids. Add-back therapy is essential to mitigate bone loss and vasomotor symptoms associated with GnRH suppression. Although effective, therapy duration is typically limited due to long-term bone health considerations, and symptom recurrence may occur after discontinuation.

Name: Elebsiran

Indication: Indicated for the treatment of chronic HBV infection

VIR 2218 inhibits expression of all HBV proteins, including hepatitis B surface antigen. This restores the patient's own immune response to HBV. VIR 2218 silences all HBV RNA transcripts, that are required for viral replication and viral protein expression. Clinical development is underway in multiple countries worldwide.

Phase II trial commenced in 2024 in China (NCT06491563).
Phase II trial commenced in 2023 with trial sites in China and Thailand (NCT05970289).

Name: Emiplacel
Developers: European Commission (EC); University of Tokyo (including the Graduate School of Agricultural and Life Sciences); Pluristem Therapeutics Inc. (formerly Pluristem Life Systems); Berlin-Brandenburg Centre for Regenerative Therapies (BCRT); CHA Biotech Co., Ltd.; Israel Innovation Authority
Indication: Prevention or treatment of preeclampsia by reducing inflammation and placental injury
Mechanism of action: Cell replacements; Dendritic cell modulators; Cell differentiation modulators
Key features and challenges:
Emiplacel is a human placental stromal cell therapy being developed by Pluristem Therapeutics by using its proprietary bio-therapeutic approach for the treatment of peripheral arterial disorders (PAD), pulmonary arterial hypertension, intermittent claudication, ischaemic heart disorders, SARS-COV-2 acute respiratory disease, preeclampsia and muscle and tendon injuries. Mesenchymal stromal cells prevent allostimulation in vivo and control checkpoints of Th1 priming, migration of human dendritic cells to lymph nodes and NK cell activation. 
Pluristem indicated in November 2013 that, based on positive efficacy and safety results in preclinical trials, the company will pursue the clinical development of emiplacel cells in preeclampsia. Emiplacel cells were efficacious in animal models of preeclampsia and administration of the cells to pregnant rats did not result in maternal or foetal toxicity. The company reported that in a preclinical study, emiplacel cells provided beneficial effects by reducing inflammation and placental injury in toll-like receptor agonist-induced mouse model with preclampsia. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26685104/)
In 2015, Pluristem reported that there was improvement in several parameters of preeclampsia on treatment with emiplacel cells in animal models in a study conducted in collaboration with the Cardiovascular Research Institute (CVRI) of the Texas A&M College of Medicine. Further, emiplacel cells demonstrated safety in both mother and foetus in another study conducted by Charles River Laboratories. Pluristem is conducting additional preclinical studies requested by the US FDA, including an efficacy study in animal model for over expression of sFLT 1, before initiating Phase I development of emiplacel in preeclampsia. Preclinical data was expected in the first half of 2016. 
Further, in December 2015, emiplacel cells received an orphan drug designation from the US FDA for the treatment of severe preeclampsia. Pluristem had filed an orphan drug application in February 2014. It received orphan designation for the treatment of preeclampsia from the EMA in June 2021.  (https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/human/orphan-designations/eu-3-21-2448)
Recent updates:
Dec 2015: Emiplacel cells received an orphan drug designation from the US FDA for the treatment of severe preeclampsia. Pluristem had filed an orphan drug application in February 2014. However, no updates on development have been reported since 2017.
June 2021: It received orphan designation for the treatment of preeclampsia from the EMA in June 2021.  (https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/human/orphan-designations/eu-3-21-2448)

Name: Emodepside
Developers: Drugs for Neglected Diseases initiative (DNDi); Bayer Healthcare; Astellas Pharma; University Hospital Bonn, Universitaetsklinikum Bonn (UKB); University of Health and Allied Sciences, Ghana; Hammersmith Medicines Research; Mahidol Oxford Tropical Medicine Research Unit (MORU)
Indication: Indicated for the broad-spectrum treatment of soil-transmitted/intestinal helminthiasis

Key features and challenges:

It has been investigated successfully in a Phase I human clinical trial and is now in a Phase II trial of its efficacy. Phase II trial (NCT05180461 - estimated completion October 2026), and a Phase III trial (NCT06736691) that is set to be completed at the end of 2025.

Name: Emodepside
Developers: Jennifer Keiser
Indication: Investigated for treatment of whipworm (T. trichiura) infections in adolescents and adults
Mechanism of action: Binds presynaptic LAT-1 receptors in neuromuscular junctions to stimulate inhibitory neuropeptide release, causing pharyngeal paralysis
Key features and challenges: A small-molecule anthelmintic that binds presynaptic latrophilin-like (LAT-1) receptors at neuromuscular junctions, stimulating inhibitory neuropeptide release and causing pharyngeal paralysis of the parasite. Taken orally. Also investigated against hookworm infection and onchocerciasis.

Indication: Indicated for the treatment of soil-transmitted helminthiasis

Recent updates: A Phase 3 trial (NCT06800248) evaluating its efficacy and safety versus mebendazole in adolescents and adults with soil-transmitted helminth infections is expected to begin in 2026 and is not yet recruiting.

Developers: Drugs for Neglected Diseases initiative (DNDi); Bayer Healthcare; Astellas Pharma; Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation; Swiss Tropical & Public Health Institute (Swiss TPH)

Oral emodepside, as a macrofilaricidal, for the treatment of onchocerciases, filariasis, hookworm infections and trichuriasis is being developed collaboratively by Bayer Healthcare and Drugs for Neglected Diseases Initiative Foundation. Name: Empagliflozin
Developers: Boehringer Ingelheim (including Merial); Eli Lilly and Company; Duke Clinical Research Institute
Indication: Indicated for treatment of PCOS-related metabolic dysfynction
Mechanism of action: Sodium-glucose transporter 2 inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Empagliflozin is an oral sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor that reduces renal glucose reabsorption, thereby promoting glycosuria and lowering plasma glucose levels. It is approved for the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus and has demonstrated cardiovascular and renal benefits in high-risk populations.

Interest in empagliflozin for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is based on its capacity to improve body weight, adiposity, and insulin resistance—key metabolic drivers of PCOS.

A 2019 randomized controlled trial (NCT03008551) compared empagliflozin with metformin in overweight and obese women with PCOS over 12 weeks. Empagliflozin led to significant improvements in anthropometric measures and body composition compared with metformin. However, no significant differences were observed in hormonal or broader metabolic parameters between the two groups.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30866088/
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03008551
A Phase IV trial initiated in 2022 (NCT05200793) aimed to compare empagliflozin or linagliptin as alternatives to metformin in non-diabetic women with PCOS. Results have not yet been published.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05200793
A more recent Phase II/III study initiated in 2024 (NCT06140108) is evaluating the effects of empagliflozin versus metformin on metabolic dysfunction in women with PCOS, including those with comorbidities or multimorbidity. Outcomes focus on metabolic endpoints, though results are pending.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06140108
Although empagliflozin has demonstrated favorable effects on weight and body composition, evidence for direct endocrine or ovulatory benefits in PCOS remains limited. Current guidelines do not recommend SGLT2 inhibitors as standard therapy for PCOS, and their use in this population is considered investigational.
Key challenges include limited long-term data in reproductive-age women, potential adverse effects such as genital infections and volume depletion, and uncertainty regarding impact on ovulation, fertility, and pregnancy outcomes. Additionally, comparative effectiveness relative to established agents such as metformin or GLP-1 receptor agonists remains under investigation.

Name: Emtricitabine (FTC) and tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) Fixed Dose Combination (FDC) tablets
Developers: ViiV Healthcare
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of HIV-1 infection.
Target: DNA polymerase beta, DNA polymerase gamma, DNA polymerase I, DNA polymerase II, HIV reverse transcriptase; HIV integrase
Mechanism of action: DNA polymerase beta inhibitors, DNA polymerase gamma inhibitors, DNA polymerase I inhibitors, DNA polymerase II inhibitors, HIV reverse transcriptase inhibitors; HIV integrase inhibitors
Key features and challenges: A small-molecule oral fixed-dose combination of two nucleos(t)ide reverse transcriptase inhibitors that block HIV reverse transcriptase to suppress viral replication. Taken orally. Also investigated in hepatitis B.
Recent updates: A Phase 2 trial (NCT07202546) evaluating regimens in treatment-naive persons with HIV-1, in which it serves as a backbone, began in 2026 and is not yet recruiting.

Name: Enalapril
Developers: Brigham and Women's Hospital
Indication: Management of postpartum hypertension and improvement of postpartum cardiovascular function in severe preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: ACE inhibitor
Key features and challenges:
Enalapril is an orally-active and long-acting nonsulphydryl antihypertensive agent that suppresses the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system to lower blood pressure. It was developed from a targeted research programme using molecular modelling. Being a prodrug, enalapril is rapidly biotransformed into its active metabolite, enalaprilat, which is responsible for the pharmacological actions of enalapril. The active metabolite of enalapril competitively inhibits the ACE to hinder the production of angiotensin II, a key component of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system that promotes vasoconstriction and renal reabsorption of sodium ions in the kidneys. Ultimately, enalaprilat works to reduce blood pressure and blood fluid volume. It is widely marketed for hypertension and is used and investigated for hypertension in the postpartum period. 
Clinical trials are underway to evaluate whether enalapril (compared with nifedipine) is better at decreasing the amount of medical resources used in the postpartum period by women who have high blood pressure in pregnancy and the postpartum period. While both antihypertensives are commonly use in the postpartum period for women with hypertension in pregnancy, it is not clear which medication works better. Nifedipine is more traditionally used and well-validated by current medical literature. However, enalapril's mechanism of action is better suited to the dysregulation of blood pressure that can occur with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. This clinical trial will investigate whether enalapril is superior to nifedipine in terms of medical resources used in the postpartum period. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT04236258)
Additionally, hypertensive diseases in pregnancy are associated with future cardiovascular disease and, therefore, enalapril is also under study to provide an opportunity of targeted therapeutic interventions aimed at reducing cardiovascular morbidity. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33012200/)
It should be noted that enalapril, and ACEs in general, are not recommended for use during pregnancy, limiting their use for preterm preeclampsia.
Recent updates:
2024: The below is in Phase IIII
2020: Clinical trial recruiting to test enalapril (compared with nifedipine) in postpartum hypertension.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT04236258

Name: End-diastolic volume (EDV)
Developers: Sri Devaraj Urs Medical College (SDUMC)
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS via detection of vascular changes
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Measures end-diastolic blood flow velocity to evaluate ovarian perfusion changes associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
End-diastolic volume (EDV) is a Doppler ultrasound measurement that assesses the total blood volume in a vessel at the end of the diastolic phase. In the context of PCOS, EDV is used to evaluate ovarian blood flow, which is often altered in women with the condition. Increased ovarian blood flow and hypervascularity in PCOS can result in higher EDV values. EDV measurements help identify these vascular changes, which are linked to PCOS symptoms like infertility and anovulation, making it a useful tool for diagnosing PCOS alongside other methods such as hormonal assessments and ovarian morphology imaging.

Recent studies have explored the role of EDV in diagnosing PCOS through ultrasound evaluations. A 2023 study found that increased EDV, along with elevated peak systolic velocity (PSV), was observed in PCOS patients compared to controls, suggesting its potential as a diagnostic indicator. (https://www.jcdronline.org/admin/Uploads/Files/644e4cb31bd2f3.42209931.pdf)

Another study from 2019 reported that PCOS patients exhibited increased EDV, PSV, and stromal vascularity, with decreased resistive index and pulsatility index, indicating altered ovarian blood flow patterns. (https://www.ijss-sn.com/uploads/2/0/1/5/20153321/32_ijss_mar_oa32_-_2019.pdf)

Name: EndoDTect
Developers: Endodiag
Indication: Diagnostic of endometriosis
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Blood-based biomarker assay quantifying inflammatory and hormonal markers to identify endometriosis-related pathophysiology.
Key features and challenges:
Endodiag is a biotech company focused on the development of diagnostics for endometriosis. In 2017, the company obtained a €4.5m funding grant from the European Union for the validation of EndoSearch, a noninvasive diagnostic tool using endometrial tissue samples to diagnose endometriosis without requiring laparoscopy. (https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/767720) 
A clinical trial for the validation of a cluster of biomarkers in endometrium and blood was conducted between 2018 and 2022.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03376451)

While EndoSearch is no longer referenced on Endodiag's website, the company is now developing EndoDTect, a blood test based on the analysis of a combination of biomarkers. Their patent portfolio focuses on the in vitro use of anti-CD71 antibodies to identify and eliminate endometriotic cells. CD71 is a receptor present on the surface of all human cells, in numbers that increase with the cell’s proliferative capacity. By binding the CD71 receptor, anti-CD71 antibodies can identify endometriotic cells, which behave a little like cancer cells in the way they proliferate. Endodiag have one granted patent in France, and pending applications in Europe, Japan, and the US. It is unclear whether this new diagnostic test is based on research conducted for EndoSearch or not. The website announces ongoing validating studies to confirm the predictive value of EndoDTect for disease detection.
(https://www.endodiag.com/early-diagnosis)

Name: EndoPAT
Developers: Itamar Medical Ltd
Indication: Indicated for monitoring of the endothelium function in pregnant women at high risk of preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Mechanism of action: Quantifying the ability of peripheral microvessels to dilate in response to a physiological stimulus
Key features and challenges:
EndoPAT is a non-invasive diagnostic device that assesses endothelial function by measuring peripheral arterial tone using finger plethysmography. It evaluates reactive hyperemia index (RHI), which reflects endothelial-dependent vasodilation. Endothelial dysfunction is a central feature in the pathophysiology of preeclampsia (PE), often preceding clinical manifestations. Early detection of endothelial impairment may therefore support risk stratification and timely intervention in pregnant women at risk of PE.
A 2024 study evaluated endothelial function during pregnancy and its association with subsequent development of preeclampsia (https://journals.eco-vector.com/jowd/article/view/633048). 
Endothelial dysfunction was detected in the first trimester in 59 (55%) patients. During the second trimester, 46 (64%) of 72 assessed patients demonstrated endothelial dysfunction despite ongoing complex therapy, while in the third trimester, endothelial dysfunction was observed in 4 (1%) of 46 patients. Moderate preeclampsia developed in the third trimester (35–39 weeks) in 28 (25.9%) of 108 patients overall. At study initiation, 15 patients with endothelial dysfunction received complex therapy, whereas 13 received acetylsalicylic acid alone. Among 46 women followed throughout the entire pregnancy, only 4 (8.7%) developed preeclampsia.
These findings suggest that assessment of endothelial dysfunction, potentially through tools such as EndoPAT, may help identify women at increased risk of preeclampsia and monitor response to preventive therapies such as acetylsalicylic acid.
Key challenges include the limited sample size and observational nature of the study, which restrict causal interpretation. Standardization of endothelial function thresholds, reproducibility across populations, and integration into routine antenatal care pathways require further validation. Additionally, the incremental predictive value of EndoPAT over established screening methods (e.g., uterine artery Doppler, angiogenic markers) remains to be determined. Larger prospective studies are necessary to establish clinical utility, cost-effectiveness, and optimal timing of endothelial function assessment in preeclampsia prevention strategies.

Name: Endocare
Developers: Lucine
Indication: Treatment of endometriosis pain
Target: central nervous system to reduce perceived pain
Mechanism of action: Pain mitigation
Key features and challenges:
Endocare is a digital therapeutic (DTx) solution developed initially by Lucine and subsequently by Butterfly Therapeutics for the management of chronic pelvic pain associated with endometriosis. It is a stand-alone software medical device comprising a mobile application and a virtual reality (VR) headset. The intervention delivers 20-minute immersive VR sessions designed to provide non-pharmacological pain relief through audiovisual stimulation in interactive 3D environments. The mechanism targets central nervous system modulation of pain perception, aiming to reduce pain intensity beyond traditional two-dimensional digital interventions. Endocare is CE-marked as a Class I medical device but is not yet commercially available (https://www.butterfly-therapeutics.com/en/home/endocare-en/).
A first randomized controlled trial (NCT04650516), completed in 2021 and involving 45 participants, demonstrated that a single 20-minute Endocare session significantly reduced pelvic pain compared with a control intervention, with analgesic effects persisting for up to four hours (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04650516
; https://www.jmir.org/2022/9/e39531).
A second randomized controlled trial published in 2023 enrolled 102 participants who used the VR intervention at home twice daily for 2–5 days (https://www.jmir.org/2023/1/e47869). 
The study reported superior pain relief compared with a sham control, with maximum pain reduction exceeding 50% by the second day of treatment. Participants also demonstrated reduced overall pain medication use. Repeated home-based VR sessions were reported to be safe and well tolerated.
Key challenges include the short duration of intervention periods in existing trials and limited long-term outcome data. Effects appear primarily symptomatic and centrally mediated, without addressing underlying lesion progression. Accessibility depends on availability of compatible hardware and digital literacy. Regulatory classification as a Class I device may vary across jurisdictions. While Endocare demonstrates promising short-term analgesic efficacy and a favorable safety profile, further studies are needed to evaluate sustained benefit, cost-effectiveness, and integration into multimodal endometriosis care pathways.

Name: Endocheck
Developers: Aspira Women's Health
Indication: Detection of protein biomarkers associated with endometriosis
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Analyzes circulating or endometrial biomarkers to detect molecular signatures associated with endometriotic lesions.
Key features and challenges:
EndoCheck is a diagnostic tool developed by Aspira Women's Health utilizing a deep neural network algorithm to detect endometriosis through protein biomarker analysis. Designed as an "aid in diagnosis," it aims to enhance the accuracy of diagnosing endometriosis in women presenting with chronic pelvic pain.

An observational trial focused on validating EndoCheck's clinical performance compared to laparoscopic surgical assessment started in 2022. The primary goal is to achieve at least 94% sensitivity and 79% specificity for the test. Secondary objectives include evaluating the test's performance across different pain severities and clinical factors. The study involves women scheduled for gynecologic surgery (n=600) and retains serum cell-free DNA for analysis.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05245695?tab=table)

Name: Endothelium-dependent Vasodilatation test
Developers: Assistance Publique - Hôpitaux de Paris
Indication: Prediction of preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Aggregates genetic variants associated with hypertension to estimate inherited susceptibility to preeclampsia.
Key features and challenges:
French researchers are working on a combined test to predict preeclampsia, using validated angiogenic biomarkers alongside measurements of endothelial function.
 
This clinical study, launched in 2023, is exploring whether changes in endothelium-dependent vasodilation in pregnant women with stable hypertension are linked to the development of preeclampsia later in pregnancy. It involves measuring endothelial dysfunction using a laser-Doppler technique combined with acetylcholine iontophoresis, which tests endothelial health by triggering nitric oxide production and microvascular dilation. The study also measures central aortic pressure (both systolic and diastolic) and the aortic augmentation index through applanation tonometry with the SphygmoCor system, as well as carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity using the same device. These results are then compared with serum levels of known preeclampsia biomarkers, including sFlt-1, placental growth factor (PIGF), vascular endothelial growth factors (VEGF), soluble endoglin (sEng), anti-angiotensin II receptor (AT1), circulating copeptin, interleukin IL-17, and urinary biomarkers like neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL) and endothelial microparticles (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04520048)​

Name: Enoxacin
Developers: Fisher BioServices Inc
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: DNA topoisomerase 2-beta inhibitor
Key features and challenges:
Enoxacin is an oral broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone antibacterial agent traditionally used in the treatment of urinary tract infections and gonorrhea. Beyond its antimicrobial activity, emerging research has suggested potential metabolic effects, including promotion of adipose tissue thermogenesis and protection against diet-induced obesity and insulin resistance.
Given the strong association between polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), insulin resistance, adipose dysfunction, and metabolic inflammation, agents that enhance thermogenesis and improve metabolic regulation have attracted investigational interest. White adipose tissue browning and modulation of gut microbiota have been proposed as potential mechanisms influencing both metabolic and reproductive features of PCOS.
A 2022 preclinical study evaluated enoxacin in a dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA)-induced mouse model of PCOS. Enoxacin treatment attenuated reproductive endocrine abnormalities, improved glucose intolerance, and ameliorated ovarian dysfunction. Mechanistic analyses indicated that enoxacin promoted white adipose tissue browning, improved metabolic parameters, and partially restored gut microbiota dysbiosis. These metabolic improvements were associated with reductions in reproductive dysfunction in the PCOS model.
https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/pharmacology/articles/10.3389/fphar.2022.978019/full
Despite promising mechanistic findings, evidence supporting enoxacin in PCOS remains limited to preclinical animal models. No human clinical trials have evaluated its safety, endocrine effects, or reproductive outcomes in women with PCOS. Additionally, as a fluoroquinolone antibiotic, enoxacin carries known safety considerations, including potential musculoskeletal, neurological, and antimicrobial resistance concerns, which may limit its long-term use in a non-infectious chronic condition.
Enoxacin represents a repurposing candidate with experimental metabolic and reproductive effects in PCOS models. However, its role in PCOS management remains highly investigational and requires clinical validation to assess translational relevance, safety, and therapeutic feasibility in humans.

Name: Enoxaparin - PCOS
Developers: Sanofi; G.L. Pharma; Italfarmco; Thrombosis Research Institute
Indication: Treatment of PCOS infertility
Mechanism of action: Factor Xa inhibitors; Thrombin inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Enoxaparin sodium is a low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) derived from porcine mucosal heparin and administered subcutaneously. It exerts anticoagulant effects primarily through potentiation of antithrombin III, resulting in inhibition of factor Xa and, to a lesser extent, thrombin. Enoxaparin is widely approved for the prevention and treatment of thromboembolic disorders, including deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, and unstable angina.
https://adisinsight.springer.com/drugs/800011021
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) has been associated with increased risks of miscarriage, implantation failure, and adverse pregnancy outcomes, potentially related to hypercoagulability, inflammation, and endothelial dysfunction. Anticoagulation during the periimplantation period has therefore been explored as a strategy to improve reproductive outcomes in selected PCOS populations, particularly those with recurrent pregnancy loss or thrombophilic tendencies.
A 2020 preregistered randomized controlled trial (ChiCTR2000036527) evaluated the use of low molecular weight heparin in women with PCOS during the periimplantation period. The multicentre study in Shanghai enrolled 188 participants and compared pregnancy outcomes between an experimental group receiving heparin and a control group receiving estrogen–progestin therapy alone. Primary outcomes included ongoing pregnancy rate and live birth rate, alongside other pregnancy-related endpoints.
https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=59389
While anticoagulation may theoretically improve endometrial receptivity and reduce thrombotic risk at implantation, enoxaparin does not address the underlying endocrine or metabolic disturbances characteristic of PCOS. Potential risks include bleeding complications, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, and the need for parenteral administration, which may limit routine use outside specific high-risk reproductive contexts.
Enoxaparin represents an adjunctive, pregnancy-focused intervention in PCOS rather than a primary disease-modifying therapy. Its role remains investigational in this population and would likely be restricted to selected subgroups pending robust evidence demonstrating improved live birth outcomes and favorable safety profiles.

Name: Entervax
Developers: Prokarium Ltd; University of Oxford (including Oxford University Clinical Research Unit Vietnam (OUCRU), Nuffield Department of Women's and Reproductive Health (NDWRH))
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against Salmonella enterica serovars Typhi and Paratyphi A infections
Mechanism of action: Contains a recombinant form of Salmonella typhi ZH9 strain, bio-engineered to also express Salmonella Paratyphi A antigens - flagellin H:a and lipopolysaccharide O:2. It acts as an immunostimulant.
Key features and challenges: Entervax is an oral, bivalent Salmonella vaccine that has been shown to be highly immunogenic in preclinical studies and a successful phase I human clinical trial. It is currently being investigated in a Phase II trial. It's progenitor candidate - M01ZH09, which was being developed by Emergent Biosolutions, and the University of Vermont College of Medicine was extensively studied in preclinical and multiple human clinical trials, and was shown to be safe, well tolerated and effective in preventing typhoid infections (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15995948/) (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16148184/) (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16140433/) (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20668668/) (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20188175/).

Name: Env (A,B,C,A/E)/gag (C) DNA, gp120 (A,B,C,A/E) Protein vaccine with GLA-SE adjuvant (PDPHV-201401)
Developers: University of Massachusetts Medical School (including MassBiologics); US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease (NIAID)
Indication: Indicated for the prevention of HIV-1 infection
Target:
env (A,B,C,A/E)/gag (C) DNA vaccine: Envs from HIV-1 clades A, B, C, and A/E and clade C Gag
gp120 (A,B,C,A/E) protein vaccine: Recombinant Proteins gp120A, gp120B, gp120C, gp120AE
Mechanism of action: Heterologous vaccine regimen. Designed to elicit humoral and cellular immune responses.
Key features and challenges:
Phase I trial: NCT03409276/HVTN 124 (completed May 2020) and NCT04927585 (completed December 2023).

PDPHV 201401 is a second-generation, polyvalent vaccines comprised of DNA vaccine with five DNA plasmids that prime the immune system and protein vaccine with four gp120 recombinant proteins that provides boost, being developed by Worcester HIV Vaccine, under a license from the University of Massachusetts Medical School for the prevention of HIV infections. The candidate is developed using the polyvalent DNA-prime/protein-boost technology to target multiple subtypes of HIV-1. The DNA component consists of five plasmids, four of which encodes the gp120 proteins of the HIV-1 clades A, B, C and AE and one codes the Gag protein from HIV-1 clade C. The protein component includes four recombinant gp120 proteins produced from CHO cells which are an exact match to the proteins in the gp120 DNA component. The recombinant proteins can be supplemented with a glucopyranosyl lipid adjuvant in a stable emulsion (GLA-SE) and can help in improving the DNA-primed immune responses to recombinant gp120 proteins. The plasmids are administered intramuscularly by mixing in in equal weights. The protein component is also administered through intramuscular injection following mixing in equal weights at bedside with GLA-SE. Clinical development is ongoing in the US.
Recent updates: Phase I trial completed in 2023 (NCT04927585).

Developers: Walter Reed Army Institute of Research (WRAIR) (including Military HIV Research Program); EMMES Corporation; US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease (NIAID)

Name: EnvSeq-1 Envs, GLA-SE adjuvant
Developers: Duke University; Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center (including the HIV Vaccine Trials Network (HVTN)); US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease (NIAID)
Indication: Indicated for the prevention of HIV-1 infection
Target: EnvSeq-1 Env proteins (CH505TF, CH505w53, CH505w78, CH505 M5)
Mechanism of action: Designed to elicit humoral immune response.
Key features and challenges:

The EnvSeq-1 vaccine candidate comprises a series of four HIV-1 envelope glycoprotein (Env) proteins—CH505TF, CH505w53, CH505w78, and CH505w100—derived from an HIV-1-infected patient who developed CD4-binding site-specific broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs). These proteins are formulated with the adjuvant GLA-SE to enhance the immune response.

Name: Epitope-based RVFV vaccine (M glycoprotein)
Product: Vector control products Reservoir targeted vaccines
Developers: Adeleke University; Clemson University
Indication: Prevention of RVFV infection in livestock
Mechanism of action: Uses predicted B-cell, CTL, and HTL epitopes from the M glycoprotein, joined with linkers and a Bos taurus-specific β-defensin adjuvant, to induce strong humoral and cellular immune responses.
Key features and challenges:
-Construct contains six CTL peptides, three HTL peptides, and two B-cell peptides with favorable antigenicity, non-allergenicity, and non-toxicity.
-Codon-optimized for E. coli K-12 expression and successfully cloned in silico into pET-28a(+) vector.
-Molecular docking showed strong interactions with TLR7 and TLR8, indicating potential innate immune activation.
-Immune simulations predicted sustained antibody responses (IgM, IgG1, IgG2) for up to 350 days post-vaccination.
-Challenges: Results are purely in silico; requires in vitro validation, animal studies, and eventual challenge trials.
Recent updates:

-As of Sept 2025, no experimental lab-based validation yet reported, but computational approaches to RVFV vaccine design are expanding, with interest in combining multi-epitope designs with delivery platforms such as nanoparticles or viral vectors.

Name: Epitope-focused immunogens
Developers: University of Lübeck
Indication: Indicated for the control of Hepatitis C infection.
Mechanism of action: Neutralizes multiple genetically diverse HCV strains.
Key features and challenges:
Abstract
Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection causes ~290,000 annual human deaths despite the highly effective antiviral treatment available. Several viral immune evasion mechanisms have hampered the development of an effective vaccine against HCV, among them the remarkable conformational flexibility within neutralization epitopes in the HCV antigens. Here, we report the design of epitope-focused immunogens displaying two distinct HCV cross-neutralization epitopes. We show that these immunogens induce a pronounced, broadly neutralizing antibody response in laboratory and transgenic human antibody mice. Monoclonal human antibodies isolated from immunized human antibody mice specifically recognized the grafted epitopes and neutralized four diverse HCV strains. Our results highlight a promising strategy for developing HCV immunogens and provide an encouraging paradigm for targeting structurally flexible epitopes to improve the induction of neutralizing antibodies (https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.ado2600).

Name: Ertapenem
Developers: University of Amsterdam, Universiteit van Amsterdam (UvA) (including University medical center)
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Ertapenem works by binding to and inhibiting bacterial penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs). Upon binding to PBPs, ertapenem inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by interfering with the lengthening and strengthening of the peptidoglycan portion of the cell wall, thereby inhibiting cell wall synthesis.
Key features and challenges:
Ertapenem is a long-acting carbapenem antibiotic with broad-spectrum activity against Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. It is administered parenterally and is commonly used for moderate to severe infections caused by susceptible organisms. As resistance to extended-spectrum cephalosporins increases globally, ertapenem has been investigated as a potential alternative treatment for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, particularly for anogenital infections.
In a 2020 randomized clinical trial, participants with gonorrhea were assigned to receive intramuscular (IM) ceftriaxone 500 mg (control), IM ertapenem 1000 mg, IM gentamicin 5 mg/kg (maximum 400 mg), or oral fosfomycin 6 g (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1473309921006253). 
The primary outcome was microbiological cure, defined as a negative nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) 7–14 days after treatment. Results demonstrated that single-dose 1000 mg ertapenem was non-inferior to single-dose 500 mg ceftriaxone for the treatment of gonorrhea. In contrast, gentamicin did not meet non-inferiority criteria. These findings support ertapenem as a potential effective alternative for anogenital N. gonorrhoeae infections, particularly in the context of emerging ceftriaxone resistance.
Key challenges include the requirement for parenteral administration, potential impact on antimicrobial stewardship given carbapenems are considered last-resort agents, and the need to preserve carbapenem efficacy for other multidrug-resistant infections. Broader evaluation against ceftriaxone-resistant strains, assessment of resistance development, and cost-effectiveness considerations will influence its role in treatment guidelines.
Overall, ertapenem has demonstrated non-inferiority to ceftriaxone for anogenital gonorrhea and represents a promising alternative option. Its future utility will depend on resistance patterns, stewardship considerations, and further clinical evaluation in resistant infections.

Name: Ervebo vaccine + Inmazeb
Developers: Inserm ANRS MIE
Indication: Ebola virus disease post-exposure prophylaxis
Target:
Ervebo: The glycoprotein (GP) of Zaire ebolavirus. Ervebo is a recombinant VSV vector expressing this Ebola GP, which is the key surface protein facilitating virus entry into host cells.
Inmazeb: Multiple epitopes across the Zaire ebolavirus glycoprotein. Inmazeb includes three human monoclonal antibodies—atoltivimab, maftivimab, and odesivimab that bind distinct, non-overlapping sites on GP.
Together, in a post-exposure prophylaxis scenario, Inmazeb provides immediate passive immunity by neutralizing any circulating virus, while Ervebo rapidly primes the immune system to develop durable, long-term protection—offering a potent dual-approach defense.
Mechanism of action:
Ervebo is a replication-competent viral vector that infects cells post-intramuscular injection, leading to transient expression of Ebola GP and prompting the immune system—both humoral (antibodies) and cellular (T cells)—to mount a defense. It triggers rapid GP-specific IgG production, observed within 3–7 days in nonhuman primate models, conferring early protective immunity.
Inmazeb:
Virus neutralization: By binding GP, these antibodies block the virus’s ability to bind to host cell receptors, inhibiting viral attachment and entry.
Additionally, Inmazeb’s antibodies can stabilize GP in its pre-fusion form—preventing conformational changes needed for fusion—and promote immune clearance via processes like ADCC (antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity) and phagocytosis.
Recent updates:
The phase 3 trial is currently underway or on standby, given its critical role in outbreak management.
Both products are licensed individually (Ervebo for prevention; Inmazeb for treatment), and the combination is now formally being tested as a PEP paradigm. Source: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06841614

Name: Ervebo vaccine + Obeldesivir
Developers: Inserm ANRS MIE
Indication: Post-exposure prophylaxis or early therapeutic intervention to prevent or treat Ebola disease, including Sudan ebolavirus strain
Mechanism of action:
Ervebo: Live-attenuated recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus expressing Ebola Zaire glycoprotein, delivering potent neutralizing antibody and cellular immune responses.
Obeldesivir (ODV): Broad-spectrum antiviral inhibiting viral polymerase and replication; shown to protect non-human primates from lethal SUDV challenge as late as 10 days post-infection, with 80–100% survival depending on species
Key features and challenges: Ebola virus disease (EVD) remains a significant public health challenge due to its high mortality rates and potential for rapid transmission among close contacts of infected individuals. Despite advances in treatment and prevention, including the development of the Ervebo vaccine (ERV), there is a critical need to optimize post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) strategies to protect high-risk contacts, such as those with direct exposure to bodily fluids of symptomatic cases or corpses of confirmed or probable cases. The EBOPEP trial seeks to evaluate whether combining ERV with Inmazeb (IMZ), a monoclonal antibody cocktail, or Obeldesivir (ODV), an antiviral agent, offers enhanced protection compared to ERV alone. The trial's main objective is to compare the efficacy of two combination PEP strategies (ERV+IMZ and ERV+ODV) against ERV alone in reducing the incidence of EVD at Day 21 among high-risk contacts. The secondary objectives include assessing the safety and tolerance of the three PEP strategies, comparing the severity of EVD cases among the intervention arms, evaluating the proportion of deaths attributable to EVD in each group, and describing the progression of viral load in participants with confirmed EVD. These objectives aim to provide a comprehensive understanding of the clinical and epidemiological benefits of the proposed PEP strategies.
Recent updates:
Phase III trial ongoing (PACTR202502853321394)
Recent outbreak responses involving Sudan ebolavirus in Uganda included both interventions under WHO’s Solidarity‑Ebola adaptive framework, comparing arms of vaccine alone, antiviral alone, and their combination. Preclinical rhesus macaque data support significant survival benefits from combination, even when initiated late post-exposure.

Name: Erythritol
Developers: Jawaharlal Nehru University
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of malaria caused by P. falciparum
Key features and challenges: Erythritol, a sugar substitute, targets multifunctional transporter protein Plasmodium aquaglyceroporin (PfAQP) responsible for maintaining hydro-homeostasis.
Recent updates: Preclinical study published in 2022 (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.04.28.489976v1).

Name: Esketamine
Developers: Janssen Cilag International Nv; Johnson & Johnson; Leiden University Medical Center
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of endometriosis associated pain, inflammation, and depression
Mechanism of action: non-competitive N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonist
Key features and challenges:
Esketamine, the S-enantiomer of ketamine, is a powerful NMDA receptor antagonist with central nervous system depressant properties. It works by modulating glutamate neurotransmission, which helps alleviate symptoms of treatment-resistant major depressive disorder. Administered as an intranasal spray, esketamine offers a rapid onset of action compared to traditional antidepressants. Its unique mechanism of action and fast-acting nature distinguish it as a promising option for patients who have not responded to other treatments.
(https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/182137).
A randomized controlled trial launched in 2024 aims to investigate the efficacy of esketamine compared to a placebo in treating chronic pelvic pain from endometriosis. The study measures pain levels using the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) and also evaluates secondary outcomes such as side effects, quality of life, depressive symptoms, and pain coping strategies. Endometriosis, a condition affecting about 10% of reproductive-aged women, causes severe pain, infertility, and diminished quality of life, with inadequate current treatment options often leading to increased opioid use. Esketamine, known for its analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antidepressant effects, has not been studied specifically for endometriosis-related pain, making this trial an important investigation into its potential benefits. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06161805)
Recent updates: TM 13/12/2025: Study protocol located from EMBASE (http://dx.doi.org/10.1177/22840265241302377).

Name: Estradiol - PE
Developers: University of Kragujevac
Indication: Treatment of preeclampsia-associated hypertension
Mechanism of action: Oestrogen receptor agonists - reducing blood pressure in preeclampsia by modulating plasma oxidative stress
Key features and challenges:
Estradiol (E2) is a naturally occurring estrogen steroid hormone widely used in menopausal hormone therapy, hormonal contraception, gender-affirming therapy, and treatment of hormone-sensitive conditions. During pregnancy, circulating estrogens play a critical role in uterine vascular remodeling and placental development. Estrogen receptor activation in cytotrophoblasts and uterine arterial walls promotes outward hypertrophic remodeling of the uterine vasculature, supporting adequate uteroplacental perfusion.
In preeclampsia (PE), reduced estrogen levels have been associated with impaired uterine vascular remodeling, diminished uteroplacental blood flow, and fetal growth restriction. Preclinical studies in rat models of preeclampsia have demonstrated that exogenous estradiol administration attenuated hypertension, proteinuria, fetal growth restriction, neonatal mortality, oxidative stress, inflammation, and endothelial dysfunction (2020: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31985028/). Similar protective effects have been observed with 2-methoxyestradiol (2ME2), a principal estradiol metabolite (2020: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32333783/). Drug repurposing modeling studies have also identified estradiol as a potential therapeutic candidate for preeclampsia (2021: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33546161/).
Limited clinical studies have evaluated short-term intramuscular estradiol therapy in women with preeclampsia, reporting improvements in antioxidant status and reductions in blood pressure (e.g., https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19903522/). However, data remain sparse and largely exploratory.
Key challenges include potential teratogenic and endocrine-disrupting effects with prolonged estrogen exposure during pregnancy, uncertainty regarding optimal dosing and timing, and lack of large randomized controlled trials demonstrating clinical benefit. While mechanistically plausible and supported by preclinical evidence, estradiol therapy for preeclampsia requires substantial clinical validation to establish safety and efficacy before consideration for routine use.
Recent updates:

2020: The effects of estradiol on inflammatory and endothelial dysfunction in rats with preeclampsia. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31985028/)

2020: Treatment with 2-methoxyestradiol increases endothelial nitric oxide synthase activity via scavenger receptor class BI in human umbilical vein endothelial cells. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32333783/)

2018: Estradiol decreases blood pressure in association with redox regulation in preeclampsia. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28920713/)

Name: Ethamsylate
Developers: Ain Shams University
Indication: Reduce blood loss/haemostatic resuscitation in postpartum haemorrhage
Mechanism of action: Stimulating TXA2 and PF2a-mediated platelet disaggegation
Key features and challenges:
Ethamsylate (etamsylate) is a haemostatic agent used to prevent and control bleeding from small blood vessels and capillary beds. It has been employed in conditions such as menorrhagia, neonatal intraventricular haemorrhage, and other forms of capillary bleeding. Ethamsylate is reported to exert angioprotective and proaggregant effects, promoting platelet adhesion and aggregation. Its haemostatic mechanism involves stimulation of thromboplastin formation at sites of vascular injury, reduction of prostacyclin (PGI₂) synthesis, and enhancement of platelet function, thereby limiting capillary haemorrhage.
Ethamsylate has been investigated in the context of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH). A clinical trial conducted between 2015 and 2016 evaluated the efficacy of tranexamic acid in combination with ethamsylate for PPH management (NCT02604719: https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT02604719). However, no results have been reported. A subsequent trial initiated in 2020 is assessing ethamsylate in PPH, with results pending (NCT04656067: https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT04656067
; PACTR202009885648906: https://pactr.samrc.ac.za/TrialDisplay.aspx?TrialID=23713).
Key challenges include limited high-quality evidence supporting its use in PPH, absence of published results from completed trials, and uncertainty regarding comparative effectiveness versus established uterotonics and antifibrinolytics. Its role in PPH management remains investigational pending robust clinical outcome data.

Name: Etonogestrel/ethinylestradiol vaginal ring
Developers: Merck (also known as Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany), including Sigma-Aldrich, MilliporeSigma and EMD Serono; Organon & Co.; University of Pennsylvania; University of Oulu
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: Estrogen receptor agonists; Progesterone receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
The etonogestrel/ethinylestradiol vaginal ring is a combined hormonal contraceptive delivering continuous low-dose ethinylestradiol and etonogestrel via a vaginal route. It is widely used for contraception and provides stable systemic hormone levels with lower daily fluctuation compared to oral contraceptives. In polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), combined hormonal contraceptives are commonly used to regulate menstrual cycles, suppress ovarian androgen production, reduce free testosterone levels, and improve androgen-related symptoms such as acne and hirsutism.

Earlier clinical investigations have evaluated the metabolic and endocrine effects of combined hormonal contraceptives in PCOS, including comparisons between oral formulations and the vaginal ring. A completed randomized trial (NCT01588873) assessed the long-term effects (59 weeks) of ethinylestradiol/desogestrel versus ethinylestradiol/etonogestrel (vaginal ring) on metabolic and inflammatory parameters in women with PCOS. The primary endpoint was change in the Matsuda index (insulin sensitivity), with secondary endpoints including high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (CRP) and Free Androgen Index (FAI). The study aimed to determine the differential metabolic and endocrine impacts of oral versus vaginal hormonal delivery systems.
https://www.clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01588873

https://adis.springer.com/trials/700217130

More recently, an ongoing study (NCT04257500) is evaluating the metabolic effects of the contraceptive vaginal ring in overweight and obese women with PCOS over a 4-month period. The study plans to enroll 40 participants, with the primary endpoint being the incidence of metabolic syndrome. Secondary assessments include hormonal and metabolic markers, aiming to clarify whether the vaginal route offers metabolic advantages or reduced risk compared with traditional oral contraceptives in high-risk PCOS populations.
https://www.clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04257500
https://adis.springer.com/trials/700318468
Overall, evidence suggests that the etonogestrel/ethinylestradiol vaginal ring effectively regulates menstrual cycles and suppresses androgen activity in PCOS, consistent with the established role of combined hormonal contraception as first-line therapy for menstrual dysfunction and hyperandrogenism. However, the metabolic effects remain an area of active investigation. Combined hormonal contraceptives may variably influence insulin sensitivity, lipid profiles, and inflammatory markers, particularly in overweight or obese women with PCOS who already carry elevated cardiometabolic risk.
Key challenges include limited large-scale, long-term comparative data specifically in PCOS populations, heterogeneity in metabolic response, and the need to balance androgen suppression benefits against potential cardiometabolic effects. As with other estrogen-containing contraceptives, thrombotic risk must also be considered in high-risk individuals. The vaginal ring remains an approved contraceptive device, but its positioning in PCOS management is primarily symptom-directed rather than disease-modifying.

Name: Etravirine
Developers: Naval Medical University, Shanghai
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of CHIKV infection
Mechanism of action:
-Binds to RdRp pocket, interfering with RNA synthesis.
-Inhibits replication of CHIKV (and WNV, YFV, TBEV) in vitro.
-In mice, reduces viral load, inflammatory cytokines, footpad swelling, and mortality.
Key features and challenges:
-In vitro: IC₅₀ against CHIKV ≈ 9.6–9.9 µM (Huh7, Vero, HUVEC cells).
-In vivo: In mouse CHIKV models (ROSS and LR2006 OPY1 strains), oral dosing (40 mg/kg) reduced swelling, viral burden, and inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-10, CCL-2).
-Improved survival (30% protection in lethal CHIKV model).
-Broad-spectrum anti-arboviral effect (CHIKV, WNV, YFV, TBEV).
-Repurposing opportunity: already FDA-approved for HIV.
Recent updates:
August 2024:
-First study to demonstrate etravirine as a broad-spectrum anti-arbovirus candidate.
-Ongoing work suggested molecular docking supports strong RdRp binding in alphaviruses and flaviviruses.
-Provides rationale for further evaluation as a repurposed therapeutic for CHIKV and related arboviruses.

Name: Ex-miRNA biomarkers + sFlt1:PlGF ratio
Developers: University of California San Diego School of Medicine
Indication: Diagnostic and prognostic assessment of preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: miRNAs detect sub-clinical placental distress in the first or early second trimester, and the sFlt-1:PlGF ratio is highly effective in predicting PE in the third trimester
Key features and challenges:
Extracellular microRNA (ex-miRNA) biomarkers are being investigated as novel, non-invasive tools for early diagnosis and prognostic stratification of preeclampsia (PE). A 2024 study analyzed small RNA sequencing data from prospectively collected maternal serum samples in women undergoing evaluation for suspected PE and identified distinct ex-miRNA expression patterns across different hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.adg7545).
Using an iterative machine learning approach, researchers identified three bivariate ex-miRNA biomarker pairs that, when applied sequentially, differentiated PE cases by severity and distinguished PE from controls. In the derivation cohort, the model achieved a sensitivity of 93%, specificity of 79%, positive predictive value (PPV) of 55%, and negative predictive value (NPV) of 89%. In a small independent validation cohort, sensitivity was 91% and specificity was 57%. Importantly, combining the ex-miRNA biomarkers with the established sFlt-1:PlGF protein ratio improved diagnostic performance compared with either modality alone, achieving sensitivity of 89.4%, specificity of 91.3%, PPV of 95.5%, and NPV of 80.8%.
Key challenges include the need for large-scale external validation, standardization of miRNA extraction and sequencing methodologies, and translation of sequencing-based biomarkers into clinically scalable assays. While the combined biomarker approach demonstrates improved predictive performance, integration into routine care will depend on feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and reproducibility across diverse populations and clinical settings.
