Name: Exenatide
Developers: AstraZeneca; Radboud University; Regional and University Hospital of Besancon; Xinqiao Hospital of Chongqing
Indication: PCOS Insulin resistance, glucose insensitivity, weight, metabolic dysfunction, fertility
Mechanism of action: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
Exenatide is a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist originally derived from Heloderma lizard venom and developed for the treatment of type 2 diabetes. It enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppresses glucagon release, and slows gastric emptying, thereby improving glycaemic control and promoting weight loss. It is available as a subcutaneous injection (5 µg and 10 µg formulations), with additional long-acting preparations explored in metabolic indications.
https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800007685
As interest in incretin-based therapies expanded beyond diabetes, exenatide began to be evaluated in PCOS due to the central role of insulin resistance and obesity in disease pathophysiology. Early and subsequent clinical studies demonstrated improvements in insulin sensitivity, weight reduction, lipid parameters, and menstrual cyclicity in women with PCOS treated with exenatide, particularly when compared to or added to metformin.
https://www.wjgnet.com/1948-9358/full/v13/i1/5.htm
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1155/2023/4288004
In 2021, a randomized clinical study comparing exenatide once weekly (EQW), dapagliflozin, combination therapy, and other metabolic agents in overweight/obese women with PCOS showed that dual therapy (exenatide + dapagliflozin) provided superior metabolic improvements compared to monotherapy, reinforcing the concept that incretin-based combinations may offer additive benefits.
https://academic.oup.com/jcem/article/106/10/3019/6294193
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02635386
Combination strategies have been central to exenatide’s development in PCOS. Meta-analyses and clinical trials report that exenatide combined with clomiphene citrate significantly improves ovulation and pregnancy rates compared to clomiphene alone.
https://rbej.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12958-023-01075-9
Similarly, multiple trials have shown that exenatide plus metformin improves anthropometric measures, insulin resistance indices, and androgen levels more effectively than metformin alone.
https://bmcendocrdisord.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12902-023-01497-x
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34732660/
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04969627
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03151005
More recently, research has expanded to metabolic comorbidities. A 2023 NIH-funded project is investigating the effect of exenatide on hepatic glucose metabolism in PCOS patients with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), reflecting growing recognition of hepatic insulin resistance in PCOS pathogenesis.
https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/10692902
In parallel, QR 108, a controlled-release injectable formulation of exenatide, is under preclinical development for endocrine disorders, suggesting ongoing innovation in formulation and delivery platforms.
https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800050010
Despite its promising metabolic and reproductive benefits, exenatide faces several challenges in PCOS care. It is not formally approved for PCOS, and current international guidelines list GLP-1 receptor agonists as emerging or adjunct options rather than first-line therapy. Most PCOS studies are relatively small, single-centre trials with short follow-up durations, and long-term data on live birth rates and reproductive safety remain limited. Gastrointestinal adverse effects, injectable administration requirements, and cost may also limit widespread adoption. Additionally, careful pre-conception planning is required, as GLP-1 agonists are not recommended during pregnancy.

Name: ExoCounter Assays for Placental Small Extracellular Vesicles
Developers: University of Oxford (including Oxford University Clinical Research Unit Vietnam (OUCRU), Nuffield Department of Women's and Reproductive Health (NDWRH)); JVCKENWOOD Corporation
Indication: Detection of early onset preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for research use only
Mechanism of action: Quantifies circulating placental extracellular vesicles to detect altered trophoblast signaling associated with placental dysfunction and preeclampsia.
Key features and challenges:
Researchers from Oxford have investigated the potential of extracellular vesicles released from the placenta as an early biomarker of preeclampsia.
They used ExoCounter, a novel device developped by JVCKENWOOD, that immunophenotypes size-selected small extracellular vesicles <160 nm. To investigate disease-specific and gestational age-specific changes, they analyzed placental small extracellular vesicles (psEV) counts in maternal plasma samples taken at each of the 3 trimesters from women who had (1) normal pregnancy (n=3); (2) women who developed early-onset preeclampsia (EOPE; n=3); and (3) women who developed late-onset preeclampsia (n=4) using 3 antibody pairs, CD10-placental alkaline phosphatase (PLAP), CD10-CD63, and CD63-PLAP. They further validated the findings in first-trimester serum samples among normal pregnancy (n=9), women who developed EOPE (n=7), and women who developed late-onset preeclampsia (n=8).

The study confirmed that CD63 was the major tetraspanin molecule coexpressed with PLAP—a known placental extracellular vesicles marker on psEV. Higher psEV counts for all 3 antibody pairs were detected in the plasma of women who developed EOPE than the other 2 groups in the first trimester, which persisted through the second and third trimesters. Significantly higher CD10-PLAP (P<0.01) and CD63-PLAP (P<0.01) psEV counts were validated in the serum of the first trimester of women who developed EOPE compared with normal pregnancy.

Application of the specific ExoCounter assay developed for this study could identify patients at risk of developing EOPE in the first trimester, thereby providing a window of opportunity for early intervention. A patent application has been filed relating to this work. (https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/HYPERTENSIONAHA.123.20907)

Name: Extracellular Vesicles-mediated recombinant IL-10 ( eIL-10)
Developers: University of Texas Medical Branch at Galveston
Indication: Reduce the incidence of infection-associated preterm birth
Mechanism of action: Characterizes microbial community composition to identify dysbiosis associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes.
Key features and challenges:
IL-10 is a potent anti-inflammatory cytokine that has been shown to be a pregnancy compatible immune effector. Previous studies have shown that IL-10 has reduced the experimental fetal growth restriction and demise, protection against LPS induced abortion and fetal growth restriction in mice and reduced uterine contraction induced by the IL-1β. The question arises as to whether such potent biologicals will target fetal inflammatory responses more efficaciously. 

To address this, researchers electroporetically packaged IL-10 as a drug in HEK293T cell-derived EVs, now called eIL-10. IL-10 was chosen based on reports that recombinant IL-10 (rIL-10) can reduce the risk of inflammation-associated PTB. A deficiency of IL-10 in the amniotic fluid of women with amniotic infection has been reported as a factor associated with fetal inflammation and PTB in animal models as well as in in vivo nonhuman primate and mouse models. IL-10 inhibits the activation of NF-κB in a cell and stimulant-dependent manner. By administering eIL-10, the drug protected the cytokine from its short half-life in the circulation, allowing its passage to the fetus so as to overcome the limitations of prior studies which showed that rIL-10 requires administration into the amniotic cavity for its success in reducing PTB.

In this study, the developers combined exosome-based drug delivery and eIL-10’s ability to control unscheduled inflammation and ascending infection-associated PTB.  CD1 mice were vaginally inoculated with E. coli (1010CFU) and subsequently treated with either PBS, eIL-10 (500ng) or Gentamicin (10mg/kg) or a combination of eIL-10+gentamicin. Fetal inflammatory response in maternal and fetal tissues after the infection or treatment were conducted by suspension Cytometer Time of Flight (CyTOF) using a transgenic mouse model that express red fluorescent TdTomato (mT+) in fetal cells. eIL-10 administration was safe, stable, specific, delayed PTB by over 72 hrs and delivered live pups. The delivery of drugs using EVs overcomes the limitations of in-utero fetal interventions. Protecting IL-10 in EVs eliminates the need for the amniotic administration of recombinant IL-10 for its efficacy.
(https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10437065/)

Name: Extracellular vesicle (EV)-based vaccine
Developers: University of Florida
Indication: Indicated for the prevention of Salmonella enterica Serovar Typhimurium infection.
Mechanism of action: Unknown.
Key features and challenges: OBJECTIVES/GOALS: The goal of this study is to determine the immune protection provided by a novel extracellular vesicle (EV)-based vaccine generated using lab-strain Salmonella against wastewater-derived Salmonella. METHODS/STUDY POPULATION: We isolated Non-Typhoidal Salmonella (NTS) from raw influent wastewater samples collected from two wastewater reclamation facilities (WRF) in Gainesville, FL. Whole genome sequencing was performed on each isolate and compared to sequences of clinically-derived isolates in FL during our study period to identify a clinical and subclinical isolate for assessing EV based vaccine protection. Mouse serum and stool samples were collected from a cohort of EV-vaccinated mice. Surrogates of protection against Salmonella used anti-Salmonella IgA in the feces of these mice, and anti-Salmonella IgG in serum of the mice, by using ELISAs coated with whole cell lysate collected from the two wastewater-derived isolates. RESULTS/ANTICIPATED RESULTS: We have previously shown that an EV vaccine provides protection against Salmonella enterica Serovar Typhimurium, the serovar used in the generation of the EV vaccine. We anticipate that the EV vaccine generates additional protection against the community-acquired strains, which will be characterized by increases in fecal IgA and serum IgG against two community Salmonella isolates that is similar to responses against the serovar used to generate the EV vaccine (Typhimurium). DISCUSSION/SIGNIFICANCE: This study will improve the translation of our vaccine studies by demonstrating the efficacy of our novel EV vaccine against circulating Salmonella isolates (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-clinical-and-translational-science/article/417-a-cts-team-approach-to-developing-an-effective-vaccine-for-nontyphoidal-salmonella/F257EA61A8CBA5B88657287B060899CB).

Name: Ezetimibe - Endometriosis
Developers: Merck & Co; Schering-Plough Corporation
Indication: Indicated for the prevention of endometriosis angiogenesis and inflammation
Mechanism of action: selectively inhibiting the absorption of cholesterol and phytosterol by the small intestine without altering the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins and nutrients.3 The primary target of ezetimibe is the cholesterol transport protein Niemann-Pick C1-Like 1 (NPC1L1) protein. NPC1L1 is expressed on enterocytes/gut lumen (apical) as well as the hepatobiliary (canalicular) interface and plays a role in facilitating internalization of free cholesterol into the enterocyte in conjunction with the adaptor protein 2 (AP2) complex and clathrin.2 Once cholesterol in the gut lumen or bile is incorporated into the cell membrane of enterocytes, it binds to the sterol-sensing domain of NPC1L1 and forms a NPC1L1/cholesterol complex. The complex is then internalized or endocytosed by joining to AP2 clathrin, forming a vesicle complex that is translocated for storage in the endocytic recycling compartment.
Key features and challenges:
Ezetimibe is a lipid-lowering medication that works by inhibiting the intestinal absorption of cholesterol and phytosterols, making it a unique option for managing cholesterol levels. Discovered in the early 1990s, its distinct mechanism involves blocking the sterol transporter Niemann-Pick C1-Like 1 (NPC1L1), which is crucial for cholesterol uptake in the intestines. Unlike other cholesterol-lowering agents, ezetimibe does not interfere with the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, triglycerides, or bile acids. It is used as an adjunct to diet in treating primary hyperlipidemia, mixed hyperlipidemia, homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, and homozygous sitosterolemia.
A clinical trial started in 2021  investigated whether ezetimibe which is a cholesterol absorption inhibitor with anti-inflammatory and antiangiogenic properties, has therapeutic effect on endometriosis in an experimental rat model. https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04844996)
Results from this study were published in 2022, showing Ezetimibe decreased the size of the endometriotic explants with its anti-inflammatory and anti-angiogenic properties.(https://europepmc.org/article/MED/35294604)

Name: Faecal microbiota transplant - PCOS
Developers: University of California San Diego School of Medicine
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: Restore microbial diversity and balance in the gut, improving gut health, reducing systemic inflammation, and potentially alleviating metabolic and reproductive symptoms in PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Faecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) is a therapeutic approach involving transfer of processed stool from a healthy donor to a recipient to restore gut microbial diversity and balance. Growing evidence suggests that gut microbiome dysbiosis may contribute to the pathophysiology of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), potentially influencing insulin resistance, chronic inflammation, androgen excess, and metabolic dysfunction.
Preclinical studies have demonstrated that alterations in gut microbiota composition are associated with hyperandrogenism and metabolic abnormalities in PCOS models. Experimental manipulation of the microbiome in animal models has shown that gut microbial shifts may influence glucose metabolism, inflammatory pathways, and reproductive hormone regulation, supporting a mechanistic link between microbiome composition and PCOS phenotype.
In 2023, a National Institutes of Health (NIH)-funded research project was initiated to investigate the relationship between androgen receptor activation and gut microbiome dysbiosis in a letrozole-induced mouse model of PCOS. The study examines whether androgen receptor signaling is required for microbiome alterations, whether dysbiotic microbiota alone can induce metabolic dysfunction, and whether faecal microbiota transplantation can reverse PCOS-like metabolic and reproductive abnormalities. The project incorporates metagenomics and metabolomics to identify specific microbial taxa and metabolic pathways involved in disease modulation.
https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/10546503
These investigations aim to clarify whether microbiome modulation, including FMT, could serve as a therapeutic strategy to improve insulin sensitivity, reduce hyperandrogenism, and restore metabolic homeostasis in PCOS.
However, several challenges remain. Current evidence is primarily preclinical, with no completed interventional FMT trials in women with PCOS. The complexity of microbiome-host interactions, variability in donor selection, lack of standardized protocols, and regulatory considerations surrounding FMT limit immediate clinical application. Safety concerns, including infection transmission and long-term microbiome stability, also require careful evaluation. Furthermore, causality between microbiome dysbiosis and PCOS pathogenesis remains under investigation, and it is unclear whether dysbiosis is a primary driver or secondary consequence of metabolic dysfunction.
Overall, faecal microbiota transplantation represents a mechanistically plausible but early-stage therapeutic concept for PCOS. While emerging preclinical data support further investigation, robust human clinical trials are required to determine safety, efficacy, durability of response, and feasibility before integration into clinical practice.

2025:

Name: Favipiravir + Ribavirin
Developers: Toyama Chemical Company
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of CCHF
Mechanism of action:
-Favipiravir inhibits viral polymerase via incorporation into viral RNA, causing chain termination or lethal mutagenesis.
-Ribavirin, a broad-spectrum antiviral, also impedes viral replication by multiple mechanisms.
-The combination provides enhanced efficacy - protecting mice even when treatment is delayed post-infection.
Key features and challenges:
-Uniform protective efficacy: Adult immunocompetent mice infected with mouse-adapted CCHFV (MA-CCHFV) were fully protected from death and clinical disease when treated with both favipiravir and ribavirin - even with delayed administration.
-Persistent viral RNA in survivors: Though survival was achieved, viral RNA remained detectable in treated animals, indicating incomplete viral clearance despite clinical recovery.
Recent updates: 2023: Demonstrated robust protection in a novel lethal CCHFV mouse model using combination therapy. Study builds on veteran research showing favipiravir's superiority to ribavirin monotherapy and aligns with WHO guidelines that explore drug repurposing for CCHF.

Name: Fc3/FH*
Developers: Planet Biotechnology, Inc; University of Massachusetts Medical School (including MassBiologics); Oak Crest Institute of Science
Indication: Prevention of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Complement-dependent bactericidal activity
Key features and challenges:
Fc3/FH* is a complement-based immunotherapeutic candidate designed to target Neisseria gonorrhoeae by overcoming its complement evasion mechanisms. Gonococci evade complement-mediated killing through binding of host regulatory proteins such as factor H (FH) and C4b-binding protein (C4BP), which inhibit the alternative and classical complement pathways, respectively. Fc3/FH* consists of a chimeric fusion protein comprising human IgG3 Fc linked to FH domains 18–20, engineered to redirect complement activation toward the bacterial surface.
Preclinical studies demonstrated that Fc3/FH* induces complement-dependent killing of N. gonorrhoeae in vitro and reduces bacterial burden and duration of infection in a mouse vaginal colonization model. The molecule is effective against all tested PorB1B strains but exhibits limited activity against PorB1A strains, killing approximately 13% of tested isolates. To address this gap, additional complement-based fusion proteins have been evaluated. FH(6-7)/Fc3 demonstrated binding to PorB1A strains and achieved approximately 60% killing, while C4BP-IgM bound 90% of PorB1A strains and achieved 92% bactericidal activity in vitro.
The ongoing development strategy aims to generate optimized C4BP/Fc3 fusion constructs with improved characteristics and to evaluate the in vitro efficacy of FH(6-7)/Fc3 and C4BP/Fc3, alone and in combination with Fc3/FH*. Lead candidates will be tested in human FH/C4BP transgenic mouse models, with evaluation against representative PorB1A and PorB1B strains to establish broad strain coverage (https://reporter.nih.gov/search/2vwUiDqqE0O2Fenei-55sw/project-details/10932016).
Key challenges include ensuring broad efficacy across genetically diverse gonococcal strains, minimizing potential interference with host complement regulation, assessing safety in the context of complement modulation, and advancing from murine models to human studies. Manufacturing complexity and immunogenicity of Fc fusion proteins must also be addressed.
Overall, Fc3/FH* and related complement-targeting Fc fusion constructs represent a novel host-directed immunotherapeutic strategy for gonorrhea. Combination approaches targeting both PorB1A and PorB1B strains may provide broader protection and support further preclinical advancement.

Name: Fetal thymus size - PTL
Developers: King's College London; Artificial Intelligence Research Center; Karadeniz Technical University
Indication: Prediction of PTL/PTB.
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: A fetal MRI was performed on a 1.5T or 3T MRI scanner: T2 weighted images were obtained of the entire uterine content, specifically the fetal thorax. A slice-to-volume registration method was used to reconstruct three-dimensional images of the thorax. Thymus segmentations were performed manually. Body volumes were calculated by manual segmentation and thymus: body volume ratios were generated.
Key features and challenges:
The fetal thymus is a key organ in immune system development and has been shown in animal models to decrease in size in the presence of antenatal infection. Because intrauterine inflammation is a known contributor to spontaneous preterm birth (PTB), fetal thymus volume has been investigated as a potential imaging biomarker of fetal inflammatory response and PTB risk.
In 2020, a pilot study evaluated fetal thymus volume and thymus-to-body volume ratios using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in women at high risk of preterm birth between 20 and 32 weeks’ gestation. Fetuses that subsequently delivered very preterm had reduced thymus volumes relative to body size, and smaller thymus volume was associated with spontaneous PTB. The authors suggested that reduced thymus size may reflect fetal inflammation, while noting that larger studies are required to confirm findings and clarify associations with chorioamnionitis.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32865812/)
A clinical trial conducted in Turkey between 2018 and 2019 examined the relationship between fetal thymus volume and preterm labour in twin pregnancies; results have not been published.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04055701)
Additional ongoing research is using MRI to assess fetal thymus and placental characteristics to identify markers of intrauterine infection and to evaluate associations with lung and brain development and adverse neonatal outcomes in preterm births.
(https://classic.clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT05164432)
Overall, fetal thymus size measured by MRI represents an investigational imaging biomarker for identifying inflammation-associated preterm birth risk. While preliminary findings suggest an association between reduced thymus volume and spontaneous PTB, further prospective validation is required before clinical application.

Name: Fezolinetant - Uterine fibroids
Developers: Astellas Pharma
Indication: Uterine fibroid management (unspecified)
Mechanism of action: Neurokinin 3 receptor antagonists
Key features and challenges:
Fezolinetant is an orally administered, small-molecule, non-hormonal neurokinin-3 (NK3) receptor antagonist developed by Astellas Pharma. It blocks neurokinin B (NKB) signaling at the kisspeptin/neurokinin B/dynorphin (KNDy) neurons within the hypothalamus, thereby modulating thermoregulatory pathways. While primarily developed for vasomotor symptoms (VMS) associated with menopause, fezolinetant has also been explored in gynecological conditions including uterine fibroids (uterine leiomyoma).
https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800039455
In 2017, Euroscreen completed a Phase IIa randomized, placebo-controlled study evaluating daily oral fezolinetant in women with uterine leiomyoma. The trial assessed tolerability and clinical efficacy, including impact on bleeding, fibroid volume, and pain. Publicly available summaries indicate completion; however, detailed peer-reviewed efficacy data specific to fibroid volume reduction remain limited.
https://adis.springer.com/trials/700239816
Subsequent development activities have largely focused on safety and tolerability rather than dedicated fibroid efficacy trials. Between 2019 and 2023, multiple Phase I and tolerability studies were conducted evaluating pharmacokinetics, dose-ranging, and safety profiles, primarily in healthy participants or in populations treated for vasomotor symptoms rather than uterine fibroids specifically.
https://adis.springer.com/trials/700319096
https://adis.springer.com/trials/700325389
https://adis.springer.com/trials/700325450
https://adis.springer.com/trials/700330374
https://adis.springer.com/trials/700334710
Regulatory approvals have been granted for menopause-related vasomotor symptoms (MR-VMS) in the United States, European Union, Iceland, Norway, Liechtenstein, Australia, and Switzerland. However, fezolinetant is not approved for uterine fibroids.
Although NK3 antagonism provides a non-hormonal mechanism that may help manage vasomotor symptoms—particularly in women receiving hypoestrogenic therapies for fibroids—direct antifibroid effects (e.g., reduction in fibroid size or durable bleeding control independent of hormonal suppression) remain unproven. No recent Phase III uterine fibroid trials have been reported.
Fezolinetant represents a clinically validated therapy for vasomotor symptom control, with limited and early-stage exploration in uterine fibroids. Its role in uterine leiomyoma appears adjunctive (symptom management) rather than disease-modifying, and further clinical data would be required to establish a defined therapeutic position in fibroid management.

Name: Fibrinogen concentrate
Developers: Octapharma AG; CSL Behring; Laboratoire français de Fractionnement et de Biotechnologies; Yale University; Octapharma; CSL Ltd (including Seqirus)
Indication: Prevention, treatment or control of postpartum haemorrhage.
Mechanism of action: Fibrinogen is a physiological substrate of three enzymes: thrombin, factor XIIIa, and plasmin. This initiates the coagulation cascade which results in blood clotting.
Key features and challenges:
Fibrinogen (coagulation factor I) is an endogenous plasma glycoprotein that is converted by thrombin into fibrin during vascular injury, forming a fibrin-based clot that occludes damaged blood vessels and limits bleeding. Fibrin also binds and modulates thrombin activity. Human fibrinogen concentrate (e.g., RiaSTAP, CSL Behring) is a pasteurised, lyophilised plasma-derived product indicated for the treatment of acute bleeding episodes in patients with congenital fibrinogen deficiency, including afibrinogenaemia and hypofibrinogenaemia.
Although primarily indicated for congenital deficiency, fibrinogen concentrate has been investigated in postpartum haemorrhage (PPH). Observational studies have shown that low fibrinogen levels early in PPH are associated with progression to severe haemorrhage, increased transfusion requirements, and worse outcomes. A fibrinogen level below 2 g/L in the early phase of PPH has been identified as a predictor of severe bleeding. Fibrinogen concentrate enables rapid, high-dose replacement without the need for blood group crossmatching and, compared with fresh frozen plasma or cryoprecipitate, offers standardized dosing and reduced risk of transfusion-related complications.
The Fibrinogen in Haemorrhage of Delivery (FIDEL) trial (NCT02155725), completed in 2018, found that early and systematic administration of fibrinogen concentrate did not reduce blood loss, transfusion requirements, or postpartum anaemia compared with placebo, although it prevented a decline in plasma fibrinogen levels without increasing thromboembolic events (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33713384/),
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT02155725). 
A separate randomized study (NCT02528708) was suspended due to slow recruitment and feasibility challenges (https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT02528708). A 2020 systematic review concluded that there is insufficient evidence to support routine early administration of fibrinogen concentrate in PPH to reduce allogeneic blood transfusion or improve clinical outcomes (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32037228/).  Clinical research in this area remains ongoing.
Key challenges include inconsistent evidence regarding clinical benefit in non-deficient obstetric populations, uncertainty regarding optimal timing and dosing, and cost considerations compared with conventional blood products. While biologically plausible and predictive markers support targeted use, routine early administration has not demonstrated clear outcome advantages. Further high-quality, adequately powered trials are needed to define its role within PPH management algorithms.

Name: Fibrinogen-like protein 1
Developers: Tongji University School of Medicine
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS via detection of metabolic dysfunction
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Quantifies FGL1 levels to reflect hepatic metabolic dysfunction and inflammatory signaling associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Fibrinogen-like protein 1 (FGL-1) is a liver-derived protein involved in metabolic regulation, immune response, and tissue repair. In the context of PCOS, studies have found that FGL-1 levels are significantly elevated in women with the condition, correlating with markers like fasting glucose, insulin resistance, and liver enzymes. 

A 2022 study investigating FGL-1 in PCOS found that serum FGL-1 levels were significantly higher in women with PCOS compared to controls across BMI, insulin resistance, and liver function subgroups. Elevated FGL-1 was strongly correlated with BMI, HbA1c, fasting glucose, HOMA-IR, ALT, AST, HDL-c, and serum uric acid. ROC analysis identified 21.02 ng/ml as the optimal cutoff for predicting PCOS, with 74.3% sensitivity and 70.6% specificity. Logistic regression confirmed that high FGL-1 levels were independently associated with increased PCOS risk, suggesting its potential as a predictive biomarker for the condition. (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40618-022-01844-0)

Name: FibroScan
Developers: Bezmialem Vakif University
Indication: Investigated as a non-invasive tool to assess hepatic steatosis and fibrosis in women with PCOS, who have high risk of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and metabolic dysfunction.
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: Hepatic stiffness (fibrosis) and hepatic fat accumulation (steatosis), assessed through liver stiffness measurement (LSM) and controlled attenuation parameter (CAP).
Mechanism of action: FibroScan uses a mechanical vibration pulse transmitted through the intercostal space to the liver. The device measures the velocity of shear waves as they propagate through hepatic tissue; faster propagation indicates stiffer (more fibrotic) liver. The Controlled Attenuation Parameter (CAP) simultaneously quantifies ultrasound signal attenuation to estimate hepatic steatosis. The technique provides rapid, reproducible, quantitative assessment of liver fat and fibrosis, without biopsy.
Key features and challenges:
FibroScan is a non-invasive transient elastography device widely used for quantitative assessment of liver steatosis and fibrosis. It is FDA-cleared and globally utilized in the evaluation of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and related metabolic liver disorders. The device provides two primary quantitative outputs: Liver Stiffness Measurement (LSM, expressed in kilopascals) to estimate fibrosis, and Controlled Attenuation Parameter (CAP, expressed in dB/m) to quantify hepatic steatosis.
https://liverfoundation.org/fibroscan
https://www.echosens.com/fibroscan-technology
NAFLD is highly prevalent in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), largely driven by insulin resistance, central obesity, and metabolic syndrome features. Clinical studies indicate that approximately 40–60% of women with PCOS exhibit NAFLD, a substantially higher prevalence compared with BMI-matched controls. Transient elastography has been shown to reliably detect hepatic steatosis in PCOS populations and demonstrates correlations with insulin resistance indices and other cardiometabolic risk factors.
Building on this background, the ongoing clinical trial NCT07027332 is specifically evaluating the use of FibroScan in women with PCOS and metabolic risk factors. The study examines CAP and LSM values in relation to hormonal parameters, menstrual irregularities, insulin resistance, and cardiometabolic biomarkers. This addresses an important clinical gap, as routine PCOS evaluation typically does not include structured hepatic assessment despite the elevated risk of NAFLD in this population.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07027332
Several challenges remain. Most FibroScan diagnostic cut-offs were validated in general NAFLD populations rather than in reproductive-age women with hyperandrogenism, and PCOS-specific thresholds have not been established. Measurement accuracy may be affected by body habitus and high visceral adiposity, particularly in obese individuals, who represent a large proportion of the PCOS population. Furthermore, FibroScan does not determine the underlying etiology of liver disease and must be interpreted in conjunction with clinical history, laboratory findings, and other imaging modalities where appropriate.
Recent updates:
2024–2025: PCOS-targeted study using FibroScan to measure hepatic fat/fibrosis patterns among PCOS phenotypes.
Source: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07027332

Name: FineBirth device
Developers: INNITIUS
Indication: Diagnosis of threatened PTL; prediction of PTL.
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: Cervical tissue's consistency, maternal clinical parameters
Mechanism of action: Non-invasive monitoring of uterine electrical activity to detect abnormal contraction patterns associated with impending preterm labour.
Key features and challenges:
The FineBirth Device (developed by Innitius) is an intravaginal probe that measures cervical tissue's consistency, which is a highly specific, direct marker of pending birth. It is a promising novel device to objectively quantify the patient's cervical consistency, diagnose threatened preterm labour, and predict the risk of spontaneous preterm birth. It uses torsional waves, a type of shear elastic waves that propagate through soft tissue to identify changes in cervical tissue consistency. The shear modulus is combined with other clinical parameters of the pregnant woman, and an artificial Intelligence algorithm provides a real-time assessment of whether the woman is experiencing a true or false preterm labour threat and informs health professionals in providing appropriate care. 
 
A clinical usability assessment was conducted on 77 pregnant women in Spain (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37094638/), with results published in July 2023. Initial use of the device did not achieve the desired reproducibility results; therefore, a lateral microcamera was added to the intravaginal probe, which resulted in improved reproducibility and acceptable values. 
In 2023, Innitius was awarded a European Innovation Council grant to fully develop and validate the accompanying AI software, do a multicentre pivotal clinical trial, and obtain regulatory approval.
(https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/190144075)
Innitius has planned for the device to enter the market by the end of 2024/beginning of 2025.

Name: Flow cytometry-based antimicrobial susceptibility test
Developers: Linnaeus University, Linnéuniversitetet; Orebro University
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoea and antimicrobial susceptibility
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: flow cytometry-based antimicrobial susceptibility testing
Key features and challenges:
A 2024 study reported on the development and evaluation of a flow cytometry-based method of antimicrobial susceptibility testing for N. gonorrhoeae, examining seven clinically relevant anti-gonococcal antibiotics and 17 well-characterized WHO N. gonorrhoeae reference strains.
The 2016 WHO gonococcal reference strains, and WHO Q, R and S (n = 17) were tested against seven clinically relevant antibiotics (ceftriaxone, cefixime, azithromycin, spectinomycin, ciprofloxacin, tetracycline and gentamicin). A dose-dependent response was seen in susceptible isolates for all tested antimicrobials. Using a single antibiotic concentration and a 50% remaining cell population cut-off, the overall sensitivity and specificity for resistance detection were 93% and 99%, respectively. By providing results in <5 h for gonococcal isolates, flow cytometry-based antimicrobial susceptibility testing can become a rapid screening method for antimicrobial resistance or antimicrobial susceptibility in gonococci. (https://academic.oup.com/jac/article/79/4/815/7604320#445946721)

Name: Fluorescent Imaging using Indocyanine green
Developers: St. Joseph Hospital Chicago
Indication: Indicated for the intraoperative detection of Endometriosis lesions.
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Uses indocyanine green fluorescence to visualize lesion perfusion and delineate endometriotic implants intraoperatively.
Key features and challenges:
A 2024 study aimed to evaluate whether the use of indocyanine green (ICG) aids in identification and removal of clear or ambiguous endometriosis lesions, not visualized under traditional WL imaging.
A retrospective chart review of patients with symptoms suspicious for endometriosis where ICG was used during laparoscopy to assist in identification of suspected endometriosis lesions. Data collection included patient demographics, medical history, surgical history, preoperative symptoms, and localization of lesions. Data was collected from hospital electronic health record system and from a private practice.
In total, 211 suspected lesions were excised, of which 115 had histologically proven endometriosis. 196 lesions were detected using ICG and 112 were confirmed to be endometriosis. These results were statistically significant (P=.024) with a sensitivity of 97.4% and a negative predictive value of 80%, demonstrating that ICG can significantly improve the intraoperative detection of endometriosis lesions. Research is ongoing with more data being collected.
This study shows that ICG fluorescence significantly improves the intraoperative detection and resection of ambiguous or clear endometriosis lesions and improves histopathologic diagnosis when compared to WL imaging. Indocyanine green has the potential to increase the detection of endometriosis and improve patient outcomes (https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/abstract/2024/05001/fluorescent_imaging_using_indocyanine_green_for.72.aspx).

Name: Foley catheter
Developers: Life Specialist Hospital
Indication: Indicated for the temporary control or reduction of postpartum uterine bleeding when conservative management of uterine bleeding is warranted.
Mechanism of action: Provides direct intrauterine pressure/tamponade to promote haemostasis.
Key features and challenges:
Balloon tamponade was initially described in 1983 using a Foley catheter. This led to the development of commercially available products such as the Bakri balloon in 2001. However, the Foley catheter is still used as an intrauterine balloon tamponade device, particularly in low-resource settings. While its own 30mL balloon may be used, other improvised balloons (e.g. gloves, condoms) may be attached to the end of the catheter and inflated. 
In a systematic review of the treatment of PPH in low-resource settings, the Foley catheter was used in three out of the 13 studies (n = 5 women). These treatments took place in Pakistan, Nigeria and Zimbabwe. Protocols varied among the three studies. None of the three studies reported how long the UBT was left in situ or the process of deflation. The Foley catheter arrested the haemorrhage in three of the five women but no further data were recorded for the other two women (https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1471-0528.2012.03454.x).  
Another study assessed uterine packing versus Foley's catheter tamponade for controlling postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) secondary. Using a prospective observational study design with 92 patients, the study found that the use of uterine packing resulted in stoppage of active bleeding in 93.3% of cases compared to only 68.1% in the Foley's catheter group (p < 0.05). Although the rate of minor complications namely fever, pain and urinary complaints were higher in the uterine packing group, it does not reach to a significant difference when compared to the Foley's catheter (p > 0.05). Six cases who failed to Foley catheter tamponade underwent emergency hysterectomy with no cases in the uterine packing group (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27855529/).

Name: Follitropin alfa - Endometriosis
Developers: CinnaGen
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of endometriosis-related infertility
Mechanism of action: Ovarian follicle stimulants
Key features and challenges:
Follitropin alfa is a recombinant human follicle-stimulating hormone (rhFSH) used to stimulate follicular development in assisted reproductive technologies (ART). Cinnal-F, developed by CinnaGen, is a biosimilar formulation of follitropin alfa launched in Iran in 2013 and available in pre-filled pens (450 IU/0.75 ml and 900 IU/1.5 ml). It is administered subcutaneously and classified under infertility therapies (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800040389). 
A Phase III trial initiated in 2014 compared its efficacy and safety with the originator product in 90 participants, supporting its use in infertility treatment.
In the context of endometriosis, follitropin alfa is not a disease-modifying therapy but is used to manage endometriosis-associated infertility through ovarian stimulation in in vitro fertilization (IVF) protocols. A double-blind, randomized clinical trial involving 94 infertile women with endometriosis published in 2022, compared letrozole plus follitropin alfa (LA) versus placebo plus follitropin alfa (PA) within a long agonist IVF protocol (https://kneopen.com/article/html/ijrm/11444/18595). 
Participants in the LA group received 5 mg letrozole daily from cycle day three. The LA group required significantly lower total doses of follitropin alfa and demonstrated lower estradiol levels compared with the PA group, suggesting that adjunctive letrozole may reduce gonadotropin requirements and estrogen exposure during stimulation in women with endometriosis.
These findings indicate that follitropin alfa remains a standard component of ART protocols in women with endometriosis-related infertility, with combination strategies potentially optimizing ovarian stimulation and hormonal profiles.
Key challenges include the fact that follitropin alfa does not treat underlying endometriotic lesions or inflammation and may increase estradiol levels, which could theoretically exacerbate estrogen-dependent disease activity. Outcomes are primarily focused on fertility rather than symptom control or lesion regression. Individualized stimulation protocols are required to balance ovarian response, estrogen exposure, and endometriosis severity. Further comparative studies are needed to refine stimulation strategies in this patient population.

Name: Follitropin delta - Endometriosis
Developers: Ferring Pharmaceuticals
Indication: Indicated for the prevention and treatment of endometriosis infertility
Mechanism of action: Ovarian follicle stimulants
Key features and challenges:
Follitropin delta is a recombinant follicle-stimulating hormone (rFSH) developed by Ferring Pharmaceuticals for treating infertility in both men and women. Administered subcutaneously, it promotes multi-follicular development in women undergoing assisted reproductive technologies. Derived from the PER.C6 human cell line, the drug is approved in numerous countries, including Canada, EU member states, Australia, Brazil, and Japan, and is under review in China and the US.
Follitropin delta has received approvals for use in controlled ovarian stimulation from various regulatory bodies, including Health Canada (March 2018), ANVISA (March 2018), and the Swissmedic (November 2017). It is also approved in Japan (March 2021) and Australia (March 2017). Ongoing reviews and trials are aimed at expanding its availability and assessing its efficacy in different patient populations.
Clinical trials investigating this candidate for fertility treatments in patients with endometriosis are as follows:
FE 999049 (Rekovelle): a daily subcutaneous injection for ovarian stimulation, with doses ranging from 6 to 12 μg based on anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) levels and body weight; dosing continued until follicular maturation criteria were met, with a maximum of 20 days of treatment (https://adis.springer.com/trials/700287289).
Phase III ESTHER-1 trial: demonstrated natural variations in AMH levels had minimal impact on ovarian response when using Rekovelle (follitropin delta) for stimulation, showing non-inferiority compared to follitropin alfa in ongoing pregnancy and implantation rates, with a higher proportion of patients achieving optimal oocyte yield and fewer cases of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (https://adis.springer.com/trials/700236520).
A randomised, controlled, open label, parallel group, multicentre trial comparing the efficacy and safety of individualised FE 999049 (follitropin delta) dosing, using a long GnRH agonist protocol and a GnRH antagonist protocol in women undergoing controlled ovarian stimulation. (https://www.clinicaltrialsregister.eu/ctr-search/trial/2017-002783-40/results)

Name: Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy
Developers: Uskudar University
Indication: Diagnosis of endometriosis via molecular analysis of blood samples
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Analyzes biochemical spectral signatures of biological samples to identify molecular composition patterns associated with endometriosis.
Key features and challenges:
Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy is a non-invasive analytical technique used to identify and quantify molecular components based on their unique infrared absorption patterns. FTIR spectroscopy has shown potential for rapid diagnosis of various diseases, including COVID-19, in research studies. However, limited awareness among clinicians and the resulting disconnect between researchers and healthcare providers impede the clinical adoption of this technology. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1572100023004805)

In FTIR spectroscopy, an infrared light beam passes through a sample, and the absorbed wavelengths are recorded to create an FTIR spectrum. This spectrum provides a molecular fingerprint of the sample, reflecting the vibrational transitions of different chemical bonds. By analyzing the positions and intensities of absorption peaks, FTIR can determine the presence and concentration of various proteins, lipids, and other biomolecules in a sample, making it valuable for diagnostic applications.

A 2022 study by Uskudar University explored the use of FTIR spectroscopy to differentiate between serum samples from women with endometrioma and healthy controls. By analyzing 100 serum samples from 50 patients with endometrioma and 50 healthy individuals, the study aims to correlate the FTIR spectral peaks with endometrioma volume and determine the chemical structure of the samples. The analysis utilized multivariate techniques, including Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Partial Least Squares (PLS) with Variables Importance in Projection (VIP), to identify significant spectral regions for diagnosis. Results indicated that specific FTIR spectral ranges (1500-1700 cm^-1 and 2700-3000 cm^-1) are indicative of endometriosis, with increased protein and lipid fractions correlating with endometrioma volume. The findings suggest that lipid content could be particularly useful in diagnosing endometriosis with endometrioma.
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1386142521008234?via%3Dihub)

Name: Fucoidan
Developers: Taipei Medical University
Indication: A natural marine-derived sulfated polysaccharide evaluated for therapeutic effects on uterine fibroids.
Target:
Fucoidan acts through multi-pathway modulation rather than a single molecular target. Key biological actions include:
-Anti-inflammatory effects (↓ CRP, ↓ inflammatory signaling)
-Anti-proliferative properties
-Anti-fibrotic activity (reported in fibrosis models)
-Modulation of lipid metabolism (↓ TG, ↓ LDL)
-Immune modulation (WBC changes)
Mechanism of action: Fucoidan is a sulfated polysaccharide known to reduce inflammation, modulate immune responses, downregulate fibrotic pathways, and influence lipid metabolism. Although its anti-fibrotic and anti-proliferative properties have been observed in other disease models, no mechanism had been studied in uterine fibroids prior to the current clinical trial. The Early Phase 1 study investigates whether fucoidan can reduce leiomyoma size and number through possible modulation of inflammatory biomarkers, hormonal balance, metabolic parameters, and uterine tissue remodeling.
Key features and challenges:
Fucoidan is a marine-derived sulfated polysaccharide commonly used as a dietary supplement and previously studied for its anti-inflammatory, anti-proliferative, and anti-fibrotic properties in oncology and chronic inflammatory conditions. This Early Phase 1 clinical trial (NCT06959966) is the first to evaluate fucoidan in uterine fibroid patients, assessing its potential to reduce fibroid size and number over six months of oral administration. The study also examines lipid metabolism, hematologic parameters, inflammatory markers (HS-CRP), liver and kidney function, and glycemic effects, reflecting fucoidan’s broad physiological activity.
However, the therapeutic mechanism for uterine fibroids remains unclear, and fucoidan’s polysaccharide nature results in variable bioavailability and heterogeneous composition. Dosing optimization, long-term safety, reproductive outcomes, and the risk of interactions with other medications (e.g., anticoagulants) remain uncertain. Evidence is currently limited to one small Early Phase 1 randomized controlled trial with 18 participants. Larger trials are needed to establish safety, mechanism, and clinical efficacy.
Source: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06959966
Recent updates:
First-ever Early Phase 1 RCT (NCT06959966) evaluating fucoidan for uterine fibroids completed in January 2023; results not yet published.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06959966

A fully convolutional dense network (FCDN) model to predict preeclampsia (PE) with circulating cell‐free RNA (cfRNA) has been proposed. The Individual Risk Score (IRS) output of the proposed FCDN model contributes to the literature on consistently monitoring the risk of PE, evaluating the effect of prophylactic treatments, and providing accurate as well as rapid screening and diagnosis of PE in populous developing countries with a high incidence of PE, such as China.

Name: Furosemide
Developers: Sanofi
Indication: Treatment of postpartum high blood pressure in preeclamptic patients
Mechanism of action: Loop diuretics; Sodium-potassium-chloride symporter inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Furosemide is a potent loop diuretic that increases renal excretion of sodium and water by inhibiting reabsorption in the loop of Henle and renal tubules. It has a rapid onset and short duration of action and is widely used in the management of fluid overload and hypertension outside pregnancy. In the context of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, furosemide has been investigated primarily in the postpartum period rather than during ongoing pregnancy.
Recent clinical studies suggest that short courses of postpartum furosemide in women with severe preeclampsia may facilitate more rapid normalization of blood pressure and reduce the need for additional antihypertensive medications. However, evidence has not consistently demonstrated reductions in length of hospital stay or delayed postpartum complications. Its role appears to be supportive in selected postpartum cases rather than disease-modifying.
Drug repurposing analyses integrating differentially expressed genes associated with preeclampsia/eclampsia (PE/E) have identified furosemide (alongside droperidol) as a potential candidate capable of modulating relevant gene expression pathways (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32724400/). However, these findings are exploratory and require clinical validation.
Key challenges include the fact that furosemide is generally not recommended during pregnancy due to concerns about reduced placental perfusion and potential fetal effects, limiting its use largely to the postpartum setting. Additionally, diuretics do not address the underlying placental pathology of preeclampsia. Further controlled studies are required to clarify optimal dosing, timing, and patient selection in postpartum hypertensive management.
Recent updates:
January 2021: a randomised clinical trial (Phase III) of Furosemide vs placebo for the management of severe antepartum hypertension is undergoing recruitment.

February 2021: scPharmaceuticals met with FDA regarding NDA approval, and intends to launch furosemide controlled release in 2023.

Name: G-porA-RPA assay
Developers: University of Queensland
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoea and antimicrobial susceptibility
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: recombinase polymerase amplification
Key features and challenges:
G-porA-RPA assay is an instrument-free, point-of-care molecular diagnostic candidate utilizing recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) technology coupled with lateral flow detection for the identification of Neisseria gonorrhoeae and assessment of ciprofloxacin susceptibility. The assay targets the gonococcal porA pseudogene (NG-porA-RPA) for infection detection.
The NG-porA-RPA assay demonstrated suitability for detecting gonococcal infection in DNA extracts from clinical urethral swabs and urine samples, including under simplified hand incubation conditions. For antimicrobial susceptibility testing, the NG-gyrA-RPA08 assay was developed to detect ciprofloxacin susceptibility, achieving 83% sensitivity (25/30) for identifying susceptible clinical samples.
However, challenges were observed in single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) discrimination using RPA technology. The gyrA assay was unable to distinguish S91F-only strains, limiting its utility in settings where such strains are prevalent. These findings highlight inherent complexities in SNP detection using RPA, particularly its tolerance for mismatches.
Overall, proof-of-concept data indicate that RPA-based diagnostics may offer a rapid, instrument-free approach for detecting N. gonorrhoeae and guiding antibiotic stewardship strategies, aligning with global priorities to improve targeted antimicrobial use (https://academic.oup.com/jac/article/77/11/2933/6650068).

Name: GMA 312

Name: GS 1144+GS 1966
Developers: Gilead
Indication: Indicated for HIV treatment.
Mechanism of action: Uncertain.
Key features and challenges:
GS-1966+GS-1144 is a heterologous vaccine regimen containing GS-1966, a ChAdV, and GS-1144, a samRNA-LNP, which both encode a novel conserved element HIV-1 immunogen spanning Gag, Pol, and Nef.
In a Phase Ib study, researchers evaluated GS-1966+GS-1144 for its safety and immunological activity, in people with HIV in the US who are using antiretroviral therapy.  The study monitored 34 people in 3 cohorts who received the vaccine at different doses and versions, and 15 people who received a placebo,
for 48 weeks.  Results showed that the vaccine was generally safe and well tolerated, with most people experiencing mild to moderate, short-lived flu-like symptoms. Vaccinated individuals from cohort 3 who received the bivalent vaccine showed higher T-cell activity than those who received placebo, but the difference was not statistically significant.  Further investigations are underway into additional metrics of T-cell functionality that may provide more insight into the impact of GS-1966+GS-1144, including evaluation of T-cell breadth and T-cell polyfunctionality (https://www.askgileadmedical.com/docs/conference/Benson_HIV%20Glasgow%20Poster%202024%20Final_25Oct24@pdf).

Name: GS-1720
Developers: Gilead

LA INSTI evaluated under a phase I open-label master protocol has recently been completed in the US, Dominican Republic, and Thailand (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05585307). 
Preliminary results presented at CROI 2024.  An initial analysis of pharmacokinetics (drug absorption and duration in the body) in HIV-negative participants demonstrated suitability to weekly dosing. 
Subsequently, four groups of seven people living with HIV who were not on ART received doses of 30 mg, 150 mg, 450 mg, or 900 mg, respectively, on two consecutive days, leading to an average viral load decline ranging from 1.74 – 2.44 log10 after 11 days of follow up. There were no serious adverse events related to the drug and no participant has so far displayed evidence of integrase inhibitor resistance (analyses of the 30 mg and 900 mg dose cohorts are not yet completed). The desired drug levels were achieved in 
recipients of the 450 mg or 900 mg doses and all experienced viral load declines greater than 2 log10
(https://www.treatmentactiongroup.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/pipeline_ARV_2024_final.pdf).
Phase-II/III clinical trials in HIV-1 infections (Combination therapy) in Puerto Rico (PO) is recruiting (NCT06544733)

Name: GSK3739937

In September 2024, ViiV Healthcare suspended the phase I trial of VH 3739937 in the treatment of HIV infections, based on the preliminary findings in a preclinical study of a similar maturation inhibitor. This double-blind, prospective, randomized, sequential trial to assess safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetic (PK) of VH 3739937 in healthy participants enrolled 67 participants in the US (https://adisinsight.springer.com/drugs/800059772).

A phase I study in HIV-negative volunteers has been completed; the results were published in Pharmacology Research and Perspectives in June 2023, showing good tolerability and the potential for once-weekly dosing (https://www.treatmentactiongroup.org/wp content/uploads/2024/07/pipeline_ARV_2024_final.pdf).

Name: GSK484
Developers: Medicines for Malaria Venture (MMV); GlaxoSmithKline (GSK)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of malaria caused by multiple Plasmodium spp
Mechanism of action: Cell inhibitors
Key features and challenges: GSK484, a therapeutic being developed by GSK in collaboration with Medicines for Malaria Venture (MMV), is targeted at the treatment of uncomplicated malaria and resistance management. Originating from the pyrazine chemical series identified in *Plasmodium falciparum* intraerythrocytic studies, GSK484 exhibits rapid parasite-killing activity in both in vitro and in vivo settings. With a low predicted dose of 100 mg and an extended half-life of approximately 200 hours, the drug holds significant promise for effective and long-lasting malaria treatment.  Clinical development is currently ongoing in the United Kingdom, complemented by preclinical studies in Switzerland. However, challenges remain, including accurate human pharmacokinetic predictions for low-clearance compounds and the reliance on palladium for two steps in the synthetic route. These factors will require careful consideration as the drug progresses through development.
Recent updates:
Dec 2024: In December 2023, GlaxoSmithKline initiated phase I trial to characterize the safety of GSK 4024484 in healthy participants within a controlled pharmacokinetic (PK) range (NCT06171113; 218708). 

Metabolite identification ongoing to confirm human PK prediction. Photosafety study ongoing.

Name: GT-CuO NPs
Developers: University of Southampton; Federal University of ABC,  Universidade Federal do ABC (UFABC)
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: generation of DNA-damaging reactive oxygen species
Key features and challenges:
GT-CuO NPs are biogenic green tea–derived copper oxide nanoparticles being investigated as a potential antimicrobial candidate against Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The nanoparticles were synthesized using a green chemistry approach and evaluated for biophysical properties, in vitro antibacterial activity, and cytotoxicity in mammalian cell cultures. Their performance was compared with commercially synthesized CuO nanoparticles (Com-CuO NPs).
GT-CuO NPs demonstrated lower cytotoxicity to mammalian cells compared with commercial CuO nanoparticles. No significant increases in bax, bcl2, il6, or il1β mRNA expression were observed following exposure to GT-CuO NPs, whereas commercial CuO nanoparticles induced notable elevations in these markers. In antibacterial testing, GT-CuO NPs achieved 50% and 100% bacterial killing at concentrations of 0.625 µg/mL and 3.125 µg/mL, respectively. In comparison, commercial CuO nanoparticles required concentrations of 15.625 µg/mL and 30 µg/mL to achieve similar effects. Ceftriaxone achieved 50% and 100% killing at concentrations of 3.125 µg/mL and 30 µg/mL, respectively.
These findings indicate that biogenic CuO nanoparticles may offer enhanced antibacterial activity with reduced cytotoxicity relative to chemically synthesized counterparts. GT-CuO NPs represent a potential alternative strategy to address multidrug-resistant N. gonorrhoeae infections and warrant further investigation.
(https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsami.4c02357).

Name: Ganirelix - Endometriosis
Developers: Merck & Co; Gedeon Richter plc; Organon & Co.
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Endometriosis.
Mechanism of action: Gonadotropin releasing hormone inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Ganirelix is a third-generation GnRH antagonist used for preventing premature ovulation during IVF treatments. Administered subcutaneously, it effectively suppresses LH and FSH surges, thus facilitating controlled ovarian stimulation. The drug is well-tolerated, with common adverse effects including injection site reactions and headache.
Developed by Roche and licensed to Organon BioSciences, Ganirelix was launched in the US in 1999, Europe in 2000, and Japan in 2009. Following its acquisition by Schering-Plough and subsequent merger with Merck & Co, Ganirelix has maintained a significant role in fertility treatments. (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800002536)
A 2023 preclinical study investigated the effects of metformin and ganirelix on subcutaneous endometriotic tissues in a mouse model. It found that both drugs reduced gene expression related to autophagy, suggesting that they might suppress endometriosis through an autophagy-based mechanism. (https://tjoddergisi.org/articles/doi/tjod.galenos.2023.85616)

Name: Gazelle platform for hemozoin detection
Developers: Hemex Health
Indication: Indicated for the diagnosis of P. falciparum and P.vivax infection
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Key features and challenges: Hemozoin was discovered and linked to malaria in the 1800s18; however, it has not been used as a primary means of diagnosing malaria. While it is possible to see hemozoin in certain stages of the parasite’s life-cycle using microscopy (in this case, it is commonly referred to as malaria pigment), it is not always detectable by traditional microscopy. Recent advances in sensing and lab-on-a-chip technologies have advanced hemozoin detection devices; a recent review article noted more than ten different research efforts. Most hemozoin-based technologies are hand-held devices that use fingerpick blood samples collected into a disposable sample chamber or cartridge. Reagents, if necessary, are contained within the cartridge, and results are available in 1-5 minutes.

Name: Gc-MP + Alum MP + AddaVax™ MP
Developers: Mercer University
Indication: Prevention of gonorrhoea
Target: Serum IgG, IgG1, IgG2a, and vaginal mucosal IgA antibodies
Mechanism of action: Induction of humoral, cellular, and protective immune responses
Key features and challenges:
Gc-MP + Alum MP + AddaVax™ MP is a whole-cell inactivated Neisseria gonorrhoeae vaccine candidate formulated as microparticles and delivered transdermally using dissolving microneedles. The formulation combines gonococcal microparticles (Gc-MP) with adjuvant microparticles, including Alhydrogel® (Alum MP) and AddaVax™ MP, to enhance immunogenicity.
Preclinical evaluation demonstrated induction of significant gonococcal-specific humoral immune responses, including serum IgG, IgG1, IgG2a, and vaginal mucosal IgA antibodies in immunized mice compared with control groups receiving blank microneedles or no treatment. Serum bactericidal assays confirmed that antibodies generated following immunization with Gc-MP + Alum MP + AddaVax™ MP exhibited bactericidal activity against live N. gonorrhoeae.
Immunized mice showed enhanced bacterial clearance following gonococcal challenge, whereas control groups did not begin clearing infection until day 10. The formulation also induced enhanced expression of cellular immunity markers CD4 and CD8 on T cells in the spleen and lymph nodes, indicating activation of cellular immune responses.
Overall, microneedle-based delivery of whole-cell inactivated gonococcal microparticles with adjuvant microparticles induced humoral, cellular, and protective immunity in preclinical models, as per a study published in 2023 (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0378517323006026?via%3Dihub).

Name: GenSci048
Developers: Changchun GeneScience Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd.
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of moderate to severe Endometriosis-related pain.
Mechanism of action: Neutralizes IL-1β.
Key features and challenges:
GenSci048 is an investigational therapeutic candidate under clinical development for the treatment of moderate to severe endometriosis-associated pain. While detailed mechanistic information has not been publicly disclosed, the compound is being evaluated as a non-surgical intervention targeting pain symptoms associated with endometriosis, a chronic inflammatory and estrogen-dependent condition characterized by ectopic endometrial tissue growth and significant pelvic pain burden.
A multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase IIa clinical trial (NCT06963177) is currently recruiting participants to assess the efficacy and safety of GenSci048 in patients with moderate to severe endometriosis-associated pain (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06963177). The study is designed to generate early-stage clinical evidence regarding therapeutic benefit and tolerability. The estimated primary completion date is January 6, 2030. The placebo-controlled and double-blind design supports methodological rigor in evaluating treatment response and safety outcomes in this population.
Key challenges include the early stage of development and limited publicly available data regarding the mechanism of action, pharmacokinetics, and long-term safety profile. As endometriosis-associated pain often involves multifactorial mechanisms including inflammation, neuropathic sensitization, and hormonal influences, demonstration of clinically meaningful and sustained pain reduction will be critical. Additionally, comparison with established hormonal and non-hormonal therapies will be necessary to define its therapeutic positioning. Robust Phase II and subsequent Phase III data will be required to establish efficacy, safety, and potential advantages over existing treatment options.

Name: Genetically Attenuated Pf∆mei2 (GA2)
Developers: Leiden University Medical Center
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against malaria caused by P. falciparum
Mechanism of action: Elicits immune response which inhibits sporozoites
Key features and challenges: The GA2 parasite, a new genetically attenuated malaria parasite, which is derived from the NF45 Plasmodium falciparum strain and has been engineered to arrest development in the liver before entering the bloodstream, was recently created. It should therefore not be able to cause malaria in humans. The idea is that the GA2 parasite will prime the immune system for recognition of non attenuated parasites in the future without causing disease itself. In other words, exposure to the innocuous GA2 parasite could confer protection against pathogenic malaria parasites.
Recent updates: Phase I trial commenced in 2025 (NCT06293339). Phase I trial completed in 2024 (NCT05468606). Phase I/II trial completed in 2022 (NCT04577066).

Name: Genetically Modified Male Bias
Developers: Target Malaria Consortium
Indication: Prevention and control of Anopheles mosquito-borne arboviral diseases
Mechanism of action: Reducing or altering vector populations through genetic manipulation – non-gene-drive approach
Key features and challenges:
Following development of the non gene drive sterile male, the Target Malaria team developed a genetically modified Anopheles gambiae  mosquito that could successfully mate and produce offspring, but in which the genetic modification would only persist for a limited period of time before disappearing. This mosquito does not carry a gene drive element that biases inheritance.

The effect of the modification in the laboratory mosquito population is that most progeny are male; hence the name “male bias”. Male mosquitoes do not bite and therefore do not transmit disease.

The non gene drive male bias mosquitoes were created by using a nuclease gene that, when activated during sperm production, fragments the X chromosome of the sperm, resulting in a mosquito that mainly has Y-bearing sperm and thus produces predominantly male offspring.

The nuclease gene is inserted into a mosquito autosome. An autosome is any chromosome that is not a sex chromosome.  Anopheles gambiae  mosquitoes have two pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes. Non-driving genes on autosomes are inherited by 50% of offspring.

Name: Genistein
Developers: Swami Vivekananda University; Burdwan Raj College; Oriental Institute of Science and Technology Vidyasagar University
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of CHIKV infection
Target: CHIKV envelope glycoproteins E1 and E2
Mechanism of action:
-Binds to CHIKV E1 and E2 envelope proteins, which mediate viral attachment and fusion.
-Predicted to inhibit viral entry by destabilizing E1/E2 function.
-Forms multiple hydrogen bonds, van der Waals and aromatic interactions within the E1/E2 binding pockets
Key features and challenges:
-Binding energy: ΔG = –8.3 kcal/mol (E1), –7.1 kcal/mol (E2).
-Stable ligand–protein complexes in 50 ns MD simulations (low RMSD, stable hydrogen bonding).
-Passed ADMET and Lipinski’s Rule of Five filters (drug-like properties).
-Natural availability: abundant in soybeans, legumes, chickpeas, broccoli, clover sprouts.
Recent updates:
2025: 
-First computational evidence of Genistein as a CHIKV E1/E2 inhibitor.
-Authors emphasize the need for in vitro and in vivo validation to confirm antiviral efficacy.

Name: Genital InFlammation Test (GIFT) - Gonorrhea
Developers: University of Cape Town (UCT) (including South African Tuberculosis Vaccine Initiative and the Lung Institute)
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoea
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Mechanism of action: detection of cytokine biomarkers interleukin (IL)-1α and IL-1β
Key features and challenges:
The Genital Inflammation Test (GIFT) is a new and inexpensive, true point-of-care diagnostic tool to identify inflammation associated with STIs/BV, to improve case detection in women. The patented technology aims to reduce the prevalence of STIs/BV and risk of HIV infection and improve sexual and reproductive health in regions using syndromic management. GIFT is an equipment-free point-of- care screening device that detects biomarkers of genital inflammation, caused by sexually transmitted infections and bacterial vaginosis. GIFT is a lateral flow test that can be offered to women in a similar manner to a pregnancy test. This device detects the presence or absence of genital inflammation based on target cytokines measured. Women who test positive using GIFT can then either be referred for more detailed investigation of the condition increasing their inflammation or treated directly, depending on public health guidelines and given specific treatment to reduce their risk of HIV acquisition and adverse reproductive outcomes.
(https://gift.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/GIFT_square_brochure-FINAL.pdf)
A study involving the GIFT started in 2023 has two distinct components: a biomedical (‘diagnostic study’) and a qualitative, modelling and economic (‘an integration into care study’) part. The diagnostic study aims to evaluate GIFT’s performance in identifying asymptomatic women with discharge-causing STIs (Chlamydia trachomatis (CT), Neisseria gonorrhoeae (NG), Trichomonas vaginalis (TV) and Mycoplasma genitalium (MG)) and BV. Study participants will be recruited from women attending research sites and family planning services. Several vaginal swabs will be collected for the evaluation of cytokine concentrations (ELISA), STIs (nucleic acid amplification tests), BV (Nugent score) and vaginal microbiome characteristics (16S rRNA gene sequencing). The first collected vaginal swab will be used for the GIFT assay which will be performed in parallel by a healthcare worker in the clinic near the participant, and by a technician in the laboratory. The integration into care study aims to explore how GIFT could be integrated into routine care. 
Study protocol: https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/14/5/e084918.
Study details: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05723484.

Name: Genital InFlammation Test (GIFT) - Mycoplasma genitalium
Developers: South African Technology Innovation Agency (TIA); University of Cape Town (UCT) (including South African Tuberculosis Vaccine Initiative and the Lung Institute); Burnet Institute
Indication: Detection of Mycoplasma genitalium
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Mechanism of action: detection of cytokine biomarkers interleukin (IL)-1α and IL-1β
Key features and challenges:
Genital InFlammation Test (GIFT) is a prototype lateral flow point-of-care diagnostic designed to detect genital inflammation associated with sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and bacterial vaginosis (BV) in women. The device detects cytokine biomarkers interleukin (IL)-1α and IL-1β and is intended to provide a low-cost alternative to syndromic management approaches commonly used in resource-limited settings.
The test aims to improve case detection of asymptomatic STIs and BV, particularly among women at increased risk, including young women, pregnant women, female sex workers, and women living with HIV. By identifying genital inflammation, GIFT is designed to support timely treatment and may contribute to reducing HIV acquisition risk and improving sexual and reproductive health outcomes.
A 2023 study outlined the rationale and design for multicountry evaluations in South Africa, Zimbabwe, and Madagascar to assess the performance and feasibility of integrating GIFT into routine care. The primary objective is to determine the sensitivity and specificity of the device at the point of care among non-pregnant sexually active women aged 18–35 years accessing family planning services, using nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) for Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Trichomonas vaginalis, and Mycoplasma genitalium, along with BV diagnosis by Nugent scoring, as reference standards. These evaluations are expected to inform strategies to strengthen STI and BV management in low- and middle-income countries.
(https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/14/5/e084918).
