Name: Genoplex chip - Mycoplasma Genitalium
Developers: GENESystem
Indication: Detection of Mycoplasma genitalium
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: multiplex detection; qPCR
Key features and challenges:
Genesystem developed a novel qPCR-based diagnostic platform, called Genoplex chip, which enables the simultaneous detection of multiple sexually transmitted pathogens with a single test. Genoplex chip realized high multiplex detection (up to 14 pathogens by a single pipetting), making it easy and fast to process more targets than conventional qPCR.
In a 2023 study, Genoplex chip was used for diagnosing sexually transmitted infection (STI) to verify the usefulness in diagnostics, including Chlamydia trachomatis (CT), Ureaplasma urealyticum (UU), Mycoplasma hominis (MH), Mycoplasma genitalium (MG), Neisseria gonorrhoeae (NG), Trichomanas vaginalis (TV), Ureaplasma parvum (UP), Gardnerella vaginalis (GV), Candida albicans (CA), Treponema pallidum (TP), Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV1) and Herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV2). They found that with Genoplex chip, various targets can be quantitatively detected in one sample and more accurate results can be provided in efficient way. This novel system gives an opportunity to overcome the limitations of current molecular diagnostics by innovative multiplex detection technology. Therefore, it is expected that the Genoplex chip system will attract attention in the molecular diagnostics market.
(https://academic.oup.com/clinchem/article/69/Supplement_1/hvad097.572/7283782).

Name: Genoplex chip - Trichomoniasis
Developers: GENESystem
Indication: Detection of T. vaginalis
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: multiplex detection; qPCR
Key features and challenges:
Genoplex chip is a quantitative PCR (qPCR)-based multiplex diagnostic platform developed by Genesystem for the simultaneous detection of multiple sexually transmitted infection (STI) pathogens. The flat-shaped microfluidic chip enables detection of up to 14 pathogens from a single sample using a single pipetting step, allowing more efficient and higher-throughput testing compared with conventional qPCR assays.
The platform is designed to detect and differentiate 12 major STI pathogens, including Chlamydia trachomatis, Ureaplasma urealyticum, Mycoplasma hominis, Mycoplasma genitalium, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Trichomonas vaginalis, Ureaplasma parvum, Gardnerella vaginalis, Candida albicans, Treponema pallidum, herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), and herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2). Target gene amplification is performed using the Genechecker UF-300 PCR system.
A 2023 study reported that the Genoplex chip enables quantitative detection of multiple targets within a single sample and provides accurate results with improved efficiency. The system is intended to address limitations of existing molecular diagnostics through innovative multiplex detection technology, supporting streamlined STI diagnosis in clinical settings (https://academic.oup.com/clinchem/article/69/Supplement_1/hvad097.572/7283782
; https://www.genesystem.co.kr/en/technology).

Name: Gestrinone subdermal bioabsorbable pellet
Developers: São Paulo State University; Science Valley Research Institute
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Endometriosis.
Target: Progesterone receptor, Glucocorticoid receptor, Androgen receptor; Gonadotropin-releasing hormone receptor; Estrogen receptor; Sex hormone-binding globulin.
Mechanism of action: Estrogenic, progestational, androgenic, antiestrogenic and antiprogesterone actions.
Key features and challenges:
Gestrinone is a synthetic steroid with anti-estrogenic, anti-progestogenic, and mild androgenic activity that suppresses gonadotropin secretion and reduces endometrial proliferation. It has historically been used for the management of endometriosis-associated pain. The subdermal bioabsorbable pellet formulation is designed to provide sustained drug release, potentially improving adherence and maintaining stable serum concentrations while reducing the need for daily oral dosing (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB11619).
In 2025, a multicenter randomized controlled trial was initiated to evaluate the safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetic profile of subdermal gestrinone pellets in women with documented deep infiltrative endometriosis who had persistent symptoms after surgery (NCT05570786; https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07853890.2025.2527352#abstract). 
A total of 100 participants are being randomized 1:1 to receive either an 85 mg gestrinone subdermal bioabsorbable pellet or placebo. Both treatment arms also receive a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS 12). The treatment duration is six months, with assessments at baseline, three months, and six months.
The primary endpoint is safety, defined as the proportion of patients who do not experience serious adverse events (SAEs) within six months of pellet insertion. SAEs include death, life-threatening events, hospitalization, permanent disability, congenital anomalies, venous thromboembolism, or other significant medical occurrences. Secondary evaluations include androgenization effects, laboratory parameter changes, pelvic pain intensity, quality of life (SF-36 and EHP-30 questionnaires), daily uterine bleeding patterns, and analgesic use, collected via a mobile application. The pharmacokinetic profile of the gestrinone pellet is also being characterized.
This represents the first prospective controlled study assessing subdermal bioabsorbable gestrinone pellets in this population. While the sustained-delivery formulation may offer clinical advantages, potential challenges include androgenic side effects, thromboembolic risk, and long-term safety considerations. Clinical outcomes from this trial will be essential to determine whether this delivery system improves tolerability and efficacy compared with existing hormonal therapies for endometriosis.

Name: Gigartina skottsbergii (marine macroalgae)
Developers: Centro de Desenvolvimento Tecnológico (CDTec)
Indication: Preventing infection with Trichomonas vaginalis
Target: metabolic pathways and enzymes: methionine gamma lyase; purine nucleoside phosphorylase; triophosphate isomerase; lactate dehydrogenase
Mechanism of action: Inhibition of T. vaginalis enzymes; disruption of T.vaginalis metabolic functions; inhibit the glycolytic pathway essential for the survival of T. vaginalis by interfering with TvLDH and inducing oxidative stress through TvxR
Key features and challenges:
Gigartina skottsbergii, a red macroalga native to the subantarctic region, is recognized for its rich source of bioactive compounds with diverse biological activities, including anti-inflammatory, anti-tumor, antioxidant, and antimicrobial properties. The lipid extracts derived from this macroalga have shown potential in the development of novel therapeutics, particularly against the protozoan parasite Trichomonas vaginalis, which causes trichomoniasis. Traditional treatment of trichomoniasis with metronidazole is hindered by issues of drug resistance and side effects, making the exploration of safer, more effective alternatives critical. 
A 2023 study evaluated the antiparasitic effects of lipid extracts Gigartina skottsbergii stage gametophidic (GFG), Gigartina skottsbergii stage tetrasporophidic (GFT), and Gigartina skottsbergii stage cystocarpic (GFC) from Gigartina skottsbergii against Trichomonas vaginalis, assessing the extracts' efficacy at different developmental stages of the macroalga. Using Gas Chromatography-Flame Ionization Detection (GC-FID), the research characterized the fatty acid profile of these extracts, identifying several compounds known for their bioactive properties. The results indicated significant inhibition of T. vaginalis trophozoite viability, with the GFG extract showing the highest inhibition index. Additionally, in silico molecular docking analyses suggested that fatty acids from the extracts interact with key enzymatic targets involved in the parasite's metabolism, such as TvLDH and TvxR. Importantly, the extracts exhibited low cytotoxicity in mammalian cell lines, reinforcing their potential as safe and effective alternatives for trichomoniasis treatment. Overall, the findings highlight the promising role of natural products derived from marine organisms in developing new antiparasitic therapies. 
(https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0285426)

Name: Glove tamponade
Developers: Government Medical College and Hospital (Nanded)
Indication: Indicated for the temporary control or reduction of postpartum uterine bleeding when conservative management of uterine bleeding is warranted.
Mechanism of action: Provides direct intrauterine pressure/tamponade to promote haemostasis.
Key features and challenges:
A surgical glove (commonly size 8) may be used as an improvised intrauterine balloon tamponade device for the management of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), particularly in low-resource settings. The glove is secured to an intravenous infusion set or catheter and inflated with saline, typically up to 500 mL, to exert mechanical pressure within the uterine cavity. As with other improvised balloon tamponade approaches, the method offers a low-cost and readily available alternative where commercial devices are inaccessible.
A study conducted in a tertiary care teaching hospital in India evaluated intrauterine glove tamponade in women with PPH following both vaginal and caesarean deliveries (2021: https://www.msjonline.org/index.php/ijrms/article/view/9207). Among 32 women (20 vaginal deliveries and 12 caesarean sections), haemostasis was achieved in 31 cases, corresponding to a reported success rate of 95%. The glove tamponade was retained in situ for 24 hours. One patient required additional intervention due to unsuccessful haemostasis.
Key challenges include limited evidence from small, single-centre studies, lack of standardized assembly and inflation protocols, and potential risks such as infection, concealed haemorrhage, or retained materials. While cost-effective and accessible, further comparative and multicentre studies are needed to validate safety and effectiveness relative to established balloon tamponade systems.

Name: Glutathione
Developers: Bezmialem University School of Medicine
Indication: PCOS inflammation and abnormal follicle growth
Target: glutathione peroxidase; methylglyoxal; glutathione S-transferase; N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine; Leukotrienes;
Mechanism of action: Leukotriene synthesis; detoxifies methylglyoxal; non-enzymatic conjugation (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine); glutathione peroxidase cofactor; glutathione S-transferase cofactor
Key features and challenges:
Glutathione is a tripeptide composed of glutamic acid, cysteine, and glycine, found in most mammalian tissues. It functions primarily as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative damage by scavenging free radicals and reducing peroxides. Glutathione plays a critical role in detoxifying harmful substances by conjugating with toxins, making them more water-soluble for excretion. It acts as a cofactor for several enzymes, including glutathione peroxidase, and is involved in the formation and maintenance of protein disulfide bonds. Additionally, it supports the immune system and aids in the transport of amino acids across cell membranes. (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/Glutathione)

A 2023 preclinical study compared hormonal, metabolic and inflammatory markers of glutathione with metformin and Diane-35 in a rat model of PCOS induced by dehydroepiandrosterone. This study showed glutathione plays anti-inflammatory and antioxidant roles, similar to metformin, by lowering serum IL-6, insulin, testosterone, CRP, and MDA levels; decreasing atretic/cystic follicle count; and improving antral follicle count and folliculogenesis in PCOS patients. (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/09513590.2024.2302086#abstract)

Name: Glyceryl trinitrate - PE/E
Developers: Pfizer; Queen's University (Kingston, Ontario); G. Pohl-Boskamp GmbH & Co. KG; Nometics Inc; Novadel Pharma Inc; Seelos Therapeutics
Indication: Treatment of hypertension in preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: GTN induces vasodilation via NO production
Key features and challenges:
Glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) is an organic nitrate with vasodilator activity. GTN is converted into nitric oxide activating guanylyl cyclase, thereby increasing cGMP concentration, and resulting in smooth muscle relaxation. 
In May 2000, the US FDA granted approval for GTN (0.3mg, 0.4mg and 0.6mg) for the acute relief of an attack or acute prophylaxis of angina pectoris due to coronary artery disease. GTN sublingual tablets have been developed by Pfizer and are available in the US, Canada and China.
Studies have shown a significant reduction in the maternal blood pressure and umbilical artery resistance without any significant adverse effects after intravenous infusion of GTN. Transdermal GTN patches and sublingual GTN have been the focus of recent studies, which consistently showed a significant reduction in blood pressure and resistance in the uterine artery without an adverse effect on foetal Doppler parameters. The safety profile of these drugs is well established in the non-pregnant population. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24313856/; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15117599/).
A clinical trial published in 2015 reported that GTN infusion was better than hydralazine as an antihypertensive therapy in the acute management of patients with severe preeclampsia (https://doi.org/10.4103/1687-7934.172670). 
A new clinical trial began in 2023 ai Assiut University to compare the use of Phentolamine Versus Glyceryl Trinitrate for their effect on renal function in Pre-eclampsia patients in ICU. 
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05687669?term=glyceryl%20trinitrate&cond=preeclampsia&rank=1)
The major disadvantage of organic nitrates in general, and GTN in particular, is the development of tolerance upon continuous dosing, necessitating the requirement of regular ‘nitrate-free’ intervals. It is not well-established whether GTN offers any competitive advantage over the existing treatment options in preeclampsia.
Recent updates:
2024: Phase IIII trial of Comparison Between the Use of Phentolamine Versus Glyceryl Trinitrate for Their Effect on Renal Function in Pre-eclampsia Patients in ICU. https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05687669?term=glyceryl%20trinitrate&cond=preeclampsia&rank=1

Dec 2015: Phase II trial into the effect of glyceryl trinitrate infusion in acute management of patients with severe pre-eclampsia finds that it may be a good a good alternative to standard treatment, especially as no adverse events to the mother or fetus were observed.

Jul 2009: Trial finds that in women with severe preeclampsia, eclampsia, and HELLP syndrome, infusion of GTN can be used as an alternative agent to well‐known drugs and causes no significant adverse effect to the mother and fetus.

Name: Glycovax-002
Developers: Glycovax Pharma Inc.
Indication: Prevention of SARS-CoV-2 infection and disease
Target: SARS-CoV-2 structural antigens (glycoconjugate design; precise epitope not disclosed, but intended to elicit neutralizing antibodies against viral glycoproteins).
Mechanism of action: Induces protective immune response by presenting carbohydrate-based antigens linked to a carrier protein, enhancing immunogenicity and stimulating neutralizing antibody responses against SARS-CoV-2.
Key features and challenges:
-Novel approach: glycoconjugate platform, traditionally successful in bacterial vaccines (e.g., Hib, pneumococcal).
-Potential for strong, durable immune responses with repeated dosing.
-Challenge: limited data for glycoconjugate vaccines in viral infections; clinical immunogenicity needs validation.
Recent updates:
-Registry last updated 24 Sept 2024; study is active with enrollment target of 36 adults.
-Three-dose regimen spaced 2 weeks apart; DSMB-guided dose escalation design.

Name: Glycyl-H-1152
Developers: University of Newcastle
Indication: For myometrial contraction blocking to prevent preterm birth
Mechanism of action: Measures metabolic and fibrinolytic biomarkers to assess placental dysfunction and risk of impaired fetal growth.
Key features and challenges:
Glycyl-H 1152 dihydrochloride is a glycyl analog of the Rho-kinase inhibitor H 1152 dihydrochloride that displays improved ROCKII selectivity. ROCK increases the sensitivity of uterine myocytes to Ca2+ through increased phosphorylation of MLC. ROCK expression (mRNA abundance and protein levels) is upregulated at the end of pregnancy and is likely involved in the processes that underpin the increased myometrial contractility at term. Thus, by inhibiting ROCK, this tocolytic reduces the sensitivity of uterine myocytes to Ca2+. 

It has also been found to inhibit both spontaneous and OT-stimulated pregnant human myometrial contractions ex vivo; however, comprehensive dose–response analyses were yet to be conducted to determine the potency of GH compared to other tocolytics.

To address this gap, myometrial strips were obtained from term, not-in-labor women, and treated with cumulative concentrations of 2-APB in addition to other tocolytics. Comprehensive dose–response curves were then generated. A single treatment with each drug at the determined IC50 concentration was confirmed to reduce contraction performance (AUC) by approximately 50%. The overall order of contraction-blocking potency in decreasing order was nifedipine > rolipram > glycyl-H-1152 > HC-067047 > 2-APB > indomethacin > aminophylline. Of the tocolytics examined, glycyl-H-1152 was the most potent inhibitor, emerging as a potential novel tocolytic for preventing preterm birth.
(https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43032-022-01000-2#author-information)

Name: GneX12
Developers: Therapyx; Brown University
Indication: Prevention of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Helper-inducer T-lymphocyte stimulants; Immunostimulants; Interleukin 12 replacements
Key features and challenges:
GneX12 is a patented therapeutic vaccine in development specifically for women with Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection. It is a novel formulation of recombinant human interleukin-12 (IL-12) and enhances both Th1 and humoral immune responses against gonorrhoea infection. (https://reporter.nih.gov/search/uAsmRBNJVkChT9Mew-gURA/project-details/10757512)
The candidate when given with antibiotics, induces protective immunity against re-infection within the host. The candidate also results in rapid activation of pre-existing anti-tumour T-effector cells as well as the development of a highly effective local and systemic anti-tumour immune response, thereby causing complete eradication of tumours. TherapyX used its EXStaM technology which is based on the phase-inversion nano-encapsulation (PIN®) technology in-licensed from the Brown University, for the treatment of gonorrhoea and for cancer. Preclinical development is underway in the US.
TherapyX's EXStaM technology (or PIN® technology) is based on encapsulation of protein based products into protective microparticles. These can be stored and are suitable for oral and mucosal delivery. Mocroencapsulation of therapeutics preserves bioactivity, enables controlled tissue specific release, reduces toxicity and increases shelf stability. Microparticles are made from poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA), which is already used in devices approved by the US FDA. PLGA is biodegradable and biocompatible. (https://adisinsight.springer.com/drugs/800058662)

Name: GoDx POC assay - Trichomoniasis
Developers: Godx, Inc.
Indication: Detection of T. vaginalis
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Mechanism of action: Point-of-care nucleic acid amplification test detecting Trichomonas vaginalis–specific genetic sequences for rapid diagnosis.
Key features and challenges:
GoDx, Inc. proposes to develop a hand-held, low-cost, and sensitive point-of-care diagnostic to deliver rapid STI test results, which would simplify screening and allow for immediate treatment at the initial visit. To develop a rapid test for chlamydia, gonorrhea, and trichomoniasis, the focus is on innovations to integrate nucleic acid extraction, amplification, and detection to develop and test a prototype device by the end of Phase II. The sample preparation device would require fewer than three user steps to purify nucleic acids for downstream detection. Benchmarks will be obtained for the sensitive and specific amplification of genetic markers in Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Trichomonas vaginalis using an isothermal amplification technique followed by lateral flow detection. The test will also amplify genetic predictors of antibiotic susceptibility to aid in the tracking and treatment of antibiotic resistant gonorrhea. The final stage will be integrating the assays into a test device delivering both STI and AMR test results in 30 minutes, with performance on par with laboratory-based STI tests. The diagnostic tool will be simple and low-cost, making it ideal for use in LMICs where laboratory infrastructure is lacking, affordable for better screening programs worldwide, and easy enough for eventual in-home testing.
(https://reporter.nih.gov/search/wp7REvBocU-eKQYujpnTuQ/project-details/10268054)

Name: Gold Nanoshells-Based Lateral Flow Assay
Developers: Cornell University; Laboratorio para Investigaciones Biomédicas, Escuela Superior Politécnica del Litoral
Indication: Indicated for the detection of anti-Chagas IgG antibodies
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care

Name: Gorilla Adenovirus Vectored Networked Epitopes Vaccine (GRAdHIVNE1 Vaccine)
Developers: International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI); Ragon Institute of MGH, MIT and Harvard; ReiThera SRL; Mutala Trust; Desmond Tutu Health Foundation (DTHF); Africa Health Research Institute
Indication: Indicated for the prevention of HIV-1 infection
Mechanism of action: CD8+ T cell responses
Key features and challenges:
A Phase 1 trial for the GRAdHIVNE1 vaccine, is being designed to evaluate safety, tolerability, and immunogenicity in healthy individuals (PLWoH) including healthy People Living with HIV (PLWH). Planning is currently underway in South Africa. 

This study builds on insights from prior T-cell vaccine trials and pre-clinical non-human primate studies, which demonstrated that robust CD8+ T cell responses, are crucial for viral control but require broad, polyfunctional responses that can also effectively counteract HIV's diversity and immune evasion strategies. Inclusion of PLWoH and PLWH in this study is important for safety, tolerability and immunogenicity data that can inform further development of the vaccine for prevention and therapeutic use. Prior clinical trials, using adenovirus vectors and exploring different vaccine approaches, demonstrated safety and potential immunogenic benefits in PLWH, despite not achieving sustained viral suppression post-treatment interruption Understanding these dynamics is key to evaluating the full therapeutic potential of vaccine induced immune responses in controlling HIV as well as inform the potential of the vaccine in aborting the establishment of a disseminated infection in the setting of prevention. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06617091)

Name: Griffithsin (GRFT)
Developers: University of Nebraska Lincoln; Texas Biomedical Research Institute (Texas Biomed, formerly Southwest Foundation for Biomedical Research); National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID)
Indication: Indicated as a prophylactic prevention of infection of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) caused by Ebola virus
Mechanism of action: GRFT binds with nanomolar affinity to N-linked glycans on Ebola GP (and other viral glycoproteins), blocking viral entry by sterically hindering receptor engagement and fusion. It functions as a direct viral entry inhibitor.
Key features and challenges:
-Broad-spectrum antiviral: Active against EBOV, HIV, SARS-CoV, Nipah virus, and others.
-Low cytotoxicity: Exhibits favorable safety in vitro and in animal studies.
Multiple formulations: Has been evaluated as recombinant protein, intranasal spray, and topical microbicide.
-Proof-of-concept for outbreak use: Rapidly deployable protein therapeutic with cross-viral potential.
Recent updates:
2014: Demonstrated potent EBOV inhibition in vitro and pseudovirus assays; efficacy in mouse models.
2020s: Continued exploration as plant-produced biologic for rapid scale-up and delivery against multiple emerging viruses.

Name: Guizhi Fuling Pill
Developers: China Medical University
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Endometriosis.
Mechanism of action: Increases population of peritoneal macrophages with enhanced phagocytic activity + upregulation of CD79a+/CD19+/Ighm+ expression in a macrophages subpopulation, indicating a novel trans-differentiation from B cells to macrophages.
Key features and challenges:
Guizhi Fuling Pill (GFP) is a traditional Chinese medicine formulation historically used for gynecologic disorders characterized by “blood stasis,” including endometriosis. Although prior clinical and preclinical studies have reported symptomatic improvement in patients with endometriosis, the underlying immunological mechanisms have remained incompletely understood. Endometriosis is associated with immune dysregulation within the peritoneal cavity, particularly impaired macrophage-mediated clearance of ectopic endometrial cells.
A 2025 preclinical study investigated the effects of GFP on peritoneal immunity, lesion growth, and adhesion formation in a mouse model of endometriosis exhibiting features of blood stasis and stagnation (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5280940). 
Flow cytometry and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analyses revealed that GFP treatment increased the population of peritoneal macrophages and enhanced their phagocytic activity. Notably, a macrophage subpopulation expressing CD79a⁺/CD19⁺/Ighm⁺ markers was significantly upregulated, suggesting a novel B cell–to–macrophage (B-to-MΦ) trans-differentiation promoted by GFP. Transcriptomic profiling indicated that transcriptional reprogramming mechanisms may underlie this cellular transition. Furthermore, pharmacologic inhibition of CSF1R-mediated macrophage differentiation using PLX5622 attenuated the therapeutic effects of GFP, resulting in reduced macrophage phagocytosis and increased lesion growth. These findings underscore the central role of peritoneal macrophages in endometriosis pathogenesis and suggest that GFP exerts therapeutic benefit through immune microenvironment modulation.
Key challenges include the reliance on animal models and early-stage mechanistic data. The B cell–to–macrophage trans-differentiation pathway requires confirmation in human tissues. Standardization of GFP composition, dosing, and quality control is necessary for reproducibility and regulatory consideration. Additionally, clinical efficacy, safety, and long-term outcomes remain to be established in randomized controlled trials. While GFP demonstrates promising immunomodulatory properties, further translational research is required to validate its therapeutic role in endometriosis management.

Name: HA targeting mAbs (11.4 mAb, 23.3 mAb)
Developers: Wonkwang University; Seoul National University (SNU)
Indication: Prevention and treatment of influenza A, caused by H5N1
Target: Hemagglutinin (HA) RBS region (130-loop and 190-helix of H5 HA)
Mechanism of action: Bind to HA RBS, blocking receptor interaction and viral entry; neutralize H5 clade 2.3.4.4b viruses; can provide prophylactic protection when administered before infection and therapeutic benefit when given post-infection.
Key features and challenges:
-Potency: Both mAbs showed low IC50 values (0.33–0.36 µg/mL) against H5 2.3.4.4b.
-Specificity: Neutralization limited to clade 2.3.4.4b; no activity against clades 2.3.4.4h or 2.3.2.1c.

-Challenges: Narrow clade specificity; potential for escape mutations at RBS residues (S136, N199, T143, N205).
Recent updates:
2025:
-Korean groups are pursuing antibody engineering (CDR modifications) to improve cross-neutralization beyond clade 2.3.4.4b.
-No reports of progression into non-human primates or clinical stages; research remains focused on escape mutation analysis and vaccine design facilitation.

Name: HAT 002
Developers: HBM Alpha Therapeutics
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: Unknown
Key features and challenges:
HAT 002 is a human monoclonal antibody candidate under preclinical development for the treatment of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). It is being developed by HBM Alpha Therapeutics using proprietary antibody discovery platforms.
The candidate is generated using Harbour BioMed’s Harbour Mice technology, which produces fully human monoclonal antibodies in both traditional two heavy/two light chain (H2L2) formats and heavy-chain-only antibody (HCAb) formats. The integration of Harbour Mice with the HBICE and single B-cell cloning platform enables efficient identification and optimization of next-generation therapeutic antibodies.
https://adisinsight.springer.com/drugs/800072254
https://www.harbourbiomed.com/news/204.html
Although detailed information regarding HAT 002’s molecular target and mechanism of action has not been publicly disclosed, the development of a monoclonal antibody approach in PCOS suggests a strategy aimed at modulating a specific hormonal, inflammatory, or metabolic signaling pathway implicated in disease pathophysiology. Antibody-based therapies offer high target specificity and the potential for durable biologic effects compared with small-molecule interventions.
At present, HAT 002 remains in preclinical development in the United States, with no publicly available clinical trial data. No human safety, pharmacokinetic, or efficacy data have been reported.
Several challenges limit current assessment. The absence of disclosed target information restricts evaluation of biological plausibility and differentiation from existing therapies. PCOS is a heterogeneous endocrine-metabolic disorder, and the identification of a single antibody target that meaningfully modifies disease trajectory may be complex. Additionally, monoclonal antibody therapies typically involve higher production costs and parenteral administration, which may limit accessibility compared with oral therapies commonly used in PCOS management. Regulatory and clinical development pathways for biologics in non-life-threatening chronic conditions such as PCOS may also require extensive long-term safety data.
HAT 002 represents an early-stage biologic approach to PCOS with potential for high target specificity. However, in the absence of publicly available mechanistic and clinical data, it should be considered an investigational preclinical candidate pending further disclosure and progression into human trials.

Name: HC067047
Developers: Stanford University (including the Center for Innovations in Global Health)
Indication: Prevention or treatment of preterm labour/birth through tocolytic/relaxant effects on myometrial contraction
Mechanism of action: Reducing myometrial contraction via TRPV4 inhibition
Key features and challenges:
Transient receptor potential vanilloid 4 (TRPV4) is a calcium-permeable ion channel expressed on myometrial smooth muscle cells (mSMCs), where it regulates Ca²⁺ influx and uterine contractility. TRPV4 expression increases with gestation and is required for oxytocin-induced contractions, identifying it as a potential therapeutic target for delaying preterm labour.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25529150/)
A 2016 preclinical study evaluated the TRPV4 inhibitor HC-067047 in mouse models of preterm labour induced either by progesterone receptor inhibition or lipopolysaccharide (LPS). Intraperitoneal administration of HC-067047 significantly prolonged time to delivery when given eight hours after the labour-inducing stimulus. Repeated smaller doses (10 mg/kg every 8 hours) were more effective than a single large dose in both models.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26702092/)
In 2022, researchers from the University of Newcastle compared the contraction-blocking potency of HC-067047 with other novel and established tocolytic agents in ex vivo human myometrial tissue obtained from term, not-in-labour women. Dose–response analyses demonstrated an IC₅₀ of 48 µM for HC-067047. When ranked by contraction-blocking potency, the order was: nifedipine > rolipram > glycyl-H-1152 > HC-067047 > 2-APB > indomethacin > aminophylline. Although HC-067047 demonstrated inhibitory effects on myometrial contractility, it was less potent than clinically used nifedipine and certain investigational agents.
(https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43032-022-01000-2#Abs1)
Overall, HC-067047 has demonstrated efficacy in preclinical models of inflammation- and progesterone withdrawal–induced preterm labour and shows contraction-blocking activity in human myometrial tissue ex vivo. However, its relative potency compared with established tocolytics and the absence of clinical trial data indicate that further translational research is required before clinical application.

Name: HD domain containing 3 (HDDC3)
Developers: Shengjing Hospital of China Medical University
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Measures HDDC3 expression or protein levels to identify metabolic and oxidative stress pathways implicated in PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
HDDC3 is a gene encoding a protein with an HD (histidine-aspartate) domain, commonly associated with functions such as hydrolase activity or involvement in nucleotide processing. While its specific biological role in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is not fully clear, recent research suggests HDDC3 may play a role in immune system regulation and inflammation, which are key factors in PCOS pathogenesis.

A study published in 2022 identified HDDC3 as a key biomarker for PCOS and examined its role in immune infiltration during PCOS pathogenesis. The specimens used in the study was follicular fluid obtained via a vaginal puncture procedure. Using bioinformatics and clinical validation, 1265 differentially expressed genes were analysed, with HDDC3 (AUC: 0.918) emerging as a strong diagnostic candidate. HDDC3 showed significant correlations with immune cells, including positive associations with T regulatory cells, activated mast cells, and monocytes, and a negative association with activated memory CD4 T cells. Immune infiltration analysis revealed altered levels of activated mast cells and eosinophils in PCOS. These findings highlight HDDC3’s potential as a diagnostic marker and its involvement in immune regulation mechanisms in PCOS.
(https://ovarianresearch.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s13048-022-01013-0)

Name: HDP-gestosis score
Developers: All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS); Acharya Shri Chander College of Medical Sciences; Federation of Obstetric and Gynaecological Societies of India; World Gestosis Organization
Indication: Diagnosis and prediction of PE
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Target: Risk factors: medical history and maternal characteristics
Mechanism of action: Combines maternal biomarkers, Doppler indices, and clinical factors to estimate individualized risk of preeclampsia in twin pregnancies.
Key features and challenges:
The HDP-Gestosis score was developed by a consortium of Indian doctors to improve PE screening in low-resource contexts. 
(https://www.fogsi.org/wp-content/uploads/gcpr/hdp-fogsi-gestosis-icog-gcpr-2019.pdf). 
The score involves several existing and emerging risk factors of PE, most of them relating to medical history and maternal characteristics and some of them common to the Fetal Medicine Foundation's algorithm, such as autoimmune diseases or diabetes. 
 
A score of 1, 2 and 3 is allocated to each clinical risk factor as per its severity in the development of preeclampsia. When the total score is 3 or more, pregnant woman are considered ‘At risk for Preeclampsia’. 
 
Risk factors with a value of 1: age older than 35 years, age younger than 19 years, maternal anaemia, obesity (BMI >30), primigravida, short duration of sperm exposure (cohabitation), woman born as small for gestational age, family history of cardiovascular disease, polycystic ovary syndrome, inter pregnancy interval longer than 7 years, conceived with assisted reproductive (IVF/ ICSI) treatment, MAP>85 mm of Hg, chronic vascular disease (dyslipidaemia), and excessive weight gain during pregnancy. 

Risk factors with a value of 2: maternal hypothyroidism, family history of preeclampsia, gestational diabetes mellitus, obesity (BMI > 35 kg/M2), multifetal pregnancy, and hypertensive disease during previous pregnancy. 

Risk factors with a value of 3: pregestational diabetes mellitus, chronic hypertension, mental disorders, inherited/acquired thrombophilia, maternal chronic kidney disease, autoimmune disease (systemic lupus erythematosus, anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome, and rheumatoid arthritis), and pregnancy with assisted reproductive (OD or surrogacy) treatment.
 
A prospective study conducted in 2020-2021 tested the HDP-gestosis score diagnostic and predictive abilities among a cohort of pregnant women seen between 11 and 18 weeks of gestation. Among the 71 women developing PE in the cohort, 59 cases were correctly predicted by HDP-gestosis score >  = 3, while among the remaining 12 cases of PE, eight patients had an HDP-gestosis score of 2 and four patients had an HDP-gestosis score of 1. 
For the HDP-gestosis score of >  = 3, true positives were 59, false positives were 10, and false negatives were 12. The Sensitivity, Specificity, PPV, NPV, and diagnostic accuracy of HDP-gestosis score (> = 3) for predicting PE were 83.1%, 97.51%, 85.51%, 97.03%, and 95.35%, respectively. 
(https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9483246/).​ 
Another study started in 2023 to test the accuracy of the gestosis score in predicting preeclampsia, with a previsional sample of 400.
(https://www.ctri.nic.in/Clinicaltrials/pmaindet2.php?EncHid=OTQ0NzY=&Enc=&userName=)

Name: HMI 115
Developers: Bayer Healthcare; Hope Medicine Inc.
Indication: Treatment of endometriosis associated pain

Key features and challenges:
HMI 115 is a subcutaneously administered prolactin (PRL) receptor monoclonal antibody, initially developed by Bayer under the name BAY 1158061, now developed by Hope Medicine for the treatment of alopecia (hair loss), endometriosis and other chronic diseases with dysregulated PRL signalling. The drug blocks the PRL receptor-mediated pathway in a non-competitive manner. Clinical development is underway in Australia, Germany, China and the US.
This drug has emerged as a promising candidate for the treatment of endometriosis and other prolactin (PRL)-mediated diseases. Endometriosis is a chronic condition often linked to hormonal imbalances, including elevated levels of PRL, which can exacerbate symptoms and disease progression. Given HMI 115/BAY 1158061's ability to block PRL receptor signaling, it holds potential for mitigating the effects of elevated PRL in endometriosis patients. Although initial studies in postmenopausal women showed no significant impact on serum PRL levels (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29806538/), the favorable safety and pharmacokinetic profiles of HMI 115/BAY 1158061 support its further exploration as a therapeutic option in endometriosis. The drug's low immunogenicity and consistent absorption suggest it could be developed into a viable treatment for managing endometriosis by targeting PRL-mediated pathways, offering a novel approach to addressing this challenging condition. 
Hope Medicine also launched a randomized, multicenter, double-blind Phase II Study to evaluate the safety and efficacy of HMI-115 in women with moderate to severe endometriosis-associated pain over a 12-week treatment period in 2021 with the aim of completing in 2024.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05101317 ; https://adis.springer.com/trials/700368433)

Name: HOMA/adiponectin ratio
Developers: University of Tehran
Indication: Diagnostic of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Combines insulin resistance (HOMA) and adiponectin to quantify insulin resistance severity and metabolic risk associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
HOMA (Homeostatic Model Assessment) is a method used to estimate insulin resistance and beta-cell function based on fasting glucose and insulin levels. Adiponectin is an adipokine secreted by fat cells that enhances insulin sensitivity and has anti-inflammatory properties. In PCOS, insulin resistance is common, and HOMA is often elevated, reflecting impaired glucose metabolism. Conversely, adiponectin levels are typically reduced in PCOS, contributing to metabolic dysfunction and increased risk of type 2 diabetes. Together, HOMA and adiponectin are key indicators of the metabolic disturbances associated with PCOS.

A study published in 2023 investigated adiponectin/leptin (A/L) and HOMA/adiponectin (H/A) ratios in Iranian women with PCOS, infertility, or recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL). The A/L ratio was decreased, and the H/A ratio increased in PCOS, strongly predicting the condition (AUC: 0.867 and 0.861). However, these ratios could not differentiate between PCOS-infertile and PCOS-RPL groups, suggesting they are biomarkers for PCOS but not for associated infertility or RPL.
(https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11845-023-03408-4#Ack1)

Name: HRS5091

Key features and challenges: HRS 5091 is an oral, class II, selective HBV capsid inhibitor with pan-genotypic activity being developed by Jiangsu Hengrui Medicine for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B. HRS 5091 is designed as a SBA (sulfamoyl benzamides) and functions as a HBV nucleocapsid assembly regulator. It promotes the assembly of HBV core protein dimers and inhibits the core protein from encapsulating viral pregenomic RNA (pgRNA) thereby resulting in the formation of a "empty" virus-free genome. Name: HRS9531
Developers: Fujian Shengdi Pharmaceutical Co. Ltd.
Indication: Treatment of PCOS - Metabolism
Target: Targets metabolic pathways associated with insulin resistance and hyperinsulinemia
Mechanism of action: The exact mechanism of action of HRS9531 has not been disclosed in the public registry. Based on the trial’s objective—to improve insulin resistance, glucose metabolism, and lipid abnormalities in PCOS—it is presumed that HRS9531 acts on pathways regulating glucose uptake, insulin signalling, lipid metabolism or hepatic metabolic processes. Its intended effects include lowering fasting glucose, improving HOMA-IR, reducing serum lipids, and potentially modulating reproductive hormone disturbances related to hyperinsulinemia in PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
HRS9531 is a novel investigational oral therapeutic currently being evaluated for the management of psychological and psychosocial symptoms associated with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). An ongoing randomized, placebo-controlled Phase 2 trial (NCT06595797), sponsored by Shenyang Huari Biotechnology Co., is assessing the short-term effects of HRS9531 on depressive symptoms, anxiety, self-esteem, and menstrual cycle regularity in women diagnosed with PCOS.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06595797

The study utilizes validated psychological assessment instruments, including the Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS), Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS), and Self-Esteem Scale (SES), alongside the Heredity Medical Scale (HMS) for Traditional Chinese Medicine symptom patterns. This design indicates that HRS9531 is positioned primarily as a mental health and quality-of-life–oriented therapeutic, rather than as a direct endocrine or metabolic intervention for core PCOS pathophysiology.

If effective, HRS9531 could address an important unmet need, as no approved PCOS-specific therapies currently target psychological wellbeing directly, despite high rates of anxiety, depression, and reduced quality of life among affected women.

However, the candidate faces several significant challenges. First, no publicly available information describes its molecular target, mechanism of action, pharmacologic class, or translational rationale, limiting scientific interpretation and complicating future regulatory positioning. Second, development remains at an early stage, with no published preclinical or Phase 1 human data available to inform safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, or long-term risk. Third, the current trial focuses primarily on psychological scales and menstrual frequency, without evaluating key metabolic, androgenic, ovulatory, or cardiometabolic parameters that define PCOS. This may restrict its positioning as a comprehensive PCOS therapy. Finally, the regulatory trajectory remains unclear, with limited public information regarding intellectual property, safety monitoring frameworks, or broader development plans.

Overall, HRS9531 represents a novel and exploratory therapeutic approach targeting the mental health burden of PCOS. While conceptually addressing an important gap in care, its development is characterized by substantial uncertainty due to limited publicly available data, early-stage testing, and an undisclosed mechanism of action

Name: Haemostatic parameters (various)
Developers: Bhagat Phool Singh Government Medical College for Women; Rivers State University (Nigeria)
Indication: Prediction of preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Modulates maternal gut and vaginal microbiota to reduce systemic and local inflammation associated with preterm labour.
Key features and challenges:
​Normal pregnancy is associated with a range of alterations to the haemostatic components, in preeclampsia pregnancy these alterations can be rapidly increased which can combine to give an increased risk of haemorrhage and thrombosis. 
 
Several studies have investigated haemostatic parameters since the 1980s, however their results do not appear to have been incorporated in diagnostic tools, which might indicate poor predication ability. A 1992 Taiwanese study on the predictive value of the haemostasis parameters in the development of preeclampsia found significant differences between PE women and the control group for tissue plasminogen activator (upregulated in PE) and antithrombin III (decreased in PE) (https://www.thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/abstract/10.1055/s-0038-1648415). 

A 2021 clinical trial in India examined various haemostatic assay parameters—such as platelet count, mean platelet volume, platelet distribution width, serum fibrinogen, serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and D-dimer—in normotensive pregnancies and in women with preeclampsia. The goal was to determine if notable changes in these parameters occur in PE, which could aid in predicting preeclampsia and assessing its severity. (https://www.ctri.nic.in/Clinicaltrials/pmaindet2.php?EncHid=NTEwOTI=&Enc=&userName=)
 
A 2022 Nigerian study on haemostatic parameters in preeclampsia patients found that the mean of prothrombin (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time of preeclampsia patients were significantly prolonged. There was no significant difference in mean value of fibrinogen in preeclampsia patients when compared to healthy pregnant and non-pregnant women (https://web.archive.org/web/20221007053158id_/http://www.nwpii.com/ajbms/papers/AJ20220301.pdf).

The tool uses intensity peaks and compares three SERS substrates, finding maximum enhancement with Au sputtered Ag nanorods, and can differentiate between X4 and R5 tropism using HIV-1 strains from subtypes A, B, C, and D, with principal component analysis confirming its ability to quantify viral load and distinguish strains. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1011134422002445)

Name: Handle-region peptides (HRP)
Developers: Emergent Biotechnologies
Indication: HRP may help improve local placental perfusion
Target: Targeting the renin-angiotensin system (RAS) specifically within the placenta.
Mechanism of action: The hypothesis behind HRP is that blocking the interaction between (pro)renin and (P)RR could improve local placental perfusion and extend pregnancy duration, thereby improving clinical outcomes. Evidence suggests that upregulation of the renin-angiotensin system (RAS) in the placenta contributes to preeclampsia pathogenesis, making HRP a targeted approach to mitigate these effects.
Key features and challenges:
Handle-region peptides (HRP) are investigational decoy peptides designed to target the handle region of the (pro)renin receptor ((P)RR). The (P)RR is implicated in activation of the renin–angiotensin system (RAS) and downstream signaling pathways involved in vascular dysfunction, inflammation, and maladaptive placental development. Dysregulation of RAS signaling has been associated with the pathophysiology of preeclampsia (preE), making the (P)RR a potential therapeutic target.
The HRP strategy aims to competitively inhibit activation of the (P)RR, thereby reducing downstream pathogenic signaling linked to angiogenic imbalance and endothelial dysfunction. By modulating RAS-related pathways, HRP may influence angiogenic factors and improve placental and systemic vascular function in preeclampsia.
In early development (Phase 1), the biological activity of HRP is being assessed in vitro using cytotrophoblast (CTB) assays and markers of angiogenesis. Subsequent preclinical evaluation includes testing HRP and extended half-life peptide formulations in animal models of preeclampsia to determine efficacy and safety. Successful demonstration of benefit in animal models is intended to support advancement to Phase 2 preclinical development and preparation of data required for an Investigational New Drug (IND) application.
https://reporter.nih.gov/search/h_eTNHuVzkKRG5wupmB6_g/project-details/10480975#description
At present, HRP remains in early-stage preclinical development. No published animal efficacy data or human safety data are available. Key translational challenges include optimizing peptide stability, half-life extension, delivery methods, placental pharmacokinetics, and ensuring maternal–fetal safety. Given the complexity of RAS signaling during pregnancy, careful evaluation of off-target vascular or renal effects will be required.
Handle-region peptides represent a mechanistically targeted, receptor-based therapeutic approach for preeclampsia. While biologically plausible and innovative, the strategy remains exploratory pending comprehensive preclinical validation and future clinical investigation.

Name: Hemostatic Intra-Uterine Suction Cup
Developers: Grenoble Alpes University Hospital (CHUGA); HEMOSQUID
Indication: Indicated for the temporary control or reduction of postpartum uterine bleeding when conservative management of uterine bleeding is warranted.
Mechanism of action: Uterine walls will append to the walls of the suction cup after a depressure in the device is applied, leading to collapse and contraction of the atonic postpartum uterus, constricting blood vessels to achieve haemostasis.
Key features and challenges:
The Hemostatic Intra-Uterine Suction Cup is an investigational medical device developed by HEMOSQUID for the management of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) secondary to uterine atony. The device is designed to apply controlled negative pressure within the uterine cavity, with the aim of drawing the uterine walls into apposition against the suction cup surface. This mechanism is intended to promote mechanical haemostasis by collapsing the uterine cavity and compressing bleeding vessels, particularly along the anterior and posterior uterine walls. The device is flexible to accommodate uterine size, can be positioned and removed transvaginally, and is intended for short-duration application, typically up to five minutes.
A clinical trial evaluating the device was registered in 2016 (NCT02816203), with the registry entry last updated in 2020; however, no results or further status updates have been reported (https://hemosquid.com/). In 2024, HEMOSQUID rebranded as Matria Health Technology, though no additional public updates regarding clinical development or commercialization of the device are available (https://matria-health-technologies.com/).
Key challenges include the absence of published clinical data, unclear trial status, and limited transparency regarding ongoing development. Without reported safety and efficacy outcomes, its comparative positioning relative to established vacuum-induced uterine tamponade systems remains uncertain. Further clinical evidence will be necessary to determine feasibility, safety profile, and potential integration into postpartum haemorrhage management pathways

Name: Hemozoin Detection Device (rotating-crystal magneto-optical detection (RMOD))
Developers: Budapest University of Technology and Economics; University of Augsburg
Indication: Indicated for the diagnosis of P. falciparum and P.vivax infection

Key features and challenges: Hemozoin was discovered and linked to malaria in the 1800s18; however, it has not been used as a primary means of diagnosing malaria. While it is possible to see hemozoin in certain stages of the parasite’s life-cycle using microscopy (in this case, it is commonly referred to as malaria pigment), it is not always detectable by traditional microscopy. Recent advances in sensing and lab-on-a-chip technologies have advanced hemozoin detection devices; a recent review article noted more than ten different research efforts. Most hemozoin-based technologies are hand-held devices that use fingerpick blood samples collected into a disposable sample chamber or cartridge. Reagents, if necessary, are contained within the cartridge, and results are available in 1-5 minutes.

Name: Henagliflozin
Developers: Jiangsu HengRui Medicine
Indication: PCOS obesity, insulin resistance
Mechanism of action: Sodium-glucose transporter 2 inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Henagliflozin is an orally administered sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor developed by Jiangsu Hengrui Medicine for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus. By inhibiting renal SGLT2, it reduces glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubules, thereby increasing urinary glucose excretion and lowering blood glucose levels. Henagliflozin has been launched as monotherapy in China and is under further development in combination regimens.
https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800041987
Given the central role of insulin resistance, obesity, and metabolic dysfunction in many PCOS phenotypes, SGLT2 inhibitors have attracted interest as potential therapeutic options beyond diabetes. A clinical trial initiated in 2023 (NCT05966792) is evaluating henagliflozin in overweight or obese women with PCOS, focusing on improvements in metabolic and clinical outcomes. While metformin remains the most widely used insulin-sensitizing agent in PCOS, response rates are variable, and emerging evidence suggests that SGLT2 inhibitors may offer comparable improvements in insulin resistance and weight-related parameters.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05966792
Despite this mechanistic rationale, henagliflozin remains investigational in PCOS. Published data specifically evaluating henagliflozin in PCOS are limited, and much of the supportive rationale is extrapolated from broader SGLT2 inhibitor studies in metabolic disease. The precise endocrine effects on androgen levels, ovulatory function, and fertility outcomes are not yet established. Additionally, potential adverse effects associated with SGLT2 inhibitors—including genitourinary infections, volume depletion, and rare ketoacidosis—require careful consideration in reproductive-age women.
Overall, henagliflozin represents a metabolically targeted candidate for overweight or insulin-resistant PCOS phenotypes, but its clinical role will depend on results from ongoing randomized trials clarifying reproductive, metabolic, and safety outcomes in this population.
