Name: Herb - Achillea millefolium extract
Developers: Kerman University of Medical Sciences
Indication: Reduction of uterine bleeding
Mechanism of action: Unclear
Key features and challenges:
Achillea L. (Compositae or Asteraceae) is a widely distributed medicinal plant throughout the world. Phytochemical investigations of Achillea species have revealed that many components from this genus are highly bioactive, including secondary active metabolites such as flavonoids, phenolic acids, coumarins, terpenoids (monoterpenes, sesquiterpenes, diterpenes, triterpenes) and sterols. Achillea species are reported as tonic, anti-inflammatory, anti-spasmodic, diaphoretic, diuretic and emmenagogic agents and have been used for treatment of haemorrhage, pneumonia, rheumatic pain and wounds healing in Persian traditional literature (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22615655/).

Evidence on effectiveness of A. millefolium on PPH is limited. A. millefolium and Hypericum perforatum ointments reduce perineal pain level, redness, oedema and ecchymosis, and therefore aid wound healing after episiotomy. However, bleeding was not investigated as an outcome (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28027682/).

A clinical trial investigating the use of hydro-alcoholic extract of A. millefolium on early postpartum haemorrhage was registered in 2019 (IRCT20160112025983N2; https://en.irct.ir/trial/35953). Another trial is also investigating the use of A. millefolium rectal suppository on the prevention of postpartum haemorrhage (https://irct.behdasht.gov.ir/trial/70618).

Name: Herb - Motherwort
Developers: Sichuan University (SCU)
Indication: Prevention and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage
Mechanism of action: Stimulation of contractions in uterine smooth muscle, which may contribute to the restoration of the uterus to its normal size after birth
Key features and challenges:
Herba Leonuri (motherwort) is a traditional Chinese medicine that has been used for centuries in the management of gynaecological and obstetric conditions. It contains multiple bioactive constituents, including alkaloids, flavonoids, diterpenes, and fatty acids. Leonurine, one of its principal active components, exhibits antioxidant, anti-apoptotic, free radical–scavenging, and anti-inflammatory effects, and may improve microcirculation. Leonurine is also reported to stimulate uterine smooth muscle contraction, which may facilitate uterine involution after childbirth and contribute to prevention of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH).
A 2018 systematic review evaluating motherwort injection as an adjunct to carboprost in the prevention of PPH reported favourable outcomes, although the included studies were limited in size and methodological quality (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30288846/). 
In 2019, a systematic review assessing motherwort injection for women undergoing caesarean section similarly found potential benefit but highlighted that most trials were underpowered and of low quality (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29882344/). 
A 2020 systematic review of motherwort injection combined with oxytocin for prevention of PPH after vaginal delivery suggested improved outcomes compared with oxytocin alone; however, the authors concluded that the overall evidence quality was low and emphasized the need for rigorously designed randomized controlled trials (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31354850/). 
Another 2020 review also noted that Herba Leonuri should be used with caution in the first trimester of pregnancy (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7391530/). 
More recently, a 2022 large cohort study conducted in China reported favourable outcomes in PPH prevention among women undergoing caesarean section who received intravenous motherwort in combination with oxytocin compared with oxytocin alone (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35401190/).
Key challenges include variability in study quality, small sample sizes in randomized trials, and heterogeneity in dosing regimens and combination therapies. Most available evidence originates from single-country settings, limiting generalizability. Regulatory approval and standardization of formulations remain inconsistent internationally. High-quality, multicentre randomized controlled trials are required to establish definitive efficacy and safety profiles.

Name: Herb - Olive leaf extract (OLE) - PE/E
Developers: Eleven March University
Indication: Indicated for the prevention and treatment of Preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: Provides polyphenolic compounds (e.g., oleuropein) with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects that improve endothelial function and reduce oxidative stress associated with preeclampsia.
Key features and challenges:
Olive leaf extract is derived from the leaves of the olive tree (Olea europaea) and has been used for centuries in traditional medicine. It contains several beneficial compounds, with oleuropein being the most notable due to its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial properties. Unlike olive oil, which is extracted from the fruit, olive leaf extract is concentrated and can be found in various forms, including capsules, liquids, and teas. 

2024 Study: This study aimed to evaluate the therapeutic potential of olive leaf extract (OLE) and nifedipine, alone and in combination, in improving pregnancy outcomes in rats induced with Nω-nitro-L-arginine methyl ester hydrochloride (L-NAME). Rats were treated with single and combination treatments of nifedipine and OLE for four weeks, after being induced with L-NAME for six weeks. Following gestational day assessment and systolic blood pressure testing, the rats were sacrificed, and blood samples were collected for Neutrophil Gelatinase-Associated Lipocalin (NGAL), Malondialdehyde (MDA), proteinuria and Creatinine (SCr) Levels examinations. The results revealed the combination of nifedipine and OLE significantly improved the results of several biomarker analyses associated with PE, including increased NGAL levels, a significant decrease in MDA levels, decrease in proteinuria and elevated creatinine levels. (https://pharmacia.pensoft.net/article/122471/)

Name: Herb - Plantago extract
Developers: Mashhad University of Medical Sciences
Indication: Prevention of postparum anaemia and reduction of postpartum bleeding
Mechanism of action: Unknown
Key features and challenges:
Plantago major (P. major), commonly known as great plantain, is a medicinal plant widely used in Traditional Persian Medicine. Plantago major contains several active compounds such as flavonoids, polysaccharides, terpenoids, lipids, iridoid glycosides and caffeic acid derivatives, and is used in treatment of various diseases including wounds, infection, fever, bleeding and inflammation. 

Clinical trials show that rectal plantago suppositories can reduce mean amount of blood loss four hours after delivery compared to oxytocin (https://ijogi.mums.ac.ir/article_13819.html?lang=en), and that oral plantago syrup reduced the mean reduction in haemoglobin and haematocrit levels after delivery, which means potential use in preventing complications of postpartum anaemia. A more recent triple blinded clinical trial demonstrated that rectal suppositories of Dill and Plantago are both effective for decreasing PPH, but Plantago rectal suppository can more effectively reduce PPH (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2210803321001068).

The effect of plantago on heavy menstrual bleeding has also been investigated (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31486196/; https://pjmhsonline.com/2020/july-sep/1678.pdf).
Recent updates: N/A

Name: Herb - Puerarin
Developers: University of Science and Technology of China
Indication: Persistent high blood pressure
Target: Inhibiting TNF and NF-κB signaling pathways
Mechanism of action: Doppler assessment of maternal ophthalmic artery flow indices to detect systemic vascular changes associated with placental insufficiency.
Key features and challenges:
Puerarin, a natural isoflavone isolated from Pueraria Lobate (Wild) Ohwi exerts anti-apoptosis and anti-inflammatory effects and demonstrates significant therapeutic potential in preeclampsia.  After administration of Pue, it was that observed that LPS-evoked PE symptoms (hypertension, proteinuria, and fetal growth restriction), were reversed

Pue could decrease the blood pressure and urine protein and increase the content of NO in the rat model of PE. However, this report only focused on the therapeutic effect of Pue on a rat model of PE and the detailed mechanism of action has not been investigated, the purpose of the study is to explore these issues. These findings highlight Puerarin as a promising therapeutic agent for managing PE by targeting multiple pathways involved in its pathogenesis. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1567576921006378?via%3Dihub)

In a 2022 study, Puerarin (PLR), derived from Radix puerariae, shows promising therapeutic potential in preeclampsia (PE). It effectively corrects gut dysbiosis in PE mice by promoting beneficial bacteria like Blautia and Turicibacter, which are associated with reduced hypertension, proteinuria, and LPS levels. PLR enhances gut barrier integrity, preventing LPS leakage and subsequent placental protection.These findings suggest that PLR could be a beneficial intervention for PE treatment, highlighting its role as a potential intestinal nutrient supplement for maternal health. (https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6643/14/23/5025)

Name: Herb - Sumac
Developers: Mashhad University of Medical Sciences
Indication: Indicated for the prevention of postpartum haemorrhage.
Mechanism of action: Unknown
Key features and challenges:
Sumac is the common name for a genus (Rhus) that contains over 250 individual species of flowering plants in the family Anacardiaceae. This genus is found in temperate and tropical regions worldwide, with representative members by geographic location. This spice comes from the berries of a wild bush that grow in all Mediterranean areas. Sumac is widely used in Turkey, Iran and Arab countries as a condiment, either in pure form or in combination with other spices. In Iran, R. coriaria is traditionally used as a table spice especially along with rich dishes and is highly recommended for adjustment of the blood lipids in diabetic patients (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25587314/). 
A study in Iran is determining the effect of sumac capsule (500mg) on postpartum hemorrhage in women at risk of bleeding. The study is a triple-blind clinical trial (research unit, researcher, statistical analyst) which is performed on 72 eligible mothers. Women in the study group will be given a 500mg Sumac capsule in addition to the routine oxytocin immediately after placental abruption and 2 hours later. The study finished recruiting patients in September 2022, however the end date of the study is unknown. (https://en.irct.ir/trial/62487)

Name: Herb - Tanshinol
Developers: Shaanxi Province Key R&D Program
Indication: Inhibiting the development of PE at the cellular level,
Mechanism of action: Combines quantitative tissue characterization with ultrafast Doppler perfusion imaging to detect placental structural and vascular abnormalities linked to growth restriction.
Key features and challenges:
Tanshinol, derived from Salviorrhiza, has garnered attention for its diverse therapeutic potential, including anti-inflammatory, anti-fibrotic, and antibacterial properties. While it has been explored in contexts such as osteoporosis and cancer, its role in treating preeclampsia (PE) remains unclear, necessitating further investigation into its therapeutic mechanisms. 

In summary, the present study identified tanshinol as a novel therapeutic compound that promotes the proliferation, migration, invasion, and tube formation of HTR-8/SVneo cells. In addition, tanshinol inhibited the rate of apoptosis in the PE cell model. This study only explored the role of tanshinol in inhibiting the development of PE at the cellular level, and subsequent in vivo experiments will have to be conducted to further validate the findings of this study.
(https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/01443615.2023.2274527)

Name: Herbs - Amomum villosum Lour.
Developers: Southern Medical University ; Shenzhen Institute for Drug Control; Shenzhen Tsumura Medicine Co. LTD; TCM-Integrated Hospital of Southern Medical University
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: Alleviates preeclampsia by modulating maternal gut health to improve placental function
Key features and challenges:
Amomum villosum Lour (WOA) is a traditional herbal medicinal plant investigated for potential therapeutic effects in preeclampsia (PE). A 2025 preclinical study evaluated its protective efficacy in an experimental model of PE (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378874124015162). WOA administration significantly reduced maternal hypertension and proteinuria and promoted fetal intrauterine growth in a dose-dependent manner, resulting in improved pregnancy outcomes.
Mechanistically, WOA modulated angiogenic imbalance by reducing the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio, suggesting restoration of placental vascular signaling. The study also demonstrated inhibition of placental ferroptosis through upregulation of FPN1, FTH1, xCT, and GPX4 proteins. Tight junction proteins (ZO-1, Occludin, Claudin1) in both placenta and colon were increased, indicating strengthened barrier integrity. WOA altered gut microbiota composition, notably enriching Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia. Fecal microbiota transplantation experiments indicated that WOA’s protective effects were dependent on gut microbial composition. Supplementation with Bifidobacterium bifidum and vanillic acid (a major WOA component) ameliorated PE-like features, and in vitro findings suggested that vanillic acid promoted B. bifidum enrichment.
Key challenges include the fact that evidence is currently limited to preclinical models, with no human clinical trials reported. Standardization of herbal preparations, dose optimization, safety profiling in pregnancy, and regulatory considerations will be essential before clinical translation. While the findings suggest a novel gut–placenta axis mechanism, robust human validation studies are required to determine therapeutic potential.

Name: Herbs - Apigenin
Developers: University of Health Sciences, Istanbul, Turkey; Tottori University Faculty of Medicine, Japan; Korea University
Indication: Treatment of endometriosis by reducing oxidative stress and improving tissue health
Target: Multiple signaling pathways and molecules within cells, including various kinases (such as PI3K, AKT, and MAPK), transcription factors (like NF-κB), and enzymes involved in oxidative stress (such as inducible nitric oxide synthase, iNOS). One of its most notable targets is the estrogen receptor (ER), which plays a role in hormone-related cancers.
Mechanism of action:
Anti-inflammatory Action: inhibits the activation of the NF-κB 

Antioxidant Activity: enhances the activity of antioxidant enzymes and scavenges free radicals, reducing oxidative stress in cells.

Anti-cancer Properties:  induces cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in cancer cells by modulating signaling pathways like PI3K/AKT and MAPK. It also downregulates the expression of pro-survival proteins and upregulates pro-apoptotic factors

Estrogenic and Anti-estrogenic Effects: can bind to estrogen receptors, exerting both estrogen-like effects and blocking estrogen activity
Key features and challenges:
Apigenin is a naturally occurring flavonoid found in a variety of fruits, vegetables, and herbs, with particularly high concentrations in parsley, celery, and chamomile. Known for its vibrant yellow color, apigenin has garnered significant attention for its diverse pharmacological properties, including anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anti-cancer effects. It functions by modulating multiple cellular signaling pathways and targets, such as kinases, transcription factors, and enzymes involved in oxidative stress. With its ability to influence processes like cell cycle regulation, apoptosis, and hormone receptor activity, apigenin is being studied for its potential therapeutic applications in conditions ranging from chronic inflammation and cancer to neurodegenerative diseases.
A 2009 study by the Tottori University Faculty of Medicine found that Apigenin inhibits TNFα-induced cell proliferation in endometriotic stromal cells. Apigenin reduces the mitogenic activity and inflammatory reaction via the suppression of NFκB pathway and could therefore be a novel therapeutic agent in the treatment or prevention of endometriosis.
(https://www.fertstert.org/article/S0015-0282(09)01478-2/fulltext)
A 2018 Korean study investigated the effects of apigenin on two well-established human endometriosis cell lines (VK2/E6E7 and End1/E6E7). Apigenin reduced proliferation and induced cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in the both endometriosis cell lines. In addition, it disrupted mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) which was accompanied by an increase in concentration of calcium ions in the cytosol and in pro-apoptotic proteins including Bax and cytochrome c in the VK2/E6E7 and End1/E6E7 cells. Moreover, apigenin treated cells accumulated excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS), and experienced lipid peroxidation and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress with activation of the unfolded protein response (UPR) regulatory proteins. Furthermore, the apigenin-induced apoptosis in endometriosis cells was regulated via the ERK1/2, JNK, and AKT cell signaling pathways. 
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28617956/)
A Turkish study published in 2023 explored the potential of Apigenin's strong antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, as treatments for endometriosis in a rat model. The results showed that apigenin significantly reduced oxidative stress and improved the histopathological scores of endometrial implants in comparison to untreated groups. Specifically, serum levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-37 were notably decreased in the apigenin-treated group. The study concludes that apigenin, by reducing oxidative stress and improving tissue health, holds promise as a novel therapeutic agent for endometriosis. (https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/eurj/issue/75618/1209679)

Name: Herbs - Asparagus racemosus root extract
Developers: SAM Global University
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Preeclampsia
Target: PlGF; sFLT1; HMGB1; Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha;;  Decorin, and Interleukin-6; Toll-like receptor 4/Nuclear Factor kappa B; Malondialdehyde (MDA);
Mechanism of action: Mechanism of action is via its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and pro-angiogenic properties
Key features and challenges:
Asparagus racemosus root extract is a botanical preparation derived from the roots of Asparagus racemosus, a medicinal plant traditionally used in Ayurvedic medicine for its anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. In the context of preeclampsia (PE), a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy characterized by systemic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and angiogenic imbalance, this extract has been investigated for its potential to modulate inflammatory mediators and restore vascular homeostasis.
Preclinical evidence from a 2025 study evaluated the therapeutic effects of A. racemosus root extract in an L-NAME-induced rat model of preeclampsia. On gestational day 20, plasma samples were analysed using ELISA to quantify inflammatory and angiogenic biomarkers. Histopathological examination of placental and cardiac tissues assessed structural abnormalities, and immunohistochemical analysis evaluated FLT1 and PlGF expression in placental trophoblasts and cardiac tissue (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0378874125011213). The preeclampsia group demonstrated significantly elevated plasma levels of HMGB1, Decorin, and TNF-α, along with reduced VEGF and PlGF concentrations. Dysregulated IL-6 and sFLT1 levels further indicated pronounced inflammatory and angiogenic imbalance. Histopathological findings revealed placental and cardiac tissue damage, while immunohistochemistry confirmed increased FLT1 expression and decreased PlGF in trophoblasts. Treatment with A. racemosus extract was associated with marked improvement in inflammatory markers, partial restoration of angiogenic balance, and improved tissue integrity.
Key challenges include the absence of human clinical studies evaluating safety, pharmacokinetics, optimal dosing, and efficacy in pregnant populations. The complexity and variability of herbal extracts may introduce issues related to standardization, bioactive compound consistency, and regulatory approval pathways. Additionally, potential maternal–fetal safety considerations and herb–drug interactions require careful evaluation. While preclinical findings are promising, rigorous translational research and well-designed clinical trials are necessary to establish clinical utility in preeclampsia management.

Name: Herbs - Astragalus - PE/E
Developers: First Clinical College of Shanxi Medical University
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: Activates the Nrf2 signaling pathway in the placenta, which helps to counteract high levels of oxidative stres
Key features and challenges:
Astragalus (Astragalus membranaceus) is a traditional herbal medicine investigated for its potential therapeutic role in preeclampsia (PE), particularly due to its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. A 2025 preclinical study evaluated Astragalus in a rat model of PE induced by NG-nitro-L-arginine methyl ester (L-NAME) (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S014340042500236X).
In this model, treatment with Astragalus significantly reduced maternal hypertension and 24-hour urinary protein levels. Improvements were also observed in placental morphology (diameter and weight) and fetal outcomes, including pup length, weight, and reduced malformation rate. Biochemically, Astragalus modulated angiogenic imbalance by increasing placental growth factor (PlGF) and reducing soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1) levels. Oxidative stress markers were improved, with reductions in malondialdehyde (MDA) and increases in antioxidant enzymes such as glutathione peroxidase (GSH-Px), catalase (CAT), and superoxide dismutase (SOD). Molecular analyses demonstrated activation of the Nrf2/Keap1/NQO1 signaling pathway, supporting a mechanism mediated through antioxidant defense enhancement.
Key challenges include the current limitation to animal model data, lack of human clinical trials, variability in herbal composition and standardization, and the need to establish safety profiles during pregnancy. While mechanistically promising, rigorous clinical studies will be required to determine translational potential and regulatory feasibility for use in preeclampsia management.

Name: Herbs - Broccoli extract
Developers: Shiraz University of Medical Sciences (SUMS)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Endometriosis.
Mechanism of action: Enhances superoxide dismutase serum levels.
Key features and challenges:
Broccoli extract (BE) is rich in bioactive compounds such as sulforaphane, which possess antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. Given the established roles of oxidative stress and inflammatory cytokines in the pathogenesis of endometriosis, broccoli-derived phytochemicals have been explored as potential non-hormonal therapeutic agents.
In a 2024 preclinical study, endometriosis was surgically induced in 40 mature female rats (https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/hmbci-2023-0071/html). 
The animals were divided into five groups and treated for six weeks: control (saline 0.9%), broccoli extract (BE, 3,000 mg/kg/day), soy isoflavones (SI, 50 mg/kg/day), a combination of BE and SI (3,000 mg/kg/day + 50 mg/kg/day), and diphereline (3 mg/kg intramuscularly) as a standard comparator. At the end of treatment, implant volume, histopathological grading, and serum oxidative and inflammatory markers—including superoxide dismutase (SOD), malondialdehyde (MDA), and tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α)—were assessed.
The diphereline group demonstrated a significant reduction in implant volume (p = 0.002). Histopathological grading of endometrial implants was significantly reduced in both the BE/SI combination group and the diphereline group compared with controls (p = 0.001). Additionally, serum SOD levels were significantly increased in the BE-only group compared with controls (p = 0.034), suggesting enhanced antioxidant activity. The combination of BE and soy isoflavones was associated with decreased lesion growth and improved histopathological grades.
These findings suggest that broccoli extract, particularly in combination with soy isoflavones, may exert therapeutic effects through antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms in a rat model of endometriosis. However, evidence remains limited to preclinical models. Further studies are required to establish optimal dosing, long-term safety, pharmacokinetics, and clinical efficacy in humans before consideration as an alternative or adjunctive therapy for endometriosis.

Name: Herbs - Chikusetsusaponin IVa
Developers: Soochow University
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Endometriosis.
Target: IGF1R/PI3K signal pathway, pyroptosis indicators, pain-related proteins.
Mechanism of action: Activates the IGF1R/PI3K signal pathway, inhibits pyroptosis of endometrial stromal cells, and inhibits expression of pain-related proteins.
Key features and challenges:
Chikusetsusaponin IVa (CHS IVa) is a natural extract from the Panax japonicus (T.Nees) C.A.Mey (P. japonicus), which can regulate immune responses. It remains unclear whether the CHS IVa can treat endometriosis (EMs) and via what possible mechanism.
A 2024 study thus aimed to investigate the possible mechanism and impact of CHS IVa on EMs.
The EMs models were established in mice by autologous transplantation or chemicals (lipopolysaccharide and adenosine triphosphate), inducing the pyroptotic endometrial stromal cells. Next, the CHS IVa was used to treat the EMs mice. The therapeutic impact of CHS IVa was assessed by hematoxylineosin staining, immunofluorescent staining, western blot (WB), and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA).
The results of immunofluorescence and WB indicated that pyroptosis indicators, including Gasdermin-D (GSDMD), Caspase-1, NOD-like receptor thermal protein domain associated protein 3 (NLRP3), and interleukin (IL)-1β, were substantially expressed in the ectopic endometrial lesions of EMs mice. The ELISA results showed that the abdominal cavity of EMs mice had higher concentrations of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α than the non-EMs animals (control group). As shown in the molecule docking experiments, CHS IVa exhibited high binding affinity with GSDMD, IL-1β, Caspase-1, and NLRP3. Moreover, after treatment with CHS IVa, the expression levels of GSDMD, IL-1β, Caspase-1, and NLRP3 decreased in the EMs mice. Meanwhile, the expression level of pain-related proteins, such as pro-nerve growth factor (pro-NGF) and transient receptor potential vanilloid-1 (TRPV1), was inhibited via the treatment of CHS IVa. According to the antibody chip analysis, the insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor/phosphatidylinositide 3-kinases (IGF1R/PI3K) signal pathway was essential to the CHS IVa’s treatment of EMs. Finally, according to the WB experiments, after the treatment with CHS-Ⅳa, the expression of IGF1R, PI3K, and related phosphorylated proteins increased compared to the mice in lipopolysaccharide + adenosine triphosphate (LPS + ATP) groups.
CHS IVa can activate the IGF1R/PI3K signal pathway, inhibit the pyroptosis of endometrial stromal cells, and relieve the inflammation and EMs.

Name: Herbs - Nano-herbal Phaleria macrocarpa - PE/E
Developers: HKBP Nommensen University; University of Northern Sumatra
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: Targets the underlying pathophysiology of PE—specifically oxidative stress, inflammation, and endothelial dysfunction, through its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and angiogenic-modulating properties
Key features and challenges:
Phaleria macrocarpa is a medicinal plant traditionally used in Southeast Asian herbal medicine and recognized for its anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. Nano-herbal formulations of Phaleria macrocarpa have been developed to enhance bioavailability and therapeutic efficacy. Given that preeclampsia (PE) is characterized by hypertension, systemic inflammation, oxidative stress, and organ dysfunction, plant-derived compounds with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity have been explored as potential adjunctive therapies.
A 2024 preclinical study evaluated the therapeutic effects of nano-herbal Phaleria macrocarpa in a rat model of preeclampsia 
(https://pharmacia.pensoft.net/article/127565/element/8/175001//). 
Preeclampsia was induced through intraperitoneal administration of prednisone and 6% NaCl over 14 days. Pregnant rats were allocated into multiple groups, including negative control (C−), positive control (C+), nifedipine-treated (C1), and three treatment groups (T1, T2, T3) receiving varying doses of the nano-herbal formulation. Blood pressure measurements were recorded on gestational days 5, 13, and 20, and complete blood count and organ weight analyses were conducted at the end of treatment. Preeclamptic rats exhibited blood pressure levels approximating 140/90 mmHg. Among the treatment groups, the highest dose (T3: 720 mg/kg body weight) demonstrated significant improvements in blood pressure, hematological parameters, and organ weight profiles, with outcomes comparable to nifedipine. The findings suggest dose-dependent efficacy, with the T3 regimen providing the most pronounced protective effects.
Key challenges include the reliance on animal models and the absence of human clinical data evaluating safety, pharmacokinetics, and efficacy in pregnant populations. Standardization of nano-herbal formulations, batch consistency, and regulatory oversight are critical considerations for translation to clinical use. Additionally, long-term maternal and fetal safety outcomes remain unknown. While preclinical findings suggest potential antihypertensive and organ-protective benefits, further validation through rigorous translational and clinical research is necessary before clinical application in preeclampsia management can be considered.

Name: Herbs - Nitrate-enriched beetroot juice
Developers: University of Sao Paulo (USP) (including FUSP, FMUSP, and HCFMUSP)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment and/or prevention of Preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: Provides dietary nitrates converted to nitric oxide, promoting vasodilation and improving endothelial function to reduce hypertensive risk.
Key features and challenges: 2024 CT: The study will include women diagnosed with either early-onset pre-eclampsia or late-onset pre-eclampsia, following the guidelines of the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists. Participants will be required to sign informed consent forms following a thorough explanation of the study. A total of four groups will be established, with twenty-four pregnant women randomly assigned to each group using a free online program. In each group (early-onset and late-onset pre-eclampsia), forty-eight pregnant women will receive nitrate-enriched beetroot juice (Beet It®, James White, UK), while another forty-eight will receive an equivalent amount of placebo juice. The trial will commence in the morning, between 7:30 and 8:30 am, after a standardized, low-nitrate breakfast provided by the hospital. Participants will be instructed to avoid nitrate-rich foods the previous evening and will receive guidance from the project team and the hospital's nutrition service. The hospital's nutritional team will oversee the dietary procedures. Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring will be conducted for six hours following the ingestion of juice or placebo. Saliva samples will be collected to assess nitrate reductase activity, and blood samples will be drawn to measure nitrate, nitrite, and nitrosothiol (nitric oxide metabolites), as well as to perform biochemical analyses of oxidative stress. Doppler ultrasound and Doppler velocimetry evaluation will be conducted at the peak action time of nitrate, which is estimated to occur two hours post-ingestion, based on previous research (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06387784)

Name: Herbs - Ping-Chong-Jiang-Ni Formula
Developers: Jiangxi University of Traditional Chinese Medicine
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Endometriosis.
Mechanism of action: Alterations in the expression of migration- and invasion-related proteins, including vimentin and E-cadherin.
Key features and challenges:
The Ping-Chong-Jiang-Ni Formula (PCJNF), a compound of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), has demonstrated remarkable clinical effectiveness and is widely utilized in the treatment of endometriosis (EMs). Previous studies have shown that PCJNF inhibits the proliferation and induces the apoptosis of ectopic endometrial stromal cells (EESCs) by modulating the JNK signalling pathway. 
In a 2024 study, it was found that PCJNF effectively alleviates EMs-associated pain by reducing inflammatory mediators, including tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and nerve growth factor (NGF). Furthermore, PCJNF down-regulates the expression of transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1), phosphorylated TRPV1 (p-TRPV1), and protein kinase C (PKC). To further investigate the therapeutic potential of PCJNF, a 2025 study conducted a comprehensive tandem mass tag (TMT) proteomics analysis, identifying 4,984 proteins co-expressed in human EESCs treated with PCJNF and control serum. Based on these findings, the study explored the inhibitory effects of PCJNF on the migration and invasion of EMs cells in vitro. Reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) analysis of 12 genes revealed a significant upregulation of FER and TRIP13 in ectopic lesions, which was further validated by immunohistochemistry. Given the crucial role of TRIP13 in EMs, we employed small interfering RNA (siRNA) to knock down its expression, observing a marked reduction in the migration and invasion abilities of EMs cells. Conversely, overexpression of TRIP13 using short hairpin RNA (shRNA) enhanced these processes. Additionally, after PCJNF treatment, we observed significant alterations in the expression of migration- and invasion-related proteins, such as vimentin and E-cadherin.  These findings suggest that TRIP13 may serve as a potential therapeutic target for EMs and that PCJNF offers a promising new approach for integrating Traditional Chinese Medicine with modern medical treatments (https://www.jfda-online.com/journal/vol33/iss2/6/).

Name: Herbs - Sanleng Wan
Developers: The Affiliated Guangdong Second Provincial General Hospital of Jinan University
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Endometriosis.
Mechanism of action: Modulation of the sphingolipid metabolism via the S1P/S1PR1-Akt axis.
Key features and challenges:
Traditional herbal medicine Sanleng Wan (SLW), composed of Curcuma phaeocaulis Valeton (Chinese name: Ezhu) and Sparganium stoloniferum (Buch.-Ham. ex Graebn.) Buch.-Ham. ex Juz. (Chinese name: Sanleng), has been recognized for its therapeutic potential in managing gynaecological conditions, including endometriosis, dysmenorrhea and pelvic masses.  In a 2025 study, researchers investigated the potential mechanism by which SLW inhibits endometriosis, utilizing serum metabolomics, network pharmacology, molecular docking, SPR affinity analysis and preliminary in vivo validation.  In a rat model, it was found that SLW inhibited the growth of endometriotic lesions and suppressed fibrosis.  Metabolomic analysis revealed distinct serum metabolites associated with SLW treatment.  A total of 76 significant metabolites were identified in the serum of the SLW-treated group, including L-threonine, (S)-homostachydrine, DL-arginine, and L-homoarginine, among others.  These metabolites were involved in various metabolic pathways, including sphingolipid signalling, tyrosine metabolism, fatty acid degradation, arachidonic acid metabolism, pyruvate metabolism, linoleic acid metabolism, and glycerophospholipid catabolism.  Molecular docking and SPR affinity analysis demonstrated that compounds including ferulic acid, zederone, curcumin, zedrone, curcumol, and curdione contribute to the modulation of targets within the S1P/S1PR1-Akt signaling axis.  Notably, compared with the model endometriosis group, SLW treatment significantly downregulated the protein expression levels of TGF-β, SphK2, S1P, and S1PR1 in ectopic endometrial tissues of rats, while markedly reducing the p-Akt/Akt ratio.  
At present, human efficacy and safety remain untested.  Standardisation of SLW (composition, dosing, bioavailability) is required for reproducible studies.  Finally, larger, well-controlled in-vivo and clinical studies will be necessary to confirm therapeutic value.
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0378874125008414?via%3Dihub).

Name: Herbs - modified Shaofu Zhuyutang
Developers: Gansu University of Traditional Chinese Medicine (GSUTCM); Tongfang CNKI (Beijing) Technology Co., Ltd
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Endometriosis.
Target: MDM4/p53/GPX4 signalling pathway; TRL4/NF-κB/NLRP3 signalling pathway.
Mechanism of action: Decrease in PI3K, p-PI3K, Akt, p-Akt, MDM4, and GPX4 protein and mRNA expression and increase in p53 protein and mRNA expression; reduction in TRL4, MyD88, TRAF6, p-NF-κB p65, NLPR3 proteins, and TRL4, MyD88, TRAF6, NF-κB, and NLPR3 mRNA expression.
Key features and challenges:
Jiawei Shaofu Zhuyu Decoction is a modified version of the traditional Chinese herbal formula Shaofu Zhuyu Decoction (SZD), used to treat gynaecological conditions like dysmenorrhea and endometriosis caused by blood stasis and cold accumulation in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) theory.
In a 2024 study, the effects of Jiawei Shaofu Zhuyu Decoction on ferroptosis in ectopic endometrial tissue of EMT rats were explored. It was found that, compared to the blank and sham surgery groups, the model group exhibited ferroptosis resistance in ectopic endometrial tissue. After treatment, Jiawei Shaofu Zhuyu Decoction and gestrinone induced ferroptosis in ectopic endometrial tissue, manifested as ultrastructural changes such as cell membrane rupture, cytoplasmic oedema, mitochondrial swelling, and vacuolation. Serum levels of IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α were significantly elevated in the model group but decreased after treatment. In the model group, Fe²⁺ and MDA levels in ectopic endometrial tissue decreased, while GSH levels increased; after treatment, these indicators changed, with Fe²⁺ and MDA levels increasing and GSH levels decreasing. Iron deposition and the relative fluorescence intensity of GSH and GPX4 were enhanced in the model group but weakened after treatment. The protein and mRNA expression levels of PI3K, p-PI3K, Akt, p-Akt, MDM4, and GPX4 increased in the model group, while p53 protein and mRNA expression decreased. After treatment, these indicators changed, with PI3K, p-PI3K, Akt, p-Akt, MDM4, and GPX4 protein and mRNA expression decreasing and p53 protein and mRNA expression increasing (https://www.syfjxzz.com/en/article/doi/10.13422/j.cnki.syfjx.20242245/).
A second 2025 study investigated the mechanism of action of modified Shaofu Zhuyutang in antagonizing cellular pyroptosis and fibrosis in ectopic endometrial tissues of endometriosis through the Toll-like receptor 4/nuclear factor-κB/NOD-like receptor protein 3(TRL4/NF-κB/NLPR3) signalling pathway. Seventy-two SPF-grade female SD rats were randomly divided into a sham-operated group (n = 12) and a modelling group (n = 60). The rats in the sham-operated group underwent a caesarean section, while the rats in the modelling group were used to establish an endometriosis model through the auto-transplantation method. After successful modelling, the animals were randomly divided into the model group, progesterone group (0.25 mg·kg(-1)), and modified Shaofu Zhuyutang low-, medium-, and high-dose groups (7.5, 15, 30 g·kg(-1)), with 12 animals in each group. After 4 weeks of drug administration, voluntary activity and heat pain latency were observed. The rats were sacrificed for tissue collection, and Masson staining were used to observe histopathological changes in the endometrial tissues. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) was used to measure serum levels of interleukin-18(IL-18), interleukin-1β(IL-1β), tumour necrosis factor- α(TNF- α), and transforming growth factor- β(TGF- β). Immunohistochemistry (IHC) was used to detect the protein expression area of tumour necrosis factor-related factor 6 (TRAF6) and NLPR3 in the endometrial tissues. Immunofluorescence (IF) was used to detect the relative fluorescence intensity of Caspase-1 and gasdermin D(GSDMD) in the endometrial tissues. Western blot was employed to measure the relative expression of TRL4, myeloid differentiation factor 88 (MyD88), TRAF6, NF- κB p65, phosphorylated NF- κB p65(p-NF- κB p65), and NLPR3 proteins in endometrial tissues. Real-time fluorescence quantitative polymerase chain reaction (Real-time PCR) was used to detect the mRNA expression of TRL4, MyD88, TRAF6, NF-κB, and NLPR3 in the endometrial tissues. Compared with the sham-operated group, rats in the model group showed reduced voluntary activity and shorter heat pain latency. Serum levels of IL-18, IL-1β, TNF-α, and TGF-β were elevated. The relative expression areas of TRAF6 and NLPR3 proteins were increased, and the relative fluorescence intensity of Caspase-1 and GSDMD was enhanced. The relative expression of TRL4, MyD88, TRAF6, NF-κB p65, p-NF-κB p65, and NLPR3 proteins, along with the expression of TRL4, MyD88, TRAF6, NF-κB, and NLPR3 mRNA, were significantly increased (P<0.01). Compared with the model group, rats in the progesterone group and the modified Shaofu Zhuyutang medium- and high-dose groups exhibited improved voluntary activity, longer heat pain latency, the fibrosis of endometrial tissue is alleviated. Serum levels of IL-18, IL-1β, TNF- α, and TGF- β were decreased. The relative expression areas of TRAF6 and NLPR3 proteins decreased, and the relative fluorescence intensity of Caspase-1 and GSDMD weakened. The relative expression of TRL4, MyD88, TRAF6, p-NF-κB p65, NLPR3 proteins, and TRL4, MyD88, TRAF6, NF-κB, and NLPR3 mRNA expression were reduced (P< 0.05, P<0.01). Modified Shaofu Zhuyutang may thus play a therapeutic role in endometriosis by interfering with key proteins in the TRL4/NF-κB/NLPR3 signalling pathway, reducing NLRP3 inflammasome-induced cellular pyroptosis, antagonizing the fibrosis process in ectopic endometrial tissues, improving the inflammatory microenvironment in the pelvic cavity, and alleviating pain (https://pesquisa.bvsalud.org/portal/resource/pt/wpr-1064063).

Name: Hesperidin
Developers: Durban University of Technology (previously Durban Institute of Technology); University of the Witwatersrand (RHRU) (including Wits RHI); University of Manchester; University of KwaZulu-Natal, Durban, Republic of South Africa
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: Hesperidin is converted by intestinal microflora to its aglycone form, hesperetin, which enters the bloodstream to exert its therapeutic effects. Its anti-inflammatory effect is often associated with the inhibition of NFκB, TNF-α, and IL-6 expression.
Key features and challenges:
Hesperidin is a naturally occurring flavonoid glycoside predominantly found in citrus fruits and recognized for its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and vasoprotective properties. It has been investigated in cardiovascular research due to its potential to modulate endothelial function, reduce oxidative stress, and exert antihypertensive effects. Given that preeclampsia (PE) is characterized by hypertension, proteinuria, endothelial dysfunction, and placental insufficiency, hesperidin has been explored as a potential therapeutic agent in experimental models of the disorder.
A 2023 preclinical study evaluated the effects of hesperidin in an arginine vasopressin (AVP)-induced rat model of preeclampsia. 
(https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/fcp.12952). 
Female Sprague–Dawley rats were implanted with mini-osmotic pumps delivering AVP (200 ng/h) to induce PE-like features. Hesperidin (200 mg/kg body weight) was administered orally for 14 days. Systolic and diastolic blood pressures were measured at gestational days (GD) 7, 14, and 18, and animals were euthanized on GD 21 for assessment. Hesperidin-treated rats demonstrated significant reductions in blood pressure (P < 0.05) and urinary protein levels (P < 0.001) compared to untreated AVP groups. Additionally, placental and individual pup weights increased significantly (P < 0.001). Alterations in hematological and biochemical markers, including white blood cell count and lymphocyte levels, were also observed (P < 0.05), suggesting modulation of inflammatory responses.
These findings indicate that hesperidin may exert antihypertensive and renoprotective effects in experimental preeclampsia, potentially mediated through diuretic action, vascular relaxation, and reduction of oxidative stress and inflammation.
Key challenges include the limitation of evidence to animal models, with no clinical trials evaluating hesperidin in pregnant women with preeclampsia. Dose translation from animal studies to humans remains uncertain, and safety data in pregnancy are limited. Additionally, the multifactorial pathogenesis of PE necessitates confirmation that observed blood pressure and proteinuria improvements translate into meaningful maternal and neonatal outcomes. Further preclinical validation and well-designed clinical studies are required before hesperidin can be considered a viable therapeutic candidate in preeclampsia management.

Name: Hetero RBD-Fc protein vaccine
Developers: Fudan University
Indication: Prevention of coronavirus infections
Target: Receptor binding domains (RBDs) of SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and multiple SARS-CoV-2 variants (D614G, Delta, BA.1, BA.2.75, BA.5, BF.7, XBB.1.5, etc.)
Mechanism of action: Fc-fused heterodimeric/tetrameric RBD proteins display multiple coronavirus RBDs in one immunogen, inducing broad neutralizing antibodies and T-cell responses that block viral receptor engagement (ACE2 or DPP4) and neutralize diverse coronavirus pseudoviruses.
Key features and challenges:
-Broad coverage: Heterodimers combining SARS-CoV-2 and MERS RBDs elicited neutralizing responses against both viruses; heterotetramers extended breadth to all SARS-CoV-2 VOCs, SARS-CoV, WIV1, GD-Pangolin, and MERS.
-Fc fusion benefits: Improves half-life, facilitates purification, enhances immunogenicity.
-Strong T-cell responses: Heterotetramers increased germinal center B cells and CD8+ effector memory T cells vs homodimers.
-Flexibility in dosing interval: Neutralizing titers remained robust across 14–42 day spacing.
-Challenges: Data so far limited to mice; no authentic virus challenge or larger animal models yet. Adjuvant (MnJ) induced systemic reactions; delivery optimization needed. Translational pathway toward human testing remains uncertain.
Recent updates:
-This vaccine concept is among several next-generation Fc-fusion RBD constructs explored in 2024–2025 to achieve universal coronavirus coverage. Similar hetero RBD-Fc approaches (chimeric RBDs, mosaic immunogens) are being tested in China and internationally for broader betacoronavirus immunity.
-Fc-fusion subunit vaccines continue to show promise as safer, more stable alternatives to mRNA in LMIC contexts; Zhao et al. highlight their adaptability to new variants

Name: Hexestrol (HES)
Developers: Kyoto University; Phillips University Marburg; Hokkaido University, Sapporo; Japan Science and Technology Agency (JST)
Indication: Treatment of Lassa fever
Target: Lassa virus glycoprotein complex (LASV GP2 transmembrane region, residues around F446; binding pocket involves F434, T438, Y441).
Mechanism of action: Binds directly to LASV glycoprotein transmembrane domain; blocks membrane fusion step of viral entry, preventing release of viral RNA into cytoplasm. Activity independent of estrogen receptor signaling.
Key features and challenges:
-In vitro inhibition of authentic LASV replication (IC50 = 0.31–0.61 µM; CC50 ~49.6 µM; Selectivity Index ~79).
-Active against multiple LASV strains (Josiah, Togo) and some New World mammarenaviruses (Sabiá, Tacaribe) but not JUNV or MACV.
-Resistance mutation identified at F446L in GP2; resistant viruses show impaired growth due to destabilized prefusion GP.
-Mechanistic modeling confirms stable binding in GP2/SSP interface.
-Advantage: drug-repurposing potential. 
-Limitations: only in vitro data, resistance possible, no animal efficacy data yet.
Recent updates:
May 2024:
-Identified alongside CP100356 hydrochloride as novel LASV entry inhibitors in library screens.
-Expanding exploration of estrogen-related scaffolds for arenavirus entry inhibitors.

Name: High resolution flow (HR-Flow) ultrasonography
Developers: The Affiliated Yixing Hospital of Jiangsu University
Indication: Indicated for the prediction of Preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for research use only
Mechanism of action: Images the microvascular characterization of the placental villi to detect reduced perfusion and high-resistance states
Key features and challenges: A 2025 study explored the use of high-resolution flow (HR-Flow) ultrasonography to assess placental villous vascularization in late pregnancy as a way to predict pre-eclampsia (PE). In this case–control study, forty women with hypertensive disorders were split into hypertension (n=18) and PE (n=22) groups, with another 40 healthy volunteers as the control group. Researchers found that the degree of placental villous branching was significantly lower in the PE group compared to the hypertension and control groups (p<0.05). The pulsatility index (PI), resistance index (RI), and the ratio of peak systolic to end diastolic flow velocity in secondary villi were notably higher in both PE and hypertension groups versus controls (p<0.05). Sensitivity for predicting PE peaked at 95.5% when villous branching was ≤2.5 alongside PI ≥0.625, while specificity reached 93.1% when RI was ≥0.485. The results suggest HR-Flow ultrasound can be a useful tool for predicting PE (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-09094-9)

Name: High-throughput multiplex  6-codon assay
Developers: Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoea and antimicrobial susceptibility
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: multiplex high-resolution melting assay
Key features and challenges:
High-throughput multiplex 6-codon assay is a molecular diagnostic candidate designed to predict decreased susceptibility to cephalosporins in Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The assay incorporates high-resolution melting (HRM) technology in a multiplex format and targets six codons associated with resistance, enabling rapid detection of resistance-associated single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs).
The method demonstrated 100% sensitivity and specificity for distinguishing specific SNPs in resistance-associated genes, with a detection limit as low as 10 copies per reaction. The assay can be applied directly to clinical samples without the need for culture and successfully identified all cephalosporin-resistant isolates evaluated in the study.
A study published in 2022, showed that this high-throughput approach enables rapid antimicrobial resistance testing and may support individualized treatment decisions while facilitating surveillance of cephalosporin-resistant strains (https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/aac.01709-21).

Name: Honokiol
Developers: National Ilan University
Indication: Treatment and prevention of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Reduces the extracellular release of IL-1β, NLRP3, and apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing a caspase recruitment domain (ASC) in N. gonorrhoeae-infected macrophages
Key features and challenges:
Honokiol is a bioactive biphenolic compound derived from Magnolia species and has demonstrated anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and antimicrobial properties. It has been investigated for activity against Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the causative pathogen of gonorrhoea, particularly in the context of antimicrobial resistance and host inflammatory response modulation.
In vitro studies have shown that honokiol exhibits direct anti-gonococcal activity against N. gonorrhoeae. Beyond antibacterial effects, honokiol modulates host immune responses by inhibiting activation of caspase-1, caspase-11, and gasdermin D (GSDMD), key mediators of inflammasome-driven pyroptosis. Treatment reduced extracellular release of pro-inflammatory mediators including interleukin-1β (IL-1β), NLRP3 inflammasome components, and apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing a caspase recruitment domain (ASC) in infected macrophages.
Mechanistic investigations further demonstrated that honokiol decreases hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) production and reduces phosphorylation of ERK1/2 in N. gonorrhoeae-infected macrophages, suggesting suppression of oxidative stress and downstream inflammatory signaling pathways. 
Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38828053/
These findings indicate that honokiol may exert dual antimicrobial and immunomodulatory effects.
However, evidence remains limited to in vitro studies. No in vivo animal model data or human clinical trials have evaluated honokiol for gonococcal infection. Safety, pharmacokinetics, optimal dosing, and potential resistance development remain uncharacterized. Additionally, as a plant-derived compound, regulatory pathways and formulation standardization would require clarification prior to clinical development.
Honokiol represents an early-stage investigational candidate with combined antimicrobial and host-directed anti-inflammatory properties against N. gonorrhoeae. Further translational research is required to determine its clinical feasibility and therapeutic potential in gonococcal infection.
Recent updates: Discovery article published in 2024, demonstrating anti-gonococcal activity (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38828053/)

Name: HormoneBayes
Developers: University of Essex
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for research use only
Mechanism of action: The framework requires multiple LH measurements taken at regular intervals (e.g., every 10 minutes over a few hours) to evaluate secretion patterns, inter-pulse intervals, and clearance rates. These blood samples serve as the input for computational modeling, which estimates hypothalamic function and identifies abnormalities in reproductive hormone regulation.
Key features and challenges: HormoneBayes is a Bayesian framework designed to analyse luteinizing hormone (LH) pulsatility, with the aim of diagnosing reproductive disorders like polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). LH pulsatility is typically altered in PCOS, and while it can be measured to assess hormonal dysfunction, routine clinical practice often lacks the tools for detailed analysis. HormoneBayes offers a solution by using Monte Carlo methods to model LH dynamics, estimate key parameters, and identify LH pulses. This method can distinguish between healthy and pathological hormonal patterns, including in women with PCOS, making it a valuable tool for personalised, data-driven diagnosis and management of reproductive hormone disorders. (https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011928)

Name: Hsp70s Inhibitor
Developers: Virginia Commonwealth University
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Inhibition of bacterial 70- kD heat shock proteins
Key features and challenges:
Hsp70s inhibitor is a small-molecule therapeutic candidate targeting 70-kDa heat shock proteins (Hsp70s), which function as molecular chaperones essential for protein homeostasis in Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Hsp70s play a critical role in bacterial survival and growth within the host, making them a potential target for novel antimicrobial strategies.
The development strategy focuses on the rational design of specific and potent inhibitors that target the open substrate-binding domain (SBD) conformational state of Hsp70s. Designed inhibitors are intended to be evaluated for their ability to inhibit growth of clinical multidrug-resistant N. gonorrhoeae isolates.
Targeting Hsp70s represents a host-pathogen interaction–informed therapeutic approach, with the potential to generate novel antimicrobial agents against gonorrhea. Further evaluation is required to establish efficacy and translational potential (https://reporter.nih.gov/search/mAwSRzqGkECLvAGLk_eRwA/project-details/9776461).

Name: HtrA4 and first-trimester uterine artery pulsatility index
Developers: Chulalongkorn University
Indication: Prediction of preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: Serum high-temperature requirement protease A4 levels and uterine artery pulsatility
Mechanism of action: Combines maternal serum HtrA4 levels with uterine artery Doppler resistance to identify impaired placentation associated with preeclampsia.
Key features and challenges:
A study published in 2023 by researchers at Chulalongkorn University (Thailand) aimed to investigate the predictive value of serum levels of high-temperature requirement protease A4 (HtrA4) combined with first-trimester uterine artery pulsatility index in predicting preeclampsia in singleton pregnancy. 
Pregnant women at gestational age 11–13+6 weeks, who visited the antenatal clinic at King Chulalongkorn Memorial Hospital between April 2020 and July 2021 were included. Serum HtrA4 levels were measured and transabdominal uterine artery Doppler ultrasound was performed to evaluate this combination for calculating the predictive value of preeclampsia. While 371 singleton pregnant women enrolled in this study, 366 completed it. Thirty-four (9.3%) women had preeclampsia. Mean serum HtrA4 levels were higher in the preeclampsia group than in the control group (9.4 ± 3.9 vs 4.6 ± 2.2 ng/ml, p < 0.001). The mean uterine artery pulsatility index (UtA-PI) was higher in the group with early onset preeclampsia than in the control group (2.3 ± 0.5 vs 1.7 ± 0.5, p = 0.002). The sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) were 76.5%, 90.7%, 45.6%, and 97.4%, respectively, when using serum HtrA4 levels above 1.8 multiples of the median for the gestational age as a cut-off value for predicting preeclampsia. A combination of serum HtrA4 levels and UtA-PI > 95th percentile yielded sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV of 79.4%, 86.1%, 37% and 97.6%, respectively, for the prediction of preeclampsia. A combination of serum HtrA4 levels and uterine artery Doppler in the first trimester thus had good sensitivity for predicting preeclampsia.
(https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-35243-z)

Name: Human chorionic gonadotropin - PTL
Developers: University of California, Irvine
Indication: Delaying preterm labour
Mechanism of action: Maintaining the corpus luteum and production of progesterone during pregnancy.
Key features and challenges:
Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), a polypeptide hormone produced by the human placenta. Endogenously produced hCG interacts with the LHCG receptor of the ovary and promotes the maintenance of the corpus luteum during the beginning of pregnancy. This allows the corpus luteum to continuously secrete the hormone progesterone during the first trimester. 

Progesterone is generally considered to enhance myometrial quiescence by its ability to down-regulate myometrial gap junctions and thus inhibit contractions. Preclinical evidence suggests that hCG may have a similar role. hCG also appears to regulate levels of cytokine production (IL-6 and TNF) in a dose-dependent manner. Experiments using mice with PGF2α-induced preterm labour demonstrated that treatment with hCG prior to progesterone induction could delay time to delivery. Human in vivo experiments also show that pretreatment with hCG markedly suppressed the myometrial activity in non-pregnant women (reviewed in: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11394205/; original research: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10521741/).

Clinical trials in humans have been limited however. Five clinical studies testing hCG in the treatment of preterm births have been undertaken: four of them were on women with active labour and the fifth was on women with a previous history of preterm births. The studies on women with active labour were compared with MgSO4 treatment. The results showed that while hCG was equally effective, it did not have the side effects of MgSO4. In the prophylactic study, hCG was found to be equally effective as vaginal micronized progesterone tablets with a better compliance rate than progesterone (review: http://dx.doi.org/10.17140/WHOJ-1-e002).

The safety of exogenous administration of hCG remains uninvestigated. Nonetheless, hCG is an endogenous hormone normally present in high serum levels throughout gestation (generally peak at 50,000 to 100,000 IU). Interestingly, urinary hCG or recombinant hCG (rhCG) is used in assisted reproduction for the final maturation of oocytes in women treated with IVF. rHCG is derived from genetically engineered Chinese hamster ovary cells through recombinant DNA technology. However, the safety of rhCH has not been evaluated.

Despite promising initial results, there are no large scale clinical trials with hCG, like those conducted with 17-hydroxy-progesterone caproate (17-OHP-C) and progesterone, there is no on-going or planned investigation.

In 2023, Shaheed Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto Medical University is undertaking an RCT assessing HCG versus MgSO4 as a tocolytic agent in Pakistan (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05828966#study-overview)
Recent updates: 2024: New RCT information added

Name: Hu‑CO2 vaccine (H5 Human COBRA 2 vaccine) +/-Addavax
Developers: University of Georgia (UGA) (including the Center for Vaccines and Immunology); University of Saskatchewan
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against influenza A, caused by H5N1
Target: Hemagglutinin (HA) of H5 clade 1 (VN/04) and cross-clade H5 antigens
Mechanism of action: Induces cross-reactive neutralizing antibodies targeting conserved H5 HA epitopes; protection enhanced by Addavax adjuvant to boost humoral and cellular immunity.
Key features and challenges:
-Designed using COBRA (computationally optimized broadly reactive antigen) method to broaden cross-reactivity across H5 clades.
-In ferret studies, vaccination overcame limitations of immune imprinting (H3N2 background) by redirecting immune responses to protective Group 1 HA antigens.
-Provided full survival protection against lethal H5N1 challenge in H3N2-imprinted ferrets, with minimal weight loss and reduced clinical signs compared to controls.
-Addavax adjuvant enhanced antibody titers and protection.
-Challenges: Effectiveness in humans with diverse imprinting backgrounds remains to be proven; requires evaluation against newly emerging clade 2.3.4.4b/c strains.
Recent updates:

-Previous COBRA iterations (H5N1 COBRA VLPs) have shown efficacy in mice, ferrets, and nonhuman primates (2011–2021 studies), supporting progression of Hu-CO2 as a leading universal H5 candidate.

Name: Hydralazine - PCOS
Developers: Novartis; Hetero; Fresenius Kabi
Indication: PCOS hyperandrogenism, cystic and atretic follicles, fertility
Mechanism of action: Undefined mechanism
Key features and challenges:
Hydralazine is a direct-acting vasodilator and antihypertensive agent, chemically described as a 1-hydrazino derivative of phthalazine. It functions primarily by relaxing vascular smooth muscle, thereby reducing peripheral resistance and blood pressure.
https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/Hydralazine
Interest in hydralazine as a potential therapy for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) emerged from computational drug-repurposing analyses. A 2022 molecular docking and molecular dynamics study screened FDA-approved drugs and identified hydralazine as a candidate with potential binding affinity to targets relevant to PCOS pathophysiology, suggesting theoretical activity comparable to letrozole in silico.
https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07391102.2023.2190411
Preclinical validation has been explored in animal models. A 2024 study using a letrozole-induced PCOS Wistar rat model demonstrated that hydralazine (30 mg/kg) significantly reduced serum testosterone and luteinizing hormone (LH) levels. Treatment was associated with a reduction in cystic and atretic ovarian follicles and increased numbers of healthy antral and Graafian follicles, as well as corpus luteum volume, suggesting restoration of ovulatory function.
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0753332224003883?via%3Dihub
Despite these promising preclinical findings, hydralazine is not currently indicated or clinically studied for PCOS in humans. Its primary approved use remains hypertension management. No registered clinical trials evaluating hydralazine in women with PCOS have been reported.
Key challenges include the absence of human clinical data, unclear mechanistic relevance beyond computational predictions and rodent models, and potential safety considerations given hydralazine’s systemic vasodilatory effects. Known adverse effects—including hypotension, reflex tachycardia, and rare drug-induced lupus—would require careful evaluation in reproductive-age populations. Additionally, the therapeutic rationale for repurposing an antihypertensive agent in PCOS requires further mechanistic clarification.
Hydralazine represents an early-stage, repurposed candidate identified through computational screening and supported by preclinical rodent data. However, its role in PCOS remains highly investigational pending translational studies and human clinical evaluation.

Name: Hydralazine - PE
Developers: EKR Therapeutics (Previously PDL BioPharma, Inc); Barbeau Pharma
Indication: Treatment of complications linked to hypertension in pregnancy, including severe preeclampsia and eclampsia
Target: Unidentified primary target in arterial endothelium; DNA methyltransferases; Collagen prolyl hydroxylase
Mechanism of action: Reducing systemic vascular resistance and arterial pressure via multiple, direct effects on vascular smooth muscles
Key features and challenges:
Hydralazine is a potent arteriolar vasodilator which relaxes arterial smooth muscle by inhibiting accumulation of intracellular free Ca2+ via an unidentified primary target; the mechanism by which vasodilation is induced by hydralazine remains to be elucidated. Dihydralazine [(4-hydrazinylphthalazin-1-yl)hydrazine] is structurally similar to hydralazine and has similar vasodilating effect. In 2005, manufacturing of IV dihydralazin was terminated worldwide for economic reasons while IV hydralazine is still generically available in the US. (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/PL00022208)
Barbeau Pharma was developing an IV formulation of hydralazine for the treatment complications linked to hypertension in pregnancy, including severe preeclampsia and eclampsia (PE/E). Interestingly, when prescribed for hypertension during pregnancy, the side-effects can mimic symptoms of PE/E (such as headaches). The antihypertensive product was undergoing clinical evaluation for complications of hypertension in pregnancy. However, no recent development has been reported. 
Intravenous (di)hydralazine has been regarded as the drug of choice in preeclamptic patients for many years. Recently, however, a meta-analysis of 21 available randomised clinical trials for the treatment of severe hypertension (including 1,085 women) showed that hydralazine was associated with poorer maternal and perinatal outcomes than other antihypertensive drugs, particularly nifedipine and labetalol. Hydralazine was associated with a trend toward more persistent severe hypertension, compared to nifedipine or isradipine. Seemingly contradictory, hydralazine was also found to be associated with more maternal hypotension than other antihypertensive drugs (labetalol, nifedipine, isradipine, ketanserin or uradipil). Other maternal complications occurred more often with hydralazine than with other antihypertensive drugs; caesarean section, placental abruption and maternal oliguria. Hydralazine was associated with more adverse effects on foetal heart rates, APGAR scores and a trend towards an increase in stillbirth. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15805801/)
Recent updates:
2022: Active based on this trial, https://www.thaiclinicaltrials.org/show/TCTR20221014007

Hydralazine is used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension). It is also used to control high blood pressure in a mother during pregnancy (pre-eclampsia or eclampsia) or in emergency situations when blood pressure is extremely high (hypertensive crisis). 

March 2015: Randomized Controlled Trial of Labetalol Versus Hydralazine for Severe Hypertension in Obstetric Patients NCT02050529 completed (results unavailable).

2005: Meta-analysis revealed that hydralazine was associated with greater risk of maternal and foetal adverse effects than other anti-hypertensives (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15805801/)

Name: Hydrochlorothiazide
Developers: University of Texas Medical Branch at Galveston
Indication: Postpartum management of preeclampsia/eclampsia
Mechanism of action: Inhibiting reabsorption by the sodium-chloride symporter, also known as Solute Carrier Family 12 Member 3 (SLC12A3)
Key features and challenges:
Hydrochlorothiazide is the most commonly prescribed thiazide diuretic but its use is declining in favour of angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors. Hydrochlorothiazide was granted FDA approval on 12 February 1959. Hydrochlorothiazide is transported from the circulation into epithelial cells of the distal convoluted tubule by the organic anion transporters OAT1, OAT3, and OAT4.6. From these cells, hydrochlorothiazide is transported to the lumen of the tubule by multidrug resistance associated protein 4 (MRP4) and there, prevents the reabsorption of sodium and water from the distal convoluted tubule, allowing for the increased elimination of water in the urine. Hydrochlorothiazide has a wide therapeutic window as dosing is individualized and can range from 25-100mg.
Hydrochlorothiazide has been considered in clinical studies as an antihypertensive in the postpartum period. However, the majority of controlled studies have been in normotensive pregnant women rather than hypertensive patients. Hydrochlorothiazide can cause volume contraction and electrolyte disorders but may be useful in combination with methyldopa and vasodilator to mitigate compensatory fluid retention. Its role as a hypertensive is reviewed in https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18259046/. 
A Phase III trial is underway to evaluate the effectiveness of hydrochlorothiazide on prevention and relapse of preeclampsia or gestational hypertension on postpartum hypertensive women. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT03298802)
Recent updates:

Name: Hydroxychloroquine
Developers: VG Life Sciences Inc. (formerly Viral Genetics); University of Texas Health Science Center San Antonio
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: Antimetabolites; Phospholipase A2 inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Hydroxychloroquine is an antimalarial and immunomodulatory agent widely used in autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus. Although its precise mechanisms are not fully understood, hydroxychloroquine is known to exert anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, and metabolic effects, including improvements in glycemic control and lipid profiles in patients with chronic inflammatory conditions.
Interest in hydroxychloroquine as a potential therapy for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) stems from the recognition that chronic low-grade inflammation, insulin resistance, and dyslipidemia are central features of the disorder, particularly in obese phenotypes. In 2021, a clinical study commenced in China to evaluate the effects of hydroxychloroquine on glucose metabolism, lipid parameters, and chronic inflammation in obese women with PCOS. The primary objective is to determine whether hydroxychloroquine can improve metabolic dysfunction and inflammatory status in this population.
As of late 2024, the trial has not been marked as complete and no results have been publicly released. Consequently, evidence supporting hydroxychloroquine in PCOS remains preliminary and investigational. Potential concerns include long-term safety considerations such as retinal toxicity and cardiomyopathy, which necessitate careful monitoring in other indications. Further high-quality randomized controlled trials are required to establish its efficacy, safety, and appropriate positioning within PCOS management strategies.
https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=160099&u_atoken=eda556cb06993fd7a0dd226492c14cc3&u_asig=ac11000117310284781518778e004b

Name: Hyivy Health Floora device
Developers: Hyivy Health
Indication: Treatment of endometriosis pain
Mechanism of action: Multitherapy vaginal wand performing heat therapy and auto dilation in combination with biosensors
Key features and challenges:
The Hyivy Health Floora device is a Class II, home-use intravaginal medical device designed to alleviate symptoms associated with hypertonic pelvic floor disorders, including those related to endometriosis. The device consists of a multi-therapy vaginal wand that combines controlled heat therapy and auto-dilation with integrated biosensors. These sensors collect patient-reported and physiological data, which can be transmitted to healthcare providers to monitor progress and inform individualized care plans (https://hyivy.com/for-patients/). 
The therapeutic rationale in endometriosis is based on addressing pelvic floor muscle hypertonicity, which can contribute to chronic pelvic pain and dyspareunia.
Clinical evaluation is underway. A proof-of-concept, single-arm pilot study initiated in 2024 is assessing the effectiveness of the Hyivy intravaginal device in reducing self-reported pelvic pain among individuals with endometriosis 
(NCT05643131; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05643131). 
The study plans to enroll 25 participants and is expected to complete in 2025, with the primary endpoint focused on changes in pain levels following device use.
Key challenges include the early stage of clinical validation, small sample size in the pilot study, and absence of randomized controlled trial data. Demonstration of clinically meaningful and durable pain reduction compared with standard pelvic floor physiotherapy or other non-pharmacologic interventions will be important. Regulatory classification as a medical device may facilitate market entry; however, payer coverage and integration into clinical care pathways remain considerations.
Overall, the Hyivy Floora device represents a non-hormonal, device-based approach targeting pelvic floor dysfunction in endometriosis-associated pain. Robust clinical evidence from larger controlled studies will be necessary to define its effectiveness and positioning in routine care.

Name: Hypericum gaitii Haines (E38)
Developers: Ministry of Science and Technology Government of India
Indication: Indicated for the treatment or preventionof CHIKV infection
Target:
