-The extract seems to interfere with CHIKV life cycle at multiple phases (entry and post-entry).
-Some individual phytocompounds (e.g. Avenanthramide A) predicted to interact with CHIKV nsP2 protease, capsid protein, and host factors like NF-κB.
Mechanism of action:
-Suppresses CHIKV replication by reducing viral RNA and protein expression, reducing production of new infectious particles; shows virucidal activity (direct inactivation).
-In silico predictions for individual constituents suggest binding to viral proteases, helicases, capsid, etc. Also suggests interactions with host innate immunity machinery.
Key features and challenges:
-Potent in vitro activity: CHIKV IC₅₀ in Vero cells ~1.89-4.16 μg/mL, in C2C12 muscle cells as well.
-Good selectivity index (SI): ≥ ~53 in Vero cells, >42 in C2C12 for CHIKV, indicating toxicity is low relative to antiviral activity.
-Virucidal activity shown (extract can inactivate virus particles directly).
-Chemical profiling identified ~13 main compounds; several (Mannopine, 2′-Deoxymugineic acid, Avenic acid A, Avenanthramide A) have favorable ADMET predictions and docking with viral and host targets.
Recent updates:
2025: 
-A study demonstrates for the first time that E38 extract strongly inhibits CHIKV in two cell lines (Vero, C2C12) at low micromolar (µg/mL) doses; shows potency in reducing viral RNA, protein expression, and new virion production.
-Also showed virucidal effect (inactivates virus particles).
-Identified specific compounds (e.g. Avenanthramide A) with promising docking to viral proteases and helicase, suggesting possible focal points for fractionation, isolation, or synthetic optimization.

Name: Hyperspectral imaging
Developers: Heidelberg University
Indication: Indicated for the detection of endothelial dysfunction in Preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Capture and analysis of the specific light absorption and scattering properties of skin tissue, enabling the quantification of microvascular oxygenation and perfusion
Key features and challenges:
Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) is a non-invasive optical imaging technology that captures spatial and spectral information across multiple wavelengths, enabling assessment of tissue oxygenation, hemoglobin distribution, and microcirculatory perfusion. In the context of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, hyperspectral imaging is being explored as a potential tool to detect endothelial dysfunction and microvascular alterations associated with preeclampsia.
The 2025 EPICS study (Endothelial dysfunction for Prognosis In patients with preeClampSia) is the first prospective observational study evaluating hyperspectral imaging in women with preeclampsia. The study aims to determine whether microcirculatory changes detected by hyperspectral imaging differ between women with preeclampsia, pregnancy-induced hypertension, normotensive pregnant women, and non-pregnant controls. It also investigates associations between microcirculatory perfusion parameters and biochemical markers such as EASIX and other indicators of endothelial dysfunction. Additionally, the EPICS study evaluates the predictive performance of hyperspectral imaging—alone or in combination with biochemical markers—for adverse maternal and perinatal outcomes and for estimating the remaining time to delivery in women with preeclampsia.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06912477).
Key challenges include the need for validation in larger and diverse populations, standardization of imaging protocols and interpretation thresholds, and integration into routine clinical workflows. The predictive value of hyperspectral imaging relative to established biomarkers and clinical parameters remains to be determined through further prospective studies.

Name: Imidazo [1,2-b]pyridazine derivatives
Developers: University of Khartoum (including the Mycetoma Research Center); University of Tours, Université de Tours (UT); University of Rotterdam
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of mycetoma
Mechanism of action: Unknown.
Key features and challenges:
Imidazo [1,2-b]pyridazines have been identified as potential candidates for treating eumycetoma.

Out of the 47 compounds investigated, 25 displayed IC50 values that fall between those of the commonly used antifungals itraconazole (IC50 = 1.1 ± 0.4 μM) and amphotericin B (IC50 = 9.7 ± 0.7 μM), which serve as benchmarks in the treatment of eumycetoma. Furthermore, 16 of these compounds exhibited IC50 values under 5 μM, with compound 14d emerging as the most potent, achieving an IC50 of 0.9 μM. This compound also demonstrated minimal cytotoxic effects on NIH-3T3 murine fibroblasts, with an IC50 of 14.3 μM, resulting in a selectivity index of 16, the highest among the synthesised compounds and reference antifungals.

Findings suggest that imidazo [1,2-b]pyridazine derivatives have substantial potential as candidates for treating eumycetoma, offering potential improvements over current therapeutic options. Further in vivo evaluation using Galleria mellonella larvae and mammalian experimental models are needed to comprehensively assess the efficacy and safety profiles of these compounds. 

Future research should focus on exploring the mechanisms underlying the enhanced activity of these compounds and investigating their potential in combination therapies, and efforts should be directed towards evaluating the pharmacokinetic properties of the most promising candidates.
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0223523424006019?via%3Dihub).

Name: Imidazole carbamate compounds
Developers: Mexican National Pediatric Institute, Instituto Nacional de Pediatría; Mexican National Polytechnic Institute, Instituto Politécnico Nacional (IPN)

Target: Gene expression; Microtubule Formation; glucose uptake and utilization
Mechanism of action: Reduce expression of glycolytic genes (CK, PFK, TPI, and ENOL) and genes involved in metabolism (G6PD, TKT, TALDO, NADHOX, ACT, and TUB); Inhibition of Microtubule Formation; inhibition of glucose uptake and utilization
Key features and challenges:
Imidazole carbamate compounds (AGR-1 to AGR-5) are investigational trichomonacidal agents derived from structural modification of metronidazole. The alcohol tail of metronidazole was replaced with five different carbamate groups to increase lipophilicity and enhance antiparasitic activity. A 2020 study reported the synthesis and initial characterization of these compounds (https://www.mdpi.com/1420-3049/25/4/793).
Subsequent evaluation demonstrated that AGR-1, AGR-2, AGR-3, AGR-4, and AGR-5 exhibited greater trichomonacidal activity than metronidazole against a metronidazole-susceptible strain of Trichomonas vaginalis, achieving 100% elimination of parasite viability. Reported IC50 values were 0.67 µM (AGR-1), 0.40 µM (AGR-2), 0.64 µM (AGR-3), 0.96 µM (AGR-4), and 1.45 µM (AGR-5). Both the imidazole carbamates and metronidazole reduced expression of key glycolytic genes (CK, PFK, TPI, ENOL) and metabolic genes (G6PD, TKT, TALDO, NADHOX, ACT, TUB), suggesting disruption of parasite metabolic pathways as a shared mechanism of action.
The compounds demonstrated low cytotoxicity in Caco-2 and HT29 cell lines, and pharmacokinetic properties were reported to be comparable to metronidazole. A 2024 study recommended further evaluation in animal models of vaginal infection to assess toxicity, tissue permeability, and local drug presence prior to clinical advancement (https://www.mdpi.com/1420-3049/29/11/2585).
Overall, imidazole carbamate derivatives represent a modified nitroimidazole-based therapeutic strategy with enhanced in vitro activity and potential to address limitations associated with metronidazole treatment.
Recent updates: A preclinical study published in 2024 determined the compounds showed low cytotoxicity in the Caco-2 and HT29 cell lines, and the results of the ADMET analysis indicated that these compounds have pharmacokinetic properties similar to those of MTZ (https://www.mdpi.com/1420-3049/29/11/2585)

Name: In2Care® EaveTube
Developers: IN2CARE
Indication: Prevention and control of malaria in children and adults in areas with ongoing malaria transmission where the principal malaria vector(s) exhibit pyrethroid resistance.
Target: Anopheles mosquitoes juvenile hormone binding site receptors
Mechanism of action: Sodium channel modulation (Deltamethrin and Beta-cyfluthrin) or  Acetylcholinesterase inhibition (Bendiocarb)
Key features and challenges:
In2Care® EaveTubes are made of plastic and contain a removable mesh with a static coating of a powder-formulated insecticide. The tubes are inserted into the eaves of houses during construction. Alternatively, they are installed behind ventilation openings or retrofitted into the wall by drilling, cutting or chiselling. The static-coated mesh transfers a sufficient dose of pyrethroid insecticide particles to be lethal to both pyrethroid-resistant and susceptible wild-type mosquitoes. The In2Care team has interacted with VCAG since 2014, working towards generating evidence of disease impact against malaria for their EaveTubes product. The results of the first trial conducted in Côte d’Ivoire were presented to VCAG at its 11th meeting in November 2019. These results demonstrated a substantial impact on malaria incidence, albeit when deployed in combination with house screening as part of the lethal house lures intervention class. Supporting entomological studies were also presented to VCAG, which demonstrated efficacy against mosquitoes in the absence of screening.
The “lethal house lure” is an innovative housing modification designed to prevent mosquito entry and eliminate host-seeking mosquitoes. This intervention combines screening potential entry points—such as eaves, windows, and doors—with insecticide treatment on some or all of these screens. The screening channels warm, human-scented air from inside the structure to the upper eaves, effectively attracting mosquitoes. Once drawn to the treated screens, mosquitoes are exposed to the insecticide. By both restricting entry and targeting mosquitoes, lethal house lures serve as a dual-action solution to enhance protection against mosquito-borne diseases.

Currently under Vector Control Advisory Group (VCAG) review for assessment of public health value as of 01/03/2020.
Recent updates: The applicants informed VCAG that their trial in Uganda had recently been completed. While data analyses were still ongoing, the applicants provided initial results of the intervention implementation, interim cross-sectional results and some entomological results. The applicants expect that the full study results will be submitted to VCAG for review in the spring of 2024. For the trial in Côte d’Ivoire, the applicants summarized baseline prevalence data and implementation progress, and provided an updated study protocol with amendments. The baseline prevalence survey was conducted from the end of May to mid-June 2023, while clinical follow-up with intervention will start in October 2023 and is planned to f inish in October 2025. https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240087699

Name: Indinol Forto
Developers: Alcea
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Endometriosis.
Mechanism of action: Modulates estrogen receptors.
Key features and challenges:
Indinol Forto® is an oral formulation containing indole-3-carbinol (I3C), a compound derived from cruciferous vegetables that modulates estrogen metabolism and may influence proliferation of estrogen-dependent tissues. Given the hormone-driven pathophysiology of endometriosis, agents that alter estrogen signaling or metabolism represent potential therapeutic strategies. Indinol Forto® is being evaluated as a non-hormonal alternative for managing endometriosis-associated pelvic pain.
A prospective, open-label, randomized, parallel-group Phase III clinical trial (NCT07164183) is currently recruiting to compare the efficacy and safety of Indinol Forto® 200 mg capsules versus dienogest 2 mg tablets (Visanne®), an established progestin therapy for endometriosis (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07164183). 
The study is designed as a non-inferiority trial. Eligible participants are women aged 18–45 years with surgically confirmed endometriosis (laparoscopy or laparotomy within 2 weeks to 60 months prior to enrollment) and at least moderate pelvic pain for a minimum of two months before study entry. Following a screening menstrual cycle, participants are randomized to receive either Indinol Forto® 200 mg twice daily or dienogest 2 mg once daily for 24 weeks, with monthly follow-up visits. Pain assessment is conducted daily using a Visual Analog Scale (VAS), capturing both cyclic and non-cyclic pelvic pain as well as vaginal bleeding intensity. The primary endpoint is the change in average daily pelvic pain score during the sixth treatment period compared with baseline screening values. The estimated study completion date is November 2026.
Key challenges include the open-label design, which may introduce reporting bias in subjective pain outcomes. Demonstration of non-inferiority to an established hormonal therapy will require clinically meaningful pain reduction and acceptable safety and tolerability. As a non-hormonal agent, its mechanism of action and long-term efficacy relative to progestins remain to be clarified. Pending Phase III results will determine whether Indinol Forto® offers a viable alternative for women seeking non-hormonal management options for endometriosis-associated pain.

Key features and challenges:
Key features:
-Based on 138 plasma samples from the INSIGHT cohort (46 sPTB cases, 92 controls) collected at 16–24 weeks (mid-pregnancy).
-Olink 384-protein inflammatory panel used to quantify 368 high-quality proteins (following QC).
-27 inflammation-related proteins showed differential expression; 16 contributed meaningfully to predictive modelling (page 14–15).

-Biomarkers reflect multiple PTL-related pathways: inflammation, placental biology, immune activation, ECM remodelling, tissue metabolism (page 4).

Name: Insulin - PCOS
Developers: Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences
Indication: Treatment of hormonal balance, folliculogenesis, and insulin resistance associated with PCOS
Target: Ornithine decarboxylase; Phosphokinase; Protein tyrosine kinase
Mechanism of action: Ornithine decarboxylase stimulants; Phosphokinase stimulants; Protein tyrosine kinase stimulants
Key features and challenges:
Insulin is a peptide hormone central to glucose metabolism and cellular energy regulation. In polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), insulin resistance and compensatory hyperinsulinaemia are common and contribute to hyperandrogenism by stimulating ovarian theca cell androgen production and reducing sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG). While insulin-sensitizing agents such as metformin are standard treatments in PCOS, direct insulin administration has also been investigated experimentally for its potential effects on ovarian physiology and insulin-signaling pathways.
PCOS is characterized by dysregulated insulin signaling, altered steroidogenesis, follicular arrest, and increased apoptosis within ovarian tissue. Impaired expression of insulin receptor substrate (IRS) proteins and downstream signaling molecules; including PI3K and AKT pathways, has been implicated in the metabolic and reproductive dysfunction observed in PCOS.
A 2023 preclinical study evaluated insulin treatment in a dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA)-induced mouse model of PCOS. DHEA exposure increased serum testosterone, progesterone, and estradiol levels while reducing the expression of insulin-signaling genes (Irs1–4, Pdk1, Pi3k, Akt1–3) and increasing Caspase-3 expression, indicating enhanced apoptosis. Structural ovarian damage was observed, including reduced ovarian tissue volume, fewer follicles, and decreased corpus luteum numbers. Insulin administration reversed many of these abnormalities, restoring hormonal balance, upregulating insulin-signaling gene expression, reducing apoptotic markers, and improving folliculogenesis and ovarian morphology.
https://www.ijfs.ir/article_252117.html
Despite these findings, evidence remains limited to animal models. In clinical settings, systemic insulin therapy is not used to treat PCOS due to the risk of hypoglycaemia and exacerbation of hyperinsulinaemia-related androgen production. Therapeutic strategies in humans typically aim to reduce insulin resistance rather than increase circulating insulin levels.
Insulin represents a mechanistic research tool in PCOS models rather than a clinically viable therapeutic intervention. While experimental data suggest that modulation of insulin signaling pathways can improve ovarian structure and function, direct insulin administration is unlikely to represent a practical treatment approach in women with PCOS without further translational evidence and safety evaluation.
Recent updates: Short-term insulin treatment showed improvement in hormonal balance, folliculogenesis, and insulin resistance in the ovaries of the PCOS mice model in a study published in 2023 (https://www.ijfs.ir/article_252117.html)

Indication: Treatment for PCOS, particularly managing obesity
Target: Insulin receptors in muscle, liver and fat cells
Mechanism of action: Intranasal insulin works by absorption into the bloodstream after inhalation, stimulating insulin receptors in muscle, fat, and liver tissues, which helps in glucose uptake and utilisation.
Key features and challenges:
Intranasal insulin (INI) is a centrally acting formulation of insulin delivered via the nasal route to target hypothalamic and central nervous system pathways without significant systemic insulin exposure. It has been developed to enhance postprandial thermogenesis, modulate energy expenditure, and improve metabolic regulation. Central insulin signalling plays an important role in appetite regulation, sympathetic activation, and adipose tissue metabolism, mechanisms that are frequently dysregulated in obesity and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
Obesity exacerbates the metabolic and reproductive features of PCOS, and women with PCOS often demonstrate reduced postprandial energy expenditure (PPEE), contributing to difficulty achieving weight loss. Impaired thermogenic responses, rather than increased caloric intake alone, may partly explain this phenotype. Strategies that enhance postprandial thermogenesis (PPT) are therefore of therapeutic interest in PCOS.
Preclinical studies in an ovine model of PCOS demonstrated that INI increases sympathetic activation in subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT), enhances thermogenic activity, and improves energy balance without systemic hyperinsulinaemia. These findings provided mechanistic rationale for translation into human studies.
A University of Edinburgh study is currently evaluating INI in obese women with and without PCOS. The study assesses changes in PPEE using indirect calorimetry and evaluates SAT metabolic activity via microdialysis techniques. The objective is to determine whether INI enhances thermogenesis and whether the response differs in women with PCOS compared to controls.
https://www.endocrinology.org/endocrinologist/143-spring-22/features/energy-balance-obesity-and-polycystic-ovary-syndrome/
https://gtr.ukri.org/projects?ref=MR%2FW015439%2F1
Given the high prevalence of obesity, insulin resistance, and reduced energy expenditure in PCOS, targeting central insulin pathways represents a novel metabolic strategy. Unlike systemic insulin therapy, intranasal delivery aims to minimise peripheral metabolic effects while leveraging central thermogenic pathways.
However, clinical evidence in PCOS remains limited. Available data are primarily preclinical or early mechanistic human studies, with no large randomized controlled trials evaluating long-term metabolic, endocrine, or reproductive outcomes. Safety considerations include potential hypoglycaemia risk (although reduced with intranasal delivery), tolerability, and the need for longer-term evaluation in reproductive-age women.
Intranasal insulin represents an investigational metabolic therapy for PCOS focused on energy expenditure modulation rather than direct androgen suppression. While the mechanistic rationale is strong, its role in PCOS management remains exploratory pending results from controlled clinical trials assessing weight, endocrine, and reproductive endpoints.
Recent updates: Conference presentation in 2025 with results suggest proof of concept and provide additional safety data for INI in the improvement of PPEE in obese women with PCOS (https://www.endocrine-abstracts.org/ea/0110/ea0110oc5.5#:~:text)

Name: Insulin-like peptide 5 (INSL5)
Developers: Zhejiang Chinese Medical University
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Quantifies INSL5 levels to assess altered metabolic and gut–endocrine signaling associated with insulin resistance in PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Insulin-like peptide 5 (INSL5) is a hormone involved in energy regulation, appetite control, and reproduction. Its association with metabolic and hormonal imbalances highlights its potential as a biomarker for PCOS.

A study published in 2022 examined the relationship between INSL5 and anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) in women with PCOS. It included 117 women with PCOS and 100 healthy controls, with serum INSL5 levels measured using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. The results showed a significant positive correlation between INSL5 and AMH levels in women with PCOS, with AMH levels increasing across higher INSL5 quartiles. 

After adjusting for factors like age, BMI, and hormonal levels, the association remained significant. The study concluded that INSL5 and AMH levels are elevated in PCOS and may be linked to increased androgen secretion and chronic anovulation. However, the diagnostic value of AMH was better than that of INSL5 (0.902 vs. 0.693) and the combination of AMH and INSL5 cut-offs did not significantly improve the accuracy of diagnosis value.

Name: Iodoquinol
Developers: University of Pretoria (UP)
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Target: Largely unknown but potentially bacterial ferrous ions.
Mechanism of action: Lately unknown but may act by chelation of ferrous ions essential for metabolism.
Key features and challenges:
Iodoquinol (diiodohydroxyquinoline) is a quinoline derivative traditionally used in the treatment of amoebiasis and is being explored for potential repurposing against Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The compound has demonstrated antimicrobial activity and represents a potential alternative strategy to address rising antimicrobial resistance in gonorrhea.
A 2023 study evaluating eight novel compounds from the Pathogen Box reported potent activity against resistant strains of N. gonorrhoeae, with minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) and minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) values of ≤10 µM (https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/aac.00348-23). 
Iodoquinol was identified among compounds showing activity against resistant isolates, supporting further investigation of its antimicrobial potential.
Key challenges include limited gonorrhea-specific pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic data, potential toxicity concerns associated with systemic quinoline derivatives, and the need for in vivo validation in relevant infection models. Additional studies are required to assess resistance development risk and clinical feasibility.
Overall, iodoquinol represents a repurposing candidate with demonstrated in vitro activity against resistant N. gonorrhoeae, warranting further preclinical evaluation. Its established clinical history in other indications may facilitate translational development.

Name: Isirin
Developers: Sichuan University (SCU)
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Target: Androgen-induced gut microbiota dysbiosis and fecal metabolites
Mechanism of action: Modulate androgen-induced gut microbiota dysbiosis and fecal metabolites
Key features and challenges:
Irisin is a myokine cleaved from fibronectin type III domain-containing protein 5 (FNDC5) and is released in response to physical exercise. It plays a role in glucose and lipid metabolism, energy homeostasis, and browning of white adipose tissue. Given the central role of metabolic dysfunction and insulin resistance in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), irisin has attracted interest as a potential mechanistic link between exercise and improvement in PCOS phenotypes.
Clinical studies evaluating circulating irisin levels in women with PCOS have reported inconsistent findings, with some studies identifying altered serum levels compared to healthy controls, while others have found no significant differences. This variability may reflect heterogeneity in PCOS phenotypes (e.g., lean vs. obese), differences in metabolic status, and study design limitations.
Preclinical evidence has provided more mechanistic insight. A 2024 experimental study demonstrated that irisin improved both reproductive and metabolic abnormalities in a PCOS mouse model. Specifically, irisin reduced androgen-induced gut microbiota dysbiosis and altered fecal metabolite profiles, suggesting a potential role in modulating the gut–metabolism–reproductive axis. These findings support the hypothesis that irisin may mediate some of the beneficial effects of exercise in PCOS.
However, irisin remains an exploratory candidate, with evidence currently limited to preclinical models and observational human data. Further well-designed clinical studies are required to clarify its therapeutic relevance, optimal dosing strategies, and safety profile in women with PCOS.

Its mechanism is similar to nitroglycerin, though with a slower onset of action.
A Phase I clinical study, published in 2005, evaluated ISD for the prevention of preterm labour reported a reduction in preterm labour risk of approximately 70%, with a generally acceptable safety profile.
(Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15919396/)
A subsequent clinical study conducted between 2017 and 2018 compared a nitroglycerin transdermal patch with isosorbide dinitrate in the context of preterm labour management; however, results have not been reported.
Overall, limited early-phase evidence suggests potential tocolytic effects of ISD. However, the available data are preliminary, and published results from later-stage clinical trials are lacking, preventing firm conclusions regarding efficacy and safety in PTL/PTB management.

https://www.anzctr.org.au/Trial/Registration/TrialReview.aspx?ACTRN=12621001218886

Ivermectin, traditionally used for parasitic diseases, is gaining attention as a malaria control tool due to its unique ability to target mosquito vectors. When ingested by humans or livestock, it renders their blood toxic to mosquitoes, reducing mosquito lifespans and disrupting *Plasmodium* parasite development, thereby lowering malaria transmission.

Effective against *Anopheles* (malaria) and *Aedes* (other diseases) mosquitoes, ivermectin has a well-established safety profile and fits seamlessly into existing public health campaigns. However, its short-lived effect requires repeated dosing, presenting logistical challenges. Ongoing research is optimizing dosing regimens and exploring its integration with other interventions like insecticide-treated nets.

As climate change reshapes mosquito habitats, ivermectin’s adaptability offers a promising complementary strategy in the fight against malaria.

Name: JSF-2659
Developers: The State University of New Jersey
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Target: Bacterial DNA gyrase (GyrB) and topoisomerase IV (ParE)
Mechanism of action: Interferes with DNA biosynthesis by inhibiting bacterial DNA gyrase (GyrB) and topoisomerase IV (ParE)
Key features and challenges:
JSF-2659 is an orally bioavailable phosphate prodrug of the tricyclic pyrimidoindole compound JSF-2414, developed to target the ATP-binding regions of DNA gyrase (GyrB) and topoisomerase IV (ParE) in Neisseria gonorrhoeae. This dual-targeting mechanism is designed to enhance antibacterial potency and reduce the likelihood of resistance development.
A 2022 preclinical study reported that JSF-2414 demonstrated potent in vitro activity against N. gonorrhoeae, including multidrug-resistant strains. 
(https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/aac.00414-22). 
To enable oral administration, the phosphate prodrug JSF-2659 was developed and evaluated in two animal models of vaginal gonococcal infection, where it reduced bacterial burdens to the limit of detection. Beyond gonorrhea, JSF-2659 also demonstrated efficacy in models of vancomycin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection and Clostridioides difficile–induced colitis, indicating broad-spectrum activity against high-threat pathogens.
Key challenges include the need for comprehensive safety, toxicity, and pharmacokinetic evaluation in humans, as well as confirmation of resistance suppression in clinical settings. Further translational studies are required to determine optimal dosing strategies and long-term resistance risk.
Overall, JSF-2659 represents a promising dual-targeting antimicrobial candidate with demonstrated preclinical efficacy against multidrug-resistant N. gonorrhoeae. Its oral bioavailability and broad-spectrum activity support continued clinical development.

Name: K207.C
Developers: Kookmin University
Indication: Treatment of MERS-CoV infection
Target: MERS-CoV receptor binding domain (RBD) of the spike protein.
Mechanism of action: Simultaneous binding to two distinct epitopes on the RBD using parental antibodies K111.3 and K111.1; blocks RBD–hDPP4 interaction, preventing viral entry.
Key features and challenges:
-Derived from a fully human antibody library using phage display.
-Parental antibody K111.3 showed potent neutralization (IC50 ~1 nM); paired with non-competing K111.1 to create bispecific construct.
-K207.C showed 5-fold greater potency (IC50 0.17 nM) than parental mAb K111.3 in pseudovirus neutralization.
-High binding affinity: KD = 0.52 nM (vs 29.2 nM for K111.3).
-Stability: High solubility, no aggregation, and thermal stability (Tm ~76.8–78.9 °C) comparable to approved antibodies.
-Advantages: Combines cocktail-like breadth with simpler manufacturing and lower dosing needs.
-Challenges: Efficacy shown only in vitro with pseudoviruses; no in vivo animal studies yet. Translation into therapeutic product requires further validation.
Recent updates:
May 2024:
-Study confirmed enhanced neutralization of K207.C.
-Bispecific antibody approaches for coronaviruses are gaining attention in 2024–2025, particularly as alternatives to cocktails; K207.C is cited in reviews as a novel pan-CoV bispecific scaffold with translational potential.

Mechanism of action: Host-immunomodulation; reduces MPXV antigen in primary keratinocytes; topical application improves dermal pathology with full resolution by Day 12.
Key features and challenges: Potent antiviral activity (VK2 IC50s in 12–50 nM cohort); nontoxic up to 1,000 nM in VK2; requires detailed MoA mapping, resistance-risk assessment, and systemic PK/tox.
Recent updates:
Cancer-immunology literature in 2024–2025 continues to connect KRAS inhibition with enhanced Type I IFN/STING signaling—supports plausibility of antiviral host-direction.
Field momentum toward combination host- and virus-directed therapies (e.g., parallel novel antivirals in Ph2) may define future positioning of KRAS-pathway modulators.

Name: Kanona cell-free DNA based non-invasive prenatal testing
Developers: Kanona, Inc; Kanona, Inc
Indication: Prediction of early-onset preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Analyzes circulating placental cell-free DNA patterns to detect placental dysfunction and risk of hypertensive pregnancy disorders.
Key features and challenges:
Kanona, Inc is working on a cell-free DNA diagnostic to predict early-onset preeclampsia. The approach uses sequencing data from non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) for aneuploidy screening to detect placenta-specific epigenetic signatures. In testing over 1,000 samples, early research showed that nucleosome positioning patterns can be reliably inferred from existing sequencing data, and machine learning models can help predict early-onset PE. With NIH funding, the company plans to fine-tune technical and analytical factors, validate results in a new cohort, and improve the method for PE risk classification using placental samples and deeper first-trimester cfDNA sequencing. This will be followed by phase II external validation, with the ultimate aim of offering an easy-to-perform PE prediction test alongside NIPT without extra blood draws or specialized lab processes ((https://reporter.nih.gov/search/TZHvVSSb8EGZtoD27HqplA/project-details/10822733))
(https://reporter.nih.gov/search/TZHvVSSb8EGZtoD27HqplA/project-details/10822733)

Name: Ketoximines
Developers: Erasmus University (including Erasmus University Medical Center)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Mycetoma.
Mechanism of action: Unknown.
Key features and challenges:
The open-source drug discovery program for mycetoma, MycetOS, screened a series of compounds for in vitro activity against M. mycetomatis.
Ketoximines were one series selected for further testing, and were subsequently identified as a novel lead compound given that they were highly active against M. mycetomatis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9516133/).

Name: Killed whole cell pneumococcal vaccine
Developers: Murdoch Children's Research Institute (MCRI); University of Melbourne (including the Australian Venom Research Unit (AVRU) and Bio21 Institute); Deakin University; University College London (UCL); London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (LSHTM) (including MEIRU); Boston Children's Hospital
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of pneumococci infection.
Target: Pneumococcal surface antigens CbpA, PspA (family 1) and PiaA.
Mechanism of action: Induces antibody response.
Key features and challenges:
The potential of a killed whole cell pneumococcal vaccine (WCV) to reduce existing pneumococcal carriage and mucosal disease when given therapeutically to infant mice colonized with pneumococci was invested. A single dose of WCV was found to reduce pneumococcal carriage density in an antibody-dependent manner. Therapeutic vaccination induced robust immune responses to pneumococcal surface antigens CbpA, PspA (family 1) and PiaA. In a co-infection model of otitis media, a single dose of WCV reduced pneumococcal middle ear infection. Lastly, in a two-dose model, therapeutic administration of WCV reduced nasal shedding of pneumococci. Taken together, the data demonstrates that WCV administered in colonized mice reduced pneumococcal density in the nasopharynx and the middle ear, and decreased shedding. WCVs would be beneficial in low and middle-income settings where pneumococcal carriage in children is high
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0264410X24001312?via%3Dihub).

Name: Kisspeptin
Developers: Syngene International
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: regulates GnRH neurons
Key features and challenges:
Kisspeptin is one of a family of RFamide-related peptides (RFRP) that is now recognized as an essential endogenous regulator of the GnRH neuroendocrine system. Two clusters of neuronal cell bodies that synthesize kisspeptin exist in the hypothalamus.
A 2021 study revealed an unexpected protective role of kisspeptin against Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and insulin resistance in the hypothalamus and has provided a new treatment strategy targeting hypothalamic ER stress and insulin resistance with kisspeptin as a potential therapeutic agent.
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0925443921001757?via%3Dihub).
In 2023, a Phase 1 trial begun that aims to assess response to kisspeptin as well as the baseline patterns of luteinizing hormone (LH) secretion in individuals with polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS). In this study, all subjects will undergo the same interventions. Baseline LH secretion patterns of individuals with PCOS will be compared to their LH secretion patterns while receiving a kisspeptin infusion. The estimated completion in December 2025. 
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05971849).
In a 2023 review of PCOS patients, KP administration, such as KP10 and KP54, increased LH and estradiol (E2) levels but did not significantly alter FSH levels, indicating selective hormonal regulation. KP-based therapies have shown potential in fine-tuning reproductive hormone secretion for better management of ovulatory dysfunction in PCOS. (https://academic.oup.com/edrv/article/45/1/30/7226658)

Name: Kisspeptin - PCOS
Developers: Imperial College London; Xi'nan Gynecological Hospital, China
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Quantifies kisspeptin levels to assess hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis dysregulation associated with ovulatory dysfunction in PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Kisspeptin, a neuropeptide involved in regulating the reproductive endocrine axis, shows promise as a potential diagnostic biomarker for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Studies have found that serum kisspeptin levels are significantly higher in women with PCOS compared to controls, suggesting a strong association with the condition. Kisspeptin plays a crucial role in stimulating gonadotropin-releasing hormone and luteinizing hormone (LH) release, and its elevated levels may be linked to the hormonal imbalances seen in PCOS, such as increased LH secretion. A meta-analysis of multiple studies has shown that kisspeptin can differentiate PCOS patients from healthy women, making it a potential diagnostic tool for the condition, though further research is needed to validate its clinical application. (https://academic.oup.com/edrv/article/45/1/30/7226658)
(https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jog.14767)

The 2025 clinical study aimed to evaluate the levels of serum kisspeptin, NKB, and GaBa in chinese patients with polycystic ovary syndrome (PcOs) and explore their association with hormonal  profiles, as well as the relationship between these levels in PcOs patients and controls. From December 2022 to December 2023, medical records of 60 individuals diagnosed with PcOs 
and 32 healthy subjects were obtained. serum kisspeptin, NKB and GaBa levels were quantified using enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (elisa) kits. to assess the correlation, either Pearson’s or spearman’s analytical method was employed between serum kisspeptin, NKB, and GaBa levels and hormonal profiles. The results showed that serum kisspeptin and  NKB levels were significantly lower in PcOs patients (p﹤.05), while GaBa levels were elevated compared to those in the control group (p﹤.05). in PcOs patients, kisspeptin was notably positive-correlated with lh and lh/Fsh (p﹤.05), but no significant correlation was found between NKB, GaBa, and hormonal profiles. in PcOs, GaBa levels had a strong positive correlation with NKB levels (r = 0.613, p = .000), but this was not observed in the control group. in control patients, kisspeptin levels were positively associated with NKB (r = 0.475, p = .011), strongly negatively correlated with GaBa levels (r = −0.773, p = .000), but these were not observed in the PcOs group. The study concluded that patients with PcOs have dysregulated levels of serum kisspeptin, NKB, and GaBa and that they may have paradoxical effects under physiological and pathological situations (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/09513590.2025.2463533)

Name: KnowNow TB-LAM Lateral Flow Assay Kit
Developers: Qoolabs
Indication: Indicated for triage and screening of individuals with presumptive tuberculosis.
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Key features and challenges: An immunoassay detecting a M. tuberculosis antigen by lateral-flow assay. Run as a rapid strip or cassette test from a sputum sample.

Name: Kynurenine
Developers: Tommy’s, Together for Every Baby
Indication: Treatment of preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: Relaxes blood vessels.
Key features and challenges:
Kynurenine is a small molecule that is formed naturally when an amino acid called tryptophan is broken down in the body. It is a metabolite of the amino acid l-tryptophan used in the production of niacin. Kynurenine is synthesized by the enzyme tryptophan dioxygenase, which is made primarily but not exclusively in the liver, and indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase, which is made in many tissues in response to immune activation. Kynurenine and its further breakdown products carry out diverse biological functions, including dilating blood vessels during inflammation and regulating the immune response. Some cancers increase kynurenine production, which increases tumor growth. It is also indicated in a number of cognitive and psycological disorders. 
Preclinical studies have shown that kynurenine relaxes blood vessels that are taken from women with normal pregnancies and those with pre-eclampsia. Developers are now investigating whether kynurenine or tryptophan could be used to treat other aspects of pre-eclampsia. Tommy's is currently testing whether kynurenine reduces blood pressure in pregnant rats, and if it is safe for their babies. If initial experiments are successful, clinical trials will be souight to test whether kynurenine is an effective treatment for women with pre-eclampsia. (https://www.tommys.org/research/research-topics/pregnancy-complication-research/pre-eclampsia/kynurenine-potential-treatment-women-pre-eclampsia)
Recent updates: 2021, Kynurenine Relaxes Arteries of Normotensive Women and Those With Preeclampsia. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8154175/#:~:text=Kynurenine%20dilates%20systemic%20arteries%20from,treatment%20of%20hypertension%20in%20pregnancy.

Name: L ICON3
Developers: Eikonoklastes Therapeutics
Indication: Indicated for the prevention and treatment of endometriosis
Mechanism of action: Antibody-dependent cell cytotoxicity
Key features and challenges:
L-ICON3 is a third-generation immunoconjugate therapeutic designed to target tissue factor and treat endometriosis, along with cancers such as triple negative breast cancer, ovarian cancer, and malignant melanoma. It combines a factor VIII peptide with the Fc region of an IgG3 antibody to bind specifically to tumor cells, neo-vasculature, and tumor stem cells. This targeted approach aims to activate complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC) and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) to destroy cancer cells while minimizing off-target effects.
As of November 2022, L-ICON3 is in preclinical research for endometriosis, with studies underway in the US. The focus is on evaluating the drug’s efficacy and safety in managing endometriosis by targeting the disease's underlying pathology with its advanced immunoconjugate technology. The development is part of a broader preclinical and early research program that also explores L-ICON3's potential in treating cancers. (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800059690)

Name: L-DBF
Developers: US National Institutes of Health (NIH); PATH (including Meningitis Vaccine Project (MVP) and Malaria Vaccine Initiative (MVI)); University of Kansas; University of Missouri-Columbia (Mizzou); University of Maryland, Baltimore (including CVD)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization for the prevention of bacillary dysentery caused by both Shigella sonnei and Shigella flexneri
Target: Fusion protein of two Type III secretion system antigens, invasion plasmid antigens B (Ipa B) and D (Ipa D), LTA1
Mechanism of action: The IpaB/IpaD subunit vaccine elicits a strong systemic immunity, with the presence of antibody-secreting cells in various compartments, as well as eliciting specific cytokine-secreting cells.
Key features and challenges:
The virulence of Shigella relies upon a type III secretion system (T3SS) which injects host altering effector proteins into targeted intestinal cells. The Shigella T3SS contains two components, invasion plasmid antigen D (IpaD) and invasion plasmid antigen B (IpaB), that have been identified as broadly protective antigens.

Using this approach, PATH and other collaborators have designed a genetically fused IpaD-IpaB protein subunit vaccine (DB fusion), which has demonstrated significant immune responses against Shigella flexneri and S. sonnei in a mice lethal pulmonary challenge as well as offering limited protection against S. dysenteriae.
LTA1 was later genetically fused to DBF to create a monomeric adjuvant-antigen conjugate L-DBF.
Recent updates: Preclinical results published in 2023 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10512073/).

Name: L-tryptophan
Developers: Sam Ratulangi University; Syiah Kuala University (USK)
Indication: Treatment of resistant gonorrhoea infections
Mechanism of action: Modulates bacterial metabolic pathways to disrupt growth and survival of Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
Key features and challenges: In a 2025 in vitro study, Liquid Chromatography–Mass Spectrometry/Mass Spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) was used to identify metabolites from the hemolymph of larvae immunized with non-pathogenic Escherichia coli. Key molecular targets of these metabolites were then pinpointed using network pharmacology and molecular docking. The interaction network showed L-glutamic acid as the most connected compound (25 interactions) among 15 identified amino acid-derived metabolites. Gene interaction analysis highlighted guaA, which encodes guanosine monophosphate synthetase, with the highest interaction degree (27). Binding free energy analysis revealed L-tryptophan had the strongest binding (-5.9 kcal/mol) to the guanosine monophosphate receptor. The study suggests guanosine monophosphate synthetase (GMPS) as a promising target against gonorrhea, with L-tryptophan emerging as a potential lead compound. Targeting GMPS could disrupt vital metabolic pathways in N. gonorrhoeae, offering a fresh approach to fighting antibiotic-resistant strains. Combining metabolite profiling, network pharmacology, and molecular docking, this research presents a robust framework for drug discovery and advances the fight against resistant pathogens (https://scialert.net/abstract/?doi=pjbs.2025.283.294)
Recent updates: In vitro study published in 2025 identified L-trytophan as a lead compound (https://scialert.net/abstract/?doi=pjbs.2025.283.294).

Name: L. Lactis-based intranasal vaccine against Group A Streptococcus
Developers: Pontifical Catholic University of Chile, Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile; The University of Tennessee Health Science Center
Indication: Indicated for the prevention of Group A Streptococcus infection.
Target: Group A Strep M protein (N-terminal fragments)
Mechanism of action: Designed to elicit humoral immune response.
Key features and challenges: Preclinical study: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29704396/. Intranasal live bacterial vaccine comprising 10 strains of Lactococcus lactis, each expressing one group A strep N-terminal fragment of M protein.

Name: L9LS (monoclonal antibody)
Developers: US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease (NIAID); Walter Reed Army Institute of Research (WRAIR) (including Military HIV Research Program); University of California, San Diego (UCSD); Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT); Harvard University
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of malaria caused by P. falciparum
Mechanism of action: Inhibits CSP, preventing  proteolytic processing
Key features and challenges:
Scientists from NIH’s Vaccine Research Center (VRC), developed L9LS, a laboratory-made version of a naturally occurring malaria parasite neutralising antibody called L9, derived from the blood of a volunteer who had received an investigational malaria vaccine. 

The scientists also led a Phase I clinical trial where,L9LS fully protected 15 of 17 (88 percent) participants from malaria infection during the 21-day challenge period. All volunteers in the control group that underwent CHMI, but did not receive L9LS, became infected and were promptly treated without complications. Encouragingly, four of the five participants who received a low, subcutaneous dose of the mAb were protected from malaria (NCT05019729).

The mAb is undergoing Phase II trials in Mali in adults investigating a single subcutaneous dose (NCT05816330) and a Phase I trial infants using intramuscular administration to evaluate the impact of L9LS on subsequent R21/Matrix-MTM vaccine immunogenicity (NCT06461026).

There are two other active trials - active trial in children with severe anaemia or severe malaria to prevent malaria after hospital discharge (PACTR202409607254081) and an ongoing trial of one-time subcutaneous (SC) administration in healthy Kenyan children aged 5 months to 10 years (PACTR202205899641128)
Recent updates: Phase II results- Subcutaneous administration of L9LS to children was protective against P. falciparum infection and clinical malaria over a period of 6 months. https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2312775 and https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05816330?cond=L9LS%20mAb&limit=10&rank=2

Name: LAMP-LFD assay
Developers: Genomix CARL; University of Malaya (including the Tropical Infectious Diseases Research and Education Centre, TIDREC); Acharya Nagarjuna University
Indication: Indicated for the diagnosis of P. falciparum infection and infection with other malaria strains
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: Plasmodium spp. nucleic acid sequence (18S rRNA gene)
Key features and challenges: Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29943720/ and https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/20d0/59239fe140122dbcf2a147619325369fd3dc.pdf

Name: LASER Guardian™
Developers: Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine (LSTM)
Indication: Prevention and control of malaria in children and adults in areas with ongoing malaria transmission where the principal malaria vector(s) exhibit pyrethroid resistance.
Target: Anopheles vector tracking profiles and spatial environments
Key features and challenges: A vector-control approach directed at Anopheles populations, using vector tracking profiles and spatial-environment data to characterise and target mosquito distribution.

Name: LASSARAB + aPHAD‑SEat
Developers: University of Maryland, Baltimore (including CVD)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against LASV infection
Target: Lassa glycoprotein precursor complex (GPC), presented via rabies virus backbone
Mechanism of action: Induces humoral (non-neutralizing IgG) and FCγ‑mediated functions—including ADCC and ADCP—against LASV GPC and rabies virus glycoprotein, providing protection in nonhuman primates via Fc‑receptor pathways
Key features and challenges:
-Dual antigen presentation: LASV GPC plus rabies antigens (potential dual protection).
-Thermostable lyophilized formulation suitable for endemic settings.
-Uses established RABV inactivated vaccine platform with proven safety profile in humans.

Preclinical challenge data published in npj Vaccines (Aug 2024) demonstrated 100% protection in non-human primates following LASV challenge after two-dose immunization; strong humoral responses without detectable neutralizing antibodies were observed, confirming immune-mediated Fc functionality as the protective mechanism
Recent updates: Phase 1 trial (NCT06546709) began in January 2025 and is currently enrolling 55 healthy adult volunteers (ages 18–50) to evaluate the safety, tolerability, and immunogenicity of two-dose LASSARAB + aPHAD‑SEat versus licensed rabies vaccine control.

Name: LASV GPC mRNA-LNP
Developers: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health; University of Texas Medical Branch at Galveston; La Jolla Bioengineering Institute; Academic Medical Center (AMC), Academisch Medisch Centrum Amsterdam
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against LASV infection
Target: Lassa virus glycoprotein complex (GPC; Josiah strain, clade IV)
Mechanism of action: Encodes wild-type LASV GPC, expressed in host cells to elicit antibody and Fc-mediated effector responses. Induces non-neutralizing binding antibodies (linear epitopes GP1 NTD and GP2 T-loop) and Fc-mediated functions (ADNP, ADCP, ADNKA, ADCD) that contribute to protection.
Key features and challenges:
-Two 10 µg IM doses (day 0, 28) fully protected Hartley guinea pigs from lethal LASV Josiah challenge.
-Protection occurred despite weak or absent neutralizing antibody responses in most animals.
-Robust non-neutralizing antibody responses, Fc-mediated effector mechanisms implicated in protection.
-Histopathology: vaccinated animals showed no disease pathology; normal lung/liver tissues compared to controls.
-Limitations: cellular immune responses not characterized; results limited to guinea pig model.
Recent updates:
2023:
-Study highlighted as first demonstration that mRNA vaccines can protect against authentic LASV in guinea pigs without neutralizing antibodies.
-CEPI and partners increasing investment in mRNA-based Lassa vaccines for rapid outbreak response.

Name: LASV GPC nanoparticle
Developers: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID); National Institutes of Health; Frederick National Laboratory for Cancer Research
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against LASV infection
Mechanism of action: Presents stabilized LASV GPC trimers on nanoparticles to elicit robust neutralizing antibody responses, including against apex and cross-protomer epitopes; enhances immunogenicity through multivalent antigen display.
Key features and challenges:
-Immunization of guinea pigs (trimer prime → nanoparticle boosts) induced strong neutralizing responses (ID50 ~500 against LASV Josiah, some breadth to Pinneo strain lineage II).
-In rhesus macaques, both GPC trimer and nanoparticle elicited neutralizing titers (up to 1800 ID50 in trimer group, ~636 ID50 in nanoparticle group).
-Stable under high temperature, pH, osmolarity, and freeze-thaw stress.
-Limitation: Guinea pigs required multiple immunizations (up to 13) for peak titers, impractical for field use. Neutralization breadth against diverse LASV lineages limited.
Recent updates: Patent applications filed by NIH for GPC trimer and GPC trimer nanoparticle vaccine constructs. Broader nanoparticle vaccine approaches (I53-50 NP, Encapsulin NP) being pursued for arenaviruses.

Name: LASV prefusion-stabilized GPC mRNA-LNP
Developers: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health; University of Texas Medical Branch at Galveston; La Jolla Bioengineering Institute; Academic Medical Center (AMC), Academisch Medisch Centrum Amsterdam
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against LASV infection
Mechanism of action: Encodes a structurally stabilized version of LASV GPC (mutations: E329P, R207C, G360C, furin cleavage site substitution) to favor the prefusion conformation. Elicits stronger binding antibody titers against prefusion epitopes and cross-reactive binding to clade II and V LASV GPC. Fc-mediated effector responses (ADNP, ADCP, ADNKA, ADCD) implicated in protection.
Key features and challenges:
-Two 10 µg IM doses (day 0, 28) conferred 100% survival in Hartley guinea pigs challenged with LASV Josiah.
-Prefusion construct induced significantly higher binding antibody titers vs WT GPC construct.
-Some animals developed low-level neutralizing activity (~50% neutralization).
-Broader cross-clade reactivity (Clade II and V) than WT construct, suggesting potential for heterologous protection.
-Protection occurred despite variable neutralizing antibody responses.
-Histopathology: vaccinated animals remained healthy; reduced viral NP staining in organs compared to WT construct.
-Limitations: mechanism of protection still unclear; cellular immunity not studied; guinea pig-only model.
Recent updates:
-Prefusion-stabilized design approach mirrors RSV and SARS-CoV-2 vaccine strategies for improved immunogenicity.
-Notable for potential cross-clade activity, but broader LASV lineage protection needs confirmation in NHP studies.
-Moderna has ongoing arenavirus mRNA vaccine programs.

Name: LASgpc-mRNA-LNP
Developers: Osaka University (including Research Institute for Microbial Diseases (BIKEN) and the School of Pharmaceutical Sciences)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against LASV infection
Mechanism of action: Delivers in vitro–transcribed mRNA encoding LASgpc into host cells, which express the viral glycoprotein and induce antigen-specific CD8⁺ T cell responses (cell-mediated immunity), conferring protection against lethal challenge. Protection observed without detectable neutralizing antibodies.
Key features and challenges:
-Two doses (i.v. or i.m.) protected C57BL/6 and CBA mice from lethal rLCMV/LASgpc2m challenge.
-Strong induction of LASgpc-specific CD8⁺ T cell responses, but minimal or absent antibody responses.
-Protection in highly susceptible CBA mice correlated with CD8⁺ T cell activity.
-No neutralizing activity detected in sera, consistent with limited role of antibodies in acute LASV protection.
-Use of modified nucleoside (5-methoxyuridine) improved antigen expression and reduced innate immune activation.
-Limitations: efficacy demonstrated in surrogate rLCMV/LASgpc mouse models; not yet tested in guinea pigs or NHPs with authentic LASV.
Recent updates:
2023: 
Study showed related LASV mRNA-LNP vaccines (WT and prefusion GPC) protect guinea pigs, supporting translation beyond surrogate models.
-Growing interest in mRNA vaccines as non-live alternatives to live-attenuated LASV vaccines, especially relevant for pregnant women (safer profile vs live vaccines).
-No registered clinical trials yet (as of Sept 2025).

Name: LBA & LAM Combination
Developers: Tecnologico de Monterrey, Campus Querétaro; University of Oslo
Indication: Indicated for the prevention of Mpox virus disease
Mechanism of action: Induces neutralizing antibodies across IMV and EEV
Key features and challenges: High NAb titers after two doses; cross-neutralization; optimization of dose split between components

Name: LBA (B6R-A29L) and LAM (A35R-M1R)
Developers: Universidad de Las Americas
Indication: Prevention of mpox infection
Target: MPXV B6R (extracellular enveloped virion antigen) + A29L (intracellular mature virion antigen)
Mechanism of action: nduces antigen expression in host cells, eliciting humoral and cellular immunity; generates neutralizing antibodies and CD4+/CD8+ T cell responses against IMV and EEV forms.
Key features and challenges:
-Two doses in mice induced strong IgG and T-cell responses.
-Provided full protection against lethal vaccinia challenge.
-Immunogenic but less potent alone compared to quadrivalent formulations.
-Requires lipid nanoparticle delivery; thermostability and scalability yet untested.
Recent updates: Multi-antigen strategies (Rmix4, Rmix6, AR-MPXV5/4a) now surpass bivalents, suggesting cocktails will dominate next-gen mpox vaccines.

Name: LBAAM (B6R–A35R–A29L–M1R)
Developers: Universidad de Las Americas
Indication: Prophylactic prevention of mpox infection
Target: MPXV B6R, A35R (EEV antigens); A29L, M1R (IMV antigens)
Mechanism of action: In vivo expression → broad antibody + T-cell immunity
Key features and challenges:
-Broader neutralizing profile than bivalents.
-Full protection in lethal VACV challenge.
-Stronger cellular immunity; best performing in comparative study.
Recent updates: Quadrivalents (LBAAM, BNT166, Rmix6) emerging as lead mpox mRNA platforms.

Name: LC16m8-based NIV vaccine
Developers: National Institute of Infectious Diseases (NIID)
Indication: Prevention of NiV disease
Target: NiV G glycoprotein (attachment protein) and NiV F glycoprotein (fusion protein)
Mechanism of action: Recombinant LC16m8 replicates in host cells and expresses NiV G and/or F proteins, inducing neutralizing antibodies that block receptor binding and membrane fusion, preventing viral entry.
Key features and challenges:
-LC16m8 is a third-generation smallpox vaccine strain with strong safety record (>100,000 children immunized in Japan without severe adverse events).
-Recombinant LC16m8-G and LC16m8-F both induced neutralizing antibodies in Syrian golden hamsters.
-Antibody titers were higher than those induced by earlier vaccinia-based NiV vaccine vectors (e.g., NYVAC).
-Three rounds of immunization boosted neutralizing antibody titers >16-fold.
-Preexisting immunity to vaccinia virus reduced antibody induction, though simultaneous inoculation with G and F at different sites improved responses.
-Challenge efficacy not yet reported; only immunogenicity evaluated.
-Potential concern: existing vaccinia immunity may limit efficacy in humans.
Recent updates:
Dec 2023 Publication:
-Authors highlight the superior immunogenicity vs. NYVAC vectors and suggest future NiV challenge studies are warranted. No reports of advancement to NHP or clinical stages.

Name: LCMnp-mRNA-LNP
Developers: Osaka University (including Research Institute for Microbial Diseases (BIKEN) and the School of Pharmaceutical Sciences)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against LASV infection
Mechanism of action: Induces strong NP-specific CD8⁺ T cell responses; provides antigen-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) that control infection with rLCMV/LASgpc surrogate viruses in mice.
Key features and challenges:
-Robust induction of NP-specific CD8⁺ T cell immunity in C57BL/6 mice.
-Provided full protection against lethal challenge with recombinant LCMV expressing LASV glycoprotein (rLCMV/LASgpc2m).
-No LASV-specific antibodies detected (as NP is not surface-exposed).
-Efficacy model is based on LCMV surrogate system, not authentic LASV.
-Challenge: NP is not the natural immunodominant antigen in humans for protective immunity, raising translational uncertainty.
Recent updates:
-Published alongside LASgpc-mRNA-LNP as a proof-of-concept for antigen-specific T cell vaccines against LASV.
-Highlights possibility of NP-based mRNA vaccines for arenaviruses, though clinical relevance remains uncertain.

Name: LDE methotrexate
Developers: Faculdade de Medicina da Universidade de São Paulo
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of endometriosis
Target: LDL receptor; dihydrofolate reductase; Tetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase; Thymidylate synthase
Mechanism of action: Antimetabolites; Immunosuppressants; Tetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase inhibitors; Thymidylate synthase inhibitors; dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor; anti-inflammatory
Key features and challenges:
LDE is a nanoemulsion that mimics Low Density Lipoprotein's lipid structure but lacks proteins. It binds to LDL receptors via apolipoprotein E, enabling cellular uptake through LDL-receptor-mediated endocytosis. Various chemotherapeutic agents have been encapsulated in Cholesterol-rich nanoemulsion (LDE) preparations, including LDE–carmustine, LDE–paclitaxel, LDE–etoposide, and LDE–methotrexate (MTX). In the context of endometriosis, particularly for lesions that are challenging to excise surgically, LDE serves as an effective drug carrier. MTX, an antiproliferative and immunosuppressive agent with anti-inflammatory properties, has been utilized in cancer, chronic inflammatory diseases, and ectopic pregnancy. Animal studies have demonstrated that LDE–MTX exhibits significantly lower toxicity and superior pharmacological effects compared to conventional MTX, showing promise in treating conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, heart transplantation, atherosclerosis, myocardial infarction, and Marfan disease.
(https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00404-023-07246-8)
LDE is indicated for sepsis, glioblastoma, and drug delivery. Methotrexate is indicated for juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, Mycosis fungoides, Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, Precursor cell lymphoblastic leukaemia-lymphoma, Psoriasis, Psoriatic arthritis, and Rheumatoid arthritis.
One study assessed the effects of LDE–MTX on endometriosis over 180 days, finding no clinical complaints or significant toxicities, with normal levels for various hormones. Improvements were observed in symptoms like deep dyspareunia, chronic pelvic pain, and dyschezia, though dysmenorrhea showed a non-significant trend for reduction, and bowel lesions remained unchanged. The findings suggest LDE–MTX is a safe and promising treatment for deep infiltrating endometriosis, warranting further investigation with extended treatment periods and placebo-controlled trials. (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00404-023-07246-8; https://ensaiosclinicos.gov.br/rg/RBR-7jx2byj)

Name: LF TRC assay
Developers: RedVault Biosciences
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoea
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: isothermal Target Reporter Construct technology
Key features and challenges:
LF TRC assay is a low-cost, rapid point-of-care diagnostic candidate under development by RedVault Biosciences for the detection of Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. The assay is based on proprietary isothermal Target Reporter Construct (TRC) technology that utilizes bacterial small RNAs (sRNAs) as primers for DNA replication, rather than conventional nucleic acid templates used in standard NAATs.
The platform is designed to incorporate TRC amplification into a lateral flow (LF) test strip format to enable rapid detection. The development strategy includes identification of gonococcal and chlamydial sRNAs in clinical urine samples, optimization of the TRC-based lateral flow assay, and demonstration of feasibility in clinical specimens. Upon successful completion of early-stage development, Phase II plans include integration of sRNA isolation, TRC amplification, and LF detection into a simplified point-of-care device workflow (https://reporter.nih.gov/search/a3l0pi4G9kWatY5WjoxFzw/project-details/10480246).
Key challenges include validation of sRNA stability and consistency in clinical samples, demonstration of sensitivity and specificity comparable to established NAAT platforms, and successful integration of multiple workflow steps into a user-friendly device. Regulatory pathway considerations and scalability for decentralized settings will also require evaluation.
Overall, the LF TRC assay represents a novel isothermal diagnostic approach leveraging sRNA targets for rapid CT/NG detection. Further validation is needed to establish clinical performance and implementation feasibility.

The company will utilize its composite peptide technology that allows conserved antigens from other viruses and bacteria to be quickly added. Preclinical development is underway in the US. Name: LION-MARV vaccine
Developers: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID); National Institutes of Health
Indication: Prevention of Marburg virus infection
Mechanism of action: Replicon RNA derived from alphavirus encodes MARV GP. Upon delivery with LION nanocarrier, RNA self-amplifies intracellularly, producing high antigen levels that stimulate both humoral and cellular immune responses.
Key features and challenges:
-First assessment of repRNA/LION platform for MARV.
-Single intramuscular dose (10 µg) fully protected hamsters against lethal MARV challenge.
-Reduced viremia and tissue viral loads compared to controls; no disease symptoms.
-Induced antigen-specific IgG and Fc effector functions (ADCP, ADCD), though neutralizing titers were weaker than VSV-MARV.
-Advantages: improved safety compared to lipid nanoparticle (LNP) RNA formulations due to localized biodistribution; dose-sparing.
-Limitations: lower neutralization activity than VSV-MARV, protection mainly through non-neutralizing antibody and T-cell responses
Recent updates:
-Builds on repRNA/LION work previously used for SARS-CoV-2 and Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever vaccines.
-Not yet advanced into NHP studies for MARV, which will be the next critical step.

Name: LION‑SUDV vaccine
Developers: National Institutes of Health; National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization to protect against Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) caused by Zaire Ebola virus
Mechanism of action: The replicon RNA encodes SUDV GP and is amplified in host cells, producing abundant antigen for prolonged stimulation. The LION nanocarrier electrostatically adsorbs RNA on its surface, improving stability and reducing systemic inflammation compared with lipid nanoparticles. Induces multifunctional humoral immunity (neutralization, antibody-dependent phagocytosis).
Key features and challenges:
-Single-dose efficacy: 100% survival in guinea pigs after lethal GPA-SUDV challenge when vaccinated 21 days prior.
-Multifunctional antibody response: Neutralizing antibodies plus strong ADCP and ADNP activity.
-Sterile protection: No viremia, no viral loads in spleen/liver, and minimal pathology.
-Compared platforms: Outperformed LION-EBOV (50% survival) and matched VSV-SUDV (positive control).
-Cross-formulation: LION-Combination (EBOV+SUDV GP) also gave full protection.
Recent updates:
April 2025:
-Demonstrated uniform guinea pig protection with a single dose.
-Authors call for NHP studies to confirm efficacy before clinical translation.

Name: LNP-CNPY3
Developers: Army Medical University; Chongqing University of Technology

Key features and challenges:

-In mouse studies, CNPY3-LNP co-administration with ZIKV E protein antigens significantly increased neutralizing antibody titers (FRNT50 > 1:10,000) and germinal center B cell formation.
-Also enhanced Tfh differentiation and long-lived plasma cell induction.
-Strategy could reduce doses needed for effective protection.
-Still exploratory; translational relevance to humans unknown.

Name: Lab-on-a-chip
Developers: Stockholm University; Mount Kenya University
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoea
Health care facility level: IVDs for research use only
Mechanism of action: Microfluidic device automates sample processing and nucleic acid detection to enable rapid, low-volume diagnosis of gonorrhea at the point of care.
Key features and challenges:
The lab-on-a-chip is a compact platform using IFAST and a colorimetric LAMP assay to extract and detect genomic N. gonorrhoeae DNA. It combines the steps of DNA extraction, concentration, purification, amplification, and detection into one handheld device, offering a colorimetric readout for easy, naked-eye interpretation of results.

The platform can detect as few as 500 copies/mL in spiked synthetic urine and showed no cross-reaction when tested with DNA from other common STIs. About the size of a credit card, the device handles DNA extraction and purification without needing power or centrifuges, and the detection process only requires a simple block heater, giving a clear positive or negative result in just an hour. These features make it a promising option for accurate, affordable, and accessible gonorrhea monitoring in resource-limited areas. (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00216-023-04734-3#Fun)

Name: Lactobacillus plantarum 299v
Developers: Lund University; University of Illinois at Chicago
Indication: Indicated to prevent iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Rapid nucleic acid amplification and detection of Mycoplasma genitalium–specific genetic sequences for point-of-care diagnosis.
Key features and challenges:
Lactobacillus plantarum is a widely distributed and versatile lactic acid bacterium. It represents part of the microbiota of many foods and feeds, including dairy, meat, fish, vegetable fermented products (e.g., must, sauerkraut, pickled vegetables, sourdoughs), and silage. It is also a natural inhabitant of the human and animal mucosa (oral cavity, gastrointestinal tract, and vagina, etc.). Research has shown that one-time or short-term dosing of the probiotic Lactobacillus plantarum 299v enhances iron absorption in non-pregnant populations. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/lactobacillus-plantarum and https://classic.clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT03646487)

A study by the University of Illinois at Chicago aimed to answer two questions regarding Lp299v for the prevention of iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy: Is daily oral Lp299v a feasible and tolerable intervention for pregnant individuals to uptake, and does daily oral Lp299v in pregnancy impact maternal and neonatal cord haematological and iron status parameters? Of the 20 enrolled and randomised participants, 58% (7/12) from the Lp299v group and 75% (6/8) from the placebo group were retained. Adherence to supplementation was 72% for Lp299v/placebo and 73% for the prenatal vitamin. A slower decline in maternal haematological and iron parameters across pregnancy was observed in the Lp299v group compared to placebo. (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9966742/)

Name: Lactoferrin - PTL/PTB
Developers: Showa Pharmaceutical University
Indication: Prevention of preterm labour resulting from inflammatory changes (sterile)
Mechanism of action: Decreases pro-inflammatory cytokine levels, such as interleukin (IL)-6
Key features and challenges:
Lactoferrin (Lf) is an approximately 80-kDa iron-binding glycoprotein, belonging to the transferrin family, with well-known bacteriostatic and bactericidal properties. It is produced and stored in specific (secondary) neutrophil granules and released during neutrophil activation and degranulation. Nowadays, Lf has a well-known therapeutic indication for combating iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) in pregnant women.

Studies have investigated the effectiveness of recombinant human lactoferrin (rhLF) on cervical ripening using a rabbit model of PTL with positive results. This suggests that rhLF may have a potential to prevent preterm delivery caused by cervical infection and ripening (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17031657/).

A pilot study results showed a correlation between the oral administration of 200 mg of recombinant human Lf with both the normalization of vaginal flora (vaginal infection disappearance) and the decrease in IL-6 cervicovaginal fluid levels in women at risk of preterm delivery (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21922138/; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22292525/).

A 2019 study found supplementation with vaginal lactoferrin in women with first trimester bacterial vaginosis may be an option to reduce the risk of preterm delivery (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31722591).

A 2022 study in Japan evaluated the effectiveness of lactoferrin in suppressing PTB using various relevant test examples. The findings suggest that LF may play a role in inflammatory protection in pregnant human cervical tissue. The antibacterial and anti-cytokine effects of LF in human-derived mucus-producing cervical cell lines were also demonstrated. It was also clarified that LF suppresses PTB and improves the prognosis of pups in inflammation-induced PTB animal models. Thus, it was identified that LF, a prebiotic contained in breast milk, can be clinically applied to suppress PTB in humans and to prevent PTBs in high-risk pregnancies.
(https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10534-022-00471-9)

Name: Large-Volume RT-LAMP HIV RNA Detection Test
Developers: University of Washington
Indication: HIV RNA detection for point-of-care diagnostics
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Mechanism of action: Isothermal amplification via RT-LAMP
Key features and challenges:
A large-volume reverse transcription loop-mediated isothermal amplification (RT-LAMP) has been developed for the detection of HIV RNA from fingerstick plasma without the need for nucleic acid extraction. This method overcomes challenges of small sample volumes and assay inhibition by performing isothermal amplification at larger reaction volumes, which increases sensitivity and allows for higher sample concentrations. The approach demonstrated successful detection of HIV RNA with a viral load as low as 1200 copies per mL. This test uses a larger volume, reducing sensitivity loss and improving assay performance, while also reducing reagent costs by identifying lower-cost options.
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0003267024003611?via%3Dihub)

Name: Late-onset PE prediction via machine learning
Developers: Yonsei University
Indication: Predict late-onset preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: Health records, including systolic blood pressure, serum blood urea nitrogen and creatinine levels, platelet counts, serum potassium level, white blood cell count, serum calcium level, and urinary protein
Mechanism of action: Analyzes amniotic fluid metabolite signatures to identify fetal–placental metabolic disruption associated with growth restriction.
Key features and challenges:
A 2022 study by Yonsei University aimed to develop models using machine learning to predict late-onset preeclampsia using hospital electronic medical record data. The performance of the machine learning based models and models using conventional statistical methods were also compared. A total of 11,006 pregnant women who received antenatal care were included. Maternal data were retrieved from electronic medical records during the early second trimester to 34 weeks. The prediction outcome was late-onset preeclampsia occurrence after 34 weeks' gestation. Pattern recognition and cluster analysis were used to select the parameters included in the prediction models. Logistic regression, decision tree model, naïve Bayes classification, support vector machine, random forest algorithm, and stochastic gradient boosting method were used to construct the prediction models. C-statistics was used to assess the performance of each model. The overall preeclampsia development rate was 4.7% (474 patients). Systolic blood pressure, serum blood urea nitrogen and creatinine levels, platelet counts, serum potassium level, white blood cell count, serum calcium level, and urinary protein were the most influential variables included in the prediction models. C-statistics for the decision tree model, naïve Bayes classification, support vector machine, random forest algorithm, stochastic gradient boosting method, and logistic regression models were 0.857, 0.776, 0.573, 0.894, 0.924, and 0.806, respectively. The stochastic gradient boosting model had the best prediction performance with an accuracy and false positive rate of 0.973 and 0.009, respectively. The combined use of maternal factors and common antenatal laboratory data of the early second trimester through early third trimester could effectively predict late-onset preeclampsia using machine learning algorithms. Future prospective studies are needed to verify the clinical applicability algorithms.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31442238/)
