Name: Lefamulin - Gonorrhea
Developers: Nabriva Therapeutics
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Target: Peptidyl transferase center (PTC) of the ribosomal bacterial 50S subunit
Mechanism of action: Inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding selectively and specifically to the A- and P-sites of the peptidyl transferase center (PTC) in domain V of the 23s rRNA of the 50S subunit.
Key features and challenges:
Lefamulin is a pleuromutilin antibiotic being evaluated for potential use in the treatment of Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections. Lefamulin inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the peptidyl transferase center of the 50S ribosomal subunit and is currently approved for the treatment of community-acquired bacterial pneumonia.
A 2022 pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) study evaluated lefamulin activity against N. gonorrhoeae, including dose–range and dose–fractionation analyses to characterize bacterial killing dynamics and assess the emergence of resistance (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/pharmacology/articles/10.3389/fphar.2022.1035841/full). 
The study modeled free lefamulin concentrations in human plasma and estimated drug exposure in urogenital tissues using a rat model. Findings supported further investigation of an oral dosing regimen of 600 mg every 12 hours for 5 days for uncomplicated gonorrhea.
Key challenges include the lack of direct human pharmacokinetic data from urogenital infection sites, which limits precise exposure-response modeling for sexually transmitted infections. Clinical studies are required to confirm efficacy, optimal dosing, and resistance suppression in gonococcal infections.
Overall, lefamulin represents a repurposing candidate with established clinical use in other indications and supportive PK/PD data against N. gonorrhoeae. Further clinical evaluation is needed to determine its role in gonorrhea treatment.

Name: Lefamulin - Mycoplasma Genitalium
Developers: Nabriva Therapeutics
Indication: Indicated for treatment of mycoplasma genitalium.
Mechanism of action: Immunomodulators; Peptidyltransferase modulators; Protein 50S ribosomal subunit modulators
Key features and challenges:
Lefamulin (BC 3781) is a semi-synthetic pleuromutilin antibiotic that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis through binding to the 23S rRNA of the 50S ribosomal subunit. It is marketed under the trade name Xenleta for the treatment of community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (CABP) and has demonstrated activity against gram-positive, gram-negative, and atypical pathogens, including drug-resistant strains. Pleuromutilins do not exhibit cross-resistance with other antibiotic classes.
In 2016, in vitro studies reported potent activity of lefamulin against respiratory pathogens, including atypical organisms (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800031605). 
A 2022 clinical study (NCT05111002) investigated lefamulin for treatment of Mycoplasma genitalium infections not cured by prior antibiotics and assessed whether sequential doxycycline administration improved outcomes (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05111002). 
In December 2023, the sponsor terminated this Phase I/II trial after enrolling 12 participants in the United States (https://adis.springer.com/trials/700344566).
Key challenges include limited clinical efficacy data for M. genitalium, early trial termination limiting conclusions on therapeutic benefit, and the need for robust evaluation in multidrug-resistant sexually transmitted infection settings. Additional studies are required to determine optimal dosing strategies and resistance suppression potential.
Overall, lefamulin represents a repurposing candidate with a novel mechanism of action and established clinical approval in other indications. Its role in treating M. genitalium remains to be clarified through further clinical investigation.

Name: Letrozole + Gonadotropin (FSH/hMG)
Developers: The Seventh Affiliated Hospital Sun Yat-sen University
Indication: Treatment of PCOS - Fertility
Target:
Letrozole: aromatase enzyme (CYP19A1)
Gonadotropins (FSH/hMG): FSH and LH receptors
Mechanism of action:
Letrozole inhibits aromatase, reducing circulating estrogen and releasing the hypothalamic–pituitary axis from negative feedback, which increases endogenous FSH and promotes follicular recruitment.
Sequential addition of exogenous low-dose FSH or hMG augments follicular growth and maturation, aiming to achieve higher ovulation and pregnancy rates with controlled mono-follicular or limited multi-follicular development, while keeping the total gonadotropin dose and risk of OHSS as low as possible.
Key features and challenges:
Mazdutide is a once-weekly injectable dual agonist of the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor and glucagon receptor (GLP-1R/GCGR), developed to promote weight loss, improve glycaemic control, and reduce hepatic steatosis in individuals with obesity or metabolic dysfunction. Dual incretin agonists have attracted significant attention because GLP-1 receptor agonists alone have demonstrated meaningful metabolic and endocrine benefits in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), including reductions in body weight, improved insulin resistance, decreased free androgen index (FAI), and improved menstrual cyclicity.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29945711/

Phase 1b and Phase 3 studies in populations with obesity or type 2 diabetes have reported substantial weight reduction (approximately 6–15%, depending on dose and duration), along with improvements in HbA1c, lipid profiles, and hepatic fat content.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36945387/

https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40128614/

These findings contributed to regulatory approval by China’s National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) as the first dual GLP-1/glucagon receptor agonist for chronic weight management.
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11379296/

https://www.innoventbio.com/pipeline/ibi362

Given the high prevalence of obesity, insulin resistance, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) in PCOS, these metabolic effects form the primary rationale for evaluating mazdutide in this population.

A Phase 1/2 open-label trial (NCT06519656) is currently assessing mazdutide in obese women with PCOS. The study evaluates changes in free androgen index (FAI), small antral follicle count (2–9 mm), metabolic parameters, and anthropometric outcomes over 24 weeks, using a dose-escalation schedule (2 mg to 6 mg weekly).
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06519656

Evidence from GLP-1 receptor agonists such as liraglutide and semaglutide supports this approach, with multiple trials demonstrating improvements in insulin sensitivity, reductions in body weight, lower testosterone and FAI, improved menstrual regularity, and reduced hepatic fat in women with PCOS.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34169523/

https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36939890/

By combining GLP-1 and glucagon receptor agonism, mazdutide may offer enhanced metabolic and hepatic benefits compared to GLP-1 agonists alone, potentially translating into greater endocrine improvement in PCOS.

Despite strong mechanistic rationale, PCOS-specific evidence remains limited. Current data consist of a single small Phase 1/2 open-label study without randomized comparative data. Safety considerations typical of GLP-1–based therapies, including gastrointestinal adverse events, rare pancreatitis risk, and the need for long-term safety evaluation in young reproductive-age women, remain relevant.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40128614/

Although mazdutide has received approval for obesity in China, it has no regulatory approval or established off-label use for PCOS. Cost, geographic accessibility, and limited PCOS-specific clinical data may constrain adoption pending results from larger, controlled trials.

Overall, mazdutide represents a high-potential metabolic therapy for PCOS, supported by strong translational rationale and broader GLP-1 agonist evidence. However, its role in PCOS management remains investigational until adequately powered randomized controlled trials evaluate its effects on endocrine, reproductive, and long-term metabolic outcomes.
Recent updates: Phase III trial commenced in 2025 and is expected to complete in 2029 (https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=254549)

Name: Letrozole - Uterine fibroids
Developers: Novartis
Indication: uterine fibroids growth
Mechanism of action: Aromatase inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Letrozole is a non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor primarily approved for the treatment of hormone receptor–positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women. It inhibits the aromatase enzyme responsible for converting androgens to estrogens, resulting in significant reductions in circulating estrogen levels. Due to estrogen suppression, treatment may increase the risk of bone mineral density loss and fractures, necessitating monitoring in long-term use.
The estrogen-lowering mechanism of letrozole has led to investigation of its off-label use in estrogen-dependent conditions, including uterine fibroids. Early clinical studies with small sample sizes reported reductions in menstrual bleeding, pelvic pain, and fibroid volume following letrozole therapy.
(Sources: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0015028207039714
; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0301211513004600)
A clinical trial registered in 2021 aimed to compare the effects of cabergoline, letrozole, and triptorelin on uterine size, bleeding volume, and fibroid size in women with uterine fibroids, reflecting continued comparative evaluation of letrozole within hormonal treatment strategies.
(Source: https://irct.behdasht.gov.ir/trial/60616)
In 2024, an NIH-funded project was initiated to support a full-scale randomized trial investigating the effect of letrozole on fibroid volume reduction and symptom improvement.
(Source: https://reporter.nih.gov/search/cXDRL-si-EOdWa1eoZ70hw/project-details/10912014)
An ongoing randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial that began in 2024 and is expected to conclude in 2027 is evaluating letrozole for the treatment of uterine fibroids. The primary outcome assesses leiomyoma-related symptom severity using the Uterine Fibroid Symptom and Quality of Life (UFS-QOL) Symptom Severity Scale over 12 weeks. Secondary outcomes include changes in quality of life, fibroid and uterine volumes, heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic pain, sexual function, urogenital distress, serum cholesterol and estradiol levels, and hot flash frequency.
(Source: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06143631)
Overall, letrozole is being investigated as a potential medical therapy for uterine fibroids based on its estrogen-suppressive mechanism. While preliminary studies suggest possible reductions in fibroid volume and symptom burden, robust randomized trial data are pending to establish efficacy, safety, and long-term clinical positioning.

Name: Leukemia inhibitory factor
Developers: University of Missouri-Columbia (Mizzou)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Endometriosis.
Target: Transcription factor forkhead box A2 (FOXA2) expression.
Mechanism of action: Unclear - reduces lesion burden in FOXA2-deficiency.
Key features and challenges:
Leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF) is a pleiotropic cytokine involved in endometrial receptivity, epithelial differentiation, and implantation. It is transcriptionally regulated by forkhead box A2 (FOXA2), a transcription factor expressed in uterine glandular epithelium that controls genes related to proliferation, differentiation, fertility, and hormonal responsiveness. Reduced FOXA2 expression has been observed in the eutopic endometrium of women with endometriosis, suggesting disruption of key regulatory pathways.
A recent preclinical study, published in 2025 investigated the functional role of FOXA2 and its downstream signaling in a surgically induced mouse model of endometriosis. Mice received transplantation of either control Rosa26mTmG/+ endometrial tissue or Pgrcre/+Foxa2f/fRosa26mTmG/+ (Foxa2d/dRosa26mTmG/+) tissue into the peritoneal cavity. Endometriosis significantly reduced FOXA2 expression in eutopic endometrium compared with sham controls, alongside decreased expression of its downstream target gene CXCL15. Mice harboring Foxa2-deficient ectopic lesions exhibited significantly increased lesion number and weight compared to controls. Additionally, progesterone receptor expression in the endometrial epithelium was significantly reduced in the Foxa2-deficient group, indicating impaired hormonal responsiveness. 
(https://faseb.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1096/fj.202403182R).
Importantly, administration of leukemia inhibitory factor significantly reduced ectopic lesion formation in Foxa2-deficient endometriosis mice compared with vehicle-treated controls. These findings suggest that FOXA2 loss promotes lesion development and that restoration of LIF signaling may counteract disease progression.
Key challenges include the reliance on genetically engineered mouse models, with no human clinical data currently available. The systemic effects of exogenous LIF administration, including potential immune or reproductive impacts, require careful evaluation. Optimal dosing, delivery method, and safety in reproductive-age women remain undefined. While the FOXA2–LIF axis represents a mechanistically compelling therapeutic target, further translational studies are necessary to determine feasibility and clinical applicability in endometriosis management.

Name: Leuprolide oral
Developers: AbbVie; Enteris BioPharma
Indication: Indicated for the prevention and treatment of endometriosis
Mechanism of action: Gonadotropin releasing hormone stimulants
Key features and challenges:
Oral leuprorelin, developed by Enteris BioPharma using its Peptelligence® delivery platform, is a gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analogue being investigated for the treatment of endometriosis. This oral formulation is intended to replace monthly depot injections with a daily tablet, potentially improving convenience and adherence. Leuprorelin acts by initially stimulating and subsequently downregulating pituitary GnRH receptors, leading to suppression of luteinising hormone (LH), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), and ovarian estradiol production. While injectable and implantable leuprorelin formulations are widely marketed for hormone-dependent cancers and gynecological conditions, the oral formulation is primarily being explored for endometriosis (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800023068).
Early clinical development focused on pharmacokinetics and safety. A completed trial evaluated an optimized Peptelligence oral leuprolide formulation to determine safety and pharmacokinetics across multiple dose regimens, with comparisons to historical subcutaneous and intramuscular depot formulations (https://adis.springer.com/trials/700343779). 
Subsequent Phase I and II studies demonstrated effective suppression of estradiol levels and favourable pharmacodynamic profiles, with data presented in 2022 supporting comparable hormonal suppression to injectable GnRH agonists.
More recently, published data in 2023 reported that at least two dosing regimens of oral leuprolide (Ovarest) achieved profound suppression of gonadal steroids comparable to approved GnRH agonists and antagonists, alongside improvements in pelvic pain symptoms (https://www.fertstert.org/article/S0015-0282(23)01411-5/fulltext). 
Ongoing clinical evaluation includes a study assessing pharmacodynamic profiles and efficacy of different dosing regimens of oral leuprolide tablets (Ovarest) in women with endometriosis started in 2022, focusing on serum hormone levels and pain outcomes (NCT05096065; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05096065).
Key challenges include the need to demonstrate sustained efficacy, long-term safety, and tolerability comparable to established depot formulations, particularly with respect to hypoestrogenic adverse effects and bone mineral density. As an oral peptide formulation, consistent bioavailability and adherence to daily dosing may also influence real-world effectiveness. Regulatory positioning will depend on clear differentiation from existing injectable GnRH agonists and emerging oral GnRH antagonists.
Overall, oral leuprorelin represents a potentially more convenient GnRH agonist option for endometriosis with encouraging early clinical data. However, confirmation of long-term safety, durability of response, and competitive differentiation is required to define its clinical role.

Name: Levetiracetam
Developers: GlaxoSmithKline (GSK); Otsuka Pharmaceutical Co. Ltd; UCB (Union Chimique Belge)
Indication: Prevention of convulsions in severe preeclampsia and imminent eclampsia
Mechanism of action: SV2A protein modulators
Key features and challenges:
Levetiracetam was first approved for use in the United States in 1999 and is structurally and mechanistically unrelated to other anti-epileptic drugs. Levetiracetam possesses a wide therapeutic index and little-to-no potential to produce, or be subject to, pharmacokinetic interactions. It is proposed as being effective in controlling seizures during pregnancy and relatively free of teratogenic side effects, providing it a role in the treatment of preeclamptic/eclamptic associated seizures. However, hard data on its efficacy and teratogenicity during pregnancy are limited.  Recent studies have shown some positive safety results during pregnancy. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29861526/)
Because levetiracetam is relatively easy to administer compared with magnesium sulphate, it has been suggested as an alternative. Currently  because its less efficacious, its use is recommended only when there are true contraindications to magnesium sulphate. However clinical studies are ongoing to assess efficicacy and safety of this drug versus magenesium sulphate for treatment of preeclampsia/eclampsia associated seizures.(https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/Abstract/2020/05001/Contraindications_to_Magnesium_Sulfate_and.443.aspx)
Recent updates:
2023: Levetiracetam is an alternative for patients with myasthenia gravis with eclampsia as magnesium and phenytoin cause increased muscle weakness, which could lead to a myasthenia crisis. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK554392/#:~:text=%5B2%5D%20Levetiracetam%20or%20valproic%20acid,lead%20to%20a%20myasthenia%20crisis.
May 2020: Contraindications to Magnesium Sulfate and Alternative Seizure Prophylaxis for Severe Preeclampsia. (https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/Abstract/2020/05001/Contraindications_to_Magnesium_Sulfate_and.443.aspx)

Name: Levofloxacin
Developers: University of Pretoria (UP)
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Target: Bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV
Mechanism of action: Levofloxacin exerts its antimicrobial activity via the inhibition of bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV.
Key features and challenges:
Levofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV and is used to treat infections caused by susceptible bacteria. Although resistance to fluoroquinolones is common in Neisseria gonorrhoeae, levofloxacin continues to be evaluated in combination strategies to enhance antimicrobial efficacy.
A 2023 study investigated combinations of eight compounds with ceftriaxone, the current first-line treatment for gonorrhea, and reported an additive effect between ceftriaxone and levofloxacin against N. gonorrhoeae strains (https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/aac.00348-23). 
Levofloxacin demonstrated bactericidal activity and showed greater activity than ciprofloxacin against several organisms, supporting its potential role in combination therapy approaches.
Key challenges include widespread fluoroquinolone resistance among gonococcal strains, the risk of rapid resistance selection, and limited utility in regions with high prevalence of gyrA-mediated resistance. Molecular resistance testing would be required to guide appropriate clinical use.
Overall, levofloxacin represents a potential adjunct or combination therapy candidate against N. gonorrhoeae, particularly where susceptibility is confirmed. Its established clinical use supports feasibility, though resistance patterns significantly limit standalone application.

Name: Linagliptin - Uterine fibroids
Developers: Boehringer Ingelheim (including Merial); Eli Lilly and Company
Indication: uterine fibroid fibrotic process and collagen deposition
Mechanism of action: Dipeptidyl peptidase 4 inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Linagliptin is an orally administered dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4/CD26) inhibitor developed by Boehringer Ingelheim and Eli Lilly for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus. It inhibits DPP-4 activity and is primarily used to improve glycaemic control through incretin pathway modulation.
Uterine fibroids (UF) are characterized by excessive extracellular matrix deposition and fibrosis. Fibroblast activation protein-α (FAP) is implicated as a pro-fibrotic enzyme contributing to collagen remodeling and fibroid-associated fibrotic architecture. Because DPP-4 and FAP belong to the same dipeptidyl peptidase family and share structural similarity in catalytic domains, DPP-4 inhibitor ligands have been hypothesized to also bind FAP and potentially attenuate fibrosis-related pathways relevant to UF.
A 2024 discovery study combined in-silico screening and in-vivo validation to assess DPP-4 inhibitors as potential FAP inhibitors. Using STITCH database mining and molecular docking, linagliptin demonstrated the strongest predicted binding affinity to FAP among evaluated DPP-4 inhibitors (dock score −8.562 kcal/mol). In a rat model of estrogen- and progesterone-induced uterine fibrosis, linagliptin reduced fibrotic progression and decreased expression of transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β), a central mediator of collagen synthesis and fibrosis. Histological assessment using Masson trichrome staining confirmed reduced collagen deposition in the uterus, supporting an anti-fibrotic effect consistent with FAP/TGF-β pathway modulation.
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0006291X24001463?via%3Dihub
Despite promising mechanistic rationale and animal data, evidence remains preclinical with no uterine fibroid–specific human trials evaluating linagliptin for fibroid size reduction or symptom improvement. Key translation gaps include confirmation of FAP inhibition in human leiomyoma tissue, dose requirements relative to standard diabetes dosing, long-term reproductive safety, and clinical efficacy endpoints (bleeding, pain, fertility outcomes).
Linagliptin represents a repurposing candidate for uterine fibroids based on antifibrotic activity demonstrated in a hormone-induced uterine fibrosis model and strong in-silico binding to FAP. However, its role in UF management remains investigational pending further mechanistic validation and controlled clinical studies.

Name: Linear Human Cathelicidin (LL-37)
Developers: Suez Canal university
Indication: Treatment or prevention of RVFV infection in humans
Target: RVFV viral envelope (membrane disruption); immunomodulatory effects on host cells
Mechanism of action: Direct virucidal activity via disruption of viral envelope; reduces viral entry and replication. Also triggers host immune modulation (cytokine induction, RIG-I pathway activation) to limit viral spread.
Key features and challenges:
-At 5 µg/ml, reduced RVFV titers by ~2 log within 24h (TCID50 assay).
-Pre-incubation with virus reduced infectivity by ~36–48%, while post-infection treatment reduced viral RNA and protein expression by up to 75%.
-Protective effect seen when Vero cells pre-treated, maintaining 47% protection for up to 4h.
-Non-toxic up to 50 µg/ml in vitro.
-Challenges: short half-life, potential systemic toxicity, requires optimized delivery methods (e.g., nanoparticles, derivatives).
Recent updates:
-LL-37 and derivatives are under active exploration as antivirals against other arboviruses (e.g., Dengue, VEEV) and respiratory viruses (RSV, Influenza A, SARS-CoV-2), showing broad-spectrum potential.
-Prior reports also explored LL-37 derivatives against RVFV MP-12, confirming dose-dependent antiviral effects.
-As of Sept 2025, no in vivo RVFV LL-37 trials have been published, but work on antimicrobial peptides as next-generation antivirals is accelerating, with nanoparticle formulations and peptide analogs being tested in animal models for related viruses.

Name: Linear antimicrobial peptide 8A
Developers: University of Cologne; University of Florence, Università degli Studi di Firenze
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: A triazole bridge at different positions produced a helical structure, and it is proposed that this modification would improve (i) proteolytic stability and (ii) membrane activity.
Key features and challenges:
Linear antimicrobial peptide 8A is a rationally designed antimicrobial peptide derived from the cell-penetrating peptide sC18*, developed to enhance antibacterial potency and structural stability. The peptide incorporates a triazole bridge to promote a preformed helical conformation, intended to improve proteolytic stability and membrane-disruptive activity.
A 2024 study reported that peptides 8A and 8B demonstrated strong antimicrobial activity against multiple bacterial species, including pathogenic Neisseria gonorrhoeae and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsinfecdis.4c00078). 
Peptide 8A exhibited favorable tolerability in human fibroblast and blood cell assays, supporting further investigation as a potential antimicrobial candidate.
Key challenges include ensuring in vivo stability, optimizing pharmacokinetic properties, and demonstrating efficacy in animal infection models. Manufacturing scalability and potential resistance development also require evaluation prior to clinical advancement.
Overall, linear antimicrobial peptide 8A represents a novel peptide-based therapeutic candidate with demonstrated in vitro activity against N. gonorrhoeae. Further preclinical validation is needed to determine its translational potential.

Name: Linear antimicrobial peptide 8B
Developers: University of Cologne; University of Florence, Università degli Studi di Firenze
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: A triazole bridge at different positions produced a helical structure, and it is proposed that this modification would improve (i) proteolytic stability and (ii) membrane activity.
Key features and challenges:
Linear antimicrobial peptide 8B is a rationally designed antimicrobial peptide derived from the cell-penetrating peptide sC18*, developed to enhance antibacterial activity and structural stability. The peptide incorporates a triazole bridge to promote a preformed helical structure, with the aim of improving proteolytic stability and membrane-disruptive activity.
A 2024 study reported that peptide variants 8A and 8B demonstrated strong antimicrobial activity against multiple bacterial species, including pathogenic Neisseria gonorrhoeae and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsinfecdis.4c00078). 
Peptide 8B showed favorable tolerability in human fibroblast and blood cell assays, suggesting a promising therapeutic index and supporting further preclinical evaluation.
Key challenges include potential peptide degradation in vivo, scalability and manufacturing complexity, and the need to confirm efficacy and safety in animal infection models. Long-term resistance potential and pharmacokinetic properties also require further investigation.
Overall, linear antimicrobial peptide 8B represents a novel peptide-based antimicrobial candidate with demonstrated in vitro activity against N. gonorrhoeae. Further preclinical studies are required to assess its translational potential.

Name: Linzagolix - PCOS
Developers: Kissei Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd.
Indication: Improving PCOS associated insulin resistance, ovarian dysfunction, and hormone regulation
Target: GnRH receptors in the pituitary gland.
Mechanism of action: GnRH Antagonist
Key features and challenges:
Linzagolix choline is an oral gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) receptor antagonist developed by Kissei Pharmaceutical, Obseva, and Bio Genuine. By competitively blocking the GnRH receptor in the pituitary, it suppresses luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) secretion, leading to a dose-dependent reduction in estradiol levels. Linzagolix is designed to maintain estradiol within a low-normal therapeutic window (approximately 20–60 pg/mL), thereby reducing symptoms of estrogen-dependent conditions while minimising hypoestrogenic adverse effects such as bone mineral density loss. It is approved in the European Union, the United Kingdom, and other regions for the treatment of uterine fibroids and is under regulatory review in additional markets.
https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800032710
Given that polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is characterised by dysregulation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian (HPO) axis, altered gonadotropin secretion, and hyperandrogenism, modulation of GnRH signalling represents a potential therapeutic strategy. By suppressing gonadotropin secretion, linzagolix may influence ovarian steroidogenesis and follicular dynamics.
A 2023 preclinical study conducted by Kissei Pharmaceuticals evaluated linzagolix in models of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and PCOS. In normal and BPH-model dogs, linzagolix significantly reduced serum LH and testosterone levels, suppressed prostate weight, and maintained testosterone within a therapeutically acceptable range. In a letrozole-induced rat model of PCOS, linzagolix improved insulin resistance and ovarian dysfunction and reduced follicle-stimulating hormone levels, without significantly altering LH or testosterone concentrations. These findings suggest potential benefits in modulating reproductive and metabolic dysfunction associated with GnRH-related disorders.
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1440-1681.13817
Despite its established role in estrogen-dependent gynecological conditions, evidence supporting linzagolix in PCOS remains limited to preclinical studies. No published randomized controlled trials have evaluated its safety or efficacy in women with PCOS. Potential risks associated with GnRH antagonists, including hypoestrogenic symptoms and bone mineral density loss with prolonged use, remain relevant considerations.
Linzagolix represents a mechanistically plausible but investigational therapeutic candidate for PCOS. While preclinical findings indicate potential endocrine and metabolic benefits, clinical validation in adequately powered human trials is required before its role in PCOS management can be determined.

Name: Lipid biomarkers
Developers: Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine; Lleida University, Spain; Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Measures lipid fractions to detect dyslipidemia and metabolic risk associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Lipid biomarkers are molecules in biological samples that reflect changes in lipid metabolism and can indicate disease presence or progression. In PCOS, lipid biomarkers, such as altered levels of triglycerides, cholesterol, and free fatty acids, are associated with metabolic issues like insulin resistance and inflammation. .

 A 2022 study analysing follicular fluid found elevated levels of ceramides and free fatty acids, alongside reduced lysophosphatidylglycerol in women with PCOS, suggesting these lipids as potential diagnostic markers. (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/endocrinology/articles/10.3389/fendo.2022.960274/full)

Another study highlighted a distinct lipidomic signature in PCOS patients, indicating alterations in glycerolipid, glycerophospholipid, and sphingolipid metabolism, which could serve as diagnostic indicators. 
(https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5796992/)

Additionally, integrated lipid metabolomics and proteomics analyses have revealed lipid metabolites and proteins closely associated with follicle quality in PCOS, offering potential biomarkers for diagnosis. 
(https://translational-medicine.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12967-024-05167-x)

Name: Longitudinal preeclampsia risk prediction models
Developers: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai (ISMMS); Harvard Medical School
Indication: Preeclampsia Risk Prediction
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: Sociodemographic, clinical diagnoses, family history, laboratory, and vital signs data
Mechanism of action: Comprehensive longitudinal predictive tool based on routine clinical data
Key features and challenges:
Longitudinal preeclampsia risk prediction models use machine learning (ML) and deep learning techniques applied to routinely collected electronic medical record (EMR) data to estimate an individual’s evolving risk of developing preeclampsia (PE) throughout pregnancy. Unlike traditional first-trimester screening approaches that rely on static risk factors, longitudinal models incorporate dynamic clinical variables—such as laboratory results, vital signs, diagnoses, and sociodemographic characteristics—captured at multiple gestational time points.

A 2022 study from the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai developed a digital phenotyping algorithm to curate 108,557 pregnancies from EMRs across their health system, standardizing pregnancy trajectories across hospital sites (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35668134/
). Using machine learning methods on a training dataset of 60,879 cases, the investigators developed predictive models for preeclampsia across antepartum, intrapartum, and postpartum periods. The models demonstrated strong performance, with area under the curve (AUC) values of 0.92 at 37 weeks’ gestation, 0.82 intrapartum, and 0.89 postpartum, and showed consistent accuracy in independent validation cohorts.
A 2023 study from Harvard Medical School further advanced longitudinal modeling by integrating sociodemographic data, clinical diagnoses, family history, laboratory results, and vital signs across multiple gestational windows (14, 20, 24, 28, 32, 36, and 39 weeks) in a retrospective cohort (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37645797/). 
The model identified both established and novel associations—such as links between red blood cell count dynamics and PE risk—and was able to detect 48.6% more at-risk patients compared with standard first-trimester risk stratification methods. The approach enables continuous risk recalibration throughout pregnancy rather than reliance on a single early screening point.
Key challenges include dependence on high-quality, structured EMR data, which may limit applicability in low-resource settings with fragmented data systems. External validation across diverse populations and healthcare infrastructures is necessary to ensure generalizability. Algorithm transparency, interpretability, and integration into clinical workflows remain important considerations. Additionally, ethical concerns related to bias, data privacy, and equitable access must be addressed. While longitudinal ML-based models demonstrate strong predictive performance, prospective implementation studies are needed to determine their real-world impact on maternal and neonatal outcomes.

Name: Lotilaner

Key features and challenges:
Lotilaner, though primarily developed for parasitic and dermatological conditions, is being explored for its potential applications in malaria control. Its innovative properties could contribute to addressing challenges in malaria eradication efforts.  Lotilaner, have shown promise in disrupting the lifecycle of mosquito vectors by targeting their neurological systems. This could reduce malaria transmission by impairing the mosquito's ability to bite or reproduce. Lotilaner’s demonstrated safety and selectivity in humans make it a strong candidate for further evaluation in malaria control strategies, especially in endemic regions where safety is paramount due to frequent exposure. Further research is needed to validate Lotilaner’s efficacy against malaria, focusing on:

1. In vivo models assessing its direct impact on Plasmodium.
2. Synergistic effects when used alongside antimalarial drugs or vector control agents.
Recent updates:
As of November 2022, phase I development of lotilaner (TP 05) for the prevention of malaria is ongoing in the US (Tarsus Pharmaceutical pipeline, November 2022).

Name: Low-cost AI ultrasound tool - PE
Developers: Emory University
Indication: Diagnosis of preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Integrated microfluidic platform concentrates and amplifies pathogen nucleic acids to enable rapid molecular detection of gonorrhea.
Key features and challenges: Researchers at Emory University have gathered point-of-care Doppler ultrasound recordings and created a preliminary machine learning method to detect intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), maternal hypertension, and preeclampsia. A follow-up study, running from September 2022 to August 2027, aims to validate these findings in two large, underserved pregnancy groups in rural Guatemala and urban Georgia. The main idea is that their low-cost AI will be just as effective at detecting these conditions as the expensive, standard diagnostic methods. The study’s goals are: 1) to validate the ultrasound-based IUGR detection algorithm against the standard two-dimensional fetal imaging; 2) to validate the maternal hypertension and preeclampsia algorithms against top-tier blood pressure devices and clinical risk prediction tools; and 3) to roll out real-time versions of these validated algorithms on an edge-computing system for field testing. If successful, this project will deliver a new screening tool for maternal hypertension, preeclampsia, and IUGR using point-of-care Doppler linked to an affordable, AI-powered edge-computing system, ideal for low-resource settings (https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/10567313)

Name: Lower placental edge thickness
Developers: Ain Shams University; Medical Teaching Institute Lady Reading Hospital, Pakistan
Indication: Prediciton of risk of preterm birth in women with placenta previa accreta
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Ultrasound measurement of placental edge thickness to identify abnormal placentation associated with increased preterm delivery risk.
Key features and challenges:
In pregnant women with placenta previa accreta, the lower placental edge thickness measured by ultrasound may correlate with gestational age at delivery and predict emergency preterm cesarean delivery. Thick lower placental edge is thought to be responsible for emergency preterm birth.

A study published in 2022 found a linear inverse relationship of placental edge thickness with gestational at delivery in pregnancies with placenta previa accreta. In this descriptive case series study, a significant negative correlation between the placental edge thickness and gestational age at delivery was seen (r= -0.566, P= 0.001) and thick placental edge of > 2cm had significant association with birth before 37 weeks(P=0.023). 
(https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9247772/)

A prospective cohort study is currently underway at Ain Shams University also examining the relation of lower placental edge thickness to gestational age at delivery in placenta accreta.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06248385)

Developers: LumiraDx UK Limited

Key features and challenges: LuimraDx is developing a rapid TB test with support from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation that is run on the portable LumiraDx instrument, a small, battery operated molecular and immunoassay instrument with the potential to be used for point-of-care TB testing at the community level. More than 5,000 LumiraDx platforms are already in use in African countries, primarily for COVID-19 testing. Name: Lupeol
Developers: Ardakan University
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: Down-regulation of NF-kappaB
Key features and challenges:
Lupeol is a naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid found in various fruits, vegetables, lupin seeds, fig latex, and rubber plants. Structurally derived from lupane, it contains a hydroxyl group at the 3β position and exhibits anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and potential anti-androgenic properties. As a bioactive plant metabolite, lupeol has been investigated for its effects on metabolic and inflammatory disorders.
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is characterised by hyperandrogenism, elevated luteinizing hormone (LH), oxidative stress, ovarian fibrosis, and impaired folliculogenesis. Compounds with anti-androgenic and antioxidant activity have therefore been explored as potential therapeutic candidates to address both structural and functional ovarian abnormalities.
A 2024 preclinical study evaluated lupeol in a mouse model of experimentally induced PCOS. Treatment with lupeol significantly reduced elevated LH and testosterone levels compared with untreated PCOS controls. Similar to flutamide, a known anti-androgen comparator, lupeol reduced ovarian fibrosis and decreased the number of atretic follicles. Lupeol also attenuated PCOS-associated lipid peroxidation and protein oxidation in serum and ovarian tissue, indicating antioxidant effects. Additionally, lupeol improved fertility outcomes by increasing pregnancy rates and reducing the proportion of arrested embryos.
https://ijbms.mums.ac.ir/article_24247.html
These findings suggest that lupeol may exert dual anti-androgenic and antioxidant effects in PCOS models, potentially improving both ovarian structure and reproductive function. However, evidence remains limited to animal studies, and no human clinical trials have evaluated its safety, pharmacokinetics, or endocrine effects in women with PCOS.
Lupeol represents an investigational phytochemical candidate for PCOS with promising preclinical data targeting hyperandrogenism and oxidative stress. Clinical validation is required to determine translational relevance, optimal dosing, and long-term safety in reproductive-age populations.

Name: Lycorine

Mechanism of action: Inhibits ZIKV replication in vitro and in vivo; suppresses viral RNA synthesis and protein translation.
Key features and challenges:

-Toxicity and off-target host effects are concerns; therapeutic window not well established.

Name: Lyophilized mRNA-LNP (Lyo-Mpox-C5)
Developers: Yither Biotech
Indication: prevention of mpox infection
Target: MPXV A27, L1 (IMV antigens) and A33, B5 (EV antigens)
Mechanism of action: Encoded viral proteins expressed in host cells induce broad humoral and cellular immune responses against both IMV and EV forms of MPXV. Lyophilization improves stability and accessibility by eliminating ultra-cold storage requirements.
Key features and challenges:
-Stable for ≥12 months at 4°C and for ≥8 hours after reconstitution at ambient temperature.
-Comparable immunogenicity and biological activity to freshly prepared liquid mRNA-LNP formulations.
-Induces strong antigen-specific IgG, neutralizing antibodies against VACV, and IFN-γ+ T-cell responses in mice.
-Scalable lyophilization process validated up to 2000 vials/batch, with consistent particle size, encapsulation efficiency, and mRNA integrity.
-Major advantage: avoids costly ultra-cold chain requirements; more practical for LMIC deployment.
-Challenges: stability at higher temperatures (≥25°C) shows gradual decline in mRNA integrity; structural “bleb-like” morphology post-reconstitution may impact performance and needs further study.
Recent updates:
-Lyophilization of mRNA-LNP is being pursued by multiple groups for mpox, COVID-19, and other pathogens, with proof-of-concept successes in SARS-CoV-2 mRNA-LNP vaccines stored at 25°C for up to 6 months.
-2023 - 2024 Publications show that progress is made in multivalent mpox mRNA candidates; lyophilization adds a critical global health access dimension by bypassing cold chain bottlenecks.
-Potential for tech-transfer to LMIC manufacturing due to robustness of freeze-drying scale-up.

Name: M1-silencing therapeutic siRNA
Developers: Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals Inc; University of Texas Medical Branch at Galveston
Indication: Prevention and treatment of influenza A, caused by H5N1
Target: Influenza A M1 gene (matrix protein 1; highly conserved across all influenza A viruses)
Mechanism of action: siRNA binds to viral M1 mRNA, inducing RNA interference (RNAi) and degradation of viral transcripts, blocking production of essential viral matrix protein, reducing replication and spread.
Key features and challenges:
-First-in-class therapeutic siRNA targeting influenza A.
-Designed to overcome resistance limitations of current antivirals (NA inhibitors, polymerase inhibitors).
-Lung-targeted delivery (intranasal/inhaled) provides direct action at site of infection.
-Showed robust antiviral activity against lethal H5N1 in preclinical models.
-Challenges: siRNA stability, delivery efficiency in humans, cost of production, regulatory hurdles for inhaled RNA drugs.
Recent updates:
2025:
-Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals is expanding its RNAi pipeline; as of 2025, no clinical trial listing for influenza siRNA, but related programs are advancing inhaled siRNA therapies in other respiratory diseases (e.g., cystic fibrosis, COPD), supporting potential platform translation.
-This siRNA remains in preclinical status but is cited in pandemic preparedness discussions for RNA-based antivirals.

Name: M1H11
Developers: Southern University at Shreveport
Indication: Treatment of mpox infection (therapeutic candidate).
Target: MPXV M1R (surface protein of intracellular mature virion, IMV; homolog of VACV L1R)
Mechanism of action: Binds to conformational epitopes on M1R (α1, α2, α4 helices). Blocks viral entry and fusion, neutralizing virus before infection of host cells.
Key features and challenges:
-Strong neutralizing activity against both VACV (Tian Tan) and authentic MPXV in vitro.
-In vivo, reduced viral lung load, weight loss, and pathology in mouse challenge models.
-Superior protection when combined with M3B2 (cocktail M1H11+M3B2 yielded best outcome).
-Mouse-origin IgG2a – will require humanization/chimerization for therapeutic use.
-Likely recognizes discontinuous conformational epitope (epitope mapping identified D66 as key residue on M1R).
Recent updates:
-Neutralizing mAbs to MPXV IMV proteins (M1R/L1R family) are increasingly being explored as countermeasures due to emerging tecovirimat resistance reports (2022–2023, US/Europe).
-The cocktail approach (M1R + another mAb) consistently yields higher protective efficacy vs. monotherapy.
-Humanization and bispecific engineering (Bis-M1M3) already under way in same group, with improved efficacy and half-life in rhesus macaques.

Name: M3B2
Developers: Southern University at Shreveport
Indication: Treatment of mpox infection (therapeutic candidate).
Target: MPXV M1R (IMV surface protein; VACV L1R homolog)
Mechanism of action: Binds to conformational epitopes on M1R (β1, β3, α5 helices + α4-β3 linker). Neutralizes IMV by preventing cell entry and fusion.
Key features and challenges:
-Strong neutralization of MPXV and VACV in vitro; binding affinity high in SPR.
-Alone, therapeutic efficacy in mice significant (reduces lung viral titers, mitigates pathology).
-Synergistic with M1H11 in cocktails – this pair provided superior protection compared to single mAbs.
-Epitope mapping indicates recognition of discontinuous conformational regions (not affected by alanine substitutions in predicted epitopes).
Recent updates:
-In tandem with M1H11, forms the basis of engineered bispecific antibody Bis-M1M3, which showed superior in vivo efficacy and extended half-life (~5.1 days in rhesus macaques).
-Supports the rationale that targeting IMV proteins is essential for protective mAb therapies, complementing EEV-targeted antibodies like B7C9.
-Other labs are also advancing anti-L1R and anti-A27 mAbs for broader coverage.

Name: MARV DNA/LAMP-1
Developers: Fourth Military Medical University China; Shaanxi Provincial Center for Disease Control and Prevention
Indication: Prevention of Marburg hemorrhagic fever (MHF)
Target: Marburg virus glycoprotein (GP; GenBank ID: MF939097.1)
Mechanism of action: Codon-optimized MARV GP gene is fused with LAMP1, directing antigen to lysosomes and endosomes. This enhances MHC class II presentation and boosts CD4+ T-cell responses, thereby improving both humoral and cellular immunity, leading to enhanced long-term protective responses.
Key features and challenges:
-Enhanced immunogenicity: Mice immunized with LAMP-GP DNA vaccine had significantly higher MARV GP-specific antibody titers compared to standard GP DNA vaccine.
-Cross-neutralization: Sera from vaccinated mice showed cross-neutralizing activity against EBOV pseudovirus.
-Cellular immunity: Increased secretion of IFN-γ, IL-2, and IL-4 from both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells; higher frequencies of GP-specific memory T cells.
-Transcriptome analysis: Enrichment of antigen processing and presentation-related pathways, especially MHC class II.
-Safety: Preliminary histopathology (H&E staining) and behavioral assessment showed no adverse effects in mice.
Recent updates:
-Builds on prior work using LAMP-targeting in DNA vaccines for EBOV and hantaviruses.
-This is the first application of LAMP-targeting in a MARV DNA vaccine.
-The strategy aligns with broader DNA vaccine optimization efforts aimed at enhancing antigen processing.
-Next steps suggested: non-human primate studies and viral challenge validation.

Name: MARV MEV
Developers: Al-Muthanna University; University of Al-Qadisiyah
Indication: prevention of Marburg virus infection
Target: Multiple MARV structural proteins (glycoprotein precursor, VP35, VP40)
Mechanism of action: The construct integrates five CTL, three HTL, and eight B-cell epitopes derived from MARV GP, VP35, and VP40 proteins, fused with linkers and an adjuvant (β-defensin, a TLR3 agonist). Predicted to elicit both humoral and cellular immune responses by activating B cells, CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
Key features and challenges:
-Designed using immunoinformatics; epitopes selected for global population coverage (~93.9%).
-Construct length: 454 amino acids, MW ~49.7 kDa.
-Predicted to be antigenic (VaxiJen: 0.57), non-allergenic, thermally stable (aliphatic index 73.3), soluble (hydrophilic GRAVY score −0.56).
-Structural quality validated in silico (Ramachandran plot: 95.58% residues in favored regions; ERRAT score: 87.4).
-Docking and molecular dynamics simulations indicate stable interaction with TLR3, with strong binding free energy (ΔGbinding ≈ −3403.8 kJ/mol).
-Immune simulation suggests robust antibody responses (IgM, IgG1/IgG2), cytokine release (IFN-γ, IL-2), and memory B/T cell formation.
Recent updates:
-Follows a growing trend in immunoinformatics-driven vaccine design for filoviruses (e.g., Ebola, MARV, Sudan virus).
-Similar MARV MEVs targeting GP and VP proteins have been proposed in other recent in silico studies (Heliyon 2023; ACS Omega 2021). None have advanced to in vitro testing yet.
-Highlights continuing research interest in computational vaccine design, though translation into experimental validation remains a challenge.

Name: MARV multi-epitope vaccine
Developers: Kalasalingam Academy of Research and Education
Indication: Prevention of Marburg virus infection
Target: Marburg virus structural proteins (VP24, VP35, GP, NP)
Mechanism of action: Constructed by selecting conserved and immunogenic CTL, HTL, and B-cell epitopes from MARV proteins (VP24, VP35, GP, NP). Epitopes were linked with suitable spacers and fused to an adjuvant (human β-defensin-3) to enhance antigenicity. Designed to elicit humoral, cytotoxic T-cell, and helper T-cell responses.
Key features and challenges:
-Epitope selection ensured broad global population coverage (>95%).
-Designed construct: ~480 amino acids, stable and soluble with predicted antigenicity score >0.6 (VaxiJen).
-Molecular docking showed strong binding to immune receptors (HLA molecules and TLR4).
-Immune simulation predicted robust antibody production (IgM, IgG subclasses) and T-cell cytokine responses (IFN-γ, IL-2, IL-4).
-Codon optimization and in silico cloning into pET28a(+) vector suggested good expression feasibility in E. coli.
-Limitations: entirely in silico; no in vitro or in vivo validation yet. Translation into real vaccine development remains uncertain.
Recent updates:
-Fits into a trend of computational vaccine designs against MARV (several published 2022–2024).
-Provides candidate epitopes that could be experimentally validated and tested in vitro/in vivo.

Name: MARV16
Developers: University of Washington (including Harborview Medical Center); Humabs BioMed SA
Indication: Treatment of acute Marburg virus infection
Target: Marburg virus glycoprotein (GP; receptor-binding domain, RBD)
Mechanism of action: Neutralizing antibody binds to the GP receptor-binding site, blocking MARV attachment/entry and mediating Fc-effector functions (ADCC, phagocytosis) for clearance of infected cells.
Key features and challenges:
-MARV16 isolated from a human survivor of Marburg infection.
-Recognizes a conserved epitope on GP RBD, overlapping with the NPC1 receptor-binding region.
-Exhibits broad neutralization across multiple MARV strains (Angola, Musoke, Ravn).
-In guinea pig lethal challenge, therapeutic administration provided full protection when given up to 3 days post-infection.
-Outperformed comparator antibodies (e.g., MR186, MR191) in breadth and potency.
-Challenges: Needs NHP efficacy validation, optimization of dosing, and manufacturing scalability.
Recent updates:
-Builds on earlier human survivor–derived antibody work (e.g., MR191, MR186) that reached NHP studies and emergency therapeutic exploration for filoviruses.
-MARV16 shows potential as a single broadly neutralizing therapeutic antibody, unlike prior cocktails (e.g., MR191 + MR186).
-Aligns with NIH/US Army efforts to establish a stockpile of filovirus monoclonals for outbreak response.
-Next steps: NHP efficacy and GMP manufacturing; potential inclusion in multi-filovirus antibody cocktails for outbreak readiness.

Key features and challenges:

-In vitro: Strong antiviral activity against CHIKV; also inhibits HSV-1.
-In vivo: Efficacy at 15 mg/kg once-daily oral dosing in mice.
-Safety: Oral LD₅₀ > 5000 mg/kg (acute study, OECD-423). Safe at 50 mg/kg/day for 9 months in rats; toxicity observed at higher doses (500–1000 mg/kg/day).
-Pharmacokinetics: Oral Tmax = 2 h, t½ ≈ 8 h, high plasma protein binding (99.5%), predicted 22 metabolites (mostly OECD Class 5 = low toxicity).
-Challenges: Mild sedation observed on prolonged dosing; requires monitoring of CNS, liver, and kidney safety for long-term use. No human studies yet.
Recent updates:
2022:
-AAC study showed potent inhibition of CHIKV nsP2 protease in vitro, in vivo, and ex vivo. 
2024: 
-Study expanded with PK/toxicology profile, supporting translational potential. 
-No clinical trial initiation as of Sept 2025.

Name: MERS two-component nanoparticle vaccine
Developers: University of Washington (including Harborview Medical Center)
Indication: Prevention of MERS-CoV infection (vaccine prophylaxis)
Target: Spike (S) subunit 2 (S2) domain of MERS-CoV (and component from HKU4 for breadth).
Mechanism of action: The nanoparticle presents multiple copies of S2 antigen to the immune system in a multivalent configuration, eliciting binding (IgG) and cross-reactive antibodies; in challenge models, immunized hDPP4 transgenic mice show reduced lung viral titers versus control, indicating interference with viral replication/infection.
Key features and challenges:
-Uses conserved S2 domain rather than more variable S1, potentially improving cross-reactive immunity and reducing escape risk.
-Two-component (MERS + HKU4 S2) “cocktail” nanoparticle design intended to broaden immune coverage across Merbecoviruses.
-In mice, single immunization with VLP-MERS S2 (prime) already yielded significant lung viral titer reduction; two doses (prime + boost) of the mixture nanoparticle achieved ~3.7 log reduction in lung virus load post challenge.
-Challenges include: durability of protection, translation to higher animals (camels, NHP), immunogenicity in diverse hosts, manufacturing of VLP nanoparticle constructs, stability, regulatory path, and ensuring that S2-directed antibodies suffice for full protection (vs neutralizing S1 / RBD responses).
Recent updates:
-The published 2024 work confirms that the two-component (MERS + HKU4 S2) nanoparticle induces cross-reactive IgG responses to four Merbecovirus S2 proteins.
-CEPI announced a $2.6M investment in 2025 to advance a nanoparticle MERS vaccine candidate (Uvax Bio’s 1c-SApNP platform), likely related or competitive technology to this class.
-The nanoparticle design (displaying viral antigen in virus-like size) is being positioned as a next-generation candidate platform for MERS.
-The biorxiv preprint (2024) made available before peer review, showing similar neutralizing and protection results, may include additional methodological details or optimizations not in earlier drafts.

Name: MERS-CoV M(pro) inhibitors
Developers: Birla Institute of Technology and Science
Indication: Post infection antiviral
Mechanism of action: Inhibit protease cleavage of viral polyproteins (pp1a / pp1ab) into functional nonstructural proteins required for viral replication, thereby blocking virus replication cycle.
Key features and challenges:
-The M^pro is highly conserved among coronaviruses (active site architecture, catalytic cysteine/histidine dyad) making it an attractive broad coronavirus antiviral target.
-Crystallographic studies across SARS, MERS, and other CoV M^pro give structural templates and insights into active site binding, enabling structure-guided inhibitor design.
-Cross-reactive inhibition is possible: some inhibitors developed for SARS-CoV / SARS-CoV-2 M^pro show activity in MERS assays in vitro (e.g. 5d / 11d compounds tested against MERS in fatal mouse models).
Challenges include:
-Achieving high potency/selectivity (low off-target protease inhibition), good pharmacokinetics (absorption, distribution, metabolic stability), cell permeability, avoiding toxicity, and overcoming potential resistance mutations.
Many M^pro inhibitors are peptidomimetics, which often suffer from poor drug-like properties (e.g. poor oral bioavailability, metabolic liabilities).
Recent updates:
-In the 2023 Cell / Structure article, co-crystal structures of the MERS-CoV main protease bound to inhibitors are reported, enabling mapping of binding interactions and informing design of next-generation inhibitors.
-A recent Nature Communications article (2025) describes ISM3312, a novel covalent broad-spectrum M^pro inhibitor active against multiple human coronaviruses, including MERS-CoV, and effective even against nirmatrelvir-resistant proteases. This suggests progress in broad coronavirus M^pro inhibitor design that may overlap with or inform MERS-targeted inhibitors.
-In the “Potent 3CLpro inhibitors” work, compounds 5d and 11d showed antiviral efficacy in fatal animal models of MERS/ SARS, providing in vivo proof of concept beyond simple biochemical inhibition.

Name: MERS-CoV RBD-mRNA vaccine
Developers: Lindsley F. Kimball Research Institute (LFKRI); University of Iowa
Indication: Prevention of MERS-CoV infection
Target: Spike (S) protein RBD of MERS-CoV (blocks DPP4 receptor engagement).
Mechanism of action: In vivo expression of RBD elicits humoral and cellular immunity; serum neutralizing antibodies correlate with protection and are expected to inhibit RBD–DPP4–mediated entry.
Key features and challenges:
-N1-methyl-pseudouridine (PseudoU)–modified RBD mRNA showed superior stability/expression vs unmodified and induced durable, broadly neutralizing antibodies. 
-Intradermal (I.D.) route at low dose (10 µg) elicited the highest neutralizing titers and robust B-cell responses. 
-Complete protection in Ad5-hDPP4–transduced mouse challenge model; lung virus undetectable post-challenge; protection correlated with nAb titers. 
-Challenges: data limited to murine models (Ad5-hDPP4); mucosal IgA not detected in serum; no clinical data yet.
Recent updates: -Multiple non-mRNA MERS vaccines continue in/near clinical testing (e.g., MVA-MERS-S Phase Ib in EU), but no clinical listings for a MERS RBD mRNA candidate as of Sept 2025.

It’s a vaccine made from a piece of the MERS spike protein (the S1 part). The spike protein is joined to a foldon (Fd) tag so it stays in its natural trimer shape, just like on the real virus. It’s mixed with an adjuvant called QS-21, which helps the body make a stronger and longer-lasting immune response.

Recent updates: A Phase 1 trial (NCT07217379) assessing the safety and tolerability of these HIV-directed antibodies, with or without a temporary treatment interruption or an oral latency-reversing agent, in people living with HIV on antiretroviral therapy began in 2025 and is recruiting as of 2025.

Name: MGfl-HYB-PCR
Developers: Minerva Consulting & Communication; University of Melbourne (including the Australian Venom Research Unit (AVRU) and Bio21 Institute)
Indication: Detection of Mycoplasma genitalium
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: PCR assay
Key features and challenges:
MGfl-HYB-PCR is a molecular diagnostic assay designed to detect Mycoplasma genitalium and characterize fluoroquinolone susceptibility by targeting mutations in codons 83 and 87 of the ParC gene. The assay utilizes post-PCR melting curve analysis with a dual hybridization probe format to differentiate wild-type (WT) and mutation-associated variants.
A 2022 study reported that MGfl-HYB-PCR demonstrated 100% specificity for detection of fluoroquinolone-susceptible (ParC WT) M. genitalium and successfully discriminated WT from common ParC mutations based on melting peak temperatures (https://academic.oup.com/lambio/article/76/6/ovad064/7180972). 
The related MGfl-MolBeac-PCR assay, which uses molecular beacon probes, additionally enabled confident detection of the ParC-S83I mutation.
Key challenges include the need for validation in diverse clinical populations, assessment of sensitivity in low bacterial load specimens, and integration into routine diagnostic workflows. Broader mutation coverage may also be required to account for emerging resistance variants.
Overall, MGfl-HYB-PCR represents a targeted molecular approach for rapid identification of M. genitalium fluoroquinolone susceptibility. Further clinical validation is required to support widespread implementation.

Name: MGparC-AsyHRM
Developers: University of Utah; ARUP Laboratories
Indication: Detection of Mycoplasma genitalium and antimicrobial susceptibility
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: AMR detection
Key features and challenges:
MGparC-AsyHRM is a molecular antimicrobial resistance (AMR) detection assay designed to simultaneously identify Mycoplasma genitalium and genotype parC mutations associated with fluoroquinolone resistance. The assay combines asymmetric high-resolution melting (HRM) analysis with unlabeled probe technology to enable mutation discrimination without culture.
A 2022 study reported that MGparC-AsyHRM enabled identification of eight parC mutations responsible for the majority of fluoroquinolone resistance cases (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9430336/). 
The method was described as high-throughput, cost-effective, and culture-free, supporting its potential use in clinical and public health settings to enhance AMR surveillance and guide treatment decisions.
Key challenges include ensuring sensitivity in low bacterial load samples, expanding mutation coverage to capture emerging resistance variants, and integrating the assay into routine diagnostic workflows. Clinical validation across diverse populations is required to confirm real-world performance.
Overall, MGparC-AsyHRM represents a rapid molecular approach for detecting fluoroquinolone resistance in M. genitalium. Further implementation studies are needed to establish its role in resistance-guided therapy and surveillance programs.

Developers: Colombian Industrial University of Santander, Universidad Industrial de Santander (UIS)

Mechanism of action: Signal transduction pathway inhibitors
Key features and challenges: A small-molecule agent that acts on parasite cell-membrane phospholipids and PI3K/Akt signalling pathways to kill the parasite. Formulated as a topical gel for cutaneous application, with the molecule also given orally. Investigated across cutaneous and visceral leishmaniasis and other indications.
Recent updates: A Phase 1 pilot trial (NCT07149753) evaluating the safety and effectiveness of several hydrogel concentrations applied topically in adults with uncomplicated cutaneous leishmaniasis is expected to begin in 2026 and is not yet recruiting.

Name: MIP3α-RelMtb
Developers: Johns Hopkins University (including the Bloomberg School of Public Health)
Indication: Prevention of TB
Key features and challenges: RelMtb is the primary enzyme regulating the stringent response, which contributes to the metabolic shift of Mtb to a persistent state. Targeting RelMtb with a vaccine to eliminate persistent bacteria through the induction of RelMtb-specific T-cell immunity in combination with antibiotics to kill dividing bacteria has shown promise in model systems. In a mouse model of Mtb infection, a vaccine created by genetically fusing relMtb to the chemokine macrophage inflammatory protein 3α (MIP3α), a ligand for the CC chemokine receptor type 6 (CCR6) present on immature dendritic cells, has been shown to enhance T-cell responses and accelerate eradication of infection in mouse models compared to a vaccine lacking the chemokine component. In this study, immunogenicity studies in the mouse and rhesus macaque models provide evidence that intranasal administrations of the DNA form of the MipRel vaccine led to enhanced lung infiltration of T cells after a series of immunizations. Furthermore, despite similar T-cell immunity seen in PBMCs between MipRel and Rel vaccinations, lung and bronchoalveolar lavage cell samples are more enriched for cytokine-secreting T cells in MipRel groups compared to Rel groups (.https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.09.04.611263v1).

Name: MIRA-CRISPR/Cas13a-LFD
Developers: Xinxiang Medical University
Indication: Detection of T. vaginalis
Health care facility level: IVDs for research use only
Target: repeated DNA sequence of T. vaginalis
Mechanism of action: Isothermal amplification coupled with CRISPR/Cas13a cleavage enables sequence-specific detection of Trichomonas vaginalis RNA via lateral flow readout.
Key features and challenges:
A 2024 study describes a novel detection method for T. vaginalis developed using a multi-enzyme isothermal rapid amplification–clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (MIRA-CRISPR)/Cas13a-lateral flow device (LFD). This assay targets the repeated DNA sequence of T. vaginalis and is performed at a constant temperature of 37 °C for approximately 1 hour. The study demonstrated that the MIRA-CRISPR/Cas13a-LFD method targeting the repeated DNA element is an efficient, reliable, and rapid detection tool for T. vaginalis. The method exhibited superior sensitivity and specificity, with the capacity to discriminate between T. vaginalis and other common pathogens in humans. The speed and visual readability of the LFD readout, combined with the high amplification efficiency and selectivity of MIRA–CRISPR/Cas13a, make this method highly suitable for point-of-care testing, particularly in resource-limited settings. Future work will aim to further refine and validate the method in a larger clinical context, potentially integrating it into standard diagnostic procedures to enable quicker and more accurate detection of T. vaginalis infections.
(https://parasitesandvectors.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s13071-023-06106-3)

Name: MK-7845
Developers: MK - 7845; Merck (also known as Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany), including Sigma-Aldrich, MilliporeSigma and EMD Serono
Indication: Treatment of coronavirus infections (including MERS-CoV)
Mechanism of action: Forms a reversible covalent adduct with catalytic cysteine (Cys145) of 3CLpro, blocking viral polyprotein processing and halting replication.
Key features and challenges:
-Potency: Nanomolar in vitro activity across SARS-CoV-2 (EC50 ~15–235 nM across variants) and MERS-CoV (EC50 ~390–463 nM).
-Spectrum: Active against SARS-CoV-1, MERS-CoV, endemic hCoVs (229E, OC43, HKU1, NL63).
-Pharmacokinetics: Oral bioavailability in mice; BID oral dosing (≥250 mg/kg) maintained plasma levels above EC90.
-In vivo efficacy: Reduced lung viral loads by 5–6 logs in hACE2 mice (SARS-CoV-2) and 2–4 logs in hDPP4 mice (MERS-CoV). High doses (500–1000 mg/kg) sometimes achieved complete viral clearance.
-Histopathology: Markedly reduced lung pathology in both SARS-CoV-2 and MERS models.
-Advantages over nirmatrelvir: Works without ritonavir boosting, potentially fewer drug-drug interactions.
-Challenges: Efficacy window narrower when treatment delayed (>12 hpi); further studies needed in advanced disease models. Translation to humans untested.
Recent updates:
-The structure of MK-7845 bound to SARS-CoV-2 3CLpro (PDB: 8UTE) was released in 2024, confirming reversible covalent binding.
-NIH/NIAID MAVDA consortium (Metropolitan Antiviral Drug Accelerator) continues to fund MK-7845 development, positioning it as a pandemic preparedness pan-CoV antiviral.
-Comparative profiling shows MK-7845 maintains activity against major Omicron subvariants (XBB.1.5, EG.5.1, JN.1) and MERS-CoV EMC 2012 strain, supporting broad utility.

Name: MK-8527
Developers: Merck (also known as Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany), including Sigma-Aldrich, MilliporeSigma and EMD Serono
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of HIV-1 infection.
Mechanism of action: Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTIs)
Key features and challenges:
Merck announced MK-8527 as an NRTTI candidate in a September 2022 press release in response to the unexpected adverse effects of high islatravir doses on CD4 T cell and absolute lymphocyte counts.
Phase I trials were completed in South Africa and Romania.
The results were presented at CROI 2024.  The drug is amenable to weekly or possibly monthly dosing. Viral load declines in people with HIV not on ART averaged a little over 1 log10 after seven days across a range of doses from 0.5 mg to 10 mg. No serious adverse events occurred, supporting further clinical development (https://www.treatmentactiongroup.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/pipeline_ARV_2024_final.pdf).

A double-blind, placebo-controlled study (active, not recruiting) will assess the safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of oral MK-8527 taken once monthly in participants at low risk for human immunodeficiency virus Type 1 (HIV-1) infection in the US, Israel, and South Africa (Estimated completion 2/2025) (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06045507).

Name: ML221
Developers: Sigma-Aldrich
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: apelin (APJ) functional antagonist
Key features and challenges:
ML221 is a selective, small-molecule antagonist of the apelin receptor (APJ), designed to inhibit apelin-13–mediated activation of APJ signaling. The apelin–APJ system is implicated in metabolic regulation, angiogenesis, and reproductive physiology, and emerging evidence suggests it may contribute to ovarian dysfunction in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
A 2024 preclinical study investigated the role of the apelin system in PCOS-associated ovarian pathogenesis using a letrozole-induced hyperandrogenic mouse model. The study evaluated both apelin-13 (agonist) and ML221 (antagonist). Treatment with ML221 ameliorated key PCOS-like features, including hyperandrogenism, cystic follicle formation, reduced corpus luteum numbers, elevated LH/FSH ratio, and upregulation of ovarian androgen receptor (AR) expression. Both apelin-13 and ML221 improved ovarian histology and reduced androgen levels, suggesting modulatory effects on cystic ovarian morphology. However, reductions in oxidative stress and apoptosis were observed with apelin-13 treatment only, indicating differential downstream pathway effects between agonism and antagonism of APJ signaling.
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S104346662400142X?via%3Dihub
Despite these promising mechanistic findings, ML221 remains at a very early stage of development. Evidence is currently limited to a single animal-model study, with no published human data, pharmacokinetic studies, or clinical trials in PCOS. The paradoxical observation that both APJ agonism and antagonism may improve certain PCOS phenotypes underscores incomplete understanding of the apelin pathway in ovarian physiology. Additionally, long-term metabolic, cardiovascular, and reproductive safety of APJ modulation has not been established.
Overall, ML221 represents an exploratory, preclinical candidate targeting the apelin–APJ axis in PCOS. While early animal data suggest potential for modulating ovarian hyperandrogenism and cystic morphology, substantial mechanistic clarification and clinical translation are required before its therapeutic relevance in PCOS can be determined.

Name: ML2640c protein inhibitors
Developers: Savitribai Phule Pune University
Indication: Investigated for the treatment of leprosy.
Mechanism of action: ML2640c protein inhibitor.
Key features and challenges: A study employed advanced computational drug discovery techniques to identify potential inhibitors against the ML2640c protein, a key factor in the Mycobacterium leprae bacterium's ability to infect and persist within host cells. Utilizing a comprehensive methodology, including virtual screening, re-docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and free energy calculations, a library of compounds were screened for their interaction with ML2640c. Four compounds (24349836, 26616083, 26648979, and 26651264) demonstrated promising inhibitory potential, each exhibiting unique binding energies and interaction patterns that suggest a strong likelihood of disrupting the protein function.  Compound 26616083 was a notably potent inhibitor due to its excellent binding affinity and stability (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11030-024-10902-z).

Name: MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio
Developers: Jordan University of Science & Technology (JUST); Chengdu Medical College
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Calculates matrix metalloproteinase-9 to TIMP-1 ratio to assess extracellular matrix remodeling and inflammatory activity associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
The MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio represents the balance between Matrix Metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9), an enzyme involved in the degradation of the extracellular matrix, and Tissue Inhibitor of Metalloproteinases-1 (TIMP-1), which regulates the activity of MMPs. A higher MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio indicates an imbalance favoring proteolytic activity, or increased tissue degradation, which may play a role in various biological processes, including follicular development and ovarian dysfunction.

In the context of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS), the MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio has been found to be elevated in women with the condition, suggesting a pro-inflammatory and pro-proteolytic environment. This imbalance may contribute to the pathogenesis of PCOS, affecting ovarian structure and function. The ratio has shown potential as a diagnostic biomarker for PCOS, with moderate accuracy in distinguishing PCOS patients from healthy controls, though further research is needed to refine its clinical use.
(https://jpet.aspetjournals.org/content/389/S3/009)
Recent updates: Study published in 2025 described concurrent upregulation of MMP-9 and TIMP-1 in PCOS, potentially reflecting dysregulated yet balanced protease-inhibitor dynamics, alongside a distinct pro-inflammatory state. (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12604328/)

Name: MMV 055/167
Developers: Medicines for Malaria Venture (MMV)
Indication:
Asexual blood stages
Causal prophylaxis
Chemoprophylaxis (TPP-2)

Mechanism of action: MMV167 is a pro-drug of MMV055 - inhibition of parasite cytochrome bc1 (Qi site)

However, one of the challenges for MMV167 is its safety profile, particularly in relation to its use as a prophylactic treatment.

Name: MMV021013
Developers: University of Pretoria (UP)
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Unknown
Key features and challenges:
MMV021013 is a small-molecule compound from the Medicines for Malaria Venture (MMV) Pathogen Box being investigated for activity against Neisseria gonorrhoeae, including resistant strains. The compound is part of a curated library of molecules with potential activity against neglected and priority pathogens.
A 2023 study evaluating eight Pathogen Box compounds reported that MMV021013 demonstrated potent in vitro activity against resistant N. gonorrhoeae strains, with minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) and minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) values of ≤10 µM (https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/aac.00348-23). 
These findings support further exploration of MMV021013 as a potential antimicrobial candidate.
Key challenges include limited data on mechanism of action, absence of in vivo efficacy studies, and the need for pharmacokinetic and toxicity characterization. Additional evaluation is required to determine resistance development risk and translational feasibility.
Overall, MMV021013 represents a preclinical repurposing candidate with demonstrated in vitro activity against resistant N. gonorrhoeae. Further preclinical studies are needed to assess its development potential.

Name: MMV024937
Developers: University of Pretoria (UP)

MMV024937 is a compound in the Malaria Box developed by Medicines for Malaria Venture (MMV), designed for early-stage antimalarial drug discovery. It is effective against Plasmodium species, including strains resistant to existing antimalarial drugs.
This compound typically shows activity against the blood-stage of malaria parasites, which is the stage responsible for clinical symptoms. Depending on its profile, it may also target other stages, such as liver-stage parasites, making it a promising candidate for malaria treatment or eradication efforts.
A 2023 study reported the activity of eight novel compounds from the Pathogen Box with potent activity against Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The Pathogen Box compounds showed potent activity against resistant strains of N. gonorrhoeae at an MIC and MBC of ≤10 µM.
(https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/aac.00348-23)

Developers: Agencia Nacional de Promoción de la Investigación; el Desarrollo Tecnológico y la Innovación (Agencia I+D+i); Fondo Argentino Sectorial (FONARSEC)
