Name: Metformin + N-Acetylcysteine
Developers: Cairo University (including Faculty Of Medicine, Kasr Al Ainy)
Indication: Treatment of PCOS - Metabolism; Hyperandrogenism; Menstrual cycle regulation
Target: AMP activated protein kinase; Gluconeogenesis; oxidative stress pathways (glutathione precursor), redox balance
Mechanism of action:
Metformin improves insulin sensitivity by reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis and enhancing peripheral glucose uptake, thereby lowering insulin levels and secondarily reducing ovarian androgen production. NAC is a precursor of glutathione and a potent antioxidant; by replenishing intracellular glutathione and reducing oxidative stress, it may protect insulin receptors, improve insulin signalling, and favourably modulate homocysteine and lipid profiles.
In combination, metformin and NAC aim to address two central mechanisms in PCOS—insulin resistance and oxidative stress—with potential additive or synergistic effects on metabolic, endocrine and clinical outcomes.
Key features and challenges:
Metformin is widely used off-label in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) as an insulin sensitizer to address hyperinsulinemia and metabolic dysfunction, with modest benefits on ovulatory function. However, persistent metabolic and reproductive symptoms are common, and long-term therapy may be limited by gastrointestinal adverse effects and effects on homocysteine and vitamin B12 levels.
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10573309

N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is an oral antioxidant and glutathione precursor with additional insulin-sensitizing properties. Early mechanistic and translational rationale for combining NAC with metformin derives from conditions characterized by insulin resistance and oxidative stress. In non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), metformin + NAC regimens improved liver enzymes, insulin resistance indices, steatosis, and fibrosis more than diet or monotherapy alone, suggesting biological complementarity between the two agents.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27920819/

More recent evidence in PCOS populations has strengthened interest in NAC as an adjunct therapy. A meta-analysis focused on metabolic outcomes (2023) reported that NAC improved fasting blood glucose and total cholesterol, with some analyses suggesting benefits comparable to or exceeding metformin, particularly with longer treatment duration.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37841396/

A systematic review and meta-analysis including 18 trials (n=2185) demonstrated that NAC reduced total testosterone and increased FSH levels, indicating beneficial effects on reproductive endocrine parameters.
https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-of-nutrition/article/effects-of-nacetylcysteine-on-ovulation-and-sex-hormones-profile-in-women-with-polycystic-ovary-syndrome-a-systematic-review-and-metaanalysis/411E42E184DE550924D72725D0519A45

A larger 2024 meta-analysis of 22 studies (n=2515) further reported that NAC significantly increased progesterone levels and endometrial thickness compared with placebo or other comparators, supporting its role as a reproductive adjunct in PCOS.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39861414/

Given the high prevalence of insulin resistance, oxidative stress, NAFLD, and cardiometabolic risk in PCOS, these findings provide a mechanistic and clinical rationale for combination therapy with metformin and NAC.

The Phase 3 trial NCT06836128 (“The Combined Effect of N-Acetyl Cysteine and Metformin in Polycystic Ovary Syndrome Patients”) is an open-label, randomized, parallel-group study enrolling 102 women with PCOS diagnosed according to the 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline. Participants are randomized to metformin + NAC (NAC 600 mg three times daily plus metformin titrated to 500 mg three times daily) versus metformin alone for 3 months. Primary outcomes include changes in LH/FSH levels and LH/FSH ratio, with secondary endpoints assessing androgen profile, menstrual irregularities, hirsutism, insulin resistance indices, and anthropometric measures.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06836128

If combination therapy demonstrates superiority over metformin alone, it may represent a relatively low-cost, oral, and accessible regimen targeting both insulin resistance and oxidative stress. NAC is generally well tolerated, and existing trials suggest a favorable safety profile that could support longer-term adjunctive use.

However, several challenges remain. Although both agents are individually marketed, the combination for PCOS remains investigational. Evidence is derived primarily from heterogeneous RCTs and meta-analyses, with substantial variability in NAC dose, treatment duration, and study populations, and no consensus on optimal dosing in PCOS.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37841396/

Furthermore, while metformin is guideline-endorsed (albeit off-label) for metabolic features of PCOS, NAC is not currently recommended as first-line therapy in international PCOS guidelines. As such, any combination regimen would initially be positioned as an adjunct rather than core standard of care.
Recent updates: Phase III trial commenced in 2025, expected to be complete in 2026 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06836128)

Name: Metformin - Endometriosis
Developers: Shionogi & Co., Ltd.; sanofi-aventis; Fudan University; University of Porto (including Ipatimup); Boston Children's Hospital
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of endometriosis
Target: AMP activated protein kinase; Gluconeogenesis; lncRNA-H19.
Mechanism of action:
AMP activated protein kinase stimulants; Gluconeogenesis inhibitors; lncRNA-H19 inhibitor.

Preclinical data suggests: Increased anaerobic glucose metabolism; lowers serum levels of tumor necrosis factor-alpha; enhances NADPH: quinone oxidoreductase (NQO1) enzyme activity; upregulates nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2; increases autophagy; downregulates mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) gene expression
Key features and challenges:
Metformin, a first-line treatment for type II diabetes, manages blood glucose by reducing hepatic glucose production, decreasing intestinal glucose absorption, and enhancing insulin sensitivity. Unlike sulfonylureas, it doesn’t increase insulin secretion but instead improves glucose uptake and utilization. In clinical trials, metformin significantly lowered fasting plasma glucose and HbA1c levels compared to placebo. Its action involves inhibiting mitochondrial complex I, which activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and impacts glucose and fat metabolism. Additionally, metformin affects glucose metabolism in the intestines, with recent research suggesting that its action in the gut might be more significant than previously thought. (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB00331)
Preclinical trials have shown Metformin may be beneficial in the treatment of endometriosis.
One study published in 2020, evaluated the impact of quercetin and metformin on endometrial tissues in a rat model of endometriosis. Results indicated that their combination significantly reduced endometrial implant size and improved gene expression related to oxidative stress and autophagy, suggesting potential therapeutic effects. (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43032-020-00377-2#Fun)
Another study published in 2022, investigated the effects of metformin, letrozole, and atorvastatin on inflammation and apoptosis in rat models of ovarian and peritoneal endometriosis. The treatments significantly reduced inflammation markers and induced apoptosis, suggesting potential therapeutic benefits for managing endometriosis. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0344033822001959?via%3Dihub)
A study published in 2023, aimed to evaluate the effects of metformin and ganirelix on subcutaneous endometriotic tissues in a mouse model. Metformin and ganirelix significantly reduced the expression of autophagy-related genes, such as Beclin2, Beclin1, and LC3BII, compared to controls. This suggests that metformin may induce an autophagy-based suppression mechanism in endometriosis. (https://tjoddergisi.org/articles/doi/tjod.galenos.2023.85616#conclusions)
Recent updates: TM 14/12/2025: Studies identified from CT.gov (vhttps://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06611501) and EMBASE (https://journals.lww.com/rdm/fulltext/2025/03000/lncrna_h19_is_downregulated_in_ectopic_endometrial.5.aspx); (https://www.rbmojournal.com/article/S1472-6483(24)00663-1/fulltext).

Name: Metformin - PE/E
Developers: King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust
Indication: Prevention or treatment of preeclampsia/eclampsia
Mechanism of action: Unclear; potentially via reduction of antiangiogenic sFlt-1 through inhibition of secretion of the protein
Key features and challenges:
Metformin, sold under the brand name Glucophage among others, is the first-line medication for the treatment of type 2 diabetes, particularly in people who are overweight It is also used in the treatment of polycystic ovary syndrome. It is widely marketed and used for these indications. 
In preeclampsia, hypoperfusion of the placenta results in placental hypoxia and ischaemia, and the maternal-foetal interface is subjected to relatively strong oxidative stress. Subsequently, cytokines and cell debris are secreted into the circulation of the maternal blood system by the placenta, eventually leading to maternal preeclamptic symptoms and injuries to other important organs.
Metformin is suggested as a promising therapeutic candidate as it has been shown to reduce soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt-1) and soluble endoglin (sEng) secretion from endothelial cells and primary trophoblasts. These key anti-angiogenic molecules released from the placenta are responsible for the widespread endothelial dysfunction and impaired vascular relaxation observed in pre-eclampsia. Further, insulin resistance together with adipocyte dysfunction might be involved in the pathophysiology of preeclampsia in obese women, suggesting that metformin may be an avenue for treatment. 
There is interest into use of metformin to prevent preeclampsia as, observationally, it has been associated with a lower risk of pregnancy-induced hypertension and preeclampsia. Preclinical studies have found that metformin significantly improved placental development in preeclamptic mice, thereby improving the related symptoms of preeclampsia and maternal and foetal outcomes, including hypertension, proteinuria, and foetal birth weight. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31886236/). Clinical studies are planned or underway (https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT04855513). A 2018 systematic review showed benefit of metformin over insulin in reducing the risk of PE/E (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29044702/).
Recent updates:
2021: Prevention of Pre-eclampsia Using Metformin: a Randomized Control Trial (PREMET). Recruiting. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT04855513)

2019: Protocol published for Phase II trial: PACTR201608001752102.(https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/9/4/e025809)

2019: Metformin shown to improve preeclamptic symptoms and pregnancy outcomes in rat models. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31886236/)

2018: Combining metformin and esomeprazole is additive in reducing sFlt-1 secretion and decreasing endothelial dysfunction (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29466360/)

2018: Risk of pre-eclampsia in women taking metformin: a systematic review and meta-analysis. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29044702/)

Name: Metformin - PTL/PTB
Developers: University of Hong Kong (HKU)
Indication: For the prevention of Preterm Birth
Mechanism of action: Quantifies hypoxia-associated microRNA miR-210-3p to detect placental hypoxic stress linked to growth restriction.
Key features and challenges:
Metformin is a biguanide antihyperglycemic agent and first-line pharmacotherapy used in the management of type II diabetes. Metformin is considered an antihyperglycemic drug because it lowers blood glucose concentrations in type II diabetes without causing hypoglycemia. It is commonly described as an "insulin sensitizer", leading to a decrease in insulin resistance and a clinically significant reduction of plasma fasting insulin levels. 

Another well-known benefit of this drug is modest weight loss, making it an effective choice for obese patients type II diabetes. Metformin was first approved in Canada in 1972, and received subsequent FDA approval in the US in 1995

A randomized double blinded controlled trial using Metformin to prevent preterm birth in twin pregnancy is currently underway. Premature uterine and amnion stretching in twin pregnancy can trigger preterm labour by increased prostaglandin synthesis and interleukin-1, activation of activator protein-1, expression of connexin-43 and stimulation of stretch dependent focal adhesion signaling. Inflammation is another risk factor for PTB. Metformin is an anti-inflammatory agent which can suppress inflammatory cytokines production and downregulate AMP-activated protein kinase medicated connexin-43 and nuclear factor κB activation. Anti-inflammatory actions of metformin can also reduce production of nitric oxide, prostaglandin E2 and pro-inflammatory cytokines through inhibition of NFκB activation in macrophages. Another possible mechanism to prevent PTB is the inhibition of mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1, which has a role in the timing of birth, by AMP-activated protein kinase. Therefore, metformin can be potentially used to prevent PTB in twin pregnancy.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05412056)

Name: Metformin/Liraglutide
Developers: Mỹ Đức Hospital; Xinqiao Hospital of Chongqing; Beni-Suef University
Indication: Treatment of PCOS-related metabolic disturbances and infertility
Target: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor ; AMP activated protein kinase; Gluconeogenesis
Mechanism of action: AMP activated protein kinase stimulants; Gluconeogenesis inhibitors; Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists
Key features and challenges:
Metformin/liraglutide combines an insulin-sensitizing biguanide (metformin) with a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) (liraglutide). Metformin reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis, improves peripheral insulin sensitivity, and lowers circulating insulin levels. Liraglutide, a long-acting GLP-1 analogue administered subcutaneously, enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppresses glucagon release, delays gastric emptying, and promotes weight loss through appetite regulation. The combination is commonly used in type 2 diabetes, particularly in individuals with obesity or elevated cardiovascular risk.
https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800010229
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is frequently associated with insulin resistance, obesity, and metabolic dysfunction. Metformin is widely used in PCOS to improve insulin sensitivity and menstrual regularity. GLP-1 receptor agonists, including liraglutide, have demonstrated benefits in weight reduction and metabolic improvement in women with PCOS. The combination of metformin and liraglutide has therefore been investigated to determine whether additive or synergistic metabolic and reproductive benefits may be achieved.
A 2021 review of clinical trials reported that liraglutide in combination with metformin did not significantly improve fasting blood glucose, fasting insulin, or HOMA-IR compared with other pharmacologic treatments such as rosiglitazone, pioglitazone, exenatide, saxagliptin, or acarbose. These findings suggest that while metabolically active, the combination may not demonstrate clear superiority over alternative insulin-sensitizing or incretin-based therapies for these specific parameters.
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/cen.14623
Clinical trials have further evaluated the combination in PCOS populations. A study completed in 2021 (NCT03151005) compared metformin plus liraglutide with metformin plus cyproterone acetate/ethinylestradiol (Diane-35) in overweight women with PCOS, assessing lipid metabolism and cardiovascular risk markers.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03151005
A 2023 trial (NCT05965908) evaluated hormonal, metabolic, and fertility-related outcomes in infertile women with PCOS treated with metformin and liraglutide. Outcomes included follicle size, endometrial thickness, metabolic parameters, and pregnancy rates.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05965908
Although the mechanistic rationale for combination therapy is strong, targeting both insulin resistance and obesity; evidence regarding incremental benefit over monotherapy remains mixed. Gastrointestinal adverse effects are common with both agents, and liraglutide carries class-related considerations including rare pancreatitis risk and the need for injectable administration. Cost and access may also limit widespread adoption in some settings.
Metformin/liraglutide represents a metabolically focused therapeutic strategy in PCOS, targeting insulin resistance and weight reduction with potential secondary reproductive benefits. While supported by biologic plausibility and clinical investigation, its comparative effectiveness and long-term reproductive outcomes require further evaluation in adequately powered randomized controlled trials.

Name: Metoprolol
Developers: Hunan Provincial People's Hospital
Indication: Treatment of high blood pressure in preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: Beta-1-adrenergic receptor inhibitor
Key features and challenges:
Metoprolol is a selective beta-1 blocker. To this date, it is one of the preferred beta-blockers in general clinical guidelines and it is widely prescribed in the Netherlands, New Zealand, and the US.  Metoprolol was developed since 1969 by US Pharmaceutical Holdings and FDA approved in 1978. 
As part of the aetiology of preeclampsia, it is reported that marked increase in the sympathetic activity causes a higher peripheral vascular resistance and as a result causes an increase in the blood pressure. Metoprolol has been investigated in this regard.
Endothelial progenitor cells (EPCs) are critical for vascular regeneration and function, but are reduced in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy such as preelcampsia. A study aimed to determine the possible effects of antihypertensive drugs, such as metoprolol, methyldopa, and nifedipine, on EPC number and functions in patients with gestational hypertension and preeclampsia was conducted in 2019. Blood samples from 30 normal pregnant women, 67 patients with gestational hypertension and 48 patients with preeclampsia were collected.  The number of EPCs and circulating endothelial cells (CECs) in the blood was measured by flow cytometry. The administration of metoprolol, methyldopa, or nifedipine effectively restored the systolic and diastolic BP, FMD%, EPCs, and CEC numbers, as well as EPC migration capacity. This study revealed a new pharmacological action of these antihypertensive drugs against gestational hypertension and preeclampsia, thus supporting their clinical use. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30614608/). However, beta-blockers are associated with the baby being born small for its gestational age.
Another study was conducted to examine the efficiency of the short-term treatment with metoprolol and nifedipine in women with preeclampsia and to evaluate the maternal and fetal outcomes. Forty three of 73 preeclamptic women were conservatively treated with metoprolol and 30 with nifedipine. Conservative management using metoprolol in preeclamptic women provided blood pressure control comparable to nifedipine, with a prolongation of pregnancy by 7 days. Maternal and fetal complications accompanying metoprolol treatment were comparable to those of nifedipine (https://perinataljournal.com/Files/Archive/en-US/Articles/PD-1043.pdf).
Recent updates: N/A

Name: Metridx lab-developed test
Developers: Hera Biotech, Inc
Indication: Diagnostic of endometriosis via uterine tissue samples
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Mechanism of action: Laboratory-developed molecular or immunoassay detecting disease-associated biomarkers to support diagnosis of endometriosis.
Key features and challenges:
Hera Biotech is developing MetriDx, a test to to identify endometriosis-specific biomarkers in uterine tissue, collected via a pap smear, to diagnose endometriosis without the need for invasive laparoscopy. After the biopsy is collected, the tissue is analyzed in a specialized lab using a proprietary AI-driven technology. This AI technology performs a detailed micro-fluidic analysis of the cells from the biopsy to identify gene expression data points specific to endometriosis. The aim is to provide a less invasive and more accessible method for diagnosing the condition compared to traditional surgical approaches.
(https://www.herabiotech.com/)

A proof of concept study was conducted in 2023 to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of the test. It involved 75 participants with scheduled laparoscopies, either for the diagnosis of endometriosis (active group with a history of endometriosis related symptoms) or other reasons, such as tubal ligation (control group, no history of endometriosis). Participants in both groups were planned to undergo a uterine biopsy before their laparoscopy. The biopsy results, analyzed by the innovative AI technology, would be compared to the laparoscopy findings to evaluate the accuracy of this new diagnostic method. 
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05698212)
No results have been published but interim results on 38 patients shared by Hera Biotech suggest good performance with 92% sensitivity, 95% specificity and an overall accuracy (AUC) of 94%, as compared to the histopathology of excised lesions.
(https://www.biospace.com/hera-biotech-announces-positive-interim-results-from-endometriosis-diagnostic-study)

Name: Metronidazole
Developers: Tehran University of Medical Sciences (TUMS)
Indication: Indicated for the prevention of postpartum haemorrhage, in combination with misoprostol and oxytocin.
Target: Unknown in the context of PPH
Mechanism of action: Combines inflammatory blood indices with Doppler parameters to evaluate placental insufficiency and fetal compromise.
Key features and challenges:
Metronidazole is a commonly used antibiotic, belonging to the nitroimidazole class of antibiotics. It is available in capsule form, tablet form, and topical form, and suppository preparations for the treatment of various infections. Metronidazole is indicated for the treatment of Trichomonas vaginalis, bacterial vaginosis, certain types of amebiasis, and various anaerobic infections. It is also used off-label in the treatment of Crohn's disease, as a prophylactic agent after surgery, and in the treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection. It has also been studied in the prevention of preterm births and to treat periodontal disease. (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB00916) 

In a study by Tehran University of Medical Sciences, metronidazole is being used in combination with misoprostol and oxytocin and is being studied for its effect on postpartum haemorrhage following caesarean section. Name: Metronidazole and curcumin gel
Developers: Eastern Mediterranean University
Indication: Investigated for the treatment of Trichomoniasis.
Target:
Metronidazole: Possible protozoal DNA
Curcumin: Angiogenesis; Cyclo-oxygenase 2; Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator; Mast cell; Thromboxane synthase
Mechanism of action:
Metronidazole: DNA synthesis inhibitors
Curcumin: Angiogenesis inhibitors; Cyclo-oxygenase 2 inhibitors; Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator modulators; Immunosuppressants; Mast cell stabilisers; Thromboxane synthase inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Metronidazole and curcumin gel is a topical combination therapeutic candidate developed for the treatment of Trichomonas vaginalis infection. Metronidazole, a nitroimidazole antibiotic widely used for trichomoniasis, exhibits antiparasitic activity but is associated with suboptimal cure rates, recurrence, and emerging resistance (DrugBank; 2023 study https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1773224723005919?via%3Dihub). 
Curcumin, a bioactive compound derived from Curcuma longa, has demonstrated antiparasitic and antioxidant properties, including interference with parasite signaling pathways and iron transport, and may reduce oxidative stress–related host cell damage.
A 2023 study evaluated a topical gel formulation containing metronidazole and curcumin in a PLX407/PLX188/PHR gel base and reported statistically significant in vitro antiparasitic activity against T. vaginalis (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1773224723005919?via%3Dihub). The combination maintained and slightly enhanced metronidazole efficacy compared with metronidazole solution alone. The gel demonstrated favorable physicochemical properties and stability for up to 90 days, supporting its potential as a localized delivery system to improve therapeutic outcomes while reducing systemic exposure.
Key challenges include the need for in vivo validation of efficacy and safety in vaginal infection models, confirmation of clinical benefit over standard metronidazole therapy, and evaluation of long-term resistance dynamics. Regulatory considerations for combination topical formulations must also be addressed.
Overall, the metronidazole–curcumin gel represents a localized combination strategy aimed at enhancing antiparasitic efficacy while minimizing systemic side effects. Further preclinical and clinical evaluation is required to establish its therapeutic value.

Developers: Tongji Hospital

Key features and challenges:
Tongji Hospital (China) started a clinical trial in 2023 aiming to evaluate the diagnostic efficiency of a three-dimensional poly(dimethylsiloxane) scaffold for isolating circulating endometrial cells (CEC) from peripheral blood samples. This innovative approach is designed as a non-invasive diagnostic method for endometriosis, aiming to improve detection efficiency compared to traditional diagnostic methods. By analyzing blood samples from patients with and without endometriosis, the chip assesses its capability to accurately identify and isolate CECs, potentially offering a more accessible and cost-effective solution for diagnosing this chronic condition.

The study involves collecting blood samples from two groups of patients—those diagnosed with endometriosis and those without. A total of 20 samples from each group will be tested using the microfluidic chip. The study's objective is to evaluate the percentage of cases in which circulating endometrial cells are identified in the samples. By comparing the detection rates between the two groups, the study aims to determine the diagnostic efficiency of the microfluidic chip in distinguishing patients with endometriosis from those without.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05749341)

Name: Microfluidic-chip-based LAMP
Developers: Tsinghua University
Indication: Detection of T. vaginalis
Health care facility level: IVDs for research use only

Compared to conventional LAMP assays in tubes, the system exhibits enhanced sensitivity. Additionally the performance of the chip was validated by testing 47 clinical samples, yielding results consistent with the diagnostic methods used by the hospital. Therefore, the system not only offers a promising solution for concurrent diagnosis of T. vaginalis and HPV infections, particularly in resource-limited areas, due to its cost-effectiveness, ease of use, and rapid and accurate detection performance, but can also contribute to future research on the co-infection of these two pathogens. Moreover, the system possesses the capability to simultaneously detect up to 22 different types of pathogens, making it applicable across a wide range of domains such as diagnostics, food safety, and water monitoring. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37606537/)

Key features and challenges: After 24 h, MvFL inhibited the proliferation of L. amazonensis promastigotes, with an IC50 of 88 µg/mL; however, hemolytic activity was not observed. MvFL also reduced macrophage infection by amastigotes with an IC50 of 52 µg/mL. Furthermore, treatment with MvFL reduced the number of amastigotes internalized by infected murine peritoneal macrophages by up to 68.9% within 48 h. Name: Mifepristone-loaded nanostructured lipid carriers
Developers: Zhejiang University School of Medicine
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Endometriosis.
Mechanism of action: Reduction of the size of endometriotic cysts via the induction of autophagy.
Key features and challenges:
Mifepristone, a progesterone receptor antagonist, was initially used to terminate early pregnancy. As scientific research advanced, it emerged to be effective in the treatment of various tumors and tumor-like conditions such as endometriosis. Despite the therapeutic potential of mifepristone, its therapeutic effect is still far from ideal because the drug is difficult to dissolve and to accumulate in the target tissue sites. To address this issue, mifepristone-loaded nanostructured lipid carriers (Mif-NLC) were prepared by a simple solvent diffusion method and their anti-endometriosis performance and mechanisms were initially investigated. By optimizing the preparation protocol, the authors obtained uniform and spheroidal Mif-NLC with an average particle size of 280 nm. The encapsulation rate and drug loading capacity were 64.67% ± 0.15% and 2.7% ± 0.014%, respectively, as measured by UV spectrophotometry. The in vitro release kinetics indicated that mifepristone was released from NLC in a sustained-release manner. Compared with free mifepristone, Mif-NLC exhibited enhanced cellular uptake and inhibition of invasion activity in primary mesenchymal cells of endometriosis. A certain reduction in the size of endometriotic cysts was observed in animals compared to controls. The induction of autophagy via Mif-NLC may serve as the molecular mechanism underlying this effect. Furthermore, observation of uterine structures showed negligible toxic effects. This suggests that mifepristone encapsulated in NLC can improve its bioavailability and anti-endometriosis efficacy, which provides a new strategy for the treatment of endometriosis (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13346-024-01661-3)
(https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB00834).

Name: Miltefosine + paromomycin or LAmB
Developers: Drugs for Neglected Diseases initiative (DNDi)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Leishmaniasis
Key features and challenges:
Based on the good efficacy of the miltefosine and paromomycin (MF+PM) combination therapy in South Asia, and on the need for an alternative and safer treatment to replace sodium stibogluconate, a Phase III study was launched in 2018 to compare a combination regimen of miltefosine and paromomycin against the current standard visceral leishmaniasis treatment, sodium stibogluconate and paromomycin (SSG+PM). The trial was conducted by AfriKADIA Consortium partners in Kenya, Ethiopia, Sudan, and Uganda.

Study results published in the journal Clinical Infectious Diseases in September 2022 showed that treatment with MF+PM was as effective as the SSG+PM, but with fewer injections, a shorter treatment duration, and no risk of SSG-related cardiotoxicity. The availability of a safer, more field-adapted, patient-friendly treatment will particularly benefit children, who represent a high proportion of the population at risk in eastern Africa.

DNDi’s Phase II study in Sudan has demonstrated the suitability of two combination treatments – miltefosine and paromomycin (MF+PM) and liposomal amphotericin B and miltefosine (LAmB+MF) – as safe, effective, shorter treatments for patients with PKDL.
Recent updates: Awaiting WHO recommendations.

Developers: Drugs for Neglected Diseases initiative (DNDi)

Mechanism of action: Miltefosine induces apoptotic-like cell death by altering phospholipid metabolism, while localized thermotherapy denatures structural proteins
Key features and challenges: A combination approach in which a small molecule alters parasite cell-membrane phospholipid metabolism to induce apoptotic-like cell death, paired with localised thermotherapy that denatures structural proteins. The components are delivered orally and topically. It has additionally been investigated for cutaneous leishmaniasis.

Name: Mineral - Calcium - PTL/PTB
Developers: Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation; Harvard School of Public Health (HSPH)
Indication: Reducing risk of preterm labour/birth
Target: Parathyroid hormone and vitamin D homeostasis
Mechanism of action: Calcium reduces parathyroid hormone and 1,25-OH-vitD levels and thus reduces peripheral vascular resistance
Key features and challenges:
During pregnancy, substantial transplacental calcium transfer occurs, particularly in the third trimester, to support fetal skeletal mineralization. This places increased demand on maternal calcium homeostasis. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends daily supplementation of 1.5–2.0 g of elemental calcium for pregnant women in populations with low dietary calcium intake.
A Cochrane review of 27 studies reported that calcium supplementation reduced the average risk of preterm birth; however, this protective effect was not statistically significant at lower doses (<1 g/day). These findings suggest that dosage may influence clinical effectiveness.
Calcium supplementation has also received attention for its role in reducing the risk of preeclampsia, which may indirectly decrease medically indicated preterm birth. However, direct evidence supporting calcium supplementation specifically for prevention of spontaneous preterm labour remains limited.
Implementation challenges include uncertainty regarding the minimal effective dose and optimal dosing strategy. Calcium may interfere with iron absorption, and separating calcium from iron–folic acid supplementation may require multiple daily administrations, potentially reducing adherence. Some studies have reported associations between calcium supplementation and adverse outcomes such as HELLP syndrome, postnatal bone resorption, and cardiovascular effects, although dose dependency remains unclear.
A large randomized clinical trial conducted in India and Tanzania compared 1,500 mg versus 500 mg calcium supplementation during pregnancy (NCT03350516). The trial was completed in 2022; results have not yet been published.
(Source: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03350516)
Recent updates:
November 2018: A large trial in India and Tanzania to compare the effectiveness between 1500 mg or 500 mg calcium supplement began (NCT03350516). 

2024: The trial was completed in December 2022. Results have not been published

Name: Mineral - Magnesium - PTL/PTB
Developers: Institute of Integral Medicine Professor Fernando Figueira (IMIP)
Indication: Reducing risk of preterm labour/birth
Mechanism of action: Undefined mechanism
Key features and challenges:
Magnesium is one of the essential minerals which works with many enzymes to regulate body temperature, synthesise nucleic acids and proteins as well as maintaining electrical potentials in nerves and muscle membranes. Common causes of magnesium deficiency include inadequate dietary intake or gastrointestinal absorption, increased losses through the gastrointestinal or renal systems and increased requirement for magnesium, such as in pregnancy. Magnesium supplements are available as different salts: oxide, citrate, gluconate, aspartate and stearate.

A 2014 Cochrane review shows that oral magnesium supplementation compared to no magnesium was associated with no significant difference in preterm birth (seven trials; 5981 women) (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24696187/). This result was supported by results from the BRAMAG trial (NCT02032186), which measured a composite neonatal outcome comprising preterm birth, still birth, neonatal death or NICU admission, and small-for-gestational-age birth weight and reported no benefits of oral magnesium citrate (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32316938). In addition, magnesium citrate also did not reduce the risk of maternal complications, including preeclampsia/eclampsia, severe gestational hypertension, placental abruption, or maternal stroke or death during pregnancy.

Inversely, a 2017 paper did find beneficial effects of magnesium supplementation on the incidence of preterm birth and other preganncy-related conditions (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5590399/).

A 2024 Cochrane review determined while magnesium sulphate may result in little to no difference in severe maternal outcomes (death, cardiac arrest, respiratory arrest), it probably increases maternal adverse effects severe enough to stop treatment. (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11082932/)

Interventional trial expected to complete in early 2026 is examining effectiveness of magnesium for tocolysis in women with threatened preterm labour. (NCT05345132)
Recent updates:
2020: The BRAMAG trial reported that magnesium citrate did not improve neonatal or maternal outcomes (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32316938).

2021: Interventional trial completed in 2021 examining effects of magnesium in reducing occurance of preterm labour. No results have been posted.

2026: Interventional trial expected to complete in early 2026 is examining effectiveness of magnesium for tocolysis in women with threatened preterm labour. (NCT05345132)

Name: Mip inhibitor
Developers: University of Wurzburg, Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg; University of Western Australia (UWA)
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Inhibition of macrophage infectivity potentiator (Mip) protein
Key features and challenges:
Mip inhibitor is a small-molecule therapeutic candidate targeting the macrophage infectivity potentiator (Mip) protein, a virulence-associated peptidyl-prolyl cis/trans isomerase implicated in bacterial survival and host interaction. Rapamycin-derived Mip inhibitors have been developed to enhance binding affinity and enzymatic inhibition across multiple bacterial species, including Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
A 2023 study reported that these inhibitors demonstrated nanomolar affinity for the Mip protein of Burkholderia pseudomallei and exhibited strong anti-enzymatic activity against Mip proteins from Neisseria meningitidis and N. gonorrhoeae (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37389560/). 
Treatment resulted in reduced bacterial cytotoxicity in macrophages and improved macrophage-mediated bacterial killing, suggesting potential as a host-directed or anti-virulence therapeutic strategy.
Key challenges include the need for validation of in vivo efficacy in gonococcal infection models, assessment of pharmacokinetics and safety in systemic use, and determination of resistance development risk. Translational feasibility and specificity toward gonococcal targets also require further investigation.
Overall, Mip inhibitors represent a novel anti-virulence therapeutic strategy with demonstrated in vitro activity against N. gonorrhoeae. Further preclinical evaluation is required to determine their clinical development potential.

Name: Mirabegron
Developers: University of Nevada, Reno
Indication: Prevention of preterm birth.
Mechanism of action: Measures caveolin-1 as a marker of endothelial signaling and vascular dysfunction associated with placental insufficiency.
Key features and challenges:
Mirabegron is a monocarboxylic acid amide obtained by formal condensation of the carboxy group of 2-amino-1,3-thiazol-4-ylacetic acid with the anilino group of (1R)-2-{[2-(4-aminophenyl)ethyl]amino}-1-phenylethanol. It is a member of 1,3-thiazoles, an aromatic amide, a member of ethanolamines and a monocarboxylic acid amide.

Prolonged-release mirabegron tablets is launched and the suspension formulation of mirabegron is approved in the US for the treatment of neurogenic detrusor overactivity in paediatric patients. Clinical development for suspension formulation is ongoing in several countries.

It has a role as a beta-adrenergic agonist. The β3 adrenergic receptor-mediated relaxation of the human myometrium is claimed to be cAMP-dependent protein kinase-dependent. This is scientifically displeasing given the failure of β2 agonists as tocolytics and suggests a non-canonical signaling role for β3AR in myometrium. 
The addition of the β3 agonist mirabegron to pregnant human myometrial strips in the tissue bath relaxes oxytocin-induced contractions. Mirabegron stimulates nitric oxide production in myometrial microvascular endothelial cells, and the relaxation of uterine tissue in vitro is partially blocked by the addition of the endothelial nitric oxide synthase blocker Nω-Nitro-L-arginine. 

Recent data suggest that both endothelial and smooth muscle cells respond to β3 stimulation and contribute to relaxation through disparate signaling pathways. The repurposing of approved medications like mirabegron (Mybetriq™) tested in human myometrium as uterine tocolytics can advance the prevention of preterm birth.
(https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/13/6/1005)

Name: Mirvie RNA platform - PE
Developers: Mirvie
Indication: A method to identify distinct RNA profiles in maternal plasma that are predictive of preeclampsia.
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: cell-free RNA profiles in maternal blood
Mechanism of action: Analyzes biochemical spectral fingerprints of biological samples to identify metabolic signatures associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
The Mirvie RNA platform was developed to predict pregnancy complications before they become symptomatic using a blood test. The platform combines analysis of tens of thousands of RNA messages from the fetus, the placenta, and the pregnant woman with machine learning (https://www.mirvie.com/). This product is in development, it has not been cleared by the FDA, and is unavailable for sale in the United States. 
 
A 2022 study conducted by Mirvie analysed RNA in 524 blood samples collected at 14.5 weeks before delivery with the Mirvie RNA platform. cfRNA signatures were identified (seven genes: CLDN7, PAPPA2, SNORD14A, PLEKHH1, MAGEA10, TLE6, and FABP1) and able to predict pre-eclampsia with a sensitivity of 75% and a positive predictive value of 32.3% (s.d., 3%). cfRNA signatures of normal pregnancy progression and pre-eclampsia were independent of clinical factors, such as maternal age, body mass index and race, which cumulatively accounted for less than 1% of model variance. The cfRNA signature for pre-eclampsia also contained gene features linked to biological processes implicated in the underlying pathophysiology of pre-eclampsia, which could contribute to a better understanding of the pathology (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-021-04249-w).​ 

In August 2023, Mirvie announced receiving a $4.6 million grant from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation to support studies in Cameroon, Ghana, and Zambia to understand preeclampsia among pregnant women in low- and middle-income countries (LMIC) using the Mirvie RNA platform.
Recent updates:
This product is in development. It has not been cleared by the FDA and is not available for sale in the United States.
Received clinical laboratory improvement amendments (CLIA) certification in September 2023 (https://www.mirvie.com/mirvie-media-releases/mirvie-becomes-first-rna-based-pregnancy-health-focused-company-to-receive-clinical-laboratory-improvement-amendments-clia-certification)

Name: Mirvie RNA platform - PTL
Developers: Mirvie
Indication: A method to identify distinct RNA profiles in maternal plasma that are predictive of early and very early sPTB.
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: cell-free RNA profiles in maternal blood
Mechanism of action: Cell-free RNA is extracted from a single serum sample. Plasma is processed via a next-generation sequencing pipeline for cell-free RNA using the Mirvie RNA platform.
Key features and challenges:
The Mirvie RNA platform is an investigational blood-based test designed to predict pregnancy complications before clinical symptoms arise. The platform analyses cell-free RNA (cfRNA) transcripts derived from the fetus, placenta, and pregnant individual, integrating large-scale transcriptomic profiling with machine learning algorithms. The product is currently in development, has not received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) clearance, and is not commercially available in the United States.
(https://www.mirvie.com/)
In 2022, a study evaluated whether second-trimester maternal plasma cfRNA profiles could identify a molecular signature associated with subsequent spontaneous preterm birth. The findings indicated that cfRNA expression patterns in maternal blood months before delivery were associated with later spontaneous PTB. The predictive signal was linked to alterations in collagen and extracellular matrix pathways, suggesting early molecular changes consistent with premature cervical remodelling.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35398029/)
The platform is currently being evaluated in a multi-center, prospective observational cohort study involving second-trimester blood collection. Maternal plasma undergoes transcriptomic and multi-omic analysis, and biological markers are integrated with detailed clinical pregnancy data, including outcomes such as preterm birth and preeclampsia, to validate the investigational predictive model. Results have not yet been reported.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06074601)
Overall, the Mirvie RNA platform represents a molecular, systems-level approach to early prediction of spontaneous preterm birth. While early transcriptomic findings are promising, prospective validation and regulatory review are required before clinical implementation.
Recent updates:
This product is in development. It has not been cleared by the FDA and is not available for sale in the United States.
Received clinical laboratory improvement amendments (CLIA) certification in September 2023 (https://www.mirvie.com/mirvie-media-releases/mirvie-becomes-first-rna-based-pregnancy-health-focused-company-to-receive-clinical-laboratory-improvement-amendments-clia-certification)

Name: MitoTEMPO (MT)
Developers: Zhejiang University
Indication: MitoTEMPO is a mitochondria-targeted antioxidant evaluated for prevention of preterm birth and fetal injury in an LPS-induced mouse model of inflammation-driven preterm labour.
Target:
-Mitochondrial superoxide and associated ROS pathways.
-Keap1 (Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1).
-Nrf2/ARE (antioxidant response element) signalling.
Mechanism of action: MitoTEMPO acts as a mitochondria-targeted antioxidant that reduces maternal oxidative stress and inflammation. In LPS-induced preterm birth models, it enhances placental mitochondrial function, decreases ROS accumulation, promotes Keap1 degradation, and activates Nrf2, leading to downstream antioxidant and anti-inflammatory signalling. This prevents inflammatory cascades that trigger preterm labour and protects fetal brain development.
Key features and challenges:
MitoTEMPO (MT) is a mitochondria-targeted antioxidant that selectively scavenges mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS). By accumulating within mitochondria, MT mitigates oxidative stress and preserves mitochondrial function. Oxidative injury and inflammation are key contributors to infection-driven preterm labour (PTL), particularly in the context of placental and maternal tissue dysfunction.
Preclinical studies have demonstrated that MT reduces lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammatory responses in placental and maternal tissues. In animal models, MT administration prevented preterm birth and reduced fetal injury, including protection against fetal brain damage and improvements in both acute and long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes.
In vitro studies using trophoblast cells showed that MT suppresses ROS accumulation and inflammatory signaling through degradation of Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1) and activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. Activation of the Nrf2/antioxidant response element (ARE) pathway was identified as essential for therapeutic efficacy, supporting a pathway-specific antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanism.
https://www.liebertpub.com/doi/10.1089/ars.2023.0382
Despite compelling mechanistic data, evidence remains entirely preclinical. No human clinical studies have evaluated MT in pregnancy, and safety, pharmacokinetics, and placental transfer characteristics are unknown. Mitochondria-targeted antioxidants are experimental and not approved for obstetric use. Additionally, demonstrated efficacy is limited to LPS-induced PTL models, and generalizability to other PTL phenotypes, such as sterile inflammation or cervical insufficiency, remains uncertain.
MitoTEMPO represents a mechanistically novel antioxidant strategy targeting mitochondrial oxidative injury in PTL. While preclinical findings suggest potential for preventing inflammation-driven preterm birth and fetal injury, substantial translational research is required before clinical application in human pregnancy can be considered.
Recent updates: 2024: Publication of preclinical data showing MitoTEMPO prevents LPS-induced preterm birth, reduces placental oxidative stress, and protects against fetal brain injury (https://www.liebertpub.com/doi/10.1089/ars.2023.0382)

Name: Mitomic Endometriosis Test
Developers: MDNA Life Sciences; Pearsanta
Indication: Diagnosis of endometriosis via blood protein biomarkers' detection
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Measures mitochondrial DNA mutations or expression profiles to identify cellular stress patterns associated with endometriosis.
Key features and challenges:
The Mitomic Endometriosis Test (MET) is a diagnostic blood test developed by MDNA Life Sciences to detect endometriosis by analyzing specific protein biomarkers in the blood (8.7kb mitochondrial DNA deletion). The test aims to identify the presence of endometriosis and its subtypes or stages, potentially reducing the need for invasive laparoscopic surgery if the results are conclusive.

A 2019 study evaluated mitochondrial DNA deletions as potential biomarkers for endometriosis, by quantitative polymerase chain reaction (QPCR) using well-characterized clinical specimens from all subtypes and stages of endometriosis in a case–control format (n = 182). It found that deletions (1.2 and 3.7 kb) detected in blood differentiated between endometriosis and controls (area under the curve [AUC] 0.71–0.90). Differences in deletion levels were statistically significant (p < 0.05) for all disease subtypes and stages (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/10.2217/bmm-2018-0419).

Building on this result, the MET test was developed and its accuracy is currently being evaluated in a study started in 2020. The study will recruit 600 female patients scheduled for their first laparoscopy to diagnose suspected endometriosis. Participants will have an extra blood sample taken for MET analysis and will continue with their planned laparoscopic procedure. Data collected from the MET results, along with details from the surgery and patient-reported symptoms, will be used to evaluate the test's accuracy in diagnosing endometriosis and its subtypes. The study will span from January 2020 to May 2027, conducted across approximately 12 sites (https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN13298303) ; (https://mdnalifesciences.com/mitomic-tests/).

Name: Mix-12/MPX-EPs vaccine
Developers: Shenzhen Bay Laboratory
Indication: Prevention of mpox infection
Target:
-Humoral: MPXV EV + MV surface proteins (12 key neutralizing antigens)
-Cellular: Epitope-enriched MPXV proteome regions presented via HLA-I to CD8⁺ T cells.
Mechanism of action:
Mix-12 provides broad neutralizing antibody diversity against EV and MV surface proteins.
MPX-EPs drives strong CD8⁺ T-cell activation (CTLs), with ubiquitin-tag facilitating proteasomal degradation and epitope presentation.
Co-administration (MPX-m-Mix) synergizes humoral and cellular immunity, providing sterilizing protection against MPXV in mice.
Key features and challenges:
-Humoral potency: Mix-12 induced the highest neutralizing antibody titers (NT₅₀ ~ 1:1195), outperforming Mix-4 and Mix-8.
-Cellular potency: MPX-EPs independently conferred CTL-mediated protection; depletion of CD8⁺ T cells abrogated protection.
-Combination efficacy: MPX-m-Mix achieved complete protection in humanized HLA-A*02:01/DR1 mice challenged intranasally with 10⁷ PFU MPXV; no lung viral load or pathology detected.
-Durability: Neutralizing antibodies and lung-resident memory CD8⁺ T cells persisted up to 150 days post-boost.
-Bias: Induced Th1-dominant responses (IFN-γ, TNF-α, Granzyme B).
-Challenges: Very complex formulation (12 mRNAs + 1 CTL construct); manufacturing, cost, and regulatory pathway may complicate scale-up. Needs validation in NHPs.
Recent updates:
-Part of a new generation of polyvalent mpox mRNA vaccines (e.g., Zuiani et al. BNT166, Ye et al. Rmix6, Li et al. MPXV-1103).
-This is the first mpox vaccine to demonstrate synergistic humoral + CTL protection in a humanized HLA mouse model.
-Broader implications: Dual immune activation strategy may serve as a template for future orthopox and pandemic vaccines.
-A patent application has been filed covering this antigen design.

Name: Modified vaccinia Ankara - Bavarian Nordic - Paediatric
Developers: Universiteit Antwerpen; Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp; University College Dublin; Bavarian Nordic
Indication: Active immunization for the prevention of mpox disease among children
Target: B6 (B6R) envelope glycoprotein, B2, C18, A29L and H3L surface proteins
Mechanism of action: Immunostimulant
Key features and challenges:
Modified vaccinia Ankara is a third-generation, live, non-replicating, prophylactic vaccine, developed by Bavarian Nordic as an intradermal and subcutaneous injection for the prevention of smallpox bioterror attack, monkeypox and vaccinia virus infections. This product consists of a highly attenuated strain of Modified Vaccinia Ankara (MVA) virus that does not replicate in human cells, thus alleviating the safety concerns of previous smallpox vaccines that were based on various replicating vaccinia virus strains. IMVAMUNE® is expected to be effective and offer protection against smallpox in 3 days following a single injection, compared with traditional vaccines that only show protection after 10-14 days. The vaccine is launched in the US and Canada for prevention of smallpox and monkeypox disease. The vaccine is available in the European Union, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and approved in Switzerland for prevention of small pox, monkeypox and for the prevention of disease caused by vaccinia virus. The subcutaneous liquid-frozen formulation is available in the US, Canada and approved in the United Kingdom for the prevention of small pox and monkeypox. The vaccine is also approved for use as under emergency use authorization for the prevention of monkeypox infection in Democratic Republic of the Congo and Nigeria. The vaccine is approved in Singapore for the prevention of small pox and monkeypox. The freeze-dried formulation of the vaccine is under regulatory review in the US for the prevention of small pox and monkeypox. Clinical development is underway in Mexico, South Korea, Germany, Puerto Rico.

CEPI has awarded USD 6.5 million to support a Phase 2 clinical study evaluating the immunogenicity and safety of the MVA-BN® non-replicating vaccine in children from 2 years to less than 12 years of age compared to adults aged 18-50 years of age for the prevention of smallpox, mpox and related orthopoxvirus infections. Subject to regulatory approvals, the study plans to enroll a total of approximately 460 healthy individuals in endemic regions without previous mpox infection or poxvirus vaccination, who will receive two doses of the MVA-BN vaccine. Bavarian Nordic will be the sponsor of the trial which will be conducted in one or more African countries with planned initiation later in 2024 (https://cepi.net/bavarian-nordic-and-cepi-partner-advance-mpox-vaccination-africa#:~:text=CEPI%20has%20awarded%20USD%206.5%20million%2A%20to%20support,prevention%20of%20smallpox%2C%20mpox%20and%20related%20orthopoxvirus%20infections.).

Name: Moenomycin
Developers: McMaster University; Zhejiang University
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Moenomycin penetrates the Gram-negative gonococcal outer membrane. Moenomycin causes intracellular accumulation of peptidoglycan precursors, cell blebbing, and rupture of the cell envelope, all consistent with cell wall biosynthesis inhibition
Key features and challenges:
Moenomycin is a natural product antibiotic that inhibits peptidoglycan biosynthesis by targeting transglycosylation in bacterial cell wall formation and is being investigated as a therapeutic candidate against multidrug-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Although historically considered active primarily against Gram-positive bacteria, moenomycin has demonstrated the ability to penetrate the outer membrane of N. gonorrhoeae.
A 2021 study identified moenomycin from a microbial natural product screen as a potent antigonococcal agent, demonstrating minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of 0.004–0.03 μg/mL against multidrug-resistant strains (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33826296/). 
The compound induced intracellular accumulation of peptidoglycan precursors, cell blebbing, and cell envelope rupture, consistent with inhibition of cell wall biosynthesis. Serial exposure over 14 days resulted in slow resistance development compared with azithromycin. A 2022 study further evaluated moenomycin against 575 clinical isolates and in a murine vaginal tract infection model, where intramuscular administration (10 mg/kg for two consecutive days) cleared infection within 1–3 days following treatment (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35762496/). 
Time-kill assays confirmed bactericidal activity with >10⁴-fold reduction after 4 hours of exposure.
Key challenges include optimization of pharmacokinetic properties for human use, formulation considerations given historical limitations of moenomycin derivatives, and assessment of safety in systemic administration. Translation from murine models to human clinical efficacy will require careful evaluation.
Overall, moenomycin demonstrates potent in vitro and in vivo activity against multidrug-resistant N. gonorrhoeae. Further preclinical optimization is needed to support advancement as an alternative therapeutic option.

Name: Molecular assay (ParC) wildtype sequences
Developers: University of Melbourne (including the Australian Venom Research Unit (AVRU) and Bio21 Institute)
Indication: Detection of Mycoplasma genitalium and antimicrobial susceptibility
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Detects mutations in the ParC gene associated with fluoroquinolone resistance to inform antimicrobial susceptibility in Mycoplasma genitalium.
Key features and challenges:
A 2022 study developed two proof-of-concept molecular tests that focus on detection of M. genitalium and characterization of WT parC sequences that are strongly linked to fluoroquinolone susceptibility. They screened a total of 227 M. genitalium-positive samples using novel molecular beacon and dual hybridization probe assays. These assays were able to detect M. genitalium and characterize fluoroquinolone susceptibility in 143/227 (63%) samples, based on clear differences in melting peak temperatures. The results of these molecular assays were in 100% agreement with ‘gold standard’ Sanger sequencing. Name: Molnupiravir
Developers: National Institute for Infectious Diseases, Tokyo
Indication: Treatment of mpox infection (therapeutic candidate, repurposed drug)

Key features and challenges:
-IC₅₀ = ~1.35 µM; IC₉₀ = ~3.25 µM in VeroE6 MPXV assays.
-Showed stronger potency than cidofovir; protected cells from MPXV cytopathic effects at ≤10 µM.
-Pharmacokinetic modeling: antiviral effect achieved briefly but declines rapidly due to short half-life (~1 hr plasma t½).
-Mathematical models predicted mild clinical effect against mpox compared to its efficacy in SARS-CoV-2 (requires ~4–10× higher concentration for equivalent inhibition).
-Orally bioavailable and already FDA-approved for COVID-19, enabling repurposing.
-Limitation: transient activity window; high dose may be required for clinical impact against mpox.
Recent updates:
-Molnupiravir continues to be studied as a broad-spectrum antiviral (coronaviruses, alphaviruses, norovirus, chikungunya).
-Concerns remain about mutagenesis risk to host DNA, limiting long-term or prophylactic use.
-Repurposing for mpox is considered lower priority compared to tecovirimat or DHODH inhibitors (e.g., atovaquone, brequinar).

Name: Moraxella osloensis + chemokine CC motif ligand 2
Developers: Hallym University Medical Center
Indication: Prediction of preterm labour
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: vaginal microbiome, immune-checkpoint proteins and inflammatory cytokines
Mechanism of action: Measures serum TSH to detect thyroid dysfunction that may mimic or exacerbate PCOS-related menstrual irregularities.
Key features and challenges: Microenvironmental factors like microbe-driven inflammation and immune-checkpoint proteins that influence immune cells have been linked to both cervical insufficiency and preterm delivery. A 2023 study set out to examine and compare how the microbiome and inflammatory factors, including cytokines and immune-checkpoint proteins, interact in patients with these conditions, and to assess their predictive value. Researchers collected 220 swab samples from 110 pregnant women recruited at the High-Risk Maternal Neonatal Intensive Care Center between February 2020 and March 2021, including 63 cervical insufficiency patients receiving cerclage and 47 controls. Endo- and exocervical swabs and fluids were taken at the same time, followed by shotgun metagenomic sequencing and measurement of 34 immune-checkpoint proteins and inflammatory cytokines. The results showed that immune-checkpoint proteins could be detected in both sample types, revealed distinct microenvironments associated with cervical insufficiency and preterm birth, and pinpointed clinically useful cervical locations. Notably, the presence of Moraxella osloensis (odds ratio = 14.785; P = 0.037) and chemokine CC motif ligand 2 levels above 73 pg/mL (odds ratio = 40.049; P = 0.005) in endocervical samples were linked to preterm birth. Combining these two factors provided strong predictive performance (AUC = 0.846, 95% CI = 0.733–0.925).(https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2023.1228647/full)

Name: Moxidectin - Lymphatic filariasis
Developers: Medicines Development for Global Health (MDGH) Ltd; Washington University in Saint Louis; Case Western Reserve University
Indication: Investigated for the treatment of Lymphatic filariasis.
Target: In Onchocerca volvulus, Glutamate-gated chloride channel, GABA-A gated chloride channel, and ABC transporters.
Mechanism of action: In O. volvulus, moxidectin selectively binds to the parasite's GABA-A and glutamate-gated chloride ion channels which are vital for the function of invertebrate nerve and muscle cells. It presents activity against the parasite but it does not kill it. Once moxidectin is bound, there is an increased permeability leading to an influx of chloride ions and flaccid paralysis of the parasite.
Key features and challenges:
Moxidectin is a potent, broad-spectrum endectocide (antiparasitic that is active against endo- and ecto-parasites) with activity against nematodes, insects, and acari. It was first used in cattle followed by an approved use in general animals. It is a semi-synthetic methoxine derivative of nemadectin which is a 16-member pentacyclic lactone of the milbemycin class. Moxidectin differs by the absence of a disaccharide moiety on carbon 13, a substituted olefinic side chain at carbon 25 and a unique methoxime moiety at carbon 23. Due to these modifications, moxidectin is classified as a second generation macrocyclic lactone. Moxidectin was developed by Medicines Development for Global Health (MDGH) and FDA approved in June 13, 2018 (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB11431).

MDGH are studying the effects of Moxidectin on lymphatic filariasis.  MDGH are collaborating in a Phase 2/3 lymphatic filariasis study being conducted in Côte d'Ivoire by the Death to Onchocerciasis and Lymphatic Filariasis (DOLF) project run by Washington University, St. Louis, USA, with the Regional Hospital of Agboville (Côte d'Ivoire) and Case Western Reserve University (USA) as collaborators. This study was initiated in Q3 2020 and will evaluate the safety and efficacy of moxidectin in combination with albendazole and diethylcarbamazine. Preliminary results from this study were presented at the 2022 American Society of Tropical Medicine & Hygiene meeting in Seattle, Washington, USA (https://www.medicinesdevelopment.com/diseases/lymphatic-filariasis).
Recent updates: A preliminary study compared four different moxidectin or ivermectin combination regimens for lymphatic filariasis and concluded that moxidectin plus albendazole is superior to ivermectin plus albendazole, which is the current standard of care for annual mass drug administration for lymphatic filariasis in Africa, in sustained clearance of microfilaremia at 12 months after a single treatment. Authors also note that moxidectin plus albendazole efficacy at 12 months is similar to ivermectin plus albendazole and diethylcarbamazine (IDA) and moxidectin plus albendazole and diethylcarbamazine (MoxDA) combinations (https://www.medicinesdevelopment.com/news/american-society-of-tropical-medicine-and-hygiene-annual-meeting-2).

Name: Mueller polarimetric colposcopy
Developers: Bicetre hospital
Indication: Tool for evaluating cervical microstructure modification during pregnancy to predict preterm birth.
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Mueller polarimetric colposcopy evaluates cervical microstructure modification during pregnancy. The "polarimetric biomarkers" are the most relevant polarimetric parameters (or a combination of them) characterizing the cervical microstructure modifications during a normal pregnancy. Using different algebraic methods, they can be the main polarimetric parameters obtained from the measured Mueller matrices.
Key features and challenges:
Mueller polarimetric imaging is an optical technique that enables detection and quantification of microstructural changes in collagen fibres within biological tissues. It has previously been investigated in the context of identifying precancerous cervical lesions, demonstrating its ability to characterise tissue microarchitecture.
(2017 – https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28572602/)
Given that cervical remodelling during pregnancy involves progressive alterations in collagen organisation and biomechanical properties, Mueller polarimetric colposcopy (MPC) has been adapted to assess cervical microstructure in obstetric applications. The technology integrates a miniaturised Mueller polarimetric imager with a conventional colposcope, allowing acquisition of Mueller matrices in a clinical setting with minimal disruption to routine examination practice.
A clinical trial conducted between 2020 and 2024 is evaluating MPC for analysis of cervical microstructural modifications occurring during pregnancy. Preliminary evidence suggests that certain polarimetric parameters correlate with gestational age, indicating potential utility in identifying early cervical remodelling associated with risk of preterm labour and birth. Study results have not yet been published.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04661553)
Technical challenges include the need for compact device design while maintaining rapid and accurate image acquisition under real-world clinical conditions. Device miniaturisation and integration into standard colposcopic platforms aim to address these limitations.
Overall, Mueller polarimetric colposcopy represents an investigational imaging approach for quantitative assessment of cervical collagen architecture. While conceptually aligned with early detection of cervical remodelling preceding PTL/PTB, further clinical validation is required to establish predictive performance and practical implementation.

A study was performed using two routes: proteome-mediated therapeutic target identification and mapping as well as multi-epitopic peptide-based novel vaccine development using state of the art of computational biology for the TN strain of M. leprae.
For multi-epitope peptide-based vaccine development, the four common types of B and T cell epitopes were identified (SLFQSHNRK, VVGIGQHAA, MMHRSPRTR, LGVDQTQPV) and combined with the suitable peptide linker. The vaccine component had an acceptable protective antigenic score (0.9751). The molecular docking of vaccine components with TLR4/MD2 complex exhibited a low ACE value (−244.12) which signifies the proper binding between the two molecules. The estimated free Gibbs binding energy ensured accurate protein-protein interactions (−112.46 kcal/mol). The vaccine was evaluated through adaptive immunity stimulation as well as immune interactions. The molecular dynamic simulation was carried out by using CHARMM topology-based parameters to minimize the docked complex. Subsequently, the Normal Mode Analysis in the internal coordinates showed a low eigen-value (1.3982892e−05), which also signifies the stability of molecular docking. Finally, the vaccine components were adopted for reverse transcription and codon optimization in E. coli strain K12 for the pGEX-4T1 vector, which supports in silico cloning of the vaccine components against the pathogen (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1567134822000429?via%3Dihub).

Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: Maternal characterisitics (BMI, history of preterm birth and second trimester loss) + serum C-reactive protein
Mechanism of action: Combines postoperative cervical measurements and clinical variables to predict residual risk of preterm birth after cerclage placement.
Key features and challenges: Researchers at Zhejiang University School of Medicine explored factors linked to preterm birth in women who had undergone ultrasound-indicated cerclage. In this retrospective study, 87 pregnant women with prior preterm births or second-trimester losses received the procedure between January 2004 and April 2021. They looked at BMI, obstetric history, and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels. Higher BMI (OR = 1.224, p < 0.05), a history of preterm birth and second-trimester loss (OR = 3.153, p < 0.05), and CRP levels over 5 mg/L (OR = 8.097, p < 0.05) were found to be independent risk factors for delivering after 28 weeks. The combined predictor including these factors had an AUC of 0.849 (95% CI: 0.701–0.998, p < 0.05). Elevated CRP was also a significant independent risk factor for gestational age at delivery. The study concluded that high BMI, repeated adverse obstetric history, and abnormal CRP could be used together to identify women at higher risk for preterm birth before 28 weeks after surgery. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1028455923000293?via%3Dihub)

Name: Multiparameter screening tool: anogenital distance and medical history
Developers: The Royal Women's Hospital; University of Melbourne (including the Australian Venom Research Unit (AVRU) and Bio21 Institute)
Indication: To rule out endometriosis in patients with pelvic pain
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Mechanism of action: Combines anatomical measurements and clinical risk factors to stratify likelihood of endometriosis.
Key features and challenges:
The University of Melbourne is developing a screening tool to rule out endometriosis in individuals with pelvic pain based on medical history and anogenital distance.
A study registered in 2021 planned to recruit participants scheduled for laparoscopy. They will complete a pre-operative questionnaire about their demographics, symptoms, and medical history. Additionally, their anogenital distance (AGD) will be measured under anesthesia just before surgery. The presence or absence of endometriosis will be documented during the laparoscopy, and pre-operative variables will be used to create a predictive model for determining the likelihood of not having endometriosis.
The study will assess the accuracy of the predictive model using metrics such as sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. The definitive diagnosis of endometriosis will be based on a combination of laparoscopic and histopathological findings. The goal is to create a tool that helps predict the absence of endometriosis pre-operatively, potentially reducing unnecessary surgeries and guiding more appropriate treatment for pelvic pain.
(https://anzctr.org.au/Trial/Registration/TrialReview.aspx?ACTRN=12621000357853)
No results have been published and the clinical trial website has not been updated since registration (2021).

Name: Multivariable prediction model
Developers: Barcelona Center for Maternal-Fetal and Neonatal Medicine
Indication: Predict PTB within 7 days and microbial invasion of the amniotic cavity in women with preterm labour
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: ultrasound cervical length, maternal C-reactive protein, amniotic fluid glucose, and interleukin-6.
Mechanism of action:
The model to predict spontaneous preterm delivery within 7 days included
gestational age at admission, ultrasound cervical length measurement, amniotic
fluid glucose, and interleukin-6. The model to predict the microbial invasion of the amniotic cavity included maternal C-reactive protein and amniotic fluid glucose.
Key features and challenges:
The multivariable prediction model is designed to identify women at risk of spontaneous delivery within seven days and to detect microbial invasion of the amniotic cavity (MIAC) among patients admitted with preterm labour (PTL) and intact membranes before 34 weeks’ gestation. MIAC and intraamniotic inflammation (IAI) are recognized contributors to preterm birth and are important determinants of clinical management and neonatal outcomes.
In 2020, the model was clinically validated in a cohort of women presenting with PTL before 34 weeks. Predictive variables incorporated into the model included ultrasound-measured cervical length at admission, maternal C-reactive protein (CRP), gestational age, amniotic fluid glucose, and interleukin-6 (IL-6) concentrations. The model demonstrated high diagnostic performance in identifying women at risk of imminent delivery and intraamniotic infection.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32147290/)
Overall, this multivariable approach integrates clinical, biochemical, and ultrasound parameters to support short-term risk stratification in symptomatic PTL. While initial validation indicates strong diagnostic performance, further external validation studies are required to assess generalisability and implementation feasibility across diverse clinical settings.

Name: Mundulone
Developers: Vanderbilt University Medical Center
Indication: tocolytic therapy for the management of preterm labor
Mechanism of action: Measures maternal iron stores and inflammatory status associated with impaired fetal growth.
Key features and challenges:
The isoflavone natural-product mundulone, and its derivative mundulone acetate (MA) have recently been identified as potent antagonists of Ca2+-mobilization from primary myometrial cells, thus having a tocolytic effect. 

Mundulone is extracted from the bark of Mundulea sericea and its structure was elucidated in 1959 as part of the isoflavone subclass of flavonoids. Isoflavones have several pharmacological effects, including modulation of smooth muscle contractions in the uterus and vasculature. Moreover, a recent review on natural products for tocolysis found that most plant extracts for inhibition of uterine contractions belong to flavonoid or terpene classes, making mundulone and MA belong to a promising class of tocolytic compounds.

Based on previous fundings, the compounds inhibit in vitro myometrial Ca2+-mobilization. The recent preclinical study sought to examine the uterine selectivity of Ca2+-mobilization inhibition, determine cytotoxicity, identify synergistic combinations of mundulone and MA with current clinically- utilized tocolytics, establish the ex vivo tocolytic efficacy and potency and confirm uterine selectivity at the tissue level and, evaluate the in vivo efficacy to delay delivery onset using a mouse model of PL and PTB.

The study showed that mundulone had greater efficacy in the inhibition of intracellular-Ca2+ from myometrial cells; however, MA showed greater potency and uterine-selectivity. Cell viability assays revealed that MA was significantly less cytotoxic. Organ bath and vessel myography studies showed that only mundulone exerted concentration-dependent inhibition of ex vivo myometrial contractions and that neither mundulone or MA affected vasoreactivity of ductus arteriosus, a major fetal off-target of current tocolytics. 

Mundulone exhibited synergism with two clinical-tocolytics (atosiban and nifedipine), and MA displayed synergistic efficacy with nifedipine. Of these synergistic combinations, mundulone + atosiban demonstrated a substantial improvement compared to mundulone alone. The ex vivo and in vivo synergism of mundulone and atosiban was substantiated, yielding greater tocolytic efficacy and potency on isolated mouse and human myometrial tissue and reduced preterm birth rates in a mouse model of PL compared to each single agent. Collectively, these studies provide a strong foundation for the future development of mundulone as a stand-alone single- and/or combination-tocolytic therapy for management of PL.
(https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2023.06.06.543921v1.article-info)
