Name: Mycophenolic acid (MPA)
Developers: National Institute for Infectious Diseases, Tokyo
Indication: Treatment of mpox infection (therapeutic candidate, repurposed drug)
Target: IMP dehydrogenase (IMPDH1/2), the rate-limiting enzyme in guanosine nucleotide biosynthesis.
Mechanism of action:
-Inhibits IMPDH, depleting intracellular GTP pools required for MPXV DNA/RNA synthesis.
-Blocks post-entry phase of MPXV replication, reducing DNA replication and virion production.
-Guanosine supplementation rescues viral replication, confirming IMPDH-dependent mechanism
Key features and challenges:
-Exhibits broad-spectrum anti-orthopoxvirus activity (active against MPXV clade I, IIa, IIb strains, vaccinia virus, and cowpox virus).
-In vitro potency: IC₉₀ values 0.026–0.89 mM, lower than brincidofovir.
-Selectivity index (SI): ~10.6 (less potent than newer IMPDH inhibitors such as AVN-944 or merimepodib).
-Does not induce interferon-stimulated genes at effective concentrations, suggesting direct metabolic restriction.
-Limitations: Host-directed mechanism may impair lymphocyte proliferation (MPA is an immunosuppressant). Safety concerns restrict systemic therapeutic use.
Recent updates:
-IMPDH is being validated as a novel host target for mpox therapeutics. Several IMPDH inhibitors (AVN-944, merimepodib) show stronger anti-MPXV activity than MPA in vitro.
-MPA has a long history as an immunosuppressant in organ transplantation; its repurposing for antivirals is limited by systemic toxicity.
-Pan-antiviral potential: MPA inhibits replication of Zika, dengue, SARS-CoV-2, hepatitis C/E, and Lassa viruses.
-Current mpox therapeutic R&D is shifting toward next-gen IMPDH inhibitors with higher potency and better safety profiles.

Name: Myo-inositol
Developers: National University of Singapore (NUS)
Indication: For the prevention of preterm birth
Mechanism of action: Quantifies NrCAM as a biomarker of fetal or placental stress pathways associated with impaired growth.
Key features and challenges:
Inositol is a collection of nine different stereoisomers but the name is usually used to describe only the most common type of inositol, myo-inositol. Myo-inositol is the cis-1,2,3,5-trans-4,6-cyclohexanehexol. It is an inositol having myo- configuration. It has a role as a member of compatible osmolytes, a nutrient, an EC 3.1.4.11 (phosphoinositide phospholipase C) inhibitor, a human metabolite, a Daphnia magna metabolite, a Saccharomyces cerevisiae metabolite, an Escherichia coli metabolite and a mouse metabolite. 

Inositol, a carbocyclic sugar alcohol present in all living cells, is naturally found in plants and enriched in a wide variety of foods including cereals, legumes, nuts, seeds and fruits. In humans, inositol can be synthesized endogenously from glucose. The human kidney produces up to 4 grams of inositol daily, while a western diet can provide about 1 gram per day. It is commonly prepared from an aqueous extract of corn kernels by precipitation and hydrolysis of crude phytate. These molecules have structural similarities to glucose and are involved in cellular signaling. It is considered a pseudovitamin as it is a molecule that does not qualify to be an essential vitamin because even though its presence is vital in the body, a deficiency in this molecule does not translate into disease conditions.

Myo-inositol, the most abundant of 9 stereoisomers of inositol, is involved in a wide array of physiologically important roles. Inositol can be incorporated into a wide range of inositol derivatives with important structural and bioactive functions. Lipid-containing inositol derivatives such as phosphatidyl-inositol (PI) are an integral part of lipid cell membranes, where they regulate membrane fluidity, permeability, electro-potential and transmembrane transport. Many inositol derivatives such as inositol phosphates act as intercellular and intracellular signaling molecules and play important roles as second messengers in many hormonal signaling pathways including those of insulin and pituitary-derived trophic hormones. Some inositol derivatives such as inositol-phospho-glycans (IPGs) even act as endocrine factors, having effects at distant tissues.

Myo-inositol (also known as inositol) has been affirmed as generally recognized as safe (GRAS) by the FDA. As such, the ingredient is used in food with no limitations other than current good manufacturing practice. It’s commonly used as a nutrient supplement and in special dietary foods (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfcfr/CFRSearch.cfm?fr=184.1370)

In the context of pregnancy, myo-inositol is postulated to be a critical player in maintaining normal pregnancy physiology since underlying inositol dysregulation is implicated in several pregnancy pathologies such as GDM and pre-eclampsia. Several small open-label clinical trials of inositol supplementation for GDM prevention in metabolically at-risk pregnant women have observed trends of a reduction in PTB as a secondary outcome, pointing to the possible role of myo-inositol in reducing the incidence of PTB. When pooled, a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs (total n=927 women) showed that myo-inositol supplementation starting from the end of the first trimester resulted in a significant reduction in the risk of PTB (risk reduction [RR] 0.36 [95%CI 0.17-0.73]; p = 0.005). Another meta-analysis comprising a secondary analysis of just 3 of these RCTs in Italian women at risk of GDM (n=595) showed halving in the incidence of PTB (10/291 [3.4%] vs 23/304 [7.6%]; P=0.03) following myo-inositol supplementation (4g/day). 
(https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7614523/#R21)

Name: N,N-Dimethylformamide (DMF)
Developers: St. John's University
Indication: For the prevention of preterm birth
Mechanism of action: Profiles urinary polyamines to identify metabolic alterations associated with impaired placental function and fetal growth restriction.
Key features and challenges:
It has been discovered that the common drug excipient, N,N-dimethylacetamide (DMA), delays inflammation-induced preterm birth in mice by inhibiting NF-κB. Since this finding, it has come to light that a group of widely used, structurally related aprotic solvents, including DMA, N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) and dimethylformamide (DMF), have anti-inflammatory efficacy.

DMF suppresses LPS-induced TNFα secretion from RAW 264.7 cells and IL-6 and IL-8 secretion from HTR-8 cells at concentrations that do not significantly affect cell viability. Like DMA, DMF protects IκBα from degradation and prevents the p65 subunit of NF-κB from translocating to the nucleus. In vivo, DMF decreases LPS-induced inflammatory cell infiltration and expression of TNFα and IL-6 in the placental labyrinth, all to near baseline levels. Finally, DMF decreases the rate of preterm birth in LPS-induced pregnant mice (P<.0001) and the rate at which pups are spontaneously aborted (P<.0001). 

In summary, DMF, a widely used solvent structurally related to DMA and NMP, delays LPS-induced preterm birth in a murine model without overt toxic effects. Re-purposing the DMA/DMF/NMP family of small molecules as anti-inflammatory drugs is a promising new approach to delaying or reducing the incidence of inflammation-induced preterm birth and potentially attenuating other inflammatory disorders as well.
(https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43032-022-00924-z)

Name: N-Acetyl Cysteine (NAC)
Developers: AstraZeneca; Boehringer Ingelheim (including Merial)
Indication: Uterine fibroid inflammation and oxidative stress
Mechanism of action: Antioxidant; anti-inflammatory
Key features and challenges:
N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is a synthetic derivative of the amino acid cysteine. It is widely used as a medication due to its multiple therapeutic properties. NAC is known for its role as a mucolytic agent, which means it helps break down and thin mucus, making it easier to expel. This property is particularly useful in treating chronic respiratory conditions such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and cystic fibrosis. Additionally, NAC is used as an antidote for acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose. It works by replenishing glutathione, a vital antioxidant in the liver, thus preventing or mitigating liver damage caused by excessive acetaminophen. (https://adisinsight.springer.com/drugs/800021262)

The drug also has significant antioxidant properties, which help neutralize harmful free radicals and reduce oxidative stress. This makes NAC a subject of research for various other conditions where oxidative stress is a contributing factor. While NAC is well-established for its primary uses, its application in new areas, such as the treatment of uterine fibroids, requires further investigation. The effectiveness and safety of NAC for such emerging indications need to be confirmed through rigorous clinical trials and research. (https://adisinsight.springer.com/drugs/800021262)

Findings from a 2021 published study demonstrated the positive impact of NAC on uterine fibroids' size after 12 weeks, positioning the drug as a potential non-hormonal treatment for leiomyoma of the uterus. The authors noted that beyond reducing fibroids' size, the possibility of treatment failure in controlling abnormal uterine bleeding cannot be ignored.  (https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ijgo.13611)

A similar 2023 registered CT will assess the impact of Dienogest and N-Acetyl Cysteine on volume reduction of uterine leiomyoma. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06115408#study-plan)

Name: N-acetylcysteine
Developers: AstraZeneca; Arbor Pharmaceuticals; Hacettepe University
Indication: Indicated for the prevention and treatment of endometriosis pain and abnormal tissue growth
Mechanism of action: Antioxidants
Key features and challenges:
N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is a thiol-containing compound with antioxidant and antiproliferative properties. As a precursor to glutathione, NAC exerts both direct and indirect antioxidant effects by scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS) and increasing intracellular glutathione levels. In the context of endometriosis, oxidative stress and inflammation are implicated in lesion persistence and pain generation, providing a mechanistic rationale for NAC use. Preclinical and early clinical studies have suggested that NAC may reduce endometriotic lesion size, alleviate pain, lower Cancer Antigen 125 (CA125) levels, and potentially improve fertility outcomes.
A double-blind, randomized clinical trial initiated in 2021 is evaluating the effects of NAC on oxidative stress markers and pregnancy outcomes in women with endometrioma undergoing IVF/ICSI cycles (NCT05460858; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05460858). 
The study, conducted at the Royan Institute, enrolled 140 participants randomized to receive 1200 mg of NAC daily or placebo for six weeks in addition to standard IVF protocols. Outcomes include oxidative stress markers in blood and follicular fluid, pregnancy outcomes, and pain severity. Results have not yet been published.
In 2022, a clinical study involving 120 patients assessed quarterly oral NAC administration (600 mg, three tablets daily for three consecutive days per week for three months). Significant improvements were observed in dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and chronic pelvic pain (p < 0.0001), along with reductions in NSAID use (p = 0.001), ovarian endometrioma size (p < 0.0001), and serum CA125 levels (p < 0.0001) (https://www.mdpi.com/1660-4601/20/6/4686).
Key challenges include limited large-scale, multicenter randomized controlled trials, heterogeneity in dosing regimens, and lack of long-term outcome data. As an over-the-counter supplement in many jurisdictions, regulatory oversight and standardization may vary. Confirmation of sustained clinical benefit and reproductive outcomes in well-powered studies will be necessary to establish its role in routine endometriosis management.
Overall, NAC represents a low-cost, mechanistically plausible adjunctive therapy targeting oxidative stress in endometriosis. However, broader validation through rigorous randomized trials is required to clarify its clinical positioning and long-term impact.
Recent updates: TM 13/12/2025: Study identified from EMBASE (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-00195-z).

Name: N-alkyl-arylsulfonamide derivatives of lupeol acetate
Developers: Universidad de Quintana Roo
Indication: Investigated for the treatment of metronidazole susceptible and resistant Trichomonas vaginalis
Mechanism of action: Unknown.
Key features and challenges:
Pentacyclic triterpenes are a class of natural products that are used as starting materials in the search for new bioactive molecules.  Lupeol, a lupanetype pentacyclic triterpene, and its derivatives are known for their wide range of pharmacological properties, including anti-inflammatory, anti-microbial, anti-protozoal, anti-proliferative properties, among others.  Previous work isolated lupeol acetate from the fruit of a Chrysophyllum cainito L. (C. cainito) plant and reported on its anti-inflammatory activity, non-toxicity, and modest reduction of Trichomonas vaginalis viability. Sulfonamide derivatives have also been shown to have biological properties, including antibacterial, antifungal, antiparasitic, antioxidant, and antitumor properties, and have been used in the modification of pentacyclic triterpenes.
A 2021 published study that sought to generate a novel series of antiprotozoal agents introduced N-alkyl-arylsulfonamides at position 30 of lupeol acetate isolated from C. cainito fruits to synthesize and test the synergistic effects of Nalkyl-arylsulfonamide derivatives with metronidazole against strains of T. vaginalis.  Of the 18 derivatives that were synthesized, 10 compounds exhibited an IC50<100 lM against a metronidazole-sensitive strain of T. vaginalis.  Of these, seven (Compounds 12, 15, 18-22) also showed activity against metronidazole-resistant strains.  Compounds 20 (N-cyclohexyl-p-chlorobenzenesulfonamidolupeol acetate) and 22 (N-cyclohexyl-p nitrobenzenesulfonamidolupeol acetate) exhibited a similar IC50 against both susceptible and resistant T. vaginalis strains and enhanced the efficacy of metronidazole in a partial and total synergistic way, respectively.  Additionally, these two compounds exhibited selectivity indexes over 30, indicating that they are not cytotoxic to mammalian cells.  
These data provide evidence of the trichomonicidal effect of N-alkyl-arylsulfonamide derivatives of lupeol acetate, and thus are highly promising novel antiparasitic agents (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34930096/).

Key features and challenges:
N-methylpyrrolidin-2-one is a member of the class of pyrrolidine-2-ones in which the hydrogen attached to the nitrogen is replaced by a methyl group. It has a role as a polar aprotic solvent. N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone appears as a clear colorless liquid with a "fishlike" odor. Denser than water. Flash point 199 °F. Contact may irritate skin, eyes and mucous membranes. May be toxic by ingestion. It is used as a solvent for chemicals and resins in the microelectronics and pharmaceutical industries; [HSDB] Widely used to replace other solvents, e.g., for paint stripping and lube oil extraction; it is used as a solvent for pesticides, coatings, adhesives, dyes, pigments, polymers, and polyurethane foam cleanup.

It has been recently discovered that the common drug excipient, N,N-dimethylacetamide (DMA), delays inflammation-induced preterm birth in mice by inhibiting NF-κB. Since this finding, it has come to light that a group of widely used, structurally related aprotic solvents, including DMA, N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) and dimethylformamide (DMF), have anti-inflammatory efficacy.  

NMP demonstrates immunomodulatory and anti-myeloma properties that are partly explained by acetyllysine mimetic properties and non-specific bromodomain inhibition. An orally administered NMP has been evaluated in a phase 1 dose-escalation trial to establish its maximum tolerated dose (MTD) in patients with relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (RR–MM). Secondary endpoints were safety, pharmacokinetics (PK), overall response rate and immunological biomarkers of activity 

Re-purposing the DMA/DMF/NMP family of small molecules as anti-inflammatory drugs is a promising new approach to delaying or reducing the incidence of inflammation-induced preterm birth and potentially attenuating other inflammatory disorders as well.
(https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43032-022-00924-z)

Name: N582707
Developers: University of Warwick; Ferring Pharmaceuticals
Indication: Prophylactic use in preterm labour management beyond its use as an acute tocolytic drug
Mechanism of action: Detects submicroscopic chromosomal copy number variants to identify genetic causes of fetal growth restriction.
Key features and challenges:
There has been an interest in developing prostaglandin F2α (PGF2α) antagonists as a new treatment for preterm birth, although much of the rationale for their use is based on studies in rodents where PGF2α initiates labour by regressing the corpus luteum and reducing systemic progesterone concentrations. 

In a 2023 study, utilizing an immortalised myometrial cell line, MYLA, derived from myometrial tissue obtained from a pregnant, non-labouring patient, researchers have developed a novel class of PGF2α receptor (FP) antagonist. Compared to four published FP receptor antagonists, the novel FP antagonist N582707 was the most potent compound [Fmax 7.67 ± 0.63 (IC50 21.26 nM), AUC 7.30 ± 0.32 (IC50 50.43 nM), and frequency of Ca2+ oscillations 7.66 ± 0.41 (IC50 22.15 nM)]. RNA-sequencing of the MYLA cell line at 1, 3, 6, 12, 24, and 48 h post PGF2α treatment revealed a transforming phenotype from a fibroblastic to smooth muscle mRNA profile. PGF2α treatment increased the expression of MYLK, CALD1, and CNN1 as well as the pro-labour genes OXTR, IL6, and IL11, which were inhibited by FP antagonism. Concomitant with the inhibition of a smooth muscle, pro-labour transition, FP antagonism increased the expression of the fibroblast marker genes DCN, FBLN1, and PDGFRA. 

These findings suggest that in addition to the well-described acute contractile effect, PGF2α transforms myometrial smooth muscle cells from a myofibroblast to a smooth muscle, pro-labour–like state and that the novel compound N582707 has the potential for prophylactic use in preterm labour management beyond its use as an acute tocolytic drug.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38155905/)

Name: NG IMRS-PCR
Developers: Mount Kenya University
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoea
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: repeat sequences in N. gonorrhoeae genome
Mechanism of action: PCR and isothermal amplification coupled with lateral flow readout
Key features and challenges:
NG IMRS-PCR is a molecular diagnostic assay developed using a de novo genome mining strategy to identify Neisseria gonorrhoeae–specific repeat sequences for amplification-based detection. The assay is designed for use with both conventional PCR and isothermal amplification platforms coupled with lateral flow readout, supporting flexible diagnostic deployment.
A 2023 preprint study described the development of this approach, demonstrating increased analytical sensitivity and specificity for detection of N. gonorrhoeae, with potential utility for screening asymptomatic infections (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4592874). 
The method is adaptable to miniaturized isothermal amplification systems and microfluidic laboratory-on-a-chip devices, enabling potential integration into point-of-care testing platforms.
Key challenges include the need for peer-reviewed validation, clinical performance assessment across diverse specimen types, and confirmation of reproducibility in decentralized settings. Regulatory approval and scalability for routine diagnostic implementation will also require further development.
Overall, NG IMRS-PCR represents a genome-informed molecular diagnostic strategy with potential for sensitive and specific gonorrhea detection. Further clinical validation is required to establish its suitability for point-of-care use.

Name: NG lateral flow assay
Developers: Cornell University
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoea
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Mechanism of action: lateral flow assay
Key features and challenges:
NG lateral flow assay (LFA) is a paper-based, colorimetric diagnostic designed for point-of-care detection of Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The assay utilizes whole bacterial cells without pretreatment, allowing recovery of viable organisms following testing and eliminating the need for preheating or multiple lysis steps.
A 2022 study reported that the assay achieved high diagnostic accuracy using a single sample application step, supporting ease of use in decentralized or at-home settings (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2590262822000272?via%3Dihub). 
Notably, viable N. gonorrhoeae cells could be recovered from the positive test line, enabling integration into antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) workflows to support resistance monitoring and personalized treatment decisions. The reader-free system was estimated to cost approximately USD $0.38 per test, highlighting potential affordability in low-resource settings.
Key challenges include the need for validation across diverse clinical specimens, assessment of sensitivity in low bacterial load samples, and confirmation of performance relative to established NAAT platforms. Regulatory approval and large-scale manufacturing feasibility must also be addressed.
Overall, the NG lateral flow assay represents a low-cost, viable-cell–preserving diagnostic approach for gonorrhea detection. Further clinical validation is required to establish its implementation potential in decentralized settings.

Name: NG-MAST
Developers: University of Montreal, Universite de Montreal
Indication: Investigation of Gonorrhoea treatment failure
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: N. gonorrhoeae multi antigen sequence typing
Key features and challenges:
NG-MAST (Neisseria gonorrhoeae multi-antigen sequence typing) is a molecular typing method used to differentiate Neisseria gonorrhoeae strains, particularly in the context of interpreting test-of-cure (TOC) results and distinguishing treatment failure from reinfection. Traditionally performed on cultured isolates, NG-MAST has been adapted for use directly on nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) clinical specimens to address declining culture availability.
A recent study evaluated NG-MAST typing directly on clinical samples transported in cobas PCR media and reported good performance on cervical, anal, and urine/urethral specimens (https://stihiv2023.eventscribe.net/fsPopup.asp?PosterID=585903&mode=posterInfo). 
However, performance was suboptimal for throat samples, likely due to the presence of commensal Neisseria species at that anatomical site. The method was considered useful for investigating suspected treatment failure in NAAT-based TOC settings.
Key challenges include limited reliability in pharyngeal specimens, potential interference from commensal organisms, and dependence on sufficient DNA quality in NAAT samples. Alternative or complementary typing approaches may be required for accurate evaluation of treatment failure at extragenital sites.
Overall, NG-MAST applied directly to NAAT specimens offers a molecular tool to support differentiation of reinfection versus treatment failure in gonorrhea. Its utility may be site-dependent, requiring optimization for pharyngeal infections.

Name: NGO0690+NGO0948+NGO1701
Developers: Tufts University
Indication: Prevention of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Induces cross-reactive antibodies with complement-mediated serum bactericidal activity against diverse N. gonorrhoeae strains
Key features and challenges:
NGO0690 + NGO0948 + NGO1701 are surface-exposed Neisseria gonorrhoeae protein antigens under investigation as combination vaccine candidates. These antigens were identified from an initial group of six targets and selected based on their ability to induce cross-reactive antibodies with complement-mediated serum bactericidal activity (SBA) against diverse gonococcal strains.
A 2023 funded study proposed further evaluation of these three antigens, including optimization of antigen dosing and adjuvant strategies to enhance immune responses and SBA (https://reporter.nih.gov/search/YhLwKVCcvUKp8kxXqiwryg/project-details/10700802). 
Preliminary data demonstrated protective potential in a murine female vaginal colonization model. Planned investigations include validation of protection in vivo, expansion of strain coverage (including incorporation of the 2C7 LOS epitope mimotope TCMP2), and characterization of the functional roles of these proteins in virulence, fitness, and immune recognition. While correlates of protection in humans remain undefined, SBA and reduction of vaginal colonization in mouse models are used as preclinical benchmarks.
Key challenges include the absence of established human correlates of protection, variability in antigen expression across gonococcal strains, and the need to demonstrate durable and broad immune protection. Translation from murine models to human efficacy remains a critical hurdle in gonococcal vaccine development.
Overall, the NGO0690, NGO0948, and NGO1701 antigen combination represents a preclinical multicomponent vaccine strategy with demonstrated serum bactericidal activity and murine protection data. Further optimization and validation are required prior to clinical advancement.

Name: NK3R antagonist
Developers: Fudan University
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: Reduces GnRH and LH release.
Key features and challenges:
Neurokinin 3 receptor (NK3R) antagonists are emerging neuroendocrine modulators targeting the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). NK3R is expressed on KNDy (Kisspeptin–Neurokinin B–Dynorphin) neurons, which regulate gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) pulsatility. Increased GnRH pulse frequency in PCOS drives excessive luteinizing hormone (LH) secretion and subsequent ovarian androgen production. By antagonising NK3R, these agents aim to reduce GnRH and LH pulsatility, thereby lowering androgen levels and potentially restoring ovulatory function.
A 2021 preclinical study evaluated the NK3R antagonist MLE4901 in a dihydrotestosterone (DHT)-induced mouse model of PCOS. While reproductive abnormalities such as cycle irregularity and ovulatory dysfunction were not corrected, NK3R antagonism significantly reduced body weight, adiposity, and adipocyte hypertrophy. However, no significant improvements were observed in serum triglycerides or glucose levels. These findings suggested potential metabolic benefits despite limited reproductive effects in this model.
A 2022 experimental study further examined NK3R antagonists in PCOS-like mice and reported reductions in fat volume, adipocyte size, and inflammatory cytokines. Treatment enhanced oxidative metabolism, regulated adipokines, and reduced lipid accumulation by suppressing genes such as PPAR-γ and FABP4. These results reinforced the hypothesis that NK3R blockade may address both metabolic and inflammatory disturbances associated with PCOS.
Also in 2022, a review of neuroendocrine mechanisms in PCOS highlighted the role of KNDy neuron dysregulation in driving increased GnRH pulsatility and hyperandrogenism, positioning NK3R antagonists as a rational therapeutic strategy for modulating this pathway. A 2023 review further noted that neurokinin B antagonists may partially suppress the reproductive endocrine axis, offering a targeted, non-surgical approach to reducing gonadotropin hypersecretion in PCOS.
Despite promising mechanistic rationale and supportive animal data, clinical evidence in women with PCOS remains limited. Effects on ovulation, fertility outcomes, long-term metabolic parameters, and safety in reproductive-age populations require further evaluation. Additionally, partial suppression of the reproductive axis necessitates careful dose optimization to avoid unintended hypoestrogenic effects.

Name: NLS -1
Developers: H. Lee Moffitt Cancer Center and Research Institute; McGill University (including The Royal Institution for the Advancement of Learning); ---olyU Technology and Consultancy Company Limited; The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Wayne State University
Indication: Indicated to limit lesion development in endometriosis

Key features and challenges:
NLS 1, or epigallocatechin gallate octaacetate (Pro-EGCG), is a small molecule derived from green tea designed to improve the stability and bioavailability of EGCG. Through acetylation, NLS 1 prevents the generation of reactive radicals, addressing EGCG's chemical instability. Preclinical studies show that NLS 1 has superior antioxidation and anti-angiogenesis properties compared to EGCG, demonstrating effectiveness in reducing endometriosis lesions and preserving normal ovarian function.
NLS 1 is in preclinical development, with ongoing research in Hong Kong. Aptorum Group holds exclusive licenses for NLS 1 from several institutions and has entered agreements for its development and commercialization. A notable agreement with Exeltis in 2021 covers Europe and Latin America, with an option to expand to the US, while Aptorum retains global development rights. The licensing agreements include significant milestone payments for regulatory and sales achievements.
NLS 1 targets endometriosis by reducing lesion size and weight, inhibiting angiogenesis, and preserving reproductive tissue. Preclinical studies have shown that NLS 1 is more effective than existing treatments, including EGCG and hormone-based therapies, making it a promising candidate for improving endometriosis management.

Name: NPC-SE36 +/- CpG
Developers: Nobelpharma; European Vaccine Initiative (EVI); Burkina Faso National Centre for Research and Training on Malaria (CNRFP); Osaka University (including Research Institute for Microbial Diseases (BIKEN) and the School of Pharmaceutical Sciences)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against malaria caused by P. falciparum
Mechanism of action: Elicits immune response to PfSERA5, preventing merozoite egress
Key features and challenges:
The SEmalvac project aims at advancing the clinical development of the Plasmodium falciparum serine repeat antigen-5 (SERA5), a blood-stage malaria vaccine. SERA5 is indispensable during blood-stage growth, is suggested to be involved in parasite egress and in parasite immune evasion. SERA5 may likely overcome two major challenges for malaria vaccine antigens as it shows limited polymorphism and has immunodominant IgG epitopes that do not require strict tertiary structures to elicit protective antibodies. A recombinant form of SERA5 N-terminal domain (SE36) was prepared and formulated with aluminium hydroxide gel to yield BK-SE36 vaccine. The safety and immunogenicity of BK-SE36 was demonstrated in a phase Ia clinical trial in malaria naive Japanese adults, and in a phase Ib trial conducted in healthy subjects aged 6–32 years from a malaria endemic area in Uganda.

In pre-clinical model, the immune response is improved when BK-SE36 is formulated with a TLR 9 ligand consisting of CpG motifs that can selectively promote cellular and/or humoral immune responses. The BK-SE36 vaccine formulated with CpC adjuvant (BK-SE36/CpG) was found safe in a phase Ia clinical trial in healthy adults in Japan and elicited antibody titres 3-4-fold higher than BK-SE36 vaccine alone. In the SEmalvac2 project, launched in parallel to the SEmalvac project, the safety and immunogenicity of the BK-SE36/CpG vaccine will be assessed in healthy malaria exposed adults and children living in Burkina Faso.

After results were posted in 2023, development of BK-SE36/CpG has been paused, with future development now under NPC-SE36 +/- CpG by Japanese SME Noblepharma.
Recent updates: Phase I results published in 2023 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10613650/).

Name: Nabiximols

Key features and challenges:
Nabiximols (Sativex®) is a cannabis-based oromucosal spray containing delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabidiol (CBD), developed by GW Pharmaceuticals (now a subsidiary of Jazz Pharmaceuticals). It modulates the endocannabinoid system through activation of cannabinoid receptors, influencing pain signaling, inflammation, and neuromodulation. Nabiximols has been approved in multiple countries for the treatment of multiple sclerosis–related spasticity and has also been studied for cancer-related and neuropathic pain. The endocannabinoid system has been implicated in gynecological pain pathways, including endometriosis-associated chronic pelvic pain (CPP), providing a mechanistic rationale for therapeutic exploration in this condition.
Despite broader clinical development efforts for indications such as cancer pain and glioblastoma, Jazz Pharmaceuticals discontinued the nabiximols program in September 2022 due to insufficient clinical data to support regulatory approval for certain expanded indications (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800013810). A related exploratory Phase II proof-of-concept study starting in 2026, is evaluating dronabinol (Marinol®), a synthetic Δ9-THC formulation, for endometriosis-associated chronic pelvic pain (NCT06834997) (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06834997). This investigation reflects ongoing interest in targeting cannabinoid pathways to modulate pain perception and inflammatory processes in endometriosis.
Key challenges include limited high-quality clinical evidence specifically evaluating nabiximols or cannabinoid-based therapies in endometriosis populations. Psychoactive effects associated with THC, regulatory variability across jurisdictions, and concerns regarding long-term safety and dependency potential may limit widespread adoption. Additionally, discontinuation of broader nabiximols development programs underscores regulatory and evidentiary hurdles. Further well-designed, placebo-controlled clinical trials are required to establish efficacy, optimal dosing, safety profile, and long-term outcomes in women with endometriosis-associated pain.

Name: Naltrexone - PCOS
Developers: Transparency Life Sciences; DrugAbuse Sciences
Indication: Treatment of PCOS infertility
Mechanism of action: Opioid receptor antagonists
Key features and challenges:
Naltrexone is an opioid receptor antagonist primarily approved for the management of opioid and alcohol dependence. By blocking opioid receptors, it modulates endogenous opioid activity, which has been implicated in neuroendocrine regulation. Emerging evidence suggests that the endogenous opioid system may influence gonadotropin secretion, insulin dynamics, and ovarian function—pathways relevant to the pathophysiology of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
Hyperinsulinemia and insulin resistance are common in PCOS and contribute to hyperandrogenism and anovulation. While metformin remains a standard insulin-sensitizing therapy, interest has grown in alternative mechanisms targeting central neuroendocrine pathways.
A 2022 clinical study compared naltrexone (50 mg daily for 8 weeks) with metformin in 120 women with PCOS (BMI 25–30 kg/m²) diagnosed according to Rotterdam criteria. The study evaluated ovarian response parameters, including serum estradiol levels on the day of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) administration, gonadotropin requirements, number and size of mature follicles, and treatment duration. The naltrexone group demonstrated higher numbers of mature follicles and higher serum estradiol levels compared to the metformin group, suggesting a potential positive effect on ovarian responsiveness in infertility treatment settings.
http://www.cjmb.org/text.php?id=555
Despite these findings, naltrexone remains investigational in PCOS. Evidence is limited to small or single-center studies, and there is insufficient data on long-term ovulation rates, pregnancy outcomes, metabolic effects, or endocrine normalization. The mechanism by which opioid receptor antagonism influences ovarian function in PCOS is not fully elucidated, and broader metabolic benefits remain unclear compared with established therapies. Additionally, potential neuropsychiatric effects and the need for careful patient selection must be considered.
Overall, naltrexone represents an unconventional and exploratory approach targeting neuroendocrine regulation in PCOS-associated infertility. While preliminary findings suggest possible enhancement of ovarian responsiveness, larger randomized controlled trials are required to define its efficacy, safety, and place in PCOS management.

Name: Nano-liposomes containing Bunium persicum
Developers: Birjand University of Medical Sciences
Indication: Investigated for the treatment of trichomoniasis.

Key features and challenges:
Nano-liposomes containing Bunium persicum are investigational lipid-based formulations designed to enhance delivery of B. persicum essential oil for the treatment of Trichomonas vaginalis infection. Bunium persicum (syn. Elwendia persica), commonly known as black cumin, is an aromatic plant with documented antimicrobial, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antifungal, and antibacterial properties.
A 2023 study evaluated nano-liposomal lipid carriers encapsulating B. persicum essential oil and reported significant in vitro antiparasitic activity against T. vaginalis (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1684118222000974?via%3Dihub). 
The formulation achieved IC50 values of 14.41 μg/mL at 12 hours and 45.19 μg/mL at 24 hours post-administration. The nano-liposomal systems demonstrated favorable physicochemical characteristics, including improved entrapment efficiency, controlled release, appropriate particle size, stability, and suitable surface zeta potential, supporting enhanced delivery of active compounds.
Key challenges include the need for in vivo efficacy and safety evaluation in vaginal infection models, assessment of mucosal tolerability, and standardization of essential oil composition. Scalability and reproducibility of nano-formulation manufacturing must also be addressed prior to clinical translation.
Overall, nano-liposomal B. persicum formulations represent a plant-derived delivery-enhanced strategy with demonstrated in vitro activity against T. vaginalis. Further preclinical validation is required to determine their therapeutic potential.

Name: Nanoceria
Developers: University of Missouri-Columbia (Mizzou)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Endometriosis.
Target: Signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3)
Mechanism of action: Inhibition of abnormal STAT3 activation.
Key features and challenges:
Nanoceria (cerium oxide nanoparticles) are redox-active nanomaterials with multi-enzymatic antioxidant properties that enable scavenging of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and modulation of inflammatory signaling pathways. Given that endometriosis is characterized by chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and immune dysregulation—particularly macrophage polarization and STAT3 pathway activation—nanoceria has been investigated as a potential non-steroidal theranostic agent.
A 2025 preclinical study evaluated nanoceria in vitro and in vivo as a therapeutic strategy for endometriosis (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0168365924009295?via%3Dihub). 
In vitro experiments demonstrated that nanoceria exerted multi-enzymatic antioxidant effects and promoted the transition of pro-inflammatory (M1-like) macrophages toward an anti-inflammatory phenotype in J774 macrophage cells. In an endometriosis mouse model, nanoceria passively accumulated within ectopic lesions, suggesting lesion-specific targeting in inflammatory microenvironments. Nanoceria conjugated with indocyanine green enabled non-invasive imaging and tracking of lesion localization, supporting its theranostic (therapeutic + diagnostic) potential.
In vivo treatment significantly reduced ectopic lesion development, with evidence indicating that aberrant STAT3 activation contributes to endometriosis pathogenesis and may be mitigated by nanoceria. Importantly, treatment reportedly minimized off-target reproductive effects, including interference with implantation and decidualization, suggesting a potential advantage over hormonal therapies.
Key challenges include the current restriction to preclinical animal models and limited long-term safety data. The biodistribution, persistence, and potential accumulation of cerium oxide nanoparticles in reproductive or systemic tissues require thorough toxicological evaluation. Regulatory pathways for nanoparticle-based theranostics remain complex, particularly in reproductive-age populations. Additionally, reproducibility of immune modulation effects in human endometriotic tissue has not yet been established. While nanoceria demonstrates promising immunomodulatory and imaging capabilities, substantial translational research is required before clinical implementation.

Name: Naphthylisoquinoline alkaloids
Developers: Ahmadu Bello University, Nigeria; University of Wurzburg, Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg

Key features and challenges:
A series of 23 naphthylisoquinoline (NIQ) alkaloids and related naphthoquinones were subjected to in vitro screening against two fungal strains of M. mycetomatis.  
Seven NIQs, mostly dimers, showed promising in vitro activities against at least one strain of the mycetoma-causative pathogens, while the naphthoquinones did not show any activity. A synthetic NIQ dimer, 8,8'''-O,O-dimethylmichellamine A (18), inhibited all tested fungal strains (IC50 = 2.81–12.07 µg/mL). Name: Naproxen
Developers: Pharos University in Alexandria,; Pharos University in Alexandria,
Indication: Reducing renal injury in PE
Mechanism of action: Naproxen significantly reduced renal levels of arachidonate end products (PGE2, PGF2α, TXA2), which play crucial roles in the inflammatory response associated with PE.
Key features and challenges:
Naproxen is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes and reduces prostaglandin and thromboxane synthesis. NSAIDs are commonly used for pain and fever during pregnancy, but their interaction with preeclampsia (PE)-associated renal injury has not been well characterized. PE is associated with endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and renal impairment, and renal injury can persist beyond delivery. In this context, modulation of inflammatory and arachidonic acid pathways has been explored as a potential strategy to mitigate PE-related renal dysfunction.
A 2023 preclinical study investigated renal injury and NSAID effects in an L-NAME rodent model of PE, comparing naproxen with celecoxib and diclofenac 
(https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-44617-2#Abs1). 
PE dams demonstrated hallmark signs of renal damage at gestational day 20, including increased urine protein and reduced creatinine clearance, with abnormalities persisting through weaning (three weeks post-labor). Naproxen administered during the last week of pregnancy was associated with improved biochemical, glomerular, and tubular indicators of renal injury compared with the other NSAIDs. It also reduced upregulated renal levels of arachidonic acid end products, including PGE2, PGF2α, and TXA2, and was linked to diminution of PE-mediated inflammatory, oxidative, fibrotic, and autophagic processes. These findings suggest a potentially preferential renoprotective effect of naproxen in this preclinical PE model.
Key challenges include the known risk profile of naproxen and other NSAIDs in pregnancy, where dose and duration can be associated with adverse renal effects, including acute and chronic kidney injury and tubulointerstitial nephritis. Translation from animal models to human PE care is also limited by differences in timing of exposure, underlying PE heterogeneity, and fetal safety considerations, particularly with NSAID use later in gestation. While the preclinical findings suggest possible benefit for PE-associated renal programming, further mechanistic work and carefully designed clinical studies are required to clarify safety, optimal dosing, and maternal–fetal outcomes before clinical relevance can be established.

Name: Nateglinide
Developers: Adiyaman University
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: Nateglinide's activity depends on the presence of functional β cells and glucose. It enhances the effect of extracellular glucose on ATP-sensitive potassium channels, stimulating insulin release. In PCOS models, its actions may include antioxidant effects, anti-inflammatory activity, and the reduction of ovarian follicle degeneration.
Key features and challenges:
Nateglinide is an oral meglitinide-class antihyperglycemic agent traditionally used in type 2 diabetes to enhance early-phase insulin secretion and improve postprandial glycemic control. Its exploration in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is based on the central role of insulin resistance, oxidative stress, and inflammation in PCOS pathophysiology. Beyond glycemic regulation, nateglinide has demonstrated antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects in experimental models, suggesting potential benefits for ovarian dysfunction associated with PCOS.
A 2022 preclinical study evaluated the effects of nateglinide and octreotide in a letrozole-induced rat model of PCOS. Compared with untreated PCOS animals, nateglinide-treated rats exhibited fewer cystic and degenerated follicles and improved ovarian histology. PCOS animals showed significantly elevated testosterone, TNF-α, IL-6, IGF-1, and malondialdehyde (MDA), alongside reduced glutathione (GSH) levels, reflecting oxidative stress and inflammation. Nateglinide treatment normalized IGF-1 and MDA levels and increased GSH concentrations, indicating antioxidant activity. Both nateglinide and octreotide appeared to reduce ovarian damage through modulation of TLR-4–mediated inflammatory pathways and attenuation of oxidative stress.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36524509/
Although these findings highlight mechanistic plausibility; particularly in addressing insulin resistance, oxidative imbalance, and inflammatory signaling, evidence remains limited to animal models. No large-scale human clinical trials have evaluated nateglinide in women with PCOS, and its impact on ovulation, menstrual regulation, fertility outcomes, and long-term metabolic parameters is unknown. As an insulin secretagogue, there is also a theoretical concern regarding hypoglycemia or weight effects, which would require careful evaluation in reproductive-age populations.

Name: Nemo Fetal Monitoring System (NFMS) - PE
Developers: Nemo Healthcare
Indication: Detection of preeclampsia in the early second trimester
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Multiplex molecular assay detects Neisseria gonorrhoeae DNA and resistance-associated mutations to guide targeted antimicrobial therapy.
Key features and challenges:
In the process of fetal adaptation to placental insufficiency, the fetal heart has a major role. Ante partum assessment of the cardiac function and uterine activity could therefore be essential for the evaluation of pregnancies complicated with a pregnancy related disease such as hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, fetal growth restriction, or end in premature birth. 
 
The Nemo Fetal Monitoring System uses electrophysiological signals to monitor both maternal and fetal heart rate outside the abdomen. The development of this device aimed at offering an alternative to either invasive (fetal scalp electrode or intrauterine pressure catheter) or poorly reliable (Doppler ultrasound influenced by movement of mother or fetus, or high body mass of mother) measurements of fetal heart rate. The device uses algorithms to filter contractions and the fetal heart rate from unprocessed abdominal electrophysiological signals, eliminating noise or interference. 
 
NFMS can measure cardiac time intervals, fetal heart rate variability (fHRV), maternal heart rate variability (mHRV), CTG waveform patterns, contraction amplitude, contraction frequency, velocity, and entropy. Two-dimensional speckle tracking echocardiography (2D-STE) is a non-Doppler technique that applies computer software analysis of images generated by conventional ultrasound techniques to calculate parameters of motion (displacement and velocity) and deformation (strain and strain rate) in all three axes and thus providing a comprehensive assessment of cardiac function. 2D-STE can measure strain, strain rate, velocity, desynchrony, sphericity index, and shortening fraction. 
 
The BEATS study is currently comparing cardiac recording using Nemo Fetal Monitoring System® and two-dimensional speckle tracking echocardiography (2D-STE) in a cohort to establish potential differences between normal pregnancies and pregnancies who develop hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, fetal growth restriction, or end in premature birth, that could later be used for detection of these pregnancy-related diseases. (https://www.onderzoekmetmensen.nl/en/trial/25988) 
 
CE-approval for the NFMS was obtained on 9 October 2018. FDA approval process was ongoing in 2018

Name: Nemo Fetal Monitoring System (NFMS) - PTL
Developers: Nemo Healthcare

Mechanism of action: Fetal and maternal heart rates can be determined using ECG signals and uterine activity measurements are obtained via EMG signals during uterine contractions. Nemo Base contains smart algorithms that filter the received electrophysiological signals.
Key features and challenges:
The Nemo Fetal Monitoring System (NFMS), developed by Nemo Healthcare, is a non-invasive electrophysiological monitoring device used to assess fetal heart rate, maternal heart rate, and uterine activity during pregnancy. The system is commercially available and marketed in several European countries. It is designed for use from approximately 21 weeks’ gestation until delivery.
NFMS utilizes the Nemo Patch, which contains six surface electrodes placed on the maternal abdomen. Fetal and maternal heart rates are derived from electrocardiographic (ECG) signals, while uterine activity is measured through electromyographic (EMG) signals during contractions. The rechargeable Nemo Base applies signal-processing algorithms to filter and isolate relevant electrophysiological parameters before transmitting data to a central monitoring system. The portability of the device enables potential home-based remote monitoring.
(https://nemohealthcare.com/en/products/)
The BEATS study is evaluating cardiac recordings obtained using the Nemo Fetal Monitoring System® in comparison with two-dimensional speckle tracking echocardiography (2D-STE) to assess differences between uncomplicated pregnancies and those that develop hypertensive disorders, fetal growth restriction, or preterm birth. Preliminary findings suggest that certain electrohysterographic (EHG) parameters differ between women who subsequently deliver preterm and those delivering at term. Specifically, entropy values may be lower, while contraction frequency, intensity, and propagation velocity may be higher in pregnancies that result in preterm birth.
(https://www.onderzoekmetmensen.nl/en/trial/25988)
Overall, NFMS represents a non-invasive, electrophysiology-based monitoring platform with potential applications in identifying pregnancies at risk of preterm birth. While early data suggest differences in uterine electrical activity patterns preceding preterm delivery, further validation is required to establish predictive accuracy and clinical utility in PTL management.

Mechanism of action: real-time PCR
Key features and challenges:
Nested real-time PCR (macrolide and fluoroquinolone resistance) is a molecular diagnostic assay designed to simultaneously detect Mycoplasma genitalium and identify resistance-associated mutations in the 23S rRNA and parC genes. A 2023 study reported development and evaluation of this method for detection of macrolide- and fluoroquinolone-resistant genotypes (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/cellular-and-infection-microbiology/articles/10.3389/fcimb.2023.1271392/full).

Overall, the nested real-time PCR assay represents a genotype-guided diagnostic approach for antimicrobial resistance detection in M. genitalium. Further clinical validation is required to support widespread implementation.

Developers: Kephera Diagnostics, LLC
Indication: Indicated for the detection/diagnosis of Tapeworm (taeniasis / cysticercosis)
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Key features and challenges: A rapid serological immunoassay that detects antibodies against Taenia. It uses a lateral-flow strip or cassette format read directly without instrumentation. The assay is performed on capillary whole blood.

Name: Neutrophil-to-Lymphocyte Ratio - PTL
Developers: Şanlıurfa Education and Research Hospital (Turkey); Kasturba Medical College, Manipal
Indication: Prediction of preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM)
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Quantifies circulating mannose to assess metabolic dysregulation and insulin resistance associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
In 2021, a study registered at Kasturba Medical College in India aimed to explore whether the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio and platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio could help predict the time of birth in women with Threatened Preterm Labor. However, the results of this study were not available. (https://www.ctri.nic.in/Clinicaltrials/pmaindet2.php?EncHid=NTM1MTI=&Enc=&userName=CTRI/2021/04/032474)

In 2023, researchers at Şanlıurfa Education and Research Hospital in Turkey compared maternal blood test results from pregnancies with preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) to those from mothers of healthy, full-term babies. They looked at platelet, lymphocyte, and neutrophil counts, as well as the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) and platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR). For the PPROM group, samples were taken at diagnosis, while for the control group, they were collected at hospital admission for delivery. The NLR was significantly higher in the PPROM group (p=0.001), with a cutoff value of 6.73 for predicting PPROM (AUC=0.671, 95% CI=0.58-0.75, p<0.001) (https://www.cureus.com/articles/147657-neutrophillymphocyte-and-plateletlymphocyte-ratio-in-preterm-premature-rupture-of-membranes#!/)

Name: Neutrophil/lymphocyte ratio
Developers: Medicana Bursa Hospital; Hangzhou women’s hospital
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS and of metabolic issues in PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Calculates neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio to assess systemic inflammation associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
The Neutrophil-Lymphocyte Ratio (NLR), a marker of systemic inflammation, is typically elevated in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), reflecting increased inflammation. High NLR levels in PCOS are associated with insulin resistance, metabolic dysfunction (e.g., dyslipidemia and obesity), and hormonal imbalances. While primarily used to monitor inflammation and metabolic issues in PCOS patients, its potential diagnostic performance is of interest. A 2020 study found higher NLR in women with PCOS, with an optimal cut-off of ≥2.26 for detecting the condition. 
(https://ia801607.us.archive.org/21/items/evaluation-of-inflammatory-markers-in-patients-diagnosed-with-polycystic-ovary-syndrome-pcos/10.4328ACAM.20728.pdf)
Similarly, a 2022 study showed significantly higher NLR, along with hs-CRP and MPV, in obese PCOS patients compared to non-obese and control groups, indicating NLR's potential as a marker for inflammation in PCOS, particularly in obese individuals.
(https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9302324/)

Name: Ng-MurI inhibitors
Developers: University of Delhi (including ACBR, LHMC, Miranda House and UCMS)
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Inhibition of glutamate racemase (a critical enzyme in cell wall biosynthesis) in Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
Key features and challenges:
Ng-MurI inhibitors are investigational small-molecule candidates targeting glutamate racemase (MurI) in Neisseria gonorrhoeae. MurI catalyzes the interconversion of L-glutamate and D-glutamate and plays a critical role in peptidoglycan biosynthesis, contributing to bacterial cell wall formation. In addition to its role in cell wall metabolism, MurI has been implicated in gyrase-related functions, making it a potential dual-functional antimicrobial target.
A 2022 study employed homology modeling, molecular docking, and pharmacophore analysis to characterize the structural and functional relationship between Ng-MurI and D-glutamate (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36106953/). 
The study identified candidate compounds with favorable fitness and docking scores that demonstrated biologically relevant interactions within the MurI active site. These findings support the potential of these molecules as lead compounds for the development of novel Ng-MurI inhibitors.
Key challenges include the need for experimental validation of in silico findings, confirmation of in vitro and in vivo antimicrobial activity, and assessment of specificity to avoid off-target effects. Pharmacokinetic profiling and resistance development potential must also be evaluated.
Overall, Ng-MurI inhibitors represent a rationally designed, target-based antimicrobial strategy against N. gonorrhoeae. Further preclinical validation is required to determine their viability as therapeutic candidates.

Name: NiV G-ferritin
Developers: National Institutes of Health; National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID)
Indication: Prevention of NiV disease
Target: Nipah virus G glycoprotein head domain (receptor-binding protein)
Mechanism of action: Multivalent display of NiV G head domain on ferritin nanoparticle stimulates strong and broad neutralizing antibody responses, blocking ephrin-B2/B3 receptor binding and preventing viral entry.
Key features and challenges:
-Induced faster, broader, and stronger antibody responses than soluble NiV G (sG).
-Complete protection in Syrian golden hamsters against lethal NiV-M challenge with no detectable viral RNA in tissues.
-Cross-neutralization observed against NiV-B and Hendra virus (HeV).
-Durable responses: antisera from mice neutralized NiV even 6 months after last immunization.
-Generated a panel of 27 mAbs targeting 4 antigenic sites on NiV G, including 2 novel epitopes.
-Challenges: cellular immune responses weak/not detected; efficacy in NHPs not yet tested; further safety and stability data needed for human translation
Recent updates:
Aug 2024 Publication:
-Reported potential for single-dose efficacy and plan further evaluation in higher-order models.

Name: NiV RT-nfoRPA LFD / NiV RT-exoRPA LFD / NiV RT-RAA LFD
Developers: University of the Sunshine Coast; Australian Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO); Defence Materials Technology Centre (DMTC)
Indication: Indicated for the detection of NiV infection
Target: NiV nucleic acid sequence (Nucleocapsid protein gene)
Key features and challenges:
Tests based on single-temperature isothermal amplification technology (RT-nfoRPA, RT-exoRPA, or RT-RAA), coupled with Lateral Flow Detection for easy and rapid (<30min) result and interpretation.
The tests were shown to be specific for detection of NiV, not detecting other acute febrile viruses (i.e., flaviviruses, CHIKV).
RT-nfoRPA-LFD showed 100.0% diagnostic sensitivity (95% CI: 79.4–100.0%) and 100.0% diagnostic specificity (95% CI: 29.24–100.0%).
Can be deployed on the field.

Name: NiV∆N VRP
Developers: University of Tokyo (including the Graduate School of Agricultural and Life Sciences)
Indication: Prevention of NiV disease
Target: NiV structural and nonstructural proteins expressed by the replicon (minus N) that elicit broad immune responses
Mechanism of action: Single-cycle replication of NiVΔN VRP in host cells allows antigen expression without production of infectious progeny, stimulating humoral and cellular immunity while avoiding uncontrolled viral spread.
Key features and challenges:
-Safety advantage: deletion of N gene makes replicon propagation impossible in vivo.
-Induces both neutralizing antibodies and strong CD8+ T cell responses.
-In hamsters, provided sterilizing immunity with no detectable viral RNA after challenge.
-In African green monkeys (AGMs), two doses conferred complete protection against lethal NiV-Bangladesh challenge.
-Challenge: replicon system requires helper cell line for production, may limit scalability.
Recent updates: NiVΔN VRP remains a leading preclinical NiV vaccine. No human trials yet, but the complete protection in both hamsters and AGMs highlights it as a strong clinical candidate. Ongoing efforts are focused on scalable VRP production.

Name: Nibrozetone
Developers: EpicentRx; SciClone Pharmaceuticals; The University of Queensland
Indication: Indicated for prevention and treatment of endometriosis
Target: CD47 antigen; Free radical; Inflammasome; Macrophage; NLRP3 protein; Proto-oncogene protein c-myc; SIRPA protein
Mechanism of action: CD47 antigen inhibitors; Free radical stimulants; Inflammasome inhibitors; Macrophage stimulants; NLRP3 protein inhibitors; Proto-oncogene protein c-myc inhibitors; SIRPA protein inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Nibrozetone (RRx 001) is an innovative small molecule under development by EpicentRx. As a nitric oxide prodrug, it functions as an anticancer agent and radiation sensitizer through the Redox-Active Drug (RAD)/CyNRGY platform. It works as an innate immune checkpoint inhibitor, targeting the CD47 signal regulatory protein-alpha axis, and repolarizes immune-suppressive cells in the tumor microenvironment. By increasing oxygenation in tumors, nibrozetone enhances susceptibility to radiation therapy, overcoming hypoxia-induced resistance in tumors. Its development spans various cancers, including CNS, colorectal, and ovarian cancers, as well as non-cancer conditions like sickle cell anemia and endometriosis.
EpicentRx has pursued a range of development activities for nibrozetone, including phase I and phase II trials across various cancers and conditions. The drug has received Fast Track Designation from the FDA for preventing severe oral mucositis in head and neck cancer patients. Collaborations with companies like Actinium Pharmaceuticals and SciClone Pharmaceuticals have advanced its global development. However, some trials, such as those for lymphoma and solid tumors, have been discontinued or terminated due to low enrollment or shifting strategic priorities.
Nibrozetone is also being explored for the treatment of endometriosis. In preclinical study published in 2024, it has shown promise in addressing conditions associated with chronic hypoxia and inflammation, which are relevant to endometriosis. 
(https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.08.12.607591v1.full).
The drug's ability to enhance oxygenation and modulate immune responses may offer novel therapeutic benefits in managing endometriosis, although further research and clinical trials are needed to establish its efficacy in this context.
(https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800035095)

Name: Niclosamide
Developers: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA); Dankook University
Indication: Treatment of mpox; potential topical therapy for lesions
Target: Multiple host pathways (e.g., Wnt/β-catenin, STAT3; reported effects on cellular DNA synthesis/actin networks) relevant to viral replication.
Mechanism of action: Host-directed antiviral; suppresses MPXV antigen and infection in human epithelial/keratinocyte models; proposed topical utility due to systemic tolerability limits.
Key features and challenges: Strong in-cell antiviral activity (VK2 IC50s within 12–50 nM cohort) but toxicity at ~80–100 nM in VK2 constrains window; systemic bioavailability historically poor—topical or advanced formulations may be required.
Recent updates:
-Nanohybrid niclosamide formulations reported in 2025 show improved bioavailability and anti-mpox activity potential, supporting reformulation for systemic/topical use.
-Broader repurposing screens in 2024–2025 continue to flag niclosamide and kinase-pathway inhibitors as promising host-directed candidates against mpox.

Name: Nicorandil - PTL/PTB
Developers: Chugai Pharmaceutical Co
Indication: Prolong gestation in threatened preterm labour
Mechanism of action: Induces vasodilatation of arterioles and large cornonary arteries via potassium channels and cGMP pathways, potentially with added anti-platelet effects
Key features and challenges:
Nicorandil is an anti-angina medication that has the dual properties of a nitrate and ATP-sensitive K+  channel agonist. In humans, the nitrate action of nicorandil dilates the large coronary arteries at low plasma concentrations. At high plasma concentrations nicorandil reduces coronary vascular resistance, which is associated with increased ATP-sensitive K+ channel (KATP) opening.
Nicorandil stimulates guanylate cyclase to increase formation of cyclic GMP (cGMP). cGMP activates protein kinase G (PKG), which phosphorylates and inhibits GTPase RhoA and decreases Rho-kinase activity. Reduced Rho-kinase activity permits an increase in myosin phosphatase activity, decreasing the calcium sensitivity of the smooth muscle. It has therefore been investigated as a potential tocolytic, smooth muscle relaxant. 
A Phase II trial is currently underway to compare nicorandil to nifedipine for tocolysis in preterm labour (https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT04846621).
A clinical trial published in 2025, demonstrated Nicorandil and Nifedipine are equally effective as tocolytic drugs in postponing labor in women who have preterm labor that has already started for 48 hours after administration. Nicorandil was found to be safer and have fewer adverse effects than Nifedipine. (https://www.clinicaterapeutica.it/2025/176/3/05_1048_Adel.pdf)
Recent updates:
2025: Clinical trial, published in 2025, demonstrated Nicorandil and Nifedipine are equally effective as tocolytic drugs in postponing labor in women who have preterm labor that has already started for 48 hours after administration. (https://www.clinicaterapeutica.it/2025/176/3/05_1048_Adel.pdf)

2024: Phase II has completed

2021: Comparative Study Between Nicorandil and Nifedipine for the Treatment of Preterm Labour. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT04846621)

2015: A randomized trial of 200 pregnant women in Egypt reported that nicorandil is as effective as nifedipine for tocolysis in preterm labour, but is more likely to cause maternal and foetal tachycardia (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26476796). **This paper has been retracted; Reason:  The submission date is impossible. Patients were recruited at 24 to 34 weeks (mean 31 w). 18% of participants delivered after 37 weeks. Average recruitment 26 per month. Recruitment ended September 2014 but the paper was received by journal on 23 October 2014.**

Name: Nifuroxazide
Developers: Naval Medical University, Shanghai; First Affiliated Hospital of Navy Military Medical University; Yunnan Minzu University
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of CHIKV infection
Mechanism of action: Suppresses CHIKV replication; minimal/no effect on binding, endocytosis, or membrane fusion; reduces replicon reporter expression and viral RNA; improves disease readouts in mice
Key features and challenges:
-Orally dosed, widely used antibacterial with established safety profile (facilitates repurposing).
-Demonstrates low-µM inhibition in Huh7 and HUVEC cells; weak effect in neuronal cells (cell-type dependence).
In vivo (C57BL/6 footpad model) reduced viral loads and footpad swelling when given 50 mg/kg p.o. from −1 to 3 dpi.
-Precise molecular target unknown; no human CHIKV data; potential cytotoxicity at higher doses in some cell types; translational dosing/PK/PD unknown
Recent updates:
Aug 2025:
No registered clinical studies or additional CHIKV in vivo studies on nifuroxazide identified since publication.
-CHIKV antiviral papers reference the Viruses study but do not report new CHIKV data for nifuroxazide.

Name: Nitazoxanide (6-12 month old infants)
Developers: Johns Hopkins University (including the Bloomberg School of Public Health)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Cryptosporidiosis in children age 6-12 months
Target: EIF-2 kinase; HN protein; Oxidoreductase; Receptor protein-tyrosine kinase
Mechanism of action: EIF-2 kinase modulators; HN protein inhibitors; Oxidoreductase inhibitors; Receptor protein-tyrosine kinase modulators
Key features and challenges:
Nitazoxanide is an antiprotozoal treatment for cryptosporidiosis, working by inhibiting the enzyme pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PFOR), essential for the parasite’s metabolism. It reduces the severity and duration of diarrhea in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised patients. Nitazoxanide is approved by the FDA for use in children and adults aged 1 year and older for the treatment of cryptosporidiosis. For younger children, such as those under 1 year, the use of nitazoxanide is generally considered off-label.

A clinical trial evaluates if nitazoxanide (NTZ) can reduce diarrhea and the presence of Cryptosporidium in stools in children aged 6-12 months. Participants will receive NTZ or a placebo for 3 days, with regular visits and blood/urine samples to assess the treatment's effectiveness. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06600711)
Recent updates: Phase III trial commenced in 2025 to investigate the approved drug in children aged 6-12 months (NCT06600711).

Name: Nitric Oxide-donating azole derivatives
Developers: China Pharmaceutical University
Indication: Treatment of cryptococcal meningitis
Mechanism of action: The mechanism of action involves NO release, inhibiting biofilm formation and fungal growth, while enhancing brain permeability to bypass the blood-brain barrier when administered intranasally.
Key features and challenges:
NO-donating azole derivatives are a class of antifungal compounds that release nitric oxide (NO) to inhibit biofilm formation and fungal growth, and in the context of cryptococcal meningitis, they show promise as a treatment by enhancing antifungal activity and improving brain permeability.

A 2023 study developed NO-donating azole derivatives with potent antifungal activity against Cryptococcus neoformans and its biofilms, with compound 3h, administered intranasally, demonstrating significant anti-cryptococcal meningitis effects by bypassing the blood-brain barrier, positioning it as a promising treatment candidate for further research. (https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jmedchem.3c01308)

Developers: Brazilian State University Paulista, Universidade Estadual Paulista (Unesp); Sapienza University of Rome, Università degli Studi di Roma La Sapienza
