Name: Nm dOMVs
Developers: Uniformed Services University; US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
Indication: Prevention of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: MOA unclear, but Nm dOMV vaccines stimulate complex immune responses that result in varying levels of protection from Ng.
Key features and challenges:
Nm dOMVs (Neisseria meningitidis detoxified outer membrane vesicles) are vaccine-derived vesicles being investigated for cross-protective immunity against Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Epidemiological evidence has suggested that meningococcal OMV vaccines may confer partial protection against gonorrhea.
A 2021 study evaluated Nm dOMVs lacking major outer membrane proteins (PorA, PorB, and RmpM) and reported enhanced antibody cross-reactivity against heterologous Neisseria strains compared with wild-type dOMVs (https://academic.oup.com/jid/article/225/4/650/6366578). 
In murine models, immunization with OMP-deficient Nm dOMVs significantly improved gonococcal clearance, associated with serum and vaginal IgG antibodies that cross-reacted with N. gonorrhoeae. Identified putative gonococcal targets included PilQ, MtrE, NlpD, and GuaB, supporting their relevance for vaccine development.
Key challenges include variability in cross-protection across strains, the need to confirm durability and magnitude of protective immunity in humans, and clarification of correlates of protection. Translation from murine models to human efficacy remains a major hurdle in gonococcal vaccine development.
Overall, Nm dOMVs represent a cross-species vaccine strategy leveraging meningococcal vesicles to induce protection against N. gonorrhoeae. Further clinical and translational studies are required to define their role in gonorrhea prevention.

Name: Non-replicating Tiantan vaccinia virus-based vaccine (NTV)
Developers: Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences
Indication: Prophylactic prevention of mpox
Target: Mpox virus clade IIb A35R, B6R, H3L, and M1R antigens
Mechanism of action: Induces cross-protective humoral and cellular immune responses through expression of conserved vaccinia and MPXV antigens. Neutralizing antibodies and polyfunctional CD8+ and CD4+ T-cell responses contribute to protection.
Key features and challenges:
-Derived from Tiantan vaccinia virus (TTV) by deletion of 26 genes linked to virulence, host range, and replication.
-Demonstrated robust immunogenicity in mice, rabbits, and macaques.
-Provides near-complete protection in rhesus macaques following prime-boost and partial protection after single dose.
-Demonstrates long-lasting immunity (≥8 months) with high CD8+ T-cell memory response.
-Excellent safety in cynomolgus macaques, even at triple standard dose, with no replication in human cells.
-Manufacturing advantage: replicates efficiently in chicken embryo fibroblasts → scalable production.
Recent updates:
-As of 2025, the NTV vaccine is advancing toward pre-IND stage, with Phase I clinical trial preparations underway in China.
-Demonstrated superior safety compared to replication-competent smallpox vaccines (e.g., ACAM2000).
-Proposed as a candidate suitable for emergency use and immunocompromised populations (e.g., PLHIV).

Name: Noninvasive plasma cell–free RNA signatures
Developers: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing
Indication: To predict preterm preeclampsia and early-onset preeclampsia before diagnosis
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Profiles circulating placental and maternal cell-free RNA transcripts to detect gene expression patterns indicative of placental dysfunction and preeclampsia.
Key features and challenges:
Plasma cell-free RNA holds unique insights from human tissues and could be valuable for noninvasive monitoring of maternal, placental, and fetal changes during pregnancy. This study explored various RNA types linked to preeclampsia in plasma and aimed to create tools for predicting preterm and early-onset preeclampsia before symptoms appear. Using a new sequencing method called polyadenylation ligation-mediated sequencing, researchers analyzed cell-free RNA from 715 healthy pregnancies and 202 affected by preeclampsia prior to symptom onset. The findings provided a detailed view of RNA profiles in preeclampsia and led to the development of two advanced prediction models with significant clinical potential. The study showed that messenger RNA, microRNA, and long noncoding RNA could all serve as biomarkers for preeclampsia, offering hope for future prevention. These abnormal RNA changes may also help uncover the causes of preeclampsia and open new paths for reducing pregnancy complications and fetal risks.
 (https://www.ajog.org/article/S0002-9378(23)00323-X/fulltext).

Name: Novel CT/NG Dx system
Developers: Novel Microdevices, Inc. (formerly Novel Dx)
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoea
Health care facility level: IVDs for research use only
Mechanism of action: multiplex nucleic acid amplification
Key features and challenges:
A rapid, automated, multiplex nucleic acid amplification test for CT/NG has been proposed to enable immediate testing and treatment of infected individuals in a single visit.
Aim 1 ​will integrate assay controls and optimise the multiplex assay for CT/NG. Aim 2 will involve developing the “Beta” Novel Dx device that will meet the FDA and CLIA waiver guidance requirements. Aim3 will involve conducting more in-depth analytical studies for sensitivity, inclusivity, exclusivity, cross-reactivity of our optimised sample to answer assay. Aim 4 will place the Novel Dx system in clinical settings and conduct end-user performance and usability evaluations. The outcome of Phase II will provide sufficient data as well as a refined system design to inform a decision regarding multicenter clinical trials and product launch.
(https://reporter.nih.gov/search/4730gfC7QUyjD-sASy17Ew/project-details/10010797)

Name: Novel Mechanism of Action antibiotic
Developers: CFD Research Corporation
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Natural product–derived small molecule that inhibits essential Neisseria gonorrhoeae cellular pathways via a novel, previously unexploited antibacterial target.
Key features and challenges:
The 2024 study seeks to develop a new class of antibiotics against Neisseria gonorrhoeae (NG). CFD Research has discovered a novel natural product (NP) with potent NG activity, which they seek to develop. Aim 1 will build on our established medicinal chemistry program to diversify and optimize the NP’s scaffold for improved potency, cytotoxicity and drug-like properties. Aim 2 will test the in vivo efficacy of the best analogues from Aim 1 in an established mouse model of NG infection. During Phase II, these data will drive further medicinal chemistry design and synthesis of a lead series. Mechanism of action will be elucidated. Followed by in vivo toxicity, and pharmacokinetics to produce an optimized lead compound for further preclinical development as a novel NG antibiotic.
(https://reporter.nih.gov/search/5Hio4J1JTUOFxM8HZze2FQ/project-details/10921601)

Name: Novel molecular Rapid Diagnostic - Mycoplasma genitalium
Developers: Cardiff University; Cwm Taf University Health Board (NHS)
Indication: Detection of Mycoplasma genitalium
Health care facility level: IVDs for research use only
Mechanism of action: Rapid nucleic acid amplification and detection of Mycoplasma genitalium–specific genetic sequences for point-of-care diagnosis.
Key features and challenges: An ongoing study commenced in 2019 aims to clinically evaluate a novel, rapid molecular diagnostic for Mycoplasma and Gonorrhoea infections. This diagnostic detects both infection and also detects any antimicrobial resistance. The tests detect these organisms and provides information about antimicrobial resistance in a laboratory. The main aim is to determine if a novel molecular test for rapid detection of Mycoplasma and Gonorrhoea infections and antimicrobial resistance is sensitive and specific in symptomatic patients attending a sexual health clinic. The secondary aim is to determine whether the novel molecular test for detection of antimicrobial resistance in Mycoplasma and Gonorrhoea infections is more accurate than standard laboratory culture techniques. The study is ongoing and results are yet to be published. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05391035)

Name: Novobiocin derivative (compound 47)
Developers: Microbial Chemistry Research Foundation (MCRF) (Including Institute of Microbial Chemistry, ICM / BIKAKEN)
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Inhibition of DNA gyrase subunit B (gyrB)
Key features and challenges:
To develop novel drugs against resistant N. gonorrhoeae, a 2023 study focused on the antibiotic novobiocin. This natural product has a different mechanism of action from existing drugs for gonorrhea, which may make it effective against resistant strains. It was applied to resistant N. gonorrhoeae, and moderate antibacterial activity was confirmed. Based on this result, the development of an antigonococcal drug with Novobiocin as the lead compound. As a result, it was found that compound 5 with an methylpyrrole ester structure have a very potent antibacterial activity. This derivative also showed excellent antigonococcal activity against resistant strains in vitro, however it has poor water solubility and pharmacokinetics. Therefore, a basic substituent was introduced into the molecule and resulted in an amphoteric compound with improved water solubility. As a result of synthesizing various derivatives, compound 47 containing imidazole was found with strong antigonococcal activity and greatly improved water solubility. This derivative has also improved metabolism and blood concentration in vivo, and is expected to be orally absorbed. Based on these results, compound 47 is a very promising anti-gonococcal lead compound and has great potential for further development.
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0968089623002298)

Name: NucoVac-11
Developers: Panacea Biotec

Name: NxTekTM Malaria P.f/P.v.
Developers: Abbott Laboratories
Indication: Indicated for the diagnosis of P. falciparum or P.vivax infection where more than 5% of cases would be missed with HRP2 detection alone due to the prevalence of Pf HRP2/3 deletions in symptomatic patients.
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Target: Plasmodium falciparum histidine-rich protein 2 (HRP-2), Plasmodium falciparum lactate dehydrogenase (pLDH)  and Plasmodium vivax lactate dehydrogenase (pLDH)
Key features and challenges: In general, Pv parasitemias are lower than Pf's, suggesting that more sensitive tests would be more important in Pv than in Pf. The new Pv tests target a 10x improvement in detection limit compared to existing Pv RDTs. What this translates to in terms of case management remains to be seen.

Name: ODA 570
Developers: Ocean Biomedical; Brown University
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against malaria caused by P.falciparum
Target: P. falciparum  Glutamic acid-rich protein of (GARP)
Mechanism of action: Protozoan protein modulators
Key features and challenges: Ocean Biomedical is developing malaria vaccine candidate, for the prevention and treatment of malaria. Ocean Biomedical utilises its whole-proteome differential screening platform to analyse the proteome of blood-stageP. falciparumparasites. The vaccine contains PfGARP as a parasite antigen that is localised to the exofacial surface of the RBC membrane in trophozoite-infected RBCs, that targets the blood stage ofP. falciparum. This anti-PfGARP vaccine attenuates the growth of parasites by arresting and killing trophozoite-infected RBCs in the absence of immune effector cells or complement. Preclinical development is underway in the US.

Name: ODA 579
Developers: Ocean Biomedical
Indication: Treatment of malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum
Key features and challenges: ODA 579 is an anti-PfGARP (P. falciparum glutamic-acid-rich protein) small molecule, being developed by Ocean Sihoma (subsidiary of Ocean Biomedical) for the treatment of Malaria. Name: ORG43553
Developers: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai (ISMMS)
Indication: Treatment of PCOS - Fertility; Metabolism
Target:
-Primary: Luteinizing hormone / chorionic gonadotropin receptor (LHCGR; LH-R).
-Secondary: Weak agonist activity at FSH receptor at higher concentrations.
Mechanism of action:
ORG43553 is a nanomolar-potent, signaling-selective allosteric agonist that binds within the transmembrane domain of LHCGR and preferentially activates the cAMP pathway while showing biased signalling vs phospholipase C (PLC).
 In classical reproductive models, oral ORG43553 mimics LH/hCG to stimulate steroidogenesis and induce ovulation, with EC50 ≈3.7 nM for human LH-R and high oral bioavailability in rats (≈79%) and dogs (≈44%).
More recent work shows that LHCGR is expressed in white adipose tissue and hypothalamic neurons; activation of LHCGR by LH, hCG or ORG43553 reduces adipocyte differentiation, enhances mitochondrial respiration, and increases energy expenditure and beiging of adipose tissue, largely independent of testosterone, positioning ORG43553 as a potential anti-obesity agent.
Key features and challenges:
ORG43553 is an orally active, low–molecular-weight agonist of the luteinizing hormone/choriogonadotropin receptor (LHCGR), originally developed as an alternative to injectable human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) for triggering ovulation in assisted reproduction.

Preclinical studies (2009) demonstrated potent activation of human LHCGR (EC50 ~3.7 nM), induction of steroidogenesis in Leydig cells, high oral bioavailability in animal models, and successful ovulation induction in rodents with fertilisable oocytes capable of implantation.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19088107/

First-in-human randomized, placebo-controlled, single-rising-dose studies (2013) in pituitary-suppressed healthy women showed that ORG43553 (25–900 mg) was generally well tolerated, rapidly absorbed (Tmax 0.5–1 hour), and capable of inducing ovulation at doses ≥300 mg, with ovulation rates exceeding 80%.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23515453/

Subsequent mechanistic analyses further characterized ORG43553 as a signalling-selective allosteric agonist. It binds to an allosteric site in the LHCGR transmembrane domain, strongly activates the cAMP pathway, but weakly stimulates phospholipase C (PLC), while non-competitively inhibiting LH-induced PLC activation. This biased agonism profile may allow stimulation of ovulation while potentially reducing risks such as ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS). In vivo work confirmed ovulation after oral dosing and suggested a shorter effective half-life than hCG.
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10248450/

Preclinical safety assessments also indicated a lower propensity for OHSS-like ovarian enlargement or vascular permeability compared with hCG.
https://cyberleninka.ru/article/n/tienopirimidiny-novyy-klass-nizkomolekulyarnyh-regulyatorov-reproduktivnoy-funktsii-zhenschin.pdf

More recently (2023–2025), research has explored metabolic and body-composition effects. Genetic and functional studies indicate LHCGR expression in white adipose tissue, and activation by LH, hCG, or ORG43553 reduced diet-induced obesity in mice by decreasing fat mass and visceral adiposity while increasing energy expenditure without increasing food intake.
https://academic.oup.com/jes/article/7/Supplement_1/bvad114.097/7290110

Cell-based and translational work further suggests reduced lipid droplet accumulation, enhanced mitochondrial oxygen consumption, and UCP1-independent thermogenesis via PLC–Ca²⁺–ERK and ATF3/PGC-1α–mediated pathways.
https://www.jshs.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/63rd-NJSHS-Abstract-Book-1.pdf

Despite mechanistic novelty and early human ovulation data, development as a fertility drug appears to have been discontinued. ORG43553 is not approved by any regulatory authority, and no active clinical programmes for infertility, obesity, or PCOS are currently registered. All obesity-related findings remain preclinical.

Overall, ORG43553 is a first-in-class allosteric LHCGR agonist with demonstrated ovulation-induction capacity and emerging preclinical metabolic effects. However, in the absence of active development programmes or PCOS-specific clinical data, it should currently be considered an early-stage concept candidate rather than an active clinical programme for obesity-related PCOS.
Recent updates: Preclinical development of ORG43553 received funding from US NIH in 2025 and will continue through to 2029 (https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/11086693)

Developers: University of Oxford (including Oxford University Clinical Research Unit Vietnam (OUCRU), Nuffield Department of Women's and Reproductive Health (NDWRH)); University of Liverpool; University of Birmingham
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Target: MtrE (Surface Antigen); IgA Protease; Gonococcal Outer Membrane
Mechanism of action: Monoclonal antibody binds MtrE surface protein to deliver cytotoxic payload and inhibit bacterial survival.
Key features and challenges: Retro-orbital (RO) blood collection is widely used, but it can cause serious complications. More researchers are turning to saphenous vein (SV) sampling as a gentler alternative that supports better animal welfare. This study compared RO and SV methods in developing a Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Ng) vaccine, testing Adhesin Complex Protein (ACP) and multiple transferable resistance E protein (MtrE) as antigen candidates. Epitope mapping showed both ACP and MtrE have multiple, highly accessible B-cell and T-cell epitope clusters, highlighting their strong immunological potential. After intranasal immunization with rACP, rACP+CpG, and rMtrE+CpG, we measured the specificity, strength, timing, and quality of immune responses. Out of 45 comparisons, only eight showed significant differences in antibody levels, and bactericidal assays found no difference between RO and SV in antigen-immunized groups. However, antibodies from SV samples after rACP or ACP+CpG restored 30.05% and 75.2% of human lysozyme activity, compared to 19.3% and 59.9% in RO, suggesting SV may be more reliable for assessing functional antibody responses. Along with these immune benefits, SV sampling reduces stress, avoids eye damage, and improves animal welfare, making it a strong alternative to RO. Standardizing SV in vaccine research could boost data reliability, meet ethical standards, and improve the relevance of preclinical studies (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.02.23.639724v1)

Name: Octreotide
Developers: Novartis; Moffitt Cancer Center
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: Growth hormone-releasing hormone inhibitors; Somatostatin receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
Octreotide is a synthetic somatostatin analogue used clinically for acromegaly and for symptom control in neuroendocrine tumors. It mimics endogenous somatostatin by inhibiting secretion of growth hormone and several other peptides, and modulates endocrine and metabolic pathways.
Interest in octreotide in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) stems from the interaction between growth hormone, insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), and ovarian steroidogenesis. Dysregulation of insulin and IGF-1 signaling contributes to hyperandrogenism and follicular arrest in PCOS, providing a mechanistic rationale for evaluating somatostatin analogues in this setting.
A 2022 preclinical study investigated the effects of octreotide and nateglinide in a letrozole-induced rat model of PCOS. Compared with untreated PCOS rats, both the octreotide- and nateglinide-treated groups demonstrated significant reductions in cystic and degenerated follicles. Treatment was associated with improvements in ovarian histology and attenuation of oxidative stress and inflammatory markers, with proposed mechanisms involving modulation of TLR-4 signaling and enhancement of antioxidant pathways.
https://www.europeanreview.org/article/30563
Despite these encouraging preclinical findings, octreotide remains investigational in PCOS. No human clinical trials have been published evaluating its effects on ovulation, androgen levels, metabolic outcomes, or fertility in women with PCOS. Additionally, octreotide’s systemic endocrine effects, injectable administration, and potential adverse events—including gastrointestinal disturbances and glucose metabolism alterations—may limit its practicality in a chronic reproductive disorder.

Name: Omega-3 fatty acids - PTL/PTB
Developers: University of Chicago; South Australian Health and Medical Research Institute (SAHMRI)
Indication: Prevention of preterm labour
Mechanism of action: Omega-3 fatty acids alleviates endothelial damage caused by production of inflammatory cytokines and sFlt-1
Key features and challenges:
Omega-3 fatty acids (FAs) are polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) involved in human lipid metabolism. The principal forms relevant to pregnancy are α-linolenic acid (ALA), found in plant oils, and eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), primarily derived from marine sources. DHA and EPA are recognized for their anti-inflammatory properties and have been investigated for prevention of preterm labour/birth (PTL/PTB).
Interest in omega-3 FAs and gestation length dates back to a 1985 observational study comparing Faroe Islanders and Danish women, which reported longer gestations and higher birthweights among women with substantially higher fish intake (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1052396/). 
Mechanistically, omega-3 FA metabolites are involved in inflammatory signaling pathways that regulate cervical ripening and the initiation of labour. A 2016 study suggested that insufficient local accumulation of omega-3 FAs may predispose to premature cervical ripening and increased uterine contractility, particularly in susceptible women (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27842314/).
A 2018 Cochrane review reported that omega-3 supplementation during pregnancy reduced the risk of preterm birth <37 weeks and early preterm birth <34 weeks compared with no supplementation; however, most included trials were conducted in high-income settings (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6516961). 
In 2020, a randomized clinical trial (CTRI/2020/08/027146) was initiated to compare high-dose DHA (1000 mg/day) versus low-dose DHA (200 mg/day) for prevention of early preterm labour; results have not yet been published. A trial funded through the University of Chicago evaluating prenatal DHA supplementation in African American women in low-income urban environments was completed in January 2022, though PTL-specific outcomes have not yet been reported (https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/9864081). 
Most recently, a 2024 review summarized therapeutic dosing strategies, safety considerations, and mechanistic pathways through which DHA may reduce PTB risk (https://www.eurekaselect.com/article/132541).
Many professional organizations recommend 300–500 mg/day of omega-3 FAs during pregnancy. However, intake in many LMIC settings remains below recommended levels, except in coastal regions with high fish consumption. Key challenges include variability in dosing regimens, heterogeneity of trial populations, and uncertainty regarding optimal DHA versus combined EPA/DHA supplementation strategies. While evidence supports a modest reduction in early and overall preterm birth risk, further large, diverse population trials are needed to clarify dose–response effects and generalizability across settings.
Recent updates:
2024: A review focusing on the favorable benefits of Ω-3, particularly DHA during pregnancy and postpartum, therapeutic dose recommendations, safety considerations, particularly during pregnancy, and the mechanistic pathway that might prevent or reduce the frequency of PTB accidents. (https://www.eurekaselect.com/article/132541)

2018: Cochrane Review Omega‐3 fatty acid addition during pregnancy. (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6516961).  

A clinical trial comparing inidence of early preterm labour between high dose (1000mg/day) and low dose DHA 200mg/day (CTRI/2020/08/027146) is planning for recruitment as of August 2020.

The University of Chicago has received funding to conduct a clinical trial on prenatal DHA supplementation for African American women living in low-income urban environments (https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/9864081). The project is expected to complete by January 2022.

Name: Ophthalmic artery doppler, maternal characteristics and medical history
Developers: State University of Ceará
Indication: Diagnosis and prediction of preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: ophthalmic artery Doppler (first diastolic peak velocity)
Mechanism of action: Composite hematologic and nutritional index identifying systemic inflammation and endothelial dysfunction associated with preeclampsia risk.
Key features and challenges:
Neurological complications of severe PE, often due to loss of autoregulation in the maternal brain blood vessels, account for much of the illness and death linked to the condition. Changes in cerebral blood flow can appear weeks before PE develops; for instance, the resistance index (RI) and pulsatility index (PI) in the maternal middle cerebral artery tend to be lower in women who later develop it. Because orbital vessels share functional, embryological, and anatomical traits with intracranial vessels, Doppler studies of these vessels reveal details about small cerebral arteries that can’t be seen with transcranial imaging. Research on the maternal ophthalmic artery in PE has generally found lower RI and PI alongside faster blood flow, pointing to reduced vascular resistance.
  
A 2014 univariate logistic regression analysis revealed that the estimated detection rates of PE from screening based on UtA-PI and PD1 alone were 16% and 19%, respectively, at a fixed false-positive rate of 10%. However, the multiple regression analysis demonstrated that models combining maternal factors with UtA-PI and PD1 provided significantly improved prediction of PE, with the former achieving a detection rate of 58% and the latter a detection rate of 48%. The highest detection rates in these models were for the outcome of early PE, at 67% with UtA-PI or PD1, and 68% when combined. Among the outcomes studied, late PE had the lowest detection rates, with the addition of UtA-PI and PD1 to maternal factors in fact lowering the detection rate achieved by maternal factors alone. The areas under the ROC curves did not demonstrate statistically significant differences for screening by maternal factors with UtA-PI and maternal factors with PD1 in the prediction of PE (P = 0.97) and early PE (P = 0.21). The efficiency of maternal ophthalmic artery PD1 as a predictive marker was approximately equal to that of uterine artery Doppler PI. Maternal ophthalmic artery Doppler analysis in the first trimester of pregnancy made the same contribution to multiparametric predictive models for PE as does uterine artery Doppler PI, although it did not add to the detection rate achieved by the latter alone in multiparametric predictive models. Therefore, given that uterine artery Doppler interrogation is becoming a well-established component of obstetric sonography, it will not be replaced by ophthalmic artery sonography in such testing regimens (https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/uog.13338). 
 
A 2023 meta-analysis of ophthalmic artery Doppler measurements found strong predictive value for preeclampsia. Peak ratio (PR) and second systolic velocity peak (P2) outperformed other indexes, with PR showing an AUC of 0.885, 84% sensitivity, 92% specificity, and a low false-positive rate of 0.08. P2 had an AUC of 0.926, 85% sensitivity, and 88% specificity. The resistance index, pulsatility index, and end-diastolic velocity also performed well and were consistent across studies but had lower AUC values of 0.833, 0.794, and 0.772, respectively. The study concluded that ophthalmic artery Doppler is a useful complementary tool for diagnosing both overall and severe preeclampsia (https://bmcpregnancychildbirth.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12884-023-05656-9).

Name: Optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD)
Developers: University of Melbourne (including the Australian Venom Research Unit (AVRU) and Bio21 Institute); Griffith University (including the Institute for Glycomics and GRIDD)
Indication: Indicated for the prediction of Preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Mechanism of action: Using Doppler and sonographic imaging to measure nerve sheath diameter
Key features and challenges:
Optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) measurement by ocular ultrasound is a non-invasive technique used to assess intracranial pressure and cerebral hemodynamics. In hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, altered cerebral perfusion and endothelial dysfunction may contribute to neurological complications, prompting investigation of ONSD as a potential predictive marker for preeclampsia.
A 2024 prospective observational cohort study evaluated maternal ophthalmic artery Doppler parameters and sonographic ONSD measurement in the third trimester for prediction of preeclampsia, and compared their performance with serum biomarkers (sFlt-1:PlGF ratio) (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2210778924000497). The study enrolled 101 women (51 with healthy singleton pregnancies and 50 with suspected but initially excluded preeclampsia), of whom 27 subsequently developed preeclampsia. Mean arterial pressure (MAP), ophthalmic artery pulsatility index, resistive index, peak ratio, and ONSD were assessed. Univariate analysis demonstrated significant differences in MAP (p < 0.001), ophthalmic artery pulsatility index (p = 0.003), resistive index (p = 0.01), peak ratio (p < 0.001), and ONSD (p = 0.01) among women who later developed preeclampsia. Multivariate analysis identified ONSD as the strongest independent predictor of preeclampsia in this cohort.
Key challenges include relatively small sample size, need for external validation in larger and more diverse populations, and requirement for operator training in ocular ultrasonography. Standardization of measurement thresholds and integration with established biomarkers will be necessary to determine clinical utility in routine screening or risk stratification pathways.

Oteseconazole, an azole antifungal targeting fungal 14α-demethylase (CYP51), is being evaluated in a Phase II/III platform trial designed to address challenges in cryptococcal meningitis treatment, such as limited 5-FC availability, reliance on a single supplier for liposomal amphotericin, drug toxicity, and rising fluconazole resistance. The trial explores new regimens with improved safety and efficacy, including oteseconazole administered as 600 mg orally twice daily for 10 days, followed by 600 mg weekly during weeks 3–6. The regimen includes a single dose of liposomal amphotericin B (10 mg/kg IV) and excludes fluconazole and flucytosine.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06666322; https://adis.springer.com/trials/700377716)

Name: Ouabain
Developers: University of Texas Medical Branch at Galveston; Federal University of Paraiba (UFPB)
Indication: Treatment of congenital Zika syndrome (CZS) and ZIKV infection during pregnancy.
Mechanism of action: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibitor with antiviral and immunomodulatory activity. Inhibits Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, leading to modulation of intracellular signaling pathways and cytokine production; reduces ZIKV replication in human neural stem/progenitor cells (hNS/PCs) and murine placental/fetal tissues; exerts anti-inflammatory effects (lower TNF, IL-1β in placenta), thereby preventing ZIKV-induced fetal growth restriction and neurogenesis impairment.
Key features and challenges:
Features:
-Reduces viral burden in hNS/PCs, placenta, yolk sac, and fetal head.
-Prevented ZIKV-induced microcephaly-like outcomes (restored fetal and head size).
-Mitigated impaired neurogenesis in human neural stem cells.
-Demonstrated immunomodulatory effects by lowering inflammatory cytokines.

Challenges:
-Ouabain is a cardiac glycoside with a narrow therapeutic index and potential cardiotoxicity, limiting systemic use.
-Safety in pregnant humans unknown.
Recent updates:
2025 Publication: 
-First demonstration that ouabain protects fetal development in a murine congenital ZIKV model while reducing viral burden and inflammatory cytokines in placental tissue.
-Expands evidence for repurposing cardiac glycosides as antivirals, though no movement yet into primate studies or clinical trials for ZIKV.

Key features and challenges:
Ov-103 is one of two lead vaccine candidates being developed by The Onchocerciasis Vaccine for Africa (TOVA) - a multinational consortium working towards the development of a recombinant sub-unit vaccine against Onchocerca vulvulus. Multiple preclinical studies have demonstrated the efficacy of this candidate both alone (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31525197/), and in combination with Ov-RAL-2 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33500417/) in eliciting protective immunity against Onchocerca vulvulus in mouse models. It has recently been shown to protect against Onchocerca ochengi infection in a bovine model (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35746469/).

A 2024 preclinical study, in preparation of Phase I trials, find Ov-RAL-2 and Ov-103 as potential onchocerciasis vaccine candidates (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0312315)
Recent updates: A 2024 preclinical study, in preparation of Phase I trials, find Ov-RAL-2 and Ov-103 as potential onchocerciasis vaccine candidates (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0312315)

Name: Ovarian artery indices
Developers: University of Lahore; SBÜ Ankara Training and Research Hospital; Bacha Khan Medical College
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS via assessment of ovarian vascular changes
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Doppler measurement of ovarian artery resistance to assess altered ovarian perfusion associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Ovarian Doppler refers to a diagnostic imaging technique that uses Doppler ultrasonography to assess blood flow within the ovaries. It measures the velocity, resistance, and patterns of blood flow in the ovarian arteries, helping to evaluate ovarian function and detect abnormalities. In PCOS, altered pulsatility suggests ovarian vascular changes, contributing to reproductive and hormonal issues.

Several studies have investigated the relationship between ovarian arterial pulsatility and PCOS. 
A meta-analysis of 27 studies examined the use of Doppler ultrasonography to assess ovarian blood flow in women with and without ovarian dysfunction, including those with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). The study found that women with PCOS had significantly higher vascularization index (VI), flow index (FI), and vascularization flow index (VFI), and significantly lower pulsatility index (PI) and resistance index (RI) compared to healthy controls. Doppler indices were also correlated with ovarian markers, such as antral follicle count in women undergoing IVF and testosterone and luteinizing hormone levels in PCOS patients. These findings support the use of Doppler ultrasound in evaluating ovarian dysfunction, though further research is needed due to high statistical heterogeneity.(https://atm.amegroups.org/article/view/108818/html)

A 2019 study in Pakistan found that women with polycystic ovaries exhibited significantly altered ovarian blood flow, including higher pulsatility and lower resistive index values compared to healthy controls, suggesting impaired ovarian vascularity in PCOS, which could contribute to ovarian dysfunction. 
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31062996/)

A 2021 Turkish study revealed that the ovarian arterial pulsatility index (PI) was higher during anovulatory cycles compared to ovulatory cycles, indicating impaired ovarian blood flow, with the resistance index (RI) differing between the two phases, further suggesting vascular dysfunction in PCOS.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34478423/)

Additionally, research highlighted that ovarian artery Doppler indices, including pulsatility and resistance indices, were significantly altered in women with PCOS compared to healthy controls, emphasizing the value of Doppler ultrasonography in assessing ovarian vascular health in PCOS.
(https://pakistanbmj.com/journal/index.php/pbmj/article/view/549)

Name: Ovarian stromal echogenicity
Developers: Lithuanian University of Health Sciences, Lietuvos Sveikatos Mokslu Universitetas (LSMU); Near East University Hospital, Cyprus
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Ultrasound assessment of stromal echogenicity to identify increased stromal volume and fibrosis characteristic of polycystic ovaries.
Key features and challenges:
Ovarian stromal echogenicity refers to the appearance of the ovarian stroma on an ultrasound scan. It is influenced by the amount of collagen, blood flow, and other tissue characteristics. In conditions like PCOS, the ovarian stroma often appears hyperechoic (brighter) due to increased tissue density and fibrosis. Changes in stromal echogenicity can indicate underlying ovarian dysfunction, such as in PCOS.

A 2022 study found that hyperechogenic stroma was present in 98% of PCOS patients and 4% of healthy women, indicating a significant difference in stromal echogenicity between the two groups. 
(https://www.degruyter.com/document/doi/10.1515/med-2022-0505/html)

A 2022 study compared ovarian stromal thickness (ST) and blood flow in PCOS, polycystic ovarian morphology (PCOM), and normal ovarian morphology (NOM) groups. PCOS patients had higher androgen levels, insulin resistance, hirsutism, ST, and stromal blood flow than PCOM and NOM. The free androgen index was strongly correlated with ovarian ST, suggesting ST as a diagnostic indicator for PCOS. No significant differences in ST or Doppler findings were found between PCOM and NOM groups. (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/01443615.2022.2054684)

A 2017 study observed that the stromal index, which is the ratio of mean stromal echogenicity to mean echogenicity of the entire ovary, was higher in the PCOS group, partly due to increased stromal density. 
(https://academic.oup.com/humrep/article-abstract/14/3/618/632879)

Name: Ovarian tumor domain-containing protein 1
Developers: Capital Medical University
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Endometriosis.
Mechanism of action: Inhibits the expression of fibrosis-related proteins in HEMCs in vitro via coordinated deubiquitination coupled with MADH7-mediated transcriptional reprogramming.
Key features and challenges:
Ovarian tumour domain-containing protein 1 (OTUD1) is a deubiquitinating enzyme implicated in regulation of inflammatory and fibrotic signaling pathways. Fibrosis is a key pathological feature of endometriosis and contributes substantially to pain, adhesion formation, and infertility. Transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) signaling is central to fibrogenesis, and the inhibitory SMAD protein MADH7 (SMAD7) functions as a negative regulator of this pathway. Dysregulation of TGF-β signaling has been linked to excessive extracellular matrix deposition and lesion progression in endometriosis.
A 2025 study was the first to evaluate the role of OTUD1 in endometriosis using human primary stromal endometriosis cells (HEMCs) and a C57BL/6N mouse model (https://academic.oup.com/molehr/article-abstract/31/2/gaaf014/8120094?redirectedFrom=fulltext
). In vitro, OTUD1 overexpression inhibited fibrosis-related protein expression in HEMCs. Mechanistically, OTUD1 exerted its effect through coordinated deubiquitination of target proteins coupled with MADH7-mediated transcriptional reprogramming, thereby modulating TGF-β–associated fibrotic pathways. In vivo, modulation of OTUD1 activity was associated with reduced lesion growth and diminished abdominal inflammation. These findings suggest that OTUD1 functions as a regulator of fibrogenesis in endometriotic tissue and may have therapeutic potential in attenuating lesion progression.
Key challenges include the early-stage, preclinical nature of the evidence, with no human interventional data available. The feasibility of targeting a deubiquitinating enzyme therapeutically, including delivery mechanisms and specificity, remains uncertain. Off-target effects on other ubiquitination-dependent pathways must be carefully evaluated. Additionally, the complexity of fibrosis and immune signaling networks in endometriosis suggests that modulation of a single pathway may not be sufficient for comprehensive disease control. Further translational research is required to determine whether OTUD1 can be safely and effectively targeted in clinical settings.

Name: Oxantel Pamoate
Developers: Jennifer Keiser
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of soil-transmitted helminthiasis

Key features and challenges: A small-molecule anthelmintic that acts as a selective cholinergic agonist at parasitic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, inducing depolarising neuromuscular blockade and paralysis of intestinal helminths. Name: Oxaspiropiperidine nsP2hel inhibitor
Developers: University of North Carolina Chapel Hill; University of Toronto
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of CHIKV infection
Mechanism of action:
-Direct binding to nsP2 helicase confirmed by ¹⁹F NMR
-Inhibits nsP2 ATPase activity (IC₅₀ ~0.84 µM) and RNA unwinding (IC₅₀ ~130 nM)
-Acts as a type-1 allosteric inhibitor, non-competitive with RNA or ATP
-Selectivity: >100-fold preference for alphavirus nsP2 over other viral helicases.
Key features and challenges:
-(R)-enantiomer highly potent; (S)-enantiomer >100-fold less active.
-EC₅₀ against CHIKV replication ~0.1 µM (vs 29 µM for inactive enantiomer).
Broad-spectrum activity against alphaviruses (CHIKV, VEEV, WEEV) but not flaviviruses (DENV, WNV) or Ebola virus.
-Demonstrates enantioselectivity, making it a high-quality probe + matched negative control.
-Structural flexibility (thermal motion in piperidine core) linked to inhibitory potency
Recent updates:
2025: 
-Resolution of racemic oxaspiropiperidine into enantiomers identified (R)-1 (RA-NSP2-1) as the active probe.
-Validated broad antialphaviral activity with high selectivity and biochemical confirmation of mechanism.
-Proposed as a chemical probe pair (RA-NSP2-1 active, RA-NSP2-1N inactive) to study alphavirus nsP2 function.
-Potential starting point for drug optimization pipelines against alphavirus threats.

Name: Oxytocin - PCOS
Developers: Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujib Medical University; University of Porto (including Ipatimup)
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: Improve metabolic and reproductive functions
Key features and challenges:
Oxytocin (OT) is a hypothalamic nonapeptide hormone released from the posterior pituitary, traditionally recognised for its roles in parturition, lactation, and social bonding. Emerging evidence suggests that oxytocin may also influence metabolic regulation, cardiovascular function, and reproductive physiology—domains that are central to the pathophysiology of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).

A 2024 systematic review synthesised available human and animal data examining the relationship between oxytocin and PCOS. The review highlighted that women with metabolic syndrome, obesity, or diabetes; conditions frequently comorbid with PCOS, often exhibit lower circulating oxytocin levels. In preclinical models, oxytocin administration reduced body weight, food intake, adipocyte size, and serum triglycerides, supporting a potential metabolic benefit. Oxytocin’s presence in cardiac tissue and its vascular regulatory effects also suggest possible relevance for cardiovascular risk modulation in PCOS populations.
(https://www.mdpi.com/1467-3045/46/6/313)
From a reproductive perspective, oxytocin may play a role in folliculogenesis and hormonal regulation. PCOS-related anovulation and impaired follicular maturation are linked to dysregulated estradiol signalling, and oxytocin has been implicated in modulating ovarian function. However, clinical trials evaluating fertility-related outcomes have yielded mixed findings, and consistent therapeutic benefit has not yet been established.
Genetic investigations have identified associations between oxytocin receptor (OXTR) variants and PCOS phenotypes, including hyperandrogenism, anovulation, and metabolic risk profiles. The review also discussed potential shared neuroendocrine features between PCOS and autism spectrum disorder (ASD), noting observational data suggesting increased ASD prevalence among women with PCOS and in their offspring. While intriguing, these associations remain exploratory and require mechanistic clarification.
Despite a biologically plausible role across metabolic, reproductive, and neurobehavioral domains, oxytocin’s therapeutic application in PCOS remains investigational. Human interventional data are limited, optimal dosing and delivery strategies are undefined, and long-term safety in reproductive-age women has not been established.
Overall, oxytocin represents a multifaceted but underexplored candidate in PCOS research, with promising preclinical findings and emerging human associations, yet insufficient clinical evidence to support routine therapeutic use at present.
Recent updates: Phase III trial investigating oxytocin triggering ovulation induction cycles in infertile women with polycystic ovary syndrome completed in 2024 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06725004)

Name: Oxytocin - heat-stable/inhaled
Developers: Monash University (including CDCO); GlaxoSmithKline (GSK); Johnson & Johnson
Indication: Prevention and treatment of PPH
Mechanism of action: Oxytocin receptor agonists
Key features and challenges:
Inhalable oxytocin is a low-cost, heat-stable, easy-to-administer, inhaled form of oxytocin, designated as GR 121619, that was being developed by GlaxoSmithKline (GSK), in collaboration with Monash Institute of Pharmaceutical Sciences (MIPS), for managing postpartum haemorrhage in resource-poor settings. In 2020, GSK returned the rights to the product to Monash, who are continuing the project with support from GSK, and Janssen Pharmaceuticals. In Dec 2020, Monash signed a development agreement with Iconovo AB to provide inhaled oxytocin in the ICOone® device to progress the Phase I trials planned for 2021. In March 2021 Janssen Pharmaceuticals and Monash Institute of Pharmaceutical Sciences enter a sponsored research agreement for development of inhaled oxytocin.
The dry powder formulation is designed to be delivered using a device/inhaler. The programme was initiated to overcome issues associated with available injectable formulations of oxytocin, which require trained personnel for administration and temperature-controlled storage and supply. These conditions are usually not available in low-resource settings, hence, delivery of dry powder, heat-stable formulation by an inhaler could allow administration of oxytocin by birth attendants, health workers and mothers themselves. 
Pulmonary delivery of dry powder formulation in an in vivo postpartum model has showed pharmacokinetic profile and faster pharmacodynamic response similar to intramuscular injection. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28781129/).  In December 2015, GlaxoSmithKline completed a phase I study that assessed the safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics of inhaled oxytocin in healthy female volunteers (NCT02542813; 201558). The randomised, single-blind study was initiated in September 2015, that enrolled 16 participants in the UK. In March 2019, GlaxoSmithKline, in collaboration with Monash University, terminated a phase I clinical trial, which compared the pharmacokinetics, safety and tolerability of inhaled oxytocin with intramuscular oxytocin in pregnant women and with intravenous oxytocin in healthy non-pregnant women (205920; NCT02999100; EudraCT2016-002672-27). The reason for termination was cited as the company's inability to dependably measure plasma oxytocin levels during third stage labour, irrespective of administration method (intramuscular or inhaled). The open-label, parallel assignment trial, which was initiated in November 2016, enrolled 35 patients in the UK and Australia. 
In 2022, a new Phase I pharmacokinetic and safety comparison study of oxytocin via dry powder by inhalation and by IV and IM injection was registered in Australia. Trial completion is listed as January 2023. (https://anzctr.org.au/Trial/Registration/TrialReview.aspx?ACTRN=12622001077752).

Name: Oxytocin impregnated gauze
Developers: Neyshabour University of Medical Sciences
Indication: Indicated for the treatment and prevention of postpartum haemorrhage following caesarean delivery.
Mechanism of action: Measures end-diastolic blood flow velocity to evaluate ovarian perfusion changes associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges: The effect of using oxytocin impregnated gauze compared with saline-soaked gauze and dry gauze on postpartum bleeding in women after caesarean section is being studied. In the intervention group, 5 ampoules of 10 units of oxytocin will be mixed in 500 cc of normal saline of cold at a temperature of 4 ° C and then poured into a sterile receiver. After the placenta comes out, two small striped gauzes will be put in the receiver to absorb the solution completely, then the gauzes will be placed in the uterus by the surgeon for one minute and the whole uterus cleaned with it. In the other study groups, the same will be done but the gauze will be dry, or soaked in saline solution only. Outcomes studied include the bleeding amount, haemoglobin and haematocrit concentrations before and after caesarean delivery, and blood rate, heart rate and temperature. It is unclear when the trial is expected to be completed. (https://irct.behdasht.gov.ir/trial/63209)

Name: P2-VP8 (NRRV)
Developers: PATH (including Meningitis Vaccine Project (MVP) and Malaria Vaccine Initiative (MVI)); Walter Reed Army Institute of Research (WRAIR) (including Military HIV Research Program); SK Bioscience; US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease (NIAID)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against rotavirus gastroenteritis
Target: Rotavirus VP8, the globular head of the spike protein of genotypes P[8], P[4] or P[6]
Mechanism of action: Induces protection by cellular and humoral immunity resulting in the generation of rotavirus-specific IgG antibody and neutralizing antibody activity.
Key features and challenges:
PATH is developing an E. coli-expressed subunit candidate vaccine which consists of the VP8 cleavage product of VP4 protein fused to the P2 universal helper T-cell epitope derived from tetanus toxin.

Through animal studies, the vaccine constructs were demonstrated to elicit serum neutralizing immune responses in animals, whiles its immunogenicity wassignificantly enhanced when the constructs were fused with the P2 epitope, which elicits a strong T-cell helper function.

The candidate has now progressed to clinical development with PATH further improving the vaccine construct with the addition ofaluminium hydroxide adjuvant and formulating two versions of the subunit vaccine:monovalent candidate vaccine (P2-VP8 type P[8]), and a trivalent vaccine candidate (P2-VP8 types P[4], P[6] and P[8]). Both versions have undergone phase I and II clinical trials with both showing promising results based on safety and immunogenicity. Specifically, the trivalent candidate vaccine elicited substantially higher neutralising antibodies to P[4] and P[6] virus strains than the monovalent candidate vaccine, while neutralization responses to a P[8] strain was comparable between the different candidate vaccines. The latest phase III trial is on-going in Africa, evaluating the safety, immunogenicity and efficacy ofthe trivalent P2-VP8 vaccine version (NCT04010448).
Recent updates:
Phase III trial commenced in 2019 (NCT04010448). 
Phase II trial completed in 2022 (NCT04344054).

Name: PA-VE-US transvaginal probe
Developers: Wayne State University
Indication: Prediction of risk of PTB in women with a short cervix, and diagnosis of PTB.
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Detection of cervical changes
Key features and challenges:
Short cervical length measured by transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) is currently the most common clinical indicator of preterm birth (PTB) risk. However, conventional ultrasound provides primarily morphological information and does not directly assess the molecular or biomechanical mechanisms underlying cervical insufficiency and preterm labour.
Investigators at Wayne State University are developing a multi-modal transvaginal imaging probe that integrates photoacoustic (PA) imaging, viscoelasticity (VE) assessment, and conventional ultrasound (US) into a single platform. The system aims to provide quantitative evaluation of cervical remodelling biomarkers. Photoacoustic imaging is intended to assess molecular and microstructural characteristics, including collagen network organisation, water content, microvascular structure, and oxygenation status. Viscoelasticity measurements are designed to quantify biomechanical properties such as tissue stiffness, softness, and viscosity. Conventional ultrasound continues to provide cervical length and structural morphology assessment.
Because TVUS is the current standard of care for cervical surveillance, the combined PA-VE-US probe is designed to add approximately 3–5 minutes to a routine examination, supporting potential integration into clinical workflows. The proposed clinical applications include improved detection of women at risk of PTB—particularly those without apparent cervical shortening—and objective assessment of cervical ripening prior to labour induction.
The project includes plans to quantitatively evaluate diagnostic efficacy in assessing cervical remodelling biomarkers and predicting PTB risk. Results have not yet been reported.
(https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/10032871)

Name: PAPP-A/PAPP-A2 ratio GO-SPR biosensor
Developers: Mackay Memorial Hospital, Taipei, Taiwan
Indication: Prediction of preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: Metalloproteinases pregnancy-associated plasma protein (PAPP)-A and PAPP-A2 from placental trophoblasts
Mechanism of action: Measuring first-trimester serum PAPP-A/PAPP-A2 ratio using a graphene oxide-based surface plasmon resonance biosensor
Key features and challenges:
Pregnancy-associated plasma protein-A (PAPP-A) and pregnancy-associated plasma protein-A2 (PAPP-A2) are metalloproteinases produced by placental trophoblasts and implicated in placental development and function. Altered expression of these proteins has been associated with preeclampsia (PE), supporting investigation of their ratio as a potential early biomarker.
A 2023 study evaluated the clinical application of a graphene oxide (GO)-based surface plasmon resonance (SPR) biosensor to measure the first-trimester serum PAPP-A/PAPP-A2 ratio for prediction of preeclampsia (https://www.dovepress.com/clinical-application-of-a-graphene-oxide-based-surface-plasmon-resonan-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-IJN
; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10712333/). The GO-SPR biosensor demonstrated higher sensitivity, affinity, and selectivity compared with conventional SPR platforms. In the study, SPR angle shifts corresponding to serum PAPP-A, PAPP-A2, and the PAPP-A/PAPP-A2 ratio were measured and compared between women who later developed preeclampsia and controls. The findings suggested that the first-trimester PAPP-A/PAPP-A2 ratio measured using the GO-SPR biosensor may serve as a promising early predictive marker for preeclampsia.
Key challenges include the need for validation in larger, diverse populations, standardization of assay calibration and cut-off values, and integration into existing prenatal screening workflows. While technologically innovative, clinical utility will depend on reproducibility, cost-effectiveness, and comparative performance relative to established biomarkers such as the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio and combined first-trimester screening models.

Name: PI4KIIIα inhibitors
Developers: University of Hyderabad

Target: Lipid kinase, phosphatidylinositol-4-kinase type III alpha (PI4KIIIα)
Mechanism of action: Inhibition of PI4KIIIα to prevent initiation of viral replication.
Key features and challenges:
Abstract
According to World Health Organization reports of the year 2022, nearly 242,000 people died from hepatitis C that causes liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Phosphatidylinositol-4-kinase type III alpha (PI4KIIIα), a lipid kinase interacts with the hepatitis C virus non-structural 5 A protein (NS5A) to produce phosphoinositol-4-phosphate (PI4P), which enriches the hepatitis C virus replication complex. Patients with hepatitis C virus infection in the liver have been associated with increased levels of PI4P at the endoplasmic reticulum. To initiate viral replication, the hepatitis C virus must assemble numerous host cellular proteins into distinct membrane replication structures. A crucial element of these replication organelles is PI4KIIIα. Therefore, inhibition of PI4KIIIα is one of the most needed therapeutic approaches for the treatment of the disease. In this direction, a combination of pharmacophore-based virtual screening, molecular docking, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were studied for PI4KIIIα. The stability of the complexes throughout MD simulations was evaluated from their binding free energies, post-MD analysis, and further the drug-like properties of the selected molecules were analyzed. Six molecules were finally selected as the likely hit molecules based on binding free energies, normal mode analysis, and their drug-like properties. The findings of this work suggest that the selected small molecules may be used as lead molecules for the development of novel PI4KIIIα inhibitors. It is also anticipated that these thorough studies will be helpful in the structure-based drug design of PI4KIIIα inhibitors (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07391102.2024.2440645).

Name: POC fluorescent-based NG LFA
Developers: Foundation for Innovative New Diagnostics (FIND); DCN Diagnostics (DCNdx); University of Alabama at Birmingham
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoea
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Mechanism of action: lateral flow assay
Key features and challenges:
POC fluorescent-based NG LFA is a rapid, low-cost lateral flow assay developed for point-of-care detection of Neisseria gonorrhoeae to support etiological diagnosis in low- and middle-income countries. The assay was developed in alignment with a Target Product Profile (TPP) defined through collaboration between FIND, WHO, and the Global Antibiotic Research & Development Partnership to address diagnostic gaps in sexually transmitted infections.
A 2024 study reported that the fluorescent-based NG LFA demonstrated clinical sensitivity and specificity of 78.6% and 100%, respectively, in female vaginal swabs, and 100% and 89.7%, respectively, in male urine samples (https://journals.lww.com/stdjournal/fulltext/2024/03000/development_of_a_novel_fluorescent_based_lateral.8.aspx). 
The assay delivers results in under 30 minutes, is designed to cost less than USD $3 per test, and is intended for decentralized settings. The platform is positioned to facilitate a shift from syndromic to etiological STI management and has been prepared for technology transfer to a commercial manufacturing partner.
Key challenges include variability in sensitivity across specimen types, the need for large-scale field validation in diverse LMIC settings, and integration into existing diagnostic and treatment workflows. Sustainable manufacturing, regulatory approval, and quality assurance mechanisms will be critical for market adoption.
Overall, the POC fluorescent-based NG LFA represents an affordable, rapid diagnostic solution aligned with global TPP guidance for gonorrhea detection. Further implementation studies are required to confirm real-world performance and programmatic impact.

Name: PPH Butterfly
Developers: University of Liverpool
Indication: Indicated for the temporary control or reduction of postpartum uterine bleeding when conservative management of uterine bleeding is warranted.
Mechanism of action: Provides direct intrauterine pressure/tamponade to promote haemostasis.
Key features and challenges:
The PPH Butterfly is a medical device designed to replicate bimanual compression (BMC) for the management of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) in a less invasive manner. Traditional BMC requires insertion of one hand into the vagina while the other compresses the uterus abdominally, which can be effective but uncomfortable and physically demanding. The PPH Butterfly reproduces this compression mechanism without requiring manual vaginal insertion (https://innovations.bmj.com/content/3/1/45).
The device consists of a perforated platform with folding handles at either end. In its folded configuration, it forms a streamlined shape for insertion. Once positioned, the handles are unfolded to orient the platform horizontally within the vagina, allowing uterine compression when external abdominal pressure is applied. The handles interlock to provide stability, and their size prevents over-insertion while protecting the perineum from trauma. The handle may also be secured against the bed in the dorsal position, enabling one-handed operation. The device can be returned to its folded state for removal by sliding back one handle, minimizing discomfort.
The PPH Butterfly is intended for early-stage PPH, typically as a second-line intervention following administration of uterotonics. A prospective phase II clinical trial published in 2023 evaluated the device in 57 women (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36732101/
). Only one participant experienced additional blood loss exceeding 1000 mL following insertion. Three women (7%) required Bakri balloon placement, and 14% received blood transfusion. All but one clinician reported the device was easy to use, and 85% stated it assisted management. All 56 women who responded indicated they would opt for the device again in a future PPH event. No serious adverse events were reported; three minor events were considered possibly device-related (two minor vaginal grazes and one episiotomy infection with breakdown).
A 2023 economic evaluation in the United Kingdom compared the PPH Butterfly to standard care (https://www.ejog.org/article/S0301-2115(23)00079-9/fulltext). Mean treatment costs were £3,459.66 in the Butterfly cohort versus £3,223.93 with standard care. The device was associated with reduced total blood loss and demonstrated an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of £3,795.78 per PPH progression avoided (defined as ≤1000 mL additional blood loss from insertion). At a willingness-to-pay threshold of £8,500 per progression avoided, the probability of cost-effectiveness was estimated at 87%.
Key challenges include reliance on early-phase clinical data with limited sample size, need for further randomized controlled trials to confirm comparative effectiveness, and considerations around training and adoption within routine obstetric practice. Broader implementation will depend on robust outcome data and integration into established PPH management pathways.

Name: PPRG - H2S-responsive nanoprodrug
Developers: South China Agricultural University
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Salmonella Typhimurium infection.
Mechanism of action: Unknown.
Key features and challenges: Salmonellosis is a globally extensive food-borne disease, which threatens public health and results in huge economic losses in the world annually. The rising prevalence of antibiotic resistance in Salmonella poses a significant global concern, emphasizing an imperative to identify novel therapeutic agents or methodologies to effectively combat this predicament. In this study, self-assembly hydrogen sulfide (H2S)-responsive nanoprodrugs were fabricated with poly(α-lipoic acid)-polyethylene glycol grafted rhein and geraniol (PPRG), self-assembled into core–shell nanoparticles via electrostatic, hydrophilic and hydrophobic interactions, with hydrophilic exterior and hydrophobic interior. The rhein and geraniol are released from self-assembly nanoprodrugs PPRG in response to Salmonella infection, which is known to produce hydrogen sulfide (H2S). PPRG demonstrated stronger antibacterial activity against Salmonella compared with rhein or geraniol alone in vitro and in vivo. Additionally, PPRG was also able to suppress the inflammation and modulate gut microbiota homeostasis. In conclusion, the as-prepared self-assembly nanoprodrug sheds new light on the design of natural product active ingredients and provides new ideas for exploring targeted therapies for specific Enteropathogens (https://jnanobiotechnology.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12951-023-02256-9).

Name: PRADA
Developers: Iowa State University
Indication: Prediction of PTL
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: Serum levels of alpha- fetoprotein (AFP), corticotrophin releasing hormone (CRH), granulocyte macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), C-reactive protein (CRP), IL-10 and IL-6
Mechanism of action: PRADA is a portable, reusable, and accurate diagnostics tool with nanoantennas consisting of magnetic microbeads capture probes functionalized with polyclonal antibodies and near-infrared resonant gold nanostar antennas barcoded with Raman tags and labeled with peptides to detect the biomarkers via surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS).
Key features and challenges:
PRADA is an investigational biomarker-based diagnostic platform designed for multiplex detection of preterm labour (PTL)–associated biomarkers in maternal serum. The system uses nanoantenna technology composed of magnetic microbeads, enabling high analytical sensitivity and specificity, low sample volume requirements, and potential cost efficiency. The platform is designed to support multiplexing and may allow reuse of microfluidic components due to magnetic bead recovery.
Initial studies demonstrated multiplex detection of three biomarkers associated with preterm birth risk: alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), and granulocyte–macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF).
Between 2020 and 2022, a study further evaluated PRADA’s capacity to detect these biomarkers alongside additional inflammatory markers, including C-reactive protein (CRP), interleukin-10 (IL-10), and interleukin-6 (IL-6). Analytical performance was benchmarked against established platforms such as Luminex and ELISA. The study also aimed to develop a maternal risk scoring system to classify patients into high- and low-risk groups and compare PRADA-derived risk stratification with existing clinical diagnoses. Results from this study have not yet been published.
(https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/9872296)
The platform leverages surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS)–based detection principles, and the use of gold nanoparticles and magnetic bead technology aligns with components already integrated into certain commercial diagnostic assays. However, clinical validation data specific to PTL/PTB prediction remain unavailable.
Overall, PRADA represents an investigational multiplex biomarker platform with potential application in PTL risk stratification. Prospective clinical validation is required to determine diagnostic accuracy, predictive performance, and clinical utility prior to implementation in obstetric care.

Name: PTB prediction by machine learning LSTM
Developers: Hangzhou Normal University, China
Indication: Indicated for the prediction of PTL

Target: Maternal characterisitcs + ultrasound measurements + blood biomarkers
Mechanism of action: Measures luteal-phase progesterone to assess ovulatory function and detect anovulation associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
A 2022 study from the Hangzhou Normal University used continuous electronic medical record (EMR) data from pregnant women to construct a preterm birth prediction classifier based on long short-term memory (LSTM) networks. Clinical data (first and second trimester medical parameters) were collected from 5187 pregnant Chinese women who gave birth with natural vaginal delivery. The data included more than 25,000 obstetric EMRs from the early trimester to 28 weeks of gestation and the following parameters: 
- General characteristics: Age, prepregnancy weight, prepregnancy systolic blood pressure, prepregnancy diastolic blood pressure, 
- Physical data: gestational age, pulse rate, maternal weight at pregnancy, systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, iterine height, mother abdominal circumference
- Ultrasonic data: biparietal diameter, head circumference, femur length, fetal abdominal circumference
- Laboratory data: Triglyceride, Total bile acid, Uric acid, Platelets, cells Fasting blood glucose, Total cholesterol, Activated partial thromboplastin, Fibrinogen, Hemoglobin
Important-feature identification indicated that blood pressure, blood glucose, lipids, uric acid, and other metabolic factors were important factors related to preterm birth.
Compared with a traditional cross-sectional study, the LSTM model in this time-series study had better overall prediction ability and a lower misdiagnosis rate at the same detection rate. Accuracy was 0.739, sensitivity was 0.407, specificity was 0.982, and the AUC was 0.651 (https://medinform.jmir.org/2022/6/e33835)

Name: PX-478
Developers: Oncothyreon; ProlX Pharmaceuticals; PharmAxis Ltd
Indication: uterine fibroid growth and angiogenesis
Mechanism of action: Hypoxia-inducible factor 1 alpha inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
PX-478 is an innovative experimental drug with a targeted approach to cancer therapy. Its primary feature is its ability to inhibit hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF-1α), a crucial protein involved in the body’s response to low oxygen levels. PX-478, primarily researched for its effects on cancer, targets hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF-1α). This mechanism could potentially impact uterine fibroids by inhibiting factors involved in abnormal growth and blood supply. While this offers a promising new treatment avenue, especially for fibroids resistant to conventional therapies, its application in this context is still largely unexplored. The key challenge is that PX-478 has limited research specific to uterine fibroids. Most studies focus on its use in cancer, so its effects and safety for fibroids remain unclear. Additionally, potential side effects related to normal physiological functions need to be carefully evaluated. As such, extensive clinical trials would be necessary to determine its effectiveness and safety for treating uterine fibroids. Name: Palmitoleate
Developers: University of Nebraska Lincoln; University of Arizona
Indication: Therapeutic (treatment of ZIKV-induced neuronal damage and CZS).

Key features and challenges:
-Shown to protect placental trophoblasts and neurons against ZIKV infection.
-Reduces ER stress markers (p-IRE1α, p-eIF2α, spliced XBP1, cleaved ATF6, CHOP).
-Decreases viral RNA, envelope protein levels, and plaque-forming units.
-Safe, dietary-based candidate; potentially accessible in pregnancy.
-Challenge: efficacy demonstrated only in vitro and in hSTAT2KI mouse neuronal cultures; in vivo translational and clinical studies still required.
Recent updates: Builds on prior findings of palmitoleate’s protective role in ZIKV-infected placental trophoblasts. This 2025 study extends activity to neuronal protection, showing strong attenuation of ER stress, apoptosis, and viral replication in human neuronal cells and hSTAT2KI mouse cortical neurons. No animal in vivo efficacy studies or clinical trials yet reported.

Name: Pam3CSK4
Developers: University of Pennsylvania; Washington University in Saint Louis
Indication: Prevention and treatment of RVFV infection in humans
Mechanism of action: Activates TLR1/2 signaling, inducing strong IFN-β and interferon-stimulated gene (ISG) responses; indirectly restricts RVFV replication and protects against viral spread to the brain.
Key features and challenges:
-In vitro: Pam3CSK4 pretreatment or co-treatment blocked RVFV infection in epithelial, hepatocyte, neuronal, and myeloid cells.
-In vivo: C57BL/6 mice treated with Pam3CSK4 were protected from RVFV encephalitis and death.
-Potent inducer of type I IFNs; also reduced replication of other RNA viruses in the same study (alphaviruses, phleboviruses).
-Challenges: systemic inflammatory side effects possible; dosing/timing critical for efficacy; translation from mice to livestock/humans untested.
Recent updates:
-Pam3CSK4 is widely studied as a TLR agonist adjuvant in vaccine research; in 2024–2025, multiple studies continued to confirm its ability to boost antiviral states across unrelated viruses (influenza, SARS-CoV-2, bunyaviruses).
-No published follow-up in vivo studies yet specifically extending Pam3CSK4 to large animal RVFV models or combination therapies, but the 2023 paper positioned it as a strong “broad-spectrum antiviral candidate.”
-CEPI and WHO R&D agendas (2024–2025) continue to emphasize TLR agonists like Pam3CSK4 as promising broad-spectrum countermeasures for emerging viral threats.

Name: Pelargonium quercetorum agnew extracts

Mechanism of action: T. vaginalis growth inhibition
Key features and challenges:
Pelargonium quercetorum agnew extracts are plant-derived bioactive extracts under investigation for antiparasitic activity against Trichomonas vaginalis. Extracts from P. quercetorum have been evaluated for their potential to inhibit parasite growth and viability.
A 2023 study assessed the antitrichomonal activity of different solvent extracts of P. quercetorum and reported that ethyl acetate and n-hexane extracts demonstrated the strongest in vitro effects (https://ajcmi.umsha.ac.ir/Article/ajcmi-3455). 
Growth inhibition was observed at concentrations as low as 250 µg/mL, with complete parasite killing achieved at higher concentrations. The findings suggest that non-polar bioactive compounds within these extracts may contribute to antiparasitic activity and warrant further characterization.
Key challenges include identification and purification of the active constituents, assessment of cytotoxicity in human-relevant cell lines, and validation in animal models of vaginal infection. Standardization of extract composition and reproducibility of pharmacological activity must also be addressed.
Overall, P. quercetorum extracts represent a plant-based therapeutic strategy with demonstrated in vitro activity against T. vaginalis. Further preclinical studies are required to determine their suitability for drug development.

Name: Penicillin-Based Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors
Developers: University of Florence, Università degli Studi di Firenze
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Inhibition of carbonic anhydrase
Key features and challenges:
Penicillin-based carbonic anhydrase (CA) inhibitors are hybrid antimicrobial candidates designed to simultaneously target bacterial carbonic anhydrases and penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) in Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Carbonic anhydrases have been validated as antibacterial targets in multiple pathogens, and a multitarget approach aims to overcome resistance by disrupting complementary bacterial pathways.
A 2024 study reported that sulfonamide-based hybrid derivatives potently inhibited carbonic anhydrases from N. gonorrhoeae and Escherichia coli (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38776401/). Computational simulations indicated that the compounds retained β-lactam–like interaction with the main gonococcal PBP. A subset of derivatives demonstrated strong PBP-related antigonococcal activity against multidrug-resistant strains, with several compounds outperforming both the parent β-lactam and standalone CA inhibitors.
Key challenges include the need for in vivo validation of dual-target efficacy, assessment of pharmacokinetic and toxicity profiles, and evaluation of resistance development risk. Optimization of hybrid molecule stability and bioavailability will also be critical for clinical translation.
Overall, penicillin-based CA inhibitor hybrids represent a dual-mechanism antimicrobial strategy against multidrug-resistant N. gonorrhoeae. Further preclinical evaluation is required to determine their therapeutic development potential.

Name: Peripherally restricted kappa receptor agonists (PRKA)
Developers: Harvard Medical School; Brigham and Women's Hospital
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: PRKAs activate peripheral kappa-opioid receptors
Key features and challenges:
Peripherally restricted kappa receptor agonists (PRKAs) are compounds that selectively activate kappa-opioid receptors in peripheral tissues while minimizing central nervous system penetration, thereby reducing the risk of centrally mediated adverse effects. Interest in PRKAs for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) arises from their potential to modulate neuroendocrine signaling, inflammation, and metabolic dysfunction; key features of the disorder.
A 2021 study investigated the role of PRKAs in murine models characterized by hyperactive kisspeptin/neurokinin B/dynorphin (KNDy) neurons, which are implicated in reproductive hormone dysregulation observed in menopause and PCOS. Treatment with PRKAs resulted in reduced body temperature, decreased plasma luteinizing hormone (LH) and testosterone levels, and improved ovarian cycle regularity. These findings suggest that peripheral kappa receptor activation may suppress excessive KNDy neuron activity, thereby attenuating hyperandrogenism and restoring aspects of reproductive cyclicity.
Although these preclinical findings are promising, evidence remains limited to animal models, and direct clinical data in women with PCOS are currently lacking. Furthermore, the long-term safety, reproductive implications, and metabolic effects of PRKAs in this population have not yet been established. Consequently, PRKAs remain an early-stage, mechanistically driven candidate that warrants further translational and clinical investigation before therapeutic applicability in PCOS can be determined.
