Name: Phenolic chalcones (4′-Hydroxychalcone (4HC))
Developers: São Paulo State University
Indication: Investigated for the treatment of Trichomoniasis.
Mechanism of action:
A high reactive oxygen species production was observed in neutrophils co-incubated with T. vaginalis treated with 4HC in concentration-response manner, suggesting that 4HC was able to improve radical defence of neutrophils against T. vaginalis.  This can be suggested as an adjuvant mechanism based on immunity control, together with chalcone 4HC action.
Molecular docking simulations also demonstrated that 4HC has a promising binding affinity in the catalytic site of purine nucleoside phosphorylase of T. vaginalis.
Key features and challenges:
Phenolic chalcones (4′-Hydroxychalcone, 4HC) are synthetic and naturally derived compounds based on a 1,3-diphenylprop-2-en-1-one scaffold, investigated for antiparasitic activity against Trichomonas vaginalis. Chalcones have demonstrated broad antiprotozoal activity across multiple parasite species, and structural modifications have been explored to enhance therapeutic potential.
A 2023 study designed and synthesized 21 phenolic chalcones and evaluated their activity against T. vaginalis trophozoites. 
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0045206823005497?via%3Dihub). 
Among these, 4′-hydroxychalcone (4HC) was identified as the most active compound, with an IC₅₀ of 27.5 µM. In vitro and in vivo assessments indicated that 4HC was non-toxic to human erythrocytes. Related investigations have also shown that chalcone–metronidazole hybrids and chalconyl-triazole organosilatrane derivatives exhibit activity against both metronidazole-susceptible and resistant strains, with limited cytotoxicity in human cell lines.
Key challenges include the need for comprehensive pharmacokinetic profiling, validation in relevant animal models of vaginal infection, and assessment of long-term safety. Optimization of potency and selectivity will be essential for clinical development.
Overall, phenolic chalcones, particularly 4HC, represent promising small-molecule candidates with demonstrated in vitro antitrichomonal activity. Further preclinical evaluation is required to determine their suitability for therapeutic advancement.

Name: Pheophorbide a (PBa)
Developers: University of Benin (Uniben)
Indication: Pheophorbide a is a chlorophyll-derived compound evaluated in mouse models of LPS-induced preterm birth for its ability to prevent PTL through suppression of inflammatory cytokines, reduction of uterine contractility and protection of fetal viability.
Target:
-Inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1β etc.)
-Uterine contraction-associated pathways
Mechanism of action: Pheophorbide a inhibits LPS-induced inflammatory signalling, reduces cytokine production, and suppresses uterine contractility. In mouse models, PBa prevented preterm labour and significantly improved fetal survival, showing comparable or greater effectiveness than progesterone.
Key features and challenges:
Pheophorbide a (PBa) is a chlorophyll-derived botanical compound investigated for its anti-inflammatory and anti-contractile properties in preterm labour (PTL). As a metabolite of chlorophyll, PBa has demonstrated biological activity in modulating inflammatory signaling pathways, which are central to infection-driven PTL pathogenesis. Inflammatory cytokine activation, upregulation of contraction-associated proteins, and uterine contractility are key mechanisms implicated in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced preterm birth.
In preclinical murine models of LPS-induced PTL, PBa demonstrated superior potency compared with progesterone in preventing preterm delivery. Treatment significantly inhibited pro-inflammatory cytokines and suppressed downstream pathways associated with uterine contractility. In vitro studies further showed marked downregulation of contraction-associated proteins, suggesting multi-pathway modulation of inflammatory and myometrial activation processes.
In vivo findings indicated improved pregnancy maintenance and increased fetal survival rates in treated animals. These data suggest that PBa may offer broader anti-inflammatory effects compared with conventional progesterone therapy in infection-driven PTL models.
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1111/aji.70000?saml_referrer
Despite promising mechanistic and efficacy findings, evidence remains entirely preclinical. No toxicity, pharmacokinetic, or safety data are available in human pregnancy. Chlorophyll derivatives have not been pharmacologically characterized for obstetric indications, and potential phototoxicity; reported with certain chlorophyll metabolites, requires careful evaluation. Furthermore, efficacy has only been demonstrated in LPS-induced (infection-driven) PTL models, and generalizability to other etiologies of spontaneous preterm labour remains uncertain.
Pheophorbide a represents an early-stage botanical candidate targeting inflammatory pathways in PTL. While preclinical data suggest potent multi-pathway activity, substantial translational work is required to establish safety, mechanism, and clinical relevance in human pregnancy.
Recent updates: 2024 article demonstrates PBa strongly inhibits inflammation and uterine contractility, preventing LPS-induced PTB and improving fetal outcomes (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1111/aji.70000?saml_referrer)

Name: Pheophytin a (PTa)
Developers: University of Benin (Uniben)
Indication: Pheophytin a is a chlorophyll-derived compound evaluated in a mouse model of preterm birth for its potential to prevent LPS-induced PTL by suppressing inflammation, inhibiting uterine contractility, and improving fetal survival outcomes.
Target: Uterine inflammatory pathways; cytokine signalling; uterine contractility pathways
Mechanism of action: Pheophytin a suppresses LPS-induced inflammatory responses, reduces production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, inhibits uterine contractility, and prevents preterm labour in murine models. It demonstrated potency comparable to or greater than progesterone in reducing inflammation and improving pregnancy outcomes.
Key features and challenges:
Pheophytin a (PTa) is a chlorophyll-derived botanical compound investigated for its anti-inflammatory and anti-contractile effects in preterm labour (PTL). As a chlorophyll metabolite, PTa has been evaluated for its ability to modulate inflammatory pathways that contribute to infection-driven PTL. Inflammatory cytokine release and upregulation of contraction-associated proteins are central mechanisms in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced uterine activation and preterm birth.
In preclinical mouse models of LPS-induced PTL, PTa demonstrated significant efficacy in preventing preterm delivery. Treatment reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine production, suppressed uterine contractility, and improved fetal viability compared with control groups. In several measured parameters, PTa outperformed progesterone, suggesting broader anti-inflammatory and uterine-stabilizing effects. In vitro assays further confirmed significant inhibition of inflammatory mediators and contraction-associated proteins, supporting a multi-pathway mechanism of action.
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1111/aji.70000?saml_referrer
Despite promising preclinical findings, PTa remains entirely investigational. No human safety, pharmacokinetic, or dosing data are available. Chlorophyll derivatives have not been characterized for obstetric use, and potential toxicity; including phototoxicity and off-target effects, requires thorough evaluation. Additionally, efficacy has only been demonstrated in infection-driven PTL models, and validation in alternative models (e.g., sterile inflammation or decidual senescence) is needed to assess broader applicability. Variability in compound purity or extraction methods outside controlled laboratory settings may also affect translational feasibility.
Pheophytin a represents an early-stage botanical candidate targeting inflammatory and contractile pathways in PTL. While preclinical data suggest strong anti-inflammatory efficacy, extensive translational and safety studies are required before consideration for clinical development in pregnancy.
Recent updates: 2024 publication demonstrating PTa prevents LPS-induced preterm birth and fetal mortality better than progesterone by reducing inflammation and uterine contractility (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1111/aji.70000?saml_referrer)

Name: Phomasetin
Developers: University of Oklahoma; University of Washington
Indication: Treatment of Mycoplasma genitalium
Mechanism of action: Natural product antibiotic disrupting essential bacterial metabolic processes.
Key features and challenges: A 2024 study highlights that tetramic acid-containing natural products are well known for their strong biological activity against various diseases. In previous work, fungal-derived tetramic acid compounds showed activity against Trichomonas vaginalis. The authors now show that Mycoplasma genitalium is also highly sensitive to this chemotype and have identified initial structure–activity relationships for distinct tetramate types in phomasetin (compound 6) and pyrrolocin A (compound 10). Both compounds were further modified to enhance bioactivity, and they hold promise as pipeline-diversifying chemotypes for developing new leads against T. vaginalis and M. genitalium (https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsmedchemlett.4c00386)
Recent updates: Discovery study published in 2024 identified phomasetin as having activity against Mycoplasma genitalium (https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsmedchemlett.4c00386)

Name: Pinocembrin
Developers: Monash University Malaysia
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of CHIKV infection
Target:
CHIKV nonstructural protein 3 (nsP3 macrodomain)
Secondary: nsP1 (methyltransferase/guanylyltransferase), CHIKV envelope protein (E1–E2 complex, Pocket 1).
Mechanism of action:
-Stable binding to CHIKV nsP3 macrodomain active site, overlapping with ADP-ribose binding pocket → potential inhibition of viral replication complex activity.
-May also stabilize the E1–E2 glycoprotein dimer at “Pocket 1,” disrupting fusion and viral entry.
-Predicted oral bioavailability (meets Lipinski’s Rule of Five) and drug-like properties.
Key features and challenges:
-Docking free energies: nsP3 (–8.8 kcal/mol, strongest), nsP1 (–8.3), CHIKV E protein Pocket 1 (–8.3).
-nsP3–Pinocembrin complex remained most stable in 200 ns MD simulations (low RMSD, low RMSF, consistent H-bonding).
-MM-PBSA binding energy: nsP3 (–17.06 kcal/mol), stronger than nsP1 (–6.02) or E protein (–8.02).
-Pharmacokinetics: MW 256 Da, LogP 2.6, good drug-likeness, potential oral delivery.
-Bioactivity profiling suggests activity as nuclear receptor ligand and enzyme inhibitor.
Recent updates:
2025: 
-First comprehensive computational study of Pinocembrin vs CHIKV; highlighted nsP3 macrodomain as lead target.
-Authors note urgent need for in vitro and in vivo validation to confirm antiviral activity.

Name: Pioglitazone
Developers: Takeda Pharmaceutical Company; Fundacio Sant Joan De Deu
Indication: PCOS Insulin insensitivity, menstrual dysregulation, fertility, metabolic dysfunction, hyperandrogenism, oxidative stress, cardiovascular risk, weight management
Mechanism of action: Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma agonists
Key features and challenges:
Pioglitazone is an oral insulin sensitiser and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) agonist approved for the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus. By enhancing insulin sensitivity in peripheral tissues, it improves glucose uptake and reduces hyperinsulinaemia. Given that insulin resistance is central to the pathophysiology of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), pioglitazone has been investigated as a therapeutic option in this population.
https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800000018
Earlier clinical studies demonstrated that pioglitazone improves fasting glucose, glucose tolerance, menstrual regularity, and ovulatory function in women with PCOS. Compared with metformin, pioglitazone has shown greater efficacy in improving menstrual cyclicity and ovulation in some studies, though it is less effective for hirsutism. However, its use is limited by adverse effects including weight gain, fluid retention, potential liver enzyme elevations, and teratogenic risk, necessitating careful patient selection.
A 2021 meta-analysis reported significant reductions in lipid parameters with pioglitazone compared with placebo and other agents, including metformin and atorvastatin.
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/cen.14636
A 2022 clinical study found that combining pioglitazone with Diane-35 (ethinylestradiol/cyproterone acetate) significantly improved hormone levels, insulin resistance, lipid profiles, BMI, and waist–hip ratio compared with Diane-35 alone in women with PCOS.
https://rbej.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12958-023-01075-9
A 2023 meta-analysis suggested that triple therapy with clomiphene citrate, metformin, and pioglitazone may optimise pregnancy outcomes in women with PCOS, although none of the treatments—including pioglitazone—demonstrated significant benefit in improving clinical pregnancy rates among obese women.
https://rbej.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12958-023-01075-9
Mechanistic studies have shown that pioglitazone improves mitochondrial function in skeletal muscle by enhancing oxidative phosphorylation gene expression and increasing PGC-1α expression, likely mediated through adiponectin upregulation and PPAR-γ activation.
https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/20420188221113140
A 2023 preclinical study demonstrated that pioglitazone improved both metabolic and reproductive abnormalities in PCOS rat models and reduced hypothalamic Kiss1 expression, linking metabolic regulation with reproductive hormone modulation.
https://www.dovepress.com/effect-of-hypoglycaemic-drugs-on-kisspeptin-expression-in-the-hypothala-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-DMSO
Another 2023 study reported that pioglitazone combined with α-lipoic acid resulted in greater improvements in oxidative stress markers, BMI, and menstrual cyclicity compared with α-lipoic acid monotherapy.
https://www.europeanreview.org/article/33285
Clinical trials continue to explore pioglitazone’s role in ovulation induction and metabolic management in PCOS. A completed study compared pioglitazone plus clomiphene citrate versus metformin plus clomiphene citrate for ovulation induction in infertile women with PCOS.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03566225
A 2023 registered study is evaluating pioglitazone’s effects on gonadal and metabolic profiles in women with PCOS.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05519813
Computational pharmacokinetic and bioactivity analyses have further supported its mechanistic plausibility in ovulation induction protocols.
http://dx.doi.org/10.13040/IJPSR.0975-8232.14(5).2522-26
Despite its demonstrated metabolic and reproductive benefits, pioglitazone presents several important limitations in the management of PCOS. One of the primary concerns is weight gain and fluid retention, which may counteract its metabolic advantages, particularly in overweight or obese women who represent a substantial proportion of the PCOS population. Additionally, the drug carries potential teratogenic risks, requiring careful contraceptive planning or discontinuation in women actively attempting conception. Hepatic safety monitoring is also necessary due to the risk of liver enzyme elevation.
Pioglitazone represents a biologically plausible and metabolically effective insulin-sensitising therapy for PCOS, with demonstrated benefits on menstrual cyclicity, ovulation, and lipid profiles. However, safety considerations and positioning relative to metformin and newer metabolic agents limit its routine use, and its role remains phenotype-specific and adjunctive rather than first-line.

Name: Piper nigrum (limonene)
Developers: Hamadan University of Medical Sciences
Indication: Growth inhibition of T.vaginalis
Target: cell membranes; ATPase; respiratory chain enzymes
Mechanism of action: cell membrane disruption; ATPase inhibition; respiratory chain enzyme inhibition
Key features and challenges:
Piper nigrum (limonene) is a plant-derived compound under investigation for antiparasitic activity against Trichomonas vaginalis. Limonene, a cyclic monoterpene and major component of black pepper (Piper nigrum) essential oil, has demonstrated antimicrobial and membrane-disruptive properties.
A 2023 study evaluated limonene and black pepper seed extracts for antitrichomonal activity and reported a minimum lethal concentration (MLC) of 1250 µg/mL for limonene (https://jkmu.kmu.ac.ir/article_92283.html). 
In comparison, the n-hexane extract and essential oil exhibited stronger activity, achieving complete trophozoite killing at MLCs of 78 µg/mL and 156 µg/mL, respectively. The enhanced efficacy of the oil and extracts was attributed to potential synergistic interactions among multiple bioactive constituents. Limonene demonstrated higher cytotoxicity toward Vero cells, resulting in a lower selectivity index (SI = 2.04), whereas black pepper oil showed a more favorable safety profile.
Key challenges include the relatively high concentrations required for limonene efficacy, cytotoxicity concerns, and the need for standardization of essential oil composition. In vivo validation and pharmacokinetic characterization are necessary before clinical translation.
Overall, Piper nigrum–derived extracts show promising in vitro activity against T. vaginalis, with limonene contributing as a key bioactive component. Further preclinical evaluation is required to assess therapeutic feasibility.

Name: Piperacillin/Tazobactam
Developers: Taiho Pharmaceutical; Fujifilm Toyama Chemical Co.Ltd; Sapporo Medical University
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Target: Bacterial outer membrane protein; Penicillin-binding protein; Beta lactamase
Mechanism of action: Bacterial outer membrane protein inhibitors; Penicillin-binding protein inhibitors; Beta lactamase inhibitors; Cell wall inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Piperacillin/tazobactam is a β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combination being evaluated as a potential treatment option for multidrug-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Piperacillin is a broad-spectrum penicillin antibiotic, and tazobactam enhances its activity by inhibiting β-lactamases produced by resistant strains.
A 2024 study assessed the affinity of various β-lactam antibiotics for recombinant penicillin-binding protein 2 (PBP2) from N. gonorrhoeae using a fluorescence-labeled competition assay (https://www.liebertpub.com/doi/10.1089/mdr.2023.0256). 
The findings demonstrated that piperacillin maintained comparable affinity for PBP2 across penicillin-susceptible, cefixime-reduced-susceptible, and cephalosporin-resistant strains, including ceftriaxone-resistant isolates. In contrast, cephalosporins showed reduced affinity for PBP2 in resistant strains. These results suggest that piperacillin/tazobactam may retain activity against ceftriaxone-resistant or multidrug-resistant gonococcal strains.
Key challenges include the need for clinical efficacy data in gonorrhea, evaluation of appropriate dosing regimens, and assessment of resistance emergence. Parenteral administration requirements and potential collateral effects on microbiota may also influence implementation feasibility.
Overall, piperacillin/tazobactam represents a repurposing strategy targeting preserved PBP2 affinity in resistant N. gonorrhoeae. Clinical validation is required to determine its role in managing multidrug-resistant gonorrhea.

Name: Pixantrone maleate (topoisomerase II inhibitor)
Developers: Nagasaki University, including the Institute of Tropical Medicine (NEKKEN)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of LASV infection
Target: Host DNA topoisomerase IIα and IIβ enzymes (host factor for arenavirus replication)
Mechanism of action: Inhibits topoisomerase II function, disrupting arenavirus RNA replication and translation. Also enhances type-I interferon signaling, counteracting arenavirus immune evasion.
Key features and challenges:
-Identified via high-throughput screening of 2,595 FDA-approved compounds using an LASV minigenome system.
-Showed potent inhibition of LASV minigenome replication (IC50 ~1.01 µM; Selectivity Index 9.21).
-Inhibited JUNV minigenome replication (IC50 ~1.81 µM) and live JUNV Candid #1 strain replication (IC50 ~3.66 µM).
-Restricted recombinant LCMV infection (IC50 ~4.75 µM).

Name: PlGF and autoimmune antibodies predictive model
Developers: Shandong University
Indication: For early prediction of preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: Serum levels of 48 cytokines, total immunoglobulins (Igs), anti-phosphatidylserine (aPS) antibodies, and biomarkers including placental growth factor (PlGF), soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1), and activin A.
Mechanism of action: Integrates placental growth factor levels and autoimmune antibody markers to assess immune-mediated placental dysfunction and preeclampsia risk.
Key features and challenges:
Preeclampsia is a major cause of maternal and infant illness and death, but predicting it early is still tough due to the lack of dependable biomarkers. A 2023 study looked at first-trimester blood levels of 48 cytokines, total immunoglobulins (Igs), anti-phosphatidylserine (aPS) antibodies, and well-known PE markers like placental growth factor (PlGF), soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1), and activin A in 34 women later diagnosed with PE and 34 healthy controls. Results showed that in women who developed PE, certain cytokines (HGF, IL-2Rα, IL-9, RANTES, TNF-β) and autoimmune antibodies (total IgM, total IgG, aPS IgG) were higher, while total IgA was lower. These women also had lower PlGF levels and a higher sFlt-1/PlGF ratio. Models combining PlGF and autoimmune antibodies showed strong potential for predicting PE.
(https://translational-medicine.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12967-023-04472-1)

Name: Placenta-Specific Extracellular miRNA + biochemical (b-hCG and PAPP-A) and ultrasound (UAPI) model
Developers: Russian Ministry for Health and Social Development
Indication: Prediction of Early- and Late-Onset Pre-Eclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Detection of  miRNAs in combination with biochemical (b-hCG and PAPP-A) and ultrasound (UAPI) parameters.
Key features and challenges: A 2023 study explored predicting early- and late-onset pre-eclampsia (PE) before symptoms appear, using placenta-specific extracellular miRNA profiling. PE is driven by maternal and/or placental factors, with their combination influencing when symptoms arise (before or after 34 weeks of pregnancy) and how severe they are. Since miRNA expression changes with gestational age, researchers aimed to pinpoint placenta-specific miRNAs that distinguish early (ePE) from late-onset PE (lPE). Analyzing 67 patients with small RNA sequencing and qPCR, they identified a core set of miRNAs that, in certain combinations, could predict ePE or lPE in the first trimester with 100% sensitivity and 84–100% specificity. Literature suggests these miRNAs regulate processes like trophoblast growth, invasion, migration, syncytialization, stress responses, immune tolerance, angiogenesis, and vascular health. Measuring let-7d-3p, miR-451a, and miR-1307-3p—stable even after repeated freeze-thaw cycles—alongside biochemical markers (b-hCG, PAPP-A) and ultrasound data (UAPI), enabled the creation of a universal prediction model. This model, with a false-positive rate of 15.7% and a false-negative rate of 9.5%, was tested on 48 patients, showing false positives in 26.7% and false negatives in 5.6% of cases (https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/24/9/8006)

Name: Placenta-derived CircBRAP, plasma sFLT1 and uterine artery Doppler ultrasound
Developers: Guangdong Medical University
Indication: Prediction of PE
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: Plasma sFLT1 + CircBRAP levels + uterine artery Doppler ultrasound findings
Mechanism of action: Modulates intrauterine immune signaling and inflammatory pathways that regulate parturition and initiation of labour.
Key features and challenges:
A 2022 Chinese study explored a multi-parametric test for predicting preeclampsia in the first trimester. This test combined plasma levels of soluble Fms-related tyrosine kinase 1 (sFLT1) with uterine artery Doppler ultrasound results and CircBRAP levels. Using qRT-PCR, the researchers examined CircBRAP expression in forty-nine pairs of plasma samples and placental tissues from preeclampsia patients and healthy controls. The uterine artery pulsatility index (PI) was measured with four-dimensional color Doppler ultrasound, while sFLT1 levels were assessed via human immunoassay. Findings showed that combining sFLT1 and CircBRAP levels with UtA-PI improved predictive power for preeclampsia. The study concluded that placenta-derived CircBRAP in plasma may serve as a novel biomarker, and when used alongside sFLT1 levels and Doppler ultrasound findings, could enhance early prediction of preeclampsia, with CircBRAP potentially playing a role in the condition’s development.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35015290/).

Name: Placental MRI - PE
Developers: Southern Medical University; King's College London; Uppsala University
Indication: Diagnosis and prediction of PE
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Rapid point-of-care molecular assay detecting Neisseria gonorrhoeae nucleic acids to enable early identification of infection.
Key features and challenges:
​Increasing evidence suggests that placental magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides information not only on placental structure but also on placental function. A wide range of quantitative MRI measurements is available, and each of these measurements is sensitive to specific aspects of placental function, including hypoxia and morphological changes. MRI is of interest as it provides more stable images than ultrasound and is safe to use in pregnancy. 
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0014488621002764) 
 
Currently investigated measurements for PE: 
Placental oxygenation: MRI transversal relaxation times such as T2 and T2* and the longitudinal relaxation time T1 tissue-specific constants, which describe the time for the observed MRI signal to decay. The relaxation time depends on multiple biological and physiological features of the tissue, as it is determined by the molecular environment of the protons within the tissue. In the human placenta, the T2* relaxation depends on morphological features such as the villous structure, the blood volume fractions, the deposition of fibrin or presence of infarctions, and fibrosis. Moreover, the T2* relaxation depends on placental oxygen saturation, as it is sensitive to the amount of the paramagnetic deoxyhemoglobin molecules in the tissue. Invasive animal studies have demonstrated that changes in tissue oxygenation are reflected by changes in the T2* weighted signal intensity, also known as the blood oxygen level dependent response. In the human placenta, several studies have demonstrated a low placental T2* value in pregnancies complicated by IUGR and PE. 
 
A 2020 study by researchers from King's College London showed a striking difference between the normal and the preeclamptic placenta in the T2 weighted MR image: the preeclamptic placenta is characterised by varied lobule size and increased granularity when compared with the normal placental. In the T2* map, the preeclamptic placenta is markedly darker, and the mean T2* value of the entire placenta is significantly reduced when compared with the normal placenta. Histological features of maternal vascular malperfusion were only found in placentae from women with preeclampsia (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32336233/). 
 
Placental perfusion: A 2014 study by researchers from Uppsala University focused on placental perfusion fraction and found a substantial reduction in perfusion fraction in early preeclampsia compared to early normal pregnancy. However, in late pregnancy, a larger perfusion fraction in late preeclampsia than in late normal pregnancy was found, confirming differential profiles for early and late PE, namely that late preeclampsia is related to general hyperperfusion while early preeclampsia is related to hypoperfusion. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0143400414000095)
 
A 2023 study found that placental diffusion-derived vessel density (DDVD), a biomarker derived from diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging measuring in vivo vessel micro perfusion had diagnostic value for early preeclampsia.
(https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/HYPERTENSIONAHA.122.20311)
 
Placental metabolism: Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (MRS): Magnetic resonance spectroscopy and MRI use different software to acquire and mathematically manipulate the signal. Whereas MRI creates an image, MRS creates a graph or "spectrum" arraying the types and quantity of chemicals in the brain or other organs. MRS has a unique ability to measure metabolites from the energy and cell membrane metabolism of the placenta. 
 
A 2014 Uppsala University study focused on the phosphodiester (PDE) spectral intensity fraction of the total P signal and on the phosphodiester/phosphomonoester (PDE/PME) spectral intensity ratio. It found that women with early onset preeclampsia had a higher median PDE spectral intensity fraction and a higher median PDE/PME spectral intensity ratio than women with early normal pregnancy, while women with late onset preeclampsia did not differ in median PDE spectral intensity fraction or median PDE/PME spectral intensity ratio compared to women with late normal pregnancies. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0143400414000782) 
 
Placental MRI tool: University College London is currently designing an MRI-based tool with the aim of diagnosing preeclampsia and differentiating types of placental disorders (maternal or fetal blood supply issues). They are building computational models of whole placentas, incorporating fine structural details such as tissue and blood vessel dimensions. The aim is to use machine learning techniques to instruct an algorithm to learn from thousands of simulations on computational placentas, to deliver an imaging tool that, given a placental MRI scan as input, can show the structure, blood flow, and oxygen levels of the placenta. (https://gtr.ukri.org/projects?ref=EP/V034537/1) 
 
NB: Placental positron emission tomography (PET) could be added to the MRI techniques used to understand placental function, but studies so far have focused on animal models of pregnancy. (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.2310/7290.2015.00013)​

Name: Placental Superb Microvascular Imaging (SMI) - PE
Developers: St. Marianna University School of Medicine
Indication: Prediction and diagnosis of preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: High-sensitivity Doppler imaging visualizes placental microvascular perfusion to detect reduced vascularization associated with preeclampsia.
Key features and challenges:
Superb microvascular imaging (SMI) technology has recently been developed as an innovative Doppler US technique. With the use of SMI technology, the imaging of very slow flow states is possible due to a unique algorithm that allows for the visualization of minute vessels with slow velocities without the use of a contrast agent. Compared to conventional Doppler technologies, the advantages of SMI are high frame rates, high resolution, high sensitivity and fewer motion artifacts.

A study started in 2023 at St Marianna University (Japan), with the incorporation of superb microvascular imaging (SMI) ultrasonography to prenatal checkups in their department of Obstetrics and Gynecology. The goal is to create references (evaluation criteria) for normal placenta, and to define SMI ultrasound pathological images specific to various placental abnormalities. 

Furthermore, in a prospective cohort study, SMI ultrasonographic screening during pregnancy will be performed to verify the accuracy of detection of placental abnormalities.  After delivery, the placenta will be submitted for pathological examination to obtain microscopic findings. By comparing placental ultrasonographic findings with pathological findings, the effects of the placenta on diseases thought to be caused by the placenta, such as fetal growth restriction, will be examined, and diagnostic methods for placental diseases during pregnancy will be established.
The study focuses on both IUGR and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
(https://center6.umin.ac.jp/cgi-open-bin/ctr_e/ctr_view.cgi?recptno=R000057186

Name: Placental growth factor
Developers: University of Mississippi Medical Center; Catholic University of Leuven, (KU Leuven) (including the Rega Institute for Medical Research); Aggamin Pharmaceuticals, LLC; Oxurion
Indication: Treatment of preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: PlGF restores sFlt1:PlGF ratio and supports angiogenesis and vascular homeostasis
Key features and challenges:
Placental growth factor (PlGF) is a potent angiogenic protein expressed in the villous syncytiotrophoblast and in the media of larger stem vessels of the human placenta. Together with vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), PlGF regulates placental vascular development in an oxygen-dependent manner. In pre-eclampsia, elevated circulating soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1) and reduced levels of its ligand, PlGF, are characteristic findings. Plasma free PlGF levels are significantly lower in women with pre-eclampsia compared with normotensive controls, largely due to excess circulating sFlt-1.
A 2016 preclinical study in a nonhuman primate model demonstrated that administration of PlGF significantly reduced uteroplacental ischemia, systolic blood pressure, and proteinuria (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27091894/). 
Although circulating total sFlt-1 levels were not affected, placental sFlt-1 mRNA expression was reduced. These findings support the therapeutic potential of PlGF supplementation in restoring angiogenic balance. However, large-scale manufacturing of recombinant whole proteins such as PlGF presents significant cost and scalability challenges.
Subsequent translational efforts have focused on modified or stabilized formulations. In 2019–2020, the University of Mississippi received funding to evaluate the safety and efficacy of an elastin-like polypeptide–PlGF (ELP-PlGF) fusion construct in a relevant preclinical model of pre-eclampsia (https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/9732626). 
The ELP carrier is designed to enhance stability and limit placental transfer, thereby reducing potential fetal exposure. Additionally, Aggamin Pharmaceuticals has received funding to evaluate recombinant human PlGF (rhPlGF), including in vitro binding to free sFlt-1, efficacy in the reduced uterine perfusion pressure (RUPP) rat model, safety assessment in third-trimester pregnant nonhuman primates, and completion of a cGMP manufacturing campaign in preparation for a Phase I clinical study.
Key challenges include high manufacturing costs, complex protein stabilization requirements, and the need to demonstrate safety in pregnant populations. While preclinical findings are encouraging, clinical translation will depend on scalable production, regulatory approval pathways, and robust human safety data.
Recent updates: The University of Mississippi has received a 2019-2020 funding to study the safety and efficacy of ELP-PlGF in a relevant preclinical animal model of preeclampsia. The project is expected to end in  30 June 2022 (https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/9732626).

Name: Placental protein 13 (PP13)
Developers: University of Calabria; Hospital SS Annunziata; University of Iceland, Háskóli Íslands
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Preeclampsia
Target: Maternal uterine vasculature; Annexin II; Actin; Glycan Receptors
Mechanism of action: Activation of the nitric oxide–cGMP pathway
Key features and challenges:
Placental Protein 13 (PP13), also known as galectin-13, is a placenta-derived protein implicated in vascular remodeling and immune modulation during pregnancy. PP13 has been investigated primarily in the context of preeclampsia, where impaired uteroplacental perfusion and abnormal vascular adaptation contribute to disease pathogenesis.
A 2024 mechanistic study evaluated the vasomodulatory effects of PP13 using pressurized myography in isolated uterine and subcutaneous arteries from pregnant and non-pregnant women. Arteries were precontracted with the thromboxane analogue U46619 and subsequently exposed to PP13. The study demonstrated that PP13 induced significant vasodilation in uterine arteries but not in subcutaneous arteries, suggesting tissue-specific vascular effects. PP13 also counteracted U46619-induced vasoconstriction, which is exaggerated during pregnancy.
Further mechanistic analyses using nitric oxide synthase inhibitors (L-NAME + LNNA) and guanylate cyclase inhibition (ODQ) demonstrated that PP13-mediated vasodilation is dependent on activation of the nitric oxide–cGMP signaling pathway. These findings provide molecular evidence that PP13 may regulate uteroplacental blood flow through endothelial nitric oxide signaling.
https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/25/14/7522
The ability of PP13 to selectively dilate uterine arteries and modulate vascular tone supports its potential therapeutic relevance in disorders characterized by impaired placental perfusion, particularly preeclampsia. By improving uteroplacental blood flow, PP13 could theoretically mitigate placental ischemia and downstream maternal endothelial dysfunction.
However, significant challenges remain. Current evidence is limited to ex vivo vascular studies, and no clinical interventional trials evaluating PP13 as a therapeutic agent have been reported. The optimal dosing strategy, route of administration, pharmacokinetics, and safety profile in pregnant populations remain undefined. As a placental protein with physiological roles in pregnancy, exogenous administration raises theoretical concerns regarding immune modulation and systemic vascular effects. Additionally, translational gaps remain between mechanistic vasodilation findings and demonstrated improvements in maternal or neonatal clinical outcomes.
PP13 represents a mechanistically compelling candidate for therapeutic modulation of uteroplacental blood flow in preeclampsia. Nonetheless, it remains an early-stage, preclinical concept requiring substantial translational and clinical validation before consideration as a therapeutic intervention.

Name: Podocyte-based testing
Developers: Sersense Inc; Mayo Clinic (including Mayo Medical School); Affinergy, LLC; Inform Bioscience
Indication: Diagnosis of preeclampsia in the second trimester
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Point-of-care assay quantifies circulating microRNA and protein biomarkers to detect placental dysfunction and endothelial injury associated with preeclampsia.
Key features and challenges:
Affinergy LLC received NIH funding in 2016 to develop a point-of-care test for the detection of preeclampsia in the second trimester. The test is based on the demonstration that glomerular podocytes are shed into the urine of preeclamptic patients and can be visualised using podocyte-specific antibodies. 
Shed podocytes can be detected in the second trimester, prior to preeclampsia diagnosis, with high sensitivity and specificity. Methods to detect podocytes rely on overnight culture and sedimentation of cells onto collagen-coated slides or Cytospin, which is prone to high false-positive rates due to contaminating red blood cells (RBCs) or casts. Inconsistencies in the method of podocyte detection and lengthy, overnight incubations susceptible to contamination weaken the utility of podocytes as a diagnostic marker of preeclampsia. To this end, Affinergy was developing a slide platform that can specifically capture and retain the diagnostic podocytes, while moving the obscuring contaminants to a separate region of the slide. Such a technology is amenable to downstream immunocytochemistry, would improve the diagnostic quality of podocyte capture, and lead to significant cost savings by minimising time and need for expensive equipment. There hasn't been any update since 2017. 
(https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/9253876). 
 
In 2015, Inform Bioscience (IB) received a European Union grant to develop a similar technology, having identified podocyte specific biomarkers in urine that indicate ongoing renal damage, and which allow for a sub-clinical diagnosis for PE. The key biomarker, podocin, had demonstrated good sensitivity and specificity and could diagnose the disease up to three months before clinical symptoms emerge. InformBio received funding to develop flow cytometry and research use only (RUO) ELISA assays for the biomarker. The project is called PREKIND (PreEclampsia diagnosis by Early Kidney Injury Detection). There hasn't been any update since 2015.
(https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/673383).

Sersense, Inc. also received NIH funding in 2018 for the development of a podocyte-based point of care device detecting extracellular vesicles (EVs) in urine of PE patients. The test, a lateral flow assay, should be able to measure the numbers of EVs and the levels of expression of EV surface markers, podocin and nephrin, which have been identified as preeclampsia biomarkers in research led by Mayo Clinic. 
(https://reporter.nih.gov/search/LLqrWWlJ4UK8tkt0PgK5tg/project-details/9621286)
This research is ongoing. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36548998/)

A study is underway in France (estimated to complete in 2026) to investigate podocyturia as a marker of preeclampsia severity. 
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03316391)
Recent updates:
Affinergy does not mention the podocyte test on their webpage. Inform Bioscience does not seem to exist as a company anymore.

CV: 27/05/2024, Project added as part of pipeline update: Sersense Inc. Candidate is now active again.

Name: Polarization sensitive optical coherence tomography
Developers: University of Sheffield (including the Sheffield Institute of Translational Neurology)
Indication: A tool to better understand cervical remodeling prior to birth to predict PTL.
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: The polarization state can be used to measure tissue’s depth-resolved phase retardance, birefringence, and relative fast axis orientation, which allows PS-OCT to differentiate anisotropic tissues, such as collagen fiber, muscle, and tendon, from other structures.
Key features and challenges:
Polarisation-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) is an imaging modality designed to characterise cervical microstructure by assessing collagen organisation and tissue birefringence. The technology enables identification of cervical epithelium and measurement of epithelial thickness, rapid imaging of collagen distribution, quantification of birefringence, estimation of three-dimensional collagen fibre alignment, and assessment of tissue depolarisation. These parameters are relevant to cervical remodelling processes that precede labour.
In 2019, preliminary in vitro studies using cervical cross-sections from hysterectomy specimens demonstrated that PS-OCT could visualise and quantify structural properties of cervical collagen. The findings suggested that the technique may improve understanding of cervical remodelling and potentially support earlier identification and stratification of preterm birth risk. The study also highlighted the need for development of a hand-held probe to facilitate clinical use.
(https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6701558/)
A research program running from 2021 to 2025 is developing a novel clinical imaging probe and associated data acquisition system to enable in vivo testing in volunteers. The objective is to translate PS-OCT from laboratory settings to clinical application for cervical assessment.
(https://gtr.ukri.org/projects?ref=EP%2FV010581%2F1)
Overall, PS-OCT represents an investigational imaging approach aimed at quantifying cervical collagen architecture and biomechanical properties associated with preterm labour risk. While early laboratory findings are promising, clinical validation studies are ongoing to determine feasibility, predictive performance, and integration into obstetric practice.

Name: Polyclonal hyperimmune IgG specific for LASV glycoprotein
Developers: Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine (BNITM); German Center for Infection Research (DZIF); Phillips University Marburg
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of LASV infection
Target: Lassa virus glycoprotein (GP; strain Josiah, clade IV)
Mechanism of action: Neutralizing antibodies against LASV GP block viral entry; passive transfer provides immediate immunity by reducing viremia and limiting viral spread to organs.
Key features and challenges:
-Produced by repeated immunization of rabbits with LASV GP VLPs.
-Pre-exposure prophylaxis: 100% protection in lethal mouse model; animals showed no weight loss, fever, or clinical signs.
-Early post-exposure treatment (1–5 dpi): 100% survival, efficient clearance of viremia and organ virus load.
-Late treatment (6–10 dpi, after symptom onset): 80% survival, reduced viremia and organ titers, but one animal succumbed.
-Broad neutralizing activity demonstrated previously against multiple LASV lineages (I–V).
-Advantages: cost-effective alternative to monoclonals; scalable; demonstrated efficacy in both prophylaxis and therapy.
-Challenges: animal-derived antibodies may raise immunogenicity/safety concerns; humanized versions preferable for clinical translation.
Recent updates:
Published June 2023:
-Expands earlier VLP immunogenicity data (Müller et al., NPJ Vaccines 2020) showing broad neutralizing activity across lineages.
-Highlights polyclonal antibodies as a lower-cost, broad-coverage therapeutic option compared to monoclonals (e.g., Arevirumab-2/3).

Name: Polyphenol - Curcuma longa (Curcumin)
Developers: University of South Carolina at Columbia; Nanjing Medical University
Indication: Reducing inflammation in preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: Curcumin inhibited the expression of pro-inflammatory factors and macrophage infiltration in placenta via TLR4, NF-κB and Akt-mediated pathways
Key features and challenges:
Curcumin is a lipophilic polyphenol derived from the rhizomes of Curcuma longa (turmeric). It exhibits antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties and has been shown to modulate multiple signalling pathways at the molecular and cellular levels. One of its principal mechanisms involves inhibition of nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) activation, a key regulator of cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) expression and inflammatory responses.
(Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5664031)
In a 2016 study using a lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced rat model of preeclampsia, curcumin (0.36 mg/kg) reduced blood pressure and proteinuria. It also decreased placental expression of TLR4 and NF-κB proteins and reduced serum levels of inflammatory mediators IL-6 and MCP-1. These findings suggested modulation of the TLR4 signalling pathway as a potential anti-inflammatory mechanism.
(Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27208407)
Another 2016 study in a mouse model of LPS-induced preeclampsia demonstrated that curcumin reduced pro-inflammatory factor expression and placental macrophage infiltration through up-regulation of phosphorylated Akt, resulting in improvement of adverse pregnancy outcomes in the model.
(Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27817102)
A 2019 study conducted in Dahl salt-sensitive rats reported that curcumin did not improve arterial pressure, uterine artery resistance, or litter size, indicating inconsistent findings in hypertensive pregnancy models.
(Source: https://faseb.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1096/fasebj.2019.33.1_supplement.574.8)
A clinical study published in 2020 evaluating curcumin supplementation in pregnant women with preeclampsia found no significant difference in serum COX-2 or IL-10 levels between treatment and control groups.
(Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32002054)
A clinical trial (NCT04633551), registered in 2020, is investigating the efficacy of a supplement containing curcumin in combination with other antioxidants for the prevention or management of preeclampsia and other adverse pregnancy outcomes.
(Source: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04633551)
Overall, curcumin demonstrates biological plausibility through anti-inflammatory and antioxidant mechanisms and has shown beneficial effects in certain animal models of preeclampsia. However, human clinical evidence remains limited and inconsistent, and its therapeutic role in PE/E has not been established.
Recent updates:
A clinical trial (NCT04633551) investigating efficacy of a supplement containing curcumin, together with other antioxidants, on preeclampsia and other adverse pregnancy outcomes, is recruiting as of November 18, 2020.

Name: Polyphenol - Dill extract
Developers: Mashhad University of Medical Sciences
Indication: Reduction of blood loss

Key features and challenges:
Anethum graveolens (Dill) (AG), from Apiaceae family, is a traditional herb that has various medical indications worldwide. Its fruit essence consists of carveol, d-Carvone, d-hydrocarveol, dihydrocarvone, limonene, carvacrol thymol, etc. Its seeds contain 3-3.5% essential oil. Dill includes tannin, which is a polyphenol with contractile properties, and has potential for inducing uterine contractions.

Clinical trials demonstrated that 0.18 gr/kg dill extract reduced the mean amount of bleeding compared to placebo (https://vlibrary.emro.who.int/imemr/an-investigation-of-effectiveness-of-oral-dill-extracts-on-postpartum-hemorrhage/), and 0.018 g/kg of dill seed was more effective in labour induction compared to oxytocin, however the sample size was small (https://sites.kowsarpub.com/jjnpp/articles/18434.html). 

Another clinical trial comparing the efficacy of dill extract versus uterine massage (https://en.irct.ir/trial/3102) was reported to take place in 2013-2014, but no results were reported. A clinical trial investigating a mixed ethanolic extract of N. sativa and A. graveolens seeds (IRCT20200214046492N1) has completed recruiting as of April 2020. 

However, a more recent triple blinded clinical trial demonstrated that rectal suppositories of Dill and Plantago are both effective for decreasing PPH, but Plantago rectal suppository can more effectively reduce PPH (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2210803321001068).

Developers: Hamedan University of Medical Sciences

Key features and challenges:
Grape seeds contain lipid, protein, carbohydrates, and 5–8% polyphenols, depending on the variety. The most abundant phenolic compounds isolated from grape seeds are catechin, epicatechin, and procyanidins, a group of important polyphenols that exert a beneficial effect on human health. Name: Polyphenol - Quercetin - PTL
Developers: Hunan Engineering Research Center of Early Life Development and Disease Prevention; Xiangya Hospital, Central South University
Indication: For the prevention of preterm birth
Mechanism of action: Exerts antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects to reduce cytokine-mediated uterine activation associated with preterm labour.
Key features and challenges:
Quercetin is a flavonol widely distributed in plants. It is an antioxidant, like many other phenolic heterocyclic compounds. Glycosylated forms include RUTIN and quercetrin. Quercetin appears as yellow needles or yellow powder. Converts to anhydrous form at 203-207 °F. Alcoholic solutions taste very bitter.

Quercetin is found in red wine, green tea and leafy vegetables, and has been shown to protect cellular structures and blood vessels from the damaging effects of free radicals. Clinical development is underway for the treatment of COPD, in the US. Earlier, the drug was also being studied for its potential in a number of diseases, including cancer, cardiovascular disorders, atherosclerosis and prostatitis. But the development in these indications was discontinued.

An earlier study has shown that quercetin prevented lipopolysaccharide-induced preterm birth. Now, researchers are interested in clarifying the potential targets and biological mechanisms of quercetin in preventing preterm birth. 105 targets for quercetin in preventing preterm birth were obtained. The biological processes of the intersecting targets are mainly involved in steroid metabolic process, drug metabolic process, oxidation-reduction process, omega-hydroxylase P450 pathway, positive regulation of cell migration, negative regulation of apoptotic process, and positive regulation of cell proliferation. The highly enriched pathways were steroid hormone biosynthesis, metabolism of xenobiotics by cytochrome P450, proteoglycans in cancer, focal adhesion, and arachidonic acid metabolism. The ten hub targets for quercetin in preventing preterm birth were AKT serine/threonine kinase 1, mitogen-activated protein kinase 3, epidermal growth factor receptor, prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase 2, mitogen-activated protein kinase 1, estrogen receptor 1, heat shock protein 90 alpha family class A member 1, mitogen-activated protein kinase 8, androgen receptor, and matrix metallopeptidase 9. Molecular docking analysis showed good bindings between these proteins and quercetin. These findings highlight the key targets and molecular mechanisms of quercetin in preventing preterm birth.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34231170/)

Name: Polyphenol - Resveratrol - PE/E
Developers: University of Melbourne (including the Australian Venom Research Unit (AVRU) and Bio21 Institute); Xidian Group Hospital
Indication: Treatment of preeclampsia by improving vascular dysfunction
Mechanism of action: Resveratrol increases sodium excretion and serum nitric oxide levels, improves uterine artery blood flow, reduces sFlt-1 and endoglin secretion and suppresses expression of inflammatory cytokines
Key features and challenges:
Resveratrol (RESV) is a stilbene-based natural polyphenolic compound produced by various plant species. It functions as an activator of sirtuin 1 (SIRT1), which regulates histone and non-histone protein deacetylation and influences pathways related to metabolism, oxidative stress, inflammation, endothelial function, and cellular survival. These properties have prompted investigation of resveratrol in disorders characterized by metabolic and inflammatory dysregulation, including preeclampsia.
(Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41698-017-0038-6)
In a 2013 pregnant mouse model with reduced uterine blood supply, resveratrol increased uterine artery blood flow velocity and fetal weight, suggesting potential vascular benefits.
(Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23667712/)
Subsequent experimental studies reported that resveratrol may reduce soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1) levels and decrease mRNA expression of pro-inflammatory molecules in trophoblasts, providing mechanistic support for its role in modulating placental angiogenesis and inflammation.
(Sources: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25501918
; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28500309)
In an L-NAME–induced rat model of preeclampsia, resveratrol reduced blood pressure and proteinuria, although no significant improvement in fetal outcomes was observed. The study also suggested beneficial effects on epithelial–mesenchymal transition in trophoblasts and modulation of angiogenesis-related factors, including VEGF and sFlt-1.
(Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30710417)
Additional experimental work proposed that the antihypertensive effects of resveratrol may involve increased sodium excretion and elevated serum nitric oxide (NO) levels.
(Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32099672)
However, findings across animal models have been inconsistent. In rats with desoxycorticosterone acetate–induced hypertension, resveratrol did not reduce blood pressure or improve placental pathology parameters.
A clinical study evaluating resveratrol as an adjunct to oral nifedipine in women with preeclampsia, published in 2017, reported improved attenuation of hypertensive symptoms compared with nifedipine alone, suggesting potential adjunctive benefit.
(Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28993436)
A clinical trial (NCT04633551), registered in 2020, is investigating the efficacy of a supplement containing trans-resveratrol in combination with other antioxidants for preeclampsia and adverse pregnancy outcomes.
(Source: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04633551)
Overall, resveratrol demonstrates biological plausibility and beneficial effects in several experimental models of preeclampsia. However, animal data remain mixed, and clinical evidence is limited to adjunctive or combination studies. Further randomized controlled trials are required to establish its efficacy and safety in PE/E management.
Recent updates:
A clinical trial investigating efficacy of a supplement containing transresveratol, together with other antioxidants, on preeclampsia and other adverse pregnancy outcomes (NCT04633551) is recruiting as of November 18, 2020.

Name: Polyscias fulva Ethanolic Extract (PFE)
Developers: University of Nairobi; United States International University-Africa
Indication: Botanical multi-compound extract evaluated for therapeutic activity against uterine fibroids.
Target:
Multi-target, including key UF-associated proteins:
-HIF1A
-ESR1 (Estrogen receptor 1)
-EGFR
-CASP3
-SRC
-TNF
-CCND1
Mechanism of action:
The ethanolic extract contains eleven identified bioactive phytochemicals, of which four compounds—β-sitosterol, pinoresinol, lichexanthone, and methyl atarate—exhibited good drug-likeness and were prioritized.
Network pharmacology identified 48 overlapping UF–compound targets and highlighted regulatory roles in:
-estrogen signaling,
-cyclin-dependent kinase regulation,
-nitric-oxide synthase modulation,
-transcription regulation,
-proliferative and inflammatory pathways.
Molecular docking (MD) showed β-sitosterol had the strongest binding affinities to key UF proteins (EGFR −9.75, HIF1A −9.21, ESR1 −8.31, CASP3 −7.13 kcal/mol).
MD simulations confirmed stable ligand-protein interactions, especially with CASP3, EGFR, and HIF1A.
In vivo, PFE significantly reduced MSG-induced uterine enlargement, lowered estrogen and progesterone levels dose-dependently, reduced cholesterol, and improved uterine histoarchitecture.
These combined findings suggest anti-proliferative, hormonal-modulating, anti-inflammatory, and pro-apoptotic activity in UF biology.
Key features and challenges:
Polyscias fulva ethanolic extract (PFE) is a plant-derived botanical formulation investigated for potential therapeutic activity in uterine fibroids (UF). Polyscias fulva contains multiple bioactive phytochemicals with predicted anti-proliferative, anti-inflammatory, and hormone-modulating properties. Network pharmacology and molecular docking analyses have identified eleven phytochemical constituents, with four compounds—β-sitosterol, pinoresinol, lichexanthone, and methyl atarate—demonstrating favorable pharmacokinetic profiles and strong predicted binding affinities to key UF-related molecular targets, including HIF1A, ESR1, EGFR, CASP3, TNF, SRC, and CCND1. β-sitosterol was identified as the dominant active compound, showing stable protein–ligand interactions confirmed by 100-ns molecular dynamics simulations.
In vivo validation in a monosodium glutamate (MSG)-induced uterine hypertrophy model demonstrated that oral administration of PFE (200–800 mg/kg) significantly reduced uterine weight, lowered serum estrogen, progesterone, and cholesterol levels, and restored uterine histological architecture. These findings suggest dose-dependent anti-inflammatory, anti-proliferative, and hormone-modulating effects. KEGG pathway analysis further supported potential involvement in estrogen signaling, hypoxia-related pathways, and cell cycle regulation.
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1093326325000440?via%3Dihub#sec6
Despite strong in silico and animal model evidence, PFE remains at an early preclinical stage. No human clinical studies have evaluated its safety, pharmacokinetics, hormonal effects, or efficacy in women with uterine fibroids. Key development challenges include lack of extract standardization and batch reproducibility, variability in phytochemical composition, absence of long-term toxicity data, and unknown reproductive safety profile.
Polyscias fulva ethanolic extract represents a multi-target botanical candidate with promising preclinical anti-fibroid activity. However, substantial toxicological, pharmacological, formulation, and clinical research is required before translation into therapeutic use for uterine fibroids.
Recent updates: A new 2025 integrative study (in silico + in vivo) demonstrated pharmacokinetic suitability, strong binding to key UF targets, and dose-dependent anti-fibroid effects in MSG-induced animal models. No clinical research has yet been initiated.

Name: Portable HIV-DNA Chemiluminescence Detection Test
Developers: Shaanxi Normal University
Indication: Detection of HIV-DNA for point-of-care diagnostics
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Mechanism of action: Chemiluminescence catalyzed by G-triplex-hemin DNAzyme, with amplification through cyclic strand displacement reaction (SDR)
Key features and challenges:
A label-free chemiluminescence method has been developed for the detection of HIV-DNA using a handheld luminometer. This method leverages a G-triplex-hemin DNAzyme (G3-hemin DNAzyme) that assembles in situ in the presence of HIV-DNA, enhancing sensitivity through a cyclic strand displacement reaction (SDR). The chemiluminescence reaction between luminol and H2O2 catalyzed by the DNAzyme results in a measurable signal, with a linear relationship between HIV-DNA concentration and chemiluminescence intensity. This approach offers a sensitive, selective, and portable solution for HIV-DNA detection, making it suitable for point-of-care testing, particularly in resource-limited settings.
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0003267024003544?via%3Dihub)

Name: Portable aptamer device
Developers: Imperial College London
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for research use only
Mechanism of action: Aptamer-based biosensor detects disease-associated biomarkers through specific binding and electrical or optical signal changes for rapid PCOS screening.
Key features and challenges: A portable aptamer device is a compact tool that uses aptamers—short RNA or DNA strands—to bind specific biomarkers like proteins or hormones in biological fluids. It provides real-time, non-invasive diagnostics, offering precise, cost-effective monitoring of conditions like PCOS. The device allows intermittent sampling and continuous monitoring to track biomarkers over time. Recent studies have shown its potential in diagnosing PCOS by detecting biomarkers such as luteinizing hormone (LH) and measuring LH pulsatility. The device also establishes normative biomarker ranges across different times of day and physiological states, including menstrual phases. It has been tested for other endocrine conditions, offering a sensitive method for monitoring hormonal imbalances. (https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN10920454)

Name: Pralatrexate (PDX)
Developers: Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine
Indication: Treatment of mpox infection (therapeutic candidate, repurposed anticancer drug)
Target: Early-stage replication processes of MPXV, particularly viral internalization and genome replication; mechanism not dependent on classical dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) inhibition.
Mechanism of action: Pralatrexate interferes with MPXV internalization and replication, disrupting viral DNA synthesis and maturation of virions. The antiviral effect is independent of its antifolate cytotoxic pathway, as supplementation with hypoxanthine and thymidine fails to rescue MPXV replication. It thus acts as a dual-phase inhibitor, primarily targeting viral internalization and replication during early infection stages.
Key features and challenges:
-In vitro potency:
i) Vero E6 cells: IC₅₀ = 7.76 nM; CC₅₀ > 10 µM; SI > 1289.
ii) HaCaT cells: IC₅₀ = 7.16 nM; CC₅₀ > 10 µM; SI > 1396.
iii) ~2× more potent than Tecovirimat (IC₅₀ = 12.73 nM).
-Mode of action: Blocks viral replication and internalization, reducing mature virion formation.
-In vivo efficacy: In MPXV-infected Spanish dormice (Dryomys nitedula), intraperitoneal PDX (1.5 mg/kg/day for 7 days) reduced viral DNA in lungs, liver, spleen, kidneys, and intestines; alleviated inflammation and preserved tissue architecture.
-Histopathology: Restored normal alveolar, splenic, hepatic, and intestinal morphology; reduced necrosis and inflammatory infiltrates.
-Safety: No body weight loss or systemic toxicity at antiviral doses; therapeutic dose ≪ oncological dose.
-Challenges: Cytotoxic potential at higher doses (mucositis, thrombocytopenia) known from oncology use
Recent updates:
Pralatrexate’s antiviral profile has expanded to VZV, SARS-CoV-2, and vesicular stomatitis virus.
Comparative screens indicate it is the most potent antifolate antiviral against MPXV, surpassing methotrexate, pemetrexed, and metoprine.
Dormouse model validated as a new small-animal system for MPXV drug evaluation.
WHO’s 2025 Emerging Pathogen Watchlist notes antifolate scaffolds (including pralatrexate) as high-priority host-targeting antiviral leads.
Further mechanistic work ongoing to clarify non-folate-mediated pathways (possibly impacting host nucleotide pools or viral entry cofactors).

Name: Prasugrel
Developers: University of Melbourne, Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: The active metabolite (converted in the liver) binds irreversibly to the ADP receptor on platelets, preventing the binding of ADP to the receptor.
Key features and challenges:
Prasugrel is a third-generation P2Y12 receptor antagonist indicated for the prevention of thrombotic cardiovascular events. As a potent antiplatelet agent, it inhibits adenosine diphosphate (ADP)-mediated platelet activation and aggregation. Alongside other newer antiplatelet agents such as clopidogrel and ticagrelor, prasugrel has been explored for potential roles beyond thrombosis, including in the prevention of preeclampsia.
Recent experimental research published in 2024, suggests that newer P2Y12 inhibitors may activate antioxidant pathways in first-trimester placental tissue, including nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) translocation and upregulation of antioxidant genes such as HO-1, NQO1, and GCLC (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0143400424005836). 
These agents were reported to reduce placental secretion of soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1), increase placental growth factor (PlGF), and improve endothelial function in experimental models. This mechanism differs from aspirin, which remains the current standard for preeclampsia prophylaxis in high-risk women.
Key challenges include the absence of clinical trial data evaluating prasugrel specifically for preeclampsia prevention in pregnant populations, concerns regarding bleeding risk with potent antiplatelet agents during pregnancy and delivery, and limited safety data in obstetric settings. While mechanistic findings are promising, rigorous clinical trials will be required to determine safety, efficacy, and comparative benefit relative to low-dose aspirin.

Name: Pravastatin - PE/E
Developers: University of Melbourne (including the Australian Venom Research Unit (AVRU) and Bio21 Institute); University of Birmingham
Indication: Prevention and treatment of preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: Pravastatin induces vasodilation via NO production and reduces preeclampsia-associated endothelial dysfunction by reducing ET-1 and sFlt-1 secretions
Key features and challenges:
Pravastatin is a selective inhibitor of hepatic 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl–coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase and is widely used for cholesterol reduction. Beyond lipid-lowering effects, pravastatin exerts pleiotropic vascular benefits, including upregulation of endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), enhanced nitric oxide (NO) production, improved endothelial function, and reduction of adhesion molecule expression (2017: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28199380/). These properties provide biological plausibility for its potential use in preeclampsia (PE), a condition characterized by angiogenic imbalance, endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and oxidative stress.
Preclinical and translational studies have demonstrated that pravastatin may reverse key pathophysiological pathways implicated in PE, including restoration of angiogenic balance and reduction of endothelial injury 
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28199380/
; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26222708
; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32199147/). The STaMP trial, a proof-of-concept randomized study evaluating pravastatin in women with severe early-onset PE, assessed effects on circulating anti-angiogenic factors. The trial did not demonstrate a reduction in maternal plasma sFlt-1 levels once early-onset PE was established; however, the study was limited by small sample size (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31715077/).
Clinical development remains ongoing. A Phase I placebo-controlled study (NCT01717586) is evaluating pharmacokinetics and preliminary safety of daily pravastatin prophylaxis in pregnant women at high risk of PE. A Phase III trial (NCT03944512) is assessing whether early pregnancy administration of pravastatin reduces a composite outcome of preeclampsia, fetal loss, and maternal death. Regarding safety, a 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis found no significant increase in congenital anomalies associated with statin exposure in pregnancy, though further large-scale studies were recommended (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34044205/).
Key challenges include historical concerns regarding statin teratogenicity, mixed results from early therapeutic trials in established PE, and the need to clarify optimal timing (prophylactic versus therapeutic use). Ongoing randomized trials will be critical to determine whether pravastatin can safely and effectively modify disease trajectory or reduce incidence in high-risk populations.
Recent updates:
2023: In animal experiments, pravastatin was found to be safe in pregnancy, with no toxic effects. Its beneficial effect has been demonstrated in several preeclampsia models https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9880057/#:~:text=In%20animal%20experiments%2C%20pravastatin%20was,several%20preeclampsia%20models%20(29).

2021: Fetal toxicity associated with statins: A systematic review and meta-analysis. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34044205/)

2020: Preclinical study reported that pravastatin reduced the secretion of ET-1 and sFlt-1 (key modulators of endothelial dysfunction) in human umbilical vein endothelial and uterine microvascular cells. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32199147/)

Name: Pravastatin - PTL/PTB
Developers: University of Edinburgh
Indication: Prevention of preterm labour/birth due to inflammation
Mechanism of action: Inhibiting expression of inflammatory cytokines; reducing ET-1 and sFLT-1 secretions
Key features and challenges:
Pravastatin is a specific inhibitor of the hepatic HMG-CoA reductase in humans. The inhibition of this enzyme produces a reduction in cholesterol biosynthesis as HMG-CoA reductase activity is an early-limiting step in cholesterol biosynthesis.
Preclinical studies demonstrated that pravastatin reduced expression of inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6) and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) in a mouse model of preterm birth (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22939729/). Another study reported that pravastatin prevented cervical remodeling through a mechanism that involves hemoxygenase-1 and complement inhibition (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24623738/).
A Phase II trial assessing the efficacy of pravastatin in prolonging time to delivery, reducing contractions and inflammation in both the mother and fetus in women with preterm labour was completed in 2019 (https://www.clinicaltrialsregister.eu/ctr-search/trial/2017-005021-21/GB). 
A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of fetal toxicity associated with statins during pregnancy observed no significant increase of birth defects after statin therapy, but noted further studies are warranted. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34044205/)
Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development Obstetric-Fetal Pharmacology Research Centers (OPRC) Network published results of a phase I clinical trial using a low dose (10 mg) of pravastatin in high-risk pregnant women. In 2021, they reported results of a follow-up, randomized trial of 20 mg pravastatin versus placebo among pregnant women with previous preeclampsia who required delivery before 34+6 weeks’ gestation with the objective of evaluating the safety and pharmacokinetic parameters of pravastatin. Primary outcomes included maternal-fetal safety and pharmacokinetic parameters of pravastatin during pregnancy. Secondary outcomes included maternal and umbilical cord blood chemistries and maternal and neonatal outcomes, including rates of preterm delivery, gestational age at delivery, and birthweight. 10 women assigned to receive pravastatin and 10 assigned to receive the placebo completed the trial. No significant differences were observed between the 2 groups in the rates of adverse or serious adverse events, congenital anomalies, or maternal and umbilical cord blood chemistries. The study confirmed the overall safety and favorable pregnancy outcomes for pravastatin in high-risk women and justifies a larger clinical trial (https://www.scholars.northwestern.edu/en/publications/a-randomized-pilot-clinical-trial-of-pravastatin-versus-placebo-i)
A Phase III trial (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03944512) was completed in the US in 2024, to assess whether daily treatment with pravastatin administered early in pregnancy prevents preeclampsia in high risk women and reduces the rate of a composite outcome of preterm birth, foetal loss and maternal death. Preterm labour is a secondary outcome measure.
