Name: RVF Clone 13 vaccine
Product: Vector control products Reservoir targeted vaccines
Developers: North-West University; Onderstepoort Biological Products (OBP)
Indication: Prevention of RVFV infection in livestock (sheep, goats, cattle)
Mechanism of action: Live attenuated virus replicates at low levels, inducing protective humoral and cellular immune responses without NSs-mediated immune suppression.
Key features and challenges:
-Provides protective immunity with a single dose; demonstrated safety in multiple species.
-Safe in later stages of pregnancy but adverse fetal outcomes reported in first trimester.
-Induces both neutralizing antibodies and CD8⁺ T-cell responses.
-Can serve as a DIVA vaccine, though commercial diagnostics not yet available.
-Challenges: vaccine is heat-labile, short shelf-life, requires cold-chain; risk of reassortment in endemic settings noted but minimal.
Recent updates:
-Formulation improvements: Recent 2023 study introduced sucrose-based lyophilized formulations to improve thermostability; sucrose preserved viral titers better than lactose.
-Pheroid® adjuvant system tested in sheep: safe but did not significantly enhance immunogenicity, though suggested for optimization.
-Regulatory status: OIE-recognized and used under emergency vaccination programs; WHO TPP (2019) highlights Clone 13 as a reference veterinary vaccine.
-As of Sept 2025: Still veterinary-only; no clinical development in humans reported, though remains a leading comparator for new RVFV vaccines.

Name: RVFV 56/74 variant 40Fp8
Developers: Centro de Investigación en Sanidad Animal CISA INIA/CSIC
Indication: Prevention of RVFV infection in livestock and potential human use
Mechanism of action: Hyperattenuated live virus lacking residual virulence, stimulates humoral and cellular immune responses while maintaining safety even in immunocompromised hosts.
Key features and challenges:
-Generated by serial passage of South African isolate RVFV 56/74 under favipiravir pressure.
-Exhibits extreme attenuation in wild-type and IFNAR-knockout (IFNARKO) mice, even after intranasal inoculation (1000 pfu) where other LAVs (rMP-12, rG1) caused 100% lethality.
-Induces protective neutralizing antibodies after single inoculation.
-Classified as Biosafety Hazard Group 2, easier handling than wild-type strains.
-Challenges: further testing needed in target livestock species (e.g., pregnant sheep, calves); long-term stability and transmission studies ongoing.
Recent updates:
-Compared to other LAVs (Clone 13, MP-12), 40Fp8 shows higher attenuation and safety margins, including in immunocompromised models.
-Current follow-up studies include stability in cell culture, transmissibility in livestock, and efficacy/safety in pregnant sheep, which are critical for veterinary deployment.
-Recognized in recent 2023–2024 reviews (Wichgers Schreur et al., Alkan et al.) as one of the next-generation live-attenuated RVFV vaccine candidates.

Name: RVFV MP-12
Developers: National Institutes of Health; National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID); University of Pittsburgh Regional Biocontainment Laboratory (RBL)
Indication: Prevention of RVFV infection in humans and livestock
Mechanism of action: Induces protective humoral and cellular immunity via replication-competent but attenuated virus.
Key features and challenges:
-Attenuated by mutagenesis; extensively studied in animals.
-Provides protection in sheep, cattle, and rodents.
-Phase 1/2 human clinical trials showed safety and immunogenicity, but conflicting reports on teratogenicity in pregnant livestock (safe in late gestation, teratogenic in early gestation at high doses).
-Stable during serial passage; good immunogenicity in humans.
-Challenges: concerns for use in pregnant animals; not yet licensed for humans.
Recent updates:
-MP-12 remains a reference comparator in RVFV vaccine studies; evaluated in maternal–fetal interface ex vivo models (sheep & human placenta explants, 2024) where it showed limited replication compared to wild-type ZH501 and ΔNSm.
-Previously entered Phase 1/2 human trials (2006–2008), with results confirming safety but limited advancement since.
-CEPI (2023–2025) identified MP-12–derived approaches as candidates for outbreak readiness.

Name: RVFV ΔNSm
Developers: National Institutes of Health; National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID); University of Pittsburgh Regional Biocontainment Laboratory (RBL)
Indication: Prevention of RVFV infection
Mechanism of action: Induces immunity while NSm deletion reduces pathogenicity; however, retains higher virulence than ΔNSs strains.
Key features and challenges:
-Demonstrated strong replication in sheep and human placenta explants, comparable to wild-type strain ZH501.
-Known to retain neurovirulence and cause pathology in animal models.
-Not suitable for pregnant livestock due to significant replication and residual virulence.
-Challenges: higher safety risks compared to ΔNSs or ΔNSs/ΔNSm; unlikely to advance as a licensed vaccine.
Recent updates:
-Confirmed to replicate robustly at maternal–fetal interface (placental explants), unlike ΔNSs/ΔNSm which showed greater attenuation.
-Prior studies (Bird et al., 2007) showed ΔNSm retains high virulence in vivo and causes delayed neurological disease in animal models.
-Remains a critical research tool to dissect RVFV virulence, but not a translational vaccine candidate.

Name: RVFV ΔNSs
Developers: National Institutes of Health; National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID); University of Pittsburgh Medical Center (including Pittsburgh Children's Hospital)
Indication: Prevention of RVFV infection
Mechanism of action: Attenuated virus lacking NSs (a major virulence factor that blocks host IFN production), stimulates protective humoral and cellular immunity.
Key features and challenges:
-Vaccinated CC057/Unc mice developed robust neutralizing antibody titers (FRNT80 1:1280–1:10240) and survived lethal WT challenge.
-Prevented CNS disease (late-onset encephalitis) in the mouse model.
-Elicited both RVFV-specific CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T cell responses.
-Challenges: previous studies showed ΔNSs retains pathogenicity in some routes (e.g., intranasal); further safety evaluation needed in livestock and NHPs.
Recent updates:
-The ΔNSs vaccine demonstrated protection from lethal RVFV encephalitis in the CC057/Unc mouse model (first reproducible percutaneous CNS disease model).
-Earlier C57BL/6 mouse studies also showed ΔNSs provided strong protection from lethal hepatitis.
-Remains under evaluation as a human vaccine candidate; CEPI and NIH include ΔNSs-derived vaccines in outbreak preparedness portfolios (2024–2025).

Name: RVFV ΔNSsΔNSm
Developers: National Institutes of Health; National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID); University of Pittsburgh Medical Center (including Pittsburgh Children's Hospital)
Indication: Prevention of RVFV infection
Mechanism of action: Dual gene deletion attenuates virus by blocking immune evasion (NSs) and reducing replication in mosquitoes (NSm), while still inducing strong immunity.
Key features and challenges:
-Safe and immunogenic in CC057/Unc mice; fully protective against lethal WT challenge at high dose.
-Generated neutralizing antibody titers similar to ΔNSs (FRNT80 1:1280–1:10240) and elicited RVFV-specific T cell responses.
-Lower doses protected from CNS disease but allowed some WT viral RNA entry into the brain, suggesting dose-dependent sterilizing immunity.
-Advantages: potentially safer than ΔNSs alone (double deletion reduces risk of reversion).
-Challenges: needs livestock and NHP validation; regulatory approval pathway ongoing under CEPI/DDVax program.
Recent updates:
-DDVax is the lead double-deletion vaccine under development; recognized by CEPI and European Commission as a promising candidate for outbreak deployment.
-Ongoing CEPI-supported program (2023–2025) advancing toward GMP manufacturing and large-animal studies.
-Demonstrated consistent safety in multiple mouse strains and shown to reduce vector competence in mosquitoes.
-Patent protection exists (USPTO: 8,673,629; 9,439,935; 10,064,933) covering ΔNSsΔNSm RVFV strains.

Name: RVFV-140
Developers: National Institutes of Health; National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID); University of Pittsburgh Medical Center (including Pittsburgh Children's Hospital)
Indication: Prevention and treatment of RVFV infection
Mechanism of action: Neutralizes RVFV by inhibiting viral fusion, preventing viral entry and replication.
Key features and challenges:
-In vitro IC50 = 13 ng/mL (moderately potent).
-Provided 83% survival in rat aerosol challenge model (5/6 rats protected).
-Demonstrated sterilizing immunity in lethal hepatic mouse model when administered prophylactically at 200 mg.
-Effective even at very low doses when combined with RVFV-268.
-Challenges: binding epitope still unmapped; needs optimization for delivery across BBB.
Recent updates:
-RVFV-140 shown to reduce lethality in both hepatic and encephalitic models.
-Combination therapy with RVFV-268 achieved protection at extremely low doses (0.02 μg) in mice.
-Current antibody engineering efforts (e.g., BBB-penetrating bispecifics, scFvs, nanobodies) are being explored to improve CNS delivery.

Name: RVFV-268
Developers: National Institutes of Health; National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID); University of Pittsburgh Medical Center (including Pittsburgh Children's Hospital)
Indication: Prevention and treatment of RVFV infection
Target: RVFV Gn glycoprotein, domain A epitope
Mechanism of action: Ultra-potent neutralization by blocking fusion and preventing viral entry; shown to cross placenta and protect fetuses.
Key features and challenges:
-In vitro IC50 = 0.2 ng/mL (ultrapotent).
-72% survival in rat aerosol challenge model (8/11 rats protected).
-No infectious virus detected in brain/liver/spleen of treated rats at 5 dpi.
-Previously shown to prevent vertical transmission in pregnant rat model.
-Challenges: Requires engineering for prolonged half-life, BBB penetration, and reduced ADE risk.
Recent updates:
-Recognized as one of the most promising RVFV therapeutic antibodies by CEPI/WHO R&D Blueprint (2024–2025).
-Shows sterilizing protection in multiple models, including maternal-fetal.
-Follow-up work focuses on antibody engineering (YTE for half-life, LALA-PG to reduce effector functions).

Name: RVFV-379
Developers: National Institutes of Health; National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID); University of Pittsburgh Medical Center (including Pittsburgh Children's Hospital)
Indication: Prevention and treatment of RVFV infection
Target: RVFV Gn glycoprotein, domain A epitope
Mechanism of action: Neutralizes RVFV by binding Gn and blocking infection.
Key features and challenges:
-In vitro IC50 = 4.6 ng/mL (potent).
-Provided 50% survival in rat aerosol challenge model (3/6 rats survived).
-Previously only tested in vitro; this was the first in vivo validation.
-Less protective than RVFV-268 or RVFV-140.
-Challenges: moderate potency; needs optimization or use in antibody cocktails.
Recent updates:
-Identified as next-tier antibody compared to RVFV-268, but included in protective mAb panels against RVFV.
-Supports rationale for antibody cocktails to ensure broader protection and mitigate escape.
-As of 2025, no NHP studies yet reported, but several RVFV mAbs (268, 140, 379) are being advanced in parallel pipelines for outbreak preparedness.

Name: Raf kinase inhibitors: Regorafenib and Dabrafenib
Developers: University of Veterinary Medicine Hannover
Indication: Zika virus (ZIKV) infection – potential antiviral for treatment of acute infection and associated complications such as congenital neurological defects and neurological syndromes.
Target: Host kinases that regulate ER morphology/protein synthesis and secretion (indirect antiviral); functionally reduces ZIKV E protein expression and NS1 secretion.
Mechanism of action: Inhibits ZIKV replication at post-entry stages by targeting host kinases (B-Raf/c-Raf, VEGFR, RET, PDGFRβ, and c-Kit). Unlike Dabrafenib, Regorafenib does not impair viral RNA replication but interferes with viral protein expression, alters ER morphology, reduces envelope (E) protein levels, blocks NS1 secretion, and limits viral egress. These effects together lead to reduced viral titers (~10-fold reduction) with minimal cytotoxicity.
Key features and challenges:
-FDA-approved oncology drug → known human PK/safety profile (facilitates repurposing).
-In vitro: ~10-fold reduction in ZIKV titers at non-cytotoxic concentrations; no activity vs DENV2 (selectivity issue). 
-NS1-secretion blockade is potentially beneficial given NS1’s role in human disease; needs in vivo confirmation for ZIKV. 
-Long-term dosing/safety for antiviral use and pregnancy safety unknown; no ZIKV animal or clinical data yet.
Multi-kinase inhibitor (B-Raf, c-Raf, VEGFR, RET, PDGFRβ, c-Kit) repurposed as host-directed antiviral
Recent updates:
2025 Publication:
-A systematic review of antivirals for epidemic-potential arboviruses lists host-directed repurposing (including kinase inhibitors) as a continuing strategy for ZIKV; no clinical programs for regorafenib identified.
-2025 patient data underscore the clinical relevance of prolonged circulating ZIKV NS1 in adults, reinforcing the rationale that agents limiting NS1 secretion (like regorafenib in vitro) may be pathogenesis-modifying—though this remains unproven in vivo.

Name: Raloxifene
Developers: Charotar University of Science and Technology
Indication: Treatment of uterine fibroids
Mechanism of action: Selective estrogen receptor modulators
Key features and challenges:
Raloxifene is a selective estrogen receptor modulator used to treat breast cancer and to prevent and treat osteoporosis. SERMs work by binding to estrogen receptors in cells, which slows down bone resorption and lowers overall bone turnover. In uterine and breast cancer cells, raloxifene acts as an estrogen blocker, while in bones it works like estrogen to help maintain bone strength (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800000856)

Past studies on treating uterine fibroids with raloxifene have shown mixed results, which has prevented it from being recommended in clinical guidelines.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23076912/; https://www.emas-online.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/fibroids.pdf)

A 2023 preclinical study explored the off-label use of raloxifene hydrochloride (RLH) to treat uterine fibroids (UF). Researchers created an RLH-loaded drug-eluting insert (DEI) for intrauterine delivery to improve targeting. Made with polycaprolactone (PCL) as the rate-controlling polymer and PEG 4000 plus Vitamin ETPGS as solubilizers, the biodegradable insert was tested for strength, drug content, release rate, and tissue effects. The results showed no interaction between RLH and the excipients, with the insert releasing 45–50% of the drug over 15 days. In tests on New Zealand white female rabbits with induced fibroids, the RLH insert significantly reduced fibroid size compared to placebo and untreated groups, confirming its potential. Overall, the study successfully developed and evaluated a targeted RLH insert that could lower required doses and reduce side effects of conventional treatment (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1773224723004045?via%3Dihub#bib10)

Name: Raloxifene
Developers: Eli Lilly and Company
Indication: Reduction of uterine fibroid size
Mechanism of action: Selective estrogen receptor modulators
Key features and challenges:
Raloxifene is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) used clinically for prevention and treatment of osteoporosis and for certain breast cancer risk–reduction indications. It binds estrogen receptors and acts as an estrogen antagonist in breast and uterine tissues while exerting estrogen-agonist effects in bone, reducing bone resorption and turnover. This tissue-selective profile has motivated investigation in uterine fibroids (UF), which are estrogen-responsive tumors.
https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800000856
Clinical studies evaluating raloxifene for uterine fibroids have produced inconsistent outcomes, with some trials suggesting limited benefit and others showing no meaningful reduction in fibroid size or symptom improvement. Due to these conflicting results and limited high-quality comparative evidence, raloxifene is not recommended in major clinical guidelines for routine UF management.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23076912/
https://www.emas-online.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/fibroids.pdf
More recently, a preclinical delivery strategy has been explored to improve uterine targeting and potentially enhance antifibroid efficacy. A raloxifene hydrochloride–loaded drug-eluting insert (DEI) for intrauterine administration was evaluated in a rabbit model and was associated with significant fibroid shrinkage, supporting the hypothesis that localized delivery may overcome limitations seen with systemic raloxifene exposure.
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1773224723004045?via%3Dihub#bib10
Despite renewed interest through localized delivery technologies, evidence remains limited to preclinical studies, and no human clinical trials have yet validated intrauterine raloxifene delivery for UF. Key challenges include establishing safety of intrauterine delivery systems, confirming reproducibility and durability of fibroid reduction, and clarifying whether symptom improvement translates to clinically meaningful outcomes in women.
Raloxifene represents a biologically plausible but clinically uncertain option for uterine fibroids. While systemic raloxifene has not demonstrated consistent clinical benefit, targeted intrauterine drug-delivery approaches may warrant further investigation to determine whether efficacy can be improved with reduced systemic exposure.

Name: Raloxifene-MERS
Developers: Sungkyunkwan University; IP Korea
Indication: Treatment of MERS-CoV infection (repurposed candidate)
Target: Host cell lipid/cholesterol metabolic pathways; viral entry stage
Mechanism of action: Alters host cell cholesterol metabolism (elevates SQLE expression, modulates membrane lipid composition), impairing coronavirus entry and replication.
Key features and challenges:
-FDA-approved since 1997 for osteoporosis and breast cancer prevention.
-Potent against MERS-CoV in vitro (EC50 ≈ 0.2 µM, non-cytotoxic).
-Effective against other coronaviruses (SARS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2, HCoV-229E, HCoV-OC43).
-Demonstrated in vivo efficacy in hamster SARS-CoV-2 model (36 mg/kg reduced viral loads in lung/nasal turbinate).
-Challenges: Mechanism not fully defined; broad host lipid metabolism impact could raise safety concerns in acute viral use.
Recent updates:
-Raloxifene was evaluated in European Exscalate4CoV COVID-19 trials (phase 2/3, NCT04586153) but results inconclusive; no MERS-specific trials.
-2024–2025: Preclinical interest continues for broad-spectrum coronavirus inhibitors.

Name: Raman spectroscopy
Developers: Uskudar University; China Medical University
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for research use only
Mechanism of action: Analyzes biochemical spectral fingerprints of biological samples to identify metabolic signatures associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Raman spectroscopy is a non-invasive technique that analyses molecular composition by measuring light scattering. In PCOS diagnosis, it can be used to detect biochemical markers in blood, urine, or ovarian tissues, offering potential for early, non-invasive detection. It can help study the molecular composition of ovarian follicles, metabolic disturbances (such as insulin resistance or lipid abnormalities), and oxidative stress in PCOS patients. Additionally, it may be useful in monitoring treatment effects by analysing changes in metabolic biomarkers over time. While promising, its clinical use in PCOS diagnosis requires further research and validation.

Two studies explored Raman spectroscopy as a potential diagnostic tool for PCOS. A 2021 study found distinct spectral differences in blood serum between PCOS and healthy women, with changes in amides and lipid groups that could serve as PCOS markers. Strong correlations were also found between hormone levels and lipid/protein imbalances in PCOS patients. 
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S030372072030441X?via%3Dihub)
A 2022 study analysed metabolic profiles in follicular fluid and plasma samples, finding the highest classification accuracy (89.32%) with follicular fluid using machine learning algorithms.
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1386142522001779?via%3Dihub)
Both studies suggest Raman spectroscopy could be a rapid and affordable method for diagnosing PCOS by detecting metabolic changes.

Name: Ramoplanin
Developers: Ology Bioservices, Inc; Pfizer; Institute of Tropical Medicine Antwerp/Prince Leopold Institute of Tropical Medicine (ITM)
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Ramoplanin blocks bacterial cell wall biosynthesis by interfering with peptidoglycan production
Key features and challenges:
Ramoplanin is the first in a new class of antimicrobials to reach clinical trials for bacterial infections (Clostridium difficile infections; Vancomycin-resistant enterococcal infections; Staphylococcal infections). 
It is a glycolipodepsipeptide produced by the fermentation of Actinoplanes spp.. Ramoplanin blocks bacterial cell wall biosynthesis by interfering with peptidoglycan production. Its development has been fast-tracked by the U.S. FDA as a treatment for multiple antibiotic-resistant Clostridium difficile infection. Unlike vancomycin, it is absorbed in the gastrointestinal tract, although it is unstable in the bloodstream, so can be taken only orally against Clostridium difficile infections of the gastrointestinal tract. (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB04952)
In a 2024 preclinical study, the effectiveness of the antibiotic ramoplanin as a treatment for N. gonorrhoeae infection was investigated. The effectiveness of ramoplanin was tested in vitro against 14 World Health Organization (WHO) reference strains of N. gonorrhoeae and found that it was active against all 14 strains tested. Furthermore, in a Galleria mellonella infection model of N. gonorrhoeae WHO P, it was demonstrated that ramoplanin was active in vivo without any evidence of toxicity. This suggests that ramoplanin might be a new promising antibiotic treatment for gonorrhoea.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38214499/)

Name: Ranibizumab
Developers: Genentech; Roche (including InterMune); Lupin; Novartis; Xbrane

Key features and challenges:
Ranibizumab is a recombinant humanized monoclonal antibody fragment targeting vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A), used to treat various ocular conditions such as neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration (AMD), diabetic macular edema, and macular edema following retinal vein occlusion. Initially approved by the FDA in 2006 and the European Commission in 2007, it is marketed as LUCENTIS and SUSVIMO. The development of ranibizumab followed the discovery of bevacizumab's efficacy in inhibiting neovascularization, leading to ranibizumab's formulation for intravitreal injection to enhance delivery to the eye. 
In addition to its primary indications, ranibizumab is used via an ocular implant for treating wet AMD in patients who have responded to at least two prior intravitreal VEGF inhibitor injections. It is approved in Canada for various conditions including neovascular AMD, diabetic macular edema, and choroidal neovascularization. In Europe, its approval extends to similar conditions, including retinopathy of prematurity in preterm infants. (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800011595)
In a study involving 52 female Wistar albino rats with experimentally induced endometriosis, ranibizumab demonstrated significantly lower histological scores compared to controls, indicating potential efficacy in managing endometriosis. Although no differences were found in ellipsoidal volumes among groups, significant reductions in cell numbers associated with Bcl-2, NF-κB, and CD31 staining were observed in the ranibizumab group. These findings suggest that ranibizumab could be promising treatments for endometriosis, warranting further investigation. (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00404-021-06104-9)

Name: Ravulizumab
Developers: Alexion Pharmaceuticals, Inc.; AstraZeneca
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: High affinity binding to the complement protein C5, blocking cleavage into C5a and C5b
Key features and challenges:
Ravulizumab is a long-acting monoclonal antibody that inhibits complement component C5, thereby preventing terminal complement activation and formation of the membrane attack complex. It is currently approved for complement-mediated disorders such as paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria and atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome. Given emerging evidence implicating complement dysregulation in the pathophysiology of severe preeclampsia and HELLP (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets) syndrome, ravulizumab is being investigated as a potential targeted therapy in these conditions.
A Phase II clinical trial initiated in 2026 is evaluating ravulizumab for the treatment of severe preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome. The study aims to assess safety, tolerability, and potential efficacy in modifying disease progression, with particular interest in maternal stabilization and prolongation of pregnancy where clinically feasible.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06333652).
Key challenges include limited clinical data in pregnant populations, potential infection risks associated with complement inhibition, and the high cost of biologic therapy. Additionally, the timing of administration relative to disease severity and delivery decisions remains a critical consideration. Robust clinical trial data will be necessary to determine whether complement inhibition can safely and effectively alter outcomes in severe hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.

Name: ReLeaf
Developers: WOMED
Indication: endometriosis pain, fertility, adhesions
Mechanism of action: unspecified
Key features and challenges:
ReLeaf is an investigational intrauterine drug delivery platform developed by Womed for the management of endometriosis-related pain. The platform builds on Womed’s proprietary intrauterine device (IUD) technology, including the Womed Leaf device, which features a patented biodegradable copolymer structure designed for ease of insertion, controlled local drug release, and targeted intrauterine therapy. In addition to ReLeaf, the company is developing related platforms such as Fibroid for preoperative fibroid treatment.
In 2024, Womed advanced its uterine drug delivery platform through European innovation funding aimed at addressing unmet needs in uterine disorders, including endometriosis and fibroids. (https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/101161066). 
The program highlights the limitations of current systemic hormonal and surgical treatments, which are often associated with significant side effects or recurrence. The ReLeaf platform is designed to deliver localized therapy directly to the uterine environment, potentially reducing systemic exposure and improving tolerability.
Key challenges include early-stage development status, the need for robust clinical data to demonstrate safety and efficacy in endometriosis-related pain, and regulatory approval pathways for combination device–drug products. While localized intrauterine drug delivery represents a promising approach, clinical validation will be essential to determine its role relative to established hormonal and surgical therapies.

Name: Real-time Multiplex PCR for STIs - Gonorrhea
Developers: Russian Federation
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoea
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: multiplex PCR
Key features and challenges: With high STI rates in the Russian Federation and challenges in diagnosing them, there’s a growing need for new, personalized approaches to patient care. A 2022 study examined the work of the Moscow Scientific and Practical Center, which uses a modern real-time multiplex PCR test for STI diagnosis. The pathogens detected included C. trachomatis (45.9%), M. genitalium (20.1%), N. gonorrhoeae (29.5%), and T. vaginalis (4.5%). Most patients (54.2–84.7%) had low pathogen concentrations (up to 10⁴ GE/mL), though males with gonococcal infection mostly showed a high bacterial load of N. gonorrhoeae DNA (72.6%). Since the test’s introduction in 2018, STI detection rates have risen sharply: gonorrhea in females by 280.6% and in males by 177.9%; chlamydia in females by 71.2% and in males by 31.1%; trichomoniasis in males by 123.1%; and M. genitalium in males by 41.1%. This advanced multiplex PCR test supports accurate diagnosis, co-infection detection, and pathogen load measurement, helping tailor treatments and ease the economic burden of STIs (https://www.mediasphera.ru/issues/klinicheskaya-dermatologiya-i-venerologiya/2022/5/1199728492022051619).

Name: Real-time Multiplex PCR for STIs - Mycoplasma genitalium
Developers: Russian Federation
Indication: Detection of Mycoplasma genitalium
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: multiplex PCR
Key features and challenges:
Real-time Multiplex PCR for STIs is a molecular diagnostic platform designed for simultaneous detection of multiple sexually transmitted pathogens, including Mycoplasma genitalium. The assay enables etiological diagnosis, identification of co-infections, and quantification of pathogen load to support individualized patient management.
A 2022 study evaluated implementation of this multiplex real-time PCR platform at the Moscow Scientific and Practical Center and reported improved diagnostic capacity for STI management (https://www.mediasphera.ru/issues/klinicheskaya-dermatologiya-i-venerologiya/2022/5/1199728492022051619). 
The assay facilitated detection of multiple pathogens in a single test and provided quantitative data that could inform personalized therapy decisions and potentially reduce the economic burden associated with misdiagnosis or inappropriate treatment.
Key challenges include the need for validation across broader geographic and epidemiological contexts, assessment of performance in low-resource settings, and cost considerations compared with single-target NAAT platforms. Integration into routine clinical workflows and antimicrobial resistance detection capabilities may also require further development.
Overall, real-time multiplex PCR represents a comprehensive molecular approach for etiological STI diagnosis, including M. genitalium. Broader implementation studies are needed to establish its impact on treatment optimization and health system efficiency.

The platform facilitated detection of multiple pathogens within a single test and provided quantitative data that could guide personalized therapy and reduce the economic burden associated with syndromic management or misdiagnosis.

Name: Real-time shear wave elastography + 3D-PDI - PE/E
Developers: Binzhou Medical University Hospital
Indication: Indicated for the prediction of preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Mechanism of action: Shear wave elastography measures placental "hardness" by inducing mechanical vibrations using acoustic radiation force. 3D-PDI provides a high-sensitivity assessment of placental microcirculation
Key features and challenges:
Real-time shear wave elastography (SWE) combined with three-dimensional power Doppler imaging (3D-PDI) is an advanced ultrasound-based approach for assessing placental stiffness and vascular perfusion. SWE quantifies tissue elasticity by measuring the elastic modulus of placental tissue, while 3D-PDI evaluates placental vascularization using indices such as vascularization index (VI), flow index (FI), and vascularization flow index (VFI). In preeclampsia (PE), abnormal placentation, increased placental stiffness, and impaired vascular perfusion are key pathophysiological features, providing a rationale for evaluating these imaging biomarkers.
A 2024 retrospective study compared 60 pregnant women diagnosed with preeclampsia with 60 normotensive pregnant controls (https://journals.lww.com/mdjournal/fulltext/2024/03080/predictive_value_of_placental_real_time_shear_wave.34.aspx). 
Elastic modulus values from different placental regions and 3D-PDI parameters (VI, FI, VFI) were measured and analyzed. Significant differences were observed between the PE and control groups in SWE and 3D-PDI measurements. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis demonstrated that individual parameters had predictive value, and that combining SWE with 3D-PDI indices improved diagnostic performance for preeclampsia compared to single-parameter assessment.
These findings suggest that integrated evaluation of placental stiffness and vascularization may enhance early prediction of preeclampsia using a non-invasive, efficient imaging approach.
Key challenges include the retrospective study design and relatively small sample size, which limit generalizability. Operator dependency, equipment variability, and lack of standardized cut-off values for SWE and 3D-PDI parameters may affect reproducibility across settings. Additionally, integration of these imaging modalities into routine antenatal screening requires validation in larger prospective cohorts and assessment of cost-effectiveness. While promising as a non-invasive predictive tool, further studies are necessary to establish clinical utility and standardized implementation protocols for preeclampsia screening.

-Highlights the synergistic role of GP38 when combined with NP.
-Vaccination induced ADCD/ADCP functions; NP antibodies mainly ADCD, GP38 antibodies ADCD+ADCP.
-First demonstration that recombinant NP+GP38 protein subunits (with safe adjuvants) reduce morbidity in survivors.
Recent updates:
July 2024:
-Demonstrated for the first time that recombinant NP alone achieves complete survival, and NP+GP38 further improves clinical outcomes by limiting morbidity.
-Supports advancing NP-based and NP+GP38 combination strategies as broadly cross-protective CCHFV vaccines.

Name: Relaxin-2 (RLX)
Developers: Boston University (including Boston University Medical Campus and Center for Global Health and Development)
Indication: Investigational peptide hormone evaluated for the treatment of uterine fibroids through anti-fibrotic, matrix-remodelling, and steroid-hormone receptor–modulating mechanisms in human uterine fibroblasts and smooth-muscle cells.
Target:
Relaxin-2 binds to and signals through:
-RXFP1 (Relaxin/insulin-like family peptide receptor 1)
Downstream effects on:
-Estrogen receptor alpha (ERα)
-Progesterone receptors (PR-A, PR-B)
-Fibrotic markers: COL1, COL3, α-SMA, fibronectin
-Matrix-remodeling markers (MMPs ↑, TIMPs ↓)
Mechanism of action:
Relaxin-2 is a peptide hormone with known anti-fibrotic and extracellular-matrix (ECM) remodelling functions. In UF models:
Attenuates TGF-β1–induced fibrosis, reducing protein and mRNA expression of:
-Collagen I
-Collagen III
-α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA)
-Fibronectin

Modulates steroid receptor expression:
-Decreases ERα overexpression induced by TGF-β1
-Decreases PR-A and PR-B expression in both uterine fibroblasts and myometrial smooth-muscle cells
-Suggests a role in correcting dysregulated hormone signalling central to UF biology.
Promotes ECM turnover:
-Increases MMPs
-Decreases TIMPs
-Alters collagen-I fiber alignment in 3D gels
Reduces fibrosis in stiffness-dependent culture models, suggesting mechanotransduction-related activity relevant to UF ECM pathology.
Key features and challenges:
Relaxin-2 (RLX) is an endogenous peptide hormone known for its anti-fibrotic, vasodilatory, and extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling properties. RLX acts through the RXFP1 receptor and has been implicated in regulation of collagen turnover, tissue compliance, and reproductive tract remodeling. Given that uterine fibroids (UF) are characterized by excessive ECM deposition, fibrosis, and aberrant smooth muscle proliferation, RLX has been explored as a potential biologic therapy targeting fibrotic pathways.
A 2024 in-vitro study evaluated RLX in primary human uterine fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells. RLX significantly attenuated transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1)–induced fibrotic responses, reducing expression of collagen I, collagen III, α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA), and fibronectin in both two-dimensional cultures and three-dimensional collagen I gel models. RLX enhanced ECM remodeling by increasing matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) expression, decreasing tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs), and altering collagen fiber organization. Additionally, RLX modulated steroid hormone signaling by reducing TGF-β1–induced overexpression of estrogen receptor-α (ERα) and decreasing progesterone receptor isoforms (PR-A/PR-B), thereby targeting hormonal drivers implicated in fibroid growth.
https://www.fertstert.org/article/S0015-0282(24)01192-0/fulltext
Despite compelling mechanistic data, evidence remains limited to in-vitro studies. No in-vivo uterine fibroid models or human clinical trials have evaluated RLX as a therapeutic intervention for UF. Development challenges include RLX’s short plasma half-life, peptide stability, need for optimized delivery systems, and potential interactions with reproductive endocrine pathways. Safety, pharmacokinetics, dosing strategies, and long-term reproductive effects in women of reproductive age remain undefined.
Relaxin-2 represents a biologically plausible anti-fibrotic biologic candidate for uterine fibroids, targeting ECM accumulation and hormone-responsive signaling. However, it remains at an early preclinical stage, and substantial translational research is required to establish feasibility and clinical potential.
Recent updates: New 2024 in-vitro evidence shows RLX reduces fibrosis markers, downregulates ERα/PRs, and enhances ECM remodelling in UF fibroblasts and smooth-muscle cells. No animal or clinical UF development reported.

Name: Remdesivir + MBP134
Developers: World Health Organisation; Uganda Ministry of Health
Indication: Treatment of Ebola virus disease (EVD), including Sudan ebolavirus (SUDV) infections.
Target: EBOV polymerases; EBOV, SUDV, BDBV glycoprotein
Mechanism of action:
Remdesivir inhibits the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, preventing viral replication across filoviruses.
MBP134 is a dual-mAb cocktail providing broad neutralizing activity across ebolaviruses, including SUDV.
In rhesus macaque models, MBP134 alone saved ~80% of animals challenged with SUDV when administered at 5 days post-infection; combined treatment with remdesivir further extended the therapeutic window to 6 days post-exposure with improved survival.
Key features and challenges: In October 2022, as this protocol was being developed, there was a growing epidemic of Ebola Disease in Uganda caused by the Sudan Ebolavirus species (SUDV). Several possible treatments for Ebola Disease have been trialled in recent years in disease caused by (Zaire) Ebolavirus (EBOV). The interventions identified as potentially beneficial in EBOV were monoclonal antibodies that are specific for EBOV and are not expected to neutralise SUDV. A World Health Organization (WHO) expert group convened to discuss a range of potential host and pathogen directed therapies has advocated for assessment of potential Ebola Disease therapeutics in a randomised controlled clinical trial. If clear evidence of efficacy, futility, or a safety signal are not achieved for any of the comparisons during the current Ebola Disease outbreak, the protocol permits the continuation of relevant arms of the trial in future Ebola Disease outbreaks until a clear outcome is achieved. This includes potential continuation in an EBOV outbreak of relevant trial interventions (e.g. host-directed / supportive care). This an open-label, adaptive, randomised platform clinical trial wit the primary aim to evaluate the impact of potential treatments on mortality in patients with Ebola Disease.
Recent updates:
In October 2022, the U.S. government deployed Remdesivir and MBP134 to Uganda during a Sudan ebolavirus outbreak, and they are now included in WHO’s adaptive Solidarity‑Ebola platform trial. This includes arms comparing Remdesivir monotherapy, MBP134 monotherapy, and the combination, with adaptive interim stopping rules for efficacy or futility—all designed for use during SUDV outbreaks.

Name: Renal function test - PTL
Developers: Capital Medical University; Weill Cornell Medicine
Indication: Prediction and diagnosis of preterm labour

Key features and challenges:
Physiological changes during pregnancy can affect the results of renal function tests (RFTs). A 2023 population-based cohort study aimed to establish trimester-specific reference intervals (RIs) of RFTs in singleton and twin pregnancies and systematically investigate the relationship between RFTs and adverse pregnancy outcomes.
The laboratory results of the first- and third-trimester RFTs, including blood urea nitrogen (BUN), serum uric acid (UA), creatinine (Crea) and cystatin C (Cys C), and the relevant medical records, were retrieved from 29,328 singleton and 840 twin pregnant women who underwent antenatal examinations from November 20, 2017 to January 31, 2021. The trimester-specific RIs of RFTs were estimated with both of the direct observational and the indirect Hoffmann methods. The associations between RTFs and pregnancy complications as well as perinatal outcomes were assessed by logistic regression analysis.
The study found that elevated third-trimester RFTs posed strong risks of preterm birth (PTB) and fetal growth restriction (FGR).

Name: Ribavirin +/- Dexamethasone - Lassa fever
Developers: Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine (BNITM)
Indication: Treatment of LASV infection
Mechanism of action: Ribavirin is thought to function through multiple distinct mechanisms. The ribavirin metabolite, ribavirin monophosphate (RMP), has been proposed as one of the primary active forms of the drug. RMP has been shown to inhibit the activity of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH), a catalyst in the synthesis of guanosine triphosphate (GTP), resulting in the disruption of critical viral replication steps. Additionally, ribavirin triphosphate (RTP) as an additional ribavirin metabolite, has been demonstrated to act as a nucleoside analog and exhibit mutagenic activity through its incorporation into the viral genome by the viral RNA polymerase. This accumulation of mutations within the virus genome is believed to result in inhibition of virus replication through a phenomenon called ‘genomic catastrophe’. RMP and RTP have been postulated to work synergistically, with RMP decreasing the availability of GTP through IMPDH inhibition and thereby lowering competition for inclusion of the mutagenic RTP by the viral RNA polymerase. Rather than disrupting viral replication, the antiviral effect of ribavirin may also be attributable to the drug reducing cell death of LASV infected cells, with the drug potentially exerting these effects through the inhibition of macrophage activation, cytokine production, and lymphocyte proliferation
Key features and challenges: Ribavirin, a guanosine analog with broad spectrum antiviral activity, was first synthesized in 1972 and has shown efficacy against both DNA and RNA viruses. Since its original synthesis, ribavirin has been tested for efficacy against multiple viruses including respiratory syncytial virus, HIV, influenza, measles, bunyaviruses, and arenaviruses, including Lassa virus, with mixed results.
Recent updates:
The UMIT‑2 multi-arm adaptive platform trial (registered as NCT06860334 / PACTR Trial 27092; starting mid‑2025) is a Phase IIb trial testing Ribavirin (IV & PO), Favipiravir, and combination therapies versus standard-of-care in hospitalized CCHF cases in Turkey and Iraq. It allows interim stopping for futility or efficacy. As of July 2025, the trial is registered but not yet recruiting.

Name: Risk Prediction Via Neural Network Ensembles
Developers: William Carey University
Indication: A computational method for early risk prediction of development of PTL via ensembles of artificial neural networks
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Neural network ensembles are a type of machine learning ensemble that combines multiple neural networks to improve the performance of the overall model. Each neural network in the ensemble is trained on a different subset of the training data, and the predictions of the individual networks are then combined to make a final prediction.
Key features and challenges:
Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are machine learning algorithms designed to identify complex patterns within large datasets. Ensemble neural network approaches combine multiple models to improve predictive performance and robustness. Such computational methods are being investigated to support early risk prediction of preterm labour (PTL) and enable individualized, dynamic risk assessment in obstetric care.
In 2021, a study developed predictive models for preterm birth using neural network ensembles and logistic regression approaches. During the first trimester, 13 variables were identified as significantly associated with preterm birth, with diabetes and abnormal pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A) concentration among the strongest predictors. First-trimester models achieved a maximum area under the curve (AUC) of 60% (95% CI: 58–62%). In the second trimester, 17 variables were significantly associated with preterm birth, with pregnancy complications showing the highest adjusted odds ratio (AOR 13.03; 95% CI: 12.21–13.90). Second-trimester models achieved an AUC of 65% (95% CI: 63–66%), which increased to 80% (95% CI: 79–81%) when pregnancy complications were included. Negative predictive values ranged from 94–97% for spontaneous PTB across models.
(https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0252025)
In 2022, a large-scale study applied ensembles of artificial neural networks to clinical data from 228,438 pregnancies to generate individualized PTL risk indices. The models identified patterns correlating with PTL risk, with many pregnancies that later developed PTL showing predicted risk indices above 95%, while many term pregnancies showed risk indices below 5%. These findings suggest the potential utility of ANN-based tools for stratified obstetric management.
(https://www.ajog.org/article/S0002-9378(22)01127-9/fulltext)
Overall, neural network ensemble approaches represent an emerging computational strategy for early risk stratification of preterm labour. While performance varies depending on data inputs and trimester of assessment, high negative predictive values suggest potential utility for identifying low-risk pregnancies. Further prospective validation, assessment of generalisability, and evaluation of implementation feasibility, including considerations of accessibility, equity, cost-effectiveness, and sustainability are required before routine clinical integration.

Name: Rituximab
Developers: AstraZeneca; Biogen, Inc
Indication: Indicated for the prevention and treatment of endometriosis tissue migration/lesions
Mechanism of action: Antibody-dependent cell cytotoxicity; T lymphocyte stimulants
Key features and challenges:
Rituximab is a humanized chimeric monoclonal antibody targeting the CD20 antigen on B lymphocytes. Its mechanism involves the Fab domain binding to CD20, leading to B-cell lysis through complement-dependent cytotoxicity and antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity. Rituximab is widely utilized in the treatment of various B-cell malignancies and autoimmune disorders. It is available in multiple formulations and has been approved in numerous countries, including the US, EU, Canada, Japan, and China, for a range of indications (not endometriosis). The intravenous formulation is used for conditions such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia, follicular lymphoma, and rheumatoid arthritis, while the subcutaneous formulation has been specifically approved for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma in China. Ongoing clinical development aims to expand its applications to additional conditions, including acute lymphoblastic leukemia and systemic sclerosis. (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800004275)
In an experimental rat model of endometriosis, Rituximab treatment led to a significant reduction in the volume of endometriotic implants compared to a saline control. The treatment also resulted in notable differences in B-cell count and fibrosis score between the control and Rituximab groups. These findings suggest Rituximab, an anti-B-lymphocyte antibody, may be a promising candidate for endometriosis treatment, though further research is needed. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0165037823000207?via%3Dihub)

Name: Rmix4 and Rmix6
Developers: Chinese Academy of Sciences
Indication: Prevention of mpox infection
Target:
-Rmix4: 2 IMV antigens (M1R, A29L) + 2 EEV antigens (B6R, A35R);
-Rmix6: 3 IMV antigens (M1R, A29L, H3L) + 3 EEV antigens (B6R, A35R, E8L).
Mechanism of action: Encodes key MPXV virion surface proteins that are translated in host cells post-injection, inducing neutralizing antibodies and T-cell responses targeting both intracellular mature virions (IMV) and extracellular enveloped virions (EEV). The “rapid-mix” (Rmix) transcription method simplifies manufacturing by combining plasmids prior to transcription, yielding an evenly distributed multi-antigen mRNA mixture.
Key features and challenges:
-Novel manufacturing: Simplified “Rmix” process mixes plasmids before transcription—reducing production steps vs. traditional “Lmix” (each mRNA transcribed/encapsulated separately).
-Encapsulation efficiency: ~96–97% for all mRNA components; reproducible antigen ratios across batches.
-Humoral immunity:
i) High antigen-specific IgG titres after two doses (5 µg); seroconversion after single prime.
ii) Neutralizing antibody titres (PRNT₅₀) against VACV: 803 (Rmix4) and 502 (Rmix6) at 5 µg.
-Cellular immunity:
i) Rmix6 induced stronger IFN-γ and IL-2 T-cell responses (ELISPOT & ICS) vs. Rmix4.
ii) Broad Th1-biased responses (CD4⁺/CD8⁺ cytokine expression).
-Protection: 100% survival and no weight loss after lethal VACV challenge (5×10⁶ PFU, i.p.) in mice.
-Antigen hierarchy: M1R induced the most potent neutralizing responses; BCR repertoire revealed dominant M1-targeted epitope (Asp35-dependent), suggesting potential vulnerability to immune escape.
-Advantages: Balanced antibody and T-cell responses; scalable, cost-efficient manufacturing.
Challenges:
-Risk of antigenic focus on M1R super-epitope, which may permit viral escape mutations.
Recent updates:
-Patent filed (China, 2023): “Simplified co-transcription method for multi-antigen mRNA vaccines” covering Rmix4/Rmix6.
-The approach has inspired later candidates (e.g., Ye et al. 2024, LBAAM; Tai et al. 2025, Mix-12/MPX-EPs).
-Rmix6’s inclusion of H3 and E8 increases T-cell breadth; prototype for polyvalent orthopox mRNA vaccines.
-WHO and CEPI have cited Rmix6 as a model for low-cost, rapid mRNA vaccine manufacturing pipelines for epidemic-prone pathogens.
-Translation to humanized or NHP models remains pending.

Name: Rolipram
Developers: University of Louisville; Autonomous University of the State of Hidalgo, Universidad Autónoma del Estado de Hidalgo (UAEH); EndoProtech Inc; University of Newcastle
Indication: Prolonging gestation in threatened preterm labour/birth
Mechanism of action: Reducing myometrial contraction by inhibiting prostaglandin
Key features and challenges:
Rolipram is a selective phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor (PDE4) discovered and developed by Schering AG as a potential antidepressant drug in the early 1990s. It served as a prototype molecule for several companies' drug discovery and development efforts. Rolipram has several activities that make it a continuing focus for research, particularly its neurogenerative properties. As with other PDE4 inhibitors, it has also been suggested to play a potential role in prevention/treatment of inflammation-mediated obstetric conditions, including preterm labour.

Preclinical studies have shown that selective PDE4 inhibition by rolipram prevented the rise in the proinflammatory cytokines (TNF, IL-1b, IL-6, and IL-10) in an LPS-induced mouse model of preterm delivery, and also prevented preterm delivery and fetal demise-Published in 2007. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17202375). Rolipram is more effective than theophylline and potentiates the effects of β2 agonists such as terbutaline in a rat model of LPS-induced preterm birth and in human myometrial tissue in vitro, published in 2013. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22765375/).
Rolipram inhibited spontaneous and tonic contractions by increasing cAMP accumulation and inducing changes in the subcellular localization of oxytocin-induced phosphorylated myosin light-chain in human uterine myometrial cells (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27739411/)
In 2022, University of Newcastle researchers examined and compared the contraction-blocking potency of novel tocolytics with other novel and existing agents that have seen greater scrutiny including rolipram. They determined the IC50 concentrations (inhibit 50% of baseline contractility) for 2-APB, glycyl-H-1152, HC-067047, aminophylline, rolipram, nifedipine, and indomethacin against spontaneous ex vivo contractions in pregnant human myometrium, and then compared their tocolytic potency. Myometrial strips obtained from term, not-in-labor women, were treated with cumulative concentrations of the contraction-blocking agents. Comprehensive dose–response curves were generated. The IC50 concentrations were 53 µM for 2-APB, 18.2 µM for glycyl-H-1152, 48 µM for HC-067047, 318.5 µM for aminophylline, 4.3 µM for rolipram, 10 nM for nifedipine, and 59.5 µM for indomethacin. A single treatment with each drug at the determined IC50 concentration was confirmed to reduce contraction performance (AUC) by approximately 50%. However, of all the drugs examined, the overall order of contraction-blocking potency in decreasing order was nifedipine > rolipram > glycyl-H-1152 > HC-067047 > 2-APB > indomethacin aminophylline (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43032-022-01000-2#Abs1)
Recent updates: 2024: changed from inactive to active.

Name: Rosuvastatin - PE
Developers: AstraZeneca; University of Melbourne (including the Australian Venom Research Unit (AVRU) and Bio21 Institute)
Indication: Prevention and treatment of preeclampsia by reducing preeclampsia-associated endothelial dysfunction
Mechanism of action: HMG-CoA (3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A) reductase inhibitor
Key features and challenges:
Rosuvastatin is a lipid-lowering drug that belongs to the statin class of medications. Rosuvastatin is also a unique member of the class of statins due to its high hydrophilicity which increases hepatic uptake at the site of action, low bioavailability, and minimal metabolism via the Cytochrome P450 system.
Preeclampsia is thought to share several pathophysiologic mechanisms with cardiovascular disease particularly maternal endothelial dysfunction, which has led to investigations for the potential role of statins (HMG CoA reductase inhibitors) in its prevention and early management. Statin administration has been shown to be safe in pregnancy presenting a protective role in endothelial function. Beyond lowering cholesterol levels, they also have other pleiotropic actions such as antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and anti-thrombogenic effects beneficial to preeclamptic patients.  (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28529486//)
In vitro studies that assessed the placental release of soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt-1) and soluble endoglin (sEng) which has been linked to preeclampsia showed that, Rosuvastatin reduced sFlt-1 secretion from endothelial cells, trophoblasts and preterm preeclamptic placental explants. This preliminary data suggest that statins can be a promising therapeutic alternative for the prevention and treatment of preeclampsia. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27207105/)
Preclinical studies comparing pravastatin, simvastatin and rosuvastatin has shown that pravastatin significantly reduced secretion of both ET-1 and sFLT-1, key mediators of endothelial dysfunction, adn that importantly pravastatin had no toxic effects, in contrast to rosuvastatin and simvastatin. This supports selection of pravastatin for clinical applications to combat preeclampsia over other statins. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32199147/)
Clinical trials using rosuvastatin for PE/E are nonetheless underway. (NCT04303806; NCT02314286).
A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of fetal toxicity associated wtih statins during pregnancy observed no significant increase of birth defects after statin therapy, but noted further studies are warranted. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34044205/)
Recent updates:
2021: Fetal toxicity associated with statins: A systematic review and meta-analysis (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34044205/)

April 2020: Rosuvastatin (and Simvastatin) have cytotoxic effects in endothelial in vitro models.
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2210778920300313

Name: Rytvela
Developers: CHU Sainte-Justine Research Center, Centre de Recherche du CHU Sainte-Justine; Rytvel Biotech
Indication: Prevention of preterm labour/birth
Mechanism of action: Interleukin 1 receptor antagonist protein
Key features and challenges:
Rytvela is a novel, small non-competitive IL-1R-biased ligand. Rytvela is a linear 7 amino acid peptide, and the first small drug candidate selective to the major pro-inflammatory interleukin-1 receptor. Currently, all available IL-1 inhibitors are large molecules that exhibit competitive antagonism properties by inhibiting all IL-1R signaling, including transcription factor NF-κB, which conveys important physiological roles.

Interleukin-1 (IL-1) is a potent inflammatory protein involved in many inflammatory disorders, including preterm birth (PTB). Blocking the actions of IL-1 in pregnancies at risk of delivering preterm may protect the fetus from PTB and the long-term harm of exposure to inflammation before birth. 

Preclinical studies have been corroborated the effectiveness of rytvela by three independent academic laboratories (Université de Montréal, University of Alberta in Canada, and University of Adelaide, Australia). These blinded studies performed separately and independently demonstrate that Rytvela suppresses uteroplacental inflammation, significantly reduces/suppress preterm birth (PTB), newborn death and prevents major organ disruption including of brain, yielding normal growth trajectory. (https://static1.squarespace.com/static/57c496ac6b8f5bb965c464d3/t/5a563683e2c48304100c3d11/1515599515817/Rytvela+Presse+release+NHNRC.13.12.17+%281%29.pdf)

A preclinical study was conducted in 2015 to demonstrate the efficacy of a small noncompetitive (all-d peptide) IL-1R–biased ligand, termed rytvela (labeled 101.10) in delaying IL-1b–, TLR2-, and TLR4-induced PTB in mice. The 101.10 acted without significant inhibition of NF-kB, and instead selectively inhibited IL-1R downstream stress-associated protein kinases/transcription factor c-jun and Rho GTPase/Rho-associated coiled-coil–containing protein kinase signaling pathways. The 101.10 was effective at decreasing proinflammatory and/or prolabor genes in myometrium tissue and circulating leukocytes in all PTB models independently of NF-kB, undermining NF-kB role in preterm labor (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26304990/).

RYTVEL Biotech announced in 2017 that the National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia will fund $1.4 million to conduct a new pre-clinical study from 2018 - 2022: “Preclinical evaluation of a novel allosteric IL-1R inhibitor (Rytvela) for the prevention of perinatal inflammation-induced fetal injury.”

Name: S-Allyl-L-cysteine
Developers: Korea University
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Endometriosis.
Mechanism of action: Inhibits endometriotic lesion growth by altering splenic CD4+ and CD8+ T cell subsets and inflammatory cytokine production in the spleen and endometriotic lesions.
Key features and challenges:
S-Allyl-L-cysteine (SAC) is the major constituent of aged garlic extracts. Although the therapeutic effects resulting from the antioxidant properties of SAC have been extensively studied in inflammatory diseases, the therapeutic efficacy of SAC in endometriosis has not been described. In a 2024 study, researchers thus investigated the therapeutic potential of SAC for endometriosis using a mouse model.
An endometriosis mouse model was surgically induced, and oral treatment with 30 mg/kg SAC was administered daily for 28 days. The development of endometriotic lesions was assessed by histological analysis, and the expression profiles of adhesion-, apoptosis-, and inflammation-related genes were evaluated by PCR. Flow cytometric analysis of mouse spleen was conducted to assess changes in lymphocyte subpopulations.
SAC treatment significantly inhibited endometriotic lesion growth. Transcriptional expression analysis revealed the antiadhesion and apoptosis-promoting effects of SAC. In particular, SAC showed an effective immune modulatory response by altering splenic CD4+ and CD8+ T cell subsets and inflammatory cytokine production in the spleen and endometriotic lesions.
These results elucidate the inhibitory effects of SAC on the growth of endometriosis in a mouse model and describe its immunomodulatory effects (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43440-024-00625-1).

Name: S. alvi Naturally attenuated nonpathogenic live vector vaccine
Developers: University of Florida
Indication: Prevention of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Stimulate elevated neutralising antibodies and effector T cells indicative of cell-mediated immunity
Key features and challenges:
Snodgrassella alvi naturally attenuated nonpathogenic live vector vaccine is a live bacterial vector strategy under investigation for prevention of Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection. S. alvi, a bee-restricted commensal bacterium within the family Neisseriaceae, has been proposed as a vaccine platform based on phylogenetic relatedness to pathogenic Neisseria species and its lack of human colonization capacity.
A funded preclinical project reported preliminary findings demonstrating that S. alvi was safe in mice when administered intraperitoneally at high doses and induced high IgG titers cross-reactive with N. gonorrhoeae, resulting in robust bactericidal activity (https://reporter.nih.gov/search/4Kc-pvRGzECeY9S9kHnqMw/project-details/10263891). 
In silico analyses indicated that S. alvi lacks major virulence factors associated with pathogenic Neisseriaceae, including iron acquisition systems. Planned studies include optimization of parenteral and mucosal vaccination strategies, evaluation of adjuvant requirements, and assessment of protective efficacy in a murine vaginal challenge model.
Key challenges include translation of murine immunogenicity data to human protection, regulatory considerations for live vector vaccines, and confirmation of long-term safety and immunological durability. Establishing clear correlates of protection for gonorrhea remains a critical barrier.
Overall, S. alvi represents an innovative live vector vaccine platform leveraging phylogenetic proximity to induce cross-reactive immunity against N. gonorrhoeae. Further preclinical validation is required to determine its feasibility for clinical development.

Name: SANARIA® PfSPZ-LARC2
Developers: Sanaria Inc; Seattle Children's Hospital (including Seattle Children's Research Institute)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against malaria caused by P. falciparum
Mechanism of action: Elicits immune response which inhibits sporozoites
Key features and challenges: Plasmodium falciparum (Pf) late liver stage-arresting replication-competent (LARC) sporozoite (SPZ) malaria vaccine. The PfSPZ comprising PfSPZ-LARC2 Vaccine contain a double gene deletion, of the Mei2 and LINUP genes. As a result, they undergo developmental arrest in the late liver stages without releasing merozoites into the blood stream (no blood stage parasites are produced, either asexual or sexual). Because Pf parasites with the LARC phenotype replicate in the liver before disintegrating, they amplify and diversify parasite protein expression and are expected to be a potent immunogen to induce anti-malarial immunity, equaling or exceeding the potency and efficacy of the replication-competent chemo-attenuated Sanaria® PfSPZ-CVac (chloroquine). Because the parasites are intrinsically attenuated, they are also expected to be safe and well tolerated, similar to radiation-attenuated Sanaria® PfSPZ Vaccine and to the single-gene(Mei2)-deleted GA2 parasites (also LARC phenotype) tested at the Leiden University Medical Center (LUMC), which, like PfSPZ-LARC2 Vaccine, disintegrate after replicating in the liver. PfSPZ-LARC2 Vaccine thus avoids the safety concerns associated with PfSPZ-CVac, which uses fully infectious, non-attenuated parasites to achieve replication and depends on co-administered chloroquine for attenuation. In summary, the genetically attenuated PfSPZ-LARC2 Vaccine should combine the best-in-class immunogenic potency and protective efficacy of PfSPZ-CVac (chloroquine) with the excellent safety and tolerability of intrinsically attenuated PfSPZ Vaccine and GA2 vaccine.
Recent updates: Two Phase I trials commenced in 2025 (NCT06652737; NCT06735209).

(https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/how-to-participate/org-details/910983940/project/101130516/program/43108390/details)
The SENSOPAD study focuses on evaluating the effectiveness of the device in reducing the diagnosis time for endometriosis from the typical eight years to just a few days. By continuously monitoring menstrual biomarkers, SENSOPAD aims to provide early detection of endometriosis, enabling timely intervention and treatment. The study assesses the device's accuracy in identifying biomarkers, its usability in everyday life, and its potential impact on optimizing healthcare outcomes, particularly in reducing the burden of undiagnosed ED. (https://www.elke.ntua.gr/en/research_project/sensopad-sensing-endometriosis-on-portable-auxiliary-devices-2/)

Name: SHR7280 - Endometriosis
Developers: Jiangsu HengRui Medicine
Indication: Indicated for endometriosis pain management
Mechanism of action: Gonadotropin releasing hormone inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
SHR7280 is an orally administered, small-molecule gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) receptor antagonist developed by Jiangsu Hengrui Medicine. It competitively blocks endogenous GnRH binding to pituitary GnRH receptors, thereby inhibiting secretion of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), leading to suppression of ovarian estradiol production. By reducing circulating estrogen levels, SHR7280 targets hormone-dependent conditions such as endometriosis, where estrogen drives proliferation and maintenance of ectopic endometrial tissue (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800058869).
A randomized, double-blind Phase I clinical trial (SHR7280-102; NCT04417972) evaluated the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics (PK), and pharmacodynamics (PD) of SHR7280 tablets in premenopausal women with endometriosis (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04417972). 
Initiated in July 2020 and enrolling 179 participants in China, the study assessed multiple dosing regimens. Results published in 2023 demonstrated favorable safety, PK, and PD profiles at doses of 200 mg once daily (QD), 300 mg QD, and 200 mg twice daily (BID) (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40262-023-01315-6). 
The findings supported further clinical development of SHR7280 as a GnRH antagonist for the treatment of endometriosis-associated pain, providing the basis for advancement into Phase II studies.
Key challenges include the potential hypoestrogenic side effects common to GnRH antagonists, such as vasomotor symptoms, decreased bone mineral density, and mood changes, particularly with longer-term use. Optimal dosing strategies that balance effective estradiol suppression with tolerability will be critical. Comparative efficacy versus other oral GnRH antagonists and hormonal therapies will also influence its positioning in the treatment landscape. Ongoing and future Phase II and Phase III trials will be necessary to establish sustained efficacy, long-term safety, and real-world clinical utility in endometriosis management.

Key features and challenges:
SHR7280 is an oral small-molecule gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) receptor antagonist being developed by Jiangsu Hengrui Medicine. By competitively blocking endogenous GnRH at the pituitary receptor, SHR7280 suppresses luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) secretion, thereby reducing downstream production of estradiol and testosterone. This mechanism is intended to create a reversible hypoestrogenic state, which is therapeutically relevant for estrogen-dependent conditions such as uterine fibroids.
SHR7280 is under clinical investigation across multiple indications, including female infertility (Phase III), menorrhagia (Phase II/III), endometriosis (Phase I/II), and prostate cancer (Phase I) (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800058869). For uterine fibroids specifically, a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase II/III trial initiated in 2022 is evaluating optimal dosing, efficacy, and safety in women with menorrhagia secondary to uterine fibroids (https://adis.springer.com/trials/700353995). The primary focus is reduction of heavy menstrual bleeding, a key symptom driving morbidity and surgical intervention in fibroid patients.
Key challenges include management of hypoestrogenic adverse effects such as bone mineral density loss and vasomotor symptoms, which are common with GnRH antagonists. Long-term safety, need for add-back hormonal therapy, comparative effectiveness versus existing GnRH antagonists (e.g., relugolix, elagolix), and cost considerations will influence positioning in clinical practice. Further Phase III data will be required to clarify durability of response and overall benefit-risk profile.

Developers: SRM Institute of Science and Technology (formerly SRM University)

Key features and challenges:
Lactobacillus crispatus is a lactic acid bacterium typically found in the human vaginal microbiota. Peptides from L. crispatus have shown a potential therapeutic option for targetting N. gonorrhea. A 2024 preclinical study identified an antimicrobial peptide from the bacteriocin immunity protein (BIP) of L. crispatus using the bioinformatics tool and Collection of Antimicrobial Peptide (CAMPR3). The peptide SM20 exhibited higher docking scores and ADMET properties. Therefore, SM20 could be further encapsulated with cellulose; it can be applied topically to the genital tract to target N. gonorrhea infection. The controlled release of the antimicrobial peptide from the gel can provide sustained delivery of the treatment, increasing its efficacy and reducing the risk of resistance development. (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40203-023-00185-x)

The ability of Lactobacillus crispatus to inhibit Neisseria gonorrhoeae has been identified in other published data. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32768529/)

Key challenges include dependence on dedicated instrumentation, cost considerations relative to single-pathogen NAATs, and the need for large-scale clinical validation across diverse populations. Integration into decentralized or low-resource settings may be constrained by infrastructure requirements.
Overall, the SMARTCHEK® STI Test Kit represents a high-throughput multiplex molecular diagnostic platform capable of detecting gonorrhea within a broader STI panel. Further implementation studies are required to assess scalability and real-world performance.

Name: SPIOMET
Developers: SPIOMET4HEALTH
Indication: Normalising ovulation rates and improving endocrine-metabolic status in PCOS
Target:

Spironolactone - Aldosterone
pioglitazone - Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma
Mechanism of action:
Metformin - AMP activated protein kinase stimulants; Gluconeogenesis inhibitors
Spironolactone - Aldosterone antagonists
Pioglitazone - Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma agonists
Key features and challenges:
SPIOMET is a fixed-dose combination therapy comprising spironolactone (SPI), pioglitazone (PIO), and metformin (MET), developed under the SPIOMET4HEALTH initiative to address the underlying metabolic and endocrine drivers of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) in adolescent girls and young adult women. The regimen combines an anti-androgen (spironolactone), a PPARγ agonist insulin sensitizer (pioglitazone), and a biguanide insulin sensitizer (metformin), aiming to simultaneously target hyperandrogenism, insulin resistance, and central adiposity.
https://spiomet4health.eu/the-clinical-trial/
The therapeutic rationale is based on the hypothesis that early correction of metabolic dysfunction and ectopic fat accumulation may restore ovulatory function and normalize hormonal patterns, potentially modifying disease trajectory rather than merely suppressing symptoms. This is particularly relevant in adolescents, where current management commonly relies on off-label use of combined oral contraceptives, which improve symptoms but do not directly address insulin resistance or visceral adiposity.
A Phase II randomized clinical trial (NCT05394142) is evaluating SPIOMET in adolescent girls and young adult women with PCOS. The primary endpoint is ovulation rate, while secondary outcomes include improvements in endocrine-metabolic parameters, reduction in central fat mass, safety, adherence, and quality of life. The study design also includes comparison of the fixed-dose combination against its individual components (spironolactone and pioglitazone) and placebo, to assess whether the combined formulation provides superior efficacy over monotherapy.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05394142
Despite its comprehensive mechanistic approach, SPIOMET remains investigational. Long-term safety in adolescents, particularly regarding pioglitazone-associated weight gain and fluid retention and spironolactone’s endocrine effects, requires careful monitoring. The durability of ovulatory restoration after treatment discontinuation is unknown, and regulatory pathways for a fixed-dose combination of established drugs in a new indication may present challenges. Additionally, comparative effectiveness versus established first-line therapies such as metformin alone or emerging GLP-1–based therapies remains to be clarified.
SPIOMET represents a multi-target, disease-modifying strategy aimed at early metabolic correction in PCOS. Its future role in clinical practice will depend on demonstration of sustained ovulatory recovery, metabolic improvement, and an acceptable safety profile in larger, confirmatory trials.

Name: Salsalate
Developers: Amneal Pharmaceuticals; LGM Pharma
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: The mode of anti-inflammatory action of salsalate and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs is not fully defined, but appears to be primarily associated with inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis.
Key features and challenges:
Salsalate is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) and a prodrug of salicylic acid, traditionally used to treat pain and inflammation associated with rheumatologic conditions. Beyond its anti-inflammatory properties, salsalate has demonstrated metabolic effects, including improvements in insulin sensitivity and lipid metabolism. Some of these effects are thought to be mediated through reduction of chronic low-grade inflammation, while others may occur independently of its anti-inflammatory activity.
Interest in salsalate for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is based on the recognition that PCOS is frequently associated with insulin resistance, hyperandrogenism, and systemic inflammation. In 2018, a Phase II randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (NCT03229408) enrolled 90 women with PCOS to evaluate the metabolic and endocrine effects of salsalate. Participants were randomized to receive oral salsalate at a dose of 3–4 g daily for 12 weeks or placebo. The study had two primary aims: first, to assess the impact of salsalate on ovarian androgen secretion and insulin sensitivity; and second, to evaluate its effect on lipid- and glucose-induced inflammatory responses in mononuclear cells. The trial was completed in February 2024; however, published results are not yet available.
While salsalate presents a mechanistically attractive option for targeting inflammation-driven insulin resistance in PCOS, its role remains investigational. High doses required for metabolic effects raise considerations regarding gastrointestinal tolerance, tinnitus, and other salicylate-related adverse effects. Further analysis of trial outcomes and replication in larger studies will be necessary to determine its therapeutic relevance in PCOS management.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03229408

Name: Salsalate
