Mechanism of action: The mode of anti-inflammatory action of salsalate and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs is not fully defined, but appears to be primarily associated with inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis. This inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis is done through the inactivation of cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) and COX-2, which are reponsible for catalyzing the formation of prostaglandins in the arachidonic acid pathway
Key features and challenges:
Salsalate is an orally available salicylate and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) with anti-inflammatory, analgesic and antipyretic activities. As a prodrug, salsalate is hydrolyzed to salicylic acid which inhibits the expression of cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes. This prevents the conversion of arachidonic acid into prostaglandin precursors and leads to decreased formation of prostaglandins that are involved in pain, fever and inflammation. In addition, salsalate appears to inhibit nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB), thereby preventing activation of the NF-κB-mediated pathway and the expression of genes involved in inflammation. Unlike aspirin, salsalate does not inhibit platelet aggregation.
Women who have had preeclampsia demonstrate microvascular endothelial‐dysfunction, mediated in part by reduced nitric oxide‐dependent dilation. Therefore, it has been hypothesised that acute systemic inhibition of inflammation would improve endothelium and nitric oxide‐dependent vasodilation in women with a history of preeclampsia. 
In a Phase I clinical trial, salsalate treatment augmented endothelium‐dependent vasodilation via nitric oxide‐mediated pathways in these women, suggesting that inflammatory signaling plays a role in mediating persistent endothelial‐dysfunction in women with a history of preeclampsia.
(https://doi.org/10.1096/fasebj.2020.34.s1.04108). It is also being investigated in postpartum women with previous preeclampsia for its role in preventing cardiovascular disease (NCT03482440).
Recent updates: Still active in 2021 based on this, Salsalate treatment augmented endothelium-dependent vasodilation via NO-mediated pathways in women who have had preeclampsia, suggesting that inflammatory signaling mediates persistent endothelial dysfunction following preeclampsia. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8858855/#:~:text=Salsalate%20treatment%20augmented%20endothelium%2Ddependent,persistent%20endothelial%20dysfunction%20following%20preeclampsia.

Name: Sanguinarine
Developers: Guangdong Medical University
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Interfering with the permeability of the cell wall and membrane and inducing bacterial reactive oxygen species production
Key features and challenges:
Sanguinarine is a benzophenanthridine alkaloid derived from rhizomes of the plant species Sanguinaria canadensis. The alkaloid can exist in the cationic iminium and neutral alkanolamine forms. Sanguinarine is a DNA and RNA intercalator where only the iminium ion binds.
In a 2023 study the antibacterial activities of spectinomycin and sanguinarine against 117 clinical NG isolates and time-kill curve of sanguinarine were evaluated. Almost all isolates were resistant to penicillin (91.5%) and ciprofloxacin (96.5%), 8.5% showed resistance to azithromycin, 10.3% and 10.3% had decreased susceptibility/resistance to ceftriaxone and cefixime, respectively, whereas 100% were susceptible to spectinomycin. The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) ranges, MIC50, MIC90 and MICmean values of sanguinarine were 2–64 μg/ml, 16 μg/ml, 32 μg/ml and 16.9 μg/ml, respectively, and time-kill curve showed killing of bacteria in a dose-dependent manner during the assay time of 6h, very similar to spectinomycin. Sanguinarine has great potential as an effective and novel anti-NG agent.
(https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/veterinary-science/articles/10.3389/fvets.2023.1121082/full)

Name: Saroglitazar
Developers: Zydus Life Sciences; Cadila Pharmaceuticals
Indication: PCOS hyperandrogenism and metabolic dysfunction
Target: Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha; Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma
Mechanism of action: Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha agonists; Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma agonists
Key features and challenges:
Saroglitazar is a dual peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR) alpha/gamma agonist that has shown promising lipid and glucose-lowering effects through its activation of PPAR α and γ pathways. Approved in India for treating hyperlipidemia in diabetes patients, it effectively reduces fasting blood glucose and hemoglobin A1c levels. With a predominant action as a PPAR α agonist and weaker PPAR γ effects, Saroglitazar presents a favorable safety profile, minimizing common side effects like weight gain and peripheral edema. Recent studies have explored its potential in managing conditions such as HIV-associated lipodystrophy and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).

A prospective CT last updated in 2021 aims to examine the effect of Saroglitazar 2 mg and 4 mg in the treatment of women with PCOS, specifically examining changes from baseline to week 24 in total testosterone levels. (http://www.ctri.nic.in/Clinicaltrials/pmaindet2.php?trialid=31492)

A study estimated to complete in 2024 aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of Saroglitazar Magnesium in women with well characterized PCOS for altering hepatic fat content from baseline. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03617263)

Recent updates: A Phase 1, first-in-human, dose-escalation trial in healthy adults in the United States found the three-dose intramuscular series was well tolerated, with adjuvanted formulations inducing robust anti-Sm-p80 IgG responses, and the candidate has advanced to a Phase 1b trial in endemic areas of Africa (NCT05292391).

Name: SchistoShield®
Developers: US National Institutes of Health (NIH); Access to Advanced Health Institute (AAHI) (formerly Infectious Disease Research Institute IDRI); Texas Tech University; PAI Life Sciences, Inc.; International Vaccine Institute (IVI); Gothenburg University, Göteborgs Universitet (including Vaccine Research Institute); Leiden University, Universiteit Leiden (including the Leiden University Medical Center); University of Tubingen (including the Natural and Medical Sciences Institute, NMI); University of Cambridge; Texas Tech University

First Phase II trial running for five months in 2025 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05999825)

Name: Secreted frizzled-related protein 5 (SFRP-5)
Developers: Bursa Yüksek İhtisas Training and Research Hospital
Indication: Low levels of SFRP-5 may be indicative of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Quantifies circulating SFRP-5 levels to assess metabolic and inflammatory dysregulation associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Secreted frizzled-related protein 5 (SFRP-5) is involved in modulating the Wnt signaling pathway, which plays a crucial role in various cellular processes such as cell growth, differentiation, and metabolism. SFRP-5 has been shown to influence adipogenesis and is implicated in regulating inflammation and insulin sensitivity.

SFRP-5 levels are being studied as potential biomarkers for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), as it has been found that women with PCOS tend to have lower levels of SFRP-5, possibly contributing to metabolic dysfunction seen in this condition.

A study published in 2022 investigated the serum levels of secreted frizzled-related protein 5 (SFRP-5) in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and its relationship with metabolic parameters. The study included 43 PCOS patients and 45 healthy controls. Results showed that SFRP-5 levels were significantly lower in the PCOS group compared to controls. No correlation was found between SFRP-5 and other metabolic parameters in the PCOS group. Using receiver operating curve (ROC) analysis, SFRP-5 showed a sensitivity of 74.4% and specificity of 75.6% at a threshold of ≤388.38 ng/mL for diagnosing PCOS. The study suggests that SFRP-5 could be a useful marker for diagnosing, monitoring, and treating PCOS. (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1354750X.2022.2064549)

Name: Segmental hair metabolome
Developers: Hacettepe University
Indication: Prediction and detection of preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for research use only
Target: Hair metabolites (urea cycle, glycine, serine, aspartate, methionine and purine metabolism, ammonia cycle, and phosphatidylethanolamine biosynthesis)
Mechanism of action: Analyzes hair metabolite profiles to retrospectively assess chronic metabolic and oxidative stress associated with preeclampsia risk.
Key features and challenges: The hair metabolome is proving to be a valuable resource in pregnancy research, offering stable metabolite data for studying biomarkers and metabolic mechanisms related to pregnancy and its complications. In a 2023 study, researchers from Hacettepe University in Turkey examined the hair metabolome profiles of pregnant women with PE, HELLP syndrome, and healthy controls. Hair samples from mothers were analyzed by trimester using proper preparation techniques and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) to identify strong biomarkers for screening, early detection, follow-up, and treatment of PE and HELLP. Results showed notable trimester-based differences between patients and controls, with a striking decrease in all 100 metabolites studied in the patient group (p < 0.000). Key affected pathways included the urea cycle, glycine, serine, aspartate, methionine and purine metabolism, the ammonia cycle, and phosphatidylethanolamine biosynthesis. These metabolites may serve as non-invasive biomarkers for predicting, detecting early, and monitoring PE (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11306-023-02009-7)

Name: Selective TIMP protein-based tocolytics
Developers: University of Nevada, Reno
Indication: For the prevention and treatment of preterm labour (reduce preterm births)
Mechanism of action: Inhibits matrix metalloproteinase activity to prevent cervical extracellular matrix degradation and delay cervical remodeling and contractions.
Key features and challenges:
Previous studies have shown that specific members of the matrix metalloproteinase family (MMP-2 and MMP-9) are overexpressed in preterm laboring myometrium and that these enzymes exacerbate contractile responses in human uterine smooth muscle. Therefore, MMP-2/9 may serve as therapeutic targets to block preterm labor. 

Tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs) are endogenous MMP. Researchers aim to target specific MMPs (MMP-2/9), responsible for uterine contraction in patients with preterm labor, with high selectivity while avoiding interactions with other beneficial MMPs. It is believed that selective TIMP protein-based therapeutics can be developed to promote uterine quiescence. Early research is ongoing. 
(https://reporter.nih.gov/search/Ll6tqcuMik68l_LThIAueA/project-details/10509786)

Name: Selenium nanoparticles
Developers: Zagazing University
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Target: Ovaries, endocrine system, adipose tissue, liver, immune system, and oxidative stress pathways.
Mechanism of action: SeNPs reduced androgen synthesis and the expression of androgen receptors (AR) by decreasing mRNA levels of key steroidogenic enzymes and increasing Cyp19α1 expression.
Key features and challenges:
Selenium nanoparticles (SeNPs) are nanoscale formulations of elemental selenium designed to enhance bioavailability and reduce toxicity compared to conventional selenium compounds. Selenium plays a critical role in antioxidant defence systems, particularly through its incorporation into selenoproteins such as glutathione peroxidases. In nanoparticle form, selenium exhibits enhanced antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and metabolic regulatory properties, making it a candidate for investigation in disorders characterized by oxidative stress and endocrine dysfunction, including polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
PCOS is associated with hyperandrogenism, insulin resistance, chronic low-grade inflammation, and oxidative stress. Experimental evidence suggests that SeNPs may modulate multiple pathophysiological pathways relevant to PCOS. Proposed mechanisms include suppression of steroidogenic enzyme expression (e.g., STAR, CYP11A1, CYP17A1, HSD17B3), upregulation of aromatase (CYP19A1), reduction in circulating testosterone levels, improvement in insulin sensitivity, attenuation of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6, and enhancement of antioxidant capacity.
A 2022 preclinical study in a letrozole-induced rat model of PCOS demonstrated that SeNPs reduced oxidative stress markers, improved metabolic disturbances, and attenuated inflammatory responses. Treatment was associated with improved ovarian histology and partial restoration of reproductive function.
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12011-023-03579-2
A 2023 study further evaluated SeNPs in female albino rats with experimentally induced PCOS. SeNP treatment restored estrous cyclicity, reduced body mass index and insulin resistance, improved lipid profiles, and decreased serum testosterone levels. Improvements in ovarian morphology were also observed. The study concluded that SeNPs decreased androgen synthesis and alleviated reproductive, endocrine, and metabolic dysfunction in the PCOS model.
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12011-023-03616-0
Despite promising multi-pathway effects in animal models, clinical evidence in women with PCOS is currently lacking. The safety, optimal dosing, long-term metabolic effects, and reproductive outcomes associated with selenium nanoparticle therapy remain uncharacterized in human populations. Additionally, selenium exposure requires careful monitoring due to potential toxicity at higher doses.
Selenium nanoparticles represent an early-stage investigational approach targeting oxidative stress, inflammation, and androgen excess in PCOS. While preclinical findings suggest broad therapeutic potential, translation into clinical practice will require rigorous human trials to establish efficacy and safety.
Recent updates: 2023 findings show that SeNPs, through their antioxidant and anti-inflammatory characteristics, alleviate letrozole-induced PCOS (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12011-023-03579-2)

Name: Selgantolimod
Developers: Gilead; French National Institute of Health and Medical Research (Inserm)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of chronic HBV infection
Mechanism of action: Inhibits host TLR8
Key features and challenges: Selgantolimod (formerly GS 9688) is an oral small molecule agonist of the toll like receptor 8, being developed by Gilead Sciences, for the treatment of hepatitis B virus infections. Selgantolimod is a potent and selective agonist of human TLR8 that induces IL-12 as well as other cellular immune mediators and antiviral cytokines in human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). Clinical development is underway in the US, Taiwan, New Zealand, Canada, Australia, South Korea, France and Spain.
Recent updates: Phase II trial commenced in 2023, includes trial sites in Botswana, Haiti, Peru, Brazil, Philippines, South Africa, Thailand, Uganda, Zimbabwe (NCT05551273).

Name: Semaglutide + Metformin
Developers: University of Colorado, Denver; Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujib Medical University; Chongqing Municipal Science and Technology Bureau
Indication: Treatment of PCOS - Metabolism; Menstrual cycle regulation; Hyperandrogenism; Fertility
Target: GLP-1 receptor; AMP activated protein kinase; Gluconeogenesis
Mechanism of action:
Semaglutide activates the GLP-1 receptor to increase glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppress glucagon, slow gastric emptying and reduce appetite, leading to substantial weight loss and improvements in glycaemic control, lipids and inflammatory markers.
Metformin primarily improves insulin sensitivity by inhibiting hepatic gluconeogenesis and enhancing peripheral glucose uptake, reducing compensatory hyperinsulinemia and secondarily lowering ovarian androgen production.
In combination, semaglutide + metformin aims to address both obesity and insulin resistance, two central drivers of PCOS pathophysiology. Semaglutide provides potent weight reduction and appetite control, while metformin augments insulin sensitization and has direct ovarian effects; together they may improve ovulation frequency, menstrual cyclicity, androgen excess and cardiometabolic risk more than metformin alone.
Key features and challenges:
Semaglutide is a potent once-weekly glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) approved for type 2 diabetes and obesity, with superior weight-loss efficacy compared with earlier GLP-1 RAs such as liraglutide. In adolescents and adults without polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), semaglutide has demonstrated mean weight reductions of approximately 10–16%, alongside improvements in cardiometabolic risk factors.
https://www.acc.org/Latest-in-Cardiology/Clinical-Trials/2022/12/20/23/09/step-teens
These metabolic effects are particularly relevant to PCOS, where obesity and insulin resistance exacerbate hyperandrogenism, anovulation, and long-term cardiometabolic risk. Evidence supporting GLP-1 RAs in PCOS has expanded over the past decade. Randomized trials of liraglutide and exenatide, alone or in combination with metformin, have demonstrated reductions in body weight, waist circumference, HOMA-IR, and liver fat, along with improvements in free testosterone, ovarian morphology, and menstrual cyclicity.
A 2024 meta-analysis of GLP-1 RAs in women with PCOS (176 participants across four RCTs) reported significant reductions in BMI, waist circumference, triglycerides, and total testosterone compared with placebo.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39178623/
Subsequent network meta-analyses confirm that GLP-1 RAs, particularly when added to standard therapy, are among the most effective pharmacologic options for improving anthropometric and several hormonal parameters in PCOS.
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13098-025-01730-8
Specific evidence for the semaglutide + metformin combination is emerging. A 2025 single-centre randomized open-label trial in China enrolled 100 overweight/obese women with PCOS and compared metformin monotherapy (1000 mg twice daily) with combination therapy including semaglutide (titrated to 1.0 mg weekly). After 16 weeks, the combination group achieved significantly greater reductions in body weight (−6.09 kg vs −2.25 kg), BMI, and waist-to-hip ratio, alongside larger improvements in testosterone, Chinese visceral adiposity index, and C-reactive protein. Menstrual recovery was more frequent in the combination group, and 24-week post-treatment follow-up showed higher natural pregnancy rates (35% vs 15%).
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40713699/
Additional evaluation is underway. The Phase 2/3 randomized study NCT06896981 (Bangladesh) compares semaglutide + metformin versus metformin alone in obese women with PCOS, assessing ≥5% weight loss, BMI, insulin resistance, blood pressure, and androgen parameters.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06896981
A related three-arm Chinese protocol (NCT05702905) compares metformin, semaglutide, and combination therapy, with subsequent ovulation induction and pregnancy follow-up to link metabolic improvements to fertility outcomes.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05702905
These findings align with broader evidence showing that GLP-1 RAs, particularly when combined with metformin, can improve menstrual regularity, hormonal profiles, and pregnancy rates in PCOS.
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12905-025-03594-6
Despite strong efficacy signals, several challenges remain. Current PCOS guidelines have not yet fully incorporated semaglutide or semaglutide–metformin combinations; metformin remains first-line therapy for metabolic features, and GLP-1 RAs are considered emerging options pending longer-term safety and fertility data.
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13098-025-01730-8
Most available trials are single-centre, relatively small, and short-term (typically 16–40 weeks), with limited data on live birth rates or long-term reproductive safety.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40713699/
Additional barriers include high cost, injectable administration, gastrointestinal adverse effects, and access disparities, particularly in low-resource settings. Concerns also persist regarding use in women actively attempting conception or during early pregnancy, given limited pregnancy safety data and evolving regulatory guidance; careful contraception and preconception planning are typically required.
Overall, semaglutide + metformin represents a high-potential combination for overweight or obese women with PCOS, with growing evidence of superior metabolic, inflammatory, and reproductive benefits compared with metformin alone. However, its long-term role in routine PCOS management will depend on larger, multi-centre randomized trials, long-term reproductive safety data, and formal guideline endorsement.
Recent updates: Phase II/III trial commenced in 2025 and is expected to complete later that year (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06896981)

Name: SensoMFgFET
Developers: National Technical University of Athens
Indication: Diagnosis of endometriosis via biomarkers in menstrual fluids
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Target: DNA single nucleotide polymorphisms in menstrual fluid
Mechanism of action: Field-effect transistor biosensor detects disease-associated biomarkers through changes in electrical conductance for rapid endometriosis screening.
Key features and challenges:
The SENSOPAD project (short for Sensing ENdometriosiS On Portable Auxiliary Devices) is a European collaborative research program aimed at developing new diagnostic solutions for endometriosis. 
SENSOMFGFET is a portable Point-of-Care (POC) device that utilizes advanced microfluidic systems and bio-conjugated graphene field-effect transistors (GFET) to detect specific DNA single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in menstrual fluid. These SNPs serve as early indicators of endometriosis. The device is equipped with RFID functionality, enabling easy data transfer and integration with other healthcare systems. Designed for clinical settings, SENSOMFGFET offers high precision in detecting endometriosis-related genetic markers, providing a complementary tool to SENSOPAD for more in-depth analysis when initial concerns arise.

The project is also developing SENSOPAD, a home-based test utilizing a sanitary pad integrated with advanced technology designed to detect biomarkers associated with endometriosis.

The study on SENSOMFGFET aims to validate its efficacy as a clinical diagnostic tool for endometriosis. The research evaluates the device’s ability to accurately identify early genetic markers of ED and its potential to complement at-home monitoring systems like SENSOPAD. By focusing on the precision of SNP detection and the usability of the device in a clinical environment, the study seeks to establish SENSOMFGFET as a critical component in the early detection and diagnosis of endometriosis. The study also explores the device's role in reducing diagnostic timelines and improving patient outcomes through early intervention. (https://www.elke.ntua.gr/en/research_project/sensopad-sensing-endometriosis-on-portable-auxiliary-devices-2/)

Name: Series-5824 (MT)
Developers: Drugs for Neglected Diseases initiative (DNDi); Mitsubishi Tanabe Pharma Corporation; University of Dundee; Institut Pasteur Korea; London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (LSHTM) (including MEIRU)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Chagas disease.
Key features and challenges: Through a two-year lead optimization collaboration, DNDi and Mitsubishi Tanabe Pharma (MTPC) aim to optimize a novel and very promising T. cruzi active series identified through high-throughput screening of 51,200 compounds in MTPC’s proprietary library. To date, the series has progressed to the lead stage. Project partners plan to chemically derivatize the lead series using a well-defined and diversified medicinal chemistry strategy to improve its in vitro potency against the T. cruzi parasite while maintaining its favourable drug metabolism and pharmacokinetic properties and mitigating any safety liabilities. In parallel, DNDi and MTPC will work to elucidate the mechanism of action of the series with the expert support of University of Dundee, and make use of this information to guide the lead optimization programme.

Name: Serum Mannose
Developers: Shengjing Hospital of China Medical University; University of Baghdad
Indication: PCOS diagnosis
Health care facility level: IVDs for research use only
Mechanism of action: Quantifies circulating mannose to assess metabolic dysregulation and insulin resistance associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
A 2022 study investigated the link between serum mannose levels, insulin resistance, and androgen hormones in women with PCOS, showing significantly elevated mannose levels in PCOS patients compared to controls. Findings suggest serum mannose as a potential biomarker for PCOS diagnosis, with a strong correlation to insulin resistance and high sensitivity and specificity for distinguishing PCOS from healthy individuals. 
(https://www.proquest.com/openview/4109363a18794b95e41969fc953ac476/1?pq-origsite=gscholar&cbl=2035897)
In a 2019 study on 71 patients with PCOS and 61 control subjects, serum mannose had an area under the curve (AUC) of 73% at a cutoff value of 225.79 ng/mL with a sensitivity of 66.2% and specificity of 73.8% for predicting PCOS. There were no differences between mannose, total testosterone, free testosterone, or dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate in the reliability of predicting PCOS. Combining mannose and total testosterone resulted in a higher AUC of 83.3%, and had moderate sensitivity (78.9%) and specificity (77%) for predicting PCOS. Multivariate logistic regression revealed that higher serum mannose levels were strongly associated with an increased risk of PCOS.
(https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/endocrinology/articles/10.3389/fendo.2019.00711/full)

Name: Serum NG-4
Developers: Mustansiriyah University; Kerbala University
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for research use only
Mechanism of action: unspecified
Key features and challenges:
Neuregulin-4 (NG-4) is an adipokine primarily expressed in brown adipose tissue and implicated in metabolic regulation, including glucose homeostasis, lipid metabolism, and insulin sensitivity. Given the central role of insulin resistance and metabolic dysfunction in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), NG-4 has emerged as a potential biomarker for disease identification and metabolic risk stratification.

A 2023 cross-sectional study evaluated serum NG-4 levels in 120 women (60 with PCOS and 60 healthy controls) to determine its diagnostic validity and association with metabolic parameters. The study reported significantly elevated NG-4 levels in women with PCOS compared with controls. NG-4 levels demonstrated strong correlations with hormonal and biochemical parameters, including BMI, insulin resistance indices, and lipid profiles. Notably, obesity parameters alone did not independently influence NG-4 levels; rather, PCOS status itself appeared to be independently associated with elevated NG-4 concentrations. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis showed high diagnostic accuracy (AUC 0.97), suggesting strong sensitivity and specificity for distinguishing PCOS cases from controls.
https://www.imrpress.com/journal/CEOG/50/4/10.31083/j.ceog5004089/htm

These findings suggest that serum NG-4 may serve as a promising biomarker for PCOS diagnosis and potentially for monitoring metabolic risk. Its association with insulin resistance and lipid abnormalities aligns with the metabolic phenotype commonly observed in PCOS.

However, several challenges limit immediate clinical translation. The available evidence is derived from a single cross-sectional study, limiting causal inference and external validity. The sample size was modest and geographically limited, and no longitudinal data are available to determine whether NG-4 levels change with treatment, weight loss, or hormonal regulation. Additionally, NG-4 is not specific to PCOS and is implicated in broader metabolic disorders, raising questions about specificity in populations with overlapping cardiometabolic risk. Standardized assay methods and clinically validated diagnostic thresholds have not yet been established.

Serum NG-4 represents an investigational biomarker with promising diagnostic performance in preliminary studies. Larger, multi-centre, longitudinal studies are required to confirm its diagnostic value, clarify its role in disease monitoring, and determine whether it provides incremental benefit beyond existing clinical and biochemical diagnostic criteria for PCOS.

Name: Serum fructose
Developers: China Medical University
Indication: Diagnostic of PCOS in women with dyslipidemia
Health care facility level: IVDs for research use only
Mechanism of action: Quantifies circulating fructose as a marker of altered carbohydrate metabolism associated with insulin resistance in PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Serum fructose, a sugar influenced by diet and metabolism, may contribute to PCOS diagnosis due to its connection with insulin resistance, metabolic dysregulation, and inflammation—key features of PCOS. Elevated fructose levels can worsen insulin resistance, oxidative stress, and hormonal imbalances, affecting ovarian function. While not yet a definitive diagnostic marker, it could complement assessments of metabolic dysfunction in PCOS, especially in cases involving obesity or insulin resistance. 

A 2022 study found that women with PCOS and dyslipidemia had higher fructose levels, which were linked to higher triglycerides, total cholesterol, and LDL cholesterol, and lower HDL cholesterol. Serum fructose levels ≥9.79 pmol/µl predicted dyslipidemia in PCOS with 83.2% sensitivity and 66.4% specificity, and were more predictive of PCOS than androgens in women with dyslipidemia, highlighting fructose’s role in lipid metabolism and PCOS.
(https://www.rbmojournal.com/article/S1472-6483(22)00283-8/abstract)

Name: Serum homocysteine concentration
Developers: Shanxi Medical University
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Measures circulating homocysteine to detect metabolic and cardiovascular risk associated with insulin resistance in PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Serum homocysteine concentrations measure the levels of homocysteine, a sulfur-containing amino acid, in the blood. Normal levels typically range from 5 to 15 µmol/L, with higher levels indicating potential health risks, including cardiovascular and metabolic disorders. 

A study published in 2023 on clinically young patients with PCOS and hyperandrogenism found that serum homocysteine concentrations were significantly higher in these patients compared to a control group. The PCOS group had an average homocysteine level of 15.21 μmol/L, compared to 12.56 μmol/L in the control group. Elevated homocysteine was associated with higher total testosterone levels and obesity. The study suggests that hyperhomocysteinemia could serve as a potential indicator for PCOS, highlighting the need to consider both homocysteine levels and body weight in diagnosis and treatment. (https://journals.viamedica.pl/ginekologia_polska/article/view/88393)

Name: Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) testing
Developers: Debre Tabor University
Indication: Indicated for the prediction of early onset PE
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Inadequate placental blood flow leads to prolonged hypoxia, which stimulates anaerobic glycolysis. This metabolic shift upregulates LDH activity and gene expression.
Key features and challenges:
Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is a cytoplasmic enzyme released during cellular injury and tissue breakdown. Elevated LDH levels reflect cellular damage, hemolysis, and endothelial dysfunction, processes that are central to the pathophysiology of preeclampsia (PE). Given the systemic inflammatory and vascular injury associated with PE, LDH has been investigated as a potential biomarker for disease severity and complication risk.
A 2024 hospital-based cross-sectional study conducted at Debre Birhan Comprehensive Specialized Hospital enrolled 132 participants (66 women with preeclampsia and 66 normotensive controls) to evaluate the diagnostic performance of serum LDH in PE (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/medicine/articles/10.3389/fmed.2024.1240848/full). 
Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis demonstrated an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.963 (95% CI, 0.91–1.0; p = 0.000), indicating excellent discriminatory capacity. Using Youden’s index, an optimal LDH cut-off value of 376.5 U/L was identified, with sensitivity of 87.5% and specificity of 90.8% for detecting preeclampsia-associated complications. LDH levels were significantly associated with disease duration, gestational age, and both systolic and diastolic blood pressure.
These findings suggest that serum LDH demonstrates strong diagnostic accuracy and may serve as a useful adjunctive biomarker for identifying women at risk of preeclampsia and related complications.
Key challenges include the cross-sectional design of the study, which limits assessment of predictive value over time and causality. Variability in LDH measurement methods, population characteristics, and disease severity may influence generalizability of the proposed cut-off value. Additionally, LDH is a non-specific marker of tissue injury and may be elevated in other maternal conditions, potentially reducing specificity in broader clinical settings. Prospective validation studies across diverse populations are necessary to confirm its utility as a standardized diagnostic or prognostic tool in preeclampsia management.

Name: Serum lipid profile - PE
Developers: University of Melbourne, Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology; Kasturba Medical College, India
Indication: Early detection of PE
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Analyzes circulating placental cell-free DNA patterns to detect placental dysfunction and risk of hypertensive pregnancy disorders.
Key features and challenges:
A study started in 2022 in Kasturba Medical college, India, to investigate whether serum lipid profile could serve as a biomarker for the early prediction of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and their severity.
It will enroll approximately 100 pregnant women aged 18 to 45 and examine their lipid profiles during the first trimester.
The goal of the study is to evaluate a potential link between the altered lipid and lipoprotein metabolism with the pathogenesis of preeclampsia and gestational hypertension, which in turn would help in early prediction of Preeclampsia/ Gestational hypertension.
(https://www.ctri.nic.in/Clinicaltrials/pmaindet2.php?trialid=56897)

A case-cohort study published in 2023 used 144 maternal plasma samples at 36 weeks’ gestation from patients before the diagnosis of late-onset preeclampsia (n = 22), delivery of a fetal growth restricted infant (n = 55, defined as <5th birthweight centile), and gestation-matched controls (n = 72). Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-QQQ) -based targeted lipidomics was performed to identify 421 lipids, and fitted logistic regression models for each lipid, correcting for maternal age, BMI, smoking, and gestational diabetes.
Phosphatidylinositol 32:1 (AUC = 0.81) and cholesterol ester 17:1 (AUC = 0.71) best predicted the risk of developing preeclampsia or delivering a fetal growth restricted infant, respectively. Five times repeated five-fold cross validation demonstrated the lipids alone did not out-perform existing protein biomarkers, soluble tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1) and placental growth factor (PlGF) for the prediction of preeclampsia or fetal growth restriction. However, lipids combined with sFlt-1 and PlGF measurements improved disease prediction.
(https://www.thelancet.com/journals/ebiom/article/PIIS2352-3964(23)00269-4/fulltext)

Name: Serum telomerase
Developers: University of Health Sciences, Istanbul, Turkey
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Measures telomerase activity as a marker of cellular stress and inflammatory/metabolic dysregulation associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Serum telomerase is an enzyme that helps maintain the length of telomeres, crucial for cell longevity and function. In women with Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS), research has shown that serum telomerase levels are lower compared to healthy controls, suggesting a potential link to the metabolic complications associated with PCOS.

A study published in 2023 investigated serum telomerase levels in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and their link to metabolic parameters. It found that telomerase levels were significantly lower in PCOS patients (80.0 ± 52.8 IU/mL) compared to healthy controls (113.1 ± 54.9 IU/mL). A telomerase level below 108.6 IU/mL distinguished PCOS patients with 73.33% sensitivity and 57.78% specificity. Telomerase levels were also inversely correlated with body mass index and triglycerides, and were lower in those with metabolic syndrome, suggesting telomerase could reflect metabolic complications in PCOS. (https://www.degruyter.com/document/doi/10.1515/jpem-2022-0455/html)

Name: Serum-based Noninvasive Molecular miRNA diagnostic
Developers: HerAnova Lifesciences
Indication: Indicated for the diagnosis of Endometriosis.
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Quantifies circulating microRNA expression profiles to detect gene regulatory patterns associated with endometriosis.
Key features and challenges: A 2025 prospective study evaluated whether a non-invasive, blood-based microRNA (miRNA) panel could accurately detect Endometriosis, comparing results against diagnostic laparoscopy with or without histopathology.  Seventy-six women presenting with pelvic pain or abnormal bleeding provided serum samples prior to laparoscopy. Researchers measured expression of five candidate miRNAs and one endogenous control, using next-generation sequencing, quantitative PCR, and digital PCR. Of these, 64 (84%) had concordant laparoscopic and histological diagnoses: 33 confirmed endometriosis cases and 31 controls. Applying a cut-off threshold, the miRNA test achieved an accuracy of 85%. Performance improved slightly to 86% when a random forest machine-learning model was used. Among 12 discordant cases (laparoscopy positive but histology negative), miRNA results aligned with histology in 9 and with laparoscopy in 3, suggesting potential for detecting lesion heterogeneity or minimizing false negatives. The findings suggest that a serum-based miRNA panel could offer a feasible, non-invasive diagnostic alternative to laparoscopic diagnosis of endometriosis. However, as a pilot feasibility study, further validation with larger, diverse cohorts and formal performance analysis is required before clinical implementation (https://academic.oup.com/humrep/article/40/Supplement_1/deaf097.651/8170460).

Name: Sestrin
Developers: University of Health Sciences, Istanbul, Turkey
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS via detection of oxidative stress
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Measures sestrin levels to assess oxidative stress and AMPK-related metabolic regulation associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
Sestrin proteins regulate cellular responses to oxidative stress, helping protect cells from damage and promoting antioxidant pathways. Elevated sestrin levels have been linked to increased oxidative stress, which is common in conditions like PCOS. 

A study in 2022 found that women with PCOS had significantly higher sestrin levels compared to healthy controls. The median sestrin level in PCOS patients was 6.2 ± 0.8, while in controls, it was 3.38 ± 0.4 (p < 0.001). ROC analysis showed that sestrin levels could serve as a diagnostic marker for PCOS, with high sensitivity (100%) and specificity (96.7%).  (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/09513590.2022.2163234#abstract)

Name: Sfu-AM2-19
Developers: University of Minnesota
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of cryptococcal meningitis infection
Mechanism of action: Binds to ergosterol in fungal cell membranes to form pores, inducing intracellular ion leakage and lethal cell lysis
Key features and challenges: A small-molecule polyene antifungal that binds ergosterol in fungal cell membranes to form pores, causing intracellular ion leakage and lethal cell lysis. Administered intravenously. It has also been investigated for severe systemic mycoses.
Recent updates: A Phase 2/3 platform trial (NCT06666322) evaluating it as one antifungal regimen for cryptococcal meningitis against standard of care began in 2025 and is recruiting.

Name: ShSERPin-P46 vaccine (S. haematobium serine protease inhibitor)
Developers: Not specified
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against Schistosomiasis
Mechanism of action: Neutralizes the parasite's regulatory serpins, limiting worm survival and mitigating liver/bladder tissue fibrosis
Key features and challenges: A recombinant subunit immunogen based on a Schistosoma haematobium serine protease inhibitor (serpin). It elicits responses that neutralise the parasite's regulatory serpins, limiting worm survival and mitigating liver and bladder tissue fibrosis. Given intramuscularly.

Name: She Sense
Developers: Sision Medical Limited; OnaWave Medical
Indication: Diagnostic of endometriosis
Health care facility level: IVDs for research use only
Mechanism of action: Detects disease-associated biomarkers in noninvasive biological samples to identify molecular signatures consistent with endometriosis.
Key features and challenges:
OnaWave Medical (formerly Sision Medical limited) is a west of Ireland medtech company developing products for the diagnosis and treatment of pelvic conditions. As part of the European project EndoSolve, they are developing a digital biomarker-based risk-stratification platform with associated wearable solutions that can identify patients with pelvic conditions, such as endometriosis and subfertility, based on a physiological marker which is altered by hormones (undisclosed).
The company obtained € 2.5m from the European Innovation Council in 2023 to develop She Sense, a novel, non-invasive diagnostic tool designed to simplify and enhance the detection of endometriosis. It utilizes a digital biomarker that has shown promise in pre-clinical and early human studies. The test aims to offer a more straightforward, cost-effective method for diagnosing endometriosis that does not involve pelvic exams, ultrasounds, MRIs, and laparoscopic procedures.
The grant will fund further development of the She Sense test by refining its signal processing, validating its performance in clinical settings, and developing a sustainable business model. The project's endpoint involves compiling and evaluating data from a prospective clinical study to confirm the test's sensitivity and specificity. This validation will set the stage for larger studies and potential commercialization.
(https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/101099834)
(https://onawavemedical.com/)

Name: Shear wave elastography and 2D-ultrasonic evaluation of the optic nerve
Developers: Fujian Medical University (FJMU)
Indication: Diagnosing preeclampsia and evaluating optic neuropathy in preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) and optic nerve stiffness measurement (ONSM) were measured using two-dimensional ultrasound and shear-wave elastography (SWE).
Key features and challenges:
Two-dimensional (2D) ultrasound and shear-wave elastography (SWE) have been investigated as non-invasive methods to evaluate optic nerve changes in women with preeclampsia. Preeclampsia is associated with endothelial dysfunction and potential alterations in cerebral and ocular hemodynamics, making optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) and optic nerve stiffness measurement (ONSM) potential surrogate markers of disease severity.
A 2023 study evaluated 91 singleton pregnancies to assess the diagnostic value of ONSD (measured by 2D ultrasound) and ONSM (measured by SWE) in women with preeclampsia compared with controls (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37643987/
; https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jcu.23551). Both ONSD and ONSM were significantly higher in the preeclampsia group (p < 0.05). Receiver operating characteristic analysis demonstrated no significant difference between ONSD and ONSM individually for diagnosing preeclampsia (p = 0.436). However, the combined model (ONSD + ONSM) showed significantly improved diagnostic performance compared with either measure alone (p = 0.033 and p = 0.014, respectively). The findings suggest that multimodal ultrasonic assessment of the optic nerve may enhance diagnostic accuracy.
Key challenges include relatively small sample size, need for operator expertise, and absence of standardized cut-off thresholds. Further validation in larger cohorts and comparison with established biomarkers are required before incorporation into routine clinical screening or risk stratification pathways.

Name: Sheffield Mark V Electrical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) device
Developers: University of Sheffield (including the Sheffield Institute of Translational Neurology); Sheffield Teaching Hospitals Foundation Trust
Indication: A technique to quantify cervical ripening changes to predict PTB
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: EIS was performed using a Sheffield Mark 5.0 device that makes measurements in the frequency range 76 Hz to 625 kHz using a small probe housing tetrapolar electrodes.
Key features and challenges:
Cervical electrical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) is a quantitative technique designed to assess cervical ripening by measuring tissue electrical properties. Changes in cervical impedance reflect alterations in extracellular matrix composition and hydration that precede labour. Mid-trimester EIS measurements have been investigated as a method to predict preterm birth (PTB) in asymptomatic women.
The Sheffield Mark 5 device was developed by the Department of Medical Physics and Clinical Engineering at Sheffield Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust (United Kingdom) to perform cervical EIS measurements in clinical settings.
In 2020, incorporation of EIS measurements into the QUIPP app predictive algorithm was evaluated and demonstrated improved predictive performance compared with traditional assessment alone, suggesting potential added value when combined with established risk factors and cervical length assessment.
(https://www.ejog.org/article/S0301-2115(20)30730-2/abstract)
In 2020, results from the EleCtriCaL Impedance Prediction of Preterm birth (ECCLIPPx) study indicated potential clinical utility of cervical EIS for PTB risk assessment, either as a standalone test or in combination with existing modalities. The authors emphasized the need for larger confirmatory studies to determine its role in guiding preventive interventions.
(https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/uog.22180)
In 2023, studies evaluating patient acceptability reported that cervical EIS was well tolerated among both low- and high-risk pregnant women when performed as part of a multimodal screening strategy.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36550429/)
Overall, cervical EIS using the Sheffield Mark 5 device represents an investigational approach to quantifying cervical ripening for early PTB risk stratification. While initial studies suggest predictive potential and good tolerability, further large-scale validation is required to establish clinical effectiveness and integration into routine obstetric practice.

Name: Sherlock ITN

Name: ShigActive™
Developers: Intralytix; University of Maryland, Baltimore (including CVD)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization for the prevention of bacillary dysentery caused by both Shigella sonnei, Shigella flexneri and Shigella dysenteriae
Target: Five lytic bacteriophages: SHSML-52-1, SHFML-11, SHSML-45, SHFML-26 and SHBML-50-1
Mechanism of action: Undefined mechanism
Key features and challenges:
ShigaShield is an all-natural, non-chemical antimicrobial preparation being developed by Intralytix. The product is a phage preparation composed of a combination of five lytic bacteriophage mixed in approximately equal concentrations: SHSML-52-1, SHFML-11, SHSML-45, SHFML-26 and SHBML-50-1.

The active ingredients selectively and specifically kill Shigella, including strains belonging to the three major disease-causing species. Ithas also been used to treat foods that are at high risk of Shigella contamination, which include ready to eat poultry, fish, shellfish, dairy products, fruits and vegetables.
Recent updates: Phase II trial commenced in 2023 (NCT05182749).

Name: ShigETEC
Developers: EveliQure Biotechnologies; icddr,b (formerly the International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research, Bangladesh); Gothenburg University, Göteborgs Universitet (including Vaccine Research Institute)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization for the prevention of bacillary dysentery caused by both Shigella sonnei and Shigella flexneri, and moderate to severe diarrhoea due to ETEC infection
Target: Shigella flexneri 2a 2457T strain, expressing two ETEC antigens, LTB and a detoxified version of ST (STN12S)
Mechanism of action: Induces immune response of IgG and IgA antibodies against bacterial lysates, and anti-ETEC toxin antibodies with neutralizing capacity
Key features and challenges:
Eveliqure Biotechnologies is developing an orally administered first-generation vaccine, designated as ShigETEC,for the prevention of traveller's diarrhoea, caused by Shigellaand enterotoxigenicEscherichia coli(ETEC).

The vaccine was constructed based on a live attenuated Shigella strain rendered rough and non-invasive with heterologous expression of two ETEC antigens, LTB and a detoxified version of ST (STN12S).

Eveliqure introduced the expression of non-shigella derived antigens into the strain to achieve a broader protection. Clinical development is currently underway in Hungary.
Recent updates:
Phase I trial in Bangladeshi adults and paediatrics (aged 2-5 years, 12-23 months and 6-11 months) commenced in 2023 (NCT05987488). 
In February 2022, positive immunogenicity and safety data from a phase I trial in Traveller's diarrhoea released by Eveliqure Biotechnologies.

Name: Shigella4V2
Developers: GlaxoSmithKline (GSK); LimmaTech Biologics; Johns Hopkins University (including the Bloomberg School of Public Health); US Naval Medical Research Center (NMRC); Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization for the prevention of bacillary dysentery caused by Shigella dysenteriae
Mechanism of action: Induces humoral immune response to the LPS of S. dysenteriae, S. flexneri, Shigella boydii and S. sonnei
Key features and challenges:
GSK 4069327A is a tetravalent bioconjugate vaccine being developed by LimmaTech Biologics for broad protection against Shigella dysenteriae, S. flexneri and S. sonnei to prevent bacillary dysentery in children. The intramuscularly administered vaccine utilises GlaxoSmithKline’s (formerly GlycoVaxyn) in vivo glycosylation technology to conjugate immunogenic surface polysaccharides of glycoproteins derived from Shigella dysenteriae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa strain and E. coli O157 to protein carriers of choice through an enzymatic conjugation.
Shigella 4V2 is a second generation tetravalent bioconjugate vaccine of Shigella 4V.
Recent updates:
Phase II trial of Shigella 4V2 commenced in 2025 in 9-month old infants (NCT06523231)
Phase II trial of Shigella 4V2 commenced in 2024 with controlled human infection model (NCT06615375)
Phase II trial of Shigella 4V completed in 2022 (NCT04056117)

Name: Shikimic acid
Developers: Sichuan Agricultural University (SCAU); Guangxi University, Nanning
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of CHIKV infection
Target:
-Host inflammatory and signaling pathways: IL-17 pathway, NF-κB (NFKB1, RELA), PTGS2, MAPK3, EGF.
-Viral attachment factors: TIM-1, TSPAN9, ACTG1, FHL-1.
-CHIKV envelope protein E1 (protein expression reduced in infected cells).
Mechanism of action:
-Interferes with viral adsorption and replication inside host cells.
-Downregulates expression of proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6) and viral attachment factors.
-Inhibits IL-17 signaling pathway components (e.g., NFKB1, RELA, PTGS2, EGF), disrupting inflammation that supports CHIKV replication.
Key features and challenges:
-Low cytotoxicity: CC₅₀ > 2,000 µM in BHK-21 and 293T cells.
-Safe concentration up to 1,000 µM; enhanced survival of infected cells (~25% increase in viability).
-In vitro antiviral effect: reduced CHIKV viral load by ~20–25% in infected cells at 250–1000 µM.
-Reduced expression of CHIKV E1 protein and lowered plaque formation in reinfection assays.
-Effective in both pre-infection and post-infection treatment windows, but not during co-infection.
Recent updates:
2025: 
-First study integrating network pharmacology + in vitro validation showing anti-CHIKV activity of shikimic acid.
-Identified IL-17 pathway modulation and reduction of host viral entry factors as key mechanisms.
-Requires in vivo testing to validate antiviral and anti-inflammatory efficacy.

Name: Sildenafil - PCOS
Developers: Yasouj University of Medical Sciences; Pfizer
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: Type 5 cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterase inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Sildenafil is a phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitor approved for the treatment of erectile dysfunction and pulmonary arterial hypertension. By inhibiting PDE5, sildenafil prevents degradation of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), thereby promoting smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilation. Common adverse effects include headache, dyspepsia, back pain, and myalgia.
Although not approved for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), sildenafil has been explored experimentally due to its potential vascular and endothelial effects. Impaired ovarian perfusion, endothelial dysfunction, and oxidative stress have been implicated in PCOS pathophysiology, particularly in hyperandrogenic and insulin-resistant phenotypes. Enhancement of nitric oxide–cGMP signaling could theoretically improve ovarian blood flow and follicular environment.
A 2024 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 3 clinical trial is underway to evaluate the effect of sildenafil combined with melatonin on oxidative stress markers in women with PCOS receiving metformin. The study includes 128 participants and assesses changes in oxidative stress parameters and related metabolic outcomes. Results are currently pending.
https://irct.behdasht.gov.ir/trial/69845
Despite mechanistic plausibility, sildenafil remains investigational in PCOS. There is no established evidence supporting improvements in ovulation, androgen levels, metabolic control, or pregnancy outcomes. Additionally, sildenafil does not directly address insulin resistance or endocrine dysregulation, which are core features of PCOS. Long-term safety in reproductive-age women with PCOS has not been specifically characterized, and current data are limited to small or ongoing studies.

Name: Sildenafil citrate - PTL/PTB
Developers: Hamedan University of Medical Sciences; Ain Shams University Specialized Hospital; Menoufia University
Indication: Reducing risk of preterm labour/birth
Mechanism of action: Maintaining endothelial function and vasodilation by preventing PDE5 from breaking down cGMP
Key features and challenges:
Sildenafil is an oral treatment developed by Pfizer for men with erectile dysfunction. It is a selective inhibitor of type-V phosphodiesterase, the predominant isoenzyme causing the inactivation of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) in the human corpus cavernosum. 

Sildenafil citrate enhances smooth muscle relaxation by preventing cGMP degradation (the second messenger) by phosphodiesterase enzyme (PDE5) and therefore, has been investigated as a potential therapeutic agent for preterm labour as a single agent and in comparison with other tocolytics.

In 2018, a prospective study was carried on pregnant women with preterm labor pain at Ain Shams University Hospital from March 2018 till September 2018 to assess the efficacy of sildenafil for stopping labor for 48 hrs compared to nifedipine in women with preterm labor. The conclusion from the study was that the  administration of Sildenafil in women with preterm labor pain seems to be a promising future therapy, with limiting the teratogenic influence of the drugs on the fetus (https://academic.oup.com/qjmed/article-abstract/113/Supplement_1/hcaa056.032/5829351?redirectedFrom=fulltext).

An RCT published in 2019 found that vaginal sildenafil citrate, combined with nifedipine is an effective tocolytic therapy to treat preterm labour (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30315625/). However, this study was retracted in 2021 based on concerns over the reliability of the study (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33305896/).

In 2021, the Iranian Hamadan University of Medical Sciences initiated a phase III trial to assess the effect of nifedipine with and without sildenafil citrate on management of preterm labor in pregnant women. This is a triple-blind randomized clinical trial, in which 126 eligible patients will be randomly assigned to the intervention and control groups (https://irct.behdasht.gov.ir/trial/54011)
Recent updates: 2021: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors in Pregnancy: Systematic review and meta-analysis of maternal and perinatal safety and clinical outcomes. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34116036/)

Name: Silymarin
Developers: Liaquat National Hospital & Medical College
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of tuberculosis (adjunctive/host-directed therapy).
Target: Liver cell membranes; Oxidative stress pathways
Mechanism of action: Stabilizes cell membranes, stimulates ribosomal RNA synthesis, and acts as an antioxidant to protect against drug-induced hepatotoxicity
Key features and challenges: A small-molecule hepatoprotective agent that stabilises cell membranes, stimulates ribosomal RNA synthesis and acts as an antioxidant against oxidative stress, intended to protect against drug-induced hepatotoxicity. Taken orally.
Recent updates: A Phase 1 trial (NCT07058090) comparing it with N-acetylcysteine for preventing hepatotoxicity in patients taking anti-tuberculosis drugs is expected to begin in 2025 and is not yet recruiting.

Name: Simeprevir +/- ribavirin
Developers: Jeffrey Cheah School of Medicine and Health Sciences (JCSMHS); Monash University Malaysia
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of CHIKV infection
Mechanism of action:
-Strongest binding of all tested DAAs (ΔG −9.9 kcal/mol, Ki ~0.055 nM).
-Interacts with catalytic residues HIS1083 and CYS1013 in nsP2 protease.
-In vitro: inhibits viral inactivation, attachment, and replication after infection.
-Combination with Ribavirin: synergistic at 7 μM, showing highest inhibition among tested groups.
Key features and challenges:
-IC₅₀ in Vero E6 cells: 8.65 μM (well-tolerated below this dose).
-Stronger antiviral efficacy than VOX or RIBA alone in both attachment and post-infection assays.
-Combination SIM+RIBA at 7 μM significantly suppressed viral replication.
Recent updates:
2025: 
-Demonstrated SIM as the most potent repurposed DAA for CHIKV.
-Combination with RIBA produced synergistic effects, especially in post-infection treatment models.

Name: Simoa SR-X
Developers: Quanterix
Indication: Indicated for triage and screening of individuals with presumptive tuberculosis.
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Key features and challenges: An ultrasensitive immunoassay that detects a M. tuberculosis antigen using a chemiluminescent enzyme immunoassay (ELISA/EIA) principle for single-molecule-level detection. It is run on an instrumented chemiluminescent platform. The assay is performed on venous whole blood.

Name: Simultaneous detection Multiplex qPCR
Developers: Qazvin University of Medical Science
Indication: Detection of Mycoplasma genitalium
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Quantitative PCR simultaneously amplifies multiple pathogen-specific targets to identify Mycoplasma genitalium infection.
Key features and challenges:
A 2022 study developed a multiplex real-time quantitative PCR for simultaneous detection of Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma hominis, Ureaplasma urealyticum, and Mycoplasma genitalium in infertile women. They found that the multiplex qPCR showed the rates of 47%, 16%, 46%, and 16.5% for Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma hominis, Ureaplasma urealyticum, and Mycoplasma genitalium in infertile women, respectively. In some patients, there were co-infections with two or three bacteria. The diagnostic approach used in our research could be employed as an alternative detection tool to identify the four most common STD-associated bacterial agents while detecting mixed infections.
Compared to multiple real-time quantitative PCR, multiplex real-time PCR provides higher sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and rapidity, with lower cost and minimum contamination. Above all, the whole process could be completed within 2 ​hours.
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0255085722000111?via%3Dihub).

Name: Simvastatin
Developers: University of California, San Francisco (UCSF)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Endometriosis.
Mechanism of action: Inhibition of MMP-3.
Key features and challenges:
Simvastatin is a 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl–coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase inhibitor widely used for the management of hypercholesterolemia and cardiovascular risk reduction. Beyond lipid-lowering effects, simvastatin exerts pleiotropic anti-inflammatory, anti-angiogenic, and immunomodulatory actions, which have prompted investigation into its potential role in estrogen-dependent inflammatory disorders such as endometriosis. Endometriotic lesions are characterized by aberrant angiogenesis, chronic inflammation, and altered gene expression profiles, providing a rationale for repurposing statins as disease-modifying agents (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2708947/).
A 2025 preclinical study evaluated simvastatin and primaquine as candidate therapeutics identified through computational drug repositioning based on gene expression reversal scores (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.05.28.656743v1).
Among 299 drugs screened in silico, simvastatin and primaquine ranked highly for reversing endometriosis-associated transcriptional signatures. In a validated rat model of endometriosis and pain, both agents significantly reduced vaginal hyperalgesia, a surrogate measure of endometriosis-associated pain. Bulk RNA sequencing of uterine tissue and ectopic lesions demonstrated reversal of disease-related gene expression patterns following treatment.
These findings suggest that simvastatin may attenuate endometriosis-associated pain and modulate pathogenic molecular pathways, supporting the feasibility of computational drug repositioning approaches for identifying novel therapeutic candidates.
Key challenges include the preclinical status of the evidence and absence of published randomized clinical trials in women with endometriosis. Statins are generally contraindicated in pregnancy due to potential teratogenic risk, necessitating careful consideration in reproductive-age populations. Optimal dosing, treatment duration, and long-term safety in the context of gynecologic disease remain to be established. While simvastatin demonstrates promising mechanistic and behavioral effects in animal models, rigorous clinical evaluation is required to determine translational applicability in endometriosis management.

Name: Simvastatin - PCOS
Developers: Shiraz University of Medical Sciences (SUMS)
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: Inducing vasodilation via NO production
Key features and challenges:
Simvastatin is a statin derived from Aspergillus terreus, commonly prescribed to reduce cholesterol and cardiovascular risk by inhibiting cholesterol production in the liver.

Simvastatin has been shown to decrease disease characteristics with adverse impact on health and quality of life in women affected by PCOS, including hyperlipidemia, hirsutism, hormone levels, and BMI. The evidence base supporting benefit and safety of simvastatin in women with PCOS includes systematic reviews, meta-analyses, clinical trials, and observational studies. (https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/essential-medicines/2021-eml-expert-committee/applications-for-new-indications-for-existing-listed-medicines/i.14_simvastatin.pdf?sfvrsn=4c98a900_4)
A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs investigated metformin’s impact on insulin resistance in women with PCOS. Results showed that metformin significantly lowered fasting blood glucose and fasting insulin levels compared to placebo. Similar benefits were observed when metformin was compared with simvastatin and acarbose, underscoring its utility in managing insulin resistance in PCOS (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/cen.14623)
A 2022 study involving 236 women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), aged 20–40, assessed simvastatin’s effects (20 mg/day for 3 months). The results indicated improvements in several key PCOS features, notably reductions in total cholesterol, testosterone, and LDL-C levels, suggesting potential benefits for lipid and hormone regulation in PCOS. (https://pjmhsonline.com/index.php/pjmhs/article/view/2743)
A 2023 review assessed statin therapy’s efficacy and safety in women with PCOS who were not actively trying to conceive. Due to limited and low-certainty evidence, it remains unclear if statins alone, or combined with metformin, improve menstrual regularity or spontaneous ovulation. Results regarding symptom relief (hirsutism, acne severity, testosterone levels) were also inconclusive. Importantly, adverse events were comparable across groups, with no significant differences reported. (https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD008565.pub3/full)

Name: Simvastatin - Uterine fibroids
Developers: MSD (also known as Merck & Co); Sahlgrenska University Hospital; University of Tokyo (including the Graduate School of Agricultural and Life Sciences)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of uterine fibroids to reduce the size and growth of fibroids.
Mechanism of action: By inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase, simvastatin effectively reduces the synthesis of cholesterol in the liver, leading to lower levels of LDL cholesterol (the "bad" cholesterol) in the blood.
Key features and challenges:
Simvastatin, widely known for its role in lowering cholesterol, has shown potential in the treatment of uterine fibroids due to its anti-proliferative and anti-inflammatory properties. 
Previous in vitro, in vivo, and epidemiologic studies have shown the beneficial effects of simvastatin on uterine leiomyomas by inhibiting cellular proliferation, inducing calcium-dependent apoptosis, reducing extracellular matrix deposition, and restoring the altered state of mechanotransduction signaling. 
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1043661821004400?via%3Dihub#preview-section-introduction)

As a cholesterol-lowering drug, simvastatin is primarily designed for cardiovascular conditions. Its repurposing for uterine fibroids may raise concerns about off-target effects, potential drug interactions, and whether its benefits outweigh the risks in women who do not have hypercholesterolemia. Furthermore, while simvastatin may have promising effects on fibroid cells in vitro, translating these findings into effective treatment in vivo presents a significant hurdle.

A 2024 Phase 2 study is underway to determine feasibility, safety and preliminary clinical efficacy of simvastatin to reduce leiomyoma size. The study will enroll 60 participants in total, half will receive simvastatin and the other half will receive a placebo. The study drug and placebo will be an add on to the participants ongoing medical management of fibroids until surgery. The participants will be monitored at intervals for the effect of the drug on fibroid size and symptoms using ultrasound and quality of life questionnaires.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03400826).

Name: Single Gene Targeted Nanopore Sequencing - Gonorrhea
Developers: Oxford Nanopore Technologies
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoea and antimicrobial susceptibility
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: DNA sequencing
Key features and challenges:
Single gene targeted nanopore sequencing is a portable DNA sequencing–based diagnostic platform designed for simultaneous identification of Neisseria gonorrhoeae and detection of key antimicrobial resistance (AMR) markers. The method targets specific resistance-associated gene regions and enables combined pathogen detection and genotypic AMR profiling within a single sequencing workflow.
A 2021 study demonstrated that single gene targeted nanopore sequencing showed promise for simultaneous diagnosis and AMR marker detection across multiple sexually transmitted infections, including gonorrhea (https://sti.bmj.com/content/97/Suppl_1/A154.1.citation-tools). 
A 2022 study further supported its feasibility for identifying resistance determinants in common genital STIs, highlighting its potential application in resource-limited and laboratory-constrained settings (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0262242). 
The approach offers a streamlined alternative to culture-based susceptibility testing by enabling direct molecular resistance profiling.
Key challenges include improving sequencing accuracy, reducing cost per test, accelerating turnaround time, and ensuring availability of bioinformatics expertise for data interpretation. Standardization of resistance mutation panels and validation in diverse clinical settings remain necessary.
Overall, single gene targeted nanopore sequencing represents a promising integrated diagnostic and AMR detection strategy for N. gonorrhoeae. Further optimization and implementation research are required to support routine clinical deployment.
