Name: Sitaformin (sitagliptin/metformin)
Developers: Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences; Arak university
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Target:
Metformin - hepatic mitochondria
Sitagliptin - dipeptidyl peptidase 4
Mechanism of action: Sitagliptin inhibits dipeptidyl peptidase 4, which slows mediated inactivation of incretins. Reduced inhibition of incretins increases insulin synthesis and decreases glucagon release. Metformin decreases blood glucose levels by decreasing hepatic glucose production, decreasing the intestinal absorption of glucose, and increasing insulin sensitivity by increasing peripheral glucose uptake and utilisation
Key features and challenges:
The combination of sitagliptin and metformin (sitaformin) has been shown to lower HbA1c and increase HOMA-B more effectively than either drug alone, due to their complementary effects. This combination may significantly lower glucose levels with minimal gastrointestinal side effects. Metformin increases GLP-1 levels without affecting dipeptidyl peptidase 4, while sitagliptin boosts both GLP-1 and GIP, resulting in additive effects on these hormones when combined. Additionally, a recent rat study indicated that sitaformin may alleviate PCOS by upregulating lncRNA H19, further supporting its potential to reduce insulin resistance compared to metformin or sitagliptin alone. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/metformin-plus-sitagliptin)
A 2023 study aimed to investigate the effects of sitaformin (sitagliptin/metformin) and metformin on the quality of oocyte and embryo in classic PCOS patients undergoing intracytoplasmic sperm injection. It was reported that sitaformin can be more effective in decreasing immature oocytes and increasing the quality of embryos than the use of metformin. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37040229/)
Another 2023 study assessed the effects of sitagliptin/metformin (sitaformin), metformin, and sitagliptin alone in PCOS patients, focusing on hormone modulation and oxidative stress markers to alleviate symptoms. Participants received treatment two months prior to ovulation through to ovum retrieval. Results showed significant decreases in HOMA-IR and FAI in all treatment groups compared to placebo, while leptin levels dropped most notably in the sitaformin group. AMH and MDA levels also decreased in the sitaformin and sitagliptin groups. Additionally, sitaformin significantly boosted GDF9 and BMP15 levels in cumulus cells, correlating with improved fertilisation rates and higher-quality embryos, indicating its potential benefit over metformin or sitagliptin alone. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37040229/)

Name: Sitagliptin + BeiDouGen
Developers: Peking University Third Hospital
Indication: Treatment of PCOS - Metabolism; Fertility
Mechanism of action:
Sitagliptin selectively inhibits DPP-4, thereby increasing endogenous active GLP-1 and GIP levels. This enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppresses inappropriate glucagon, and improves post-prandial glycaemia without significant hypoglycaemia risk. In women with PCOS, small clinical studies show sitagliptin can improve β-cell function, reduce insulin resistance indices and decrease visceral adipose tissue without major effects on body weight.
BeiDouGen is a branded Chinese capsule used in this trial as a PCOS-specific herbal product. It improves ovarian function and fertility in PCOS, but validated targets are unknown.
In combination, sitagliptin and BeiDouGen are hypothesised to act on insulin resistance, glucose handling, androgen excess and endometrial/ovarian function, aiming to improve ovulation and pregnancy outcomes more than either agent alone.
Key features and challenges:
Sitagliptin is an oral DPP-4 inhibitor approved globally for type 2 diabetes and increasingly studied in PCOS because of its favourable effect on glucose metabolism and visceral fat. A pilot randomized study in obese, metformin-intolerant women with PCOS (n=30) showed that sitagliptin 100 mg daily for 12 weeks improved β-cell function (HOMA-B, modified β-cell function index) and insulin sensitivity indices compared with lifestyle alone. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29144805/).
Another double-blind crossover trial in 18 women with PCOS found that 1-month sitagliptin treatment decreased peak and AUC glucose during OGTT, increased early insulin secretion, and significantly reduced visceral adipose tissue mass and volume, although sex steroids and menstrual symptoms were unchanged over this short exposure. (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7947776/).
Beyond individual trials, a 2022 meta-analysis of six randomized controlled trials (394 women) reported that sitagliptin in PCOS significantly improved HOMA-IR, BMI, total testosterone and HDL-C compared with control therapies, supporting DPP-4 inhibition as a promising metabolic and endocrine intervention in this population. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35962305/).
Preclinical studies in PCOS-like rodent models further suggest that metformin + sitagliptin combinations produce greater improvements in insulin resistance, reproductive hormone disturbances, ovarian morphology and inflammatory/angiogenic markers than either drug alone, indicating potential synergy when DPP-4 inhibition is added to an insulin-sensitizing backbone. (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/15384101.2019.1652036).
Within this context, the BeiDouGen capsule is being evaluated as a complementary Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM)-based intervention. Although its exact herbal composition is not publicly detailed, the NCT06587698 protocol positions BeiDouGen as a PCOS-targeted capsule intended to improve ovarian function and reproductive outcomes. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06587698).
TCM in PCOS models (e.g., other PCOS capsules) have been shown in animal experiments to reduce LH/FSH ratio, testosterone, insulin resistance, chronic inflammation and hypothalamic inflammatory signalling, thereby improving ovarian morphology and endometrial receptivity. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32016479/).
BeiDouGen is likely conceptually similar: a multi-component formula aiming at combined endocrine, metabolic and inflammatory pathways, but direct preclinical or clinical data on this specific product are not yet published in English.
The trial NCT06587698 “Sitagliptin or BeiDouGen Capsule Improve the Pregnancy Outcome in Patients with PCOS” is an open-label, randomized, three-arm study sponsored by Peking University Third Hospital.
By including both monotherapy arms and the combination arm, this study is designed to disentangle whether combining sitagliptin with BeiDouGen yields superior reproductive and hormonal outcomes compared with either intervention alone, thereby generating evidence to guide PCOS treatment strategies and potential integrative approaches. (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06587698).
Despite these attractive features, there are important challenges. First, the combination Sitagliptin + BeiDouGen is entirely investigational; there are no completed human outcome data yet, and no regulatory approvals or guideline recommendations for this regimen in PCOS. Second, NCT06587698 is open-label, single-country and conducted at a single major centre in China, which may limit generalisability and introduces performance/assessment bias. Third, the lack of transparent information on BeiDouGen’s exact composition and pharmacology complicates safety assessment, pharmacovigilance and replication by other groups. Herb–drug interactions, especially with sitagliptin and other concomitant medications, remain uncertain. Finally, while sitagliptin has an emerging evidence base in PCOS, its effect size on reproductive endpoints (ovulation, live birth) is still modest and less well characterised than metabolic outcomes, so the added value of combining it with a TCM capsule for fertility specifically is yet to be demonstrated.
Overall, Sitagliptin + BeiDouGen represents an innovative, fully oral, integrative approach targeting insulin resistance and ovarian function in PCOS, with a large, ongoing randomized trial focused on pregnancy outcomes. Until results are available and BeiDouGen’s composition and safety profile are better described, the combination should be considered a research-phase candidate rather than a near-term clinical option.
Recent updates: Phase III trial commenced in 2024, expected to complete in 2029 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06587698)

Name: Smart vaginal diaphragm
Developers: Department of Obstetrics, Gynecology and Reproductive Sciences, University of California San Francisco
Indication: A "smart" vaginal diaphragm that detects changes in cervical collagen to identify a pre-labour window and wirelessly alerts health providers before preterm labour begins.
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: The design allows for a self-inserted device to fit over the cervix (similar to a cervical cap) and leverages inexpensive, low-power Bluetooth (rather than cellular signal) to send an alert to a mobile device (belonging to either the user or the provider) to warn of the newly detected changes and the increased risk of preterm labor. The device is designed to be used after 20 weeks of gestation.
Key features and challenges:
The smart vaginal diaphragm is a proof-of-concept intravaginal device designed to detect early structural cervical changes associated with preterm labour. The device measures microscopic alterations in cervical tissue density related to collagen remodelling, aiming to identify women at high risk of preterm birth during the asymptomatic phase of early parturition.
In 2013, early clinical feasibility work at the University of California, San Francisco evaluated the concept of a cervical cap–like device capable of assessing cervical biomechanical properties. The design proposed a self-inserted device positioned over the cervix, using low-power Bluetooth connectivity to transmit alerts to a mobile device when significant cervical changes are detected. The device is intended for use after 20 weeks of gestation and may ultimately be worn for extended periods, similar to a pessary.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23893706/)
In 2022, further work explored user and provider perspectives on device acceptability. Participants and clinicians expressed a preference for provider insertion rather than self-insertion. Women with a prior history of preterm birth demonstrated greater support for the device compared with those without such history. Design refinements suggested a pessary-inspired model suitable for extended wear.
(https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9338600/)
Potential challenges include user comfort, hygiene considerations, impact on sexual activity, and the need for provider training. While the concept offers the possibility of early warning during the “silent” phase of cervical remodelling, clinical efficacy in reducing preterm birth has not yet been established.
Overall, the smart vaginal diaphragm represents an investigational, technology-driven approach to early detection of cervical change preceding preterm labour. Further validation studies are required to determine diagnostic performance, user acceptability in broader populations, and clinical impact on pregnancy outcomes.

Name: Somatotaxin
Developers: University of Warwick
Indication: Prevention and treatment of preterm labour
Mechanism of action: Doppler assessment of fetoplacental and cardiac flow resistance to evaluate hemodynamic compromise.
Key features and challenges:
Cytokine-suppressive anti-inflammatory drugs (CSAIDs) represent a more novel class of drugs compared to NSAIDs. In the past 10 years, several different compounds have been studied as potential modulators of intrauterine inflammatory responses. Yet, so far this has been solely in preclinical models. Two main strategies have been deployed in the design of this drug: broad-spectrum and selective cytokine/chemokine inhibition.

Broad-spectrum CSAIDs regulate cytokine signaling by targeting events upstream of cytokine expression. In PTB therapeutics, they specifically target 2 signaling pathways that are crucial in the pathophysiology of inflammation-induced PTB, namely, the NFkB and MAPK pathways. By inhibiting the NFkB complex via blockade of p60 nuclear translocation, sulfasalazine was able to inhibit the expression of several LPS-induced proinflammatory cytokines including TNFα and IL-6 in human fetal membranes ex vivo, albeit while concurrently exhibiting a proapoptotic effect in these tissues. The I-kB kinase (IKKB) inhibitors parthenolide and TPCA-1 were also shown to downregulate NFkB-dependent TNFα and IL-6 expression (along with other cytokines/chemokines) in human choriodecidual cells ex vivo, and without affecting the apoptosis pathway. TPCA-1 treatment ex vivo was also effective in suppressing IL-8 and PGE2 levels caused by in utero administration of LPS or Ureaplasma parvum in sheep. In a similar fashion, the MAPK inhibitors U0126, SB202190, and SP600125 did reduce the LPS-stimulated expression of cytokines, chemokines, and prostaglandins in human placental and membrane explants. This was also the case for the compound SB239063 in human and ovine fetal membranes. Importantly, apart from ameliorating inflammation, there is also evidence of CSAIDs potential in PTB treatment ((https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9545799/))

In a mouse model of systemic inflammation–induced PTB using intraperitoneal administration of LPS, the broad-spectrum chemokine inhibitor somatotaxin achieved a reduction in PTB rates. This was accompanied by a reduced inflammatory response in maternal gestational and nongestational tissues. It also conferred the major benefit of live-born pups with normal weight in the cases were LPS-induced PTB was preventedm (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4196657/)
Recent updates: AAA (2024); Listed in a review of recent advances in preclinical studies introducing novel approaches with therapeutic potential for PTL. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9545799/

Name: SpagoPix (SN132D)
Developers: Spago NanoMedical
Indication: Indicated for the diagnosis of endometriosis
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Magnetic resonance imaging enhancers; Radionuclide imaging enhancers
Key features and challenges:
SN132D is a manganese (Mn) -containing, polymeric nanomaterial developed as an intravenous contrast agent for tumor selective MRI. It was designed for optimal physiological targeting and preferential accumulation in malignant lesions by means of the Enhanced Permeability and Retention (EPR) effect. Unlike the conventional low molecular-weight MRI contrast agents, which enhance healthy tissue as well as diseased and therefore results in a relatively high proportion of false positive findings, SN132D is designed to selectively accumulate in diseased tissue. This could contribute to improved precision in MRI scans, e.g. for suspected cancers.
(https://spagonanomedical.se/portfolio/).
In 2023, the SPAGOPIX-01 trial finished which aimed to assess safety and tolerability as well as initial efficacy of SN132D in breast cancer patients. The trial was conducted at Uppsala university hospital and Sahlgrenska University Hospital in Sweden. Interim clinical data from the first two dosage groups show that SN132D provides imaging with selective contrast in breast tumors, without compromising safety. In addition SN132D show excellent contrast in pancreas and liver, opening for broader use in imaging of these organs.
(ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04080024).
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04080024)
In 2023, a Phase IIa, open-label, non-randomised and non-placebo-controlled study began. The study is designed to evaluate the diagnostic value and safety of a single intravenous dose of SN132D in up to 18 participants with suspected endometriosis. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) will be performed pre- and post-infusion of SN132D. Comparisons will be made to transvaginal ultrasound and conventional MRI in order to consider the diagnostic potential of SN132D in endometriosis.
The study is led by Associate Professor Dr. Ligita Jokubkiene, Senior Consultant at the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology at Skåne University Hospital in Malmö, Sweden. 
(https://adis.springer.com/trials/700356324).

Name: Speckle tracking echocardiography (STE) - PTL
Developers: Máxima Medical Center
Indication: Identification of uterine electrical activity to predict PTL/PTB.
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Fetal heart deformation will be analysed 4-weekly at 16, 20, 24, and 28 weeks gestational age using 2D-STE. NFMS recordings will be made weekly from 22 until 28 weeks of gestational age.
Key features and challenges:
Speckle tracking echocardiography (STE) is an advanced ultrasound-based imaging technique used to quantitatively assess myocardial function. By analysing the motion of naturally occurring acoustic speckles within two-dimensional ultrasound images, STE provides angle-independent evaluation of myocardial deformation. The technique enables calculation of strain, strain rate, myocardial velocities, thickening, shortening, and rotational dynamics, allowing objective assessment of cardiac function.
(2017 – https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28492566/)
(2019 – https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/uog.20233)
In obstetric research, two-dimensional STE (2D-STE) has been investigated alongside electrophysiological monitoring tools such as the Nemo Fetal Monitoring System (NFMS) to assess physiological changes during pregnancy. The rationale is that alterations in maternal or fetal cardiac function may reflect underlying placental or systemic changes associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes, including preterm birth.
A prospective cohort clinical trial enrolled women with singleton pregnancies at 16 weeks’ gestation to establish physiological reference values using NFMS and 2D-STE and to explore potential differences in pregnancies that later develop complications such as hypertensive disorders, fetal growth restriction, or preterm birth. Results have not yet been published.
(https://www.onderzoekmetmensen.nl/en/trial/25988)
Overall, STE represents a quantitative imaging modality that may contribute to understanding cardiovascular adaptations in pregnancy and their association with preterm birth. However, its role in PTL/PTB prediction remains investigational, and clinical validation data specific to preterm risk stratification are currently limited.

Name: SpeeDx InSignia
Developers: SpeeDx
Indication: Detection of gonorrhoea and antimicrobial susceptibility
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Multiplex molecular assay detects Neisseria gonorrhoeae DNA and resistance-associated mutations to guide targeted antimicrobial therapy.
Key features and challenges:
SpeeDx has developed a phenotypic test called InSignia that uses the RNA/DNA ratio of a target gene to assess bacterial viability and antibiotic susceptibility. Designed to detect resistance in gonorrhoea, the test splits a patient sample into two parts, briefly treats one with an antibiotic, then extracts and PCR-amplifies both RNA and DNA. By comparing the RNA-to-DNA ratios between the treated and untreated samples, changes in transcription reveal whether the bacteria are sensitive or resistant to the antibiotic (https://plexpcr.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/SpeeDx-RNA_DNA-Ratio-Method-Shows-Promise-for-Bacterial-Viability-Susceptibility-Testing-_-Genomeweb.pdf)

An observational study is currently underway, looking at how feasible it is to use the InSignia assay to determine the antibiotic susceptibility of NG—from collecting, handling, and transporting samples to lab analysis and data interpretation. Another focus is on how well the assay performs in assessing NG’s susceptibility to commonly used and clinically relevant antibiotics in clinical samples, compared to gold standard methods. The study is still in progress, and results have not yet been published.
(https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06352554)

Name: Sphingosine kinase inhibitor (SKI II) - nanoformulation - vaginal
Developers: St John's University, Queens; Nassau University Medical Center; Montefiore Medical Center/Albert Einstein College of Medicine
Indication: For the prevention and treatment of PTB
Mechanism of action: Sphingosine kinase inhibitor
Key features and challenges:
Sphingosine kinase inhibition has been investigated as a therapeutic strategy for preventing inflammation-induced preterm birth (PTB). Earlier preclinical work demonstrated that pharmacologic inhibition of sphingosine kinase reduced the incidence of PTB in an inflammation-induced mouse model, supporting its potential role in modulating inflammatory pathways associated with preterm labour.
(Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31793846/)
Building on these findings, researchers developed a vaginal nanoformulation of the sphingosine kinase inhibitor SKI II to enhance localized drug delivery and overcome solubility limitations. The compound was incorporated into a self-nanoemulsifying drug delivery system (SNEDDS), composed of oil, co-solvent, surfactant, and drug. SNEDDS platforms are designed to improve the bioavailability and solubility of lipophilic agents and support targeted mucosal delivery.
In subsequent preclinical studies using inflammation-induced Swiss Webster mouse models, physicochemical properties of the nanoparticle system were optimized to maximize uterine delivery while minimizing systemic exposure. Treatment with SKI II–loaded SNEDDS significantly increased the number of pups rescued from lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced PTB compared to control groups receiving blank-loaded SNEDDS or LPS with phosphate-buffered saline. Blank SNEDDS alone demonstrated a non-statistically significant trend toward improved outcomes compared to LPS control.
(Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36297454/)
Overall, vaginal nanoformulation of SKI II represents a targeted preclinical strategy aimed at reducing inflammation-induced PTB through localized sphingosine kinase inhibition. Evidence to date is limited to animal models, and clinical evaluation in humans has not yet been reported.

Name: Spironolactone
Developers: Massachusetts General Hospital
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: Spironolactone binds to and blocks mineralocorticoid receptors in the distal tubule and collecting duct of the kidney
Key features and challenges:
Spironolactone is a mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) antagonist traditionally used for the management of hypertension, heart failure, and hyperaldosteronism. Emerging evidence suggests that hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP), including preeclampsia, may induce heightened vascular smooth muscle cell MR sensitivity that persists into the postpartum period, contributing to long-term risk of chronic hypertension and cardiovascular disease. Additionally, findings from the POP-HT trial have indicated that early postpartum blood pressure control may have sustained effects on future cardiovascular risk and cardiac remodeling.
Building on this evidence, a 2026 multi-site randomized clinical trial (NCT07041281) is evaluating whether short-term pharmacologic MR blockade in the early postpartum period improves long-term cardiovascular outcomes in women with HDP and pre-pregnancy overweight or obesity (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07041281). The study will randomize 204 women delivering at Massachusetts General Hospital, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, and the University of Pittsburgh–Magee Women’s Hospital to receive either low-dose spironolactone, considered compatible with breastfeeding: or placebo in addition to usual care for three months postpartum. Primary outcomes include 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure at nine months postpartum, and secondary outcomes include echocardiographic measures of cardiac remodeling.
Key challenges include the need to confirm safety and tolerability in postpartum and breastfeeding populations, assessment of adherence during the early postpartum period, and determination of long-term cardiovascular benefit beyond short-term blood pressure control. While mechanistically compelling, clinical evidence will be required to establish whether postpartum MR blockade can meaningfully modify long-term cardiovascular risk after preeclampsia.

Name: SuVax/MarVax +/-ZaireVax + CoVaccine HT adjuvant
Developers: Soligenix Inc.; University of Hawaii, Manoa; BIOQUAL; University of Texas Medical Branch, Galveston

Target: EBOV glycoprotein, SUDV glycoprotein, MARV glycoprotein
Mechanism of action: Elicits humoral immune response
Key features and challenges: The vaccines are based on recombinant filovirus glycoproteins (GP) from EBOV, MARV and SUDV produced using the Drosophila S2 platform. The highly purified recombinant subunit vaccines formulated with CoVaccine HT™ adjuvant have not caused any safety concerns (no adverse reactions or clinical chemistry abnormalities) in preclinical testing. Candidate formulations elicit potent immune responses in mice, guinea pigs and non-human primates (NHPs) and consistently produce high antigen-specific IgG titers. The monovalent MARV or SUDV vaccine candidates completely protected cynomolgus macaques from infection with lethal doses of MARV or SUDV. Name: Sub-unit vaccine - Trichomoniasis
Developers: Hormozgan University of Medical Sciences
Indication: Vaccination against T.vaginalis
Mechanism of action: Toll-like receptors 2 and 4 interaction
Key features and challenges:
A protein-based subunit vaccine candidate targeting Trichomonas vaginalis is being developed using three key proteins, AP65, AP33, and α-actinin, which are integral to the parasite's adhesion to host cells and its pathogenicity. By selecting immunogenic regions rich in B-cell and T-cell epitopes from these proteins, the vaccine aims to induce a strong immune response, potentially offering protection against the infection. Computational evaluations suggest that the designed protein has stable interactions with immune receptors TLR2 and TLR4, highlighting its potential as an effective immunogen.
The 2024 study employs a multi-step immunoinformatics approach to develop and validate the vaccine candidate. Using bioinformatics tools, the researchers identified epitope-rich regions from the AP65, AP33, and α-actinin proteins. The candidate's stability and antigenicity were evaluated through computational methods, including molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations. These analyses demonstrated robust interactions with key immune system receptors and stability over time, suggesting the vaccine's potential effectiveness. Additionally, immune simulation studies indicated that the candidate could stimulate both B-cell and T-cell responses, laying the groundwork for future experimental and clinical validations. (https://parasitesandvectors.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s13071-024-06248-y)

Name: Subasumstat
Developers: Chosun University Hospital, Gwangju; Chonnam National University Medical School
Indication: Investigational small-molecule therapy being explored for potential antifibrotic and antiproliferative effects relevant to uterine fibroids (leiomyomas), based on its mechanism of suppressing SUMOylation—an intracellular modification process implicated in aberrant cell proliferation, inflammation, and extracellular-matrix (ECM) accumulation.
Mechanism of action: Subasumstat inhibits SUMO E1, thereby blocking SUMOylation—a post-translational modification essential for cell-cycle progression, inflammatory signaling, and stress-response pathways. Dysregulated SUMOylation has been associated with proliferation of leiomyoma smooth-muscle cells and enhanced extracellular matrix deposition. By inhibiting this pathway, Subasumstat may reduce tumor-cell proliferation, disrupt fibrotic signaling, and modulate immune–stromal interactions relevant to UF pathophysiology.
Key features and challenges:
Subasumstat (TAK-981) is a first-in-class small-molecule inhibitor of SUMOylation, a post-translational modification pathway involved in regulating cellular proliferation, stress responses, inflammation, and transcriptional activity. Originally developed for oncology and immune-modulation indications, Subasumstat inhibits the SUMO-activating enzyme, thereby disrupting SUMO conjugation and altering downstream signaling pathways implicated in tumor growth and immune activation.
SUMOylation has been linked to pathways relevant to uterine fibroid (UF) pathophysiology, including cellular proliferation, extracellular matrix (ECM) accumulation, hypoxia signaling, and inflammatory responses. A 2025 study demonstrated that inhibition of the SUMOylation pathway reduces cellular proliferation and modulates inflammatory and stress-response signaling, providing a biologically plausible antifibrotic and antiproliferative rationale for potential application in UF.
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0006291X25007144?via%3Dihub
Despite this mechanistic rationale, Subasumstat has not been evaluated in uterine fibroid models or clinical trials for UF. Current development remains focused on oncology indications. Reported adverse effects in oncology studies; including immune activation, flu-like symptoms, and hematologic abnormalities, raise concerns regarding tolerability in reproductive-age women. Additionally, Subasumstat is administered intravenously, which may limit practicality for chronic management of benign gynecologic conditions.
Data specific to leiomyoma tissue, female reproductive endocrinology, fertility, pregnancy safety, and long-term hormonal interactions are currently lacking. Comprehensive reproductive toxicology and tissue-specific mechanistic studies would be required before considering translational application.
Subasumstat represents a theoretical repurposing candidate for uterine fibroids based on pathway overlap with fibrotic and proliferative signaling. However, it remains at a hypothesis-generating stage, with substantial preclinical and safety data gaps that must be addressed prior to consideration for reproductive health indications.
Recent updates: New publications in 2024–2025 explored SUMOylation pathway inhibition in proliferative and inflammatory disease models, but Subasumstat itself has not entered UF-specific translational or clinical research.

Developers: Merck & Co; University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (including the Carolina Vaccine Institute); Columbia University (including The Joseph L. Mailman School of Public Health); Dana-Farber Cancer Institute; Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center (including the HIV Vaccine Trials Network (HVTN)); Groupe Francophone des Myelodysplasies
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Uterine fibroids.
Mechanism of action: Inhibits histone deacetylases, which can lead to changes in gene expression related to cell cycle regulation, apoptosis, and differentiation.
Key features and challenges:
Suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid, marketed under the name Vorinostat, is a cyto-differentiating agent that was originated by Columbia University and the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center as a cancer therapeutic. Vorinostat is a histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor that has demonstrated potential for the treatment and prevention of cancer; it has been launched in the US, Canada, Japan, Argentina, Chile and Greece for the treatment of cutaneous T cell lymphoma and clinical development is underway in several countries in acute myeloid leukaemia, myelodysplastic syndromes, glioma, breast cancer, HIV infections, Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, lymphoma, leukaemia, solid tumours and B-cell lymphoma, glioblastoma, gliosarcoma, brain metastases and Hodgkin's indication.
(https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800007497)

A 2022 study evaluated the effect of inhibition of histone deacetylases (HDACs) by suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid (SAHA) treatment of human uterine leiomyoma primary cells in vitro on cell proliferation, cell cycle, extracellular matrix (ECM) formation, and transforming growth factor β3 (TGF-β3) signaling. They found that SAHA treatment inhibits cell proliferation, cell cycle, ECM formation, and TGF-β3 signaling in human uterine leiomyoma cells, suggesting that histone deacetylation may be useful for treatment of uterine fibroids.
(https://www.fertstert.org/article/S0015-0282(21)02135-X/fulltext).

Developers: Virti, Inc.
Indication: Prevention of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: INI-2005, induces robust systemic and mucosal immune response following SL administration
Key features and challenges:
Sublingual (SL) Ng vaccine is a mucosal vaccine strategy designed to induce both systemic and local immune responses against Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Unlike conventional parenteral vaccines, the sublingual approach aims to stimulate mucosal immunity at the site of infection while potentially reducing reliance on cold-chain logistics and injection-based delivery.
A 2024 funded study reported identification of novel N. gonorrhoeae antigens expressed during natural mucosal infection that generate cross-reactive antibody responses (https://reporter.nih.gov/search/Rkoh6eKstUGtGQkzFxTU4w/project-details/10830447). 
The vaccine formulation incorporates a novel TLR4 agonist adjuvant, INI-2005, administered sublingually. INI-2005 demonstrated robust systemic and mucosal immune responses, favorable thermostability properties, and an acceptable safety profile in preclinical studies. The candidate combines three antigens identified through a reverse vaccinology–like approach and is undergoing validation for immunogenicity and protective efficacy.
Key challenges include establishing durable mucosal protection, defining correlates of immunity in humans, and demonstrating efficacy across diverse gonococcal strains. Regulatory evaluation of novel mucosal adjuvants and large-scale manufacturability will also be critical considerations.
Overall, the sublingual Ng vaccine represents a delivery-focused innovation aiming to enhance mucosal immunity and global accessibility. Further preclinical and translational studies are required to determine its clinical development potential.

Name: Suction Tube Uterine Tamponade (STUT) (with Levin tube)
Developers: Walter Sisulu University; University of the Witwatersrand (RHRU) (including Wits RHI); University of Fort Hare (UFH)
Indication: Indicated for the temporary control or reduction of postpartum uterine bleeding when conservative management of uterine bleeding is warranted.
Mechanism of action: A suction tube uterine tamponade (STUT) technique with a Levin stomach tube mimics postpartum physiology by applying low-level intrauterine negative pressure to induce collapse and contraction of the atonic postpartum uterus, constricting blood vessels to achieve haemostasis.
Key features and challenges:
A suction tube uterine tamponade (STUT) technique with a Levin stomach tube or a similar plastic catheter can be used to treat postpartum haemorrhage.  The suction tube is introduced through the cervix into the uterine cavity. The device is held in place until the suction is activated, the uterus collapses, and the tube is thus fixed in place. The recommended vacuum pressure is between 100 and 200 mm Hg. In clinical trials, vacuum pressure at ≥500 mm Hg was associated with the collapse of the suction tube and the inability to adequately generate intrauterine suction. The device should remain in place for 1 hour, and if adequate hemorrhage control occurs, then the suction is disconnected from the vacuum source. If no significant bleeding is observed after 20 minutes, the suction is reconnected to ensure that no blood has accumulated within the uterine cavity, and the device is removed ((https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36058519/). 
Reports indicate that STUT insertion is fast (<1 minute) and effective. Despite the absence of a cervical seal (a component of the Jada System) or an anchoring balloon (a component of the modified Bakri balloon technique), preliminary reports on this simple suction tubing indicate that collapse of the uterine cavity and increased uterine tone are sufficient to keep the device anchored securely in place. An initial feasibility study of STUT placement was conducted in 45 postpartum women after cesarean delivery without hemorrhage. This report described the stability of the tube within the uterus and successful aspiration of intracavitary blood without tube blockage. In addition, the study evaluated suction tube placement in an early cohort (immediately after hysterotomy closure) and a late cohort (after skin closure) and found no difference in the functionality of the STUT between these groups (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31206652/). 
Subsequently, Hofmeyr et al reported a case series of 3 women where STUT was used as a last resort treatment in patients with ongoing hemorrhage who failed primary medical therapy. Rapid and adequate hemorrhage control was achieved in all 3 cases ((https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32043686/)). Finally, a small internal pilot study was performed with 24 women randomized to STUT or traditional uterine balloon tamponade. Data from this study were limited but described comparable outcomes between STUT and IUBT in efficacy, tolerability, and usability (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34605016/).

Name: Suction cannula
Developers: Rajagiri Hospital
Indication: Indicated for the temporary control or reduction of postpartum uterine bleeding when conservative management of uterine bleeding is warranted.
Mechanism of action: Mimics postpartum physiology by applying low-level intrauterine negative pressure to induce collapse and contraction of the atonic postpartum uterus, constricting blood vessels to achieve haemostasis. Additionally, if the suction cannula has multiple holes, the bleeding vessels may get sucked into the holes of the cannula and mechanically close them.
Key features and challenges:
Suction cannulas are surgical instruments traditionally used to clear operative fields or prevent aspiration. In the context of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), suction cannulas have been adapted to function as intrauterine vacuum tamponade devices. By applying controlled negative pressure within the uterine cavity, they promote collapse and contraction of the atonic postpartum uterus, thereby compressing bleeding vessels and facilitating haemostasis.
A 2017 study from India evaluated a specially designed stainless steel or plastic cannula (12 mm diameter, 25 cm length) with multiple distal perforations for use in four women with atonic PPH and blood loss exceeding 1500 mL (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28405125/). The cannula was inserted transvaginally to the uterine fundus and connected to a suction apparatus generating negative pressure of approximately 700 mmHg. The negative pressure evacuated blood and clots and caused the uterine walls to collapse inward, mechanically occluding bleeding arterioles and sinusoids. The authors reported successful haemostasis in these cases.
Further clinical evaluation is ongoing. Two additional trials are registered in India investigating suction cannula–based approaches (CTRI/2022/08/045615: https://www.ctri.nic.in/Clinicaltrials/pmaindet2.php?trialid=77079
; CTRI/2020/11/029357: https://www.ctri.nic.in/Clinicaltrials/pmaindet2.php?trialid=53575). In South Africa, a related soft plastic catheter–based vacuum device is also under investigation (PACTR202003795130815: https://pactr.samrc.ac.za/TrialDisplay.aspx?TrialID=8223).
Key challenges include limited published data beyond small case series, absence of large randomized controlled trials, and variability in device design and suction parameters. Standardization of technique, safety evaluation of high negative pressures, and comparative effectiveness studies versus established balloon or vacuum systems are needed to define its role in PPH management.

Name: Sufentanil
Developers: Maternity and Child Health Hospital, Shenzhen
Indication: Pain relief in PE management
Target: Targeting trophoblast cell function via miRNA-mediated pathway
Mechanism of action: Ultrasound measurement of fetal epicardial fat thickness to assess altered fetal adiposity and cardiometabolic adaptation associated with growth restriction.
Key features and challenges:
Sufentanil(SUF) a potent analgesic commonly used in epidural labor anesthesia, has shown promise beyond pain relief in PE management. Its stable hemodynamic profile and robust analgesic effects make it an attractive candidate for alleviating complications associated with PE. Research has demonstrated that SUF treatment accelerates trophoblast cell progression in a concentration-dependent manner, both in vitro and in vivo. Notably, low concentrations of SUF enhance trophoblast cell proliferation, whereas higher concentrations exhibit cytotoxic effects. This dual action highlights the importance of optimizing SUF dosage in clinical applications for PE.

In conclusion, SUF emerges not only as a powerful analgesic for labor management but also as a potential therapeutic agent in PE by targeting trophoblast cell function via miRNA-mediated pathways. These insights pave the way for innovative approaches in PE treatment, aiming to improve maternal outcomes and fetal health through precise pharmacological interventions. Name: Sulfasalazine - PE/E
Developers: University of Melbourne (including the Australian Venom Research Unit (AVRU) and Bio21 Institute); Norman Beischer Medical Research Foundation
Indication: Prevention of preeclampsia
Target: Unknown primary target involved in transcription of NFκB
Mechanism of action: Reducing sFlt-1 and sEng and upregulating PlGF secretion from human placental tissues
Key features and challenges:
Sulfasalazine is a disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) andiIts activity is generally considered to lie in its metabolic breakdown product, 5-aminosalicylic acid released in the colon. The mode of action of sulfasalazine (SSZ) or its metabolites, 5-aminosalicylic acid (5­ASA) and sulfapyridine (SP), is still under investigation, but may be related to the antiinflammatory and/or immunomodulatory properties. Azulfidine (500mg sulfasalazine tablets) is approved by FDA for treatment of ulcerative colitis.
Preeclampsia is associated with placental oxidative stress, hypoxia and inflammation leading to soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt-1) and soluble endoglin (sEng) secretion and reduced placental growth factor (PlGF). This results in widespread endothelial dysfunction causing hypertension and multisystem organ injury. Preclinical results show that sulfasalazine reduces sFlt-1 and sEng secretion and endothelial dysfunction and upregulates PlGF. 
Sulfasalazine mitigates endothelial dysfunction in several in vitro/ex vivo assays. According to Brownfoot et al (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30824385/), sulfasalazine enhanced endothelial cell migration and proliferation, promoted blood vessel dilation (vessels obtained from women at caesarean section) and angiogenic sprouting from whole blood vessel rings. The effect of sulfasalazine on the secretion of sFlt-1 was not mediated through either the NF-kB or HO-1 pathways. Sulfasalazine has potential to treat or prevent preeclampsia and warrants investigation in clinical trials.
In February 2017, an early phase clinical trial was registered by Norman Beischer Medical Research Foundation (ACTRN12617000226303) to examine pharmacokinetics of sulfasalazine for the treatment of preterm preeclampsia. The status was last updated on 18/04/2018 as "Recruiting".
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30824385/). 

In 2023, a preclinical trial was registered by the Australian National Health and Medical Research Council for the treatment of preeclampsia in a nitric oxide synthase antagonist mouse model (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36623415/).

Combined administration of esomeprazole and sulfasalazine may provide a more effective treatment or prevention for preeclampsia compared to either as single agents (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32758704/)

18/04/2018: Status of clinical trial last updated

Key features and challenges:

The mode of action of sulfasalazine or its metabolites, 5-aminosalicylic acid (5­ASA) and sulphapyridine (SP), is still under investigation, but sulfasalazine likely blocks activation of nuclear factor‐kappa B (NF‐κB), which is one of the earliest signals in the inflammatory response in gestational tissues in vitro. Key features and challenges: Sumaya’s goal is the development of vaccines against both, P. falciparum and P. vivax infections, with an initial focus on P. falciparum. To achieve an activity against liver and blood stages, the Sumaya vaccination approach consists of two components: (i) a vector delivery system, in this case a human Adeno6 viral vector expressing full length MSP-1, to elicit a cellular immune response against liver stages and (ii) a proteinaceous component consisting of full length MSP1 to elicit a humoral immune response against merozoites. Sumaya plans to evaluate SumayaVac in challenge studies (CHMI) to assess the contribution of each component to immunity and efficacy.

Name: Synbiotic
Developers: Synbiotic Health
Indication: Indicated for maintenance of gut health
Mechanism of action: Modulate maternal systemic health to reduce the inflammatory and oxidative drivers of preeclampsia
Key features and challenges:
Synbiotics are combinations of probiotics and prebiotics designed to modulate gut microbiota composition and improve host metabolic and inflammatory responses. Given emerging evidence linking gut dysbiosis and systemic inflammation to the pathophysiology of preeclampsia (PE), synbiotic supplementation has been investigated as a potential adjunctive therapy.
A 2024 randomized, controlled, phase III triple-blinded clinical trial evaluated synbiotic supplementation in 128 pregnant women with mild preeclampsia beyond 24 weeks’ gestation (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12905-024-02922-6). Participants were randomized to receive either one oral synbiotic capsule daily or placebo until delivery. Preeclampsia was stratified as early (<34 weeks) or late (≥34 weeks). After adjustment for confounders, the synbiotic group demonstrated significantly lower systolic blood pressure (adjusted mean difference: -13.54 mmHg, 95% CI: -22.07 to -5.01) and diastolic blood pressure (adjusted mean difference: -10.30 mmHg, 95% CI: -15.90 to -4.70) compared with placebo. The incidence of progression to severe PE (p < 0.001), proteinuria (p = 0.044), and mean serum creatinine levels (p = 0.005) were also significantly reduced in the intervention group. No significant differences were observed for several other maternal or perinatal outcomes.
Key challenges include relatively modest sample size, short intervention duration, and limited data on long-term maternal and neonatal outcomes. Optimal strain composition, dosing, and timing of administration remain unclear. While findings suggest potential benefit in mild preeclampsia, larger multicenter trials are needed to confirm efficacy, clarify mechanisms, and establish clinical guidance for synbiotic use in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.

Name: Synbiotic mixture - oral
Developers: Ziekenhuis Oost-Limburg
Indication: For the prevention of preterm birth
Mechanism of action: Modulates maternal gut and vaginal microbiota to reduce systemic and local inflammation associated with preterm labour.
Key features and challenges:
Infections ascending from the vagina may be an important cause of preterm delivery in certain cases. Some women have an abnormal vaginal microbiome and are therefore at risk for infections and preterm birth. 

Synbiotics are a mixture containing probiotics and prebiotics. Probiotics are living bacteria with potential beneficial effects that can be used safely in pregnancy, while prebiotics are consumed by the bacteria. It is known that probiotics, when used for a long period of time, can maintain a healthy and stable vaginal flora that may protect against infections. Oral synbiotic (food supplement) contain 8 probiotic Lactobacillus strains, the prebiotics inulin, fructooligosaccharides (FOS) and D-mannose.

Among mothers with mild preeclampsia, Iranian researchers initiated a phase III study aimed to compare the effect of synbiotic and placebo on blood pressure and pregnancy duration as primary outcomes, and other pregnancy outcomes including mean duration of pregnancy from diagnosis to delivery at a high-risk pregnancy clinic. Compared to the placebo group, the incidence of severe PE (p < 0.001), proteinuria (p = 0.044), and mean serum creatinine level (p = 0.005) significantly declined in the synbiotic-supplemented group after the intervention. However, our analysis found no significant association for other outcomes. Synbiotics had beneficial effects on some pregnancy outcomes. Further studies with larger samples are needed to verify the advantages of synbiotic supplementation for high-risk pregnancies, particularly with regards to higher doses, and longer intervention periods (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/38297273); 

In a clinical study which started in 2023, pregnant patients with a history of preterm birth will be included in the first trimester of pregnancy to start with synbiotics or placebo. The investigators will examine the effect of synbiotics on the vaginal flora and on the pregnancy duration. The hypothesis is that synbiotics, when started early in the pregnancy, can change the disturbed vaginal flora into a stable micro-environment (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05966649).

In silico immunoinformatics pipeline was employed to identify antigenic peptides and construct a multi-epitope vaccine candidate targeting T. vaginalis. Name: TAS2R modulators
Developers: Amaro Therapeutics
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: G protein-coupled receptor modulators
Key features and challenges:
TAS2R (taste receptor type 2) modulators represent an emerging therapeutic concept in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Although TAS2R receptors were originally identified in the gustatory system, they are now known to be expressed in multiple extraoral tissues, including the gastrointestinal tract, adipose tissue, immune cells, and components of the reproductive system. As G-protein coupled receptors, TAS2Rs are implicated in metabolic regulation, inflammatory signaling, and endocrine pathways. Preclinical evidence suggests that modulation of specific TAS2R subtypes may influence insulin sensitivity, systemic inflammation, and metabolic homeostasis—pathways that are central to PCOS pathophysiology. However, the precise receptor targets, downstream mechanisms, and therapeutic relevance in PCOS remain under investigation.
Amaro Therapeutics is developing TAS2R modulators for immune-metabolic disorders, including obesity, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), diabetes, and PCOS. The proposed mechanism involves tissue-specific and systemic effects through modulation of extraoral TAS2R signaling, potentially addressing both metabolic and inflammatory components of PCOS. Development remains at an early research stage in the United States, and no clinical efficacy data in PCOS have yet been published.
At present, TAS2R modulators are considered exploratory candidates, with substantial translational gaps between mechanistic rationale and clinical application. Further studies are required to define receptor specificity, safety, pharmacokinetics, and therapeutic efficacy in PCOS populations.

Name: TBCM/ Poly6/alum
Developers: Seoul National University (SNU)
Indication: Prevention of TB
Mechanism of action: Elicits humoral and cellular immune response
Key features and challenges: A novel TB subunit vaccine consisting of TB-secreted chorismate mutase (TBCM) (Rv1885c) and a hepatitis B virus (HBV)-derived peptide (Poly6), which elicits Type I interferon responses, both with and without an alum adjuvant. Our results revealed that subcutaneous vaccination with TBCM combined with Poly6 induced stronger antigen-specific humoral and cell-mediated immune responses than TBCM alone or TBCM combined with alum adjuvant. Furthermore, adding the alum adjuvant to TBCM combined with Poly6 significantly enhanced antigen-specific immune responses. Subcutaneous vaccination with TBCM combined with both Poly6 and alum adjuvants effectively protected mice against Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) K strain infection, demonstrating its potential as a TB vaccine. Additionally, this vaccine platform exhibited therapeutic potential by significantly reducing bacterial loads and lung inflammation in mice previously infected with the virulent Mtb K strain (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0264410X25000076?via%3Dihub).

Name: TCR 1672
Developers: Beijing Tide Pharmaceutical; Sino Biopharmaceutical
Indication: Indicated for endometriosis pain management.
Mechanism of action: Purinergic P2X3 receptor antagonists
Key features and challenges:
TCR 1672 is an orally available, second-generation, highly selective P2X3 receptor antagonist being developed by Beijing Tide Pharmaceutical, a subsidiary of Sino Biopharmaceutical. The P2X3 receptor is implicated in sensory neuron hypersensitization through adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-mediated activation and subsequent calcium ion influx. Overactivation of this pathway has been associated with persistent sensory symptoms, including chronic cough and visceral pain. By selectively inhibiting P2X3 receptors, TCR 1672 is designed to reduce neuronal hypersensitivity.
The candidate is primarily being developed for refractory chronic cough. Preclinical studies in cough models demonstrated significant reductions in cough frequency, supporting its continued clinical development in this indication. In addition to respiratory applications, TCR 1672 is being explored for visceral pain conditions, including endometriosis-associated pain, as well as neuropathic and cancer-related pain. Modulation of P2X3-mediated sensory signaling provides a mechanistic rationale for its evaluation in endometriosis, where peripheral and central sensitization contribute to chronic pelvic pain.
As of January 2024, clinical development in endometriosis-associated pain is reported to be underway in a Phase I trial at an undisclosed location (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800077105). 
Publicly available data on study design, patient population, and preliminary efficacy outcomes remain limited.
Key challenges include the early stage of clinical development in endometriosis, absence of published clinical efficacy data in this population, and uncertainty regarding long-term safety and differentiation from other P2X3 antagonists under development. Demonstration of clinically meaningful pain reduction and acceptable tolerability in well-designed trials will be critical to support further advancement.
Overall, TCR 1672 represents a mechanistically novel approach targeting sensory neuron hypersensitivity in endometriosis-associated pain. However, its clinical role remains to be established pending results from ongoing early-phase trials.

Name: TDO Inhibitor - 680C91
Developers: Tocris Bioscience
Indication: Indicated for the reduction of uterine fibroids.
Mechanism of action: By inhibiting TDO, LM10 prevents the conversion of tryptophan into kynurenine, leading to increased levels of tryptophan in the system. This inhibition can affect several downstream effects.
Key features and challenges:
680C91 is an orally active, selective tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase (TDO) inhibitor with a reported Ki of 51 nM. TDO is a key enzyme in the kynurenine pathway responsible for the catabolism of tryptophan into kynurenine. 680C91 has previously been investigated in oncology and neurodegenerative conditions, including cancer immunotherapy and Alzheimer’s disease, due to its ability to modulate immune and metabolic signaling.
The kynurenine pathway has emerging relevance in uterine fibroids (UF), where immune regulation, inflammation, and estrogen-related signaling contribute to fibroid growth and extracellular matrix accumulation. By inhibiting TDO, 680C91 reduces kynurenine production, which may influence downstream immune pathways and estrogen-mediated processes implicated in fibroid proliferation. This mechanism provides a biologically plausible rationale for antifibroid effects through immune–endocrine modulation.
A 2024 preclinical study evaluated 680C91 in a mouse xenograft model of uterine fibroids. The compound was reported to be well tolerated, with no significant changes in body weight or blood chemistry parameters. After two months of treatment, mice receiving 680C91 demonstrated approximately 30% reduction in fibroid xenograft weight compared with controls, suggesting measurable antitumor activity in vivo.
https://www.fertstert.org/article/S0015-0282(23)02073-3/abstract
Despite encouraging preclinical findings, evidence remains limited to animal models. No human clinical trials have evaluated 680C91 for uterine fibroids. Broader inhibition of the kynurenine pathway raises concerns regarding systemic immune modulation and potential unintended effects on tryptophan metabolism, neurobiology, and endocrine function. Specificity, long-term safety, reproductive impact, and optimal dosing remain undefined.
680C91 represents a novel mechanistic candidate targeting immune–metabolic pathways in uterine fibroids. While preclinical data demonstrate antifibroid activity and tolerability in mice, substantial translational research is required before clinical application can be considered.

Name: TIB Molbiol LightMix(®) assays
Developers: Roche Diagnostics; TIB MOLBIOL
Indication: Detection of Mycoplasma genitalium and antimicrobial susceptibility
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Modular assays
Key features and challenges:
TIB Molbiol LightMix® assays (Mycoplasma genitalium) are modular real-time PCR assays designed for detection of Mycoplasma genitalium and associated antimicrobial resistance mutations. The LightMix® portfolio includes pre-designed singleplex or multiplex assays, as well as modular components that allow laboratories to construct customized panels compatible with LightCycler® instruments.
A 2023 study evaluated the LightMix® Modular Mycoplasma Macrolide and LightMix® Modular parC Fluoroquinolone Resistance assays and compared results to a commercial assay (ResistancePlus MG, SpeeDx) and Sanger sequencing for parC mutations (https://academic.oup.com/lambio/article/76/11/ovad124/7330186). 
The assays demonstrated reliable performance for detection of M. genitalium and identification of macrolide and fluoroquinolone resistance–associated mutations. The authors noted that interpretation of fluoroquinolone resistance results should consider the evolving understanding of resistance mechanisms.
Key challenges include incomplete characterization of fluoroquinolone resistance determinants, need for continuous assay updates as new mutations emerge, and dependence on compatible instrumentation. Broader validation across diverse clinical settings may also be required.
Overall, TIB Molbiol LightMix® modular assays provide a flexible molecular platform for detection of M. genitalium and key resistance mutations. Ongoing surveillance and mutation panel refinement are essential to maintain diagnostic relevance.

Name: TITAN mRNA vaccine
Developers: University of Cape Town (UCT) (including South African Tuberculosis Vaccine Initiative and the Lung Institute)
Indication: Investigated for the prevention of Mtb infection or TB disease.
Target: Four antigens targeted by controller-associated T cell receptors, CFP-10, PE13, PPE18, and Wbbl1.
Mechanism of action: CD4 T cell responses.
Key features and challenges:
Recent research that identified peptide targets of T cell receptors (TCRs) with conserved CDR3 motifs predicted to bind the same antigen enriched in individuals who control Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) infection (controllers) as well as advances mRNA vaccine technology have presented an opportunity to develop mRNA-based TB vaccines. The TCR Informed TB AntigeN (TITAN) mRNA vaccine includes four antigens targeted by controller-associated TCRs, CFP-10, PE13, PPE18, and Wbbl1.

A study aimed to characterise antigen-specific T cell responses to controller-associated TITAN antigens in healthy adults and individuals with TB disease.  Whole blood was collected from 25 QuantiFERON-TB Gold 
negative (QFT-) adults, 30 QFT+ adults, and 25 adults with microbiologically-confirmed TB disease, stimulated with 15-mer peptide pools spanning CFP-10, PE13, PPE18, or WbbL1. Cells were stained with an optimized antibody panel and frequencies of cytokine-expressing antigen-specific T cells measured by flow cytometry.  All QFT+ and active TB participants had CD4 T cell responses to at least one of the 4 TITAN antigens.  There was a higher abundance of cytokine expressing CD4+ cells after stimulation with all antigens in individuals with TB compared to QFT- controls.  CD4 T cell frequencies among QFT+ individuals were also significantly higher compared to QFT- controls following stimulation with all antigens 
except PE13. There were also CD8 T cell responses to PE13, PPE18, and WBBL1 in individuals with TB. Taken together, these results indicate that populations of T cells specific for the antigens intended for inclusion in the TITAN mRNA vaccine are more abundant in individuals with evidence of Mtb infection or TB disease compared to QFT- participants (https://tbvaccinesforum.org/wp-content/uploads/7GF_PA-21_Looney_Abstract.pdf).

Name: TLD-in-DcNP
Developers: University of Washington
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of HIV
Mechanism of action:
Dolutegravir (DTG) – Integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI)
Lamivudine (3TC) – Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitor (NRTI)
Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate (TDF) – Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitor (NRTI)
Key features and challenges:
TLD-in-DcNP is an investigational long-acting injectable formulation that combines three antiretroviral drugs—tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), lamivudine (3TC), and dolutegravir (DTG)—using drug-combination nanoparticle (DcNP) technology. This approach aims to transform the standard daily oral regimen into a single subcutaneous injection with extended drug release, potentially improving adherence and treatment outcomes for individuals living with HIV. Nanoparticle Formulation: The DcNP technology stabilizes the combination of TDF, 3TC, and DTG, despite their differing physical and chemical properties, into a single injectable nanoparticle suspension. 
Extended Drug Release: Preclinical studies in non-human primates have demonstrated that a single subcutaneous injection of TLD-in-DcNP maintains plasma concentrations of all three drugs above their effective concentrations for up to four weeks. 
Potential for Self-Administration: Unlike some long-acting injectable HIV treatments that require intramuscular administration by healthcare professionals, the subcutaneous route of TLD-in-DcNP may allow for self-administration, increasing convenience for patient. In summary, TLD-in-DcNP represents a novel approach to HIV treatment by leveraging nanoparticle technology to create a long-acting, all-in-one injectable regimen. If successful, this formulation could simplify treatment protocols and enhance adherence, particularly in settings where daily oral dosing presents challenges.

Name: TMCP2/GLA-SE
Developers: Infectious Disease Research Institute (IDRI); University of Massachusetts Medical School (including MassBiologics)
Indication: Prevention of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Immunostimulant
Key features and challenges:
TMCP2/GLA-SE is an experimental peptide-based vaccine candidate designed to mimic a conserved oligosaccharide epitope of gonococcal lipooligosaccharide (LOS). TMCP2 is formulated with the glucopyranosyl lipid adjuvant in stable emulsion (GLA-SE) to enhance immunogenicity and promote bactericidal antibody responses against Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
A 2022 publication arising from research funded in 2019 demonstrated that TMCP2/GLA-SE elicited bactericidal immunoglobulin G and accelerated clearance of gonococci in a murine vaginal colonization model (https://academic.oup.com/jid/article/225/10/1861/6491069
; https://reporter.nih.gov/search/kFIDLOciEkm8bJjGYWjIOQ/project-details/9625276). 
Vaccine efficacy was dependent on an intact terminal complement pathway, as protection was lost in C9−/− mice or when C7 function was blocked, indicating that membrane attack complex formation is critical for protection. Serum bactericidal activity was proposed as a potential correlate of protection.
Key challenges include defining correlates of protection in humans, ensuring broad strain coverage given gonococcal antigenic variability, and translating murine efficacy to durable human mucosal immunity. Regulatory development of peptide vaccines with novel adjuvants will require extensive safety and immunogenicity evaluation.
Overall, TMCP2/GLA-SE represents a complement-dependent peptide vaccine strategy targeting gonococcal LOS. Further translational studies are required to determine its potential for clinical development.

Name: TNX-801
Developers: Tonix Pharmaceuticals Holding Corp.
Indication: Prevention of orthopoxvirus infections (Mpox and Smallpox).
Target: Broad orthopoxvirus antigen presentation—inducing immunity to MPXV, Variola, and Vaccinia cross-reactive epitopes.
Mechanism of action:
TNX-801 is a recombinant chimeric horsepox virus, constructed from chemically synthesized DNA fragments.
It elicits robust humoral and cellular immune responses following a single immunization, producing neutralizing antibodies and T-cell activation that cross-protects against lethal Mpox and Smallpox virus challenges.
Attenuation occurs through reduced genome packaging efficiency (~10–100× less than VACV), limiting viral replication while maintaining immunogenicity.
Key features and challenges:
-Engineered from horse-derived orthopoxvirus genome (MNR-76); genome ~20 kb larger than VACV.
-Demonstrated >10–1,000-fold attenuation relative to traditional VACV-based vaccines (e.g., VACV-Lis, VACV-NYCBH).
-Single-dose efficacy in macaques against lethal MPXV challenge.
-Significantly safer in immunocompromised mice (Ifnar⁻/⁻, Ifngr⁻/⁻, Ifnar⁻/⁻Ifngr⁻/⁻) – no morbidity or mortality observed.
-Induces potent and durable immune response via dermal scarification route.
-Genome packaging/egress stage identified as main attenuation mechanism.
Challenges:
-Requires detailed characterization of long-term immunity and large-scale manufacturing.
-Regulatory concerns remain for replication-competent constructs despite attenuation.
Recent updates:
-Earlier efficacy data (Noyce et al., Viruses, 2023) show complete protection of macaques from lethal MPXV challenge after single TNX-801 dose.
-TNX-801 is being developed as a dual mpox–smallpox vaccine under Tonix’s biodefense portfolio, alongside TNX-1800 (COVID-19 recombinant version).
-Tonix announced preparation for IND-enabling studies (FDA pre-IND guidance anticipated 2025).
-Additional publications confirm cross-neutralization against SARS-CoV-2 when engineered as TNX-1800 variant (Awasthi et al., Vaccines, 2023).
-TNX-801’s natural attenuation and strong immunogenicity make it a promising next-generation alternative to MVA-BN and ACAM2000.

Name: TPHD-LAMP assay
Developers: London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (LSHTM) (including MEIRU)
Indication: to diagnose yaws
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: polA gene (DNA polymerase I) of Treponema pallidum and 16S ribosomal RNA (16S rRNA) gene of Haemophilus ducreyi
Mechanism of action: Molecular diagnostic tool that  uses isothermal amplification to detect Treponema pallidum
Key features and challenges:
A combined Treponema pallidum (TP) and HD loop mediated isothermal amplification test (TPHD-LAMP)7 8 has been developed for simultaneous detection of these two primary causes of yaws-like lesions. This test is user-friendly and does not require costly thermocyclers. Therefore, it is suitable for use in local hospital laboratories close to the patient, to test for yaws and HD. The TPHD-LAMP test has been previously evaluated in a laboratory setting8 using swab samples collected during yaws studies in Papua New Guinea and Ghana with promising results: sensitivities of 84.7% (95% CI 72.5% to 92.4%) for TP and 91.6% (95% CI 85.8% to 95.3%) for HD were reported. The respective specificities were 95.7% (95% CI 92.0% to 97.8%) and 84.7% (95% CI 77.4% to 90.1%). The sensitivities for both targets were reduced in mixed infection samples: 68.4% (95% CI 43.5% to 86.4%) for TP and 73.7% (95% CI 48.6% to 89.9%) for HD.  The TPHD-LAMP test can also potentially be adapted to include TP macrolide resistance detection, a feature which is hugely important in light of the recent detection of macrolide-resistant TPE strains, which emerged after MDA campaigns in Papua New Guinea.

Key features and challenges:
TTX 334E (formerly TTX 334) is a monoclonal antibody originally developed by Temple Therapeutics for the treatment of ovarian cancer. Its proposed mechanism of action involves inhibition of myeloperoxidase (MPO), a pro-inflammatory enzyme released by activated neutrophils and implicated in oxidative stress pathways. MPO activity has been associated with inflammatory tissue damage and has been proposed as a mediator linking oxidative stress and estrogen signaling pathways.
Endometriosis is an estrogen-dependent inflammatory disorder characterized by ectopic endometrial growth, chronic inflammation, and oxidative stress. Estradiol, the biologically active estrogen, promotes lesion growth, inflammatory signaling, and pain. Experimental data suggest that inhibition of MPO may induce apoptosis of endometriotic cells, potentially through modulation of the estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) pathway. Targeting MPO may therefore disrupt inflammatory and estrogen-mediated pathological mechanisms central to endometriosis progression.
TTX 334E entered Phase I development for chemotherapy-resistant ovarian cancer as of May 2018. As of January 2023, the candidate is reported to be in preclinical development for endometriosis (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800052114).
Key challenges include the early stage of development for endometriosis, with no published preclinical efficacy data specific to this indication and no human clinical trials to date. The translational relevance of MPO inhibition in endometriotic lesions requires further validation. Safety, dosing, route of administration, and potential effects on immune function and reproductive physiology remain undefined in this context. While mechanistic rationale exists linking MPO inhibition to modulation of oxidative and estrogen-dependent pathways, substantial preclinical and clinical investigation is required to determine feasibility and therapeutic value in endometriosis.

Name: TV Molecular RPA assay
Developers: Xinxiang Medical University
Indication: Detection of T. vaginalis
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: PCR
Key features and challenges:
TV Molecular RPA assay is a recombinant polymerase amplification (RPA)–based molecular diagnostic developed for rapid detection of Trichomonas vaginalis. The assay targets the actin gene and operates under isothermal conditions, enabling amplification without the need for conventional PCR instrumentation.
A 2023 study reported development and optimization of the RPA assay, identifying the actin gene as a suitable target and establishing optimal amplification conditions at 39°C for 30 minutes (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36632692/). 
When evaluated using 53 vaginal secretion samples, the RPA assay demonstrated higher sensitivity than wet mount microscopy and excellent specificity. Compared with nested PCR and culture methods, the assay offered faster turnaround time and did not require thermocycling equipment, supporting potential application as a point-of-care diagnostic tool.
Key challenges include validation in larger and more diverse clinical populations, assessment of performance in low-parasite-load samples, and integration into routine clinical workflows. Cost-effectiveness and scalability for decentralized settings require further evaluation.
Overall, the TV Molecular RPA assay represents a rapid, instrument-minimal molecular diagnostic approach for trichomoniasis. Further clinical validation is needed to confirm its suitability for point-of-care implementation.

Developers: Dilafor AB (including Dilaforette)
Indication: Treatment and prevention of preeclampsia

Key features and challenges:
Tafoxiparin (DF 01) is a proprietary polysaccharide and heparan sulphate mimetic under development for the treatment and prevention of dystocia (prolonged labour), labour arrest, and preeclampsia. Unlike low-molecular-weight heparins (LMWH), tafoxiparin lacks anticoagulant activity.
Clinical observations have suggested that pregnant women receiving LMWH for thrombosis prophylaxis experienced reduced incidence of prolonged labour compared with controls. However, LMWH use at delivery is limited by bleeding risk due to its anticoagulant properties.
Tafoxiparin has demonstrated similar effects to LMWH and unfractionated heparin on isolated uterine strips and cervical cells, without exhibiting anticoagulant activity. Its proposed dual mechanism of action includes promotion of myometrial contractility and enhancement of cervical softening, which may support labour progression while reducing hemorrhagic risk.
Clinical development of intravenous (IV) and subcutaneous (SC) formulations is underway in Sweden, Italy, and Finland.
(Source: https://adisinsight.springer.com/trials/700342100)
Overall, tafoxiparin is being investigated as a non-anticoagulant heparan sulphate mimetic with potential applications in labour management and preeclampsia. Clinical efficacy and safety outcomes remain under evaluation.
