Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator used to treat estrogen receptor positive breast cancer, reduce the risk of invasive breast cancer following surgery, or reduce the risk of breast cancer in high risk women. 
Recent work has investigated the role of Tamoxifen in treating PCOS-related infertility.

In a 2023 published study, Tamoxifen was analyzed for its pharmacokinetics, drug-likeness, bioactivity, and toxicity profile, aiming to contribute to the development of safer and more effective ovulation-inducing medications for PCOS-related infertility. Tamoxifen showed favorable pharmacokinetics and bioactivity but was identified as hepatotoxic, highlighting the need for safer alternatives in future treatments. (https://ijpsr.com/bft-article/computational-analysis-of-pharmacokinetics-bioactivity-and-toxicity-profiling-of-some-selected-ovulation-induction-agents-treating-polycystic-ovary-syndrome-pcos/?view=fulltext)

Several studies have compared the effectiveness of Tamoxifen to Clomiphene citrate.
A 2021 prospective study compared their effectiveness for ovulation induction in women with PCOS and found that both drugs were equally effective in induction of ovulation and achieving a pregnancy in women with PCOS.
(https://publish.kne-publishing.com/index.php/JRI/article/view/7653). 
A 2022 study suggests that tamoxifen (TMX) and clomiphene citrate (CC) both induce autophagy in ovaries with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), highlighting autophagy as a potential target for developing more effective treatments for PCOS-related anovulation. (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11033-021-06981-y#Fun)

Additionally, a 2023 registered phase 2, double-blind, randomized clinical trial will compare the therapeutic effects of letrozole, tamoxifen, estradiol, and vitamin E diet versus letrozole, tamoxifen, and estradiol diet in stimulating ovulation in infertile women with PCOS, assessing pregnancy outcomes, follicle size, number, thickness, multiple births, and drug side effects. (https://irct.behdasht.gov.ir/trial/71936)

Name: Tanshinone-I
Developers: IFTM University
Indication: Indicated for anti-inflammatory and antioxidant treatment of uterine fibroids.
Mechanism of action: Tanshinone I may affect cellular pathways related to fibroid cell proliferation, such as those involving growth factors and signaling molecules. By inhibiting excessive cell growth, Tanshinone I could help control fibroid size and symptoms.
Key features and challenges:
Tanshinone I, an active compound from *Salvia miltiorrhiza* (Danshen), offers possibilities for the treatment of uterine fibroids. This compound is known for its anti-inflammatory effects, which can help manage the inflammation often associated with fibroids. By reducing inflammatory mediators, Tanshinone I may alleviate some of the discomfort and symptoms caused by fibroid growth. Additionally, Tanshinone I exhibits strong antioxidant properties, which help protect cells from oxidative stress—a factor believed to contribute to fibroid development and growth. By neutralizing free radicals, it may prevent further damage to the uterine tissue and potentially slow down fibroid progression. Hormonal regulation is another area where Tanshinone I shows promise. Its impact on hormonal pathways could help manage the hormonal imbalances that contribute to fibroid growth. Furthermore, preliminary research suggests that Tanshinone I might induce apoptosis (programmed cell death) in fibroid cells, which could lead to a reduction in tumor size and growth.
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S094471132200719X)
Despite these promising benefits, there are several challenges to consider. One significant hurdle is Tanshinone I's low oral bioavailability, meaning that only a small amount of the compound is effectively absorbed and utilized by the body when taken as a supplement. Improving delivery systems is essential to enhance its therapeutic efficacy.

A 2023 study looks at Tanshinone-I for the treatment of uterine fibroids with molecular docking, simulation, and density functional theory investigations. 28 plant-based molecules were identified from previous literature and docked onto the prog receptors with 1E3K and 2OVH. They report that Tanshinone-I demonstrated the highest level of activity for both of the proteins. Tanshinone-I was also demonstrated through MD simulation research to form stable interactions with the receptors.
(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1319016423001202?via%3Dihub#ab010).

Name: Taraxasterol
Developers: Jiangxi Maternal and Child Health Centre
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Endometriosis.
Mechanism of action: Inhibits the proliferation and migration of ectopic endometrial cells through the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway, while promoting apoptosis.
Key features and challenges:
Taraxasterol is a bioactive pentacyclic triterpenoid compound derived from Taraxacum officinale (dandelion), a traditional Chinese medicinal herb that has been used in compound formulations for inflammatory and gynecological disorders, including endometriosis. Dandelion has been considered attractive due to its reported efficacy and relatively low side-effect profile. Taraxasterol is regarded as one of its principal active components.
A 2025 study investigated the molecular mechanisms of taraxasterol in the treatment of endometriosis using an integrated network pharmacology and experimental validation approach (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0006291X24016152?via%3Dihub). 
Initially, 148 potential drug-related targets were identified through predictive databases, alongside 1,180 disease-associated targets for endometriosis. Seventy-one overlapping targets were identified and analyzed using the STRING database to construct a protein–protein interaction (PPI) network, which was visualized with Cytoscape 3.7. Ten key hub targets were selected and preliminarily validated via molecular docking analysis.
Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses were subsequently conducted, identifying the top enriched biological processes and signaling pathways associated with the overlapping targets. Among these, the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway emerged as a central pathway potentially mediating therapeutic effects.
In vitro validation was performed using ectopic endometrial cells. Western blotting, colony formation assays, scratch assays, and CCK-8 assays demonstrated that taraxasterol inhibited cell proliferation and migration while promoting apoptosis. Mechanistically, these effects were associated with modulation of the PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling pathway.
Overall, the study suggests that taraxasterol may exert anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic effects on ectopic endometrial cells through inhibition of PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling. However, the evidence is currently limited to computational modeling and in vitro experiments. Further in vivo studies and clinical investigations are required to determine pharmacodynamics, bioavailability, dosing parameters, safety, and translational relevance before considering taraxasterol as a therapeutic candidate for endometriosis.

Name: Teicoplanin
Developers: Korea University College of Pharmacy; College of Veterinary Medicine and Bio-Safety Research Institute, Iksan, Jeonbuk; Dongkook Pharmaceutical Co, Ltd.
Indication: Potential therapeutic for ZIKV infection
Target: ZIKV Envelope (E) protein fusion loop (predicted binding pocket); host cathepsin L protease

Key features and challenges:
-Already FDA-approved for Gram-positive bacterial infections (e.g., MRSA).
-In vitro, inhibited ZIKV production in Vero cells by up to 90% when added during entry stages.
-Broad-spectrum antiviral activity against influenza, coronaviruses, RSV, measles, DENV2, and EV71.
-High EC₅₀ for ZIKV (192.5 μM) relative to cytotoxicity (CC₅₀ ~7.3 mM), yielding selectivity index ~37.9.
-Risks: antibiotic resistance, pharmacokinetic variability, limited in vivo efficacy data for antivirals.
-Potential use as a scaffold to develop non-antibacterial derivatives with stronger antiviral potency.
Glycopeptide antibiotic with antiviral activity via cathepsin inhibition and viral envelope protein binding
Recent updates:
Dec 2024 Publication (Preprint): First study showing direct ZIKV inhibition by teicoplanin, with activity during both binding and endocytosis stages.
-In silico docking suggested TP binds the E protein fusion loop (Asp99, Gly103), stabilizing the prefusion dimer.
-Prior derivatives (teicoplanin aglycone analogues) also reported antiviral effects against flaviviruses (De Burghgraeve 2012).
-Authors propose TP pharmacophores as basis for next-generation broad-spectrum antivirals, separating antibacterial and antiviral effects.

Name: Telapristone acetate - Uterine Fibroids
Developers: Repros Therapeutics
Indication: Indicated for uterine firboids pain and menstrual bleeding
Mechanism of action: Selective progesterone receptor antagonists
Key features and challenges:
Telapristone acetate is a second-generation selective progesterone receptor antagonist originally developed by the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD) in the United States and subsequently out-licensed to Repros Therapeutics (formerly Zonagen). It has been investigated as a treatment for uterine leiomyoma, endometriosis, and early-stage breast cancer.
Telapristone suppresses progesterone-mediated proliferative activity and promotes pro-apoptotic pathways, supporting its activity against progesterone-sensitive tumours such as uterine leiomyomas.
(Source: https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800014404)
Conventional treatment for uterine fibroids often involves gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists; however, these agents are typically limited to treatment durations of approximately six months due to the risk of bone mineral density loss. As a result, they are frequently used as short-term pre-surgical interventions. Telapristone has been investigated as a potential alternative, with the expectation that it may not induce bone loss, thereby allowing for longer-term medical management and potentially reducing the need for surgical intervention.
(Source: https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800014404)
Phase II clinical development has been conducted in the United States for uterine leiomyoma, endometriosis, and breast cancer. Repros Therapeutics also initiated development of a vaginal formulation (Proellex-V), which entered Phase II clinical evaluation for uterine leiomyoma. A Phase III study in patients with anaemia was placed on hold.
(Source: https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800014404

Tellurium-based AS101 is a synthetic, non-toxic tellurium derivative structurally related to cisplatin, under investigation for antimicrobial activity against Neisseria gonorrhoeae. A 2023 preclinical study evaluated the in vitro anti-gonococcal activity of AS101, including its effects on bacterial growth, biofilm formation, and infectivity (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36877078/). Key challenges include the need for in vivo validation, characterization of pharmacokinetics and safety in the context of STI treatment, and assessment of resistance development potential. Repurposing for gonorrhea will require clinical efficacy studies and regulatory pathway clarification.
Overall, AS101 represents a repurposing candidate with demonstrated in vitro anti-gonococcal and anti-infectivity activity. Further preclinical and clinical investigation is required to define its therapeutic potential in gonorrhea management.

A phase II study is being planned by the HIV Prevention Trials Network (HPTN 106), with the latest projected date for starting enrollment being July 2024. 
Results of DREAM-01 were published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in November 2023. The trial was a phase I, open label, dose-escalation, and variable osmolarity study to compare the safety, PK, PD, and acceptability of three formulations of a TFV enema. All three produced tissue concentrations above target levels and were well tolerated with no grade 2 or greater adverse events reported. 
Results from another phase I trial, DREAM-03, were presented as a poster at CROI 2022. The investigators reported that a TFV douche prior to receptive anal sex produced good drug coverage of the colorectal tract. Based on their results, the authors recommend administration prior to receptive anal sex in future studies. 
DREAM-02, a third phase I study assessing the TFV enema used in sequence with tap water enemas, has been completed with results pending. 
A phase I study of the safety, PK, PD, and acceptability of a one-dose TFV douche in adolescents aged 15–24 (ATN DREAM) has been completed. Limited preliminary results are posted in the clinicaltrials.gov registry entry and suggest that the product was safe, but to our knowledge the findings have not yet been presented or published (https://www.treatmentactiongroup.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/pipeline_PrEP_2024_final.pdf).
Recent updates: Phase II trial (HPTN 016) commenced in 2024 (NCT06560684).

Name: Terbutaline - PTL/PTB
Developers: Columbia Laboratories, Inc.; Catalent, Inc. (including Swindon UK facilities, Juniper Pharmaceuticals, Inc.); Ardana PLC
Indication: Delaying preterm labour/birth
Mechanism of action: Reducing myeometrial contraction via adrenergic beta-2 receptor agonsim
Key features and challenges:
Terbutaline is a selective β2-adrenergic receptor agonist originally developed as a bronchodilator for asthma management. It acts through sympathomimetic stimulation of β2 receptors, resulting in relaxation of smooth muscle, including the myometrium. Due to its uterine relaxant properties, terbutaline has been used off-label as a tocolytic to delay preterm labour, typically for short-term use (up to 48 hours).
Terbutaline received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval in 1974. It was subsequently used off-label for prevention and treatment of preterm labour. In 2011, the FDA issued a boxed warning and contraindication against prolonged intravenous use in pregnant women for prevention or treatment of preterm labour due to risks of serious maternal cardiovascular complications, including arrhythmias and death. Oral terbutaline was also discouraged due to lack of demonstrated efficacy and similar safety concerns.
The European Medicines Agency (EMA) has similarly restricted the use of short-acting β2-agonists for preterm labour because of safety concerns, although limited short-term intravenous use remains permitted under specific conditions.
(Source: https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/human/referrals/short-acting-beta-agonists)
Despite regulatory warnings, terbutaline continues to be used in some clinical settings and is often included in national and international guidelines for short-term management of preterm labour or fetal distress. It is also frequently used as a comparator in clinical trials evaluating newer tocolytic agents.
In 2023, a preclinical study evaluated the combined uterus-relaxant effects of terbutaline and magnesium sulfate (MgSO₄) in isolated organ bath experiments and in vivo smooth muscle electromyographic studies in pregnant rats. Both agents reduced uterine contractions in vitro and in vivo. Low-dose MgSO₄ enhanced the relaxant effect of terbutaline, particularly at lower doses. Additionally, MgSO₄ attenuated the tachycardia-inducing effect of terbutaline in late-pregnant rats.
(Source: https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1111/aogs.14532)
Overall, terbutaline demonstrates established short-term tocolytic effects but carries significant maternal cardiovascular safety concerns, leading to regulatory restrictions. Its role in PTL/PTB management is primarily limited to short-term use under careful monitoring, and it is increasingly being evaluated in comparison with or in combination with alternative agents.
Recent updates: 2011: FDA issued a Black Boxed Warning and Contraindication to the terbutaline injection label  against the use of intravenous terbutaline for pregnant women for treatment or prevention of preterm labour because of the potential for serious maternal heart problems and death. (https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/fda-drug-safety-communication-new-warnings-against-use-terbutaline-treat-preterm-labor)

Developers: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID); National Institutes of Health; Swedish Science Council; Swedish Cancer Fund

Name: Thrombin generation assay
Developers: Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development
Indication: Prediction of preeclampsia in the first trimester
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Measures plasma thrombin generation kinetics to detect hypercoagulability associated with endothelial dysfunction in preeclampsia.
Key features and challenges:
Activation of the coagulation system and increased thrombin generation have been implicated in the pathophysiology of preeclampsia, and this rationale supports the administration of low-molecular-weight heparin to prevent this syndrome in patients at risk. Yet, randomized trials of this prophylactic measure have yielded contradictory results. A possible explanation is that only a subset of patients with preeclampsia have excessive thrombin generation and would benefit from the administration of low-molecular-weight heparin. Therefore, the key questions are whether and when patients who subsequently develop preeclampsia present evidence of abnormal thrombin generation.

A study by the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development published in 2022 aimed to determine the kinetics of thrombin generation throughout gestation in women with a normal pregnancy and in those with early and late preeclampsia, and the diagnostic performance of in vivo thrombin generation parameters to predict the development of preeclampsia.
This retrospective, nested case–control study was based on a prospective longitudinal cohort of singleton gestations. Cases comprised women who developed preeclampsia (n=49), and controls consisted of patients with a normal pregnancy (n=45). Preeclampsia was classified into early-onset (n=24) and late-onset (n=25). Longitudinal changes in the parameters of the thrombin generation assay (lag time, time to peak thrombin concentration, peak thrombin concentration, endogenous thrombin generation, and velocity index) throughout gestation were compared between the study groups, and normal pregnancy percentiles were derived from the control group. They tested whether a single parameter or a combination of parameters, derived from the kinetics of thrombin generation, could identify patients who subsequently developed preeclampsia. Time-related parameters <10th percentile were considered short, and concentration-related parameters >90th percentile were considered high.
Patients who developed preeclampsia (early- and late-onset) had abnormal thrombin generation kinetics as early as 8 to 16 weeks of pregnancy; (2) patients with a combination of a short lag time and high peak thrombin concentration at 8 to 16 weeks of pregnancy had an odds ratio of 43.87 for the subsequent development of preeclampsia (area under the curve, 0.79; sensitivity, 56.8%; specificity, 92.7%; positive likelihood ratio, 7.76); (3) at 16 to 22 weeks of gestation, patients with a combination of a short lag time and a high velocity index had an odds ratio of 16 for the subsequent development of preeclampsia (area under the curve, 0.78; sensitivity, 62.2%; specificity, 92.5%; positive likelihood ratio, 8.2.
During early pregnancy, the thrombin generation assay can identify the subset of patients at a greater risk for the development of preeclampsia owing to accelerated and enhanced production of thrombin. This observation provides a rationale for testing the efficacy of low-molecular-weight heparin in this subset of patients. 
(https://www.ajog.org/article/S0002-9378(22)02164-0/abstract)

Name: Thymol
Developers: South China Agricultural University
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Endometriosis.
Mechanism of action: Estrogen antagonist and progesterone agonist.
Key features and challenges:
Thymol is a phenol obtained from thyme oil or other volatile oils. It is used as a stabilizer in pharmaceutic preparations. It has been used for its antiseptic, antibacterial, and antifungal actions, and was formerly used as a vermifuge (https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB02513).
The efficacy of thymol in treating endometriosis remains unexplored. A such, a 2024 study aimed to investigate the role of thymol in the treatment of endometriosis using a murine model and Ishikawa cells. Thirty C57BL/6 mice were administered 17β-E2 (100 ng/mouse) subcutaneously for three consecutive days to induce synchronous estrus. On the last day of injection, the mice underwent surgical induction of endometriosis. Next, the mice were divided into three groups, i.e., Control (CTRL), Thymol 30 mg/kg and Thymol 60 mg/kg, receiving oral administration of either saline or thymol (30 mg/kg/d or 60 mg/kg/d, as 0.1 mL/kg/d, respectively) for a three-week duration. Each group consisted of ten mice and was evenly divided into estrus and diestrus according to the vaginal cytology on the last day of treatment. Thymol significantly (p < 0.05) reduced the weight and volume of ectopic tissue, hindered cell proliferation, and stimulated apoptosis compared to the CTRL group. Additionally, in the thymol-treated group, the levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, tumour necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), interleukin (IL)-1β, and IL-6, as well as the numbers of neutrophils and macrophages, were significantly (p < 0.05) decreased. Moreover, a novel role of thymol in rebalancing estrogen and progesterone (E2-P4) signalling was explored, and it was distributed in the ectopic endometrium. Next, the role of thymol on Ishikawa cells was determined. The results demonstrated that thymol significantly (p < 0.05) suppressed the E2-induced proliferation of Ishikawa cells. Furthermore, molecular docking analyses suggested that thymol potentially binds to ESR1-like estrogens, indicating its antagonistic activity against estrogens. The estrogen receptor 1 (ESR1) and its target gene expression exhibited significant (p < 0.05) downregulation, while progesterone receptor (PGR) and target genes were markedly (p < 0.05) upregulated following thymol treatment in the ectopic endometrium. Most importantly, data revealed the minimal impact of thymol treatment on the eutopic endometrium and its crucial role in supporting pregnancy, thus indicating the safety of thymol in treating endometriosis. Overall, this study suggests that thymol holds promising therapeutic implications for endometriosis by virtue of its anti-inflammatory properties and ability to antagonize estrogen activity (https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/25/23/13150).

Name: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
Developers: Pusan National University School of Medicine; University of Barcelona, Universitat de Barcelona; Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine
Indication: Thyroid function assessment in PCOS to assess metabolic, hormonal, and reproductive health
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Measures serum TSH to detect thyroid dysfunction that may mimic or exacerbate PCOS-related menstrual irregularities.
Key features and challenges:
Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) is produced by the pituitary gland and stimulates the thyroid to release thyroid hormones (T3 and T4), which regulate metabolism and energy. Recent research has explored the relationship between TSH levels and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), suggesting a potential link between elevated TSH levels and various aspects of PCOS, such as thyroid function, hyperandrogenism, and oocyte maturation. However, further studies are needed to better understand these findings.

A 2021 study found that 26.7% of PCOS patients had elevated TSH levels, indicating hypothyroidism, compared to 5% in the control group. Additionally, 42.3% of PCOS patients exhibited a hypoechoic thyroid ultrasound pattern, suggesting mild thyroid damage. (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10585146)

A 2022 study showed that PCOS patients with normal thyroid function had significantly higher average TSH levels compared to non-PCOS individuals, suggesting a potential impact of TSH on oocyte maturation in PCOS patients. (https://rbej.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12958-022-01005)

A 2022 study indicated that elevated TSH levels are present in adolescents with PCOS, highlighting the need for further studies to understand the implications of these findings. (https://karger.com/hrp/article/96/5/458/835980/Raised-Thyroid-Stimulating-Hormone-in-Girls-with)

A 2021 study found that after adjusting for age and BMI, PCOS patients had higher TSH levels compared to the control group, suggesting a potential association between TSH levels and PCOS. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35315007/)

Name: Tildacerfont
Developers: Spruce Biosciences
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: Corticotropin releasing factor receptor 1 antagonists
Key features and challenges:
Tildacerfont is an orally administered small-molecule corticotropin-releasing factor type 1 (CRF1) receptor antagonist developed by Spruce Biosciences. It was initially designed for congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH), an endocrine disorder characterized by excessive adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) stimulation and adrenal androgen overproduction. By blocking CRF1 receptors, tildacerfont reduces ACTH secretion and downstream production of adrenal steroids, including androstenedione and 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP). This mechanism directly targets adrenal-driven hyperandrogenism.
https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800050153
Given that a subset of women with PCOS exhibit elevated adrenal androgens, CRF1 antagonism represents a mechanistically targeted strategy for this phenotype. In contrast to peripheral anti-androgens that block androgen receptors, tildacerfont aims to reduce androgen production at its adrenal source.
In March 2022, Spruce Biosciences initiated the Phase II P.O.W.E.R. trial, a randomized, placebo-controlled, dose-escalation study evaluating tildacerfont in adults with PCOS characterized by high adrenal androgen levels. The trial enrolled 27 participants in the United States, achieved full enrollment by May 2023, and released interim data in August 2023, followed by updated results in June 2024. The U.S. FDA had previously cleared the Investigational New Drug (IND) application in August 2021, allowing progression to Phase II development.
While tildacerfont offers a biologically precise approach to adrenal hyperandrogenism, its development in PCOS remains early-stage. Data are currently limited to small Phase II studies, and long-term outcomes related to ovulation, fertility, metabolic parameters, and cardiovascular risk remain to be established. Moreover, PCOS is a heterogeneous disorder, and not all patients exhibit significant adrenal androgen excess, potentially limiting its applicability to a defined subgroup. Safety, tolerability, and comparative efficacy versus established anti-androgen therapies also require further clarification.
Tildacerfont represents a novel, upstream endocrine-targeted candidate for adrenal-driven PCOS phenotypes. Its future role will depend on larger randomized trials demonstrating sustained androgen suppression, clinical symptom improvement, and favorable safety in reproductive-age women.

Name: Tinidazole
Developers: University of Washington
Indication: Treatment of Mycoplasma genitalium
Mechanism of action: Nitroimidazole antimicrobial causing DNA damage under anaerobic conditions to inhibit microbial survival.
Key features and challenges: A phase II trial that began in 2025 and is expected to finish in August 2026 is evaluating how effective tinidazole is for treating Mycoplasma genitalium (MG) in male patients diagnosed with non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU) at the Public Health – Seattle & King County (PHSKC) Sexual Health Clinic. Tinidazole, approved by the FDA in May 2004 for other infections like trichomoniasis, giardiasis, amebiasis, and bacterial vaginosis, has not yet been systematically tested against M. genitalium. The proposed dosing is not expected to significantly increase risks, and the study meets the criteria for an IND exemption (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07088419).
Recent updates: Phase II trial commenced in 2025 with expected completion in August 2026 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07088419)

Name: Tinidazole - Endometriosis
Developers: Mission Pharmacal
Indication: Indicated to treat endometritis to improve fertility outcomes
Mechanism of action: DNA synthesis inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Tinidazole is a nitroimidazole antimicrobial agent indicated for the treatment of trichomoniasis, giardiasis, amebiasis, and bacterial vaginosis (https://adisinsight.springer.com/drugs/800024976).
 It exerts its effect by causing DNA strand breakage in susceptible anaerobic organisms and protozoa. While not developed specifically for endometriosis, interest in tinidazole has emerged in the context of chronic endometritis (CE), a condition characterized by persistent endometrial inflammation that may coexist with endometriosis and contribute to infertility.
In 2023, a prospective cohort study evaluated whether oral antibiotic therapy for chronic endometritis improves reproductive outcomes in women undergoing Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) (https://www.ijifm.com/doi/pdf/10.5005/jp-journals-10016-1324). 
Women diagnosed with CE were treated initially with doxycycline (100 mg twice daily for 14 days), followed by a combination regimen of ciprofloxacin (500 mg twice daily) and tinidazole (600 mg twice daily) for 14 days. The study reported that evaluation and treatment of CE in infertile women undergoing ART was associated with improved reproductive outcomes.
Although tinidazole was administered as part of combination antibiotic therapy rather than as a direct endometriosis treatment, the findings suggest that management of underlying inflammatory or infectious endometrial conditions may indirectly improve fertility outcomes in women with coexisting gynecological disorders. However, there is currently no direct evidence supporting tinidazole as a targeted therapy for endometriosis lesions or endometriosis-associated pain. Further research would be required to clarify whether antimicrobial treatment has a disease-modifying effect in endometriosis beyond the management of concurrent chronic endometriosis.

Name: Tofacitinib / meglumine antimoniate
Developers: University Hospital Professor Edgard Santos, Hospital Universitário Professor Edgard Santos (HUPES)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of cutaneous Leishmaniasis
Mechanism of action: Janus kinase 1 inhibitors; Janus kinase 2 inhibitors; Janus kinase 3 inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Tofacitinib is an orally active small molecule, immunosuppressant and janus activated kinase (JAKs) 1, 2 and 3 inhibitor developed by Pfizer, for the treatment of immunological disorders, including rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, ulcerative colitis, diffuse scleroderma, ankylosing spondylitis, cutaneous sarcoidosis and granuloma annulare, COVID-19 pneumonia and dermatomycosis. Tofacitinib modulates the signaling pathway at the point of JAKs, preventing the phosphorylation and activation of Signal Transducers and Activators of Transcriptio (STATs). JAK enzymes transmit cytokine signaling through pairing of JAKs, to influence cellular processes of hematopoiesis and immune cell function. Within the signaling pathway, JAKs phosphorylate and activate STATs modulating intracellular activity including gene expression.

Investigated in combination with meglumine antimoniate in Brazil. Not yet recruiting as of Feb 2025 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06011343)
Recent updates: Phase II/III trial commenced in 2023 (NCT06011343).

Name: Topiramate
Developers: Erasmus Medical Center
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of HIV-1 infection.
Mechanism of action: Modulates ion channel conductance and enhances GABAergic activity to manage neurologic or behavioral co-morbidities within HIV cohorts
Key features and challenges: A small-molecule agent that modulates voltage-gated sodium channel conductance and enhances GABAergic activity at GABA-A receptors, investigated for managing neurologic or behavioural co-morbidities. Taken orally. It has also been investigated for neurological co-morbidities in HIV.
Recent updates: A Phase 1/2 trial (NCT07384624) evaluating it as part of a latency-reversing combination to target the HIV reservoir is expected to begin in 2026 and is not yet recruiting.

Name: Topiramate + Lenalidomide

Name: Traditional /Modified Gegen Qinlian
Developers: The Second Affiliated Hospital of Guangzhou University of Chinese Medicine
Indication: Treatment of PCOS - Menstrual cycle regulation; Metabolism; Hyperandrogenism
Target:
Multi-pathway effects including:
-AMPK activation (metabolic regulation)
-PI3K–Akt pathway modulation (insulin sensitivity)
-Anti-inflammatory cytokine reduction (TNF-α, IL-6)
-Modulation of ovarian steroidogenesis (in animal models)
-Improvement of gut microbiota associated with metabolic PCOS
Mechanism of action: Gegen Qinlian’s active components; puerarin, baicalin, berberine and glycyrrhizin work synergistically to reduce inflammation, improve glucose and lipid metabolism and modulate insulin signalling. Experimental PCOS models show the formula improves insulin resistance, lowers fasting glucose, decreases LH/FSH ratio, reduces testosterone and improves ovarian morphology. Modified versions add specific reproductive herbs (e.g., peony root, Chinese angelica) to support menstrual regulation and ovulation.
Key features and challenges:
Gegen Qinlian Decoction is a classical traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) formula historically used for gastrointestinal and inflammatory conditions. It has increasingly been studied in metabolic disorders, including polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Key bioactive constituents—such as baicalin, berberine, and puerarin—demonstrate insulin-sensitising, anti-inflammatory, and AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)-activating properties, targeting two core mechanisms implicated in PCOS: chronic low-grade inflammation and insulin resistance.

Preclinical studies in rodent PCOS models (2023) reported that Gegen Qinlian or modified derivatives reduced fasting insulin levels, improved HOMA-IR, decreased testosterone concentrations, normalized the LH/FSH ratio, and restored estrous cyclicity, suggesting combined endocrine and metabolic benefits.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36647837/

Clinical studies in related metabolic conditions, including type 2 diabetes and insulin-resistance syndromes, have consistently shown that Gegen Qinlian formulations improve glycaemic control, reduce inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α), lower C-reactive protein, and modulate gut microbiota associated with metabolic homeostasis. Although PCOS-specific trials remain limited, several TCM-based combination studies incorporating Gegen Qinlian have reported improvements in menstrual regularity, acne, hirsutism, and central obesity, suggesting indirect reproductive benefits mediated through systemic metabolic improvements.

An ongoing clinical study registered with the International Traditional Medicine Clinical Trial Registry (ITMCTR; Project ID: 2749494274758155590) is evaluating a Modified Gegen Qinlian prescription in women with PCOS. The trial assesses metabolic endpoints (fasting glucose, insulin, HOMA-IR), reproductive hormones (total testosterone, SHBG, LH, FSH), ovarian morphology on ultrasound, and menstrual cycle regulation. This reflects a multi-target TCM approach aimed at simultaneously addressing metabolic and reproductive dysfunction in PCOS.
https://itmctr.ccebtcm.org.cn/mgt/project/view/2749494274758155590

Despite promising biochemical and preclinical findings, several challenges remain. Modified TCM formulations lack standardized composition across studies, limiting reproducibility and pharmacovigilance. Mechanistic pathways are often inferred from experimental models rather than confirmed in well-designed clinical trials. High-quality, placebo-controlled Phase III/IV trials in PCOS populations are scarce, and potential herbal–drug interactions remain insufficiently characterized. Regulatory status is generally restricted to traditional medicine categories, and the formulation remains investigational for PCOS under contemporary clinical standards.
Recent updates: Phase I trial commenced in 2023 and is expected to be complete in 2026 (https://itmctr.ccebtcm.org.cn/mgt/project/view/2749494274758155590)

Name: Traditional Chinese medicinal compounds
Developers: Universiti Sains Malaysia; Qatar University; Jalan Universiti
Indication: Indicated for the prophylactic prevention and treatment of infection with Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) caused by Ebola virus
Mechanism of action: Predicted binding of TCM small molecules to EBOV proteins, potentially interfering with functions like viral replication (VP35), transcription (VP30), virion assembly (VP40), and immune evasion (VP24). Actual activity remains theoretical pending biochemical or cellular validation.
Key features and challenges:
-Multi-target potential: Compounds predicted to bind multiple viral proteins.
-Human usage history: Many compounds have traditional usage and known safety profiles, offering repurposing appeal.
Computational prioritization: In silico derived hits support focused experimental follow-up.
Recent updates: 2025: Computational screen identified eight TCM compounds with strong in silico binding and favorable ADMET predictions for EBOV targets.

Name: Tranilast
Developers: Kissei Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd.
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of uterine fibroids to inhibit fibrosis.
Mechanism of action: TGF-β is a key regulator of fibrosis and extracellular matrix production, both of which are crucial in the development and growth of uterine fibroids. By inhibiting TGF-β, tranilast reduces fibrosis and the associated growth of fibroid tissue.
Key features and challenges:
Tranilast, originally developed as an anti-allergic and anti-inflammatory medication, is now being repurposed for the treatment of uterine fibroids. This drug offers promising features, primarily due to its antifibrotic and anti-inflammatory properties. Tranilast works by targeting the TGF-β pathway, a crucial driver of fibrosis that contributes to the growth of uterine fibroids. By inhibiting this pathway, tranilast can potentially reduce the size of fibroids and alleviate symptoms such as heavy menstrual bleeding and pelvic pain. Additionally, its effects on mast cells and inflammatory cytokines further support its potential benefits.

However, the use of tranilast for uterine fibroids is not without challenges. One of the key concerns is its efficacy compared to other existing treatments, such as GnRH agonists or selective progesterone receptor modulators. While tranilast is generally well-tolerated, it may cause side effects like gastrointestinal issues or liver enzyme elevation, which could limit its use in some patients. The long-term safety of tranilast when used specifically for uterine fibroids remains uncertain, as fibroid treatment often requires prolonged management. 

Moreover, there is currently limited clinical data supporting the use of tranilast for this new indication, which may hinder its acceptance within the medical community. The drug's availability and affordability can also be problematic, depending on geographic and healthcare system differences. Finally, even though tranilast is an established drug, obtaining regulatory approval for its new use in treating uterine fibroids could be a complex and time-consuming process.

In 2023, a preclinical study looked at the efficacy of tranilast for treatment of human-derived fibroids in a mouse model. They found that there was a significant inhibition of mRNA and protein expression of fibronectin, COL3A1, CCND1, E2F1, and TGF-β3 in the xenografts from the tranilast-treated mice. These promising therapeutic effects of tranilast warrant additional animal studies and human clinical trials to evaluate its efficacy for treatment of fibroids.
(https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/24/13/10465).

A 2024 review discusses the key mediators involved in fibrosis and reviews the role of tranilast as a potential drug targeting critical fibrotic mediators in a range of fibrotic conditions. These include scleroderma, keloid and hypertrophic scars, liver fibrosis, renal fibrosis, cardiac fibrosis, pulmonary fibrosis, and uterine fibroids. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1567576924009445#:~:text=Tranilast%20shows%20antifibrotic%20effects%20in,TGF%2D%20%CE%B2%2C%20and%20MAPK.).

Name: Transdermal Typhoid conjugate vaccine - Vaxxas
Developers: SK Bioscience; Vaxxas
Indication: Indicated for the prevention of typhoid fever.
Mechanism of action: Immunostimulant.
Key features and challenges:
A second-generation, typhoid conjugate vaccine is being developed by Vaxxas in collaboration with SK bioscience for the prevention of typhoid fever. The candidate is reformulated from the antigen utilized by SK bioscience's SKYTyphoid™ vaccine [See AdisInsight Drug profile 800048060] and ‘printed’ onto thousands of tiny microprojections covering the Vaxxas patch to be delivered directly to the abundant immune cells just under the skin surface. The typhoid vaccine is delivered by Vaxxas’ proprietary high-density needle-free microarray patch (HD-MAP) platform technology. Developers: Vellore Institute of Technology (VIT University)

Target: Triple mutant DNA gyrase subunit A enzyme.
Mechanism of action: Triple mutant DNA gyrase subunit A enzyme inhibitor.
Key features and challenges:
Abstract
The rising resistance to fluoroquinolones in Salmonella Typhimurium poses a significant global health challenge. This computational research addresses the pressing need for new therapeutic drugs by utilizing various computational tools to identify potential natural compounds that can inhibit the triple mutant DNA gyrase subunit A enzyme, which is crucial in fluoroquinolone resistance. Initially, the three-dimensional structure of the wild-type DNA gyrase A protein was modelled using homology modelling, and followed by in silico mutagenesis to create the clinically relevant triple mutant (SER83PHE, ASP87GLY, ALA119SER) DNA gyrase A protein structure. The structural stability and integrity of the modelled protein were ensured through rigorous validation. Subsequently, a high-throughput virtual screening of a curated library of natural compounds was conducted to identify potential inhibitors against wild-type and triple-mutant proteins. The selected potent lead molecules comprehensively evaluated their physicochemical properties, ADME/T properties, and binding affinities via ADME/T assessment and molecular docking studies. The safest and most promising ligands were chosen for dynamics studies to analyze their dynamic behaviour and protein stability before and after the binding of ligands. Our results showed that the natural compounds from the ChemDiv database, CID: 0407–0108, N039-0003, 1080–0568, and 0099–0261 have binding energies ranging from −4.32 to −5.69 kcal/mol and exhibit excellent physio-chemical properties, affinities, and are stable in their dynamic environments over 100 ns for both wild-type and triple mutant DNA gyrase A complexes. These compounds provide a promising alternative treatment for fluoroquinolone-resistant Salmonella Typhimurium infections (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405580824002656?via%3Dihub).

Name: Tripraline

Mechanism of action: Tripraline is a short-acting GnRH agonist, it suppresses the secretion of gonadotropins (FSH and LH), leading to ovarian downregulation.
Key features and challenges:
Tripraline is a short-acting gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist used in assisted reproductive technologies (ART), including in vitro fertilization (IVF) and intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI). By initially stimulating and subsequently downregulating pituitary GnRH receptors, tripraline suppresses follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) secretion, achieving controlled ovarian suppression. This mechanism allows synchronization of follicular development and prevention of premature LH surges during controlled ovarian stimulation, which is particularly relevant for women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) who are at elevated risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS).
A 2022 study compared two IVF/ICSI stimulation protocols in women with PCOS: an early-follicular long-acting GnRH agonist (EFLL) protocol and a midluteal short-acting GnRH agonist (MLSL) protocol. In the MLSL protocol, tripraline was administered at 0.1 mg daily for 14–16 days starting in the midluteal phase to achieve ovarian downregulation prior to gonadotropin stimulation and hCG trigger. While the EFLL protocol demonstrated higher clinical pregnancy and live birth rates, it was associated with a higher incidence of gestational diabetes. The MLSL protocol using tripraline provided effective downregulation and cycle control, representing a viable alternative within ART strategies for PCOS patients.
Although tripraline is widely used within IVF protocols, its role is supportive within stimulation regimens rather than disease-modifying for PCOS itself. Outcomes are influenced by patient-specific factors such as age, body mass index (BMI), and endometrial thickness, and careful protocol selection is required to balance pregnancy outcomes against metabolic and obstetric risks.

Name: TyG index
Developers: The First People's Hospital of Chenzhou; Fudan University
Indication: Indicated for the prediction of Preeclampsia
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: The mechanism of action is based on the formula: Ln [fasting triglycerides (mg/dL) × fasting plasma glucose (mg/dL) / 2].
Key features and challenges:
The triglyceride–glucose (TyG) index is a surrogate marker of insulin resistance calculated from fasting triglyceride and glucose levels. Given the established association between metabolic dysfunction and preeclampsia (PE), the TyG index has been investigated as a potential early screening marker for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
A large retrospective cohort study conducted between January 2019 and June 2024 across three tertiary hospitals included 41,694 singleton pregnancies, of which 2,308 developed PE and 39,386 served as healthy controls. The TyG index was measured before 20 weeks’ gestation and categorized into quartiles. After adjustment for confounders, higher TyG quartiles were significantly associated with increased risk of PE (Q3: OR 1.23, 95% CI 1.06–1.43; Q4: OR 1.31, 95% CI 1.11–1.53). A modest association was observed between the highest TyG quartile and preterm birth (Q4: OR 1.18, 95% CI 1.01–1.37), although this association was attenuated after multivariable adjustment. A negative association with low birth weight (LBW) was reported for Q3 (OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.74–0.97). Subgroup analyses indicated that maternal age, pre-pregnancy body mass index, parity, and timing of TyG testing did not significantly modify these associations (interaction P > 0.05).
Receiver operating characteristic analysis demonstrated modest predictive performance for PE, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.596 (95% CI 0.584–0.608), sensitivity of 65.4%, and specificity of 49.6%. These findings suggest that while the TyG index is statistically associated with increased risk of preeclampsia, its standalone predictive accuracy is limited.
(https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12944-025-02556-z).
Key challenges include modest discriminatory performance, potential confounding by underlying metabolic risk factors, and uncertainty regarding added predictive value beyond established clinical and biochemical screening tools. Further prospective validation and integration into multivariable prediction models would be necessary to determine its clinical utility in early pregnancy risk stratification for preeclampsia.

Name: Ultrasound: Ovarian morphology (Automated AI diagnostic model)
Developers: Cornell University
Indication:
Diagnosis of PCOS
A deep-learning model designed to automatically detect ultrasonographic features of polycystic ovarian morphology
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: Ultrasound-derived ovarian morphology features including follicle number per ovary (FNPO), ovarian volume, and stromal echogenicity, the core morphological PCOS markers recognised by international diagnostic guidelines.
Mechanism of action: The candidate uses deep-learning algorithms (likely convolutional neural networks) trained on two- and three-dimensional transvaginal ultrasound images to identify diagnostic features of polycystic ovarian morphology (PCOM) such as excessive antral follicles, increased ovarian volume, and stromal abnormalities. The system aggregates image outputs with selected clinical and biochemical parameters to classify PCOS status. It aims to standardise and automate interpretation, reduce operator dependency, resolve inter-rater variability, and improve diagnostic accuracy across clinical settings.
Key features and challenges:
Ultrasound assessment of ovarian morphology is one of the core diagnostic components of PCOS, particularly in adults using the 2018 International Evidence-Based PCOS Guideline, which highlights follicle number per ovary (FNPO) and ovarian volume as the most reliable imaging markers for polycystic ovarian morphology.
(International PCOS Guideline: https://www.monash.edu/medicine/sphpm/mchri/pcos)
However, despite widespread adoption of transvaginal ultrasonography, interpretation of PCOM remains highly operator-dependent. Studies consistently document moderate to poor inter-rater reliability, especially in follicle counting and assessment of stromal echogenicity, leading to diagnostic inconsistency and delays in PCOS identification (https://www.cdc.gov/pcos/)
The candidate “Ultrasound: Ovarian morphology” proposes a deep-learning, AI-driven diagnostic model capable of automatically characterising key ultrasonographic features of PCOM. This includes follicle excess, ovarian enlargement, and stromal aberrations, using both 2D and 3D ovarian ultrasound volumes. The approach draws on a large, well-curated archive of ovarian ultrasound datasets from well-characterized populations across the reproductive lifespan, enabling robust model training and external validation. The model aims to harmonise ultrasound interpretation, reduce subjectivity, and support earlier PCOS detection by integrating imaging data with clinical and biochemical markers.
(NIH RePORT Project Source: https://reporter.nih.gov/)
Interest in automated ultrasound interpretation has been growing, supported by recent advances in medical imaging AI. For example, similar approaches in obstetrics have shown that deep-learning segmentation improves accuracy and reduces variability in ovarian and uterine measurements. E.g. (https://www.rsna.org/news/2023/may/ai-in-radiology)
Key challenges remain. First, ultrasound equipment varies significantly in image quality, resolution, and probe technology, meaning generalisability must be rigorously tested across devices and clinical sites. Second, FNPO thresholds adopted in recent international standards were based on high-frequency transvaginal probes (≥8 MHz), and AI models must account for these differences to avoid misclassification. Third, large-scale, prospective clinical validation and real-world testing are needed before integration into routine diagnostic pathways. Finally, regulatory frameworks for AI diagnostics are evolving, and approval can be complex, particularly for adaptive learning systems.
(https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/software-medical-device-samd/artificial-intelligence-software-medical-device)
Overall, this candidate represents a promising approach to standardising PCOS imaging diagnostics. Its potential lies in overcoming longstanding limitations of human-based ultrasonographic interpretation, accelerating diagnosis, and harmonising assessments globally. Evidence generation, transparency of model architecture, and device-agnostic validation will be essential for future adoption.
Recent updates:
Current ongoing project aims to develop and externally validate a deep-learning ovarian ultrasound classifier and integrate it with clinical + biochemical measures for PCOS detection.
Leveraging large, annotated ultrasound archives for model training and validation (NIH-funded initiative).
Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-75964-3

Name: Ultrasound: Ovarian stiffness/elasticity
Developers: Adnan Menderes University School of Medicine; Adana City Research and Training Hospital; Erciyes University; University of Health Sciences, Istanbul, Turkey
Indication: PCOS diagnosis
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Detection of tissue stiffness using shear-wave elastography
Key features and challenges:
Shear Wave Elastography (SWE) is a non-invasive ultrasound technique (either transvaginal or abdominal) that measures tissue stiffness or elasticity by analysing the speed of shear waves. Stiffer tissues transmit waves faster, while softer tissues slow them down, providing quantitative data to aid in diagnosis. SWE has been explored in PCOS for assessing ovarian stiffness and changes in ovarian volume and stroma. Additionally, studies have shown that lower SWE values are associated with higher serum testosterone levels. This makes SWE a potential tool to predict and monitor androgenic alterations in PCOS patients.
A 2021 study comparing ovarian tissue elasticity in women with and without PCOS found significantly higher shear wave velocity (2.12 m/sec) in PCOS patients compared to controls (1.18 m/sec). This suggests that PCOS leads to increased ovarian stiffness. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34970437/)
Another study published in 2021 evaluated the use of shear wave elastography to assess tissue stiffness changes in the ovaries of 33 women with polycystic ovary syndrome. SWE measurements and metabolic and androgenic parameters were collected during the early follicular phase. Results showed that lower SWE values were significantly associated with higher serum testosterone levels (AUC = 0.755, p = 0.041), indicating its predictive potential for androgenic alterations. However, no significant correlation was found between SWE values and metabolic parameters. The study suggests that SWE could be a useful, non-invasive tool for monitoring testosterone levels in PCOS patients. 
(https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jog.14835)
A 2022 study included 45 women with PCOS and 30 healthy controls, examining serum biomarkers (such as AMH, testosterone, and insulin resistance) and ovarian stiffness using pSWE. The results showed significantly higher ovarian stiffness and volumes in the PCOS group, with ovarian stiffness correlating strongly with AMH levels. Linear regression analysis revealed AMH as the main factor linked to increased ovarian stiffness. The study suggests that pSWE may serve as an adjunctive tool in monitoring PCOS, although further studies are needed to validate these findings with larger patient samples and transvaginal US.
(https://journals.lww.com/ultrasound-quarterly/abstract/2022/03000/ovarian_stiffness_is_significantly_increased_in.14.aspx)
A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of eight studies found that women with PCOS had stiffer ovarian tissue than healthy controls. Shear wave elastography (SWE) and strain elastography (SE) both showed significantly higher ovarian stiffness in PCOS patients, suggesting that ultrasound elastography could be a valuable diagnostic tool for PCOS. (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/09513590.2024.2352139#abstract)

Name: Umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells
Developers: ProSTEM (PT Prodia StemCell Indonesia); Foundation for Regenerative Medicine
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: In the context of PCOS, UC-MSCs show potential to decrease systemic inflammation; improve insulin sensitivity; normalise androgen levels; and promote ovarian tissue repair.
Key features and challenges:
Umbilical cord–derived mesenchymal stem cells (UC-MSCs) are multipotent stromal cells isolated from Wharton’s jelly of the umbilical cord. They can differentiate into mesodermal lineages (e.g., bone, cartilage, adipose tissue) and possess immunomodulatory, anti-inflammatory, and paracrine regenerative properties. UC-MSCs are considered an ethically acceptable and readily available source of stem cells for therapeutic applications.
Early translational and clinical observations have suggested potential relevance of mesenchymal stem cell therapy in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). A published case report described complete resolution of PCOS symptoms in a young woman following a single intravenous infusion of umbilical cord–derived MSCs, with improvements in hormonal parameters and menstrual regularity. While anecdotal, this report contributed to growing interest in stem cell–based approaches.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39308763/
A 2023 systematic review evaluated mesenchymal stem cells and their secretomes as potential therapies for PCOS. The review concluded that MSC-based therapies may downregulate androgen levels, enhance insulin sensitivity, and reduce proinflammatory cytokines, thereby targeting key pathophysiological drivers of PCOS, including hyperandrogenism, insulin resistance, and chronic inflammation.
https://www.mdpi.com/2305-6320/10/1/3
Building on preclinical and early clinical findings, several early-phase clinical trials are underway. The Phase 1/2 study NCT05279768 is investigating UC-MSCs, their secretomes, and combination therapy in women with PCOS and insulin resistance. The four-arm trial evaluates improvements in clinical and laboratory insulin resistance markers, ovulatory function, and fertility outcomes, with follow-up at 1, 3, and 6 months post-injection.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05279768
Additionally, the Phase I trial NCT06143527 is assessing the safety and preliminary efficacy of intravenously administered cultured allogeneic adult UC-MSCs in women with PCOS. Participants receive approximately 2 million cells per kilogram of body weight, with monitoring of hormonal levels and ovarian morphology via ultrasound at 3, 6, and 12 months. The study is scheduled to conclude in 2027.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06143527
Despite promising mechanistic rationale, several challenges remain. Current evidence is largely derived from preclinical studies, small early-phase trials, and isolated case reports. Long-term safety, durability of therapeutic effect, optimal dosing, and standardization of cell preparation protocols require further validation. Stem cell therapies also involve higher cost, complex manufacturing processes, and regulatory scrutiny compared with conventional pharmacologic treatments. Furthermore, heterogeneity in PCOS phenotypes may influence treatment response, necessitating well-powered, randomized controlled trials.
UC-MSC therapy represents an innovative regenerative and immunomodulatory approach targeting multiple pathogenic mechanisms in PCOS. However, it remains investigational, with ongoing early-phase trials needed to establish safety, efficacy, and feasibility before consideration for routine clinical use.

Name: Uterine artery (UtA) indices - PCOS
Developers: Akram Medical Complex; University of Lahore
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Measures blood flow in the uterine arteries via Doppler ultrasound, assessing vascular resistance
Key features and challenges:
The uterine artery Pulsatility Index (PI) is a Doppler ultrasound measure used to evaluate blood flow in the uterine arteries, often associated with various gynecological conditions, including PCOS. In women with PCOS, uterine artery PI values can be altered, reflecting changes in uterine and ovarian blood flow. These alterations are often linked to the hormonal and metabolic imbalances characteristic of PCOS. Lower PI values typically indicate increased blood flow to the uterus, while higher PI values suggest resistance to blood flow, which can be a sign of endothelial dysfunction or vascular changes. The uterine artery PI is considered a valuable diagnostic tool for assessing vascular changes in conditions like PCOS, where uterine perfusion may be compromised.

A 2022 study aimed to evaluate the sensitivity of uterine artery PI using 3D Doppler ultrasound as a diagnostic tool for PCOS. It included 120 women who met the Rotterdam criteria for PCOS, with PI and Resistance Index (RI) measurements taken for both uterine arteries using pelvic duplex and color Doppler sonography. The results showed a mean PI value of 2.1 ± 0.84 and an average RI of 0.71 ± 0.48, suggesting a strong potential for Doppler ultrasound to diagnose PCOS non-invasively. The study found that 80.83% of the diagnoses were accurate, aligning with previous research that highlighted the utility of Doppler ultrasound in identifying PCOS through its vascular indicators, particularly uterine artery PI. (https://pjmhsonline.com/index.php/pjmhs/article/view/2808)

Name: Uterine artery Pulsatility Index (UtA-PI) + diastolic notching - PE/E
Developers: Fetal Medicine Foundation (FMF)
Indication: Indicated for the prediction of Preeclampsia in Primigravida Women
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Mechanism of action: The Uterine Artery Pulsatility Index (UtA-PI) combined with diastolic notching acts as a Doppler marker reflecting high impedance to blood flow within the maternal uteroplacental circulation
Key features and challenges:
Uterine artery Doppler assessment, including measurement of uterine artery pulsatility index (UtA-PI) and evaluation for diastolic notching, is a non-invasive imaging approach used to assess uteroplacental perfusion and risk of preeclampsia (PE). Elevated UtA-PI reflects increased resistance in the uterine arteries, while persistent diastolic notching suggests impaired trophoblastic invasion and abnormal placental vascular remodeling.
A 2024 study evaluated the predictive value of second-trimester Doppler ultrasonography combined with clinical parameters for early detection of preeclampsia in primigravida women (https://impactfactor.org/PDF/IJPCR/16/IJPCR,Vol16,Issue5,Article611.pdf). Among 300 participants, 36 women (12%) developed preeclampsia. Elevated UtA-PI and the presence of diastolic notching were both significantly associated with subsequent development of preeclampsia (p < 0.001). The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was 0.83 for UtA-PI and 0.77 for diastolic notching. When combined, these Doppler findings achieved an AUC of 0.86, indicating good predictive performance. Logistic regression modeling demonstrated that integration of Doppler parameters with clinical data (e.g., blood pressure and body mass index) improved risk stratification.
Key challenges include variability in operator expertise, differences in gestational timing of assessment, and limited predictive value when used in isolation without biochemical markers. While Doppler ultrasonography is widely available and non-invasive, standardization of cut-off values and integration into comprehensive screening algorithms remain necessary to optimize predictive accuracy and clinical impact.

Name: Uterocervical angle
Developers: Haiphong University of Medicine and Pharmacy; Naval Medical Center Portsmouth; Banaras Hindu University
Indication: Prediction of PTL
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Ultrasound measurement of the uterocervical angle to identify cervical geometry changes associated with reduced cervical support and preterm labour risk.
Key features and challenges:
The uterocervical angle is a novel ultrasound parameter that is being used as a predictor of spontaneous preterm birth. The angle between the uterine wall and the cervical canal is measured during the first and the second trimester by a transvaginal ultrasound. It is measured using a line that starts from the internal cervical os (that is extended along the cervical canal) and a second line that tracks the internal segment of the anterior uterine wall. (https://radiopaedia.org/articles/anterior-cervical-angle). 

A systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to compare the uterocervical angles in term and spontaneous preterm birth cohorts and to compare the test characteristics of the uterocervical angle and cervical length in the prediction of spontaneous preterm birth. A total of 15 cohort studies with 6218 patients were included. The study concluded that uterocervical angle alone or with cervical length was not superior to cervical length alone in predicting spontaneous preterm birth. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2666577823000813) 

A number of studies have found that a uterocervical angle >110° was significantly associated with preterm birth (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14767058.2023.2262081, https://journals.viamedica.pl/ginekologia_polska/article/view/95194).
A 2023 study at the Haiphong Hospital of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Vietnam, investigated the UCAs' distribution in 1,051 singleton pregnant women at 16+ 0 - 23+ 6 weeks of gestation with low risk for sPTB and found an association with a UCA>95°. The study established normal range of UCA, as well as UCA changes throughout pregnancy (2.51 degrees per week, p < 0.001 between 16-29 weeks of gestation). A total of 42/63 (66.7%) patients with preterm birth < 37 weeks had a UCA above the 75th percentile. The majority of women with preterm birth had a UCA >= 95degree compared with those with full-term delivery (88.9% vs. 31.3%, p < 0.001). The authors concluded that a UCA value >= 95degrees can potentially predict the risk for preterm birth.
(https://bmcpregnancychildbirth.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12884-023-05597-3)

Name: Uterocervical angle-cervical length ratio
Developers: Isfahan University of Medical Sciences, Iran
Indication: Prediction of spontaneous preterm birth during the second trimester
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Target: Ultrasound measurements of uterocervical angle and cervical length
Mechanism of action: Measures lipid fractions to detect dyslipidemia and metabolic risk associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges: A 2024 prospective observational cohort study explored how two ultrasound markers—the uterocervical angle (UCA) and cervical length (CL)—could work together to predict spontaneous preterm birth during the second trimester. The study followed first-time pregnant women with single pregnancies and no known risk factors for preterm birth, from 16+0 to 23+6 weeks until delivery. At admission, transvaginal ultrasounds measured UCA and CL, and maternal histories were collected from patient records. Logistic regression identified significant predictors, while receiver operating curves (ROCs) determined the best cut-offs and accuracy. The predictive performance of each variable was compared using positive and negative likelihood ratios. Out of 357 participants, 41 (11.5%) experienced spontaneous preterm birth. Both UCA and CL remained significant predictors after adjusting for other factors (adjusted odds ratio: UCA 1.05, 95% CI 1.02–1.07; CL 0.82, 95% CI 0.75–0.90). The optimal cut-offs were 106 degrees for UCA and 33 mm for CL. A new index, UCA/CL, achieved an area under the ROC curve of 0.781 (95% CI 0.734–0.823), with a cut-off of 3.09 degrees/mm, and showed stronger likelihood ratios (positive: 3.18, 2.47, and 4.22; negative: 0.63, 0.52, and 0.51 for UCA, CL, and UCA/CL, respectively). (https://dx.doi.org/10.1002/ijgo.15361)

Name: VAL-181388
Developers: Moderna Therapeutics (including Valera)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against CHIKV infection
Target: CHIKV nucleocapsid protein (C) and glycosylated E proteins
Mechanism of action: Immunostimulant

Name: VEGF-B (polypeptide delivery)
Developers: University of Mississippi Medical Center
Indication: Reducing hypertension in preeclampsia
Mechanism of action: Activating Flt-1 receptor to improve endothelial and sequestering circulating sFlt1
Key features and challenges:
VEGF-B–based polypeptide delivery strategies are being investigated as a targeted approach to restore angiogenic balance in preeclampsia. Preeclampsia originates from an inadequately vascularized and ischemic placenta that releases anti-angiogenic factors, notably soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1). Elevated sFlt-1 binds and sequesters vascular endothelial growth factors (VEGF family members), contributing to systemic endothelial dysfunction, hypertension, and multiorgan injury.
One investigational strategy involves fusion of vascular endothelial growth factor to an elastin-like polypeptide (ELP) carrier, creating ELP-VEGF constructs designed to prolong circulation time and limit placental transfer. The ELP carrier is engineered to avoid crossing the placental barrier, thereby reducing fetal exposure while targeting maternal endothelial dysfunction. ELP-VEGF can directly activate VEGF receptors (e.g., Flk-1/KDR) and may also sequester circulating sFlt-1, increasing bioavailability of endogenous VEGF and improving endothelial nitric oxide signaling. Research in this area is being conducted by the University of Mississippi.
https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/9973513
In a placental ischemic rat model, long-term ELP-VEGF administration resulted in dose-dependent attenuation of hypertension at doses up to 5 mg/kg/day. Treatment increased total circulating sFlt-1 and enhanced renal nitric oxide signaling, consistent with improved endothelial function. No significant adverse effects on maternal or fetal body weight were observed at therapeutic doses. However, dose-dependent adverse events were reported, including ascites formation and neovascular tissue encapsulation around the delivery device.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29629873/
VEGF signaling requires precise regulation during embryogenesis. Overexpression of VEGF can lead to aberrant angiogenesis, excessive vascular fusion, vessel dilation, and embryonic lethality, as demonstrated in murine models. These findings underscore the importance of tight dose control and targeted delivery in any VEGF-based therapeutic strategy during pregnancy.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10952892
VEGF-based polypeptide delivery represents a mechanistically targeted, angiogenic rebalancing approach for preeclampsia. While preclinical data demonstrate blood pressure reduction and endothelial improvement in animal models, the strategy remains entirely investigational. Translation to human pregnancy will require rigorous evaluation of maternal safety, fetal exposure risk, dose optimization, and long-term vascular effects.

Name: Vaccinia immune globulin therapy
Developers: National Center for Global Health and Medicine
Indication: Indicated for the treatment and prevention of Mpox virus
Mechanism of action: High titers of neutralizing IgG antibodies bind to epitopes on Mpox Virus, preventing viral entry.
Key features and challenges:
VIG is purified from human blood and used to treat serious infections of the vaccinia (smallpox vaccine) virus or similar viruses. VIG (Human) is a component of plasma from persons vaccinated with vaccinia vaccine. It is the only treatment available for those viruses. The only available supply of VIG has developed a discoloration over time and therefore is considered an investigational new drug by the FDA.

A phase I study in the US has been withdrawn (NCT00006630), while a phase II study in Japan is evaluating the efficacy and safety of vaccinia immune globulin therapy for patients with mpox or smallpox (https://rctportal.niph.go.jp/en/detail?trial_id=jRCTs031220744).
Recent updates:
Vaccinia Immune Globulin Intravenous (VIGIV, CNJ-016) remains licensed for treatment of serious vaccinia vaccination complications and prophylaxis in contraindicated individuals. Expanded-access IND protocols continue under CDC guidance as of 2023 for orthopoxvirus infections. Phase 2 pharmacodynamic trials in healthy volunteers demonstrated safety and dose-dependent efficacy in attenuating Dryvax reactions. Post-marketing reports note rare but serious adverse events including TRALI and renal events.
As of July 2025, Emergent BioSolutions secured a $51.9 million contract modification for VIGIV (CNJ‑016), confirming ongoing production and stockpiling efforts.
The CDC’s Expanded Access IND Protocol (as of 2023) remains operational for orthopoxvirus treatment—including mpox and smallpox vaccine complications.
Sources:

Name: Vaginal microbiome - low lactobacilli
Developers: Stanford University (including the Center for Innovations in Global Health)
Indication: Prediction of the risk of preterm birth
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Calculates neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio to assess systemic inflammation associated with PCOS.
Key features and challenges:
The cervicovaginal environment (microbiome, innate immune system, and metabolome) is an important contributor to a healthy pregnancy. Several recent and ongoing studies have focused on the potential role of the vaginal microbiome in preterm birth and its association with pregnancy adverse outcomes. Studies require the characterization of the vaginal microbiome in healthy pregnancies and the identification of specificities associated with adverse outcomes. They have the potential to allow for microbiome profiling and the development of multibiomarker tests predictive of preterm labour.

A 2022 systematic review and network meta-analysis focused on the association between the vaginal microbiome, defined as community state types (CSTs, i.e. dominance of specific lactobacilli spp, or not (low-lactobacilli)), and the risk of preterm birth. It included 17 studies published between 2014 and 2021 and found that women presenting with “low-lactobacilli” vaginal microbiome were at increased risk (OR 1.69, 95% CI 1.15–2.49) for delivering preterm compared to Lactobacillus crispatus dominant women (https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biodatasci-020722-094144#right-ref-B116)

Developers: US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease (NIAID); Ottawa Hospital Research Institute (OHRI); University Hospital Virgen del Rocío, Hospital Universitario Virgen del Rocío
Indication: Indicated for the control of HIV-1 infection in the absence of ART.

Name: VesiVax-MtrE-IAM
Developers: Molecular Express, Inc.
Indication: Prevention of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Immunostimulant
Key features and challenges:
VesiVax-MtrE-IAM is a liposome-based vaccine candidate under development for prevention of Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection. The VesiVax platform utilizes engineered proteins capable of stable insertion into nanoscale liposomal particles, which serve as immunogenic carriers for vaccine antigen presentation.
A 2022 funded project proposed development of a VesiVax-based gonococcal vaccine incorporating the surface-exposed outer membrane protein MtrE co-formulated with immunostimulatory adjuvant molecules (IAMs) (https://reporter.nih.gov/search/eZ7U81Vga0SaOKF_UjWP_g/project-details/10385208). 
MtrE, a component of the gonococcal efflux pump system, was selected as a target antigen due to its surface accessibility and potential role in antimicrobial resistance. The liposomal formulation is intended to enhance antigen stability, immune activation, and protective antibody responses.
Key challenges include demonstrating broad strain coverage given antigenic variability, establishing correlates of protection in humans, and validating durable mucosal immunity. Manufacturing scalability and regulatory evaluation of novel liposomal formulations will also be critical considerations.
Overall, VesiVax-MtrE-IAM represents a platform-based liposomal vaccine strategy targeting a conserved gonococcal surface protein. Further preclinical validation is required to determine its suitability for clinical advancement.

Name: VesiculoVax CHIKV
Developers: Auro Vaccines
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against CHIKV infection
Target: CHIKV glycosylated E proteins (E1, E2, E3) and glycoprotein 6K
Key features and challenges: Glycoprotein-defiicient VSV encoding CHIKV structural proteins. Preclinical studies report on the development of a potent experimental vaccine for CHIKV based on a chimeric vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) expressing the entire CHIKV envelope polyprotein (E3-E2-6K-E1) in place of the VSV glycoprotein (G). These VSVΔG-CHIKV chimeras incorporated functional CHIKV glycoproteins into the viral envelope in place of VSV G. The chimeric viruses were attenuated for growth in tissue culture but could be propagated to high titers without VSV G complementation. They also generated robust neutralizing antibody and cellular immune responses to CHIKV in mice after a single dose and protected mice against CHIKV infection. VSVΔG-alphavirus chimeras could have general applicability as alphavirus vaccines.
