Name: Vidofludimus
Developers: Kagoshima University
Indication: Treatment of influenza virus infection, caused by H5
Mechanism of action: Inhibits DHODH, reducing pyrimidine pools required for viral RNA synthesis, thereby blocking influenza virus replication. Rescue experiments with uridine/cytidine/orotic acid confirmed dependence on pyrimidine metabolism.
Key features and challenges:
-Already in clinical trials for autoimmune diseases (e.g., multiple sclerosis), supporting repurposing potential.
-Active against both wild-type H5N1 and PA-I38T mutant (resistant to baloxavir) and PB2-T271A enhanced polymerase mutant.
-EC50 values: 2.10 μM (wild-type H5N1), 2.11 μM (PA-I38T mutant).
-Also active against seasonal IAV H1N1 and influenza B virus (IBV).
-Host-targeted → high barrier to resistance, but risk of host toxicity and off-target metabolic effects.
Recent updates:
-Vidofludimus is in advanced clinical development for multiple sclerosis (Immunic’s IMU-838 program, Phase 3 ongoing), with established safety profile.
-No influenza-specific clinical trials yet, but repurposing discussions ongoing in the context of H5N1 outbreaks in 2024–2025.
-Fits into growing interest in host-directed antivirals (e.g., DHODH inhibitors, IMPDH inhibitors) as broad-spectrum countermeasures.

Name: Vipoglanstat
Developers: Gesynta Pharma
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of endometriosis.
Mechanism of action: Prostaglandin-E synthase inhibitors
Key features and challenges:
Vipoglanstat is an orally active, non-peptide small-molecule inhibitor of microsomal prostaglandin E synthase-1 (mPGES-1), developed by Gesynta Pharma. By selectively inhibiting mPGES-1, vipoglanstat reduces production of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), a key mediator of inflammation and pain. Given the role of PGE2 in endometriosis-associated inflammation, lesion maintenance, and pain sensitization, mPGES-1 inhibition represents a targeted anti-inflammatory strategy distinct from broader cyclooxygenase (COX) inhibition (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800054502).
Vipoglanstat was initially developed for systemic scleroderma and has subsequently advanced into clinical development for endometriosis. A clinical study initiated in 2023 is evaluating vipoglanstat in women with endometriosis (https://adis.springer.com/trials/700366089). 
In 2025, a Phase II trial was initiated to further investigate its efficacy and safety in endometriosis (NCT07260669; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07260669). 
These studies aim to assess reduction in endometriosis-associated pain and inflammatory activity.
Key challenges include the need to demonstrate clinically meaningful pain reduction compared with established hormonal and non-hormonal therapies, as well as confirmation of safety with longer-term use. As a novel mPGES-1 inhibitor, regulatory familiarity and comparative positioning versus NSAIDs and hormonal agents will be important considerations. Robust Phase II data will be critical to determine progression to later-stage development.
Overall, vipoglanstat represents a mechanistically targeted, non-hormonal anti-inflammatory approach for endometriosis. Ongoing Phase II studies will determine whether selective mPGES-1 inhibition can translate into clinically meaningful benefit in this population.
Recent updates: TM 13/12/2025: Phase I trial identified from EMBASE (https://academic.oup.com/humrep/article/40/Supplement_1/deaf097.195/8170420)

Name: Viral budding inhibitors
Developers: Biotron Limited
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of DENV
Mechanism of action: Viral protein inhibitor
Key features and challenges:
Biotron is developing novel small molecule antiviral therapeutics targeting a range of viruses. The Company’s core expertise lies in designing and developing new drugs that target a new class of viral proteins known as viroporins.Viroporins are virus-encoded polypeptides that interact with membranes comprising at least one transmembrane segment. Viroporins participate in several viral functions, including the promotion of release of viral particles from cells. By blocking the ion channel activity of viroporins, potentially therapeutic compounds are able to inhibit viral budding and replication. 
Viral proteins targeted under Biotron's programme include M protein of Dengue virus and E protein of coronaviruses such as severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS).Early research for the treatment of Dengue is underway in the US and Australia.

Name: Vitamin - Vitamin A - PE/E
Developers: Zhejiang University
Indication: Treatment of vitamin A deficiency caused by proteinuria
Mechanism of action: Regulating pathways controlling development of foetal organs and tissues
Key features and challenges:
Vitamin A plays a critical role in embryonic growth and organ development, including the formation of the vertebrae, spinal cord, limbs, heart, eyes, and ears. Adequate maternal vitamin A status supports fetal tissue differentiation and lung maturation. Deficiency during pregnancy has been associated with impaired organ development and increased risk of adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes.
Vitamin A is also involved in steroidogenesis, and deficiency may reduce the activity of enzymes required for progesterone precursor formation, potentially affecting adrenal, gonadal, and placental steroid production. Additionally, vitamin A contributes to antioxidant defense mechanisms. Oxidative stress, characterized by increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) or reduced antioxidant capacity, has been implicated in the pathogenesis of preeclampsia. Antioxidant vitamins, including vitamin A, help neutralize free radicals and limit lipid peroxidation. Circulating vitamin A is transported by retinol-binding protein (RBP), and conditions such as proteinuria—commonly observed in preeclampsia—may reduce RBP levels and contribute to lower circulating vitamin A concentrations.
(Sources: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28877853/
; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30909386/)
A clinical trial (NCT03971604), registered in 2019, is investigating the association between vitamin A and vitamin E levels and preeclampsia.
(Source: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03971604)
Overall, vitamin A has been studied primarily in relation to its biological plausibility and antioxidant role in preeclampsia pathophysiology. However, robust clinical evidence demonstrating a preventive or therapeutic effect of supplementation on preeclampsia outcomes remains limited.
Recent updates: 2021: Current study: The Correlation Between Vitamin A / E Levels and Preeclampsia (NCT03971604)

Name: Vitamin - Vitamin B12 - PTL/PTB
Developers: Harvard School of Public Health (HSPH); University of Modena and Reggio Emilia
Indication: Enhancing foetal growth
Mechanism of action: Supporting neurodevelopment and development of RBCs via DNA synthesis and metabolism of several essential biomolecules
Key features and challenges:
Vitamin B12, also known as cobalamin, functions as a cofactor in DNA synthesis, and in both fatty acid and amino acid metabolism. It is also important in the normal functioning of the nervous system via its role in the synthesis of myelin, and in the maturation of developing red blood cells in the bone marrow. The most common cause of vitamin B12 deficiency in developed countries is impaired absorption due to a loss of gastric intrinsic factor, which must be bound to a food-source of B12 in order for absorption to occur.

Vitamin B12 has many forms, including the cyano-, methyl-, deoxyadenosyl- and hydroxy-cobalamin forms. The cyano form (cyanocobalamin), is the most widely used form in supplements and prescription drug, which was initially approved by the FDA in 1942 for vitamin B12 deficiency.

Experiments on Wistar rats indicated vitamin B12 combined with folate during pregnancy had positive impact on foetal growth (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29032242/). In a meta-analysis of 18 studies, low B12 levels in pregnancy have been associated with preterm birth, and low neonatal birthweight (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28108470/). A clinical trial (NCT03071666, VitaGreg) is underway to investigate effects of vitamin B12 supplementation during pregnancy on gestational age and neurodevelopment of infants. 
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03071666
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28851784/
Recent updates: August 2017: Systematic review published investigating maternal vitamin B12 in pregnancy and risk of preterm birth and low birth weight (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5390862/)

Name: Vitamin - Vitamin E - PE/E
Developers: Royal Victoria Hospital
Indication: Reduce the risk of preeclampsia through supplementation
Mechanism of action: α‐tocopherol may reduce inflammatory mediators, lower the expression of cell adhesion molecules, and increase peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor‐γ (PPAR‐γ) expression
Key features and challenges:
Vitamin E, first identified as an essential nutrient in 1922, refers to a group of eight fat-soluble compounds (tocopherols and tocotrienols), with alpha-tocopherol being the most biologically active form. It functions primarily as an antioxidant, protecting cell membranes from oxidative damage by neutralizing free radicals. Due to its antioxidant properties, vitamin E has been investigated for potential therapeutic applications in conditions associated with oxidative stress, including preeclampsia.
A 1994 clinical study evaluating vitamin E supplementation in women with severe preeclampsia found no improvement in fetal outcomes, maternal hypertension, or proteinuria.
(Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8050728)
Subsequent research in 2004 highlighted the biological plausibility of antioxidant therapy in preeclampsia, noting elevated inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6, TNF), increased soluble cell adhesion molecules (e.g., sICAM-1, sVCAM-1), and reduced peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPAR-γ) levels in affected women. These findings supported continued investigation of antioxidants such as vitamin E in the condition.
(Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15753150/)
However, a 2010 study assessing vitamin E supplementation in pregnant women with diabetes demonstrated no reduction in the incidence of preeclampsia.
(Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20580423/)
Overall, while vitamin E possesses mechanistic relevance due to its antioxidant properties, clinical evidence has not demonstrated consistent benefit in preventing or improving outcomes in preeclampsia. Supplementation remains widely available and is generally regarded as safe at recommended doses, though its therapeutic role in PE/E remains unestablished.
Recent updates:
A 2019 preclinical rat model suggested that vitamin E (and omega-3) supplementation was beneficial in reducing the caspase-8 and 3 in early onset preeclampsia but did not normalize BAX and Bcl-2 levels. This has implications for reducing placental apoptosis in preeclampsia (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31730868/)

On-going trial for vitamin E (including Vitamin A) and PE (NCT03971604).

Name: Vitamin D (Cholecalciferol/ 25-hydroxyvitamin D/ Ergocalciferol)
Developers: Gonabad University of Medical Sciences; Rajavithi Hospital
Indication: PTL Prevention
Target:
-Vitamin D receptor (VDR) in uterine, placental and immune tissues
-Maternal 25(OH)D levels
-Immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory pathways
Mechanism of action: Vitamin D₃ acts through the vitamin D receptor (VDR) to modulate inflammation, cytokine production, immune balance, oxidative stress, and calcium homeostasis. In PTL contexts, vitamin D may reduce inflammatory triggers, enhance uterine muscle quiescence, improve placental function and reduce infection-driven PTL pathways. Evidence supports a role for maintaining 25(OH)D >30 ng/mL for reduced PTB risk; deficiencies are associated with increased PTB, pre-eclampsia, and GDM.
Key features and challenges:
Vitamin D (including cholecalciferol [D₃], ergocalciferol [D₂], and circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D) has been extensively investigated for its role in pregnancy outcomes, including preterm birth (PTB) and preterm labour (PTL). Vitamin D insufficiency has been strongly associated with increased risk of PTB, with proposed mechanisms including immune modulation, suppression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, enhancement of antimicrobial peptide expression, and support of placental function and trophoblast integrity.
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4695683/

More recent mechanistic and clinical reviews (2024) reinforce the association between low maternal vitamin D status and adverse pregnancy outcomes, highlighting pathways involving regulation of inflammatory mediators, modulation of adaptive immunity, and effects on uterine contractility and placental vascular function.
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11668112/

Building on observational and mechanistic evidence, interventional trials are now exploring whether vitamin D supplementation can prevent or mitigate PTL/PTB. The Thai Clinical Trials Registry study (TCTR20250614004) evaluates vitamin D supplementation in pregnant women with hypovitaminosis D, assessing obstetric outcomes and biochemical parameters.
https://www.thaiclinicaltrials.org/show/TCTR20250614004

Similarly, the Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials study (IRCT74998) assesses the effect of additional vitamin D₃ supplementation on cessation and recurrence of preterm labour, aiming to determine whether targeted correction of deficiency improves short-term PTL outcomes.
http://en.irct.ir/trial/74998

Despite strong biological plausibility and consistent epidemiological associations, confirmed clinical efficacy for prevention or cessation of PTL remains unestablished. Evidence to date remains investigational, with many trials still recruiting or in early phases. Heterogeneity in baseline vitamin D deficiency across populations complicates standardization of dosing strategies and interpretation of results. High-dose regimens may require monitoring due to potential risks of hypercalcemia and renal complications, particularly with prolonged supplementation.

Name: Vitamin D - PCOS
Developers: Yale University
Indication: Diagnosis of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: unspecified
Key features and challenges:
Vitamin D testing measures serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D), the primary circulating form of vitamin D and the most reliable indicator of overall vitamin D status from dietary intake, supplementation, and endogenous synthesis. Quantification is typically performed using immunoassays or liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), with results categorized as deficiency, insufficiency, or sufficiency to guide clinical management.
In the context of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), vitamin D insufficiency has been associated with metabolic and reproductive abnormalities. A 2022 study comparing ultrasound and biochemical characteristics of adolescents with PCOS and healthy controls found that the PCOS group exhibited vitamin D insufficiency alongside elevated anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) levels (https://www.jpagonline.org/article/S1083-3188(22)00067-5/fulltext). These findings highlight potential biochemical differences in adolescent PCOS and suggest that vitamin D status may contribute to the disorder’s endocrine and metabolic profile.
Key challenges include the lack of specificity of vitamin D deficiency to PCOS, as insufficiency is common in the general population, and uncertainty regarding causal versus associative relationships. While vitamin D testing may provide supportive metabolic context, it is not a standalone diagnostic marker for PCOS. Further research is needed to clarify whether incorporation of vitamin D status meaningfully improves diagnostic accuracy or risk stratification in adolescents with suspected PCOS.

Name: Vivaxin
Developers: CT-Vacinas; Cristália Produtos Quimicos e Farmaceuticos Ltda.
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against malaria caused by P. vivax
Mechanism of action: Triggers protective antibody development to block sporozoite transit into hepatic cells, stopping vivax replication cycles
Key features and challenges: A subunit vaccine that triggers protective antibodies against the P. vivax circumsporozoite protein (CSP) to block sporozoite entry into hepatic cells and interrupt the vivax replication cycle. It is administered intramuscularly and has been investigated for malaria prophylaxis.
Recent updates: A Phase 1, first-in-human, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-escalation trial is planned to evaluate the safety, reactogenicity, and immunogenicity of three intramuscular dose levels in 48 healthy malaria-naive adults.

Name: Voriconazole - Leishmaniasis
Developers: Zagazig University
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of cutaneous Leishmaniasis
Mechanism of action: Inhibits ergosterol biosynthesis
Key features and challenges:

The digenetic protozoan Leishmania is dependent on ergosterol synthesis for growth and viability.. A 2013 study found voriconazole active against insect and mammalian stage parasites (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23392902/).
Recent updates: Study completed in 2024 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05708625)

Name: Voxilaprevir +/- ribavirin
Developers: Jeffrey Cheah School of Medicine and Health Sciences (JCSMHS); Monash University Malaysia
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of CHIKV infection
Mechanism of action:
-Binds strongly to nsP2 protease (ΔG −8.7 kcal/mol, Ki ~0.42 nM).
-Interacts via multiple H-bonds (ASN1082, LYS1091, ASP1246, GLN1241).
-In vitro: blocks viral inactivation, attachment, and replication post-infection.
-Combination with Ribavirin (RIBA): synergy at higher concentrations (20 μM), producing greater viral inhibition than either alone.
Key features and challenges:
-IC₅₀ in Vero E6 cells: 25.25 μM (well-tolerated below this dose).
-Significant post-infection inhibitory effect, stronger than RIBA alone.
-Combination VOX+RIBA enhances viral suppression, especially at 20 μM.
Recent updates:
March 2025:

-Recommended for further in vivo testing in CHIKV animal models.

Name: WC-rCTB (Dukoral) + Ty21a (Vivotif) coadministration trial. Change to phase IV
Developers: Emergent Biosolutions; Valneva
Indication: Indicated for the prevention of typhoid fever.
Target: Cholera toxin B subunit & Live attenuated S. Typhi Ty21a
Mechanism of action: Co-presents whole-cell inactivated targets with live attenuated bacterial lines to trigger dual mucosal protection loops
Key features and challenges: An inactivated oral combination that co-presents a whole-cell inactivated cholera toxin B subunit with a live attenuated Salmonella Typhi Ty21a line to trigger dual mucosal protection. It is given orally and has been investigated for simultaneous cholera and typhoid prophylaxis.
Recent updates: A prospective, randomised, open-label trial assessing coadministration versus single administration of the oral cholera and typhoid vaccines in healthy adults reported favourable safety and robust immunogenicity for both vaccines, supporting their simultaneous use without spacing precautions.

Name: WGc0201
Developers: Jiyan Liu
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of chronic HBV infection
Target: Hepatitis B virus HBx protein (mRNA transcript)
Mechanism of action: Immunostimulants
Key features and challenges: An immunostimulatory therapeutic vaccine directed against the hepatitis B virus HBx protein mRNA transcript, designed to activate virus-specific T- and B-cell responses. Administered intramuscularly.
Recent updates: An open-label, single-arm, dose-escalation Phase 1 trial (NCT07051187) evaluating its safety in patients with chronic hepatitis B who have achieved virological stability is expected to begin in 2025 and is not yet recruiting as of 2025.

Name: WIN 55,212–2 (WIN)
Developers: Oswaldo Cruz Foundation (FIOCRUZ), Fundação Oswaldo Cruz (including Evandro Chagas Clinical Research Institute, FIOCRUZ Amazonia and Instituto Leônidas & Maria Deane (ILMD))
Indication: Treatment of Trichomoniasis
Mechanism of action: Synthetic cannabinoid that interferes with protozoal cellular signaling and membrane integrity to inhibit growth.
Key features and challenges: A 2025 study highlights trichomoniasis as a growing challenge due to resistance to the current treatment, Metronidazole (MTZ), which also has side effects. Cannabis sativa, with over 100 phytocannabinoids and a history of research into therapeutic uses, including for parasitic infections, has seen a global shift in acceptance driven by legalizations and major revenue projections. In this context, the study examines cannabinoids like WIN 55,212–2 (WIN) and Cannabivarin (CBV) for their anti-parasitic effects on the growth and morphology of T. vaginalis, also exploring their pharmacokinetic properties. CBV, in particular, meets Lipinski’s rules, suggesting it could be suitable for oral drug delivery. Both cannabinoids showed they could inhibit T. vaginalis trophozoite growth and reduce the parasite’s ability to adhere to host cells. Observed changes included membrane projections, blebbing, autophagosomes, and damaged hydrogenosomes. These findings point to the need for more research into the therapeutic potential and mechanisms of cannabinoids against T. vaginalis (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0753332224016809)
Recent updates: Discovery study published in 2025 demonstrated cannabinoid compounds inhibited growht of T. vaginalis trophozoites and reduced the parasite's adhesion to host cells. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0753332224016809?via%3Dihub)

Name: WISP2/CCN5
Developers: Affiliated Hospital of Youjiang Medical University for Nationalities
Indication: Indicated as a biomarker of endometriosis.
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: WISP2/CCN5 gene expression in the eutopic endometrium.
Key features and challenges:
WISP2/CCN5 (Wnt1-inducible signaling pathway protein 2), a matricellular protein belonging to the CCN family, has recently been proposed as a potential diagnostic biomarker for endometriosis. Members of the CCN family are involved in cell proliferation, migration, extracellular matrix remodeling, and angiogenesis—processes central to the pathogenesis of endometriotic lesion establishment and progression.
A 2025 study employed machine learning approaches combined with single-cell transcriptomic analyses of eutopic and ectopic endometrial tissues to identify candidate diagnostic biomarkers (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10142-025-01631-z). 
WISP2/CCN5 expression was consistently elevated in endometriotic lesion cells and was particularly enriched in cellular clusters associated with MAPK, Wnt, and fibroblast growth factor (FGF) signaling pathways. These pathways are implicated in epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), lesion proliferation, and fibrosis. The integration of computational modeling and transcriptomic profiling suggested that WISP2/CCN5 may serve as a promising candidate for non-invasive diagnosis of endometriosis.
Key challenges include the need for validation beyond transcriptomic datasets. The biomarker’s diagnostic performance must be assessed across diverse patient populations, disease phenotypes (superficial, ovarian, deep infiltrating), stages, and menstrual cycle phases. The influence of hormonal status and comorbid gynecological or inflammatory conditions on WISP2/CCN5 expression remains unclear. Additionally, translation into a clinically practical, minimally invasive assay (e.g., blood-based test) requires further development and standardization. While computational and molecular findings are encouraging, prospective clinical validation studies are essential before WISP2/CCN5 can be implemented as a routine diagnostic biomarker for endometriosis.

Name: WRSs2
Developers: US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease (NIAID); Walter Reed Army Institute of Research (WRAIR) (including Military HIV Research Program)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization for the prevention of bacillary dysentery caused by Shigella sonnei
Target: Shigella sonnei strains WRSs2 and WRSs3
Mechanism of action: Induces mucosal and systemic immune responses
Key features and challenges:
The National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) and Walter Reed Army Institute of Research are developing a new, second-generation virG(icsA)-based S. sonnei vaccine candidates, WRSs2 and WRSs3, attenuated principally by the loss of the VirG(IcsA) protein. Besides the loss of VirG(IcsA), WRSs2 and WRSs3 also lack plasmid-encoded enterotoxin ShET2-1 and its paralog ShET2-2. WRSs3 further lacks MsbB2 that reduces the endotoxicity of the lipid A portion of the bacterial LPS. 

Studies in cell cultures and in gnotobiotic piglets have demonstrated that WRSs2 and WRSs3 have the potential to cause less diarrhea due to loss of ShET2-1 and ShET2-2 as well as alleviate febrile symptoms by loss of MsbB2. In guinea pigs, WRSs2 and WRSs3 were found to be as safe and immunogenic.

The candidates have now progressed to phase II clinical development (NCT04242264)
Recent updates: Phase II trial completed in 2024 (NCT04242264).

Name: Wb123/WbAgx biplex test
Developers: Drugs and Diagnostics for Tropical Diseases (DDTD); US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
Indication: Indicated for the diagnosis of Lymphatic filariasis
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care

Name: Wedelolactone
Developers: Medical School of Sao Jose do Rio Preto (FAMERP); Institute of Biological Information Processing IBI-7; Institut für Physikalische Biologie
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of CHIKV infection
Mechanism of action: Direct inhibition of CHIKV nsP2 protease (IC₅₀ = 2.3 ± 0.4 µM); modest reduction of viral replication in infected Vero E6 cells (IC₅₀ = 22.9 ± 6.7 µM); alters host metabolite pathways (glycolysis, amino acid metabolism, phospholipids).
Key features and challenges:
-Potent enzymatic inhibitor of nsP2 in vitro at low µM.
-Cytotoxicity (CC₅₀ = 373.5 ± 154.2 µM), yielding favorable selectivity index (~16).
-Only moderate suppression of CHIKV replication in Vero cells, suggesting poor cell permeability or bioavailability.
-Alters host cell metabolism (reduced lactate, proline, myo-inositol; increased glucose, methionine, betaine), potentially reducing viral replication capacity.
-Challenge: Translational efficacy not yet validated in vivo; requires formulation or delivery improvements.
Recent updates:
Jan 2024:
-First detailed report on CHIKV activity. 
-Subsequent citations reference WDL as a natural nsP2 inhibitor, but no animal model or clinical follow-up reported as of Sept 2025.

Name: Wenshen Xiaozheng Tang
Developers: Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of the fibrogenesis of endometriosis.
Mechanism of action: Reduces the expression and secretion of thrombospondin 4 by ectopic eMSCs.
Key features and challenges:
Wenshen Xiaozheng Tang (WXT), a traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) decoction, is effective for treating endometriosis. However, the effect of WXT on endometrium-derived mesenchymal stem cells (eMSCs) which play a key role in the fibrogenesis of endometriosis requires further elucidation.
The aim of a 2025 study was thus to clarify the potential mechanism of WXT in improving fibrosis in endometriosis by investigating the regulation of WXT on differentiation and paracrine of eMSCs.
Nude mice with endometriosis were randomly divided into model group, WXT group and mifepristone group. After 21 days of treatment, the lesion volume was calculated. Fibrosis in the lesions was evaluated by Masson staining and expression of fibrotic proteins. The differentiation of eMSCs in vivo was explored using a fate-tracking experiment. To further clarify the regulation of WXT on eMSCs, primary eMSCs from the ectopic lesions of endometriosis patients were isolated and characterized. The effect of WXT on the proliferation and differentiation of ectopic eMSCs was examined. To evaluate the role of WXT on the paracrine activity of ectopic eMSCs, the conditioned medium (CM) from ectopic eMSCs pretreated with WXT was collected and applied to treat ectopic endometrial stromal cells (ESCs), after which the expression of fibrotic proteins in ectopic ESCs was assessed. In addition, transcriptome sequencing was used to investigate the regulatory mechanism of WXT on ectopic eMSCs, and western blot and ELISA were employed to determine the key mediator.
WXT impeded the growth of ectopic lesions in nude mice with endometriosis and reduced collagen deposition and the expression of fibrotic proteins fibronectin, collagen I, α-SMA and CTGF in the endometriotic lesions. The fate-tracking experiment showed that WXT prevented human eMSCs from differentiating into myofibroblasts in the nude mice. The authors successfully isolated eMSCs from the lesions of patients with endometriosis and demonstrated that WXT suppressed proliferation and myofibroblast differentiation of ectopic eMSCs. Moreover, the expression of α-SMA, collagen I, fibronectin and CTGF in ectopic ESCs was significantly down-regulated by the CM of ectopic MSCs pretreated with WXT. Combining the results of RNA sequencing, western blot and ELISA, it was found that WXT not only reduced thrombospondin 4 expression in ectopic eMSCs, but also decreased thrombospondin 4 secretion from ectopic eMSCs. Thrombospondin 4 concentration-dependently upregulated the expression of collagen I, fibronectin, α-SMA and CTGF in ectopic ESCs, indicating that thrombospondin 4 was a key mediator of WXT in inhibiting the fibrotic process in endometriosis.
WXT improved fibrosis in endometriosis by regulating differentiation and paracrine signalling of eMSCs. Thrombospondin 4, whose release from ectopic eMSCs is inhibited by WXT, may be a potential target for the treatment of endometriosis (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378874124010237?via%3Dihub).

Name: Withaferin A
Developers: Umea University; University of Texas Medical Branch; Regional Centre for Biotechnology, India
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of CHIKV infection
Mechanism of action:
-Inhibits nsP2 protease activity; binds to protease and disrupts cleavage of viral non-structural polyproteins.
-This inhibition reduces minus-sense viral RNA synthesis.
-The oxidizing chemical property of WFA is important: reducing agents (e.g. N-acetylcysteine, glutathione ester) reverse its protease inhibition and antiviral effect in cells.
Key features and challenges:
-In cultured cells (ERMS muscle lineage; also HeLa, Huh7, C2C12), WFA has IC₅₀ ≈ 0.45 µM, CC₅₀ ≈ 8.76 µM, giving a Selectivity Index (SI) ~19.4. 
PMC.
-Reduces extracellular virus titers (~4- to 16-fold reductions) and viral RNA levels (~2.5- to 8-fold) in vitro depending on timepoint and cell line.
-In vivo in C57BL/6 mice: WFA given intraperitoneally (5 mg/kg twice daily, starting 4 h post-infection) reduced viremia, markedly reduced footpad swelling (edema), and accelerated resolution. 
-No CHIKV symptoms (or much milder) in WFA-treated mice vs untreated; edema sharply reduced.
Recent updates:
Dec 2024: 
-Publication shows WFA active in mouse model, confirming reduction of viremia and clinical signs. 
Demonstrated that WFA’s antiviral action is protease-specific and reversible with reducing agents.
-The SI (~19) is moderate, and CC₅₀ is relatively close to antiviral IC₅₀, so therapeutic window might be tight in development.

Name: Woost menstrual blood at-home test kit
Developers: Woost
Indication: Detection of biomarkers indicative of PCOS
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Mechanism of action: Analyse biomarkers in mentrual blood
Key features and challenges:
Woost Ltd is a femtech start-up focused on improving women's health diagnostics, particularly for conditions like polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). They are developing at-home test kits designed to analyze biomarkers in menstrual blood to aid in the early detection of PCOS. 
A one-year clinical study funded by an Innovate UK Smart grant is underway to demonstrate the solution’s technical feasibility. 
(https://gtr.ukri.org/projects?ref=10100544)
(https://www.theengineer.co.uk/content/news/startup-developing-screening-tool-for-polycystic-ovary-syndrome/)

Name: XVR 021
Developers: ExeVir Bio
Indication: Prevention and treatment of dengue fever caused by DENV
Mechanism of action: Neutralise specific targets associated with the dengue virus
Key features and challenges: XVR-021 is an investigational single-domain antibody (nanobody) developed by ExeVir Bio for the treatment and prevention of dengue. Currently in the preclinical stage, it is undergoing early research and development. In June 2023, ExeVir Bio received a €1.6 million grant from VLAIO to support its advancement. With no specific antiviral treatments available for dengue, XVR-021 presents a promising approach, utilising the small size and stability of nanobodies for precise viral neutralisation. (https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800074315)

Name: Xafty
Developers: Hyundai Bioscience
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of DENV
Mechanism of action: Virus internalisation inhibitor
Key features and challenges: Niclosamide, traditionally an antiparasitic agent, is being investigated for its antiviral activity against dengue virus (DENV). Research suggests it inhibits DENV infection by targeting endosomal acidification, a key step in viral replication. In vitro studies show it reduces DENV replication in human cells by neutralizing acidic intracellular vesicles, blocking viral entry and replication. To address bioavailability challenges, Hyundai Bioscience has developed a novel formulation to maintain therapeutic concentrations, targeting DENV and other mosquito-borne viruses like Zika, Chikungunya, and Yellow Fever. A basket-type clinical trial in Brazil is planned to evaluate its efficacy in patients infected with these viruses. (https://adis.springer.com/trials/700373098) (https://storage.googleapis.com/pcf_sb_39_1613727931605803249/assets/supporting/mediarelease/1884/809415536.html)

Name: Xanthoquinodins
Developers: University of Oklahoma
Indication: Investigated for the treatment of Trichomoniasis.
Mechanism of action: Unknown.
Key features and challenges:
Xanthoquinodins are fungal-derived xanthone–anthraquinone heterodimer secondary metabolites under investigation for antitrichomonal activity against Trichomonas vaginalis. Although historically underexplored, xanthoquinodins have demonstrated inhibitory effects against multiple pathogens, including protozoan parasites and fungi.
A 2023 study evaluating compounds isolated from a Trichocladium species reported that xanthoquinodins A1 and A2 exhibited potent activity against T. vaginalis, with EC₅₀ values of 3.9 μM and 6.8 μM, respectively (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37276438/). 
No cytotoxicity was observed in HepG2 cells at the highest concentration tested (EC₅₀ > 25 μM). Earlier findings also indicated that xanthoquinodin A1 reduced parasite growth, supporting its potential as a lead compound for further development.
Key challenges include limited understanding of structure–activity relationships, need for mechanistic elucidation, and absence of in vivo efficacy data. Optimization of pharmacokinetic properties and evaluation in relevant infection models are required before clinical consideration.
Overall, xanthoquinodins represent a promising class of fungal-derived natural products with potent in vitro activity against T. vaginalis. Further preclinical investigation is necessary to determine their therapeutic development potential.

Name: XfoldTB
Developers: Xfold Imaging Oy
Indication: Indicated for the detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis and drug resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid.
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Key features and challenges: Molecular assay based on LAMP in a Cartridge-based processing format; validated on sputum specimen(s); detecting Mycobacterium tuberculosis and drug resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid.

Name: Xpert MTB Host Response assay
Developers: Cepheid; QuantuMDx Group Ltd; BioMerieux; The Francis Crick Institute; University of Leicester
Indication: Indicated for monitoring of treatment response in patients with tuberculosis.
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Key features and challenges: The RNA tests, or transcriptomic assays, can detect and quantify the expression of specific gene signaturese in the RNA transcriptome that are activated by the presence of TB bacteria, thus serving as biomarkers for the presence and bacterial load of TB in the body. These tests utilise the same nucleic acid extraction and amplification technologies as rapid molecular tests. A range of transcriptomic gene signatures show promise, including Sweeney3, RISK6 and RISK11, and according to early studies the performance of these gene signatures has been found to be similar. Several companies including Cepheid, QuantuMDx and bioMerieux are developing transcriptomic biomarker-based assays for incipient TB and treatment monitoring utilising finger-prick blood samples. The performance of these assays does not yet meet the minimal criteria set in the TPP for incipient TB and treatment monitoring, including the capability to predict progression to active TB up to two years prior to the onset of active disease therefore, more R&D is needed to improve their performance.

Name: YF17D-vectored Ebola vaccine (YF-EBO)
Developers: KU Leuven, Katholieke Universiteit Leuven
Indication: Indicated for active immunization to protect against Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) caused by Zaire Ebola virus
Mechanism of action: Single-dose live vaccine that induces humoral and cellular immune responses against both EBOV GP and YF17D antigens. Protection is mediated by Th1-polarized T cell responses and EBOV GP-specific binding antibodies.
Key features and challenges:
-Dual-target vaccine: protects against both Ebola virus and Yellow fever virus.
-Attenuated phenotype: safer than parental YF17D; reduced neurovirulence in AG129 mice and neonatal BALB/c pups.
-Durability: EBOV GP expression genetically stable for ≥8 passages.
-Protection: A single dose (250 PFU) provided complete protection in Ifnar−/− mice challenged with lethal rVSV-EBOV; also protected against lethal intracranial YF17D challenge.
-Cross-reactivity: Additional constructs (YF-SUD, YF-BDB, YF-TAF) elicited antibodies cross-reactive with other ebolaviruses (SUDV, BDBV, TAFV).
Recent updates:
August 2023:
-First demonstration that a single YF17D-based dual-target vaccine protects simultaneously against EBOV and YFV.
-Proposed as a candidate for endemic regions under WHO’s Eliminate Yellow Fever Epidemics (EYE) strategy.

Name: YG 1805
Developers: Youngene Therapeutics
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: Undefined mechanism
Key features and challenges:
YG 1805 is an investigational antihyperglycaemic agent being developed by Youngene Therapeutics. The compound is under preclinical development in China and is being explored for multiple indications, including heart failure, constipation, diabetic nephropathy, and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
https://adis.springer.com/drugs/800072114
Although detailed mechanistic data have not been publicly disclosed, YG 1805 is positioned as a metabolic modulator. Given the central role of insulin resistance and hyperinsulinemia in the pathophysiology of PCOS, antihyperglycaemic agents represent a biologically plausible therapeutic strategy for improving endocrine and metabolic abnormalities associated with the condition.
At present, there are no published preclinical data specific to PCOS models, nor are there registered clinical trials evaluating YG 1805 in women with PCOS. Information regarding its molecular target, pharmacokinetic properties, dosing strategy, and safety profile has not been publicly reported.
Key challenges include the absence of disclosed mechanism of action, lack of PCOS-specific efficacy data, and the early stage of development. Additionally, competition from established insulin-sensitizing therapies (e.g., metformin, GLP-1 receptor agonists, dual incretin agonists) may require YG 1805 to demonstrate clear differentiation in efficacy, safety, or tolerability to justify clinical advancement in PCOS. Regulatory progression will depend on the generation of robust preclinical and early-phase human data.
Overall, YG 1805 represents an early-stage antihyperglycaemic candidate with potential relevance to the metabolic features of PCOS. However, given the absence of publicly available mechanistic and clinical evidence, it should currently be considered a preclinical, exploratory candidate for PCOS management.

Name: YS1646
Developers: McGill University (including The Royal Institution for the Advancement of Learning); Canadian National Institute of Scientific Research (INRS)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment and prevention of schistosomiasis
Mechanism of action: Systemic and local humoral responses to CatB
Key features and challenges:
A 2023 study showed that a repurposed an attenuated Salmonella enterica Typhimurium strain (YS1646) to express Cathepsin B (CatB), a digestive enzyme important for the juvenile and adult stages of the S. mansoni life cycle. (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41541-023-00599-w).Previous studies have demonstrated the prophylactic and therapeutic efficacy of our plasmid-based vaccine. The study shows they generated chromosomally integrated (CI) YS1646 strains that express CatB to produce a viable candidate vaccine for eventual human use (stability, no antibiotic resistance).

The biologic candidate works by effecting a humoral response to a key digestive enzyme of the parasite, Cathepsin B (CatB), rather than external tegumental proteins.

Name: Yaso-GEL
Developers: Henry M. Jackson Foundation for the Advancement of Military Medicine; Uniformed Services University
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: PPCM is proposed to directly impact gonococcal viability.
Key features and challenges:
Yaso-GEL is a topical gel formulation containing polyphenylene carboxymethylene (PPCM), a condensation polymer with contraceptive and antimicrobial properties. PPCM has demonstrated activity against several sexually transmitted pathogens and is being investigated as a non-hormonal, non-systemic multipurpose prevention product.
A 2023 study evaluated Yaso-GEL containing PPCM and reported significant in vitro and in vivo activity against Neisseria gonorrhoeae in a female mouse model (https://sti.bmj.com/content/99/6/409). The formulation demonstrated antimicrobial efficacy while maintaining its contraceptive properties, supporting its potential as a dual-function product targeting both unintended pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections.
Key challenges include translation of murine efficacy to human clinical effectiveness, assessment of safety and tolerability with repeated mucosal use, and evaluation of real-world adherence and acceptability. Clinical trials will be required to establish protective efficacy against gonorrhea in humans.
Overall, Yaso-GEL represents a multipurpose prevention strategy combining contraceptive and antimicrobial activity. Further clinical development is required to determine its role in gonorrhea prevention and broader STI control.

Name: ZF0901
Developers: Beijing Zhifei Lvzhu Biopharmaceutical
Indication: Indicated for active immunization for the prevention of bacillary dysentery caused by both Shigella sonnei and Shigella flexneri
Target: Shigella flexneri 2a and Shigella sonnei Lipopolysaccharides (LPS)
Mechanism of action: Induces humoral immune response to the LPS of S. flexneri 2a and S. sonnei
Key features and challenges: Beijing Zhifei Lvzhu Biopharmaceutical Co., Ltd is currently advancing its bivalent conjugate vaccine candidate to phase III clinical development (NCT05156528). The Shigella vaccine, also known as ZF0901 is composed of O-specific polysaccharides purified and detoxified from lipopolysaccharides (LPS) of S. flexneri 2a and S. sonnei and covalently bonded to a tetanus toxoid.
Recent updates: Phase III trial commenced in 2021 (NCT05156528).

Name: ZH548-rA2 (triple mutant RVFV)
Developers: Centro de Investigación en Sanidad Animal CISA INIA/CSIC; Centre de Recerca en Sanitat Animal (CReSA)
Indication: Prevention of RVFV infection in livestock (sheep, goats, cattle) and potential human use
Mechanism of action: Virus carries three defined amino acid substitutions (G924S, A1303T in RdRp; P82L in NSs), resulting in impaired replication and virulence, while still inducing protective humoral and cellular immunity
Key features and challenges:
-Safe in sheep: caused no clinical signs or liver pathology after high-dose inoculation (10⁷ pfu).
-Protective efficacy: vaccinated sheep were fully protected against challenge with parental virulent ZH548-rC1 strain; no liver lesions observed post-challenge.
-Immune responses: induced neutralizing antibodies by day 4–7 pi; T-cell IFNγ responses confirmed via recombinant Gn/N peptides.
-Attenuation validated in both mice and sheep.
-Challenges: exploratory pilot (n=6 sheep); larger animal and pregnant livestock studies needed; unknown cross-protection against heterologous strains (e.g., ZH501).
Recent updates:
-Builds on earlier work identifying attenuating polymerase (G924S, A1303T) and NSs (P82L) mutations.
-Considered a promising next-generation LAV with defined genetic basis for attenuation, reducing reversion risk compared to Clone 13 or MP-12.
-2023–2025 reviews (e.g., Wichgers Schreur et al., Vaccines) highlight rA2 as one of the leading rationally designed RVFV LAVs.
-Suggested combining rA2 mutations with MP-12 or Clone 13 backbones to further improve safety for ruminants and pregnant animals.

Name: ZIKV M/E saRNA (with OX40 and 4-1BB agonism)
Developers: University of California, San Diego (UCSD)
Indication: Prevention of ZIKV disease and associated complications (e.g., congenital Zika syndrome).
Mechanism of action: saRNA replicon derived from Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus (VEEV) drives prolonged antigen expression of ZIKV M/E, inducing humoral and cellular immunity. Protection is primarily mediated by CD8⁺ T-cell responses; neutralizing antibodies contribute to early viral control but wane quickly.
Key features and challenges:
Features:
-Elicits both antibody and T-cell responses in wild-type and Ifnar1−/− mouse models.
-Reduces viremia and tissue viral burden after ZIKV challenge.
-Encapsulation in LNPs yields >90% efficiency.
-Durability improved by co-administration of OX40 + 4-1BB agonist antibodies, sustaining CD8⁺ T-cell–mediated protection up to 84 days.

Challenges:
-Immunity from saRNA vaccine alone is short-lived (wanes by day 84).
-Requires external agonists/adjuvants to achieve durable protection.
-Potential regulatory complexity of combining vaccine + immunomodulatory antibodies.
Recent updates:
2025 Publication: 
-Demonstrated that a prime-boost regimen with ZIKV M/E saRNA vaccine reduced viral loads in serum and organs of Ifnar1−/− mice challenged with high-dose ZIKV.
-Identified that immunity from saRNA alone wanes rapidly, but durability can be significantly extended by co-administration of OX40 + 4-1BB agonist antibodies, which maintain protective CD8⁺ T-cell responses at 84 days post-vaccination.
-Suggests combining saRNA vaccine platforms with TNFR-superfamily agonists as a strategy for durable immunity against ZIKV and other flaviviruses.

Name: ZIKV prME mRNA-loaded PPSNs
Developers: Seoul National University (SNU); Lemonex Inc
Indication: Prevention of ZIKV infection and congenital Zika syndrome.
Target: ZIKV prM and E glycoproteins (expression generates subviral particles that mimic ZIKV antigens)
Mechanism of action: PPSNs deliver prME mRNA locally at the injection site, inducing intracellular antigen expression and subviral particle formation; elicits robust neutralizing antibodies and multifunctional CD4+/CD8+ T cell responses, conferring complete protection in mice.
Key features and challenges:
-PPSNs overcome limitations of LNPs by reducing systemic off-target expression and prolonging local translation.
-Single intramuscular dose induced high IgG titers (endpoint ~180,000) and neutralizing antibodies (FRNT50 ~3,000).
-Robust Th1-biased CD4+ and CD8+ T cell polyfunctional responses.
-Provided 100% survival against lethal ZIKV MR766 challenge and protection against Asian genotype ZIKV Brazil/16 321 in mice.
-Exhibited favorable safety profile (no toxicity, no organ pathology, normal blood chemistry).
Polyethyleneimine (PEI)-coated porous silica nanoparticle (PPSN)
Recent updates:
Sept 2024 Publication:
-First demonstration of porous silica nanoparticle–based mRNA delivery for ZIKV, showing improved biodistribution vs. LNPs (localized retention, minimal liver/spleen expression).
-PPSNs elicited stronger and more durable humoral and cellular immunity compared to LNPs in head-to-head tests.
-Manufacturing process is simpler than LNPs (no microfluidics needed), which may lower costs and accelerate scale-up.

Name: ZIKV-1-PP4
Developers: National Taiwan University College of Medicine
Indication: Prevention of ZIKV infection and disease
Mechanism of action: Induces neutralizing antibodies; enhances innate immune activation and dendritic-cell costimulation with elevated IL-12, IFN-γ, IL-1β, TNF-α, conferring reduced susceptibility upon ZIKV challenge in mice.
Key features and challenges:
High titer and homogeneous morphology; prime-boost with inactivated PP4 elicits significant neutralizing antibodies and improved post-challenge outcomes in mice; needs confirmation of sterilizing protection, durability, adjuvanting, and manufacturing/inactivation process controls for translation beyond murine models.
Inactivated whole-virus vaccine using a high-titer, plaque-purified Vero-adapted ZIKV clone (PP4)
Recent updates:
2024 Press:
-Reported this plaque-purified inactivated clone (ZIKV-1_PP4) as a new Zika vaccine candidate.
Broader field reviews (2024–2025) note no approved ZIKV vaccines to date and continued preclinical/early-clinical exploration across platforms.

Name: ZIKV-117
Developers: Vanderbilt University; Washington University School of Medicine; IDRI
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Zika virus infection
Mechanism of action: Inhibits rearrangement of the E protein
Key features and challenges: ZIKV117 treatment reduced tissue pathology, placental and fetal infection and mortality in mouse model.
Recent updates: There are 2 papers, one detailed in vivo positive results and another one showed 3D cryoEM structure of the Zika virus binding with ZIKV-117 monoclonal antibody.

Name: ZIKV-117-LALA-YTE
Developers: Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center; BIOQUAL
Indication: Prevention and treatment of ZIKV disease, including congenital Zika syndrome risk reduction.
Target: ZIKV Envelope (E) protein, Domain II dimer epitope (cross-links E dimers to block fusion).
Mechanism of action: Neutralizes ZIKV by binding E protein dimers, cross-linking them, and preventing low-pH mediated conformational rearrangements required for viral fusion and entry; Fc engineering reduces ADE and extends serum half-life.
Key features and challenges:
-Derived from parental ZIKV-117 mAb (ultrapotent neutralizer).
-Complete protection in rhesus macaques at 0.016 mg/kg (median serum 0.13 µg/mL).
-Estimated protective threshold: 0.014–0.088 µg/mL.
-LALA mutations minimize ADE; YTE substitution prolongs persistence.
-Manufactured antibody stocks provided by IDBiologics; potential scalability.
Human IgG1 neutralizing monoclonal antibody with LALA (reduced FcγR binding) and YTE
Recent updates:
Nov 2024 Publication: The first study to establish a quantitative protective threshold in non-human primates for a ZIKV mAb (0.014–0.088 µg/mL).
-Builds on earlier murine studies of ZIKV-117; confirms translation to macaques with exquisite potency.
-Highlights ZIKV-117 as the only ultrapotent Zika-specific neutralizing mAb described to date, strengthening its candidacy for clinical development.

Name: ZINC000253403245/ZINC000008876351
Developers: Indian Institute of Technology (BHU) Varanasi (IIT BHU)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Leishmaniasis
Target: Mitochondrial iron superoxide dismutase A (FeSODA); trypanothione reductase (TR)
Mechanism of action: Inhibition of both the FeSODA and TR enzymes
Key features and challenges: Mitochondrial iron superoxide dismutase A (FeSODA) and trypanothione reductase (TR) are critical enzymes in the antioxidant defense mechanism of Leishmania donovani. FeSODA is responsible for neutralizing reactive oxygen species in mitochondria, while TR is responsible for reducing trypanothione, the molecules that help the parasite fight oxidative stress in Leishmania. In this study, we used multitarget ligands to inhibit both the FeSODA and TR enzymes. We combined structure-based drug design using virtual screening approach to find inhibitors against both the targets. The ZINC15 database of biogenic compounds was utilized to extract drugs-like molecules against leishmaniasis. The compounds were screened by standard precision (SP) and extra precision (XP) docking methods. Two compounds, ZINC000008876351 and ZINC000253403245, were selected based on molecular docking based on the binding affinity for both the targets. The screened molecules ZINC000008876351 and ZINC000253403245 showed strong hydrogen bonding with the target proteins according to the Molecular mechanics with generalised Born and surface area solvation (MM-GBSA) techniques. These two compounds were also experimentally investigated on promastigotes stage of L. donovani. Under in vitro condition, the compounds show inhibitory effects on L. donovani promastigotes with IC50 values of 24.82 ± 0.61 µM for ZINC000008876351 and 7.52 ± 0.17 µM for ZINC000253403245. Thus, the screened compounds seem to have good potential as therapeutic candidates for leishmaniasis.
Recent updates: Preclinical results published in 2023 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37884555/) and 2024 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39388970/).

Name: ZKA64
Developers: SG Giuseppe Moscati Hospital; Humabs BioMed SA; Università della Svizzera italiana
Indication: Treatment and post-exposure/prophylaxis of ZIKV disease; reduction of maternal–fetal transmission is an intended application for potent anti-E antibodies (class rationale).
Target: ZIKV E protein Domain III (EDIII); ZIKV-specific with minimal DENV cross-reactivity.
Mechanism of action: Potently neutralizes ZIKV by binding EDIII and blocking virion attachment/conformational changes required for entry; the LALA Fc substitutions retain neutralization while reducing antibody-dependent enhancement risk.
Key features and challenges:
-High in-vitro potency (IC50 ≈ ~93 ng/mL) and ZIKV specificity. 
-In vivo efficacy in A129 mice when given 1 day before or 1 day after lethal challenge (LALA variant).
-ADE risk for some anti-E antibodies at sub-neutralizing titers; LALA engineering is used to mitigate this.
Human IgG1 neutralizing mAb targeting the Envelope (E) protein Domain III (EDIII) lateral-ridge epitope
Recent updates: -Recognition of EDIII by ZKA-64 used as a benchmark in newer vaccine/antigen design and VLP studies (2019–2025), reinforcing epitope specificity (no new clinical development).

Name: ZM-H1505R
Developers: Zhimeng Biopharma
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of chronic HBV infection

Key features and challenges: Antibiotic resistance is an increasing threat, requiring novel therapeutic solutions. Metal nanoparticles e.g., zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO NPs) exhibited the potential against many bacterial pathogens. Strains of Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi resistant to ceftriaxone were reported first from Pakistan in 2016. Since then, S. Typhi is a pathogen of concern globally owing to its rapidly emerging resistance potential against many last resort antibiotics. In the present study, in vitro and in vivo antimicrobial activity of ZnO NPs against multidrug resistant (MDR) and extensively drug resistant (XDR) Salmonella Typhi strains from Pakistan was evaluated. Zinc oxide green nanoparticles (ZnO GNPs), synthesized from Aloe vera, were characterized by SEM, XRD, UV-vis and Raman spectroscopy. In vitro antibacterial activity of two different concentrations of ZnO GNPs (7 and 15%) was checked using agar well diffusion method. Further, broth microdilution and time kill assays were performed using the ZnO GNPs. In vivo assays were conducted in BALB/c mice sepsis models. In all the three methods, agar well diffusion assay broth microdilution and time kill assay, different zinc oxide dihydrate precursor concentrations had shown the antibacterial activity. The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of ZnO GNPs nanoparticles against MDR and XDR S. Typhi strains was found as 16 to 64 µg/ml. In vivo experiment has shown a significant decrease in CFU/ml in the mice treated with ZnO GNPs as compared to the control group. Our findings have revealed that ZnO GNPs have significant antibacterial activity against MDR and XDR S. Typhi, both in vitro and in vivo (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42770-024-01522-8).

Name: anti-MBG human monoclonal antibody
Developers: Larix Bioscience, LLC
Indication: Effective treatment of PE
Mechanism of action: The candidate blocks MBG-mediated signaling.
Key features and challenges:
An anti-MBG human monoclonal antibody (humAb) is an investigational biologic designed to selectively bind and neutralize marinobufagenin (MBG), an endogenous cardiotonic steroid implicated in the pathophysiology of preeclampsia (PE). Elevated plasma MBG levels have been observed in pregnancies complicated by PE and are associated with vascular fibrosis, sodium retention, endothelial dysfunction, and hypertension. By targeting MBG, the antibody aims to interrupt MBG-mediated signaling pathways that contribute to placental and systemic vascular pathology.
Candidate anti-MBG humAbs have been screened for high binding affinity and specificity. The selected lead antibody demonstrated nanomolar dissociation constant (Kd), limited cross-reactivity with structurally related cardiotonic steroids, and the ability to block MBG-mediated activation of downstream signaling pathways in preclinical models. These characteristics support its development as a targeted therapeutic strategy for PE.
Current development is in the preclinical Phase 1 stage. Planned studies include pharmacokinetic evaluation (plasma half-life), dose–response characterization, and toxicology assessments, including teratogenicity testing in relevant animal models of preeclampsia. Phase 2 preclinical work will focus on generating additional safety, pharmacology, and manufacturing data required for submission of an Investigational New Drug (IND) application.
https://reporter.nih.gov/search/Indd2eZPT0qwg9o9nO8p0g/project-details/10478384
As a monoclonal antibody therapy intended for use in pregnancy, translational considerations include placental transfer, fetal exposure risk, immunogenicity, dosing optimization, and long-term maternal–fetal safety. Biologic therapies also involve complex manufacturing and regulatory pathways.
The anti-MBG human monoclonal antibody represents a mechanistically targeted biologic approach aimed at neutralizing a putative pathogenic mediator in preeclampsia. While preclinical data suggest specificity and pathway inhibition, clinical efficacy and safety in human pregnancy remain to be established.

Name: bivalent TbpB formulation
Developers: Virginia Commonwealth University
Indication: Prevention of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Immunostimulant - provide immunologic cross-protection against both asymptomatic colonisation and pathogenic inflammation caused by diverse N. gonorrhoeae strains
Key features and challenges:
A bivalent TbpB formulation is an investigational protein-based vaccine strategy targeting Neisseria gonorrhoeae transferrin-binding proteins, particularly transferrin-binding protein B (TbpB), which plays a critical role in iron acquisition during infection. Iron uptake systems are essential for gonococcal survival and virulence, making TbpB an attractive conserved surface antigen for vaccine development. Rationally designed Tbp-based vaccines aim to induce cross-protective immune responses capable of preventing both asymptomatic colonization and inflammatory disease across diverse N. gonorrhoeae strains.
In 2017, a funded research program was initiated to design engineered TbpA and TbpB antigens combined with an experimentally selected adjuvant (https://reporter.nih.gov/search/adDzWAtTaEG3AlSVt1GB6w/project-details/9309268). 
The project objectives included optimization of vaccine delivery in a humanized female mouse model of lower genital tract infection, evaluation of protective efficacy in newly developed humanized infection models, and assessment of cross-protection across multiple infection settings.
More recently, in 2024, additional funded research has supported further development of a protein-based vaccine specifically targeting gonococcal TbpB, reinforcing continued investment in this antigen as a vaccine candidate (https://reporter.nih.gov/search/RK4F7c1hkkK--nBC8EhISA/project-details/10757312).
Key challenges include translation from animal models to durable human protection, antigen variability across circulating strains, and identification of immune correlates of protection. Gonorrhea vaccine development is further complicated by the pathogen’s immune evasion mechanisms and lack of naturally acquired protective immunity following infection. Progression beyond preclinical stages will require demonstration of safety, immunogenicity, and broad strain coverage.
Overall, the bivalent TbpB formulation represents a rational, antigen-targeted vaccine strategy focused on iron acquisition mechanisms in N. gonorrhoeae. Continued preclinical development and funding support highlight its promise, although human clinical validation remains a critical next step.

Name: cLipo-DC
Developers: Anhui Medical University
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Endometriosis.
Mechanism of action: Binds to neutrophils and accumulated in ectopic lesions to inhibit glycolysis and autophagy in both 12Z and Ishikawa cells, resulting in cell death.
Key features and challenges:
cLipo-DC is a reactive oxygen species (ROS)-responsive liposomal drug delivery platform designed to selectively target ectopic endometriotic lesions. Endometriosis is characterized by chronic inflammation, persistent neutrophil recruitment, and elevated ROS levels within lesions. Conventional systemic therapies lack lesion specificity and are often associated with hormonal side effects. Targeted delivery systems may therefore improve therapeutic precision while minimizing off-target exposure.
A 2025 preclinical study developed a neutrophil-targeting liposome (cLipo) modified with surface peptides to exploit neutrophil recruitment and inflammatory homing mechanisms within endometriotic lesions (https://www.thno.org/v15p4848.htm). 
The liposomes were engineered to be ROS-responsive and were co-loaded with 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG), a glycolysis inhibitor, and chloroquine (CQ), an autophagy inhibitor, forming the formulation cLipo-DC. In a minimally invasive mouse model of endometriosis, cLipo demonstrated selective binding to neutrophils and preferential accumulation within ectopic lesions following intraperitoneal administration.
In vitro studies using human endometriotic (12Z) and endometrial cancer (Ishikawa) cell lines showed that cLipo-DC effectively inhibited glycolysis and autophagy, leading to cell death. In vivo treatment in the endometriosis mouse model resulted in significant lesion suppression without detectable adverse effects. The approach represents a novel “neutrophil hitchhiking” strategy for targeted, non-hormonal therapy of endometriosis.
Key challenges include the early preclinical stage of development, with no human safety or efficacy data available. Long-term toxicity, immunogenicity, biodistribution, and nanoparticle clearance profiles require comprehensive evaluation. Scalability, manufacturing consistency, and regulatory approval pathways for complex nanomedicine platforms also pose translational barriers. While cLipo-DC demonstrates promising lesion-specific targeting and dual metabolic inhibition in animal models, further validation in larger preclinical studies and eventual clinical trials is required before potential clinical application.

Recent updates:

Key features and challenges: 2024 Study:  In this work, we investigated the effects of human amniotic epithelial cells (hAECs) in PE rat model. The rats were induced with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) on gestational day 14.5 followed by injection of hAECs and human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells 24 h later. The hAECs treatment resulted in a reduction in blood pressure and proteinuria in the PE rat model. Furthermore, hAECs treatment decreased levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, reduced inflammatory cells aggregation, and alleviated the damage to placental spiral arteries by downregulating the expression of anti-angiogenic factor and upregulating proangiogenic factor. In vitro experiments confirmed that hAECs treatment restored the proliferation, migration, and angiogenesis of LPS-damaged human umbilical vein endothelial cells. Additionally, hAECs treatment had positive effects on fetal weight and neurological development in the PE group, with no negative effects on the physical development or fertility of offspring rats. These results suggested that hAECs transplantation may be a novel adjuvant therapeutic strategy for PE by reducing the inflammatory and enhancing placental spiral artery angiogenesis (https://academic.oup.com/biolreprod/article-abstract/111/4/906/7723470?redirectedFrom=fulltext)

Finally, they created an ensemble model-based risk stratification card with five risk levels for PE patients, achieving 94.62% accuracy and 0.99 AUC, and launched an online tool called iPlacenta for classifying placental cell types and assessing PE risk. http://bioinfor.imu.edu.cn/placenta (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36849879/).

Name: lpxc inhibitor
Developers: Taisho Pharmaceutical; Blacksmith Medicines Inc.
Indication: Treatment of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Inhibiting the biosynthesis of lipid A components with LpxC inhibitors and disrupting outer membrane integrity with CPP
Key features and challenges:
LpxC inhibitors are investigational antimicrobial agents targeting lipid A biosynthesis in Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The lipid A component of gonococcal lipooligosaccharide (LOS) is a key inducer of cytokine-mediated inflammation and contributes to bacterial survival and pathogenicity. Targeting lipid A biosynthesis, particularly through inhibition of the LpxC enzyme, represents a strategy to disrupt outer membrane integrity and reduce both bacterial viability and host inflammatory response.
Preclinical research has identified LpxC inhibitors and 12–amino acid cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) as promising candidates against N. gonorrhoeae. Ongoing studies focus on optimizing these agents and evaluating their bactericidal activity, effects on cytokine induction, hemolysis, and cytotoxicity in vitro.
(https://reporter.nih.gov/search/nDIc7jbF70mwAY89k47uVw/project-details/10363529). 
Mechanistic investigations include assessment of DNA binding, membrane permeabilization, proteolysis resistance, protein interactions, and the impact of major gonococcal efflux pumps (MtrCDE, MacAB, and NorM) on antimicrobial activity. Lead candidates identified through in vitro studies are planned for evaluation in a female mouse model of infection.
Key challenges include early-stage development status, the need to demonstrate in vivo efficacy and safety, and potential resistance mechanisms mediated by efflux pumps. While targeting lipid A biosynthesis offers a novel therapeutic approach, substantial translational and clinical development work is required before LpxC inhibitors can be considered viable treatment options for gonorrhoea.

Overall, the mLAMP-AuNPs-LFB assay represents a rapid, visual molecular diagnostic approach for gonorrhea detection. Further clinical validation is required to establish implementation potential in decentralized settings.

-The authors note plans for cross-lineage evaluation (Bangladesh vs. Malaysia strains) and possible formulation optimization to address the 19 amino acid head-domain differences across NiV clades, but no new published results are available beyond this paper.

Name: mRNA influenza A (H5N1) pre-pandemic vaccine
Developers: GlaxoSmithKline (GSK)
Indication: Prevention of H5N1 influenza virus infection in healthy younger and older adults
Target: Hemagglutinin (HA) of influenza A H5N1 subtype (pandemic risk)
Mechanism of action: The mRNA instructs host cells to produce the H5 HA antigen, eliciting humoral (HAI/neutralizing antibodies) and cellular immune responses to protect against H5N1 influenza virus infection.
Key features and challenges:
Dose-finding Phase 1/2 trial in adults 18-85 yrs, younger and older cohorts, comparing several dose levels vs placebo. 
Designed as a pandemic-preparedness vaccine using mRNA platform; potential rapid manufacture and update.
Challenges: breadth across H5Nx clades, durability of protection, and translation from early immunogenicity data to efficacy are still to be demonstrated.
Recent updates: Featured in pipeline landscape reviews indicating mRNA-based H5N1 candidates are a major focus for pandemic influenza preparedness.

Name: mRNA vaccine (non-fusion GnGc with NSm linker)
Developers: Institut Pasteur; Fondation Mérieux; Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against CCHF
Target: CCHFV surface glycoproteins Gn and Gc, linked by NSm (non-structural protein).
Mechanism of action:
-Designed to express Gn and Gc together, using NSm as a linker to mimic glycoprotein processing.
-Induces humoral and cellular immune responses against glycoproteins.
-However, NSm reduces immunogenicity: antibody titers and T-cell responses were lower compared to Gc-only (vLMc) vaccines.
Key features and challenges:
-vLMc (Gc-only mRNA) outperformed both vLMn (Gn-only) and vLMs (GnNSmGc).
vLMs induced weaker IgG and IFN-γ T-cell responses compared to vLMc.
-NSm presence associated with reduced Gn and Gc expression and weaker immune stimulation.
-Suggests NSm acts as an antagonist of vaccine immunogenicity.
-ELISPOT showed diminished IFN-γ responses in vLMs vs vLMc groups.
-Indicates future mRNA vaccine design should exclude NSm for optimal efficacy.
Recent updates:
Feb 2024:
-First demonstration that including NSm in mRNA constructs reduces immunogenicity in CCHFV vaccines.
-Highlights importance of antigen design in mRNA vaccine development.

Name: mRNA vectored Nipah virus vaccine
Developers: The Pirbright Institute; Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness; University of Parma, Università degli Studi di Parma; University of Pennsylvania
Indication: Indicated for the prevention of Nipah virus infection
Target: Soluble G glycoprotein from the Malaysia strain of NiV
Key features and challenges: Preclinical study evaluated the immunogenicity of an mRNA vectored NiV vaccine candidate in pigs. Pigs were immunized twice with 100 μg nucleoside-modified mRNA vaccine encoding soluble G glycoprotein from the Malaysia strain of NiV, formulated in lipid nanoparticles. Potent antigen-binding and virus neutralizing antibodies were detected in serum following the booster immunization. Antibody responses effectively neutralized both the Malaysia and Bangladesh strains of NiV but showed limited neutralization of the related (about 80% amino acid sequence identity for G) Hendra virus. Antibodies were also capable of neutralizing NiV glycoprotein mediated cell-cell fusion. NiV G-specific T cell cytokine responses were also measurable following the booster immunization with evidence for induction of both CD4 and CD8 T cell responses. These data support the further evaluation of mRNA vectored NiV G as a vaccine for both pigs and humans .(https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2024.1384417/full)

Name: mRNA-1018
Developers: Moderna Therapeutics (including Valera)
Indication: Prevention of H5N1 influenza in healthy adults
Mechanism of action: Host cells translate the mRNA into H5 HA antigen, triggering humoral (HAI neutralizing antibodies) and cellular immune responses that target H5N1 virus infection.
Key features and challenges:
-Early clinical data show a very high rate of seroconversion (≥ HAI titer ≥ 1:40 in ~97.8% of participants) after two doses, despite very low baseline immunity (~2.1%) in participants. 
-The vaccine builds on Moderna’s mRNA platform used for COVID-19, allowing rapid design and scalable manufacturing.
-Because it is targeted at H5N1 (pandemic subtype) it is part of pandemic preparedness rather than seasonal influenza.
-Challenges: Translation to large trials and regulatory approval still pending; funding uncertainties (e.g., U.S. HHS grant cancellation) raise development risk.
Recent updates:
-Interim clinical data indicate potent and durable immune responses in adults after two doses. 
-U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) reportedly cancelled a ~$590 million funding award for the programme in mid-2025, creating uncertainty about late‐stage development.

F component covalently linked to G monomer (pre-F/G) of Malaysian strain NiV

Developers: Moderna Therapeutics (including Valera)
Indication: Active immunization for prevention of mpox
Target: Mpox virus M1 protein, A29 (A29L) envelope protein, A35 (A35R) protein and B6 (B6R) envelope glycoprotein
Mechanism of action: Immunostimulant
Key features and challenges:

In August 2023, Moderna therapeutics initiated a phase I/II trial to evaluate safety, efficacy and immunogenicity of mRNA 1769 in healthy volunteers (NCT05995275; mRNA-1769-P101). The randomised, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging, observer-blind trial intends to enrol 350 participants in the UK [1] Phase-I/II clinical trials in Monkeypox (Prevention) in United Kingdom (IM) (NCT05995275)
