Name: mRNA-1893
Developers: Moderna Therapeutics (including Valera)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against Zika virus infection
Mechanism of action: Induces neutralizing Ab immune response
Key features and challenges: This vaccine contains envelope E structural protein prME from the RIO-U1 Zika virus isolate.
Recent updates:
No new clinical trials or sponsor updates reported since the Phase 2 trial completed its primary endpoint in July 2024. The candidate remains in Phase 2 status. Awaiting public disclosure of final results or advancement plans. No indication of discontinuation.
Phase I study published in Jan 2023 and the vaccine candidate was well tolerated and immunogenic.

Name: mRNA-1E5-LNP
Developers: Beijing Institute of Biotechnology (BIB)
Indication: Prevention and treatment of henipavirus disease
Mechanism of action: In vivo translation of mRNA yields the 1E5 antibody, which neutralizes NiV and HeV by blocking G protein–mediated receptor interaction and viral entry.
Key features and challenges:
Synthetic mRNA encoding the 1E5 heavy/light chains, optimized UTRs, LNP-encapsulated for systemic delivery
Optimized 5′/3′ UTRs (DH1 + HBA1) greatly improved translation efficiency compared to natural or Moderna UTRs.
-High antibody yields in vitro (>1500 ng/mL) and in vivo (up to 42.3 µg/mL after 1 mg/kg i.v. injection).
-Provided rapid (within hours) and durable protection in mice against NiV and HeV pseudoviruses.
-Stable for ≥2 months at 4 °C without loss of activity.
-Challenges: no live-virus (BSL-4) evaluation yet, relatively high therapeutic dose required (≥0.5 mg/kg), short serum half-life (~14 days), LNP formulation requires further optimization
Recent updates:
April 2025 publication:
-In early preclinical development with published murine efficacy. 
-No reports yet of advancement into NHP models or clinical testing. 
-Authors highlight ongoing work to optimize UTR combinations and LNP formulations, and plan to extend evaluation to live NiV/HeV under BSL-4 conditions.

Name: mRNA-3012-LNP
Developers: Beijing University of Technology (BJUT)
Indication: Prevention of mpox infection
Target: MPXV A29L, A35R, B6R, M1R, and E8L (IMV + EV antigens).
Mechanism of action: The tandem multi-antigen design ensures broad coverage of IMV and EV forms of MPXV. After intramuscular delivery, LNP-encapsulated mRNAs are translated into viral antigens, eliciting humoral (neutralizing antibodies) and cellular (Th1-biased CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T-cell) responses.
Key features and challenges:
-Induced strong IgG titers against all 5 MPXV antigens (A29L, A35R, B6R, M1R, E8L) in mice after two doses.
-Generated dose-dependent neutralizing antibodies against VACV (higher at 25 µg vs 10 µg).
-Elicited robust Th1-biased cellular responses: elevated IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-2 from splenocytes; increased CD4⁺/CD8⁺ effector memory T cells.
-Provided effective protection against luciferase-expressing VACV (rTV-Fluc) in murine challenge studies (cleared bioluminescent signals).
-Passive serum transfer from vaccinated mice protected nude mice from VACV challenge (both in vitro and in vivo).
-Safety: No acute or immunological toxicity in mice; no histopathological damage to major organs; no elevation in cytokine storm markers.
-Challenge limitation: tested against VACV (surrogate), not MPXV itself; also focused on clade IIb design.
Recent updates:
Builds on earlier tetravalent mpox mRNA vaccines (mRNA-A-LNP, mRNA-B-LNP) by reducing complexity while expanding antigen coverage with E8L.

Complements other 2023–2025 mRNA platforms (BioNTech BNT166, Moderna mRNA-1769, Hou et al. VGPox series).
This tandem-fusion strategy is part of a trend toward cost-efficient multivalent mpox mRNA vaccines, simplifying manufacturing compared to 4–12 separate mRNA mixes.
Demonstrates feasibility of E8L inclusion (a less-explored but immunogenic EV antigen), potentially expanding protective breadth against diverse MPXV clades.
Considered a leading academic prototype among Chinese mpox mRNA vaccines, with potential for progression to NHP evaluation.

Name: mRNA-A-LNP / mRNA-B-LNP
Developers: Bioinformatics Center of AMMS; National Institutes for Food and Drug Control (NIFDC), Beijing
Indication: Prevention of mpox and other orthopoxvirus infections
Target: MPXV surface proteins A29L and M1R (IMV antigens), A35R and B6R (EEV antigens)
Mechanism of action: Intramuscular delivery of LNP-encapsulated mRNAs encoding A29L, A35R, M1R, B6R induces expression of viral proteins in host cells → strong MPXV-specific IgG and neutralizing antibodies (against VACV as surrogate) + robust Th1-biased T-cell and memory B/T cell responses; prevents viral replication and pathology after challenge.
Key features and challenges:
-Induces very high antigen-specific IgG titers and potent VACV neutralizing antibody titers after booster (NT50 ~1/6000) in mice.
-Generates Th1-biased CD4+/CD8+ T-cell responses, GC B cells, and memory T cells.
-Provides complete protection against VACV challenge in mice; sera transfer protected nude mice.
-Demonstrates favorable safety: no cytokine storm, organ toxicity, or cutaneous lesions in mice.
-Challenge model used VACV, not MPXV; no NHP or direct MPXV challenge yet.
Recent updates:
-Other groups have independently confirmed A29, A35, M1, B6 as highly conserved across MPXV clades and orthopoxviruses, supporting broad coverage.
-2024–2025 studies reported microneedle DNA and nanoparticle platforms encoding the same four antigens, showing protection in animals—validating this antigen constellation.
-mRNA poxvirus vaccine platforms are being adapted for pandemic preparedness, with Chinese and US groups exploring GMP-scale MPXV mRNA production.
-Discussion in 2024/2025 reviews: potential for cross-protection against smallpox (variola) and mpox resurgence, though clinical development pathway is not yet established.

Name: mRNA-ALAB-LNP
Developers: Yither Biotech
Indication: Prevention of mpox, smallpox, and potentially other orthopoxvirus infections.
Target:
-A27, L1 (IMV entry/attachment antigens).
-A33, B5 (EEV spread antigens).
-Cross-reactivity confirmed against homologous MPXV antigens A29, M1, A35, B6
Mechanism of action: mRNA encodes a fusion protein of four conserved VACV antigens. After intramuscular delivery, antigens are expressed in host cells, inducing strong humoral (neutralizing IgG) and cellular (IFN-γ T-cell) immunity. Cross-reactive antibodies bind to MPXV homologs, providing potential broad orthopoxvirus protection.
Key features and challenges:
-Immunogenicity in mice: After 2 doses (20 µg), high IgG titers against A27, L1, A33, B5 (anti-L1 peak ~810,000; anti-A33 ~1.45×10⁶).
-Neutralization: Sera neutralized VACV infection (mean NT₅₀ = 1:1431).
-Cellular responses: Strong IFN-γ T-cell responses, especially against A33 and A27 peptides (2,747 and 904 spots/10⁶ cells).
-Cross-reactivity: Equivalent or stronger IgG responses to MPXV homologs A29, M1, A35, and B6; post-boost titers reached 2.43×10⁶ (M1), 558,000 (A35), 1.78×10⁶ (B6).
-Safety: No abnormal histopathology or acute adverse effects in mice.
-Advantages: Broad-spectrum orthopoxvirus protection from a single mRNA, simplified manufacturing vs multi-mRNA cocktails.
Recent updates:
Follows a trend of tandem multi-antigen mRNA designs (e.g., mRNA-3012-LNP, MPXVac-097) to reduce complexity of multi-mRNA cocktails.
WHO and CEPI emphasize the need for broad orthopoxvirus stockpile vaccines; ALAB is one of the first explicitly designed for cross-protection beyond mpox.
Similar quadrivalent mRNA vaccines (Sang et al. 2022; Fang et al. 2023; Zhang et al. 2023) also validated the antigen set (M1/A29, A35, B6). ALAB instead uses VACV versions, leveraging >93% sequence conservation.
A patent has been filed by Yither Biotech and Ab＆B Biotech covering this construct

Name: mRNA-LNP prM/ENV dengue vaccine
Developers: Not specified
Indication: Investigated for the prevention of dengue
Target: Dengue virus pre-membrane (prM) and Envelope (E) proteins
Mechanism of action: Instructs host host-cells to synthesize and assemble native-like dengue subviral particles, driving balanced neutralizing antibodies
Key features and challenges: An mRNA-lipid-nanoparticle immunogen encoding dengue virus pre-membrane (prM) and Envelope (E) proteins that instructs host cells to assemble native-like subviral particles, driving balanced neutralising antibodies. Given intramuscularly. Also examined for flavivirus cross-reactivity.
Recent updates: Preclinical work generated fusion-loop-deleted mRNA-LNP prM-E vaccines for DENV serotypes 2, 3 and 4 (with chimeric E for improved VLP expression) that each elicited serotype-specific neutralising titres and protected mice against lethal homotypic challenge with reduced antibody-dependent enhancement, and a tetravalent formulation protected against all four serotypes (bioRxiv 10.1101/2025.07.21.665855).

Name: mRNA-encoded TB antigens
Developers: US National Institutes of Health (NIH); US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease (NIAID); ModernaTX, Inc.; International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI); Trudeau Institute, Inc.; University of Georgia Research Foundation, Inc.

Name: mRNA-encoded membrane-bound HIV Env trimer vaccine
Developers: Not specified
Indication: Indicated for the prevention of HIV-1 infection
Mechanism of action: Utilizes mRNA to instruct host host-cells to display anchored, native-conformation envelope proteins directly on surfaces
Key features and challenges: An mRNA immunogen instructing host cells to display an anchored, native-conformation HIV envelope trimer directly on cell surfaces to focus B-cell responses on non-base, neutralising epitopes. Given intramuscularly.
Recent updates: Preclinical evaluation of mRNA-delivered soluble and membrane-bound forms of a stabilised BG505 MD39.3 Env trimer showed, in rabbits and non-human primates, that the membrane-bound form elicited reduced off-target base-directed responses and stronger neutralising antibody responses than soluble Env (bioRxiv 10.1101/2025.01.24.634423).

Name: mRNA-mab22-LNP
Developers: Tecnologico de Monterrey, Campus Querétaro; University of Oslo
Indication: Prophylactic prevention & treatment of mpox infection.
Mechanism of action: In vivo expression of A33-neutralizing antibody
Key features and challenges: As a single agent, provided complete protection against weight loss and mortality in mice; durability and dose finding needed.

Name: mRNA-mab26-LNP
Developers: Tecnologico de Monterrey, Campus Querétaro; University of Oslo
Indication: Prophylactic prevention and treatment of mpox infection
Mechanism of action: Neutralizes IMV to block entry

Developers: Tecnologico de Monterrey, Campus Querétaro; University of Oslo

Mechanism of action: Host cells translate the mRNA to secrete anti-B5 IgG that neutralizes extracellular enveloped virions and blocks spread
Key features and challenges: Rapid antibody expression and single-dose protection in mice; breadth across orthopoxviruses suggested; durability and dose optimization vs. reactogenicity remain to be established

Name: mRNA-mab301-LNP
Developers: Tecnologico de Monterrey, Campus Querétaro; University of Oslo

Mechanism of action: Neutralizes IMV by blocking A27-mediated attachment/entry

Name: mc27902/mc27902 Δesx1
Developers: Albert Einstein College of Medicine
Indication: Prevention of TB
Target: panCD and lysA genes, esx-1 secretion system
Mechanism of action: Elicits cell mediated and humoral host response
Key features and challenges: Double auxotrophic mutants of Mtb lacking the ability to synthesize leucine and pantothenate are safe and sterilized in immunocompromised mice and SIV-infected Rhesus macaques. We examined how immunization with a Mtb triple auxotrophic strain, mc27902, which cannot synthesize leucine, pantothenate, and arginine, protects immunocompetent mice from a virulent Mtb infection. The route of immunization was a crucial factor for protection with mc27902 with intravenous immunization being 100 times more effective in protecting immunocompetent mice from Mtb challenge when compared to conventional subcutaneous vaccination with BCG. To further increase the safety of the attenuated auxotroph for vaccine purposes, the type VII secretion system Esx1 responsible for BCG attenuation was deleted in mc27902. When tested by prime-boost immunization of immunocompetent mice followed by aerosol challenge with virulent Mtb, mc27902 Δesx1 provided similar protection to mc27902. This robust protection against Mtb infection conferred by mc27902 and mc27902 Δesx1 in a mouse model paves the way for new TB vaccine development using highly attenuated, auxotrophic Mtb strains (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.05.15.594337v1).
Recent updates: https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.05.15.594337v1

Name: methanolic extract of soft coral Sarcophyton regulare
Developers: Misr University of Science and Technology (MUST)
Indication: Treatment of MERS-CoV infection
Target: Coronavirus main protease (Mpro), spike (S) protein, and nsp16/nsp10 complex
Mechanism of action: Fatty acid ester derivatives in the extract (hexadecanoic acid 2-hydroxy-1-(hydroxymethyl) ethyl ester; octadecanoic acid 2-hydroxy-1-(hydroxymethyl) ethyl ester) bind to MERS-CoV Mpro, S protein, and nsp16/10 in docking studies, potentially inhibiting viral proteolysis, receptor interaction, and RNA cap methylation.
Key features and challenges:
-Potency: In vitro antiviral activity with IC50 = 4.29 μg/ml and selectivity index (SI) = 112.2, highest among tested Red Sea coral extracts.
-Bioactive components: GC-MS revealed eight major compounds, including fatty acid esters (hexadecanoic acid, octadecanoic acid derivatives) and sterols (stigmast-5-en-3-ol, oleate).
-Docking: Identified esters showed favorable binding energies across three viral targets, with multiple H-bonds (e.g., −19.5 kcal/mol for Mpro, −11.8 kcal/mol for nsp16/10).
-Advantages: First report of coral-derived natural products with anti-MERS-CoV activity; high selectivity index; multiple viral targets.
-Challenges: Findings limited to in vitro cytopathic effect assays and in silico docking; no animal model or PK/PD data; batch-to-batch variability of natural extracts; purification and standardization needed before translational development.
Recent updates:
-Review articles in 2024–2025 cite this study as pioneering evidence of Red Sea coral metabolites with anti-MERS potential.
-Fatty acid esters like hexadecanoic acid and oleic acid, previously shown to disrupt enveloped viruses (HIV, influenza, HSV), are now highlighted for possible anti-CoV development.

Name: mi3-AM
Developers: Wuhan Institute of Virology
Indication: Prevention of mpox infection
Mechanism of action: The SpyTag-SpyCatcher system covalently displays A35R and M1R antigens on the mi3 nanoparticle scaffold. This multivalent display enhances antigen stability and immunogenicity, eliciting robust B-cell (antibody) and T-cell (CD4+/CD8+) responses against both forms of MPXV virions.
Key features and challenges:
-Self-assembling nanoparticle platform (mi3, derived from KDPG aldolase) displaying MPXV antigens.
-Induced strong IgG1/IgG2a antibody responses and neutralizing antibodies against both MPXV and VACV.
-Elicited Th1-biased cellular responses (IFN-γ, TNF-α in CD4+/CD8+ T cells).
-Provided complete protection against lethal VACV-WR challenge at day 42 and day 160 post-immunization in mice.
-Superior durability: antibody titers remained high at 5 months; protection persisted long-term compared to soluble AM vaccine.
-Improved stability of unstable A35R protein when conjugated to nanoparticles.
-Potential scalability via plug-and-display design.
Recent updates:
-Nanoparticle-based vaccines are advancing as next-gen orthopox platforms; the DAM two-in-one fusion vaccine (Nat Immunol 2024) also highlighted M1R+A35R as an optimal protective pair.
-The plug-and-display mi3 scaffold has been validated in SARS-CoV-2 and influenza vaccines, enabling rapid scale-up and adaptability.
-WHO and CEPI emphasize durability and thermostability as key features for outbreak response; nanoparticle vaccines like mi3-AM may bridge gaps in cold-chain dependent mRNA platforms.
-Antigen durability and manufacturing simplicity (compared to multi-mRNA cocktails) position mi3-AM as a strong translational candidate.

Name: miLab™
Developers: noul
Indication: Indicated for the diagnosis of P. falciparum and P.vivax infection
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Key features and challenges:
The device provides results with 5 µL blood in 20 minutes; the sample is loaded into a proprietary cartridge and inserted into the machine. Smear and staining are automatically completed, followed by optical imaging and AI analysis. Currently, the device provides Pf and parasitemia levels (parasites / µL); Pv detection is in development. MiLab also performs blood counts, including a WBC five part differential and CBC estimations. A clinical validation study is ongoing in South Korea, as is an independent study in Ghana.

Developer website - https://noul.kr/en/product-mal/

Name: miR-18a-5p
Developers: Science and Technology Fundamental Resources Investigation Program; Anhui Science and Technology University
Indication: Prevention and treatment of influenza A, caused by H5N1
Target: Host protein NEDD9 (Neural precursor cell expressed, developmentally downregulated 9), required for efficient influenza replication.
Mechanism of action: Overexpression of miR-18a-5p suppresses influenza virus replication by binding the 3′-UTR of NEDD9 mRNA, downregulating NEDD9 expression. This reduces viral NP and M1 protein production, attenuates replication, decreases pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-1β), while boosting type I interferon responses, thereby limiting viral pathogenicity.
Key features and challenges:
-First demonstration of miRNA-based therapeutic effect in both mammals and birds against H5N1.
-Cross-species efficacy: protective in mice and chickens.
-Reduced lung pathology, mortality, and pro-inflammatory cytokine levels.
-Highlights host-targeted antiviral strategy (avoids direct viral resistance mutations).
-Challenges: clinical translation of miRNA therapeutics (stability, delivery, off-target effects).
Recent updates:
March 2025:
-Builds on broader trend of host-directed antivirals using miRNAs.
-miR-18a-5p is part of the miR-17-92 cluster, previously implicated in antiviral regulation in other infections (HBV, EBV, enterovirus).
-Potential candidate for next-generation RNA-based antivirals but requires delivery platform optimization.

Name: miR2PE-score
Developers: Wenzhou Medical University
Indication: Diagnosis and predicition of PE
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Measures clotting parameters to identify hypercoagulability and endothelial dysfunction associated with preeclampsia.
Key features and challenges: Researchers at Wenzhou Medical University have created a blood-based miRNA signature for early, non-invasive detection of preeclampsia. They carried out a three-phase discovery, training, and validation study, both retrospectively and prospectively, involving cross-platform and multicenter cohorts. Initial biomarkers were identified and confirmed in tissue samples using small RNA sequencing and qRT-PCR. The resulting miRNA signature, called the miR2PE-score, was developed from two validated miRNAs (miR-196b-5p and miR-584-5p) using Firth’s bias-reduced logistic regression analysis. The miR2PE-score showed strong diagnostic performance, with AUROC values of 0.920, 0.848, 0.864, and 0.812 across training, internal, and two external validation cohorts. Its non-invasive diagnostic potential was further supported by AUROC values of 0.933 and 0.787 in two prospective plasma cohorts (https://bmcmedicine.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12916-022-02495-x).

Name: mini-dbPCR-NALFIA
Developers: Academic Medical Center, The Netherlands; Mekelle University; Carlos III Health Institute, Instituto de Salud Carlos III (ISCIII)
Indication: Indicated for the detection of Visceral leishmaniasis
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Mechanism of action: Lateral flow detection combining simplified nucleic acid amplification with a rapid immunological read-out

Name: mosaic ferritin nanoparticle vaccine
Developers: Guangzhou Medical University
Indication: Prevention of betacoronavirus infections (pan-β-CoV vaccine)
Target: Receptor-binding domains (RBDs) of MERS-CoV (DPP4-binding), SARS-CoV, and SARS-CoV-2 (ACE2-binding)
Mechanism of action: Multivalent display of heterotypic RBDs on ferritin nanoparticles induces robust B-cell cross-linking and antibody responses; blocks receptor engagement (DPP4 or ACE2), neutralizes multiple coronaviruses, and confers pan-β-CoV protection.
Key features and challenges:
-Design: RBDs (MERS-CoV, SARS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2 WT) genetically fused to hybrid ferritin, assembled into ~24-meric nanoparticles.
-Immunogenicity:
       i). In mice: 10 µg prime-boost induced high IgG binding and neutralizing titers against MERS-CoV, SARS-CoV, and SARS-CoV-2 WT and VOCs (Alpha, Beta, Delta, Omicron BA.1.1, BA.2, BA.5, EG.5).
       ii). In NHPs: elicited strong IgG and neutralizing titers vs MERS-CoV EMC/2012, SARS-CoV, and SARS-CoV-2 VOCs.
-Protection:
      i). Mice fully protected from lethal SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV (hDPP4 mice), and SARS-CoV-2 WT/Beta challenge; no detectable lung virus.
      ii). Serum transfer from immunized mice/NHPs conferred passive protection in hACE2-transduced mice.
Durability: Neutralization persisted ≥5 months post-boost; protection maintained against SARS-CoV-2 VOCs.
Challenges:
      i). MERS-specific T-cell epitopes appeared subdominant in BALB/c mice (weak cellular responses).
     ii). Only aged cynomolgus macaques tested; broader age/strain validation needed.
      iii). Large-scale GMP production and stability of mosaic nanoparticles remain unproven.
Recent updates:
-Highlighted in 2024–2025 reviews as a leading ferritin nanoparticle platform for universal coronavirus vaccines.
-Compared to PCNA-based mosaic scaffolds, ferritin nanoparticles showed stronger cross-neutralization against Omicron BA.1/BA.2 and robust MERS neutralization.
-Passive serum transfer confirmed antibody-mediated protection, bolstering translational potential.

Name: nitroxoline
Developers: Goethe University Frankfurt, Johann Wolfgang Goethe-Universität Frankfurt am Main
Indication: Treatment of mpox infection (therapeutic candidate, repurposed antibiotic)
Target: Host PI3K/AKT/mTOR and RAF/MEK/ERK signaling pathways required for orthopoxvirus replication.
Mechanism of action:
Inhibits host signaling pathways (PI3K/AKT/mTOR and RAF/MEK/ERK) that are hijacked by MPXV for replication.
Acts post-entry to suppress viral DNA replication and virion production in infected cells.
Also displays antibacterial effects by metal ion chelation, though antiviral effect is independent of this property.
Key features and challenges:
-In vitro potency: IC₅₀ = 0.5–4.6 µM in human foreskin keratinocytes and fibroblasts.
-Selectivity index (SI): >10 (CC₅₀ >20 µM).
-Inhibits replication of 12 MPXV isolates (clade IIb) from 2022 outbreak.
-Active in human split-thickness skin explant model, reducing MPXV antigen expression in epidermis and dermis.
-Effective against tecovirimat-resistant MPXV strain (MPXV1rTECO, carrying F13L N267D/I372N).
-No resistance developed after repeated passage in presence of nitroxoline.
-Additive/synergistic effects with tecovirimat and brincidofovir.
-Additional antimicrobial activity against E. coli and Neisseria gonorrhoeae (MIC 4–8 µg/mL).
-Also weakly active against HSV-1 and VZV (>10 µM).
Recent updates:
-Nitroxoline is being studied for other viral infections (SARS-CoV-2, JEV, HSV-1) via host signaling inhibition.
-Its dual antiviral and antibacterial activity makes it suitable for mpox coinfections seen in the 2022–2024 outbreaks.
-No resistance observed in vitro supports its use as a combination partner with tecovirimat to delay resistance emergence.
-Pharmacokinetic modeling indicates achievable plasma concentrations (30–50 µM) exceed the antiviral IC₅₀ range.
-Further studies are proposed to evaluate systemic vs. topical use for mpox skin lesions.

Name: nomogram-based risk prediction tool
Developers: Anhui Medical University; The First Affiliated Hospital of USTC
Indication: Indicated for the prediction of PE in routine pregnancy care.
Health care facility level: IVDs for research use only
Target: Cystatin C, uric acid, glutamyl aminotransferase, blood urea nitrogen, and basal systolic blood pressure
Mechanism of action: Quantification of individual patient risk by combining demographic factors, medical history, and, crucially, biomarkers into a single, intuitive chart
Key features and challenges:
The retrospective collection of clinical data was performed on 951 pregnant women with hyperglycemia, including those diagnosed with diabetes in pregnancy (DIP) and gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), who delivered after 34 weeks of gestation at the Maternal and Child Health Hospital Affiliated to Anhui Medical University between January 2017 and December 2019. Observation indicators included liver and kidney function factors testing at 24– 29+6 weeks gestation, maternal age, and basal blood pressure. The indicators were screened univariately, and the “rms” package in R language was applied to explore the factors associated with PE in HIP pregnancy by stepwise regression. Multivariable logistic regression analysis was used to develop the prediction model. Based on the above results, a nomogram was constructed to predict the risk of PE occurrence in pregnant women with HIP. Then, the model was evaluated from three aspects: discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility. The internal validation was performed using the bootstrap procedure.
Results: Multivariate logistic regression analysis showed that cystatin C, uric acid, glutamyl aminotransferase, blood urea nitrogen, and basal systolic blood pressure as predictors of PE in pregnancy with HIP. The predictive model yielded an area under curve (AUC) value of 0.8031 (95% CI: 0.7383– 0.8679), with an optimal threshold of 0.0805, at which point the sensitivity was 0.8307 and specificity of 0.6604. Hosmer–Lemeshow test values were P = 0.3736, Brier score value was 0.0461. After 1000 Bootstrap re-samplings for internal validation, the AUC was 0.7886, the Brier score was 0.0478 and the predicted probability of the calibration curve was similar to the actual probability. A nomogram was constructed based on the above to visualize the model.
Conclusion: This study developed a model for predicting PE in pregnant women with HIP, achieving high predictive performance of PE risk through the information of routine pregnancy care (https://www.dovepress.com/a-prediction-model-of-preeclampsia-in-hyperglycemia-pregnancy-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-DMSO)

Name: nsP-Mutant
Developers: Singapore Immunology Network (SIgN); National University of Singapore (NUS)

Mechanism of action: Elicits immune response to CHIKV nsP2

Name: p*17-K4S2
Developers: Griffith University (including the Institute for Glycomics and GRIDD); University of Alberta
Indication: Indicated for the prevention of Group A Streptococcus infection.
Target: Group A Strep M protein (SpyCEP, IL-8 protease and P*17 peptide from the C terminus
Mechanism of action: Designed to elicit humoral immune response.
Key features and challenges: Tested in Phase I dose-ranging study in Canada in 2021. Conjugated to the CRM197 carrier protein. Adjuvanted with CAF01. A recent pre-clincial study demonstrated that intramuscular injections followed by a intranasal dose of P*17 (prime-pull immunisation) induced high antibody levels in both the airway mucosa and serum, as well as protection against upper respiratory tract infection and invasive disease in mice.
Recent updates: A Trial of a Peptide-based Group A Streptococcal (GAS) Vaccine Candidate in Healthy Individuals.  Active, not recruiting.  Estimated completion = 2025-12 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04882514).

Name: p38 MAPK/MEK Inhibitor Cluster (HDT)
Developers: Universidad Antonio Nariño; Fundación Universitaria de Ciencias de la Salud (FUCS)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of Lepromatous Leprosy.
Target:
Glucosamine: TNF and IFN-γ
Binimetinib: TNF and IL-1B
Talmapimod: TNF and IL-1B
Dilmapimod: TNF and IL-1B
VX-702: TNF and IL-1B.
Key features and challenges:
Bioinformatic Approach for Repurposing Immunomodulatory Drugs for Lepromatous Leprosy (LL).
ABSTRACT:
A dataset of human genes associated with LL-immune response was retrieved from public health genomic databases including the Human Genome Epidemiology Navigator and DisGeNET. Retrieved genes were filtered and enriched to set a robust network (≥10, up to 21 edges) and analyzed in the Cytoscape program (v3.9). Drug associations were obtained in the NDEx Integrated Query (v1.3.1) coupled with drug databases such as ChEMBL, BioGRID, and DrugBank. These networks were analyzed in Cytoscape with the CyNDEx-2 plugin and STRING protein network database.
Pathways analyses resulted in 100 candidate drugs organized into pharmacological groups with similar targets and filtered on 54 different drugs. Gene-target network analysis showed that the main druggable targets associated with LL were tumoral necrosis factor-alpha, interleukin-1B, and interferon-gamma. Consistently, glucosamine, binimetinib, talmapimod, dilmapimod, andrographolide, and VX-702 might have a possible beneficial effect coupled with LL treatment.
Based on the drug repurposing analysis, immunomodulatory drugs might have a promising potential to be explored further as therapeutic options or to alleviate symptoms in LL patients
(https://journals.lww.com/ijmy/fulltext/2023/12040/bioinformatic_approach_for_repurposing.4.aspx).

Name: pET-29a(+) vectored MgPa
Developers: University of the Punjab
Indication: Prevention of Mycoplasma genitalium
Mechanism of action: Recombinant MgPa antigen expressed in vector to induce protective immune responses against Mycoplasma genitalium.
Key features and challenges: A 2024 study reveals that Mycoplasma genitalium is gaining recognition for its role in serious health issues, including sexually transmitted infections, ovarian cancer, and prostate cancer. Its adhesion protein is key to the pathogen’s ability to attach to and invade host cells, making it a prime target for vaccine development. The push for a vaccine comes from growing antibiotic resistance and limited treatment options. The research centers on designing and computationally evaluating an adhesion protein-based epitope vaccine. Using an immunoinformatics approach, researchers identified multiple novel cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL), helper T lymphocyte (HTL), and linear B-cell epitopes with strong antigenic, non-allergenic, and immunogenic qualities. The vaccine’s 3D structure was validated with Ramachandran plot analysis, ProSA, and ERRAT, confirming its stability. Molecular docking showed high binding affinity with the TLR-2 receptor, supported by 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations that verified structural stability and strong receptor interaction. In silico immune simulations suggested the vaccine could trigger strong humoral and cell-mediated immune responses. Codon optimization for expression in E. coli using the pET-29a(+) vector indicated efficient production. Overall, the computational analysis points to this epitope-based vaccine as a promising candidate against M. genitalium, though in vitro and in vivo studies are still needed to confirm its safety and effectiveness before clinical trials.(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40726761/)
Recent updates: Discovery study published in 2024 demonstrated in silico immune simulations using the C-ImmSim server demonstrated the vaccine’s potential to elicit strong humoral and cell-mediated immune responses. Codon optimization for expression in E. coli using the pET-29a(+) vector predicted efficient production of the vaccine. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40726761/)

Name: pSVCTQ (tafenoquine prodrug)
Developers: University of Washington (including Harborview Medical Center); Walter Reed Army Institute of Research (WRAIR) (including Military HIV Research Program)
Indication: Indicated for the treatment of malaria caused by P. vivax
Key features and challenges: Researchers developed a polymeric prodrug to enhance the therapeutic index of tafenoquine (TQ) administered subcutaneously (SC). This modification results in lower peak blood concentrations, reducing hemolytic anemia risk. The prodrug is also engineered to optimize transport through liver cells, aiming to achieve a radical cure with a single dose while minimizing the production of hemotoxic metabolites in the liver. The prodrug is designed to remain stable in the bloodstream but is broken down by cathepsin enzymes within the body. Given the absence of non-8-aminoquinoline (non-8-AQ) options for radical cures and the practicality of SC administration in mass eradication efforts, this development could represent a significant advancement.
Recent updates: Preclinical results published in 2024 (https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.adk4492).

Name: pVAX-E2 DNA vaccine +/- E2* protein/AS03 boost
Developers: Universidade Federal de São Paulo (UNIFESP/EPM); Universidade Federal da Bahia (UFBA); Instituto Nacional de Ciência e Tecnologia de Investigação em Imunologia
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against CHIKV infection
Mechanism of action:
-DNA prime with pVAX-E2 leads to expression of E2 antigen in host cells, priming both humoral (B) and cellular (T) immune responses.
-Boost with E2* recombinant protein + AS03 adjuvant enhances neutralizing antibody titers and further stimulates CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T cell responses (polyfunctional) and IFN-γ producing cells.
Key features and challenges:
-The heterologous DNA prime / protein boost strategy delivers a strong immune response; neutralizing antibodies + cellular immunity (Th1/Th2 balanced). AS03 adjuvant improved humoral response significantly. Mice immunized showed strong neutralization.
-Challenges: So far tested only in mice; need to assess protection in challenge models, durability of immunity, safety, and dose schedule; manufacturing of recombinant E2*, ensuring consistent antigenicity; adjuvant safety; translation to larger animals and ultimately humans.
Recent updates: As of Sept 2025, no published challenge (infection) protection results in mice (or other species) beyond immunogenicity; no clinical trial registered specifically for this formulation; no data yet on duration of immunity beyond short-term post-boost; no reports yet on scale-up or manufacturing stability.

Name: pVAX-Gnc, pVAX-LAMP/Gnc
Developers: Fourth Military Medical University China
Indication: Active immunisation against Haemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantaan virus
Target: HTNV envelope glycoprotein (GP), comprising Gn spike protein
Mechanism of action:
pVAX-Gnc: Delivers Gn-derived antigen to host cells, stimulating modest immune responses.
pVAX-LAMP/Gnc: Traffics antigen into the lysosomal/MHC II compartment via LAMP1 fusion, enhancing both humoral and cellular (CD4+ T helper) immune responses and promoting memory formation.
Key features and challenges:
Enhanced immunogenicity:
pVAX-LAMP/Gnc induced strong IFN-γ secretion, potent neutralizing antibodies, and CTL responses—significantly higher than pVAX-Gnc or controls.
pVAX-Gnc elicited detectable but lower neutralizing antibody levels compared to pVAX-LAMP/Gnc.
Memory and protection: pVAX-LAMP/Gnc established long-term immune memory and conferred protection in HTNV-challenge assays in BALB/c mice.
Safety profile: Histology (H&E) showed no significant toxicity in mice to either construct.
Recent updates:
2024: Publication in Vaccines demonstrating improved immunogenicity using the Gnc antigen and LAMP-targeting strategy.
2017: Original study showed long-term protection in mice with LAMP/Gn DNA vaccine.

Name: pVAX-LAMP1-CCHFV-Gc
Developers: Air Force Military Medical University, China; The Eighth Medical Center of PLA General Hospital Beijing; Shaanxi University of Chinese Medicine, Xianyang
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against CCHF
Mechanism of action: Elicits specific humoral (neutralizing antibodies) with LAMP1 enhancing immune recognition through improved presentation. Generates protection in a tecVLP infection model (virus-like particles) in mice.
Key features and challenges:
-Enhanced immunogenicity: Mice immunized with pVAX-LAMP1-CCHFV-Gc had Gc-specific antibody GMT ~526.6 compared to ~196.7 without LAMP1, demonstrating LAMP1's boosting effect.
-Neutralizing response: Neutralizing antibody GMT in LAMP1-Gc group was 52.5 vs. 26.2 in non-LAMP1 Gc group, significantly enhanced (p = 0.033).
-Partial protective efficacy: Provided better protection against CCHFV tecVLP challenge in liver, spleen, and kidney compared to control groups, though efficacy was lower than that seen with LAMP1-NP construct.
Recent updates:
2023:
Demonstrated that LAMP1 enhances LAMP1-Gc immunogenicity and neutralizing antibody generation; partial protection against tecVLP challenge in mice was achieved—but to a lesser extent than seen with LAMP1-NP.

Name: pdmFlu vaccine
Developers: Pfizer
Indication: Prevention of pandemic influenza A infection in healthy adults
Target: Hemagglutinin (HA) antigen of pandemic influenza A (H5 subtype, clade 2.3.4.4b; strain A/Astrakhan/3212/2020)
Mechanism of action: Host cells translate the modRNA into H5 HA antigen, stimulating humoral (HA-inhibition antibodies) and cellular T-cell immune responses that provide immunity against H5 A influenza viruses. (Pfizer press release indicates “notable increases in antibody responses” vs H5 viruses).
Key features and challenges:
-Built on the same mRNA/LNP platform used for COVID-19 vaccines, allowing rapid pandemic response capability.
-Phase 1 dose-ranging study began late 2023; healthy adult cohorts (ages 18-49 and 65-84) enrolled. 
-Comparator arms include a licensed seasonal influenza vaccine and placebo, enabling assessment of relative immunogenicity. 
-Challenges: early-stage human data only; breadth of protection across divergent H5Nx clades and durability of immune responses need demonstration; manufacturing, regulatory pathways for pandemic vaccines still evolving.
Recent updates:
-The WHO / IVR investigational products list mentions pdmFlu as a modRNA H5N1 candidate. 
-Public commentary (May 2024) from Pfizer emphasised the candidate could be rapidly deployed for stockpiling if requested by health authorities.

Name: portable qPCR
Developers: Oswaldo Cruz Foundation (FIOCRUZ), Fundação Oswaldo Cruz (including FIOCRUZ Amazonia and Instituto Leônidas & Maria Deane (ILMD))
Indication: Indicated for the screening of M. leprae

Name: protein-based MERS-CoV nanoparticle vaccine
Developers: Vaccine Company Inc
Indication: Prevention of MERS-CoV infection
Target: MERS-CoV spike (S) glycoprotein ectodomain (S1 + S2, ΔTM, prefusion-stabilized).
Mechanism of action: Multivalent display of stabilized MERS-CoV SΔTM trimers on ferritin nanoparticles enhances immunogenicity; induces strong neutralizing antibodies and T-cell responses that block viral entry via DPP4 receptor engagement.
Key features and challenges:
-Design: Incorporated prefusion stabilizing mutations (2P: K1067P, V1068P) into MERS S ectodomain (ΔTM) before ferritin fusion.
-Nanoparticle characterization: Cryo-EM showed ~24 S trimers per ferritin nanoparticle; well-formed, symmetrical particles.
-Immunogenicity:
   i)Mice immunized with SΔTM-2P-ferritin nanoparticles (with AddaS03 + CpG adjuvant) developed high titers of neutralizing antibodies against MERS-CoV pseudoviruses.
    ii_Provided protection in hDPP4 transgenic mice, reducing lung viral titers and pathology after lethal MERS-CoV challenge.
-Breadth: Cross-reactive antibody responses induced against multiple Merbecoviruses.
-Challenges:
      i). Data so far limited to mice; no NHP or camelid testing yet.
      ii). Manufacturing of multivalent nanoparticle vaccines may face scale-up and stability challenges.
      iii). Durability of immunity and efficacy against diverse MERS strains remain unknown.
Recent updates:
-The preprint was revised (v3, July 2024) with additional mouse challenge data showing robust protection against MERS-CoV EMC/2012 strain.
-Structural models deposited in EMDB/PDB for the nanoparticle construct (check upon final peer-reviewed publication).
-NIH/NIAID MAVDA program (Metropolitan Antiviral Drug Accelerator) continues to support pan-CoV vaccine work including nanoparticle platforms; this candidate is mentioned in MAVDA’s 2025 pipeline reviews.

Name: rAAV1-CHIKV-SP
Developers: Wuhan Institute of Virology; Hunan Normal University
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against CHIKV infection
Target: CHIKV structural proteins (especially E2, the major neutralizing antibody target).
Mechanism of action:
-rAAV1 transduces muscle cells, leading to expression of CHIKV structural proteins.
-This induces robust antibody responses (IgG, neutralizing Abs) and Th1-biased immunity.
-Protective immunity is mediated by neutralizing antibodies against CHIKV E2 and cross-neutralization across lineages.
Key features and challenges:
-Single intramuscular dose induced strong and durable immune responses.
-Neutralizing Ab titers up to 1:640, maintained >12 weeks.
-Complete protection against heterologous CHIKV-ECSA strain challenge in mice.
-Safe profile: no adverse effects observed in C57BL/6 mice.
-Th1-biased IgG2c > IgG1 response.
-Prime-boost with heterologous AAV9 vector further increased titers (1:51,200 IgG; PRNT₅₀ = 1:320).
Recent updates:
2024: 
-First demonstration of an AAV-vectored vaccine for CHIKV.
-Highlighted potential advantages: single-dose protection, long-term immunity, and safer profile compared to live-attenuated vaccines.

Name: rACP +/- CpG
Developers: Oregon State University
Indication: Prevention of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Recombinant ACP antigen with CpG adjuvant induces humoral and cellular immune responses against gonococcal surface proteins.
Key features and challenges: In a 2025 preclinical study on developing a Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Ng) vaccine, researchers compared RO and SV sampling while testing Adhesin Complex Protein (ACP) and multiple transferable resistance E protein (MtrE) as antigen candidates. Epitope mapping showed that both ACP and MtrE have multiple, easily accessible B-cell and T-cell epitope clusters, highlighting their potential. After intranasal immunization with rACP, rACP+CpG, and rMtrE+CpG, the team evaluated the specificity, magnitude, timing, and quality of the immune responses. Of 45 comparisons, only eight significant differences were found in antibody titers, and bactericidal assays showed no difference between RO and SV for antigen-immunized groups. However, antibodies from rACP alone or ACP+CpG in SV samples restored 30.05% and 75.2% of human lysozyme activity, compared to 19.3% and 59.9% in RO, suggesting SV may better reflect functional antibody responses. Beyond immune benefits, SV sampling also reduces stress, avoids eye trauma, and supports animal welfare, making it a strong alternative to RO. Standardizing SV sampling could boost reliability, ethics, and relevance in vaccine research (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.02.23.639724v1).
Recent updates: Preclinical study assessing immunology in mice published in 2023 (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.02.23.639724v1)

Name: rAd-Rv2299c
Developers: Not specified
Indication: Prevention of disease
Target: M. tuberculosis heat shock protein (HspX homolog / Rv2299c)
Mechanism of action: Stimulates mucosal IgA and systemic cellular responses directly within the respiratory epithelium
Key features and challenges: A viral-vectored immunogen using a chimpanzee adenovirus to express the M. tuberculosis antigen Rv2299c (an HspX homolog), designed to stimulate mucosal IgA and systemic cellular responses within the respiratory epithelium. Given intranasally/by inhalation.
Recent updates: Preclinical work in mice showed rAd-Rv2299c induced a trained-immunity phenotype in dendritic cells (upregulated MHC-II and CD86, increased TNF-alpha, IL-6, IL-1beta and IL-12p70), generated polyfunctional Th1/Th17 T cells, and on challenge significantly reduced lung and spleen bacterial loads while attenuating pulmonary inflammation (Vaccines 2026;14(1):55).

Name: rAd5-EBOV-GP, rAd5-SUDV-GP, rAd5-BUDV-GP, rAd5-MARV-GP
Developers: N. Gamaleya National Research Center for Epidemiology and Microbiology
Indication: Indicated for active immunization to protect against Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) caused by Zaire Ebola virus and Sudan Ebola virus, and Marburg Virus Disease (MVD) caused by Marburg virus
Target: EBOV glycoproteins (EBOV Zaire, SUDV, BUDV, MARV)
Mechanism of action: Induces humoral immune responses by expressing GP antigens in vivo. Full-length GP and GPΔM constructs elicit strongest antibody titers; GPcl (glycan cap + mucin deleted) constructs were poorly immunogenic.
Key features and challenges:
-Constructs made for four filoviruses (EBOV, SUDV, BUDV, MARV) with three GP forms each.
-In mice, full-length GP and GPΔM induced highest IgG titers across all species.
-Neutralizing antibody (pseudovirus) responses strongest for rAd5-SUDV-GP and rAd5-MARV-GPΔM.
-Cross-reactivity: rAd5-SUDV GP constructs elicited antibodies cross-reactive with EBOV and BUDV; rAd5-MARV GPΔM showed weak cross-reactivity with EBOV and SUDV.
-GPcl forms consistently least immunogenic.
-Low anti-Ad5 neutralizing titers detected, suggesting minimal vector immunity interference.
Recent updates:
September 2024:
-Concluded that full-length GP and GPΔM constructs are most promising for further vaccine development.
-Work supported by Russian Ministry of Health “Pan-filovirus vaccine” program.

Name: rCSP +/- AP 10-602 (GLA-LSQ)
Developers: University of Maryland, Baltimore (including CVD); US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease (NIAID); EMMES Corporation
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against malaria caused by P.falciparum
Mechanism of action: Inhibits CSP, preventing  proteolytic processing
Key features and challenges: Participants experienced no serious adverse events in a Phase I trial (NCT03589794). Rates of solicited and unsolicited adverse events were similar among groups. All 26 participants who underwent controlled human malaria infection 28 days after final vaccinations developed malaria. Increasing vaccine doses induced higher immunoglobulin G titers but did not achieve previously established RTS,S benchmarks.
Recent updates: Completed Phase I trial in 2022 (NCT03589794).

Name: rDENdelta30/31-7164
Developers: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID)
Indication: Investigated for the prevention of dengue in individuals aged 18 to 59 years
Mechanism of action: Immunostimulants
Key features and challenges: A live attenuated, monovalent viral immunogen that acts as an immunostimulant, presenting attenuated dengue virus components (serotypes 1-4) to prime serotype-specific immune responses. It has also been investigated as a platform across other indications including influenza, Japanese encephalitis, measles, and meningococcal and pneumococcal infections.
Recent updates: A Phase 1 trial (NCT05691530) evaluating safety and immune responses according to prior dengue exposure, using a single subcutaneous dose, began in 2023 and is active and not recruiting as of 2025.

Name: rDIs-mcl2.2 HA
Developers: University of Tokyo (including the Graduate School of Agricultural and Life Sciences); Tokyo Metropolitan Institute of Medical Science (TMiMS); National Institute of Infectious Diseases (NIID)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against influenza A, caused by H5N1
Mechanism of action: Recombinant vaccinia virus vector expresses modified H5 HA protein, eliciting humoral (IgG, HI antibodies) and cellular (Th1-skewed T cell) immune responses, leading to rapid and durable protection against heterologous H5N1 challenge
Key features and challenges:
-Replication-deficient vector (cannot replicate in most mammalian cells), enhancing safety.
-Induces rapid protection (within 1 week) and long-term immunity (≥20 months in mice).
-Provides cross-clade protection against heterologous H5N1 strains (clades 1, 2.3.2.1).
-Demonstrated efficacy even in animals pre-sensitized with vaccinia virus, though higher dose required.
-Suitable for immunocompromised populations due to replication defect.
-Challenge: need to confirm immunogenicity and safety in humans; potential pre-existing vaccinia immunity could affect response.
Recent updates:
2025:
-Builds on prior LC16m8 vector work; rDIs provides similar protection but with greater safety due to replication defect.
-Data suggest potential for lifelong immunity from a single dose, unusual for non-replicating viral vectors.
-Comparison with other VACV-based platforms (e.g., MVA) ongoing; MVA already tested in clinical trials, making rDIs a novel alternative for safe long-term protection.

Name: rGDF-9
Developers: Indian Institute Chemical Technology (IICT)
Indication: Treatment of PCOS
Mechanism of action: GDF9 acts through two receptors on the cells surrounding the oocyte, it binds to bone morphogenic protein receptor 2 (BMPRII) and downstream to this utilizes the TGF-β receptor type 1 (ALK5). Ligand receptor activation allows the downstream phosphorylation and activation of SMAD proteins.
Key features and challenges:
Growth differentiation factor-9 (GDF-9) is an endogenous oocyte-derived peptide belonging to the transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) superfamily. It is expressed in humans and animal models and plays a critical role in ovarian physiology. GDF-9, together with bone morphogenetic protein-15 (BMP-15), is co-expressed in oocytes and can form a heterodimer known as cumulin. Cumulin enhances oocyte developmental competence and promotes granulosa cell activation. GDF-9 is particularly important in the pre-ovulatory phase, supporting cumulus cell metabolic function, including glycolysis and cholesterol biosynthesis, processes essential for follicular maturation and ovulation.
A 2023 preclinical study investigated the therapeutic effects of recombinant GDF-9 (rGDF-9), alone and in combination with the GnRH antagonist cetrorelix, in a gestational DHEA-induced PCOS rat model. The combination treatment normalized biochemical parameters, reduced estrous cycle irregularity, and improved sex hormone balance. Improvements were also observed in glucose metabolism and insulin resistance, as reflected by reduced HOMA-IR values. These findings suggest that rGDF-9, particularly when combined with cetrorelix, may ameliorate both metabolic and reproductive phenotypes associated with PCOS.
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0024320523002722?via%3Dihub
Despite promising mechanistic and preclinical data, rGDF-9 remains at an early investigational stage. Evidence is currently limited to animal models, and its impact on infertility-associated outcomes in PCOS has not yet been adequately evaluated. Furthermore, challenges related to peptide stability, delivery methods, dosing strategies, and long-term safety would need to be addressed before clinical translation.
Overall, recombinant GDF-9 represents a biologically plausible, ovarian-targeted therapeutic strategy aimed at restoring folliculogenesis and metabolic balance in PCOS, but robust clinical studies are required to determine its feasibility and therapeutic value in humans.

Name: rJEV/ZIKV(P6-740)
Developers: Utah State University
Indication: Prevention of ZIKV disease and congenital complications
Target: ZIKV precursor membrane (prM) and envelope (E) proteins.
Mechanism of action: Uses a recombinant JEV P6-740 backbone with prM-E of ZIKV to induce neutralizing antibodies and T-cell responses against ZIKV, while retaining attenuation and replication properties of JEV. Provides protective immunity against lethal ZIKV challenge.
Key features and challenges:
Features: Live-attenuated chimeric flavivirus vaccine (Japanese encephalitis virus backbone)
-Constructed by replacing prM-E genes of JEV (P6-740 strain) with those of ZIKV (PRVABC59).
-Protected mice from lethal ZIKV challenge; reduced viral loads and induced robust nAb responses.
-Exploits established safety and immunogenicity of JEV vaccine backbones.

Challenges:
-Data limited to mouse models; NHP studies needed.
-Risk of flavivirus cross-reactivity and antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) must be addressed.
-Manufacturing and regulatory pathways for chimeric vaccines can be complex.
Recent updates:
2025 Publication: 
-Demonstrated that rJEV/ZIKV(P6-740) immunization conferred complete protection against lethal ZIKV challenge in both wild-type and interferon receptor-deficient mice.
-Neutralizing antibody titers correlated with protection; strong Th1-skewed immune responses were noted.
-Study suggests this JEV backbone could be developed further as a dual-use platform for other flaviviruses.

Name: rKLi8.3 ELISA
Developers: Philipps University Marburg; Novatec Immundiagnostica GmbH; Eurofins Ingenasa S.A.; University Hospital Bonn, Universitaetsklinikum Bonn (UKB); German Center for Infection Research (DZIF); Universidade Federal de Juiz de Fora; Imam Abdulrahman Bin Faisal University
Indication: Indicated for the detection of Leishmania infantum causing VL
Health care facility level: IVDs for Health care facilities with clinical laboratories
Mechanism of action: Detects IgG antibodies in serum that bind to recombinant antigen rKLi8.3

Name: rKLi8.3 LFT
Developers: Philipps University Marburg; Novatec Immundiagnostica GmbH; University Hospital Bonn, Universitaetsklinikum Bonn (UKB); German Center for Infection Research (DZIF); Universidade Federal de Juiz de Fora; Imam Abdulrahman Bin Faisal University
Indication: Indicated for the detection of Leishmania donovani
Health care facility level: IVDs for Primary health care
Mechanism of action: Immunochromatographic assay designed to identify IgG in patient serum

Name: rLASV/IGR-CD
Developers: US Army Medical Research Institute for Infectious Disease (USAMRIID); National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID); Texas Biomedical Research Institute (Texas Biomed, formerly Southwest Foundation for Biomedical Research)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against LASV infection
Target: Lassa virus glycoprotein (GP) and viral genome attenuation determinants (IGR rearrangement, GP codon usage)
Mechanism of action: Combines two genetic attenuation strategies: (1) replacement of L segment IGR with S segment IGR, and (2) codon-deoptimization of GP gene. This produces a replication-competent LASV with reduced pathogenicity that elicits both antibody and T cell responses, conferring protective immunity.
Key features and challenges:
-Grows to high titers in Vero cells, supporting vaccine production.
-Completely attenuated in guinea pigs: no disease signs or pathological lesions.
-Single vaccination protected 100% of guinea pigs from lethal wild-type LASV challenge.
-Vaccination induced high LASV GP-specific antibody titers and reduced inflammatory cytokines post-challenge.
-Incorporates dual attenuation determinants to minimize risk of reversion to virulence.
-Advantages: durable humoral and cell-mediated immunity, strong safety profile.
-Challenges: as a live-attenuated LASV, regulatory scrutiny will be high for potential recombination/reversion risks; requires NHP testing and long-term safety studies.
Recent updates:
-Builds on earlier single-attenuation candidates (rLASV/IGR swap or GP-CD alone) that protected guinea pigs.
-rLASV/IGR-CD represents a “second-generation” live-attenuated LASV vaccine with enhanced safety.
-Data support advancing toward NHP studies to validate efficacy and durability before clinical transition.

Name: rLC16m8-mcl2.2 HA
Developers: Tokyo Metropolitan Institute of Medical Science (TMiMS); University of Tokyo (including the Graduate School of Agricultural and Life Sciences); National Institute of Infectious Diseases (NIID)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against influenza A, caused by H5N1
Mechanism of action: Attenuated vaccinia vector expresses H5 HA antigen, inducing humoral and cellular immune responses; provides durable immunity against heterologous H5N1 strains.
Key features and challenges:
-LC16m8 is a licensed smallpox vaccine in Japan, attenuated but replication-competent, providing a strong safety record in humans.
-Induces rapid and long-term protective immunity against H5N1 in preclinical models.
-Cross-protection observed against heterologous H5 clades (clade 1, 2.3.2.1).
-Effective even in vaccinia-immune hosts, though higher doses required.
-Challenge: Replication competence may limit acceptance in immunocompromised populations; compared to replication-deficient rDIs vector, less safe but potentially more immunogenic.
Recent updates:
-Builds on decades of clinical use of LC16m8 in Japan, now adapted for H5N1.
-Parallel comparison with rDIs-mcl2.2 HA in the same study: rLC16m8 showed robust protection but with higher biosafety concerns compared to replication-deficient vector.
-As of 2025, no clinical influenza vaccine trials reported for LC16m8-H5, but promising as a next-gen smallpox-derived vector platform.

Name: rMtrE+CpG
Developers: Oregon State University
Indication: Prevention of gonorrhoea
Mechanism of action: Recombinant MtrE antigen with CpG adjuvant elicits antibodies targeting efflux pump components to enhance bacterial clearance.
Key features and challenges: In 2023, a preclinical study compared retro-orbital (RO) and saphenous vein (SV) sampling for developing a Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Ng) vaccine, focusing on Adhesin Complex Protein (ACP) and multiple transferable resistance E protein (MtrE) as antigen candidates. Epitope mapping showed that both ACP and MtrE contain multiple, highly accessible B-cell and T-cell epitope clusters, highlighting their strong immunological potential. After intranasal immunization with rACP, rACP+CpG, and rMtrE+CpG, researchers evaluated the specificity, magnitude, timing, and functional quality of immune responses. Out of 45 comparisons, only eight significant differences were found in antibody titers, and human serum bactericidal assays showed no differences between RO and SV in antigen-immunized groups. However, antibodies from SV samples after rACP alone or ACP+CpG restored 30.05% and 75.2% of human lysozyme hydrolytic activity, compared to 19.3% and 59.9% for RO, suggesting SV sampling may be more reliable for assessing functional antibody responses. Along with its immunological benefits, SV sampling reduces stress, avoids eye trauma, and improves animal welfare, making it a solid alternative to RO collection. Standardizing SV sampling could boost data reliability, ethical standards, and translational relevance in preclinical research (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.02.23.639724v1)
Recent updates: Preclinical study assessing immunology in mice published in 2023 (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.02.23.639724v1)

Name: rS-MARV
Developers: Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences
Indication: Prevention of Marburg virus infection
Mechanism of action: Induces MARV GP-specific humoral and cellular immune responses, including IgG, Th1-biased cytokines, and limited neutralizing antibodies; sequential immunization strategy elicited fully humanized neutralizing antibody (mAb 60H07) in CAMouse.
Key features and challenges:
-Encodes two copies of MARV GP genes to increase antigen expression.
-Evaluated against three strains (Angola, Musoke, Ravn).
-Generated specific IgG, splenocyte proliferation, and cytokine responses in mice.
-Neutralizing antibody titers weak and transient in BALB/c mice, but sequential immunization in humanized CAMouse yielded high-affinity antibody (60H07) with cross-neutralization.
-Inactivated vaccine platform considered safer than live RABV or VSV vectors, but immunogenicity is weaker.
Recent updates:
-Identified neutralizing antibody 60H07 from immunized humanized mice, showing cross-strain neutralization (Angola, Musoke, Ravn).
-Reported strong Th1-biased immune response and protection in golden hamster challenge model (100% survival after rVSV-Angola lethal challenge).

Name: rVSV N4CT1 EBOVGP1
Developers: US Department of Defense (DOD); Profectus Biosciences, Inc.; Accelovance; Auro Vaccines; University of Texas Medical Branch, Galveston; US National Institutes of Health (NIH)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization to protect against Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) caused by Zaire Ebola virus
Key features and challenges: Conducted by Auro Vaccines, the rVSV-EBOV-001 clinical study (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT02718469; N=38) examined the safety and immunogenicity of ascending dose levels (104, 105, 106, and 107 plaque-forming units) of a VesiculoVax™ vectored Ebola GP vaccine delivered on days 0 and 28 by intramuscular injection to healthy adults. The primary outcomes were safety and tolerability; immunogenicity, assessed as GP-specific humoral immune response (at 2 weeks after each dose) and cellular immune response (at 1 and 2 weeks after each dose), was a secondary outcome.
Recent updates: The vaccine has completed phase I clinical evaluation demonstrating safety, 100% vaccine take, and immunogenicity across a range of doses. (https://aurovaccines.com/pipeline/vesiculovax-prophylactic-vaccines/)

Name: rVSV-EBOV-GP-NiV-G (PHV02)
Developers: Public Health Vaccines LLC; Crozet Bio Pharma; US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease (NIAID)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against Nipah virus infection caused by NiV M strain
Target: NiV glycoprotein (G), fusion protein (F) and nucleoprotein (N)
Mechanism of action: Elicits Ab immune response to NiV
Key features and challenges:
The PHV02 vaccine is a live, attenuated, recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) vector that expresses the glycoprotein of the Nipah virus (Bangladesh strain) and the Ebola virus glycoprotein, which is required for receptor-mediated viral entry. The rVSV-Nipah vaccine was developed by the Laboratory of Dr. Heinz Feldmann within the Laboratory of
Virology, Division of Intramural Research, National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), part of the National Institutes of Health, and has been licensed to PHV by
NIAID. PHV has been developing the vaccine in partnership with the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness and Innovations (CEPI) under and award of up to US$43.6 million that facilitates development through Phase 2 clinical trials, including supportive non-clinical and manufacturing activities (https://www.phvaccines.com/downloads/Press-Release-Feb-09-2022.pdf).

A Phase 1 Randomized, Single Center, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Dose-Response Study was initiated in 2022 in the US to evaluate the Safety and Immunogenicity of PHV02 in Healthy Adult Subjects. The trail has now been completed with findings yet to be released (NCT05178901)

Name: rVSV-H5N1dc2024
Developers: University of Pittsburgh Center for Vaccine Research; National Institutes of Health
Indication: Research tool for vaccine/therapeutic evaluation; potential vaccine platform
Target: Hemagglutinin (HA) and Neuraminidase (NA) of bovine-origin clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 (2024 US outbreak strain)
Mechanism of action: Surrogate replicating virus presents authentic H5 HA and NA glycoproteins on VSV backbone; enables neutralization, antibody-escape mapping, and resistance evaluation under lower biosafety levels.
Key features and challenges:
-Mimics key surface glycoproteins of bovine H5N1 without requiring BSL-3+/BSL-4 containment.
-Encodes a fluorescent reporter, enabling real-time tracking of infection and neutralization assays.
-High titers facilitate neutralization, antibody escape, and NA inhibitor resistance studies.
-Expands influenza research access to more labs, accelerating antiviral and antibody testing.
-Limitation: surrogate system, not a true influenza virus → cannot fully replicate influenza life cycle or pathogenesis.
Recent updates:
-2025 reports indicate rVSV-H5N1dc2024 is being distributed to collaborating labs for testing monoclonal antibodies and next-generation NA inhibitors.
-Platform considered valuable for rapid assessment of therapeutic efficacy against emerging bovine H5N1 strains outside high-containment labs.

Name: rVSV-HTNV-GP vaccine
Developers: Air Force Military Medical University, China; Fourth Military Medical University China
Indication: Active immunisation against Haemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantaan virus
Target: HTNV envelope glycoprotein (GP), comprising Gn and Gc spike proteins
Mechanism of action: A single-dose vaccination with rVSV‑HTNV‑GP induces robust humoral immune responses—high titers of neutralizing antibodies (NAbs) against HTNV and related Seoul virus (SEOV), which confer protection. It also reduces viral RNA burden and tissue inflammation in vaccinated mice.
Key features and challenges:
-Single-dose efficacy: A single administration elicits durable immune protection up to 12 months post-vaccination in mice.
-Superior immunogenicity: Induces significantly higher HTNV-specific IgG and NAbs than licensed inactivated vaccine.
-Long-lasting immunity: Neutralizing antibody responses peak around 1 month post-dose, remain strong for 3–4 months, and detectable for over a year.
-Protection: Confers long-term protection in mice - reduced viral loads and pro-inflammatory cytokine expression, and mitigated lung and liver pathology.
Recent updates:
2024: Demonstrated strong immunogenicity and protection in mice from a single-dose rVSV‑HTNV‑GP—induction of high titers of neutralizing antibodies and durable immunity lasting at least 12 months.
2025 review (MDPI Vaccines) highlights this rVSV‑HTNV‑GP candidate as achieving longer-term protection than inactivated vaccines.

Name: rVSVΔG-MARV-GP
Developers: International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI); Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC); Public Health Vaccines LLC
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against Marburg virus infection
Mechanism of action: Elicits humoral immune response
Key features and challenges: Live recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus vaccine vector (rVSV∆G-MARV-GP) encoding the MARV glycoprotein (GP). A dose-range study conducted in cynomolgus macaques showed that a single intramuscular injection with as little as 200 plaque-forming units (PFUs) was 100% efficacious against lethality and prevented development of viremia and clinical pathologies associated with MARV Angola infection. Across the vaccine doses tested, there was nearly a 2000-fold range of anti-MARV glycoprotein (GP) serum IgG titers with seroconversion detectable even at the lowest doses. Virus-neutralizing serum antibodies also were detected in animals vaccinated with the higher vaccine doses indicating that vaccination induced functional antibodies, but that the assay was a less sensitive indicator of seroconversion.
Recent updates: HB 22/07/2025: Nov 2024-ongoing Phase I clinical development of RVSV Marburg virus vaccine-Public Health Vaccines is ongoing in USA (NCT06265012) https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06265012?term=NCT06265012&rank=1

Name: rVSVΔG-MERS-S
Developers: Korean National Institute of Health (KNIH); Ilin Agricultural University
Indication: Prevention of MERS-CoV infection (vaccine prophylaxis)
Target: MERS-CoV Spike (S) glycoprotein (the full-length S protein)
Mechanism of action: The vector infects cells and expresses MERS-CoV S on its envelope / in infected cells, eliciting immune responses (neutralizing antibodies and T cells) directed against S, thereby preventing infection of MERS-CoV by blocking S–receptor (DPP4) binding or fusion.
Key features and challenges:
-Single-dose immunogenicity: In rhesus monkeys, a single IM or IN dose induced neutralizing antibodies and T cell responses. 
-Mucosal and systemic immunization: The vector was tested by both intramuscular and intranasal routes.
-Rapid development potential: The VSVΔG platform is relatively fast to engineer and produce, as used for other viral vaccines. 
-Biosafety / vector risks: As a viral vector (replication-competent or attenuated), safety concerns include vector-associated pathology, vector replication in non-target tissues, interference, reactogenicity, and vector immunity. (General considerations for rVSV vectors).
-Species barrier / receptor dependency: Immune performance via mucosal delivery was modest in wild-type mice/hamsters; robust immunogenicity was observed only in animals expressing functional DPP4 (hDPP4 transgenic or DPP4-transduced) or in species with compatible receptor. This suggests that choice of animal model with correct receptor is critical.
-Vector immunity: Preexisting or subsequent immunity to VSV vector may limit boosting or repeated doses. (General vector vaccine limitation).
-Manufacturability / stability: Large-scale production, stability, and cold chain for a live vector vaccine are challenging (common to VSV-vectored vaccines).
-Durability & dose optimization: Long-term protection, durability of immunity, and optimal dose/regimen need further evaluation (not fully addressed in initial studies).
Recent updates:
-A 2025 paper (“Functional DPP4 Receptor Is an Indispensable Factor Mediating the Immune Performance of Mucosal Vaccines for MERS”) reports that intranasal (nasal spray) delivery of rVSVΔG-MERS-S is poorly immunogenic in wild-type (WT) mice or hamsters, but in hDPP4 transgenic mice or hamsters transduced with hDPP4, strong humoral & cellular immunity and APC priming were observed. This underscores the role of receptor compatibility in vaccine performance.
-The 2025 paper also compared species DPP4 alignment, identifying residues (e.g. L294, I295, R336) that are critical for species differences in immune responsiveness to the vector.
-The broader rVSV vector vaccine field continues active development (e.g. for Ebola, Nipah, etc.), including safety and single-round replication modifications, which may influence future modifications of the MERS construct.

Name: rVSVΔG-SUDV-GP
Developers: Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC); University of Manitoba; US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease (NIAID); Boston University (including Boston University Medical Campus and Center for Global Health and Development); US Army Medical Research Institute of Infectious Diseases (USAMRIID); International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI); University of Texas Medical Branch, Galveston
Indication: Indicated for active immunization to protect against Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) caused by Sudan Ebola virus.
Key features and challenges:
Non-human primate studies are complete. No safety data in humans is yet available. The developer plans dose ranging and a manufacturer comparison study with Phase I in US, Phase I/II in Uganda in healthcare workers, with exploration of immunobridging from ERVEBO to Sudan candidate as a potential approach to authorisation. 
The candidate was included in the Tokomeza ring vaccination trial in Uganda in 2022. This was ranked highest on the basis of the proven safety and efficacy of the rVSV ZEBOV GP (ERVEBO™) vaccine with the Zaire strain developed by Merck and for which IAVI now held the licensure rights for the technology. ERVEBO is licensed in the USA, UK, EU, Switzerland, and 10 African countries. ERVEBO’s efficacy was shown in a pivotal ring vaccination trial using a single intramuscular dose.1 There is extensive experience with use of rVSV ZEBOV
GP in the field with approaching 400,000 doses given as part of outbreak control measures and experience with compassionate use in over one thousand pregnant women. The SAGE recommendation on this vaccine now includes pregnant women. In addition to adults, tens of thousands of children have been vaccinated with ERVEBO, most of whom are under 10 years of age. No safety signals have emerged to date for the VSV platform. It was deemed valid to extrapolate the efficacy and safety experience with ERVEBO to VSV-SUDV, as the
only difference was the glycoprotein insert. The NHP data for VSV-SUDV was supportive of protection, including when NHPs were vaccinated shortly after challenge. There was confidence that the yields and ease of growth of the vaccine would make this an affordable product.
Single dose

Developers: Ege University; University of California, Irvine; Sivas Republic University, Sivas Cumhuriyet Üniversitesi

Name: recombinant M. bovis BCG strain AspikeRBD
Developers: Oklahoma State University
Indication: Prevention of TB
Target: M. tb Ag85A protein and the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein
Key features and challenges: A recombinant M. bovis BCG strain AspikeRBD that expresses a fusion protein consisting of M. tb Ag85A protein and the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein was designed using synthetic biology technique. Results show that the recombinant M. bovis BCG strain successfully expressed this fusion protein. Interestingly, the recombinant M. bovis BCG strain AspikeRBD significantly induced SARS-CoV-2 spike-specific T cell activation and IgG production in mice when compared to the parental M.bovis BCG strain, and was more potent than the recombinant M.bovis BCG strain expressing SARS-CoV-2 spike RBD alone. As expected, the recombinant M. bovis BCG strain AspikeRBD activated an increased number of M. tb Ag85A-specific IFNγ-releasing T cells and enhanced IgG production in mice when compared to the parental M.bovis BCG strain or the BCG strain expressing SARS-CoV-2 spike RBD alone. Taken together, our results indicate a potential application of the recombinant M. bovis BCG strain AspikeRBD as a novel dual vaccine against SARS-CoV-2 and M. tb in humans (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/cellular-and-infection-microbiology/articles/10.3389/fcimb.2023.1273019/full) .

Name: repHA-Bovine
Developers: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID); HDT Bio
Indication: Prevention of highly pathogenic avian influenza (zoonotic transmission from cattle/poultry to humans), caused by H5N1
Mechanism of action: Encoded HA expressed in host cells, eliciting binding antibodies, T-cell responses, and protection against homologous lethal challenge.
Key features and challenges:
-Designed from first bovine H5N1 human-transmissible clade 2.3.4.4b isolate detected in US dairy cattle (2024).
-Single intramuscular dose protected mice completely against lethal homologous challenge.
-Outperformed repRNA vaccine based on older clade 1 (A/Vietnam/1203/2004), which gave only partial protection.
-Mutations in HA head domain of bovine isolate reduce recognition by antibodies elicited by historical vaccines.
-Platform can be rapidly updated for emergent strains.
-Challenge: neutralizing titers low or absent after one dose, suggesting protection mechanisms may involve non-neutralizing antibodies or T-cell immunity; boosting may be required.
Recent updates:
-Builds on HDT Bio’s repRNA/LION platform, previously granted EUA in India for SARS-CoV-2 vaccine.
-Ongoing evaluation in non-human primates for respiratory disease protection.
-US CDC reported >65 human H5N1 cases by Dec 2024 linked to bovine outbreaks, underscoring urgency for updated vaccines.
-May complement or replace stockpiled clade 1 H5N1 vaccines if current bovine clade becomes dominant.

Name: rvAc-Gn
Developers: Ningxia University, Yinchuan, China
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against CCHF
Mechanism of action: Presentation of Gn on baculovirus particles induces strong humoral (antibody) and cellular immune responses in mice—via display on a viral-like platform to improve immunogenicity.
Key features and challenges:
-High humoral immunogenicity: rvAc-Gn elicited significantly increased anti-Gn IgG levels in BALB/c mice compared to controls and to rvAc-Np or rvAc-Gn-Np constructs.
-Strong cellular responses: rvAc-Gn induced superior splenic lymphocyte proliferation (stimulation indices) versus rvAc-Np and rvAc-Gn-Np groups.
-Balanced Th1/Th2 cytokines: Serum IL-4 (Th2 marker) and TNF-α (Th1 marker) were elevated in the rvAc-Gn group—much more so than in rvAc-Np or rvAc-Gn-Np groups.
-Surface display confirmed: Gn protein correctly expressed and localized on baculovirus surface, as shown by immunofluorescence and immunoelectron microscopy
Recent updates: 2023: Demonstrated that the Gn-only display (rvAc-Gn) is more immunogenic (humoral & cellular) than Np-only or Gn+Np co-display constructs.

Name: sE1E2.LZ
Developers: University of Maryland, College Park
Indication: Indicated for active immunization of HCV infection
Mechanism of action: Designed to elicit humoral immune response.
Key features and challenges: Focused on designing a B cell-based vaccine and redesigning the E2 glycoprotein to stabilise Vn B, D and E epitopes in order to increase antigenicity. Undergoing immunogenicity testing in mice to identify optimal combinations of HCV envelope immunogens, protein expression system, and immunoadjuvant formulations. Leading candidates to be tested in macaques. Source:https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/10167618

Name: sFL-HA sa-mRNA-LNP vaccine
Developers: Ghent University Hospital, Universitair Ziekenhuis Gent (UZ Gent)
Indication: Indicated for active immunization against influenza A, caused by H5
Mechanism of action: The sa-mRNA encodes replicase and full-length HA antigen, leading to sustained intracellular amplification of antigen transcripts and robust expression of trimeric HA; formulated in LNPs for delivery and immunostimulation, inducing strong humoral, mucosal, and Th1-biased cellular immune responses.
Key features and challenges:
-sa-mRNA platform allows potent immunogenicity at very low doses (≥0.25 µg).
-Secreted full-length HA elicited high IgG, IgA, and hemagglutination inhibition (HAI) titers above the protective threshold.
-Induced robust CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell responses, with Th1-skewing (high IFN-γ and IL-2, minimal IL-4).
-Generated mucosal IgA in bronchoalveolar lavage, relevant for blocking respiratory infection.
-Biodistribution showed expression at injection site, spleen, and draining lymph nodes, transiently in other organs, not in brain.
-Compared to membrane-anchored FL-HA sa-mRNA, sFL-HA was slightly less immunogenic but still conferred protective titers.
-Challenge studies were not performed (mice are not highly susceptible to H5N1).
-Challenge: need for validation in ferrets or other influenza-susceptible models.
Recent updates:
-Builds on rapid advances in sa-mRNA platforms applied to SARS-CoV-2.
-2025 conference reports indicate Ghent University team is planning challenge studies in ferrets to assess cross-clade protection.
-Considered a promising candidate for pandemic preparedness, enabling rapid antigen swapping for emerging H5 clades.

Name: sHBsAg VLP + E2
Developers: Hvidovre Hospital; University of Copenhagen, Kobenhavens Universitet (UCPH); University of Gdansk, Uniwersytet Gdanski; Burnet Institute
Indication: Indicated for active immunization of HCV infection
Target: HCV E2 glycoprotein (residues 412-425, 434-446, 502-520, 523-535 of isolate H77c)
